Give furosemide to slow the water loss
Overcorrection risks osmotic demyelination. Guidelines support stopping the water diuresis with desmopressin and giving free water to bring the sodium back within safe limits.
qlm9jmq: A DKA patient has glucose 540, pH 7.08 and K 3.0 mEq/L. What is the correct next step per ADA?
Hold insulin; give potassium until K is above 3.3
Start insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hr right away
Give sodium bicarbonate 100 mEq first, then insulin
Give an insulin bolus, then add potassium to the fluids

Insulin drives potassium into cells and can cause fatal hypokalemia when the starting level is already low. Replace potassium first, at peripheral rates of about 10 mEq/hr per label unless monitored centrally.
qmlbjyb: A patient's hypokalemia keeps coming back despite 80 mEq of KCl. What is the most likely related problem to correct?
Low magnesium increases renal potassium wasting through ROMK channels, so potassium will not stay up until magnesium is replaced. Both also contribute to torsades risk.
q1lyzcex: An intubated asthmatic has a peak pressure of 52 and plateau of 22. BP falls to 70/40, and the capnogram never returns to baseline before the next breath. What is the best immediate action?
Disconnect the vent briefly, then lower the rate
Increase PEEP to splint the small airways
Increase the rate to correct the hypercapnia
Give a 1 L fluid bolus before anything else

This is dynamic hyperinflation (auto-PEEP) causing obstructive shock. Letting the lungs empty and lengthening exhalation restores venous return. The high peak-to-plateau gap shows airway resistance, not stiff lungs.
q67orb2: Which post-intubation sedation choice best fits a patient in status asthmaticus?
Ketamine bronchodilates and provides sedation and analgesia. Morphine releases histamine. Beta-blockers and cholinesterase inhibitors can worsen bronchospasm.
qpm5wdh: IV magnesium 2 g over 20 minutes (per guideline) is given for severe asthma. How does it cause bronchodilation?
Blocks calcium entry into airway smooth muscle
Stimulates beta-2 receptors on airway smooth muscle
Blocks muscarinic receptors in the airway
Stabilizes mast cells and inhibits mediator release
Magnesium antagonizes calcium-dependent smooth muscle contraction. Watch for hypotension and loss of DTRs.
q15hggfe: A patient with liver failure and anuric kidney failure needs a paralytic infusion for ARDS. Which agent is best?

Cisatracurium undergoes Hofmann elimination, which does not depend on the liver or kidneys. Vecuronium's active metabolite and pancuronium accumulate in renal failure, and rocuronium is cleared by the liver.
q9e3a6y: A patient with ARDS got vecuronium for 3 days plus high-dose methylprednisolone. After the drugs stop, there is profound flaccid weakness. What is the most likely cause?
Aminosteroid paralytics combined with corticosteroids are a classic cause of ICU-acquired myopathy. Limit how long paralytics are used and monitor depth with train-of-four.
qdzw7ge: Which factor is most likely to PROLONG rocuronium paralysis during transport?
Magnesium reduces acetylcholine release and potentiates nondepolarizers. Aminoglycosides and hypothermia do this too. Chronic anticonvulsants and burns cause resistance.
q8gw3wm: At a cabin altitude of 8000 feet, what happens to an air-filled ETT cuff inflated at sea level?
Cuff pressure rises, risking tracheal injury
Cuff pressure falls, risking an air leak
It does not change in a pressurized cabin
Boyle's law: at about 565 mmHg, gas expands roughly 35%. Check cuff pressure with a manometer during ascent and descent, or fill the cuff with saline.
qa1d243: A patient needs FiO2 0.40 at sea level. What FiO2 is needed for the same PAO2 at a cabin altitude of about 8000 feet (565 mmHg)?
Dalton's law: FiO2 x 760 / 565 = 0.40 x 1.35, or about 0.54. Watch for desaturation as cabin pressure falls.
q13j594c: An amiodarone infusion will run for 4 hours by peripheral line. Which preparation follows the label?
Concentration up to 2 mg/mL, with non-PVC tubing
Any concentration, but only in normal saline
Glass bottle only, protected from all light
Concentration over 3 mg/mL in standard PVC
Concentrations over 2 mg/mL need a central line because of phlebitis risk. Infusions over 2 hours need non-PVC or DEHP-free containers because amiodarone leaches plasticizer.
q9uil7i: Sodium bicarbonate is pushed through the IV line already running norepinephrine. What are the two main problems?
Pressor inactivation and a pressor bolus
Calcium carbonate precipitate in the line
No problem; flush with 5 mL and continue

Catecholamines are inactivated in alkaline solutions, and pushing anything through a pressor line flushes a bolus of drug into the patient. Bicarbonate with calcium is the combination that precipitates.
q91jguk: A nitroglycerin infusion seems less effective than expected at the programmed dose. Which equipment factor may explain this?
In-line filter removing all of it
Nitroglycerin is absorbed by PVC, so the delivered dose can be lower until binding sites saturate. Use the tubing the manufacturer recommends and titrate to effect.
qu2yyo2: Anectine is stored in an unrefrigerated flight bag. What does the label say about storage?
Stable 14 days at room temperature; date the vial
Loses all potency within 24 hours unrefrigerated
Stable indefinitely at any cabin temperature
Must be discarded after 4 hours without refrigeration
Multi-dose succinylcholine vials are stable up to 14 days at room temperature. Track out-of-fridge dates and replace stock, since heat in aircraft and vehicles speeds degradation.
q1hh2qni: A smoke inhalation patient will get both hydroxocobalamin and blood products. How should they be given?
The hydroxocobalamin label lists blood products among its incompatibilities, so give it through its own line. Draw baseline labs first because of colorimetric interference.
q12b2h2r: An awake ventilated patient has HR 118 and BP 160/90 and is fighting the vent. The crew wants to paralyze without changing sedation. What should happen first?
Give the paralytic now and add sedation later
Treat the BP with labetalol, then paralyze
Raise the rate to overpower the patient
Paralysis without adequate sedation and analgesia causes awareness and is a never-event. Fighting the vent is often pain, anxiety, hypoxia or a mechanical problem that paralysis would hide.
q8tf66w: A 64-year-old man has had substernal pressure for 30 minutes. He is diaphoretic; BP 148/90, HR 92, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air. He has no allergies or bleeding history. What is the best next action?
Have him chew non-enteric-coated aspirin per protocol
Place him on a nonrebreather mask before any medication
Wait for ALS to obtain a 12-lead before giving aspirin
Have him swallow an enteric-coated aspirin tablet whole
Early chewed aspirin reduces platelet aggregation and is indicated for suspected ACS when no contraindication exists. Oxygen is not needed when SpO2 is normal, and enteric coating delays absorption.
q1ltc99f: After chewing aspirin, a 60-year-old chest pain patient has an SpO2 of 98% on room air, is speaking in full sentences, and has clear lung sounds. Which oxygen decision is most appropriate?
Withhold supplemental oxygen and keep monitoring SpO2
Apply a nonrebreather at high flow for all chest pain
Give oxygen by nasal cannula only if he asks for it
Use a bag-valve mask to improve coronary oxygen delivery
Oxygen is given for hypoxia or respiratory distress per protocol; routine high-flow oxygen in a well-oxygenated ACS patient offers no benefit. Keep reassessing SpO2 and start oxygen if it falls.
q339jm1: A 58-year-old woman with chest pressure and nausea reports black, tarry stools for the past two days. BP 118/74, HR 104. She has no drug allergies. Regarding aspirin, the EMT should:
Withhold aspirin and report the finding to medical direction
Give full-dose aspirin because chest pain outweighs any bleeding risk
Give half of the usual aspirin dose to limit bleeding risk
Give aspirin rectally so it bypasses the stomach entirely

Black, tarry stools suggest active GI bleeding, a contraindication to aspirin, and the tachycardia adds concern for blood loss. A smaller dose or a different route does not remove the antiplatelet bleeding risk.
q15bfmmd: A 9-year-old was found with an open bottle of his grandmother's aspirin 2 hours ago. He now has ringing in his ears, vomiting, and rapid deep breathing. What is the best interpretation and action?
Likely salicylate toxicity; contact poison control and transport
Likely anxiety; coach slower breathing and release to parents
Likely a viral illness; advise rest and fluids at home
Likely mild GI upset; give milk and observe for an hour

Tinnitus, vomiting, and hyperventilation after an aspirin ingestion point to salicylate toxicity, which can worsen over hours. It needs poison control input and hospital evaluation, not home observation.
q1tg46z9: Ten minutes after chewing aspirin for chest pain, a 66-year-old man reports mild heartburn. Vitals are unchanged and he has no rash, swelling, or wheezing. This is best interpreted as:
An expected GI side effect; continue care and reassess
An allergic reaction requiring an epinephrine auto-injector
A sign the aspirin failed, so a second full dose is needed
Proof the pain is GI in origin, so ACS care can stop
GI upset and heartburn are common aspirin side effects. Without hives, swelling, wheezing, or hypotension there is no allergic reaction, and heartburn does not rule out ACS.
qmedv4c: Five minutes after chewing aspirin, a 55-year-old chest pain patient develops generalized hives, wheezing, and a BP that drops from 142/88 to 86/52. What is the priority?
Treat as anaphylaxis per protocol and request ALS
Give a second aspirin dose to finish the protocol
Give nitroglycerin to treat the ongoing chest pain
Note it as a heartburn reaction and recheck later
Hives, wheezing, and hypotension after a drug indicate anaphylaxis, which is treated per protocol (including epinephrine) with ALS support. Nitroglycerin would worsen the hypotension.
qj59dau: A 72-year-old man with chest pain becomes confused and can no longer follow commands or swallow reliably before you give aspirin. What should you do about the aspirin?
Withhold oral aspirin and manage his airway first
Place the tablets in his cheek and let them dissolve
Have a family member help him chew the tablets slowly
Crush the tablets in water and pour them into his mouth

Aspirin for ACS is chewed and swallowed, so it requires an alert patient who can protect the airway. A declining mental status makes airway management the priority and oral medication an aspiration risk.
q1ftwp9t: A 61-year-old woman with chest pain says she took her usual 81 mg daily aspirin this morning. She has no allergies or bleeding. Following typical ACS protocols, you should:
Give the ACS aspirin dose per protocol or medical direction
Withhold aspirin because she already took a dose today
Give one additional 81 mg tablet only, to avoid overdose
Delay aspirin until the hospital can check her platelet count and clotting
A low daily maintenance dose does not replace the 162-324 mg chewed ACS dose, and most protocols still give it, with medical direction as needed. Withholding it removes a proven early treatment.
qwk8c9q: A 70-year-old man has sudden right arm weakness, facial droop, and slurred speech that began 40 minutes ago. He has no chest pain. His wife asks you to give him aspirin. You should:
Withhold aspirin and transport rapidly to a stroke center
Give chewed aspirin because it helps prevent stroke
Give chewed aspirin only if his blood pressure stays above 160 systolic
Give aspirin with water since he cannot chew well
Prehospital aspirin is indicated for suspected ACS, not stroke; a stroke may be hemorrhagic, and slurred speech raises swallowing concerns. Rapid transport for imaging is the priority.
qhodffq: You are assessing a 67-year-old with chest pain before giving aspirin. Which history finding is the most important reason to withhold it?
Lip swelling the last time she took ibuprofen
She takes a daily statin for high cholesterol
She had a cardiac stent placed five years ago
She ate a full meal about one hour ago
Hypersensitivity to aspirin or other NSAIDs is a contraindication, and a prior reaction to ibuprofen suggests NSAID sensitivity. A statin, a prior stent, or a recent meal are not contraindications.
q1rp3jsj: You gave aspirin to a 63-year-old with chest pain. During transport he becomes unresponsive, pulseless, and apneic. What is your next action?
Begin CPR and apply the AED
Give a second dose of aspirin rectally
Give oral glucose in his cheek

Cardiac arrest takes priority over every medication decision; immediate high-quality CPR and early defibrillation are what change survival. No oral or sublingual medication is given to a pulseless patient.
q17todla: A 52-year-old man has chest pain that began while shoveling snow. He took acetaminophen at home for the pain. He has no allergies or bleeding history. Regarding aspirin, the best action is:
Give chewed aspirin; acetaminophen is not an antiplatelet
Withhold aspirin because he already took a pain reliever at home today
Give only half the aspirin dose to avoid an overdose
Wait to see whether the acetaminophen relieves the pain
Acetaminophen has no antiplatelet effect, so it does not replace aspirin for suspected ACS. Waiting or reducing the dose delays a proven early treatment.
q1dux4ql: A 45-year-old with chest pain has a history of asthma but has taken aspirin many times without wheezing or rash. She is not wheezing now. What is the best action?
Give aspirin per protocol and monitor for bronchospasm
Withhold aspirin because all asthmatics react to it
Assist with her albuterol inhaler first, then give the aspirin afterward
Give the aspirin rectally to avoid any bronchospasm
Asthma alone is not a contraindication; aspirin-induced asthma or NSAID hypersensitivity is. Because she has tolerated aspirin before, give it and watch for bronchospasm, a known serious side effect.
q44zzno: At a family gathering, a 62-year-old has crushing chest pain and a 14-year-old has fever, sore throat, and body aches. Both ask for aspirin. Which plan is correct?
Aspirin for the adult per protocol, but not the teenager
Aspirin for both patients, since each of them is unwell and in pain
Aspirin for the teenager only, who is at lower risk
Withhold aspirin from both until hospital arrival
Aspirin is indicated for suspected ACS in the adult, but it is avoided in children and teens with viral illness because of Reye syndrome. Withholding it from the adult delays a key ACS treatment.
qxe71h9: A 76-year-old man taking glipizide was found confused with a glucose of 44 mg/dL. After oral glucose he is alert with a glucose of 98 mg/dL and wants to stay home alone. What concern should guide your advice?
His low glucose may return for hours, so transport is advised
Oral glucose lasts all day, so recurrence is very unlikely
Glipizide raises glucose, so the low reading was an error
His normal reading means he no longer needs any food

Sulfonylureas such as glipizide can cause prolonged, recurrent hypoglycemia, especially in older adults living alone. Oral glucose works quickly but briefly, so transport and observation are strongly advised.
q1f4xr5: You are about to give oral glucose to a confused diabetic woman (glucose 39 mg/dL) when she becomes unresponsive with gurgling respirations. What is your next action?
Suction and manage the airway; do not give oral glucose
Squeeze the full tube onto her tongue while she is still
Give the gel and tilt her head back to help it go down
Rub the gel on her gums and wait for her to swallow
Oral glucose requires a patient who can swallow and protect the airway. Once she is unresponsive with gurgling, airway management and ALS for IV dextrose take priority; oral gel risks aspiration.
qbqfqj3: A 7-year-old with type 1 diabetes is pale, sweaty, and irritable after soccer practice but answers questions and swallows normally. Glucose is 52 mg/dL. What is the best action?
Give oral glucose per protocol and recheck glucose
Withhold sugar because children cannot take oral glucose
Give his scheduled insulin dose since he missed lunch
Have him lie down and rest until his color improves
A child who is awake and able to swallow can receive oral glucose for symptomatic hypoglycemia. Insulin would worsen the low glucose, and rest alone does not correct it.
qlp505c: A 45-year-old found confused in a parked car smells of alcohol and has slurred speech. His friend says he is diabetic. What is the most important step before deciding on treatment?
Give oral glucose immediately without any test
Ask him to perform a field sobriety test
Hypoglycemia can mimic intoxication, and the two often coexist. A glucose reading decides whether oral glucose is indicated; assuming intoxication can miss a treatable emergency.
q1i5s936: A 28-year-old diabetic has vomiting, deep rapid breathing, fruity breath odor, and mild confusion. Glucose reads 480 mg/dL. What is the best action?
Withhold oral glucose, give supportive care, and transport
Give oral glucose because the confusion suggests his sugar is actually low
Give oral glucose since it cannot harm any diabetic
Have him take his own insulin and then release him
Hyperglycemia is a contraindication to glucose, and these findings suggest DKA, which needs hospital care. Oral glucose would raise an already high glucose, and vomiting increases aspiration risk.
q1wm7f85: Fifteen minutes after oral glucose, a 60-year-old diabetic remains confused and her repeat glucose is still 46 mg/dL. She can still swallow. What is the best next step?
Repeat oral glucose per protocol and request ALS
Stop treatment because oral glucose has failed
Give her own insulin to help glucose enter cells
Wait another 30 minutes before rechecking glucose

Persistent hypoglycemia calls for a repeat dose per protocol while she can still swallow, plus ALS for IV dextrose. Insulin would worsen the hypoglycemia, and waiting prolongs brain glucose deprivation.
q1r8x7o0: A 68-year-old with diabetes has new left-sided weakness and slurred speech. Glucose is 41 mg/dL. He can swallow small sips. Which action comes first?
Treat the low glucose per protocol, then reassess deficits
Skip glucose and go straight to a stroke center
Give aspirin for a possible stroke, then recheck glucose during transport
Withhold glucose since it may worsen a stroke
Hypoglycemia can cause focal deficits that mimic stroke. Correct the low glucose, then reassess; if deficits persist, continue stroke-focused transport.
q2qpldi: An 81-year-old nursing home resident with dementia is more confused than usual, according to staff. Glucose is 54 mg/dL. She has a weak cough and chokes when drinking water. Which is the best decision?
Avoid oral glucose and request ALS for IV dextrose
Give the full tube quickly before she tires out
Mix the gel into a large cup of juice for her
Wait until she becomes unresponsive, then give the oral glucose gel
Oral glucose requires the ability to swallow and protect the airway; a weak cough and choking on liquids indicate aspiration risk. ALS can give IV dextrose instead.
q9i9dph: A 30-year-old woman who is 28 weeks pregnant and takes insulin for gestational diabetes is shaky, sweaty, and anxious but alert. Glucose is 50 mg/dL. What is the best action?
Give oral glucose per protocol and recheck glucose
Withhold glucose because it can harm the fetus
Have her take her scheduled insulin dose to stop the shaking and sweating
Place her supine and give nothing by mouth

Symptomatic hypoglycemia in an alert pregnant patient is treated with oral glucose, which also protects the fetus. Supine positioning late in pregnancy can cause hypotension, so the left side is preferred.
q1ors6qx: Which patient is the best candidate for EMT-administered oral glucose?
An alert, sweaty diabetic with a glucose of 50 mg/dL
An unresponsive diabetic with a glucose of 35 mg/dL
A confused diabetic with a glucose of 420 mg/dL
An alert nondiabetic with a glucose of 105 mg/dL
Oral glucose is for symptomatic hypoglycemia in a patient who can swallow and protect the airway. Unresponsiveness, hyperglycemia, and a normal glucose are all reasons not to give it.
qw73fvi: A known diabetic is sweaty and confused but able to swallow, and your glucometer has failed. He took insulin and skipped lunch. Following typical protocols, the best action is:
Give oral glucose per protocol, then reassess mental status
Withhold glucose until a reading is available at the hospital
Give his insulin because the reading cannot be confirmed
Encourage him to sleep it off while you monitor him

Many protocols allow oral glucose for a diabetic with signs of hypoglycemia when glucose cannot be measured; it is low risk in a patient who can swallow, while delay risks brain injury. Insulin would worsen hypoglycemia.
q1gdba1p: A 50-year-old with chronic alcohol use is confused and sweaty after days of not eating. Glucose is 46 mg/dL. He can follow commands and swallow. What is the best action?
Give oral glucose per protocol and recheck
Withhold glucose because he is not diabetic
Treat as intoxication and let him sleep it off
Give naloxone first to wake him up fully
Hypoglycemia is treated regardless of diabetic history; poor intake and alcohol use deplete glucose stores. Naloxone is not indicated without signs of opioid toxicity.
q1pztyeo: A 60-year-old diabetic with a glucose of 38 mg/dL receives oral glucose. Ten minutes later she is alert with a glucose of 112 mg/dL, but she still has slurred speech and a new right facial droop. What does this suggest?
A possible stroke needing rapid stroke-center transport
Expected recovery that will improve with more glucose
An allergic reaction to the oral glucose gel
Normal post-hypoglycemia confusion needing no action
Focal deficits that persist after glucose is corrected suggest a stroke, not hypoglycemia. More glucose is not indicated with a normal reading, and time to stroke care matters.
qt2onst: A 19-year-old type 1 diabetic collapsed during a marathon. She is awake, confused, and sweaty, and she can swallow. Glucose is 55 mg/dL; HR 118. What is the best initial treatment?
Give oral glucose per protocol, then recheck glucose
Give insulin to help her muscles use glucose
Give nothing by mouth at all until she reaches the emergency department
Give a caffeinated drink to raise her alertness
Exercise can drop glucose in insulin-dependent diabetics; she is symptomatic and able to swallow, so oral glucose is indicated. Insulin would worsen the hypoglycemia.
qlbpfix: An insulin-dependent diabetic who is awake but very confused will not open her mouth for oral glucose and keeps turning her head away. What is the best action?
Do not force it; protect the airway and request ALS
Squeeze the gel through her clenched teeth
Hold her head still and pry her mouth open
Wait until she falls asleep, then give the gel
Oral glucose requires a cooperative patient who can swallow; forcing it risks aspiration and injury. ALS can give IV dextrose while you protect the airway.
q1frney4: A 35-year-old diabetic who took insulin is anxious, pale, and sweaty with a pulse of 112. She is alert, and her glucose is 61 mg/dL. Her friend says it is a panic attack. What is the best action?
Treat the low glucose with oral glucose per protocol
Coach slow breathing for a panic attack
Give her own insulin to lower her heart rate
Withhold any treatment until she becomes confused or drowsy
Sweating, pallor, anxiety, and tachycardia with a low glucose after insulin indicate symptomatic hypoglycemia. Treat it now rather than waiting for neurologic decline.
q9m85sf: A 19-year-old with a known peanut allergy ate a cookie 15 minutes ago. He has diffuse hives, abdominal cramping, and has vomited twice. Breathing is unlabored; BP 118/76. He has a prescribed auto-injector. What is the best action?
Assist with his auto-injector because two systems are involved
Withhold epinephrine because his airway, breathing, and BP are all normal
Give oral glucose to settle his stomach and observe
Wait to see whether his breathing worsens before acting
Skin plus GI involvement after a known allergen exposure meets anaphylaxis criteria even without airway or BP changes. Early epinephrine is safer than waiting for airway compromise or shock.
qhexn8m: A 10-year-old (35 kg) has anaphylaxis from a bee sting. His parent holds his own prescribed 0.3 mg auto-injector and a younger sibling's 0.15 mg device. Which is appropriate?
Both devices given at the same time
Neither until a dose is calculated
The 0.3 mg auto-injector is for patients 30 kg or more, and it is prescribed to this child. The 0.15 mg device is for 15-30 kg and belongs to someone else.
q1hfm1mo: Three minutes after an auto-injector, a 45-year-old with anaphylaxis says her heart is pounding and her hands are shaking. HR 118, BP 128/80, and her wheezing has decreased. How should you interpret this?
Expected epinephrine effects with a good response
An overdose requiring immediate medical direction
Worsening anaphylaxis needing a second injection
A sign she is allergic to epinephrine itself

Tachycardia, palpitations, and tremor are common epinephrine side effects, and improving wheezing with a normal BP shows it is working. Repeat dosing is based on persistent anaphylaxis, not on side effects.
q9lfhlb: Twenty minutes after an auto-injector, a patient's hives and wheezing had resolved. During transport her voice becomes hoarse, wheezing returns, and BP falls to 88/56. What is the best action?
Give a second auto-injector per protocol and request ALS
Assume it is anxiety and coach her to breathe slowly into a paper bag
Give her albuterol inhaler only and keep monitoring
Hold further treatment since the first dose worked
Epinephrine wears off and anaphylaxis can recur; returning airway signs and hypotension call for a repeat dose per protocol and ALS. Albuterol alone does not treat airway swelling or shock.
q1e4mds1: A patient in anaphylaxis is wearing heavy jeans and has stridor. Which approach to her auto-injector is best?
Inject the anterolateral thigh, through clothing if needed
Remove the jeans fully, then inject the deltoid
Inject into the buttock to reach a larger muscle
Inject into the abdomen to avoid the clothing
Auto-injectors are designed for the anterolateral thigh and can be given through clothing to avoid delay. Removing clothing wastes time, and other sites are not the recommended location.
qb3t779: A 30-year-old asthmatic is wheezing after eating at a restaurant. Which additional finding most strongly suggests anaphylaxis rather than an asthma flare?
A history of using an inhaler

Hives and lip swelling with wheezing after a possible allergen exposure indicate anaphylaxis, which needs epinephrine. An inhaler history, a mild tachypnea, or a night cough do not distinguish the two.
q69pbsu: A teenager in anaphylaxis with stridor and BP 80/50 has only an auto-injector that expired two months ago. ALS is 15 minutes away. What is the best action?
Contact medical direction about using the expired device
Discard it and wait for ALS to arrive with a fresh dose of epinephrine
Give oral diphenhydramine and monitor her airway
Inject it into the deltoid to improve absorption

A recently expired auto-injector usually retains much of its potency, and in a life-threatening reaction with no alternative, medical direction may approve its use rather than a 15-minute delay. Antihistamines do not reverse airway swelling or shock.
q69032y: A woman who is 32 weeks pregnant develops hives, wheezing, and BP 84/50 after a dose of an antibiotic. She has a prescribed auto-injector. What is the best action?
Give epinephrine and position her on her left side
Withhold epinephrine because it may harm the fetus
Give only oxygen because pregnancy limits drug use
Position her supine and wait for ALS to evaluate her
There is no contraindication to epinephrine in anaphylaxis, and maternal shock threatens the fetus. Left lateral positioning prevents the uterus from compressing the vena cava.
q1inm8he: After assisting with an auto-injector for anaphylaxis, which reassessment finding best shows the drug is working?
Stridor resolves and BP rises to 112/70
The injection site is pale and sore
Improving airway sounds and blood pressure show that anaphylaxis is being reversed. A rising heart rate, tremor, and local pallor are side effects, not measures of response.
q1itsid2: A 68-year-old with coronary disease received an auto-injector for anaphylaxis. His wheezing has improved, but he now reports new chest pressure; HR 128, BP 176/98. What is the best action?
Report the chest pain to ALS or medical direction
Give a second auto-injector for the chest pressure
Assist with nitroglycerin without any order
Ignore it because epinephrine has no cardiac effects
Chest pain and severe hypertension are serious epinephrine adverse effects that need ALS or medical direction input. A second dose is not indicated because the anaphylaxis is improving.
qnqt11g: A 35-year-old in anaphylaxis becomes unresponsive and pulseless before you can use her auto-injector. What is your immediate priority?
Begin CPR and apply the AED
Give an injector into each thigh
Place her in the recovery position

Once she is pulseless, high-quality CPR and early defibrillation come first; ALS gives arrest-dose epinephrine IV or IO. Compressions should not be delayed for an IM injection, which is poorly absorbed without circulation.
qu9p5k0: A 40-year-old with no known allergies has hives, stridor, and BP 80/48 after a wasp sting. Your ambulance carries epinephrine auto-injectors under local protocol. He has no prescription. What is the best action?
Give the ambulance auto-injector per protocol
Withhold it because he has no prescription
Have a bystander find another person's device
Give oral diphenhydramine and wait for ALS

First-time anaphylaxis is still anaphylaxis; when the service stocks auto-injectors, protocol allows the EMT to give one without a prior prescription. Antihistamines do not reverse airway swelling or shock.
q1qt82sm: After epinephrine, an anaphylaxis patient's stridor is improving, but SpO2 is 89% and she is working hard to breathe. Which oxygen decision is best?
Give high-concentration oxygen; be ready to ventilate
Withhold oxygen since the epinephrine will correct the low SpO2 by itself
Use a nasal cannula at low flow to avoid toxicity
Delay oxygen until a second epinephrine dose is due
Hypoxia with increased work of breathing calls for high-concentration oxygen and readiness to assist ventilations. Epinephrine treats the cause but does not replace oxygen or ventilatory support.
qq398pp: A 50-year-old with a shellfish allergy has hives only on her forearms and mild itching after dinner. Breathing is normal, BP 134/82, and she has no GI symptoms. She has her auto-injector. What is the best plan?
Monitor closely and be ready to give epinephrine
Give the auto-injector now due to her allergy
Give oral glucose and release her at the scene
Inject the deltoid now as a precaution
Localized skin findings alone, with normal breathing and BP, do not meet anaphylaxis criteria. Reassess often and give epinephrine promptly if other systems become involved.
qui95pk: A 9-year-old (32 kg) in anaphylaxis received his 0.3 mg auto-injector 10 minutes ago. Stridor is worse and he is pale and lethargic. No second injector is on scene, and ALS is 8 minutes out. What is the best action?
Support the airway, give oxygen, and update ALS
Inject the used device again into the other thigh
Give his albuterol inhaler instead of epinephrine
Lay him flat and give him water to drink
A used auto-injector cannot deliver another dose. Airway support, oxygen, and an urgent ALS update for further epinephrine are the priorities; albuterol does not treat upper airway swelling.
qxu4pqu: After an auto-injector for anaphylaxis, a 40-year-old with BP 84/50 wants to stand up and walk to the ambulance. What is the best response?
Keep him lying down and move him by stretcher
Let him walk since the epinephrine is working
Have him sit upright on the curb to recover
Let him walk if he leans on a crew member
Hypotensive anaphylaxis patients can collapse suddenly when upright because venous return falls. Keep him supine (or as breathing allows) and move him by stretcher.
q1jlh2l1: A 26-year-old found next to a syringe responds only to pain, with pinpoint pupils, RR 8 and shallow, and SpO2 84%. You have opened the airway. What is the best next action?
Ventilate with a BVM and oxygen, then give naloxone
Give naloxone and wait for breathing to improve
Apply a nonrebreather at high flow and give naloxone
Place her in recovery position and recheck in 5 minutes
Slow, shallow breathing needs assisted ventilation first; a nonrebreather cannot fix hypoventilation. Naloxone is then given to restore adequate spontaneous breathing.
q1lg4djg: Thirty minutes after intranasal naloxone, a patient who had been breathing well becomes harder to arouse during transport, and his RR falls to 8. What is the best action?
Support ventilation and repeat naloxone per protocol
Assume he is sleeping and let him rest quietly
Give oral glucose since sleepiness means hypoglycemia
Withhold naloxone because he already had a dose
Naloxone can wear off before the opioid does, causing recurrent respiratory depression. Support breathing and repeat naloxone per protocol.
q13gv7zp: A 2-year-old found with an open bottle of her grandmother's oxycodone is sleepy, with pinpoint pupils and RR 8. What is the best approach?
Support ventilation and give naloxone per pediatric protocol
Withhold naloxone because it is unsafe for toddlers under any circumstances
Induce vomiting to remove any remaining tablets
Give activated charcoal by mouth right away
Pediatric opioid toxicity is treated with ventilation and weight-based naloxone. Charcoal and induced vomiting are dangerous in a child with a decreased level of consciousness.
q15v60oo: A 30-year-old who took a handful of alprazolam is sleepy but arousable, with RR 14, normal pupils, and SpO2 97%. No opioids were found or reported. Regarding naloxone, the best decision is:
Not indicated; monitor the airway and transport
Give it because every overdose responds to naloxone
Give it to keep the patient from falling asleep
Give two doses at once since benzodiazepines are strong
Naloxone reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression; it does not reverse benzodiazepines, and this patient is ventilating adequately. Monitor the airway and transport.
q5xa0oh: After naloxone, a patient wakes, vomits, and begins to aspirate while still lying on his back. What is the priority?
Roll him onto his side and suction the airway
Give a second naloxone dose to stop the vomiting
Sit him upright and have him drink water
Give oral glucose to settle his stomach
Vomiting is a common withdrawal effect after naloxone; protecting the airway by positioning and suctioning comes first. More naloxone would worsen withdrawal.
qafwxwi: Three minutes after a 4 mg intranasal naloxone dose, a suspected fentanyl overdose patient still has RR 6 and SpO2 82% despite your BVM ventilations. What is the best next step?
Keep ventilating and repeat naloxone per protocol
Stop ventilating to see if he breathes on his own
Wait 15 minutes before considering another dose
Switch to a nonrebreather and stop the naloxone
Naloxone can be repeated every 2-3 minutes, and potent synthetic opioids may need more than one dose. Ventilation must continue until breathing is adequate.
qr0i27z: A 79-year-old hospice patient with a morphine pump for cancer pain is drowsy with RR 7 and SpO2 86%. Her POLST requests full treatment. What is the best approach?
Assist ventilation; give naloxone aiming for adequate breathing
Give a large dose to fully reverse the morphine
Withhold naloxone because the morphine is prescribed for her cancer pain
Turn off the pump and let her sleep it off

In opioid-dependent patients, the lowest effective naloxone dose per protocol restores breathing while limiting severe withdrawal and a pain crisis. The goal is adequate ventilation, not full reversal.
q9blcav: A patient's RR improves from 4 to 14 after naloxone, but he remains unresponsive to voice and pain. His glucose has not been checked. What is the best next step?
Check glucose and look for other causes
Give more naloxone until he is fully awake
Assume he is asleep and transport without testing
Give activated charcoal for a co-ingestion
Once breathing is adequate, continued unresponsiveness suggests another cause such as hypoglycemia, head injury, or co-ingestants. Charcoal is contraindicated with an unprotected airway.
q1d0qk0x: A woman who is 30 weeks pregnant is found after injecting heroin with RR 6, cyanosis, and pinpoint pupils. What is the best action?
Ventilate with a BVM and give naloxone per protocol
Withhold naloxone to avoid harming the fetus
Give oxygen by nasal cannula and observe only
Wait until she reaches the hospital before giving her any medication
Maternal hypoxia directly endangers the fetus, so ventilation and naloxone are indicated; titrating to adequate breathing limits withdrawal. A nasal cannula does not correct hypoventilation.
qv5z1t8: Seconds after naloxone, a patient wakes up combative, swinging at the crew, and trying to leave. RR is 18. What should you do first?
Ensure crew safety and request additional help
Give a second dose to calm the withdrawal
Hold him down alone to keep him on the cot
Give oral glucose to treat the agitation
Agitation is a known naloxone withdrawal effect; crew safety comes first, and breathing is now adequate. More naloxone would worsen the withdrawal.
q13pg8p8: After naloxone, a patient breathes 16 times per minute with good chest rise, but SpO2 is 91% on room air. Which oxygen decision is best?
Apply supplemental oxygen and titrate per protocol
Continue BVM ventilations at a rapid rate
Withhold oxygen since breathing is now adequate
Give a second naloxone dose to raise the SpO2
Ventilation is now adequate, so BVM support and more naloxone are not needed, but mild hypoxia (often from aspiration or lung injury) warrants titrated supplemental oxygen.
qwjc7br: A 45-year-old is found with RR 8 and pinpoint pupils. His medical alert bracelet lists a severe allergic reaction to naloxone. What is the best plan?
Ventilate with a BVM and contact medical direction
Give a double dose to overcome the allergy
Give naloxone and then his EpiPen right after
Withhold ventilation until ALS gives an antidote
Hypersensitivity is naloxone's contraindication. Effective BVM ventilation treats the life threat, and medical direction can guide further care.
q1cvplr5: After naloxone, a 33-year-old who used fentanyl 20 minutes ago is awake, alert, and breathing normally. He wants to refuse transport. What is the most important point to explain?
The opioid may outlast naloxone and his breathing can slow again
Naloxone will keep protecting him from an overdose for the next several days
He can safely use again once the naloxone wears off
Naloxone fully removes the fentanyl from his body
Naloxone's effect may end before the opioid's, so respiratory depression can recur after the crew leaves. It does not remove the opioid or give lasting protection.
qo9mqa: A 15-year-old having an asthma attack wants to use her friend's albuterol inhaler because she left hers at home. What is the best action?
Contact medical direction; do not assist with the friend's inhaler
Assist with the friend's inhaler since it is the same drug
Let the friend administer it so you are not responsible
Have her take twice the usual puffs from the friend's inhaler
EMTs assist only with a patient's own prescribed inhaler unless protocol or medical direction allows otherwise. Letting a bystander give it does not change that rule.
q1pa4eb4: After two treatments with her own inhaler, a 12-year-old asthmatic becomes drowsy, her wheezing is now barely audible, and SpO2 falls to 86%. What is the best action?
Assist ventilations with a BVM and request ALS
Recognize improvement since the wheezing stopped
Assist with more puffs and recheck in 20 minutes
Have her sit upright and sleep until arrival
Drowsiness, a quiet chest, and falling SpO2 signal respiratory failure, not improvement. Assisted ventilation and ALS are needed; an inhaler cannot reach the lungs without adequate air movement.
qqo4fe7: After assisting with a prescribed albuterol MDI, which reassessment finding best shows the treatment worked?
Speaking in full sentences with less wheezing
Less respiratory effort with new drowsiness
Better speech and decreased wheezing show improved air movement. Tachycardia and tremor are side effects, and drowsiness with less effort may signal fatigue and failure.
qmh07ho: A 66-year-old with COPD and coronary disease used his albuterol inhaler with your assistance. He now reports new chest pain, and his pulse is 136 and irregular. What is the best action?
Stop the albuterol and contact ALS or medical direction
Repeat the inhaler right away since he is still a little short of breath
Assist with his nitroglycerin without checking BP
Assume anxiety and coach him to breathe slower
Chest pain, severe tachycardia, and dysrhythmias are reasons to stop albuterol and escalate care. Further doses could worsen cardiac ischemia.
q1vdzc7o: A 73-year-old with COPD has increased shortness of breath and wheezing. Which finding is most concerning?
Wheezing on expiration in both lungs
Altered mental status and the inability to speak more than a word signal impending respiratory failure. The other findings are common in COPD exacerbations.
q11s7nda: A 70-year-old with COPD and wheezing has SpO2 84% on room air and is working hard to breathe. He worries that oxygen is bad for him. Which oxygen decision is best?
Give oxygen and titrate to the protocol's target range
Withhold oxygen because COPD patients cannot receive it
Give high-flow oxygen and never reduce it in transport
Use his inhaler only and avoid oxygen until the hospital

Hypoxia should never be left untreated in COPD; oxygen is titrated to the protocol's target range while you watch mental status and breathing. Withholding it or leaving it at maximum without reassessment are both wrong.
qdci04p: A 5-year-old with asthma has wheezing and retractions. His parent has his prescribed MDI with a spacer and mask. What is the best way to assist?
Use the spacer and mask per protocol, then reassess
Remove the spacer so the medicine goes in faster
Spray the inhaler directly into his open mouth
Have him hold his breath for one full minute
A spacer with a mask helps young children inhale the medication effectively. Spraying directly into the mouth deposits most of the dose in the throat.
qnwr0dr: A 26-year-old who is 30 weeks pregnant has an asthma attack with wheezing and SpO2 92%. She has a prescribed albuterol inhaler. What is the best action?
Give oxygen and assist with her inhaler per protocol
Withhold albuterol because pregnancy is a contraindication
Wait until after delivery to treat her asthma
Have her lie flat on her back to rest
Pregnancy is not a contraindication to albuterol, and maternal hypoxia endangers the fetus. Lying supine late in pregnancy can cause hypotension and worsen breathing.
qbew5dp: A wheezing asthmatic says she broke out in hives and her lips swelled the last time she used albuterol. Her inhaler is on the table. What is the best action?
Do not assist with it; contact medical direction
Assist with half of the usual number of puffs
Assist with it since the wheezing is dangerous
Have her use it while you watch her lips closely
Hypersensitivity to albuterol is its contraindication. Give oxygen, monitor for anaphylaxis, and get medical direction rather than repeating an exposure that caused a reaction.
qe6m7y: A 35-year-old asthmatic used her inhaler twice in the last 5 minutes and is still wheezing with SpO2 93% and HR 112. What is the best next step?
Contact medical direction about further doses and reassess
Give as many puffs as she needs until the wheezing stops completely
Stop all treatment since the inhaler has failed
Give her aspirin to reduce airway inflammation
Repeat dosing timing is set by protocol or medical direction, and unlimited puffs increase side effects. Aspirin can trigger bronchospasm in sensitive asthmatics.
q7yrpfx: A wheezing COPD patient hands you two inhalers: tiotropium (Spiriva) and albuterol. For acute bronchospasm, which should you assist with per protocol?
Tiotropium, because it is the daily controller
Both at once to double the bronchodilation
Neither, since COPD wheezing cannot be treated
Albuterol is the short-acting rescue drug for acute bronchospasm; tiotropium is a long-acting maintenance inhaler not meant for acute relief.
q1huxh76: A 2-year-old has a barking cough, inspiratory stridor, and a low-grade fever. His older brother's albuterol inhaler is available. What is the best action?
Do not use the inhaler; keep him calm and transport
Assist with the brother's inhaler for the stridor
Give the inhaler with a spacer and repeat it often
Give it because stridor and wheezing are the same
The findings suggest croup, an upper airway problem that albuterol does not treat, and the inhaler is not prescribed to this child. Keeping him calm avoids worsening the airway obstruction.
q6712dz: A 67-year-old with COPD says his albuterol inhaler is not helping. He now has a fever, a productive cough, SpO2 88%, and RR 30. What is the most important next step?
Give oxygen titrated per protocol and transport
Assist with unlimited puffs until he feels better
Withhold oxygen because he has COPD
Advise a routine visit with his doctor
A failing rescue inhaler with hypoxia and tachypnea signals a serious exacerbation that needs oxygen and hospital care. More puffs add side effects without fixing the underlying problem.
q17q9td0: A 9-year-old asthmatic used his own MDI with your help and now speaks in full sentences with SpO2 97% on room air. He still has faint end-expiratory wheezes. Which oxygen decision is best?
Apply a nonrebreather at high flow for the ride
Start BVM ventilations to clear the wheezes
Give oxygen only if the parent requests it
With a normal SpO2 and good air movement, supplemental oxygen is not needed; ongoing reassessment catches any relapse. BVM ventilation is for inadequate breathing.
qswscqd: A 62-year-old with chest pain has his own prescribed nitroglycerin. BP 146/88, HR 84. He denies erectile dysfunction drug use and has already chewed aspirin. With protocol approval, what is the best next action?
Assist with one dose sublingually, then recheck BP
Assist with three tablets at once for faster relief
Have him swallow the tablet with a glass of water
Give the tablet only after his chest pain resolves
Nitroglycerin is given one sublingual dose at a time, with BP rechecked before each repeat. Swallowing it or giving several doses together risks failure or hypotension.
q2x56s5: A 58-year-old with chest pain and BP 152/90 says he took tadalafil (Cialis) about 36 hours ago. What should you do about his nitroglycerin?
Withhold it and notify medical direction
Assist with it since 24 hours have passed
Assist with half a tablet to reduce the risk
Assist with it if he lies flat during the dose
Tadalafil is long-acting, so nitroglycerin is contraindicated within 48 hours of use. The 24-hour window applies to sildenafil and vardenafil, not tadalafil.
qcdspz4: A 70-year-old with chest pain usually has a BP around 170/100, according to his records. Today his BP is 128/78 and he feels lightheaded. What is the best decision about his nitroglycerin?
Withhold it and contact medical direction
Assist with it because his SBP is above 90
Assist with two tablets to relieve pain faster
Assist with it and have him walk to the cot
A systolic BP more than 30 mmHg below baseline is a contraindication even when it is above 90. His lightheadedness suggests he is already relatively hypotensive.
qost9ah: A 66-year-old with chest pain and her own nitroglycerin has BP 104/70 and a pulse of 42, and she feels weak. What is the best decision?
Assist with it since the BP is above 90
Assist with it and recheck the pulse later
Give it with aspirin to protect her heart
Severe bradycardia is a contraindication to nitroglycerin, and the drug can cause further bradycardia and hypotension. A symptomatic slow pulse needs ALS evaluation.
qfdze38: After a second nitroglycerin dose, a 60-year-old's chest pain resolves completely. BP 124/80, HR 80. What is the best next step?
Stop nitroglycerin, keep monitoring, and transport
Give the third dose to complete the series
Cancel transport since the pain has resolved
Have him walk to the ambulance to see whether exertion brings the pain back
Nitroglycerin is stopped when pain is relieved; the full series is not required. Relief does not rule out an MI, so transport and monitoring continue.
qjxj5zk: A 65-year-old's chest pain persists after three nitroglycerin doses over 15 minutes. BP 132/84. ALS is still 10 minutes away. What is the best action?
Give no more; continue care and update ALS
Assist with a fourth and fifth dose now
Apply his nitroglycerin patch in addition
Give an epinephrine auto-injector for the pain
The usual maximum is three doses in 15 minutes; pain persisting beyond that suggests an evolving MI that needs ALS and rapid transport. Extra doses or patches raise the risk of hypotension.
q8lmyv: Before assisting an 80-year-old with her nitroglycerin, which positioning is safest?
Seated or semi-reclined with legs supported
Standing so the tablet dissolves faster
Prone on the cot to rest her chest
Walking to the ambulance to save time
Nitroglycerin can cause dizziness, hypotension, and syncope, especially in older adults. A seated or semi-reclined position reduces fall risk while allowing comfortable breathing.
qzydp5p: A 55-year-old with pulmonary hypertension takes riociguat daily and now has chest pain with BP 130/84. She also has prescribed nitroglycerin. What should you do?
Withhold nitroglycerin and contact medical direction
Assist with it because her BP is above 90
Assist with it only if the pain gets worse
Assist with two doses since she is stable
Riociguat, like PDE-5 inhibitors, can interact with nitrates and cause severe hypotension, so it is a contraindication. A normal BP now does not remove that risk.
qf59s0l: A 69-year-old with chest pain and crackles in both lung bases has SpO2 88% on room air and BP 160/96. He has his own nitroglycerin. Which action should come first?
Apply oxygen and titrate to the protocol target
Assist with three nitroglycerin doses at once
Lay him flat to rest during the assessment
Withhold oxygen because it narrows coronary arteries

Hypoxia is an immediate threat and is corrected first; oxygen is titrated to the protocol target. Lying flat worsens breathing with pulmonary congestion, and nitroglycerin is given one dose at a time.
qx2gvna: A 14-year-old has sharp chest pain after a soccer collision. His grandfather offers his own nitroglycerin. What is the best action?
Decline it; it is not for this patient
Give one tablet since chest pain is present
Give half a tablet because he is a teen
Give it only if his SBP is above 120
Nitroglycerin is rarely used in children, the tablets belong to someone else, and traumatic chest wall pain is not angina. Assess for injury and transport instead.
q1hh6o8o: Which chest pain patient is the best candidate for EMT-assisted nitroglycerin?
BP 142/88, own prescription, no PDE-5 drug use
BP 86/58, own prescription, no recent drug use
BP 138/80, took vardenafil 12 hours ago, own Rx
EMTs assist with the patient's own nitroglycerin when SBP is adequate and no PDE-5 inhibitor has been used recently. An SBP under 90, someone else's prescription, or recent vardenafil rule it out.
q14jkrnb: A 57-year-old has chest pain with BP 150/90. He has his own nitroglycerin and no aspirin allergy. Protocol allows both. Which plan is best?
Give chewed aspirin, then nitroglycerin if BP allows
Withhold aspirin until all nitroglycerin doses are used
Give nitroglycerin, then aspirin only if pain persists
Give both only after arriving at the emergency department
Aspirin should be given early for suspected ACS and does not depend on pain relief, while nitroglycerin depends on BP checks. Delaying aspirin removes its early benefit.
qvq6tzw: After one nitroglycerin dose, a 61-year-old still has chest pain. Five minutes later his BP is 92/60, down from 136/82. What is the best decision?
Withhold further doses and notify medical direction
Give a second dose since the SBP is still above 90
Give a second dose with him lying flat
Give two tablets at once to finish faster
A drop of more than 30 mmHg from baseline is a reason to stop nitroglycerin even though SBP is still above 90. Another dose could cause serious hypotension.
q1a83qxd: A patient with chest pain took one of his own nitroglycerin tablets 3 minutes before you arrived. Pain persists. BP 140/84, HR 88. What is the best next step?
Note the time, reassess, and follow protocol for the next dose
Give another dose immediately, because he still has pain after his own tablet
Withhold all nitroglycerin because he self-treated
Give three tablets now to catch up on the missed doses
The patient's own dose counts toward the series and timing; the next dose follows the protocol interval after a BP recheck. Doubling up or giving early increases the risk of hypotension.
qm80czi: A 59-year-old with chest pain is about to take her own nitroglycerin. She says she fainted the last time she took it. BP 138/84. What is the best action?
Assist with three doses to prevent a repeat
Refuse to treat until the pain stops
Have her stand while taking the tablet
A prior syncopal reaction suggests she is prone to severe hypotension or a Bezold-Jarisch response. Medical direction should weigh in, and she must not stand during any dose.
q16uzs1e: A 22-year-old swallowed an unknown number of pills 45 minutes ago. She is now drowsy and responds only to a loud voice. Poison control is on the phone. What is the best decision about charcoal?
Withhold it because her mental status is declining
Give it quickly now, before she becomes completely unresponsive
Give it through a straw while she is lying flat
Mix it with soda so she drinks it faster
Altered mental status without a protected airway is a contraindication to activated charcoal because of aspiration risk. Her airway and transport are the priorities.
q1478y65: A 3-year-old swallowed drain cleaner 20 minutes ago and is drooling, with burns around the mouth. What is the best action?
Withhold charcoal, protect the airway, and transport
Give charcoal per protocol to bind the cleaner
Induce vomiting to remove the drain cleaner
Give charcoal mixed with cold milk to bind the cleaner and soothe the burns
Caustic ingestion is a contraindication to charcoal; it does not bind the agent and can hide injuries. Drooling suggests airway swelling, so airway protection comes first.
q1kpv9rg: A 4-year-old drank lamp oil 15 minutes ago and is now coughing and breathing fast. What is the best decision?
Do not give charcoal; monitor breathing and transport
Give charcoal right away to bind the lamp oil
Make him vomit to empty his stomach
Give water and observe at home for an hour
Hydrocarbon ingestion is a contraindication to charcoal because of aspiration risk, and coughing with tachypnea suggests aspiration has already occurred. Vomiting would worsen it.
qqclvf4: An alert 30-year-old swallowed an overdose of her prescription pills 5 hours ago and feels fine. Poison control asks about charcoal. Which factor most limits its benefit?
Charcoal works best when given within about 1 hour of ingestion, before much of the drug is absorbed. Being alert is required for safe use, not a limitation.
qrnjrl0: While drinking charcoal ordered by medical direction, a 17-year-old with an intentional ingestion becomes sleepy and starts gagging. What is the best action?
Stop the charcoal, turn her on her side, and suction
Encourage her to finish the remaining dose quickly
Hold her nose so she swallows the rest of it
Lay her flat on her back and continue the dose
Decreasing mental status with gagging means aspiration risk, which is a reason to stop charcoal. Lateral positioning and suction protect the airway.
q18o5byt: Medical direction orders charcoal for an alert 25-year-old who swallowed a large amount of a medication 30 minutes ago. Which action best supports safe administration?
Have her sit upright and drink it from a covered cup
Have her lie flat on her back so it reaches the stomach and bowel faster
Mix it with ice cream to improve the taste
Wait until she becomes drowsy so she will not gag
Sitting upright reduces aspiration risk, and a covered cup with a straw improves acceptance. Ice cream reduces charcoal's binding, and a drowsy patient should not receive it.
qifziuv: A 7-year-old has a fever of 102.4 F and is acting normally. His parent gave acetaminophen 1 hour ago and asks whether to give another dose now. What is the best response?
Do not repeat it yet; doses are spaced 4-6 hours apart
Give another dose right now, since the fever is still present after an hour
Switch to aspirin, which works faster in children
Give an adult tablet so the fever breaks sooner
Pediatric acetaminophen is dosed every 4-6 hours by weight, and repeating early risks liver toxicity. Aspirin is avoided in children with viral illness because of Reye syndrome.
qv7mhav: A 50-year-old with chronic alcohol use, known cirrhosis, yellow skin, and a swollen abdomen asks whether acetaminophen is safe for his headache. What is the best response?
Avoid it; ask his physician about other options
It is safe in any amount despite liver disease
Take double the usual dose to cover the pain
Take it with alcohol to speed its absorption
Severe hepatic impairment or active liver disease is a contraindication because acetaminophen can cause hepatotoxicity. Higher doses or alcohol increase that risk.
qe184e8: A 4-year-old with fever is lethargic, hard to arouse, and has a purple rash that does not blanch. The parent asks whether acetaminophen will be enough. What is the priority?
Recognize possible serious infection and transport
Give acetaminophen and observe at home
Add ibuprofen to the acetaminophen and recheck the temperature in an hour
Give a cool bath and recheck the rash tomorrow
Lethargy with a non-blanching rash suggests a life-threatening infection such as meningococcemia. Fever medication treats a symptom and must not delay transport.
qbnddc1: A 68-year-old with knee arthritis has taken high-dose ibuprofen daily for weeks. He now has dizziness, a pulse of 112, and black, tarry stools. What is the most likely concern?
Low blood sugar from skipped meals
GI bleeding is a serious ibuprofen adverse effect, and tarry stools with tachycardia and dizziness suggest significant blood loss needing prompt transport.
q1epn5bh: A 29-year-old asthmatic with a sprained ankle asks for ibuprofen. She says aspirin once made her wheeze severely. What is the best response?
Advise against ibuprofen due to NSAID-asthma risk
Ibuprofen is safe since it is not the same as aspirin
Take ibuprofen with her inhaler to block any wheezing
Take a double dose to avoid the need for repeat doses
Aspirin- or NSAID-induced asthma is a contraindication to ibuprofen because cross-reactivity can cause severe bronchospasm. Pretreating with an inhaler does not make it safe.
qgseq1d: A 16-year-old with a sprained wrist took ibuprofen and now has hives, facial swelling, and wheezing. BP 88/54. What is the best action?
Treat as anaphylaxis per protocol and request ALS
Give acetaminophen to replace the ibuprofen
Apply ice to the wrist and reassess later
Give more ibuprofen to treat the swelling
Hives, facial swelling, wheezing, and hypotension after a drug indicate anaphylaxis, which needs epinephrine per protocol and ALS. Switching pain relievers does nothing for the reaction.
q13h6675: A 58-year-old diabetic man is confused and combative, will not follow commands and has a blood glucose of 42 mg/dL. Your partner has a patent forearm IV. What is the best next action?
Give IV dextrose per protocol, then recheck the glucose
Squeeze oral glucose gel into his cheek because he is still awake
Give IM glucagon first and save the IV line for fluids only
Recheck the glucose in 15 minutes before giving any treatment
A patient who cannot follow commands cannot safely swallow oral glucose, and with IV access in place IV dextrose works fastest. Glucagon is the choice only when IV dextrose cannot be given.
q1i214nk: You have given 100 mL of D10 to a hypoglycemic 66-year-old woman. Her glucose rose from 31 to 64 mg/dL, but she is still confused. What should you do next?
Give another D10 aliquot and reassess glucose and mental status
Stop dextrose because the glucose is now above 60 mg/dL
Give naloxone because the confusion did not fully clear
Give IM glucagon on top of the D10 already infused to boost it
D10 is titrated in 5-10 g (50-100 mL) aliquots until glucose is normal and mental status improves. A glucose still in the low 60s with persistent confusion means treatment is not finished.
q1gy0w8d: A 71-year-old man has sudden right-sided weakness and slurred speech. BP is 178/96 and his blood glucose is 312 mg/dL. A bystander says "he is diabetic, give him sugar." What is the best action?
Withhold dextrose and treat as a possible stroke with rapid transport
Give D10 because diabetics with altered speech are usually hypoglycemic
Give oral glucose because it is safer than IV dextrose
Give a half dose of D50 to be safe and recheck

Hyperglycemia is a contraindication to dextrose, and the glucose reading rules out hypoglycemia as the cause of his deficits. Giving sugar to a hyperglycemic stroke patient may worsen outcome and delays stroke care.
q12lmugd: A 4-year-old weighing 16 kg has had vomiting and diarrhea for two days. She is lethargic, her glucose is 38 mg/dL, and you have a patent IV. What is the best treatment?
D10 IV at 5-10 mL/kg, then recheck glucose
Oral glucose gel between the cheek and gum
Undiluted D50, the full 50 mL by slow IV push
IM glucagon 1 mg instead of IV dextrose
For infants and children, D10 at 5-10 mL/kg IV is the listed dose. A lethargic child cannot safely take oral glucose, and an adult D50 dose is far too concentrated and too large for a 16 kg child.
q1fqgde7: A 49-year-old woman woke up after IV D10 and now has a glucose of 118 mg/dL. Which finding is most concerning?
Swelling, coolness and blanching around the IV site
A mild headache she rates 2 out of 10
Hunger and asking for something to eat right away
Mild sweating that is now resolving

Swelling, coolness and blanching at the site suggest extravasation, which can cause tissue necrosis with dextrose. Stop the infusion at that site; hunger and resolving sweating are expected after correction.
q1ujqp34: You are titrating D10 for a 62-year-old hypoglycemic man. After 150 mL, he is alert, oriented and his glucose is 142 mg/dL. What should you do now?
Stop further dextrose and keep reassessing glucose and mental status
Infuse the rest of the 250 mL bag to complete the full dose
Give IM glucagon to prevent the glucose from dropping again
Switch to D50 so the remaining full dose can be given faster
Dextrose is stopped when glucose is normal and mental status has improved. Pushing the full bag regardless of response risks hyperglycemia, which is the most common side effect.
qkz9x6a: A 40-year-old man of unknown history is found unresponsive in his apartment. RR is 14 and deep, SpO2 97%, pupils midsize and there is no trauma. Before giving any medication, what is the most important step?
Give oral glucose gel in the cheek
Give an IV fluid bolus immediately

Hypoglycemia is a common, quickly reversible cause of unresponsiveness, and a glucose check guides whether dextrose is needed. His breathing is adequate and his pupils are not pinpoint, so naloxone is not indicated.
qf2k4p3: A 6-year-old with type 1 diabetes received D10 at the pediatric dose. Ten minutes later she is still lethargic with a glucose of 50 mg/dL. What is the best next step?
Repeat dextrose per protocol and recheck glucose and mental status
Consider her treated and transport without further medication
Give oral glucose now because she has already had IV dextrose
Change to undiluted adult D50 because the D10 did not work at all
Persistent hypoglycemia with altered mental status means the dose was not enough, so a repeat per protocol is indicated. A lethargic child still cannot protect her airway for oral glucose.
qqr9ful: An 84-year-old malnourished woman with a glucose of 36 mg/dL received glucagon 1 mg IM 15 minutes ago because no IV could be placed. Her glucose is now 37 mg/dL and she is still unresponsive. What does this most likely mean, and what is next?
Her glycogen stores are likely depleted; obtain IV or IO access for dextrose
The glucagon needs another hour to work; keep monitoring only
She is having an allergic reaction to glucagon and needs IM epinephrine now
The meter is wrong because glucagon always works; transport only
Glucagon works by releasing stored glycogen, so malnourished patients may not respond. When glucose does not rise within 15 minutes, dextrose by IV or IO is needed.
qhzr075: A 52-year-old man with a known pheochromocytoma is unresponsive with a glucose of 30 mg/dL. Two IV attempts have failed. What is the best plan?
Avoid glucagon and obtain IO access to give dextrose per protocol
Give glucagon 1 mg IM because it is the standard choice when an IV fails
Give oral glucose gel because he cannot get glucagon
Give glucagon at half the usual dose to limit side effects
Pheochromocytoma is a contraindication to glucagon because it can trigger a dangerous catecholamine surge. Dextrose can be given IO, and oral glucose is unsafe in an unresponsive patient.
q275z50: A 27-year-old diabetic received glucagon 1 mg IM. He is now awake, oriented, swallowing normally and his glucose is 92 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate next step?
Give oral carbohydrates and continue to monitor during transport
Give a second dose of glucagon to keep the glucose up
Release him without further care since his glucose is normal now
Start a D50 push to build up his glucose reserves
The effect of glucagon is short and uses up glycogen, so glucose can fall again. Once he can swallow, oral carbohydrates help maintain the glucose; another glucagon dose is not indicated.
q90hwt: You are called for several diabetic patients at the same event. Which one is the best candidate for IM glucagon?
Unresponsive, glucose 29 mg/dL, no IV obtainable
Alert, glucose 58 mg/dL, asking for juice
Confused, glucose 45 mg/dL, with a patent IV already in place

Glucagon is indicated for severe hypoglycemia when IV dextrose cannot be given. The alert patient can take oral glucose, the patient with an IV should get IV dextrose, and the hyperglycemic patient needs no glucose-raising drug.
qi3qnia: A parent gave a 9-year-old 3 mg of nasal glucagon 5 minutes before you arrived. The boy is starting to stir and moan but cannot answer questions. What is the best next action?
Recheck glucose, protect the airway and reassess as the drug takes effect
Give IM glucagon now because the nasal form is unreliable in children
Give oral glucose gel immediately while he is stirring
Give naloxone because he is not fully awake yet

The child is responding, so the priority is airway protection (vomiting is common), a glucose recheck and reassessment. A drowsy child cannot safely take oral glucose, and repeating glucagon this early is not indicated.
q11h570q: A confused 45-year-old has a glucose of 33 mg/dL and a patent, flushing IV. Your partner hands you glucagon. What is the best response?
Give IV dextrose instead, since IV access is available
Give the glucagon IM since it avoids any IV-related complications
Give glucagon IV push followed by oral glucose
Give both glucagon and dextrose to speed recovery
Glucagon is meant for severe hypoglycemia when IV dextrose cannot be given. With a working IV, dextrose acts faster and does not depend on liver glycogen.
qh8zlaq: A 67-year-old diabetic has new left arm weakness and facial droop that started an hour ago. Glucose is 41 mg/dL. He cannot swallow safely and no IV can be started. What is the best action?
Give glucagon IM and recheck glucose and neurologic signs
Withhold all glucose because this looks like a stroke
Give oral glucose gel because he is still conscious
Skip glucose treatment and transport rapidly to a stroke center
Hypoglycemia can mimic stroke, and focal deficits may resolve once glucose is corrected. With no IV and an unsafe swallow, glucagon is the appropriate route, followed by a neurologic reassessment.
q13ra7pq: A 58-year-old man has crushing chest pain. BP is 150/90 and HR 84. He says he took tadalafil (Cialis) about 30 hours ago. What is the best decision about nitroglycerin?
Withhold it; tadalafil within 48 hours is a contraindication
Give it, since more than 24 hours have passed since his last dose
Give a half dose and lay him flat to prevent hypotension
Give it only if his systolic pressure stays above 120
Tadalafil lasts longer than other PDE-5 inhibitors, so nitrates are withheld for 48 hours. The 24-hour window applies to sildenafil and vardenafil, not tadalafil.
qni22xx: A 63-year-old woman with pulmonary hypertension has chest pressure. BP is 132/78 and HR 92. Her medication list includes riociguat. What should you do about nitroglycerin?
Withhold nitroglycerin and continue ACS care and transport
Give nitroglycerin since her BP is above 90 systolic
Give nitroglycerin but only one dose
Give nitroglycerin and start a fluid bolus at the same time
Riociguat is listed with the PDE-5 inhibitors as a nitroglycerin contraindication because the combination can cause severe hypotension. A normal BP does not remove that risk.
q132wksv: A 74-year-old man with chest pain says his BP is "always around 160." Today it is 118/70 with HR 96. He is pale and diaphoretic. What is the best decision about nitroglycerin?
Withhold it; his BP is more than 30 below his baseline
Give it, since his systolic is well above 90
Give it, since a lower BP shows his heart workload is now reduced
Give two doses quickly before his BP drops further
Nitroglycerin is contraindicated with SBP under 90 or more than 30 below baseline. A drop of over 40 from his usual pressure suggests poor perfusion, so a vasodilator could cause collapse.
q1uts2yz: Two minutes after SL nitroglycerin, a 66-year-old woman becomes pale and lightheaded. HR falls from 78 to 44 and BP from 128/80 to 76/40. What is happening, and what should you do?
Bezold-Jarisch reaction; lay her supine, no more nitro, fluids per protocol
An expected headache response; give the next dose in 5 minutes as planned
A worsening heart attack that needs another nitroglycerin dose
An allergic reaction that requires IM epinephrine

Sudden bradycardia with hypotension after nitroglycerin is a known Bezold-Jarisch reaction. Further nitrates are withheld, and supine positioning with a fluid bolus per protocol supports her pressure.
q1wbcyin: A 61-year-old man has received three SL nitroglycerin doses over 15 minutes. Pain is 5 out of 10, BP is 140/86 and HR 82. What is the best next action?
Hold more SL doses unless protocol or medical control directs; transport
Give a fourth dose right away, since his BP is still above 90 systolic
Double the next dose, since the first three were not enough
Stop treatment entirely because the medication has failed

The FDA label allows up to three doses in 15 minutes, so further doses need protocol or medical control direction. Persistent pain points to ongoing ischemia that needs rapid transport, not a larger dose.
q16r7hto: After one SL nitroglycerin, a 57-year-old woman's chest pain goes from 7 to 0 out of 10. BP is 130/80 and HR 76. What should the AEMT do now?
Hold further doses and keep monitoring during transport
Give the second dose in 5 minutes to complete the series
Give two more doses to prevent the pain from returning
Cancel transport since the pain is fully relieved
Nitroglycerin is stopped once pain is relieved, so more doses add risk without benefit. Relief with nitroglycerin does not rule out ACS, so she still needs transport and monitoring.
qhnnyc7: A 69-year-old man with chest pain is ready for nitroglycerin. Which finding is most important to address before you give it?
A pain score of 8 out of 10
Severe bradycardia is a listed contraindication, and adding a vasodilator can drop his BP further. The other findings do not change the decision to give nitroglycerin.
qkx5gtm: You give a 64-year-old man an SL nitroglycerin tablet. A moment later you notice he is chewing and swallowing it. What is the best response?
Teach him to let the next tablet dissolve under his tongue
Have him swallow the next tablet with a glass of water
Give the next tablet right away to make up for the lost dose
Stop nitroglycerin, since he is unable to use it correctly
The SL route depends on absorption through the mucosa under the tongue; a swallowed tablet is poorly absorbed. Correct the technique and keep the usual dosing interval rather than doubling up.
q6j09pt: Five minutes after nitroglycerin, a 59-year-old woman says her chest pain went from 8 to 4, but she now has a pounding headache and flushing. BP is 138/84. What is the best interpretation?
An expected side effect; reassess and repeat per protocol
An allergic reaction; stop nitroglycerin and give IM epinephrine now
A stroke caused by the nitroglycerin; stop all medications
A sign of overdose; give a fluid bolus right away
Headache and flushing are common, expected effects of vasodilation. Her BP is stable and pain is improving, so a repeat dose per protocol is reasonable.
q1owic87: A 55-year-old man has chest pain that suggests ACS. BP is 142/88. He has asthma and says that aspirin once caused a severe asthma attack. What is the best decision?
Withhold aspirin and continue other ACS care
Give aspirin, since the benefit in ACS outweighs the risk
Give one 81 mg tablet instead of the full dose
Give aspirin with albuterol ready in case he wheezes
Aspirin-induced asthma is a listed contraindication because aspirin can cause severe bronchospasm in these patients. A smaller dose does not prevent the reaction.
q1t9xld7: A 68-year-old man has chest pressure and says he has had black, tarry stools for two days. He is pale with HR 108 and BP 104/66. What is the best decision about aspirin?
Withhold aspirin due to signs of active GI bleeding
Give aspirin, since ACS is more dangerous than bleeding
Give aspirin along with oral fluids to protect the stomach
Give aspirin and avoid nitroglycerin instead
Black, tarry stools with tachycardia point to an active GI bleed, which is a contraindication to aspirin. His chest pain may even be from anemia caused by blood loss.
q1x1dak7: A 62-year-old woman with chest pain took her daily 81 mg enteric-coated aspirin this morning. She has no allergies or bleeding. What is the best action?
Give 162-324 mg non-enteric-coated aspirin, chewed, per protocol
Withhold aspirin, since she already took her daily dose
Give one 81 mg tablet to top up her morning dose
Have her swallow a 325 mg enteric-coated tablet whole with water
A daily low-dose enteric-coated tablet does not provide the rapid antiplatelet effect needed in ACS. Chewed non-enteric-coated aspirin at 162-324 mg is recommended unless contraindicated.
qxkzbhn: A 70-year-old man with suspected ACS is pale and diaphoretic. BP is 84/50 and HR 104. Which medication can still be given?
Nitroglycerin, as a skin patch only
Hypotension is a contraindication to nitroglycerin by any route, but it is not a contraindication to aspirin. Aspirin should not be delayed in suspected ACS when there is no allergy or bleeding.
q13z26mp: A 16-year-old with fever, cough and body aches for three days has chest pain when coughing. His mother asks if you can give him aspirin. What is the best response?
Do not give aspirin due to the risk of Reye syndrome
Give 324 mg chewed in case this is a heart attack
Give 81 mg chewed, since he is a teen and not a small child
Give aspirin only if his fever is above 39 C (102.2 F)
Aspirin is avoided in children and teens with viral illness because of Reye syndrome. His pain with coughing does not suggest ACS, and aspirin is not given for ACS in this age group.
ql5zuu8: A 59-year-old man has chest pain and is about to chew aspirin. He then mentions his throat swelled and he got hives the last time he took ibuprofen. What should you do?
Withhold aspirin due to his NSAID hypersensitivity
Give aspirin, since his reaction was to a different drug
Give aspirin and watch closely for hives
Give a reduced dose of aspirin with oral fluids
Allergy or hypersensitivity to NSAIDs is a contraindication to aspirin because cross-reactions are common. A swelling reaction raises the concern for anaphylaxis.
qhc2ahw: A 24-year-old was stung by a bee. She has diffuse hives, wheezing, throat tightness and BP 82/50. What is the first medication to give?
Epinephrine 0.3-0.5 mg IM (1 mg/mL) in the lateral thigh
Albuterol nebulized to treat the wheezing first
An IV fluid bolus before any medication
Epinephrine 1 mg IV push of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration right away

This is anaphylaxis with airway and circulatory involvement, and IM epinephrine is the first-line treatment. Albuterol and fluids are add-ons, and IV epinephrine for a patient with a pulse is not an AEMT anaphylaxis dose.
q1xdr315: Six minutes after 0.3 mg of IM epinephrine, a 35-year-old man with peanut anaphylaxis still has stridor and BP 84/52. What is the best next step?
Repeat IM epinephrine and support the airway and BP
Wait 20 more minutes since epinephrine is slow by IM
Give albuterol instead, since epinephrine has failed
Give oral diphenhydramine and recheck in 15 minutes
IM epinephrine can be repeated every 5-10 minutes as needed when anaphylaxis persists. Antihistamines and albuterol do not reverse airway swelling or shock.
qe85n0q: After IM epinephrine for anaphylaxis, a 30-year-old woman's wheezing has cleared and BP is 128/80. She now has HR 124, a fine tremor and feels anxious. What is the best interpretation?
Expected epinephrine side effects; reassess and monitor
A new allergic reaction requiring a second epinephrine dose
An overdose requiring immediate medical reversal
Worsening anaphylaxis requiring a fluid bolus
Tachycardia, tremor and anxiety are common, expected effects of epinephrine. Her improved breathing and BP show the drug worked, so monitoring is the right plan.
qy5ebnj: A 76-year-old man with coronary artery disease develops facial swelling, hives, wheezing and BP 80/46 after a new antibiotic. Your partner hesitates to give epinephrine because of his heart history. What is the correct decision?
Give IM epinephrine; anaphylaxis has no contraindication
Withhold epinephrine and give only IV fluids
Give half the adult dose to protect his heart
Give albuterol only, since it is much safer for an older heart
There is no contraindication to epinephrine in anaphylaxis, and untreated shock is more dangerous to his heart than the drug. Monitor him closely for chest pain or dysrhythmias afterward.
q1nchjqr: A 6-year-old weighing 22 kg has lip swelling, hives and wheezing after eating cashews. Which epinephrine dose is appropriate?
The 0.15 mg auto-injector IM in the lateral thigh
The 0.3 mg auto-injector IM in the lateral thigh
0.5 mg IM, the full adult anaphylaxis dose in the thigh
1 mg IV of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration
