The 0.15 mg auto-injector is listed for children 15-30 kg. The 0.3 mg auto-injector is for 30 kg or more, and IV epinephrine is not the AEMT route for anaphylaxis.
q1033h4x: A 13-month-old weighing 12 kg develops hives, vomiting and noisy breathing after eating egg. Using epinephrine 1 mg/mL at 0.01 mg/kg IM, what is the dose?
12 kg x 0.01 mg/kg = 0.12 mg, which is 0.12 mL of 1 mg/mL. This is under the 0.3 mg maximum for children under 30 kg.
q1b4qq9f: A 41-year-old was stung by a wasp. Which finding most strongly indicates she needs IM epinephrine now?
Hives all over the body with vomiting and lip swelling
A painful, red, swollen welt limited to the sting site only
Itching and swelling of the stung hand only
Anxiety and a HR of 104 with clear lungs
Reactions that involve more than one body system, such as skin plus GI plus swelling, indicate anaphylaxis and the need for epinephrine. Local swelling and pain at the site are not anaphylaxis.
q6k5o8r: A 28-year-old with shellfish anaphylaxis improved after IM epinephrine. Twenty minutes into transport, the hives return, she is wheezing again and BP is 88/56. What should you do now?
Give another dose of IM epinephrine and reassess
Watch only, since she already received epinephrine
Give albuterol and avoid a second epinephrine dose
Give oral antihistamines and recheck the BP later
Symptoms can return as epinephrine wears off. Repeat IM dosing is allowed every 5-10 minutes as needed, and returning hypotension means she needs it now.
qksbc5f: Five minutes after IM epinephrine for anaphylaxis, a 68-year-old woman's hives and wheezing are improving, but she now has chest pain and BP 196/108. What is the best action?
Hold more epinephrine unless anaphylaxis worsens; call medical control
Give a second dose of epinephrine since the first one is working
Give nitroglycerin for the chest pain and hypertension
Ignore the chest pain because epinephrine has no effects on the heart

Chest pain and severe hypertension are serious epinephrine adverse effects, and anaphylaxis is improving. The drug is held and medical control notified; nitroglycerin is not appropriate here and could worsen hypotension if anaphylaxis returns.
q1acqdr1: A 29-year-old is found next to a syringe. He is unresponsive with RR 4, pinpoint pupils, cyanotic lips and SpO2 78%. What is the first action?
Open the airway and ventilate with a BVM and oxygen
Give naloxone IN before touching the airway
Start an IV so naloxone can be given IV
Check a blood glucose level before any other care is given
Ventilation corrects the hypoxia immediately, while naloxone takes minutes to work. Naloxone is given after effective ventilation has started.
q1dxv9se: After 0.4 mg of IV naloxone, a 45-year-old woman's RR rises from 6 to 14 with good chest rise and SpO2 96%. She is drowsy but arousable. What is the best next action?
Stop naloxone, monitor closely and keep her on oxygen
Give more naloxone until she is fully awake
Give a full 4 mg nasal dose to prevent any relapse later
Stop monitoring, since the overdose is reversed
The goal of naloxone is adequate ventilation, not full alertness. Further doses can trigger acute withdrawal without added benefit.
qh41i01: Two minutes after 4 mg IN naloxone, a 33-year-old man wakes up, is vomiting, sweating heavily and is agitated with HR 118. What is the best interpretation and action?
Acute opioid withdrawal; protect the airway and monitor
A naloxone allergy; give IM epinephrine
Not enough naloxone; give a second dose
Hypoglycemia from the overdose; give oral glucose right away

Vomiting, sweating, agitation and tachycardia after naloxone are signs of acute opioid withdrawal. The main risk is aspiration, so airway protection and monitoring come first; more naloxone would worsen it.
qqqd15m: A 50-year-old with a heroin overdose woke up after naloxone. Thirty minutes into a long transport he becomes drowsy and his RR drops to 6. What is the best action?
Ventilate as needed and give another dose of naloxone
Wait until hospital arrival, since the naloxone already worked once
Give glucagon to reverse the sedation
Give oral glucose to help keep him awake
Naloxone's effect can wear off before the opioid's, causing recurrent respiratory depression. Support ventilations and redose naloxone.
qyhi0a: A 38-year-old is unresponsive after using pain pills. Her pupils are pinpoint, but RR is 16 with good tidal volume and SpO2 is 97%. What is the best plan?
Withhold naloxone, support the airway and monitor breathing
Give naloxone now, since her pupils are pinpoint
Give naloxone IN at a full 4 mg dose to wake her
Give naloxone IV now to prevent any future respiratory depression
Naloxone is given for respiratory depression, and her ventilation is adequate. Waking her without need can cause withdrawal, vomiting and aspiration; close monitoring is the right call.
q1m8s15w: A 26-year-old found after injecting fentanyl is pulseless and apneic. Your partner is getting naloxone ready. What is the priority?
Begin CPR with ventilations and use the AED
Give naloxone IN before starting compressions
Start an IV for naloxone before beginning CPR
Give naloxone IM and wait for a response
In cardiac arrest, high-quality CPR, ventilation and defibrillation take priority. Naloxone can be considered but must not delay CPR.
qxnfqkx: A 3-year-old weighing 14 kg got into a grandparent's oxycodone. She is unresponsive with RR 6 and pinpoint pupils. After starting BVM ventilations, what is the best medication plan?
Withhold naloxone until IV access is obtained
Oral glucose gel, since children get hypoglycemic
Hold naloxone because children should not receive it

PALS-based dosing of 0.1 mg/kg (max 2 mg) gives full reversal in a pediatric opioid ingestion. Ventilation comes first, naloxone should not be delayed for IV access when IN or IM routes are available, and there is no reason to withhold it in a child.
qis0iw0: A 72-year-old hospice patient with cancer wears a fentanyl patch. He is very drowsy with RR 8 and SpO2 89%. What is the best naloxone approach?
Titrate small IV doses until breathing is adequate
Give a full 2 mg IV push for complete reversal
Give 4 mg IN and repeat it until he is fully awake and talking
Withhold naloxone because he is a hospice patient

For opioid-dependent patients, small starting doses titrated to RR restore breathing without causing sudden withdrawal and severe pain. Remove the patch, and note that hospice status alone does not mean withholding care; follow any advance directive.
qsp3hlq: A 19-year-old woman with asthma is wheezing and speaking in short phrases. SpO2 is 91%, HR 118 and RR 28. What is the best next medication?
IM epinephrine before trying any albuterol
An IV fluid bolus for her tachycardia
Nebulized albuterol is first-line for acute bronchospasm. Her tachycardia comes from distress and hypoxia, not low volume, and albuterol is expected to help.
q1xlsf7f: A 14-year-old with asthma is tripoding and drowsy. Breath sounds are faint with no wheezing, and SpO2 is 84%. What does the lack of wheezing suggest, and what is next?
Poor air movement; assist ventilations, epinephrine per protocol
Improving asthma; the albuterol is no longer needed
A non-respiratory cause of distress; withhold all bronchodilators
Mild asthma; coach slow breathing and reassess

A silent chest with drowsiness signals very little air movement and impending respiratory failure. Assisted ventilation (with in-line nebulizer) and epinephrine for severe asthma per protocol are needed.
q1j3vtku: After an albuterol neb, a 25-year-old asthmatic's wheezing is louder, but she can now speak full sentences and SpO2 rose from 89% to 95%. How should you interpret this?
Improvement, since air is moving through opening airways
Worsening, since the wheezing is now louder
A side effect of albuterol requiring the treatment to stop
Louder wheezing can mean more air is moving through narrowed airways. Full sentences and better SpO2 confirm that the treatment is working.
q1bjt43r: A 66-year-old with COPD is getting a second albuterol neb. He now reports chest pain and has a new irregular pulse of 136. What should you do?
Stop the albuterol and contact medical control
Finish the neb, since chest pain is a common side effect
Give a third neb right away to fix the breathing
Give nitroglycerin and continue the albuterol
Chest pain and new dysrhythmias are reasons to stop albuterol. These are serious effects, not the common tremor or palpitations.
qj9ol9t: A 4-year-old with wheezing refuses to keep the nebulizer mouthpiece in and keeps pulling away. What is the best way to deliver albuterol?
Use a pediatric mask attached to the nebulizer
Hold the mouthpiece a few inches from his face
Switch to IM epinephrine since he will not cooperate
Wait until he stops crying before giving anything

A snug pediatric mask delivers nebulized albuterol well in young children. Holding the mouthpiece away from the face (blow-by) wastes most of the drug, and refusing a mouthpiece is not an indication for epinephrine.
qfsqh23: A 31-year-old asthmatic improved after one neb, but during transport she worsens: SpO2 86%, speaking one or two words and tiring. What is the best action now?
Repeat albuterol per protocol and prepare to assist ventilations
Stop the neb since it is causing the problem
Hold all medication until arrival at the hospital to avoid overdose
Switch to oral fluids to thin her secretions
Albuterol can be repeated every 20 minutes, and back-to-back doses are used for worsening bronchospasm. Fatigue with low SpO2 means you should be ready to assist ventilations.
q1kar5ck: After her first albuterol neb, a 40-year-old woman's breathing improved, but she has a fine tremor, says she is jittery and HR is 112. What is the best interpretation?
Common albuterol side effects; continue to reassess
An allergic reaction; give IM epinephrine
An albuterol overdose requiring an IV fluid bolus right away
Tremor, nervousness and tachycardia are common albuterol effects. Her breathing improved, so the plan is to reassess and monitor.
qn2ewlc: A 71-year-old with COPD has a wheezing exacerbation. SpO2 is 87% and RR 26. Your protocol allows a combined neb. Why add ipratropium to albuterol?
It adds anticholinergic bronchodilation in COPD
It speeds up albuterol so less of it is needed
It reverses the tremor and racing heart that albuterol may cause
It thins mucus so the patient can cough it up
Ipratropium is an anticholinergic bronchodilator used for COPD bronchospasm and acts by a different path than albuterol, so the effects add together. It does not prevent albuterol side effects.
qzwrf62: A 78-year-old man with an enlarged prostate received several DuoNebs. He now reports lower abdominal fullness and cannot urinate. What is the most likely cause?
Urinary retention from ipratropium's anticholinergic action
A kidney stone unrelated to any of the medications he received today
Urinary retention is a listed serious effect of ipratropium, and an enlarged prostate raises the risk. It should be reported and further doses held per protocol.
q18m1lub: Shortly after an ipratropium neb begins, a 64-year-old's wheezing gets much worse and SpO2 drops from 91% to 84%. What is the best action?
Stop the ipratropium and treat as paradoxical bronchospasm
Continue the neb since early wheezing worsening is expected
Double the ipratropium dose to overcome the spasm
Remove oxygen because it is worsening the wheezing
Paradoxical bronchospasm is a listed reason to stop ipratropium. Worsening wheezing with falling SpO2 is not expected and needs urgent treatment.
q8fuv1i: After a DuoNeb, a 69-year-old woman with COPD breathes easier but complains of a dry mouth and a bitter taste. What is the best response?
Reassure; these are common, expected side effects
Stop all treatments due to an allergic reaction
Give IM epinephrine for a developing reaction
Hold further doses; these signal anticholinergic toxicity

Dry mouth and bitter taste are common ipratropium effects and are not dangerous. Her breathing improved, so continue to reassess; serious anticholinergic effects would be urinary retention or blurred vision.
q1u2v62m: A 34-year-old asthmatic got hives and lip swelling the last time she used albuterol. Your partner suggests levalbuterol instead. What is the best decision?
Avoid levalbuterol; albuterol allergy contraindicates it
Give levalbuterol, since it is a different drug
Give levalbuterol at a lower dose to limit the allergic reaction
Give levalbuterol, then albuterol if she does not react
Levalbuterol is the active isomer of albuterol, so hypersensitivity to albuterol contraindicates it. Consider other treatments per protocol.
qsg6oza: Your service uses levalbuterol for asthma. A 42-year-old woman received one acute-dose neb 20 minutes ago. She is still wheezing and speaking in phrases, SpO2 91% and HR 108. What is the best next step?
Repeat levalbuterol per protocol and reassess
Hold it, since a HR above 100 means she must stop
Switch to the lower dose used for children 6-11
Wait 4-6 hours before giving another dose

Acute bronchospasm is treated with levalbuterol repeated every 20 minutes x3 per NAEPP and EMS protocol, and she still has significant obstruction. Mild tachycardia is an expected effect; severe tachycardia or chest pain would be the reasons to stop.
qzkaal1: During a levalbuterol neb, a 52-year-old asthmatic reports palpitations and chest pain. HR is 154. What is the best action?
Stop the levalbuterol and notify medical control
Finish the neb since this is a common side effect
Give a second neb to fix the bronchospasm faster
Give aspirin and continue the levalbuterol
Severe tachycardia and chest pain are reasons to stop levalbuterol. Unlike mild tremor, these are not effects to ignore.
q1ni51bn: A 22-year-old woman is vomiting after a night of drinking. She mentions she was born with long QT syndrome. Your partner prepares ondansetron. What is the best decision?
Withhold ondansetron due to congenital long QT syndrome
Give ondansetron, since nausea from alcohol is common
Give half the usual ondansetron dose
Give ondansetron ODT, since oral forms do not affect the heart
Congenital long QT syndrome is a contraindication because ondansetron can prolong the QT interval and cause dysrhythmias. The ODT form carries the same risk.
q1b989n0: A 70-year-old man with Parkinson disease is vomiting. His medications include apomorphine injections. What is the best decision about ondansetron?
Withhold it due to the risk of profound hypotension
Give it, since Parkinson patients often have nausea
Give it IM rather than IV to reduce side effects
Give it only after an IV fluid bolus has been infused to raise BP
Using ondansetron with apomorphine is contraindicated because the combination can cause profound hypotension and loss of consciousness. The route does not change that risk.
q4a71nk: A 9-year-old weighing 25 kg has been vomiting with gastroenteritis. Your protocol allows ondansetron ODT. What is the appropriate dose?
For children 15-30 kg the ODT dose is 4 mg. 2 mg is for 8-15 kg, and 8 mg exceeds the dose for this weight band.
qpv6ccu: Fifteen minutes after 4 mg of IV ondansetron, a 45-year-old woman is still nauseated and has vomited once. Vitals are stable. What is the best next step?
Repeat 4 mg once per protocol and reassess
Give 16 mg IV because the first dose failed
Stop treatment since ondansetron did not work
Give ondansetron every 5 minutes until she stops
The 4 mg dose may be repeated once in 10-15 minutes. Large or repeated doses beyond that raise the risk of QT prolongation.
q188i61: After IV ondansetron, a 63-year-old who takes several heart medications reports palpitations and becomes lightheaded. Her pulse is now irregular. What is the best response?
Suspect a QT-related dysrhythmia; monitor and call medical control
Reassure her that headache and dizziness are common
Give a second ondansetron dose to settle her stomach
Give oral glucose because this is most likely hypoglycemia from fasting

QT prolongation and dysrhythmias are serious effects of ondansetron, and a new irregular pulse with symptoms needs close monitoring and medical direction. Mild dizziness alone would be common, but a new irregular rhythm is not.
q24e56l: A 15-year-old drank drain cleaner 20 minutes ago. He has drooling and mouth pain but is alert. A parent asks about activated charcoal. What is the best decision?
Withhold charcoal, since caustic ingestion is a contraindication
Give charcoal, since he is alert and within the first hour
Give charcoal mixed with milk to neutralize the drain cleaner first
Give charcoal through a straw to protect the mouth
Activated charcoal does not bind caustics and can make injury and endoscopy worse. Being alert and within an hour does not change that contraindication.
q1q4o153: A 36-year-old took a large amount of her prescription pills 40 minutes ago. While you prepare activated charcoal per protocol, she becomes drowsy and slurs her words. What is the best action?
Withhold the charcoal and focus on airway and monitoring
Give the charcoal quickly before she becomes less alert
Give half the dose so she can still swallow it
Have her lie flat on her back while she drinks the whole dose
Decreasing mental status is a reason to stop charcoal because of aspiration risk. Airway protection and monitoring come first.
qj7hhu5: A mother has given her 3-year-old adult-strength acetaminophen every 3 hours for two days for fever. The child is now vomiting and has right upper abdominal pain. What is the best decision?
Withhold acetaminophen and transport for a suspected overdose
Give another acetaminophen dose for the fever
Give acetaminophen rectally instead, since the child is vomiting
Give ibuprofen and acetaminophen together for the fever

Adult-strength doses given too often suggest a supratherapeutic ingestion, and abdominal pain with vomiting raise concern for hepatotoxicity. Suspected overdose is a reason to hold acetaminophen by any route.
qc2g0ia: A 31-year-old woman who is 35 weeks pregnant has a headache and asks for ibuprofen. BP is 162/104. What is the best decision?
Withhold ibuprofen and treat the high BP as a warning sign
Give ibuprofen, since it is a common and safe headache medication
Give a smaller ibuprofen dose because she is pregnant
Give ibuprofen with food to protect her stomach
Ibuprofen is contraindicated in the third trimester, and a headache with high BP late in pregnancy suggests preeclampsia. She needs evaluation and transport, not an NSAID.
qnpyn52: A 58-year-old man has had crushing chest pressure for 30 minutes. He is diaphoretic, BP 148/90, HR 96, and he took his usual daily enteric-coated low-dose aspirin this morning. What is the best next action regarding aspirin?
Give chewed non-enteric-coated aspirin per protocol
Withhold aspirin since he already took a daily dose
Have him swallow enteric-coated tablets whole with water
Wait to give aspirin until a STEMI is seen on the 12-lead

A routine daily low dose does not replace the ACS dose; chewed non-enteric-coated aspirin gives the fastest antiplatelet effect. Waiting for a STEMI is wrong because aspirin is indicated for any suspected ACS.
qhb7nyt: A 66-year-old woman has substernal chest pain with ST depression in the lateral leads. HR 112, BP 104/66. She reports black, tarry stools for two days and feels lightheaded when standing. What should the paramedic do about aspirin?
Withhold aspirin and report suspected GI bleeding
Give full-dose aspirin because ACS benefit outweighs risk
Give half the usual aspirin dose because of the stools
Give the aspirin rectally to avoid irritating the stomach
Melena with tachycardia and orthostasis suggests active GI bleeding, a contraindication to aspirin. Changing the route to PR does not remove the systemic antiplatelet effect that worsens bleeding.
q1sik74j: A 52-year-old man with chest pain and anterior ST elevation is alert with BP 138/86. While you prepare aspirin, he mentions several facts. Which one most changes your aspirin decision?
Ibuprofen once caused wheezing that required a hospital stay
He takes atorvastatin every night for his high cholesterol level
He has smoked one pack of cigarettes per day for 30 years
He ate a large meal about one hour before the pain began

Severe bronchospasm from an NSAID suggests aspirin-sensitive asthma, which is a contraindication to aspirin. Smoking and statin use are risk factors or routine meds and do not change the aspirin decision.
qvorjc1: A 70-year-old man has an inferior STEMI. He is alert, BP 136/82, HR 74, SpO2 96% on room air, pain 7/10, no allergies, and has taken nothing today. Which medication should be given first?

Early aspirin reduces mortality in STEMI and he has no contraindication. Morphine is not first-line and may hide ongoing ischemia; metoprolol and furosemide are not routine early prehospital STEMI treatment.
q1nr2n2y: A 59-year-old man has chest pressure with BP 142/88 and HR 84. While preparing nitroglycerin, you learn he took tadalafil about 36 hours ago. What is the best action?
Withhold nitroglycerin and manage pain another way
Give nitroglycerin since more than 24 hours have passed
Give one nitroglycerin and recheck BP in 5 minutes
Give a nitroglycerin spray instead of a tablet
Tadalafil within 48 hours contraindicates nitrates because the combination can cause profound hypotension. The 24-hour window applies to sildenafil and vardenafil, not tadalafil.
qjyrzze: A 64-year-old woman with chest pain had BP 138/82 and HR 80. Two minutes after her second nitroglycerin, she is pale and nauseated with BP 82/50 and HR 48. What is the next best action?
Stop nitroglycerin, lay her supine, and give a fluid bolus
Give a third nitroglycerin dose because her chest pain persists
Give IV metoprolol to control the heart rate change
Sit her fully upright so she can breathe more easily

Hypotension with bradycardia after nitroglycerin fits a Bezold-Jarisch type reaction; stop nitrates and restore preload, adding atropine if bradycardia persists with poor perfusion. A further dose would deepen the hypotension.
q1t1f5j8: A 74-year-old man in acute pulmonary edema had BP 218/124. After CPAP and repeated nitroglycerin per protocol, his breathing is much easier, but his BP is now 104/66. What should the paramedic do next?
Hold further nitroglycerin and keep CPAP on with close BP checks
Continue the nitroglycerin doses every 3-5 minutes as before to keep the BP down
Remove CPAP since the patient is clearly improving now
Give IV furosemide to finish clearing the remaining fluid

His symptoms have improved and the SBP is now near the 90-100 stop range for nitroglycerin, so further doses are held while CPAP continues. Continuing the doses risks hypotension now that afterload has been reduced.
q1rwtajw: A 77-year-old woman has chest pressure, dizziness, and HR 42 in sinus bradycardia. BP is 104/62. She asks for her nitroglycerin. What is the best decision?
Withhold nitroglycerin and treat the bradycardia first
Give nitroglycerin because the SBP is above 90
Give nitroglycerin and lay her flat if she gets more dizzy
Give nitroglycerin and atropine at the same time
Severe bradycardia is a contraindication to nitroglycerin, which can worsen hypotension and bradycardia. A BP above 90 alone does not make nitrates safe in a patient this slow and symptomatic.
qjfpyah: A 68-year-old man with a STEMI received IV morphine for refractory pain. Ten minutes later he is difficult to arouse, RR 8, SpO2 89%, BP 112/70. What is the best next action?
Assist ventilations with a BVM and give naloxone per protocol
Give a second morphine dose now since his chest pain has not returned
Place a nasal cannula and recheck him in 10 minutes
Give IV ondansetron to prevent vomiting and aspiration
An RR under 10-12 with oversedation is a stop point for morphine; support ventilation first and reverse with naloxone if needed. Low-flow oxygen alone does not fix hypoventilation.
q6va5tv: A 61-year-old woman has an inferior STEMI with ST elevation in V4R. She still has pain 8/10, BP 92/60, HR 66, lungs clear. Which is the most appropriate decision about morphine?
Withhold morphine because of borderline hypotension
Give morphine because ongoing pain increases cardiac demand
Give morphine with nitroglycerin for better relief
Give morphine IM so it absorbs more gently
Right ventricular involvement makes her preload-dependent, and morphine can cause hypotension. The IM route does not prevent hypotension and makes titration harder.
qtdqqrb: A 71-year-old man with symptomatic third-degree block is being paced with good electrical and mechanical capture. BP is now 112/68 but he is grimacing and asking you to stop. What is the best next action?
Give titrated fentanyl analgesia per protocol
Turn the pacer off until he is calmer
Withhold all analgesia because he is being actively paced
Lower the current below the capture threshold
Pacing is painful, and with capture and an adequate BP, titrated analgesia is appropriate. Dropping the current below threshold loses capture and returns him to the unstable rhythm.
qjyld2n: A 74-year-old woman with symptomatic third-degree block is being paced at 70 with confirmed electrical and mechanical capture. After a fluid bolus her BP is still 72/40, she remains confused, and her lungs are clear. What is the best next step?
Start an epinephrine infusion per protocol and titrate
Give atropine to raise the paced heart rate
Turn off the pacer and give amiodarone
Hold further treatment until hospital arrival

With confirmed mechanical capture, persistent hypotension and poor perfusion call for a vasopressor or chronotropic infusion such as epinephrine. Atropine adds nothing while the pacer controls the rate, and stopping pacing returns her to the unstable rhythm.
qt6ijpb: A 63-year-old woman with a STEMI was given fentanyl after nitroglycerin failed to relieve her pain. Five minutes later: pain 3/10, RR 16, SpO2 96%, BP 124/78, alert. How should you interpret this?
Effective analgesia without adverse effects; keep monitoring
Early respiratory depression that requires naloxone now
Inadequate response that calls for a larger repeat dose of fentanyl
Hypotension from fentanyl that needs a fluid bolus now
Pain fell with normal breathing, SpO2, BP, and mental status, so the drug worked without side effects. There is no sign of respiratory depression, so naloxone is not indicated.
q13spxz: A 72-year-old woman has palpitations. The monitor shows an irregularly irregular narrow-complex tachycardia at 168 with no clear P waves. BP 124/80, alert. What is the most appropriate decision?
Do not give adenosine; consider rate control per protocol
Give adenosine to convert this reentrant rhythm
Give adenosine to slow the rate and then cardiovert her afterward
This is atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, not reentrant SVT; adenosine is for regular reentrant rhythms. She is stable, so immediate cardioversion is not required.
q1mrkflc: A 55-year-old man with a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 receives adenosine. During the brief slowing, the monitor shows sawtooth waves at about 300 per minute before the rate returns to 150. What does this finding mean?
The rhythm is atrial flutter, so repeat adenosine will not convert it
The adenosine was pushed too slowly and should be repeated at a faster rate
This is ventricular tachycardia and requires a shock right now
The rhythm is sinus tachycardia that needs a fluid bolus
Adenosine slowed AV conduction and unmasked flutter waves; flutter is not reentrant through the AV node, so adenosine will not convert it. The QRS stayed narrow, so this is not VT.
q1h601zb: A 34-year-old woman with SVT at 210 was alert with BP 116/74 while you prepared adenosine. She now becomes confused, diaphoretic, and her BP is 76/40. What changes now?
Give adenosine more slowly and wait
Repeat vagal maneuvers for one more minute
Give a fluid bolus and recheck later
She is now unstable, so synchronized cardioversion is indicated rather than drug therapy. Adenosine may be tried while preparing only if it causes no delay; a fluid bolus does not treat the rhythm.
qfqz2vc: A 26-year-old with a history of asthma receives adenosine for SVT. The rhythm converts, but she now has diffuse wheezing and SpO2 88% that is not resolving after a minute. What is the best next step?
Treat the bronchospasm and give no further adenosine
Ignore it, as this is the normal flushing after adenosine
Give another adenosine dose to prevent the SVT returning
Give IV metoprolol to keep her from going back into SVT

Adenosine can cause bronchospasm, especially in patients with asthma; this needs treatment, not reassurance. Flushing and chest pressure are brief expected effects, but persistent wheezing with low SpO2 is a serious reaction.
qnopnna: A 60-year-old man with stable monomorphic VT at 170 and a QRS of 140 ms is receiving procainamide. He remains alert with BP 124/78, but the rhythm has not converted and the QRS now measures 220 ms. What should the paramedic do?
Continue, since a wider QRS shows drug effect
Increase the rate to convert him faster
Add amiodarone to complete the conversion

QRS widening of more than 50% from baseline is a procainamide endpoint and signals toxicity. Continuing or adding another antiarrhythmic raises the risk of hypotension, heart block, and worse dysrhythmias.
q1gx99bq: A patient with stable monomorphic VT is receiving procainamide. Midway through the load the rhythm is unchanged, the QRS is a bit narrower, and the BP falls from 128/80 to 84/52. What should the paramedic do?
Stop the infusion and reassess the patient
Speed up the infusion to convert faster
Add amiodarone to the same IV line now
Continue at the same rate and recheck the BP in 10 minutes
Hypotension is one of the endpoints for stopping procainamide. Increasing the rate or adding another QT-prolonging antiarrhythmic raises the risk of hypotension and dysrhythmias.
qz0ftmk: A 48-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis has stable monomorphic VT at 160 with BP 130/84. She is alert and has no chest pain. Which antiarrhythmic decision is best?
Avoid procainamide and choose another agent
Give procainamide since she is stable
Give procainamide but stop if she feels weak
Myasthenia gravis is a contraindication to procainamide because it can worsen muscle weakness. Waiting for weakness to appear risks respiratory compromise.
q1k3peev: A 64-year-old man has a regular wide-complex tachycardia at 170 that looks like monomorphic VT. He is alert, BP 128/80, and has no chest pain or dyspnea. Which treatment is most appropriate?
Amiodarone 300 mg as a rapid IV push

Stable VT with a pulse is treated with amiodarone 150 mg infused over 10 minutes. The 300 mg push is the cardiac arrest dose, and diltiazem is contraindicated in wide-complex tachycardia of unknown origin.
qcgcg70: A patient with stable VT is receiving amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes. Halfway through, he is still in VT but his BP has fallen from 126/78 to 80/48 and he is now drowsy. What should the paramedic do?
Stop the infusion and prepare for synchronized cardioversion
Finish the amiodarone, since stopping it early makes it fail to convert
Push the rest of the amiodarone to convert him sooner
Add a dopamine infusion and keep the amiodarone going
Hypotension is a stop point for amiodarone, and a drop in BP with altered mental status makes him unstable, so cardioversion is indicated. Pushing it faster would worsen the hypotension.
q1l36f0d: After his VT converted, a 69-year-old man has frequent PVCs. The new 12-lead shows second-degree type II AV block at a rate of 48. BP 98/62. Should amiodarone be given for the PVCs?
No; AV block without a pacemaker contraindicates it
Yes; frequent PVCs after VT always need an antiarrhythmic
Yes; give the arrest dose so VT does not return
Yes, but give half of the usual dose this time

Second- or third-degree AV block without a pacemaker is a contraindication to amiodarone, which can worsen the block. Suppressing ectopy is less important than avoiding a slower, more dangerous rhythm.
q1kgklym: A 58-year-old woman has monomorphic VT at 190. She is confused and pale with BP 70/40 and a weak radial pulse. Which action is the priority?
VT with a pulse plus hypotension and altered mental status is unstable and needs synchronized cardioversion. Antiarrhythmic infusions are for stable patients and would delay definitive care.
q1lhmqbt: During transport to a PCI center, a 60-year-old STEMI patient develops a regular wide-complex rhythm at 58 with no P waves. BP 112/70, he is alert and his pain is improving. What is the best decision?
Monitor; do not suppress it with lidocaine
Give lidocaine to suppress the ventricular rhythm
Give lidocaine and start an infusion after it

A slow ventricular rhythm like this is often an accelerated idioventricular (reperfusion) rhythm; ventricular escape rhythms are a contraindication to lidocaine, which can remove the only pacemaker and cause asystole. The patient is stable, so cardioversion is not indicated.
q6903st: A 46-year-old woman on methadone has runs of polymorphic VT that twists around the baseline and stops on its own. Between runs she is alert, BP 104/68, and the QT is markedly prolonged. Which medication is the best choice?
This is torsades de pointes with a pulse, and magnesium is the drug of choice. Procainamide is contraindicated with torsades and long QT, and amiodarone also prolongs the QT.
qlykgj9: A patient with torsades de pointes is about to receive magnesium when the rhythm continues without stopping and she becomes pulseless. What is the next best action?
Defibrillate at once, then give magnesium
Give magnesium IV push before any shock
Give amiodarone before a shock is delivered

Pulseless polymorphic VT is treated as VF with immediate unsynchronized defibrillation and CPR; magnesium can follow. Synchronization often fails in polymorphic VT because the device cannot track the QRS.
q1vvehqa: A 79-year-old woman is dizzy and confused. The monitor shows sinus bradycardia at 38. BP 78/40, skin cool and pale, lungs clear. What is the best initial treatment?
Atropine IV while preparing to pace
Adenosine rapid push to reset the node
Wait for a 12-lead before any treatment
Symptomatic sinus bradycardia with hypotension and altered mental status is treated with atropine first, with pacing ready if it fails. Nitroglycerin would lower her BP further.
qv1l9et: A 75-year-old man has third-degree AV block with a wide-complex escape rhythm at 32. He is pale, confused, and has BP 70/38. Which action should not be delayed?
A wide-complex escape rhythm in complete heart block is unlikely to respond to atropine, which works at the AV node. Pacing should start without delay; repeated atropine wastes time.
qrit974: A 66-year-old man with an inferior STEMI and symptomatic bradycardia received atropine. His HR is now 136 and his chest pain is worse, with deeper ST changes. What should the paramedic do?
Give no more atropine and reassess
Give more atropine to reach a target
Give adenosine to slow the new rate

Tachycardia with worsening ischemia is a stop point for atropine because the higher rate increases myocardial oxygen demand. This is sinus tachycardia from the drug, so cardioversion or adenosine is not appropriate.
q18vcczf: A 7-month-old with bronchiolitis is limp and gray. HR 58, SpO2 76%, RR 8 and shallow. What is the first priority?
Ventilate with a BVM and high-flow oxygen
Give atropine IV before anything else
Give epinephrine IV before ventilating the infant
Set up for transcutaneous pacing first
Bradycardia in infants is most often caused by hypoxia, so oxygenation and ventilation come first; start CPR if HR stays under 60 with poor perfusion. Atropine does not fix the underlying hypoxia.
q8gx4ok: A 72-year-old woman with symptomatic sinus bradycardia at 36 has received the maximum atropine dose with no change. Pacing will not capture despite pad repositioning. BP 70/40. What is the next best action?
Start a dopamine infusion and titrate to effect
Give more atropine beyond the maximum dose until HR rises
Give amiodarone to stabilize the rhythm
Give adenosine to reset the sinus node
Dopamine is indicated for symptomatic bradycardia after atropine when pacing fails or is unavailable. Atropine past the maximum adds no benefit, and amiodarone or adenosine would slow her further.
qxct3iu: A patient on a dopamine infusion for bradycardia and hypotension now has a HR of 118 with runs of nonsustained VT and new chest pain. BP 148/90. What is the best action?
Reduce or stop the infusion and reassess
Increase the infusion to reach a higher BP
Give amiodarone while keeping the same rate
Change to a larger IV site and keep it going
Tachydysrhythmias and chest pain are signs of too much dopamine and are stop criteria. Adding an antiarrhythmic while keeping the cause running does not fix the problem.
q1a4ocdw: A 67-year-old man with an anterior STEMI is cool and clammy with crackles halfway up both lungs. BP 74/48, HR 112, SpO2 88%. What is the most appropriate treatment for his BP?
Start a norepinephrine infusion titrated per protocol
Give a large fluid bolus to raise his preload and BP quickly
Give nitroglycerin to reduce cardiac workload
Give IV furosemide to remove the lung fluid

This is cardiogenic shock with pulmonary edema, and a vasopressor such as norepinephrine supports perfusion. Large fluid boluses worsen pulmonary edema, and nitroglycerin and furosemide lower BP further.
q15lbdqb: A 58-year-old woman has ROSC after VF arrest. After a fluid bolus, her MAP is 55 and HR 104. She is intubated with good ventilation. What is the next best action?
Start norepinephrine and titrate to a MAP of 65 or higher
Repeat cardiac arrest epinephrine doses every 3-5 minutes
Give amiodarone to prevent VF from returning
Withhold vasopressors since she now has a pulse
Post-ROSC hypotension that persists after fluids is treated with a vasopressor titrated to MAP goals. Arrest-dose epinephrine stops at ROSC and would cause severe hypertension and dysrhythmias.
q2obtm6: A 62-year-old man has an inferior STEMI with ST elevation in V4R. BP 82/50, HR 68, lungs clear, no JVD. What is the best initial treatment for his hypotension?
A fluid bolus first; vasopressor only if it persists
Norepinephrine infusion first, then fluids if needed
Nitroglycerin to improve flow through the coronary arteries
Furosemide to reduce strain on the right ventricle

Right ventricular infarction is preload-dependent, and clear lungs support careful volume first; vasopressors are for hypotension that persists after volume. Nitroglycerin and furosemide reduce preload and would worsen the hypotension.
q1oj1bzm: A post-ROSC patient on a norepinephrine infusion now has BP 168/102 (MAP about 124), HR 54, and cool, mottled fingers. What is the best action?
Titrate the norepinephrine down toward the MAP goal
Increase the infusion rate to improve the perfusion of his fingers
Give atropine for the HR and keep the same rate
Make no change; a high MAP protects the brain
MAP well above goal is a stop or titrate-down point; reflex bradycardia and cool, mottled fingers are signs of too much vasoconstriction. Giving atropine treats a side effect instead of the cause.
q19iqeom: A 70-year-old man is in cardiac arrest. Asystole is confirmed in two leads, CPR is ongoing, and IV access is established. Which medication decision is best?
Give epinephrine and continue CPR; atropine is not routine
Give atropine first because the underlying rhythm is very slow or absent
Give amiodarone to prevent VF from starting again
Withhold drugs until a shockable rhythm appears

Epinephrine is the vasopressor for all arrest rhythms and should be given as soon as possible in asystole. Atropine is no longer routinely recommended in asystole, and amiodarone is for shock-refractory VF/VT.
q1tkmb6e: A 66-year-old woman regained a pulse after a VF arrest. Four minutes later her BP is 68/40 while a vasopressor infusion is still being prepared. What is the best bridging action?
Give push-dose epinephrine per protocol and recheck
Resume arrest-dose epinephrine every 3-5 minutes until BP improves
Wait for the infusion before treating her BP
Give a rapid amiodarone push to support her BP

Push-dose epinephrine in small doses is used as a short bridge for hypotension until an infusion runs. The 1 mg arrest dose is for pulseless patients and would cause severe hypertension and dysrhythmias.
qh0aye5: A 29-year-old man is found pulseless and apneic with a syringe nearby. CPR is in progress with a BVM, and the monitor shows asystole. Which action is the priority?
Stopping CPR to give IV naloxone and wait for effect
Repeating naloxone until he starts breathing on his own

In opioid-associated cardiac arrest, high-quality CPR with ventilation and standard ACLS come first; naloxone may be given but should not delay or interrupt them. Naloxone cannot restore a pulse in a heart that is not perfusing.
q1veu9v5: An 81-year-old man has atrial fibrillation at 156. He is lightheaded, BP 84/52, and his skin is cool. What is the best decision about diltiazem?
Withhold it; consider cardioversion per protocol
Give the full weight-based dose to slow his heart rate quickly
Give a reduced elderly dose to protect his BP
Give it slowly over 10 minutes instead of 2
SBP under 90 is a contraindication to diltiazem, which causes hypotension. A smaller or slower dose does not remove that risk in a patient already showing poor perfusion.
q1jdokwr: A 70-year-old woman with AF at 148 and BP 128/80 was given IV metoprolol at an urgent care clinic 30 minutes ago with little effect. What should the paramedic do about diltiazem?
Withhold diltiazem because of the recent IV beta blocker
Give diltiazem now since the metoprolol did not work
Give diltiazem together with more IV metoprolol now to control the rate
Give diltiazem now but cut the dose in half to be safe

An IV beta blocker within hours is a contraindication to diltiazem because the combination can cause severe bradycardia, AV block, or hypotension. Lack of effect from metoprolol does not make adding diltiazem safe.
q1q2icys: A 65-year-old man with AF at 152 and BP 132/84 received diltiazem. Fifteen minutes later his HR is 92, BP 118/76, and his palpitations have eased. What is the best interpretation and action?
Rate control achieved; monitor without another dose
Rate is still too fast; give the second, higher weight-based dose
Early hypotension; stop and give a fluid bolus
The HR is now controlled with a stable BP and better symptoms, so the drug worked and a second dose is not needed. A BP of 118/76 is not hypotension.
qa970nw: A 32-year-old man has chest pain after using cocaine. He is agitated and diaphoretic, HR 128, BP 170/100. Which decision is most appropriate?
Avoid metoprolol and treat agitation with a benzodiazepine
Give metoprolol to slow the HR and lower the BP
Give metoprolol only if the 12-lead shows no ST elevation at all
Give metoprolol, then give nitroglycerin afterward
Beta blockers are avoided in cocaine-associated ACS because they can leave alpha stimulation unopposed. Benzodiazepines reduce the sympathetic drive that causes the tachycardia and hypertension.
q4c6cwq: A 63-year-old man has an anterior STEMI with crackles at both bases, HR 104, BP 96/64, and SpO2 90%. A partner suggests IV metoprolol for the tachycardia. What is the best response?
Withhold it due to heart failure and low BP
Give it because the tachycardia worsens ischemia
Give a single IV dose and then recheck the BP
Give it after furosemide clears the crackles

Decompensated heart failure and SBP under 100 in acute MI are contraindications to metoprolol. The tachycardia is likely compensating for poor pump function, and blocking it can cause cardiogenic shock.
q1etf4cn: A 78-year-old woman has crackles to the mid-lung fields, SpO2 86%, cool clammy skin, and BP 82/54. Her family asks why she is not getting her water pill. What finding makes furosemide inappropriate now?
Hypotension is a stop point for furosemide, and diuresis would worsen this picture of cardiogenic shock. The crackles and hypoxia are why a diuretic seems tempting, not reasons to withhold it.
qwobry7: A 59-year-old man on hemodialysis who makes no urine missed his last session. He has crackles, JVD, BP 196/108, and SpO2 85%. Which plan is most appropriate?
CPAP and nitroglycerin; furosemide will not help an anuric patient
IV furosemide at double his usual home dose to remove the excess fluid quickly
IV furosemide first, then CPAP if he does not improve
Withhold all drugs and transport without CPAP or treatment
Anuria is a contraindication to furosemide because the drug acts through urine production. CPAP and nitroglycerin reduce preload and afterload and help while he gets to dialysis.
q1h60qxr: An 84-year-old man has had fever, cough, and poor oral intake for four days. He has crackles in the right lower lobe, dry mucous membranes, HR 118, and BP 98/60. Should furosemide be given?
No; pneumonia with dehydration makes it harmful
Yes; crackles always point to fluid in the lungs
Yes; it will clear the crackles and raise SpO2
Yes; but only give half of the usual dose
Focal crackles with fever suggest pneumonia, not heart failure, and dehydration is a contraindication to furosemide. Diuresis would worsen his volume depletion and hypotension.
q3vp8p0: A 68-year-old man has a severe headache, blurred vision, and BP 226/124. The monitor shows third-degree AV block with a narrow escape rhythm at 46. Medical direction asks about labetalol. What is the best response?
Avoid labetalol because of the complete heart block
Give labetalol, since the BP poses the greater danger
Give labetalol and keep atropine at the bedside
Give labetalol at a reduced first dose

Second- and third-degree heart block and severe bradycardia are contraindications to labetalol, which can slow the escape rhythm further. Having atropine ready or lowering the dose does not make the drug safe.
qguhr1l: A 71-year-old woman has BP 224/118, crackles to the mid-lung fields, pink frothy sputum, and SpO2 85%. Your partner suggests labetalol to bring the BP down. What is the best plan?
Use CPAP and nitroglycerin; avoid labetalol
Give labetalol first, then start CPAP
Withhold all BP treatment until arrival

Overt heart failure is a contraindication to labetalol because beta blockade can further depress pump function. CPAP and nitroglycerin reduce preload and afterload and are first-line for hypertensive pulmonary edema.
q1481c25: A 57-year-old man has BP 244/136, a severe headache, blurred vision, and confusion. Labetalol is ordered. What is the most appropriate BP goal in the first minutes?
Lower the BP gradually per protocol
Lower it to 120/80 as fast as possible
Lower it below 100 systolic for safety
Do not lower BP until he is at the ED

In hypertensive emergency the BP is lowered in a controlled way, not normalized in minutes, because a sudden drop can cause brain or heart ischemia. Leaving it untreated is also wrong when there are signs of end-organ damage.
q80fcry: A 61-year-old man with no kidney disease collapses at a gym. He is in VF; CPR is in progress, and he has received two shocks and one dose of epinephrine. A partner suggests calcium chloride. What is the best response?
Calcium is not indicated; continue CPR and ACLS
Give calcium chloride now to strengthen contractions
Give calcium chloride before the next shock
Give calcium chloride in place of an antiarrhythmic

Calcium is contraindicated in VF that is not related to hyperkalemia and is not part of routine arrest care. It is reserved for causes such as suspected hyperkalemia or calcium channel blocker toxicity.
qdf3gd: A 70-year-old man who takes metoprolol and insulin is found diaphoretic, responding only to loud voice and not following commands. HR 54, BP 112/70, RR 16, SpO2 97%, and a fingerstick glucose is 36 mg/dL. What is the best next action?
Give IV dextrose and recheck the glucose
Give atropine for the slow heart rate
Give oral glucose gel in his cheek

Hypoglycemia explains his mental status, and his HR and BP are adequate, so IV dextrose is the priority; beta blockers can blunt the usual tachycardia. Oral glucose is unsafe because he cannot reliably swallow or protect his airway.
qquy2o7: A 66-year-old woman with AF at 150 and BP 132/80 received IV metoprolol per protocol. Five minutes later her HR is 54, BP 84/50, and she feels lightheaded. What is the best next action?
Hold further metoprolol and treat the hypotension
Give the next scheduled metoprolol dose
Add diltiazem to keep the rate controlled
Give adenosine to reset the rhythm
HR under 60 and SBP under 90 are stop points for metoprolol; more doses would worsen the bradycardia and hypotension. Adding diltiazem after an IV beta blocker is contraindicated.
q12zt60m: A 67-year-old woman with an NSTEMI is vomiting. She takes several QT-prolonging medicines, and her 12-lead shows a clearly prolonged QTc. What is the best decision about ondansetron?
Withhold it and notify medical direction
Give it at once to prevent vomiting and aspiration
Give it IM rather than IV to be safe
Give it with magnesium as a precaution
A prolonged QTc is a hold point for ondansetron, which can prolong the QT further and cause dysrhythmias. Changing the route does not remove the QT effect.
quinbq6: A 61-year-old man has monomorphic VT at 180 with a weak pulse. He is unresponsive to voice and pain, BP 64/30. Your partner draws up midazolam for cardioversion. What is the best action?
Cardiovert now; sedation is not needed
Give midazolam and fentanyl, then shock
Wait until the midazolam takes effect
An unresponsive, unstable patient needs immediate cardioversion, and sedation would delay it and worsen his hypotension. Sedation is for conscious patients when time allows.
qg8p7lc: An 86-year-old woman is being paced for complete heart block. After IV midazolam for pacing discomfort, she becomes very drowsy with RR 8 and SpO2 87%. Pacing still captures. What is the next best action?
Give more midazolam to keep her calm
Turn off the pacer to reduce stimulation
Place a nasal cannula and keep watching

Respiratory depression and oversedation are stop points for midazolam, and older patients are more sensitive to it. She needs ventilatory support now; turning off the pacer would return her to the unstable rhythm.
qf6wjxd: A 48-year-old man is found unresponsive with pinpoint pupils, shallow respirations at 5 per minute, and cyanosis. The monitor shows sinus bradycardia at 46 and BP is 98/60. Your partner reaches for atropine. What is the best action?
Ventilate with a BVM, then give naloxone
Give atropine first for the bradycardia
Start a dopamine infusion for the HR

The bradycardia is most likely from hypoxia caused by opioid hypoventilation, so ventilation and naloxone treat the cause. Atropine, pacing, or dopamine do not correct the hypoxia driving the slow rate.
q1a48lft: A 64-year-old man with ongoing ischemic chest pain and BP 176/104 needs analgesia and sedation for transcutaneous pacing. Which concern makes ketamine a less suitable choice?
It can raise BP and HR, adding cardiac demand
It almost always causes severe hypotension in older adults
It reliably causes complete heart block
It has no effect when given by IV route

Ketamine commonly causes hypertension and tachycardia, which increase myocardial oxygen demand in a patient with active ischemia. It does not usually cause hypotension, which is why it is chosen in other settings.
qv9h29i: A 57-year-old woman with diabetes has ROSC after a PEA arrest. She is intubated with MAP 70, but a fingerstick glucose is 42 mg/dL. What is the best next action?
Give IV dextrose and recheck the glucose
Give oral glucose gel through the tube
Recheck the glucose at the hospital
Give glucagon IV in place of the dextrose

Hypoglycemia is a reversible cause of poor neurologic outcome after ROSC and should be corrected with IV dextrose and rechecked. Oral glucose is contraindicated in a patient who cannot swallow or protect the airway.
q1h4zm9u: A 22-year-old woman with asthma has received two albuterol and ipratropium nebulizers. Her wheezing is now louder, she speaks in full sentences, SpO2 rose from 88% to 94% and HR went from 118 to 124. How should you interpret these findings?
She is improving; louder wheezing reflects better air movement, so continue and reassess
She is worsening; louder wheezing means bronchospasm is progressing and she needs intubation
She has albuterol toxicity; the rise in heart rate means all bronchodilators should stop
She has likely developed a pneumothorax and needs needle decompression before more treatment
Better speech and SpO2 show improved airflow; wheezing often gets louder as air moves through narrowed airways. A small expected rise in heart rate is a common albuterol effect, not a reason to stop.
qx3jjd7: A 19-year-old with asthma has had three albuterol nebulizers en route. HR is 132, SpO2 86%, he is now drowsy, and breath sounds are barely audible bilaterally. Which finding is most concerning?
Heart rate of 132 shortly after the third albuterol dose
A fine tremor of both hands

A quiet chest with falling mental status signals near-respiratory arrest from severe air trapping and fatigue; he needs assisted ventilation now. Tachycardia and tremor are expected albuterol effects and are less urgent.
qkf0f9y: A 30-year-old asthmatic was intubated 10 minutes ago. Waveform capnography shows a shark-fin pattern, the tube position is confirmed, breath sounds are equal with diffuse wheezing, and peak airway pressures are rising. What is the most appropriate medication step?
Give albuterol in-line through the ventilator circuit
Give a second dose of the paralytic and recheck
Extubate and return to BVM ventilation with a nasal airway
Give IV naloxone in case opioids are suppressing the drive
With tube placement confirmed and a shark-fin capnogram, ongoing bronchospasm is the problem; albuterol can be delivered in-line through the ventilator. More paralytic does not treat bronchospasm.
q8c6ibg: A 66-year-old with COPD is wheezing after one albuterol nebulizer, and you are considering CPAP with in-line albuterol. Which finding makes CPAP inappropriate?
Respiratory rate of 28 with accessory muscle use
Heart rate of 112 after the albuterol

CPAP requires an alert patient who can protect the airway; a decreased GCS with vomiting creates aspiration risk, so ventilate with BVM and prepare for an advanced airway instead. Hypoxia and tachypnea are reasons to use CPAP, not to avoid it.
q1nrthpy: A 71-year-old man with a COPD exacerbation is wheezing. While you prepare a combined albuterol and ipratropium nebulizer, he tells you he had a severe allergic reaction to atropine during surgery. What is the best plan?
Give albuterol alone and withhold ipratropium
Give the combined nebulizer at half the usual dose
Give ipratropium alone because albuterol is riskier
Give diphenhydramine first, then the combined nebulizer

Hypersensitivity to atropine or its derivatives is a contraindication to ipratropium, so give albuterol alone. Pretreating with diphenhydramine or reducing the dose does not make a contraindicated drug safe.
q1x1qpca: An 80-year-old woman with COPD has received several albuterol and ipratropium nebulizers through a loose-fitting mask. She now reports a painful left eye with blurred vision and halos around lights. What is the best action?
Stop the ipratropium and report possible acute angle-closure glaucoma
Continue nebulizers since blurred vision is an expected albuterol effect
Increase the oxygen flow so the mist is cleared away from her eyes
Give another ipratropium dose because her wheezing has not resolved

Ipratropium mist reaching the eye can trigger acute angle-closure glaucoma, a serious effect that calls for stopping the drug and notifying the receiving facility. It is not an expected albuterol side effect.
qx7h5tl: A 27-year-old with acute asthma needs a bronchodilator. Her allergy list shows hives and lip swelling after albuterol. The unit carries levalbuterol. What is the best decision?
Withhold levalbuterol because albuterol allergy is a contraindication
Give levalbuterol because it is a different drug from albuterol
Give levalbuterol after pretreating her with IV diphenhydramine and steroids
Give levalbuterol by MDI instead of nebulizer to limit exposure
Hypersensitivity to albuterol is a listed contraindication to levalbuterol, its closely related isomer. Choose another option per protocol rather than assume levalbuterol is safe.
q1wntlir: A 58-year-old with asthma and known coronary disease received levalbuterol 1.25 mg. Ten minutes later he has new substernal chest pressure, HR 148 and frequent PVCs, though his wheezing has improved. What is the best next step?
Stop levalbuterol, obtain a 12-lead ECG and reassess
Give the second 1.25 mg dose since the wheezing improved
Switch to continuous albuterol for a smoother effect
Give IV metoprolol to slow the rate and continue nebulizers

Chest pain, severe tachycardia and dysrhythmia are stop criteria for levalbuterol; evaluate for cardiac ischemia. Partial improvement in wheezing does not justify continuing a drug that is causing chest pain.
q1pocdwk: A 34-year-old man was stung by a bee. He has hives, a hoarse voice, inspiratory stridor and BP 84/50. Which medication should be given first?
Epinephrine 0.3-0.5 mg IM in the lateral thigh
Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV followed by reassessment
Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV to reduce airway swelling
Nebulized albuterol to open the upper airway

Airway swelling and hypotension mean anaphylaxis; IM epinephrine is the first drug and is not delayed for IV access. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts that do not reverse airway edema or shock quickly.
qdhbfkx: A 41-year-old woman with anaphylaxis has received two IM epinephrine doses and a fluid bolus. She still has diffuse hives and wheezing, with BP 78/44 and HR 132. What is the best next step?
Start an epinephrine infusion per protocol
Give 1 mg of epinephrine by IV push
Give diphenhydramine and wait for a response
Give methylprednisolone and recheck in 15 minutes

Anaphylactic shock that persists after repeated IM doses and fluids needs a titrated epinephrine infusion. A 1 mg IV push is the cardiac arrest dose and can cause severe hypertension and dysrhythmias in a patient with a pulse.
qxmrqa6: A 74-year-old man with prior MI and stents develops wheezing, facial swelling and BP 82/48 after a new antibiotic. His wife worries that epinephrine will harm his heart. What is the best decision?
Give IM epinephrine; there is no contraindication in anaphylaxis
Withhold epinephrine and give diphenhydramine and steroids
Give half the usual IM dose to protect his damaged coronary arteries
Give nitroglycerin first, then epinephrine if needed

Epinephrine has no contraindication in anaphylaxis, and untreated shock is a far greater threat to the heart than the drug. Watch for chest pain or dysrhythmia afterward, but do not withhold or underdose it.
q9o17p1: An 82-year-old man with hives received diphenhydramine 50 mg IV. Twenty minutes later the hives are fading, but he is newly confused and picking at the air, with HR 112 and warm, dry skin. Airway and BP are normal. What is the best interpretation?
Anticholinergic side effect; hold further doses and monitor
Returning anaphylaxis; give IM epinephrine right away
Expected improvement; give a second dose for the hives
Opioid-like sedation; give naloxone and reassess

Confusion and tachycardia with warm, dry skin are anticholinergic effects of diphenhydramine, to which older adults are more sensitive; hold further doses. With a normal airway and BP and fading hives, this is not returning anaphylaxis.
q1wkgqc4: A 20-month-old with croup received nebulized racemic epinephrine for stridor at rest. Ten minutes later the stridor is quieter, but she is drowsy, retractions persist, air movement is poor, and SpO2 is 86%. How should you interpret this?
Worsening obstruction with fatigue; assist ventilation
Good drug response; reassess her in 20 minutes
Expected drowsiness from the racemic epinephrine
Mild croup now; switch to oral dexamethasone

Quieter stridor with drowsiness, poor air movement and falling SpO2 signals impending respiratory failure, not improvement. Racemic epinephrine causes tachycardia and anxiety, not sedation, so the drowsiness reflects hypoxia and fatigue.
qnm69hy: A 24-year-old woman who is not pregnant has a severe asthma attack and is moving so little air that nebulized albuterol is having little effect. She is alert, HR 128, with no chest pain. Which medication is most appropriate next?
Ipratropium nebulizer as the only next drug
Diphenhydramine IV to dry the airways
Methylprednisolone as the only next drug
When poor air movement limits nebulized delivery, SQ terbutaline gives a beta-agonist systemically. A steroid or ipratropium alone will not act fast enough, and diphenhydramine has no role in asthma.
qpe5zaf: Thirty minutes after racemic epinephrine for croup, a 3-year-old has no stridor at rest and is playing. Her father asks to cancel transport. What is the best response?
Advise transport, since stridor can return as the drug wears off
Agree to cancel, since the stridor has fully resolved
Give a second racemic epinephrine dose now to prevent any recurrence
Advise an albuterol inhaler at home if stridor returns
Racemic epinephrine works for a limited time and stridor can come back, so these children need observation. Resolution of stridor is the expected response, not a sign the child is safe to leave.
q7a9kpz: A 4-month-old weighing 6 kg has a temperature of 39.2 C (102.6 F) and a runny nose. She is alert, feeding well, and breathing normally. The parent asks you to give ibuprofen before transport. What is the best response?
Do not give ibuprofen to an infant under 6 months
Give half of the 10 mg/kg dose to be safe
Give aspirin instead because she is so young

Ibuprofen dosing in children starts at 6 months of age, so it is not given to this infant; consider acetaminophen per protocol and transport for evaluation. Aspirin is avoided in children with viral illness because of Reye syndrome.
q1lnjaj7: A 45-year-old with asthma is receiving dexamethasone by IV push. Partway through, she suddenly reports intense burning and itching in her perineal area. Her vitals and airway are unchanged. What is the best interpretation?
A common effect of rapid IV push; slow the rate and reassure her
An allergic reaction; stop the drug and give IM epinephrine right away
A sign of GI bleeding; stop and start a fluid bolus
An extravasation injury; remove the IV catheter now
Perineal burning is a known common effect of rapid IV dexamethasone and is not dangerous; slowing the push helps. With no airway, skin or BP changes, this is not anaphylaxis.
q27um2s: Ten minutes after receiving methylprednisolone 125 mg IV with nebulized bronchodilators, an asthmatic patient asks why the steroid has not helped her breathing yet. What is the correct explanation and plan?
Steroids work over hours; keep giving bronchodilators
The steroid has failed; give a second 125 mg IV dose right now
The steroid failed; this means she needs intubation
Steroids act within minutes; recheck the IV line
Corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation over hours, not minutes, so bronchodilators remain the immediate treatment. A lack of effect at 10 minutes is expected and is not a reason to redose.
q7zv75y: A 50-year-old with an asthma exacerbation improves after nebulizers. You plan to give methylprednisolone, but he reports he is being treated in the hospital for a disseminated fungal infection. What is the best decision?
Withhold the steroid and report the fungal infection
Give methylprednisolone anyway since the asthma takes priority
Give the steroid IM instead of IV to reduce risk
Give double the dose to overcome the infection

Systemic fungal infection is a contraindication to methylprednisolone because steroids suppress immunity. He is improving with bronchodilators, so withhold the steroid and let the receiving physician decide.
qm5uzdg: A 28-year-old asthmatic has had three albuterol and ipratropium nebulizers. She still speaks in two-word phrases, with SpO2 89% and HR 128. She is alert. What is the most appropriate next medication?
Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 15-20 minutes
Magnesium sulfate 2 g by rapid IV push
Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV followed by reassessment
Morphine for air hunger and anxiety
For severe asthma not responding to nebulizers, magnesium is given as 2 g IV over 15-20 minutes. A rapid push increases the risk of hypotension and is reserved for cardiac arrest.
q191vj99: During a magnesium infusion for severe asthma, a 35-year-old reports flushing and warmth. BP has fallen from 128/80 to 84/50 and RR is 16. What is the best next step?
Stop the infusion, reassess, and treat the hypotension
Speed up the infusion so that the full dose finishes more quickly
Continue the infusion since flushing is expected
Give a second 2 g dose to improve bronchodilation
Flushing is common, but hypotension is a stop criterion for magnesium. Stop the infusion and support BP; continuing because flushing is expected ignores the significant BP drop.
q4rr69l: A 32-year-old asthmatic received terbutaline 0.25 mg SQ 20 minutes ago. She is still wheezing, with HR 116 and no chest pain. What is the best next step?
Repeat terbutaline 0.25 mg SQ once and reassess
Give 0.5 mg SQ now because the first dose failed
Give terbutaline every 5 minutes until wheezing stops
Do not repeat; terbutaline is a single-dose drug
Terbutaline 0.25 mg SQ may be repeated once in 15-30 minutes, with a maximum of 0.5 mg in 4 hours. Higher or more frequent doses exceed that limit.
q1vu0ifv: A 78-year-old man with COPD and an enlarged prostate has received several albuterol and ipratropium nebulizers. His breathing is better, but he now has lower abdominal pain, a firm distended bladder, and cannot urinate. What is the best action?
Hold further ipratropium and report urinary retention
Give another ipratropium dose for residual wheezing
Give furosemide IV to help him pass urine
Give an IV fluid bolus to increase urine output

Urinary retention is a known anticholinergic effect of ipratropium, especially with an enlarged prostate, so further doses are held and the finding reported. Furosemide or fluids add volume to a bladder that cannot empty.
q5m6mkv: A 25-year-old with anaphylaxis improved after IM epinephrine: airway clear, no wheeze, BP 118/74, but she still has itchy hives. What is the best next step?
Give diphenhydramine as an adjunct and keep monitoring
Give a third IM epinephrine dose to clear the remaining hives
Discontinue care since the anaphylaxis has resolved

With airway and BP restored, diphenhydramine is a reasonable adjunct for the hives. More epinephrine is not needed for isolated skin symptoms, and she still needs transport because symptoms can return.
qznq2fi: A 62-year-old with septic shock needs RSI for worsening hypoxia. His BP is 78/42 and HR 128 after one fluid bolus. What is the best action before giving etomidate?
Correct the hypotension first, per protocol
Give the induction dose quickly to finish the airway
Give the paralytic before etomidate to avoid hypotension
Skip induction and give the paralytic only

Induction and positive pressure ventilation can cause hypotensive arrest in a patient already in shock, and significant hypotension is a hold point for etomidate. Resuscitate first; paralysis without sedation is never appropriate.
qio8a0o: A patient was intubated using etomidate and rocuronium 12 minutes ago. The ETT is secure, HR has risen from 92 to 128, BP from 130/80 to 176/102, and tears are running from his eyes. No sedative has been given since induction. What is the best plan?
Start a post-intubation sedative and analgesic per protocol
Give a second etomidate dose and repeat it as needed during transport
Give more rocuronium to stop the hemodynamic response
Give labetalol for the hypertension and recheck

Etomidate wears off within minutes while rocuronium lasts much longer, so this patient is likely aware under paralysis. He needs ongoing sedation and analgesia; repeat etomidate is avoided because of adrenal suppression.
qxwo14l: A 45-year-old motorcyclist has an open femur fracture, pain 10/10, BP 84/50 and HR 126. Which analgesic is most appropriate?

Ketamine provides strong analgesia without lowering blood pressure, making it the best choice in the hypotensive trauma patient. Opioids can worsen hypotension, and ketorolac is contraindicated in trauma with possible hemorrhage.
q10tzkqe: An 84-year-old woman weighing 45 kg has a hip fracture and no liver disease. Medical direction orders IV acetaminophen, and your partner has drawn up the standard 1,000 mg adult dose. What is the best action?
Use a weight-based dose since she is under 50 kg
Give the full 1,000 mg since she is an adult
Give ketorolac instead as a safer choice
Give 2,000 mg because her pain is severe

The 1,000 mg IV dose applies to patients 50 kg or more; lighter patients need weight-based dosing to avoid exceeding safe limits. Ketorolac is not safer in an elderly trauma patient because of its bleeding and kidney risks.
q1kavgew: After a dissociative ketamine dose, a 28-year-old is calm with nystagmus, but you hear gurgling and see copious oral secretions. SpO2 is 95%. What is the best action?
Suction the airway and position to protect it
Give naloxone for possible opioid co-ingestion
Give a second ketamine dose to control him
Hypersalivation and increased secretions are known ketamine effects; suctioning and positioning maintain the airway. With adequate SpO2, this does not require intubation.
q1d3c9pb: Four patients need analgesia. For which one is ketamine least appropriate?
A 66-year-old with BP 224/126 and tearing chest pain
A 40-year-old with a tibia fracture and BP 96/60
A 25-year-old with burns who is opioid-tolerant
A 55-year-old with a dislocated shoulder and BP 138/86

Ketamine raises BP and HR, and severe hypertension is a stop point; in a possible aortic dissection that rise could be dangerous. The hypotensive and opioid-tolerant patients are often good ketamine candidates.
q14lufb9: A 300-lb man with severe facial burns, a short neck and stridor is combative. The crew has no supraglottic airway or surgical airway kit, and it is a 5-minute transport to a trauma center. A partner suggests rocuronium so he can be intubated. What is the best decision?
Do not paralyze without a rescue plan; support and transport
Give rocuronium, since paralysis makes intubation easier
Give rocuronium at half dose to keep some breathing
Give rocuronium now, then decide on a backup plan only if he desaturates

Inability to manage the airway is a contraindication to paralytics; a predicted difficult airway with no rescue option can turn into a fatal cannot-intubate, cannot-oxygenate event. A smaller dose does not preserve safe breathing.
q1e02hru: After RSI with rocuronium, two intubation attempts fail. SpO2 drops to 85%, and BVM ventilation with two providers and an OPA is difficult. What is the best next step?
Place a supraglottic airway and ventilate
Wait for the rocuronium to wear off
Rocuronium paralysis lasts a long time, so spontaneous breathing will not return soon; oxygenation through a supraglottic airway is the priority. Repeated attempts during desaturation worsen hypoxia.
q1qgjqog: A 58-year-old dialysis patient missed two sessions and is now obtunded with vomiting. The monitor shows peaked T waves and a wide QRS. You are preparing for RSI. Which paralytic decision is best?
Use succinylcholine at the usual RSI dose
Use succinylcholine at a reduced dose
Give succinylcholine IM to slow absorption

Known or suspected hyperkalemia contraindicates succinylcholine, which raises potassium and can trigger arrest. Rocuronium does not raise potassium; a smaller succinylcholine dose does not remove the risk.
qpt72ai: A 77-year-old was hospitalized for a stroke 3 weeks ago, has been bedbound since, and now has aspiration pneumonia with worsening hypoxia that requires RSI. Which finding most affects your paralytic choice?
Immobility since the stroke weeks ago
Pneumonia as the underlying cause of his hypoxia
Prior use of aspirin for stroke
Stroke with immobilization for more than 48-72 hours contraindicates succinylcholine because of the risk of severe hyperkalemia. Age and pneumonia do not change the paralytic choice.
q11h7w1j: Before RSI, a 24-year-old's mother tells you that her brother developed a dangerously high fever and stiffness during surgery under general anesthesia. What is the best decision about succinylcholine?
Avoid it because of possible malignant hyperthermia risk
Give it as planned, since the reaction occurred in another relative
Give it but pre-treat with acetaminophen
Give a smaller dose and watch the temperature
A family history of malignant hyperthermia is a contraindication to succinylcholine. Antipyretics and dose reduction do not prevent a malignant hyperthermia reaction.
qddnlcx: During transport, a patient intubated and paralyzed with vecuronium suddenly loses the EtCO2 waveform, SpO2 falls from 98% to 86%, and HR drops from 96 to 58. Sedation is running and the next vecuronium dose is due. What is the best action?
Hold the dose and check the tube and circuit now
Give the vecuronium dose on schedule
Give atropine and continue as planned

Loss of the EtCO2 waveform with falling SpO2 and bradycardia suggests a dislodged tube or disconnection, and a paralyzed patient cannot breathe on his own. Redosing vecuronium or adjusting sedation ignores the airway emergency.
qd5vn7z: After midazolam and fentanyl for procedural sedation, a 52-year-old's RR drops to 6, SpO2 to 87%, and EtCO2 rises to 62. What is the first action?
Open the airway and assist ventilation with BVM
Give flumazenil IV to reverse the midazolam effect right away
Give naloxone IN and wait for the response
Increase oxygen by nonrebreather and observe
Combined benzodiazepine and opioid sedation can cause respiratory depression; airway support and ventilation come first. Reversal agents may follow, but they do not replace immediate ventilation.
qiyu7qn: An intubated trauma patient needs post-intubation sedation. His BP is 76/40 and HR 132 despite fluids. Which sedation plan is best?
Ketamine per protocol rather than a midazolam bolus
A midazolam bolus followed by a continuous midazolam infusion
No sedation until the BP is normal
A midazolam bolus plus fentanyl for analgesia

Midazolam can cause hypotension and shock is a relative contraindication, so ketamine is a better sedative in the hypotensive patient. Withholding sedation risks awareness, especially if the patient is paralyzed.
qu8oshi: After ketamine for a painful dislocation reduction, a 34-year-old is frightened, crying and describing terrifying visions. Vitals are stable and airway is patent. What is the best management?
Reduce stimulation; small benzodiazepine dose per protocol
Give naloxone to reverse the ketamine effect
Give a repeat ketamine dose to deepen sedation
Physically restrain the patient and give haloperidol IV
This is a ketamine emergence reaction; a calm environment and, if needed, a small benzodiazepine dose per protocol can help. Naloxone has no effect on ketamine.
q5xndvj: A 66-year-old COPD patient on CPAP was given lorazepam for anxiety. He is now drowsy with RR 9, EtCO2 70 and SpO2 86%. What is the best next step?
Remove CPAP and ventilate with BVM
Increase the CPAP pressure to improve ventilation

CPAP requires a spontaneously breathing, alert patient; with hypoventilation and rising EtCO2, he needs assisted ventilation. Increasing the CPAP pressure does not fix hypoventilation from respiratory depression.
q1v1408j: A 40-year-old woman with known myasthenia gravis has a dislocated shoulder with severe muscle spasm. A partner suggests diazepam to relax the muscles. What is the best decision?
Avoid diazepam because of her myasthenia gravis
Give diazepam because it relaxes skeletal muscle
Give diazepam IM since IM is safer
Give diazepam with fentanyl for synergy
Myasthenia gravis is a contraindication to diazepam, which can worsen muscle weakness and breathing. IM diazepam is absorbed erratically and does not avoid the problem.
q1tfykzv: After a rapid IV push of a large fentanyl dose, a patient becomes apneic. You cannot ventilate with the BVM, and the chest wall is stiff. What is the best action?
Chest wall rigidity: naloxone or a paralytic per protocol
Push harder on the BVM until the chest rises
Give more fentanyl to relax the muscles
Give IV diphenhydramine for a presumed dystonic reaction
Chest wall rigidity is a known serious effect of fentanyl; it is treated with naloxone or a paralytic per protocol along with continued ventilation. It is not a dystonic reaction.
q11xbb5p: A 6-year-old (22 kg) with an obvious forearm deformity is screaming and has no IV access; two IV attempts have failed. What is the best analgesia plan?
Wait until IV access is obtained
IO fentanyl through a tibial needle
Intranasal fentanyl gives fast analgesia without IV access and avoids a painful IO for an isolated limb injury. Delaying analgesia for IV access is unnecessary.
q1pcvm3n: A 48-year-old with a tibia fracture received two doses of fentanyl. Pain is now 6/10, but she is drowsy though rousable, with RR 10 and SpO2 92%. What is the best next step?
Withhold more fentanyl, stimulate her and monitor EtCO2
Give a third fentanyl dose since pain persists
Give naloxone 2 mg IV for full and rapid reversal of the opioid
Switch to morphine and give a full dose
RR around 10 with oversedation is a stop point for fentanyl, so hold doses and watch ventilation closely. Full-dose naloxone is not needed while she is breathing and rousable.
qai852b: Four patients each need fentanyl for pain. Which patient needs the most caution?
An 82-year-old on home O2 for COPD who takes a nightly benzodiazepine
A 30-year-old with a kidney stone and normal vital signs
A 25-year-old with an ankle fracture and BP 130/82
A 45-year-old with a shoulder dislocation and no medical history
An older patient with chronic lung disease who also takes a benzodiazepine is at highest risk of opioid respiratory depression. The healthy patients with normal vitals carry much less risk.
q1jya7vb: A 29-year-old with three rib fractures is in an acute asthma attack with diffuse wheezing and SpO2 90%. He asks for pain relief. Which plan is best?
Avoid morphine; fentanyl per protocol and treat the asthma
Give morphine since it also reduces air hunger
Give a full morphine dose so he can take deep, effective breaths

Acute or severe asthma is a contraindication to morphine without airway support, and histamine release can worsen bronchospasm. Fentanyl with close monitoring and treatment of the asthma is a safer plan.
qcs520e: After morphine for a hip fracture, an 81-year-old's BP falls from 124/80 to 86/58. RR is 16, SpO2 96%, and she is alert. What is the best next step?
Stop morphine, position supine and give fluid per protocol
Give naloxone IV to reverse the hypotension from the morphine
Give the next morphine dose for pain control
Give epinephrine IM for possible anaphylaxis
Hypotension is a stop point for morphine; manage with positioning and fluids. With normal breathing and alertness, naloxone is not indicated and would remove her analgesia.
q15n4wya: During an interfacility transfer, a patient's next hydromorphone dose is due. She is hard to arouse, with RR 11 and SpO2 91%. What is the best decision?
Hold the dose and notify the sending provider
Give the dose since it is ordered on schedule
Give half the dose and recheck in 30 minutes
