Give the dose and add naloxone at the same time
RR below 12 and excessive sedation are hold criteria for hydromorphone. A scheduled order does not override clear signs of opioid toxicity.
q1bpznkv: A 6-year-old weighing 20 kg improved after nebulizers for an asthma attack. Medical direction orders dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, but she has vomited twice and has no IV access. What is the best action?
Wait for IV access at the hospital
0.6 mg/kg for 20 kg is 12 mg, and the IM route avoids losing an oral dose to vomiting. A 1.2 mg dose is a tenfold error, and waiting delays a drug that already takes hours to work.
q1msoddi: After 0.4 mg naloxone IV, an opioid overdose patient now has RR 14, SpO2 96%, and responds to voice but is drowsy. What is the best next step?
Monitor; no more naloxone is needed now
Give more naloxone until he is fully awake
Give 2 mg IV to prevent relapse
Give naloxone IM to extend the effect
Naloxone is titrated to adequate ventilation, not full wakefulness. Extra doses risk acute withdrawal, vomiting and agitation without improving safety.
q8h4ed2: After 2 mg naloxone IV, an opioid overdose patient vomits, becomes agitated, and has crackles with SpO2 84% and pink frothy sputum. What is the best next step?
Support oxygenation and ventilation; give no more naloxone
Give another 2 mg naloxone IV for recurrent opioid toxicity
Give midazolam to control the agitation
Give furosemide and repeat the naloxone

Pulmonary edema is a serious naloxone effect; oxygenation and ventilation support are the priority, and more naloxone is not indicated. The low SpO2 is from pulmonary edema, not recurrent opioid toxicity.
q1ics6w8: A 40-year-old was intubated using succinylcholine 8 minutes ago and faces a 60-minute transport. Tube placement is confirmed and sedation and analgesia have been given, but he is starting to move against the ventilator. Medical direction orders ongoing paralysis. Which is best?

A longer-acting nondepolarizing agent such as rocuronium maintains paralysis once placement and sedation are assured. Repeated succinylcholine can cause bradycardia and hyperkalemia, and etomidate is a sedative, not a paralytic.
qz81rks: A 72-year-old with renal colic has normal renal function, no bleeding history, and takes no NSAIDs. Medical direction approves ketorolac. Which single IV dose is appropriate?
Patients 65 and older get a reduced single dose of 15 mg IV. Higher doses are for younger adults and raise the risk of renal and GI harm.
qtqwy2g: A 54-year-old with renal colic takes daily aspirin for a heart stent and had a bleeding ulcer last year. Which analgesic decision is best?
Withhold ketorolac and consider an alternative
Give ketorolac since renal colic responds well to NSAIDs
Give ketorolac at a reduced dose
History of GI bleeding and concurrent aspirin use are contraindications to ketorolac. A reduced dose does not remove the bleeding risk.
qe2y89b: A 68-year-old on warfarin fell and has a wrist fracture and a mild headache. She asks for something other than opioids. What is the best decision?
Avoid ketorolac due to bleeding risk and possible head bleed
Give ketorolac since she clearly wants to avoid opioids
Give ketorolac IM to reduce bleeding risk
Give ketorolac and recheck her neuro status
Coagulopathy and possible intracranial bleeding are contraindications to ketorolac. The IM route does not reduce bleeding risk.
qatftc1: A 34-year-old with an ankle sprain asks for ibuprofen. She has asthma that previously worsened after taking aspirin. What is the best decision?
Withhold ibuprofen because of NSAID-sensitive asthma
Give ibuprofen since it is a different drug from aspirin
Give ibuprofen with albuterol on standby
Aspirin- or NSAID-induced asthma is a contraindication to ibuprofen because of cross-reactivity. Having albuterol ready does not make the drug safe.
q1bpil17: A 32-year-old at 34 weeks of pregnancy has severe back pain after a fall. She has no allergies. Which pain medication decision is best?
Avoid ibuprofen; consider acetaminophen per protocol
Give ibuprofen since she has no allergies
Give ibuprofen IV to bypass the GI tract
Give a double dose of ibuprofen for a faster, stronger effect
Ibuprofen is contraindicated in the third trimester of pregnancy. Acetaminophen is a safer option, and changing the route does not remove the fetal risk.
q17hufe9: A 55-year-old with known cirrhosis and jaundice has a painful wrist fracture. Which analgesic decision is best?
Avoid acetaminophen because of his active liver disease
Give acetaminophen since it is gentle on the stomach lining
Give IV acetaminophen to bypass the liver
Give acetaminophen with a reduced interval
Severe hepatic impairment or active liver disease contraindicates acetaminophen. The IV route does not bypass liver metabolism.
q1jfh2av: A 24-year-old with a sprained knee asks for IV acetaminophen. She says she took several OTC cold remedies today and is unsure how much acetaminophen they contained. What is the best decision?
Hold acetaminophen until the total dose is known
Give the full IV dose for her pain
Give half the IV dose as a precaution
Give acetaminophen PO instead of IV to be safer
Many OTC products contain acetaminophen, and reaching the daily max is a stop point. Hold until the total is known; changing the route or halving the dose does not prevent exceeding it.
q128su3o: Medical direction orders promethazine for a 40-year-old woman with severe motion sickness and repeated vomiting. Her only IV is a small catheter in the back of her hand. What is the best route?
Deep IM injection into a large muscle
Undiluted IV push through the hand IV
SQ injection in the back of the upper arm
Rapid IV push followed by a fast flush
IM is the preferred route for promethazine; IV use, especially through small hand veins, risks severe tissue injury, and SQ injection is contraindicated. If given IV it must be diluted and slow.
q15bo7pq: A 34-year-old man is found in a bathroom with a syringe nearby. He is unresponsive with pinpoint pupils, RR 4, SpO2 78% and HR 112. Your partner is preparing naloxone. What should you do right now?
Ventilate with a BVM and oxygen while naloxone is prepared
Give naloxone first and wait for him to breathe on his own
Intubate him before any naloxone is given so the airway is secure
Place him in the recovery position and apply a nonrebreather mask
Hypoxia is the immediate threat, so ventilation comes first and continues while naloxone is drawn up. Waiting for naloxone to work while he stays apneic and hypoxic wastes critical minutes.
q1avanj0: A 45-year-old woman who takes methadone was found with RR 6. After titrated IV naloxone she has RR 14, SpO2 96% and is awake. She now wants to refuse transport. What is your main concern?
Methadone can outlast naloxone, so breathing may slow again
Naloxone will cause several days of severe opioid withdrawal
Naloxone often causes a delayed hypertensive crisis at home
She must receive a full second dose before she can refuse

Methadone has a long duration while naloxone wears off much sooner, so respiratory depression can return after the crew leaves. Withdrawal from naloxone is unpleasant but short-lived and is not the main danger.
qe6sc57: A 2-year-old weighing 12 kg got into a grandparent's oxycodone. He is limp with RR 6 and pinpoint pupils. You are ventilating with a BVM. Using the PALS full-reversal dose, how much naloxone do you give?
1.2 mg IV, IO, IM or IN
4 mg IN as for an adult
The PALS full-reversal dose is 0.1 mg/kg (max 2 mg), so 12 kg x 0.1 mg = 1.2 mg. A flat adult dose ignores the weight-based calculation, and ventilation continues until breathing is adequate.
qvz83f6: A 26-year-old woman took an unknown amount of amitriptyline. She had one brief seizure. HR 128, BP 84/50, QRS 148 ms, and she is ventilating adequately on a BVM. What is the best next medication?
Procainamide infusion for the wide QRS

A wide QRS with hypotension after a tricyclic overdose reflects sodium channel blockade, and bicarbonate is the antidote. Procainamide and amiodarone can worsen sodium channel or QT toxicity in this setting.
q1emuod8: A 40-year-old man with a tricyclic overdose has a QRS of 138 ms. He is unresponsive with RR 6 and SpO2 88%. Before you give sodium bicarbonate, what is the priority?
Secure ventilation, because bicarbonate creates CO2 that must be exhaled
Give the bicarbonate first, since the wide QRS is the bigger and more urgent threat
Give midazolam first to prevent seizures during the infusion
Obtain an ABG on arrival before deciding on any bicarbonate

Inadequate ventilation is a contraindication to bicarbonate: the CO2 produced by bicarbonate builds up and worsens acidosis unless the patient is ventilated. Giving it to a hypoventilating patient undercuts the treatment.
q11o2kmz: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes has Kussmaul breathing, a glucometer reading of HI, HR 124 and BP 98/60. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia only. Your partner suggests sodium bicarbonate for the acidosis. What is best?
Withhold bicarbonate and give an isotonic fluid bolus per protocol
Give sodium bicarbonate 1 mEq/kg IV to correct the acidosis
Give bicarbonate only if the respiratory rate keeps increasing
Give bicarbonate first and then start IV fluids once the blood pH improves

DKA is treated with fluids and later insulin, and routine bicarbonate is not indicated without a specific reason such as hyperkalemic ECG changes or arrest. Rapid breathing here is compensation, not a reason to give bicarbonate.
qj4czgn: After IV glucagon for a propranolol overdose, a 58-year-old man's HR rises from 38 to 58 and BP improves, but he becomes drowsy and starts vomiting. What is the best action?
Position him and suction to protect the airway; consider an antiemetic
Stop all glucagon since vomiting means he is allergic to it
Give atropine to treat the vagal response that is causing all the vomiting
Give activated charcoal now that his heart rate has improved

Nausea and vomiting are common glucagon effects, and a drowsy patient is at risk of aspiration, so airway protection comes first. Vomiting is not an allergy, and charcoal is contraindicated with altered mental status.
qwtogpu: A 62-year-old woman with insulin-dependent diabetes was unresponsive with BG 32 and no IV access. Fifteen minutes after glucagon 1 mg IM she is awake, alert and swallowing, with BG 88. What is the best next step?
Give oral carbohydrates now that she can swallow safely
Give a second glucagon dose to prevent recurrence
Withhold food because glucagon causes vomiting
Leave her at home since her glucose is now normal
Glucagon raises glucose briefly by releasing stored glycogen, so an awake patient who can swallow should get oral carbohydrates to keep the glucose up. A repeat dose is not needed when she can eat.
q8n4daq: A 62-year-old dialysis patient has missed two treatments. He is weak, HR 48, BP 88/50, and the ECG shows a very wide QRS with peaked T waves. What is the first medication?
Calcium chloride 1 g IV slow push
Atropine 1 mg IV for the bradycardia
Amiodarone 150 mg IV for the wide QRS
Albuterol nebulizer as the only treatment

Hyperkalemia with ECG changes calls for calcium first to stabilize the heart muscle. Atropine and amiodarone do not address the cause, and albuterol shifts potassium but does not protect the heart quickly enough by itself.
qyijkyi: You are giving calcium chloride slowly through a hand IV for a verapamil overdose. The patient reports severe burning, and the site is swollen and pale. What should you do?
Stop giving it at that site because of extravasation
Speed up the push so the dose finishes sooner
Flush the line hard and continue at the same site
Finish the dose, then elevate the hand on arrival
Calcium chloride can cause tissue necrosis when it extravasates, and extravasation is a reason to stop. Finish the dose through a new large, secure line such as a large vein or IO.
q15aju1n: A 70-year-old woman with hyperkalemia had a wide QRS and peaked T waves. After calcium gluconate IV the QRS narrows. What is the best interpretation and plan?
The heart is stabilized, but potassium is unchanged; add shifting therapy
The potassium is now corrected, so no further treatment is needed
The improvement means the diagnosis was wrong and the calcium was not actually needed
Calcium has lowered potassium, so stop cardiac monitoring

Calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes but does not lower serum potassium. The patient still needs treatments that move potassium into cells, such as albuterol per protocol, with continuous monitoring.
quy1l8w: A patient with hyperkalemic ECG changes is receiving calcium gluconate IV. Midway through the dose, the heart rate drops from 72 to 46 and she feels lightheaded. What should you do?
Stop the calcium and reassess the rhythm and blood pressure
Push the rest of the calcium quickly to finish the dose
Give atropine and keep giving calcium at the same rate
Switch to calcium chloride and push it faster
Bradycardia is a serious calcium side effect and a reason to stop, often from pushing it too fast. Speeding it up or switching to the stronger chloride salt would make the problem worse.
qg79d9g: A farmworker sprayed with pesticide has drooling, wheezing, copious bronchial secretions, SpO2 86% and HR 52. After the first IV atropine dose, HR is 118 but the lungs are still wet with secretions. What next?
Give more atropine, doubling the dose, until secretions dry
Stop atropine because the heart rate is now over 100
Switch to albuterol to dry the bronchial secretions
Give atropine only if the heart rate falls below 60
In organophosphate poisoning the goal of atropine is drying of the airway secretions, not heart rate. Tachycardia is expected and is not a reason to stop while the lungs are still wet.
qyw27ww: You are first on scene where two field workers are vomiting and drooling after a crop-spraying accident. Their clothes are soaked with chemical. What do you do first?
Put on PPE and decontaminate the patients before treating
Give each patient atropine IM right away, before anything else
Start IVs in both patients inside the ambulance at once
Assist ventilation first, then remove the clothing later
Organophosphates are absorbed through the skin, so unprotected rescuers can be poisoned too. Responder safety and decontamination come before atropine, which is given as soon as it is safe.
q33xkde: An organophosphate-poisoned patient has dry lungs after repeated atropine doses, but he has muscle twitching, increasing weakness and shallow breaths. What is the best next step?
Give pralidoxime to treat the nicotinic muscle weakness
Give more atropine until the twitching stops completely
Give midazolam, because the twitching is a seizure
Give calcium chloride for the muscle cramps and twitching

Atropine treats muscarinic effects such as secretions but does nothing for nicotinic muscle weakness. Pralidoxime reactivates cholinesterase and can improve muscle strength, while ventilation is supported as needed.
q1drhm0r: A 20-kg child has organophosphate poisoning with weakness and fasciculations after atropine. Medical control orders IV pralidoxime. Which order fits the dosing range?
2 g IV as a rapid push over 1 minute
100 mg IV infused slowly over about 2 full hours
Pediatric IV dosing is 20-50 mg/kg (max 2 g) infused over 15-30 minutes, so 20 kg gives 400-1,000 mg. A rapid push of a full adult dose exceeds the weight-based range and the administration time.
q18w4qkb: A 44-year-old electroplating worker suddenly collapsed at work after a chemical spill. He had a seizure, BP is 80/50, he is gasping, and SpO2 reads 99%. Coworkers mention a bitter almond odor. What is the priority antidote?
Naloxone 2 mg IN for possible opioid use
Atropine 2 mg IV for the collapse

Sudden collapse, seizure and shock with a normal SpO2 after an industrial exposure suggests cyanide, which blocks oxygen use in the cells. Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide; naloxone and atropine do not treat cellular poisoning.
qa9ty22: After hydroxocobalamin for smoke inhalation, a patient's skin and urine turn red and BP rises from 96/60 to 148/88. What is the best interpretation?
Expected effects of the drug; continue care and monitoring
A severe allergy that needs epinephrine IM right away
Worsening carbon monoxide levels that need a second 5 g dose of the drug
Kidney failure, so stop all IV fluids immediately
Red skin and urine and a rise in blood pressure are common effects of hydroxocobalamin. They are not signs of allergy or treatment failure, though the color can interfere with some monitors and labs.
q3hzk64: A 24-year-old man used methamphetamine. He is agitated and paranoid, HR 150, BP 190/110, temp 40.2 C (104.4 F). He has IV access. What is the best first medication?
Midazolam per protocol to reduce agitation and sympathetic drive
Metoprolol IV to slow the heart rate and lower his blood pressure quickly
Labetalol IV to bring the blood pressure down to normal
Haloperidol alone to control the paranoia and the agitation

Benzodiazepines are first-line for stimulant toxicity: they calm the patient and lower heart rate, blood pressure and heat production. Beta blockers are avoided as initial therapy in stimulant toxicity.
qny6033: A 35-year-old man received midazolam 5 mg IM for violent agitation. Ten minutes later he is calm but snoring, with RR 8 and SpO2 89%. What is the next step?
Open the airway, assist with a BVM and monitor EtCO2
Give a second midazolam dose since the first one worked
Leave him supine in restraints and recheck at the hospital
Give flumazenil IV to completely reverse the midazolam

Respiratory depression is the main danger of sedation, so airway support and capnography come first. Flumazenil is generally avoided in the field because it can trigger seizures, and more sedation would make things worse.
qwv5xbu: A 4-year-old weighing 16 kg with a fever has been having a generalized seizure for 7 minutes. There is no IV access yet. What is the best action?
Give midazolam IN or IM using weight-based dosing
Wait for it to stop, since febrile seizures are harmless
Give rectal acetaminophen first to treat the fever
Start an IV before giving any seizure medication
A seizure longer than 5 minutes needs a benzodiazepine whatever the cause, and IN or IM midazolam avoids the delay of IV access. Antipyretics do not stop an active seizure.
q142qsuo: A 38-year-old man in status epilepticus received lorazepam 4 mg IV. After 10-15 minutes of observation he is still having a generalized seizure, SpO2 94% with assisted ventilation and BP 142/88. What is next?
Wait another 30 minutes before any further dose
Give naloxone in case this is an opioid overdose
Give a fluid bolus before any more anticonvulsant
The lorazepam label allows one repeat 4 mg dose after a 10-15 minute observation period if seizures continue. Waiting longer lets status epilepticus cause more injury.
q1mgrqdw: A 70-year-old man with severe COPD is restless and anxious. SpO2 84%, RR 8, EtCO2 68. His family asks you to give him something to calm him. What is best?
Withhold lorazepam and assist ventilation for the hypercapnia
Give lorazepam IV so that he can better tolerate the oxygen mask and calm down
Give lorazepam IM since the IM route is less sedating
Give lorazepam and recheck the EtCO2 in 30 minutes

His restlessness comes from hypercapnic respiratory failure, and severe respiratory insufficiency without airway support is a contraindication to lorazepam. A sedative could cause respiratory arrest; he needs ventilatory support.
qokhtcn: A 52-year-old man stopped drinking alcohol 2 days ago. He has tremors, visual hallucinations, diaphoresis, HR 128, BP 172/100 and temp 38.3 C (100.9 F). What is the best medication?
Diazepam IV, then reassess and repeat per protocol
Haloperidol IM as the only agent for hallucinations
Metoprolol IV to slow the heart rate and lower BP
Naloxone IN in case he took opioids along with alcohol
Benzodiazepines such as diazepam treat alcohol withdrawal and prevent seizures. Haloperidol alone lowers the seizure threshold and does not treat the withdrawal itself.
qcso7xj: An 8-year-old weighing 25 kg has been seizing for 6 minutes, and there is no IV access. Your service carries diazepam rectal gel. Which dose matches the label for this age?
Rectal gel dosing is 0.3 mg/kg for ages 6-11 years, so 25 kg x 0.3 = 7.5 mg. The 0.5 mg/kg dose is for ages 2-5, and 0.2 mg/kg is for age 12 and older.
q1spxky9: A 55-year-old malnourished man with heavy alcohol use is confused, with BG 42 mg/dL. You have thiamine and D50 ready. What is the best approach?
Give dextrose now; give thiamine as well without delaying glucose
Give thiamine and wait 30 minutes before giving any dextrose
Withhold dextrose because it will cause Wernicke encephalopathy
Give oral glucose only, since IV dextrose is unsafe in alcoholics
Hypoglycemia can cause brain injury within minutes and must be corrected right away. Thiamine is given too, but delaying dextrose for it is not justified.
q2sdvqd: A 49-year-old man with chronic alcohol use is ataxic and confused, with nystagmus. After dextrose his BG is 112, but the confusion, nystagmus and ataxia persist. What should you consider next?
Thiamine 100 mg IV for possible Wernicke encephalopathy
Another D50 dose since the confusion persists
Naloxone 2 mg IV for possible opioid co-ingestion
Haloperidol IM to manage the confusion

Confusion, ataxia and eye movement abnormalities in a malnourished drinker suggest Wernicke encephalopathy, which is treated with thiamine 100 mg IV. More dextrose is not needed with a normal glucose.
qyy2z7g: A 1-year-old weighing 10 kg has had vomiting and diarrhea. She is lethargic and not feeding, with BG 34. You have IV access. What is the best treatment?
D50 25 g IV push as for an adult
Oral glucose gel between her cheek and gum
Withhold dextrose and give a fluid bolus
Infants and young children get dilute dextrose (D10) by weight to avoid vein injury and large osmotic loads. Oral glucose is unsafe in a lethargic child who cannot protect the airway.
q1kl64id: A 66-year-old man who takes glipizide was found confused with BG 36. After D50 he is alert with BG 104. He wants to stay home. What is the key concern?
Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia often returns after dextrose
D50 will cause dangerous hyperglycemia within the hour
Glipizide will interact with the D50 to cause dangerously low potassium
His glucose will stay normal for the rest of the day
Sulfonylureas act for many hours and can cause hypoglycemia to come back after a single dextrose dose. These patients need observation, so the crew should strongly encourage transport.
qck7jem: A 71-year-old woman has new right-sided weakness and slurred speech that started 40 minutes ago. BP 168/94. Her glucometer reads 38 mg/dL. What is the best next step?
Treat the hypoglycemia with dextrose and reassess her deficits
Transport to a stroke center without treating the glucose
Lower her blood pressure first, then recheck the glucose in 15 minutes
Give aspirin for the stroke while the glucose is rechecked
Hypoglycemia can mimic a stroke, so it must be found and treated first; the deficits often resolve once glucose is restored. Aspirin and BP lowering are not field stroke treatments here.
qu2eqln: A 28-year-old man is naked, sweating, screaming and fighting police. Temp is 40.5 C (104.9 F), and he cannot be safely approached for IV access. What is the best medication strategy?
Ketamine IM per protocol for rapid, safe sedation
Haloperidol IV once an IV is started in the field
Keep him prone in restraints until he tires out
Midazolam PO mixed in a drink to calm him down

Hyperactive delirium with hyperthermia needs fast chemical sedation, and IM ketamine works quickly without IV access. Prone restraint without sedation risks sudden death, and IV or oral routes are not practical.
qbou93h: Minutes after IM ketamine for agitation, a patient develops high-pitched stridor, chest retractions, and SpO2 dropping to 84%. What should you do?
Jaw thrust and BVM with positive pressure for laryngospasm
Give a second ketamine dose to deepen the sedation
Give naloxone to reverse the ketamine effects
Place him prone and apply a nonrebreather mask

Laryngospasm is a serious ketamine complication, and positive pressure ventilation with a jaw thrust usually breaks it. Naloxone does not reverse ketamine, and the prone position makes airway management harder.
q1yc9wkr: A 74-year-old man with Parkinson's disease is confused and agitated after a fall. He is pulling at his IV. Medical control asks what agent you plan to use. What is the key consideration?
Avoid haloperidol; it can severely worsen his parkinsonism
Give haloperidol IV because it acts faster in the elderly
Give double the usual haloperidol dose because of his tremor
Haloperidol is preferred since he has a movement disorder

Parkinson's disease is a contraindication to haloperidol because blocking dopamine can sharply worsen rigidity and mobility. Look for causes of delirium and use other approaches or agents per protocol.
q1kym67f: Twenty minutes after IM haloperidol for agitation, the monitor shows a QTc of 520 ms and short runs of polymorphic VT. The patient has a pulse. What is the best action?
Withhold more haloperidol and give magnesium per protocol
Give a second haloperidol dose to prevent more agitation
Give amiodarone to suppress the polymorphic VT runs
Ignore the runs since they are self-terminating
QT prolongation is a serious haloperidol effect and a reason to stop; polymorphic VT with a long QT (torsades) is treated with magnesium. Amiodarone further prolongs the QT.
q1guzuy3: A 30-year-old woman is severely agitated after an argument. Her 12-lead shows a QTc of 480 ms. Droperidol is in your agitation protocol. What is best?
Withhold droperidol and use a benzodiazepine per protocol
Give droperidol IM, since the IM route avoids QT effects
Give droperidol at half the usual dose with monitoring
Give droperidol and repeat the 12-lead at the hospital
A QTc over 450 ms in a female is a contraindication to droperidol, which carries a QT prolongation risk. A lower dose or another route does not remove that risk.
q8n4b3g: Twenty minutes after droperidol for vomiting, a 22-year-old woman is very restless, keeps standing up and says she feels like she has to keep moving. Vitals are stable. What is happening?
Akathisia from the droperidol; stop it and treat per protocol
Worsening anxiety that needs a second, larger droperidol dose to control it
A normal sign that the nausea is resolving
An allergic reaction that needs IM epinephrine
Akathisia is a common droperidol side effect and a reason to stop further doses; it is often treated with diphenhydramine or a benzodiazepine per protocol. Giving more droperidol would make it worse.
q1gxmlu6: A 27-year-old woman who delivered 4 days ago has a severe headache and had a generalized seizure at home. BP is 164/108. She is now postictal. What is the best medication?
Magnesium sulfate 4-6 g IV over 15-20 minutes
Labetalol alone, since the pregnancy is over
Dextrose, because seizures after delivery are hypoglycemic

Eclampsia can occur up to several weeks after delivery, and magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice to treat and prevent seizures. Blood pressure control alone does not prevent recurrent eclamptic seizures.
q1o6gfhf: During a magnesium loading dose for eclampsia, a patient feels warm and flushed and is sweating. RR is 18, patellar reflexes are present and BP is 148/96. What is best?
Continue the infusion and keep monitoring reflexes and breathing
Stop the infusion and give calcium gluconate IV immediately as an antidote
Stop the infusion because she is having an allergic reaction
Speed up the infusion so the side effects pass sooner
Flushing, warmth and sweating are common, expected effects of magnesium. Toxicity shows as loss of reflexes, RR under 12, hypotension or bradycardia, and none are present.
q12ecxn5: A woman has just delivered a full-term infant. The uterus remains large, with the fundus above the umbilicus, and you feel what may be another fetus. Bleeding is moderate. Your partner draws up oxytocin. What is best?
Withhold oxytocin until a second twin is ruled out
Give oxytocin 10 units IM to control the bleeding now
Give oxytocin IV fast to speed delivery of the placenta
Give oxytocin, then perform fundal massage firmly
A possible second twin is a contraindication: oxytocin could clamp the uterus down on an undelivered infant. Give it only after all infants are delivered.
q1gd43xt: After oxytocin 10 units IM and fundal massage for postpartum bleeding, the uterus is firm at the umbilicus, but a steady stream of bright red blood continues. HR 112. What should you do next?
Look for a perineal laceration and apply direct pressure
Give more oxytocin, since a firm uterus means it is not working
Vigorously massage the fundus for another 15 minutes
Have her sit upright to slow down the flow of blood
Once the uterus is firm, ongoing bleeding suggests another source such as a laceration, which needs direct pressure. More oxytocin targets uterine tone, which is already good.
qtn59jx: A woman delivered 40 minutes ago. Despite oxytocin and fundal massage she is still bleeding heavily. HR 124, BP 86/50. Your protocol includes TXA. What is the correct administration?
1 g IV as a rapid push over 30 seconds
2 g IM divided into both thighs
For postpartum hemorrhage, TXA is given as 1 g IV over 10 minutes, and the dose can be repeated if bleeding continues after 30 minutes. A rapid push can cause hypotension.
q1p44r1y: A trauma patient with controlled external bleeding is receiving TXA 1 g IV. Your partner pushed the first part of the dose over about 30 seconds, and BP falls from 104/68 to 82/50. While you reassess for ongoing hemorrhage, what should you do about the TXA?
Slow the rest of the dose to run over about 10 minutes
Push the rest quickly so the drug works sooner
Stop TXA and give IM epinephrine for an allergy
Stop TXA for good, since hypotension rules it out

Hypotension is a known effect of giving TXA too rapidly, which is why it is infused over about 10 minutes, so the rate is slowed and the BP treated. A drop in BP is not a sign of allergy, and hemorrhage must still be ruled out in a trauma patient.
qh0ds33: A 30-week pregnant woman in preterm labor received terbutaline 0.25 mg SQ by medical control order. Now her HR is 128, and she reports chest tightness. What is the best action?
Withhold further terbutaline and obtain a 12-lead
Give the second dose since contractions persist
Give a fluid bolus and then repeat the dose
Give metoprolol to slow her heart rate
A maternal HR over 120 or chest pain is a reason to stop terbutaline. Repeating the dose increases the risk of dysrhythmia and cardiac ischemia.
qcc6awd: A woman at 31 weeks has regular contractions. Medical control is discussing terbutaline when you see the infant's head crowning with each contraction. What should you do?
Prepare for delivery; do not attempt tocolysis
Give terbutaline SQ quickly to stop the delivery
Have her cross her legs while terbutaline is drawn up
Give terbutaline and transport in the left lateral position
Delivery is imminent, so trying to stop labor is no longer appropriate and could delay care. The crew should prepare for a preterm delivery and neonatal resuscitation.
q13allgo: A 6-year-old weighing 22 kg ate a peanut cookie. He has hives, wheezing and vomiting, BP 70/40. Using 1 mg/mL epinephrine, what is the correct initial dose?
0.22 mg IM in the anterolateral thigh
0.22 mg IV push of the 1 mg/mL solution
0.5 mg IM in the deltoid muscle
Children under 30 kg receive 0.01 mg/kg IM, so 22 kg gives 0.22 mg. The 1 mg/mL concentration is never given IV push, and antihistamines do not replace epinephrine in anaphylaxis.
qrkxfyq: A 9-year-old in anaphylaxis received IM epinephrine 6 minutes ago. She is still wheezing with hives, and BP is 76/44. What is the best next action?
Repeat IM epinephrine and give fluids per protocol
Wait 20 minutes for the first dose to fully work
Give diphenhydramine instead of more epinephrine
Give methylprednisolone and wait for it to work
IM epinephrine can be repeated every 5-10 minutes when anaphylaxis persists, along with fluids for hypotension. Antihistamines and steroids are slow adjuncts that do not reverse shock.
qp20y29: A 2-year-old has a barking cough, stridor at rest, suprasternal retractions and SpO2 93%. Symptoms began suddenly overnight after a mild cold. What is the best treatment?
Nebulized racemic epinephrine and calm transport
Nebulized albuterol for the noisy breathing
Inspect the throat with a tongue blade first
Nebulized saline only, since croup resolves

Croup with stridor at rest is treated with nebulized racemic epinephrine to reduce swelling in the upper airway. Albuterol treats lower airway bronchospasm, and agitating the child can worsen the obstruction.
qc3ci35: A 4-year-old is sitting upright and leaning forward, drooling, with high fever, a muffled voice and soft stridor. He looks toxic. Your partner wants to start a nebulizer and an IV. What is best?
Keep him calm with the parent and transport quickly
Start the IV first, then give racemic epinephrine
Lay him flat and give racemic epinephrine by mask
Look in his throat to confirm the diagnosis first

Drooling, toxic appearance and tripod positioning suggest epiglottitis, where agitation can cause complete obstruction. Avoid upsetting procedures, keep him in a position of comfort, and prepare for a difficult airway.
qxnnobe: A 3-year-old has a barking cough at night but no stridor at rest, normal work of breathing and SpO2 98%. What is the most appropriate medication?
IM epinephrine in the lateral thigh
Mild croup without stridor at rest benefits from a single dose of dexamethasone, which reduces airway swelling over hours. Racemic epinephrine is reserved for stridor at rest or respiratory distress.
q1ypcfif: A 46-year-old woman with vomiting and diarrhea remains hypotensive after 2 L of fluid. Her medication list shows long-term daily prednisone for lupus, and she missed doses while sick. What does this finding change?
Consider adrenal crisis and give dexamethasone per protocol
It changes nothing, since steroids do not affect shock
Stop all fluids, since prednisone causes fluid retention
Give extra potassium for steroid-induced hypokalemia

Long-term steroid use suppresses the adrenal glands, so illness with missed doses can cause adrenal crisis that does not respond to fluids. A corticosteroid such as dexamethasone (4 mg IV per protocol) is indicated.
qyjewgc: A 68-year-old man with Parkinson's disease is vomiting. His medications include carbidopa/levodopa and apomorphine injections. Which is the best decision about ondansetron?
Withhold ondansetron because of the apomorphine
Give ondansetron 4 mg IV as for any adult
Give ondansetron ODT, since the oral form is safe
Give ondansetron and a fluid bolus together
Ondansetron with apomorphine can cause profound hypotension and loss of consciousness, so it is contraindicated. Changing the route does not remove the interaction.
q1az3jfj: A 5-year-old weighing 18 kg has had vomiting and diarrhea for a day. She is alert, mildly dehydrated, and has no IV. Your protocol allows ODT ondansetron. What is the correct dose?
For children 15-30 kg, the ODT dose is 4 mg. The 2 mg dose is for 8-15 kg, and 8 mg is above the range for her weight.
qbterve: An 18-month-old has been vomiting for 6 hours and is mildly dehydrated. A parent asks if you can give promethazine like the older sibling got. What is the best response?
Promethazine is contraindicated under age 2 because it can stop breathing
Promethazine is safe at half the adult dose in any toddler
Promethazine is fine in toddlers as long as it is given deep IM rather than IV
Promethazine can be given if the child weighs over 10 kg
Promethazine is contraindicated in children under 2 years because of fatal respiratory depression. An age-appropriate antiemetic such as ondansetron per protocol is the alternative.
q3hhy68: A 72-year-old woman with prior abdominal surgery has a distended abdomen, no bowel movement for 3 days, and is vomiting foul brown fluid. What is the best decision about metoclopramide?
Withhold it because of suspected bowel obstruction
Give 10 mg IV to speed up stomach emptying
Give it IM so that it bypasses the gut
Give it only after a fluid bolus is complete
GI obstruction is a contraindication to metoclopramide because it increases gut movement. The surgical history and feculent vomiting strongly suggest obstruction.
q1h784fv: A 30-year-old woman took a handful of her amitriptyline 45 minutes ago. On arrival she is drowsy, slurring words and her GCS is 11. She is not intubated. What is the best decision about activated charcoal?
Withhold charcoal because she cannot protect her airway
Give charcoal right away while she can still swallow
Give charcoal mixed with soda to improve its taste
Give half the charcoal dose to lower aspiration risk

Altered mental status without a protected airway is a contraindication because of aspiration risk, which is especially high with a tricyclic that can cause sudden seizures and coma. A smaller dose does not solve the airway problem.
q1vkxmi6: A 3-year-old drank from a bottle of lamp oil 20 minutes ago. He is coughing and mildly tachypneic but alert. The parent asks about the charcoal they read about online. What is best?
Do not give charcoal; it does not help and raises aspiration risk
Give charcoal 1 g/kg PO right away to bind the lamp oil before it is absorbed
Give charcoal after making the child vomit at home
Give charcoal through an NG tube to protect the lungs
Hydrocarbons are a contraindication to charcoal: it does not bind them well and vomiting increases aspiration risk. The cough already suggests aspiration, so watch his breathing closely.
q1wvxgso: A 33-week pregnant woman has a severe headache and BP 172/114. She uses an albuterol inhaler for asthma and wheezed last week. Medical control asks about labetalol. What is your best response?
Asthma is a contraindication; request an alternative agent
Labetalol is safe in asthma when it is given slowly IV
Give labetalol with albuterol to prevent bronchospasm
Give labetalol IM instead of IV to avoid bronchospasm
Labetalol blocks beta-2 receptors and is contraindicated in asthma or reactive airway disease because it can cause bronchospasm. Another antihypertensive should be chosen per medical control.
qued7h6: A preeclamptic patient received labetalol 20 mg IV for BP 170/112. Ten minutes later, BP is 146/94 and HR has fallen to 52. Your protocol calls for 40 mg next if BP is still above goal. What is best?
Hold further labetalol because of the bradycardia
Give the 40 mg dose since BP is still above 140
Give atropine and then the 40 mg dose of labetalol
Give 80 mg now to reach the BP goal faster

An HR under 60 is a stop criterion for labetalol, and 146/94 is already out of the severe range that requires urgent treatment. Further beta blockade could cause symptomatic bradycardia or heart block.
q534opx: A 7-year-old weighing 20 kg ate shrimp and has itchy hives on the trunk. Lungs are clear, no swelling of the lips or tongue, no vomiting, BP 104/66, HR 108. What is the best treatment?
Diphenhydramine and close monitoring for any progression
Epinephrine IV push of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration to stop the reaction
Nebulized albuterol to prevent future wheezing
No treatment and release to the parent at home

Isolated hives without airway, breathing, GI or circulation involvement is a mild allergic reaction that is treated with an antihistamine, with monitoring for progression to anaphylaxis. IV epinephrine is reserved for refractory shock.
q1psdv1r: An 18-month-old weighing 11 kg had a 2-minute generalized seizure with fever. On arrival she is crying and moving all limbs, with normal breathing, SpO2 98% and temp 39.4 C (102.9 F). What is the best approach?
Withhold benzodiazepines; treat fever for comfort and transport
Give IN midazolam now to prevent another seizure
Give acetaminophen now, since it reliably prevents the seizure from recurring
Give aspirin for the fever and then release her at home
A short febrile seizure that has stopped does not need a benzodiazepine; acetaminophen is given for comfort but does not prevent recurrence. Aspirin is avoided in children because of Reye syndrome.
q17e3wbw: A 58-year-old with urosepsis has MAP 56, HR 118 and lactate 4.8 after an initial crystalloid bolus. Her lungs now have faint crackles. Only an 18 g antecubital IV is available, and a central line will take 45 minutes. What is the best next step?
Start peripheral norepinephrine and titrate to MAP 65 or greater
Hold all vasopressors until the central line has been placed
Start a phenylephrine infusion as the first-line agent
Keep giving crystalloid boluses until the MAP is above 65

Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor in septic shock and can be started through a secure proximal peripheral IV with close site checks. Waiting 45 minutes for a central line prolongs hypoperfusion, and more fluid is risky once crackles appear.
qo5dk4a: You pick up a 31-year-old with an open-book pelvic fracture. BP is 74/40 and HR 138. The referring facility started norepinephrine but has not given any blood. What should change first?
Give blood and bind the pelvis before relying on the pressor
Double the norepinephrine rate to reach a MAP of 65 or greater
Add vasopressin so norepinephrine can be weaned
Give push-dose phenylephrine and keep the current plan

Hypovolemic hypotension is a contraindication to norepinephrine unless used briefly while volume is restored. This patient needs hemorrhage control and blood; raising the pressor dose squeezes an empty tank.
q1a6tnzu: Twenty minutes into transport, the MAP of a patient on norepinephrine falls from 70 to 46 over 2 minutes. The patient just had a line change at the referring bedside. HR and rhythm are unchanged. What is the best first action?
Trace the line and pump to confirm the drip is infusing
Give a 1-liter fluid bolus over 10 minutes
Add vasopressin at the septic shock dose
Push 1 mg of epinephrine IV for a presumed pulseless arrest

A sudden MAP drop right after a line change with no other change points to an interrupted or disconnected pressor. Restoring flow fixes the cause; adding drugs before checking the line treats the wrong problem.
qjbmj9y: A 64-year-old has ROSC after VF arrest. He is intubated and unresponsive with BP 78/48 (MAP 58) and HR 96. What is the best hemodynamic plan?
Start a norepinephrine infusion and titrate to MAP 65 or greater
Give 1 mg epinephrine IV push every 3-5 minutes
Allow permissive hypotension to limit any reperfusion injury
Give atropine and recheck BP in 5 minutes

Post-arrest hypotension worsens brain injury; a titrated vasopressor infusion to MAP 65 or greater is standard. Arrest-dose epinephrine pushes are for pulseless patients and cause wild swings, and permissive hypotension applies to bleeding trauma, not post-arrest care.
q1r6ct: A septic patient remains at MAP 58 on high-dose norepinephrine plus vasopressin. Bedside echo shows a poorly contracting left ventricle, and her extremities are cold. Which addition best fits?
Add an epinephrine infusion titrated to MAP
Add dobutamine and titrate to cardiac output
Add phenylephrine for more alpha tone
Start a nitroglycerin infusion to lower afterload
She needs both more pressure and more contractility, which epinephrine provides (labeled for septic shock). Dobutamine adds inotropy but often lowers BP further when the MAP is already below goal.
q1yf4ucq: A patient on an epinephrine infusion for septic shock develops frequent multifocal PVCs during transport. MAP is 72. A point-of-care potassium is 2.9 mEq/L. What is the most likely contributor?
Epinephrine-driven shift of potassium into cells
Hyperkalemia from a hemolyzed sample drawn from the line
Expected sinus tachycardia from sepsis alone
Hypokalemia and dysrhythmias are listed serious effects of epinephrine through beta-2 driven cellular potassium uptake. Replace potassium per protocol and reassess whether the dose can come down.
q12z8yyh: Two minutes after intubation with propofol, a 70-year-old's BP falls from 104/62 to 68/40. HR is 108 and the tube position is confirmed. What is the best immediate treatment while an infusion is being prepared?
Push-dose epinephrine 10-20 mcg IV, repeated per protocol
Furosemide IV to reduce the after-intubation fluid shift
A second propofol dose to deepen the anesthetic plane
Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes for the hypotension
Post-induction hypotension needs prompt vasoactive support; push-dose epinephrine per protocol bridges until an infusion runs. More propofol worsens the vasodilation that caused the drop.
q2rypib: A 4-year-old with septic shock has had repeated fluid boluses. He is still lethargic with HR 168, cool mottled legs, capillary refill 5 seconds and a narrow pulse pressure. Which vasoactive agent fits this cold-shock picture best?

Fluid-refractory cold shock in children reflects low cardiac output with high resistance, and epinephrine adds inotropy plus pressure. A pure vasoconstrictor such as phenylephrine or vasopressin raises afterload on a struggling heart.
q439gjm: A septic patient is on norepinephrine and vasopressin. After source control and fluids, MAP is now 88 and rising. Which drip should be weaned first?
When MAP is well above goal, catecholamines are tapered first, and vasopressin is usually weaned last. Stopping both at once risks rebound hypotension.
q1fnklg8: During a 3-hour transfer, a patient on norepinephrine and vasopressin develops several new findings. Which one is most concerning?
New severe abdominal pain with a rising lactate
A drop in HR from 104 to 92
Mild headache with a stable MAP of 70 and good urine output

Mesenteric ischemia is a serious effect of vasopressin (and catecholamines), and pain with a climbing lactate is an early warning. A mild sodium change or slightly slower HR does not change the plan right now.
qqyl04d: Four patients need vasoactive support during interfacility transfer. In which patient is vasopressin LEAST suited as the only vasoactive agent?
Cardiogenic shock with a low ejection fraction
Post-cardiotomy vasoplegia with good LV function
Vasodilatory shock with warm, flushed skin

Vasopressin is a pure vasoconstrictor that can decrease cardiac output; without inotropy it can lower output in a failing heart and worsen cardiogenic shock. In vasodilatory states, which are labeled indications, it restores tone without that drawback.
qum113e: A 77-year-old with known severe aortic stenosis is intubated. Afterward, BP is 78/44 and HR 92 in sinus rhythm. Which drug best fits her physiology right now?

With fixed outflow obstruction, she needs diastolic pressure for coronary flow and a slower HR for filling, and pure alpha agonism with reflex slowing does both. Inotropes and chronotropes shorten filling time, and vasodilators can cause collapse.
q4ae6om: A patient with an EF of 15% gets several phenylephrine boluses for post-intubation hypotension. BP rises to 112/70, but HR falls to 48, SpO2 drops and new crackles appear. How should you interpret this?
Afterload rose and cardiac output fell; change to an inotropic pressor
Phenylephrine worked well; continue boluses as needed
This is aspiration from the intubation and is unrelated to the drug
The patient needs more phenylephrine to keep up with the HR

Phenylephrine can lower cardiac output (a listed serious effect) and causes reflex bradycardia. In a weak heart the BP looks better while forward flow and oxygenation worsen, so an agent with inotropy fits better.
q17wus6v: A septic patient was started on dopamine at the referring hospital. During packaging she develops atrial fibrillation at 164 with frequent PVCs. MAP is 64. What is the best change?
Increase dopamine to improve the MAP
Add an esmolol infusion for rate control
Give adenosine to break the arrhythmia

Tachydysrhythmias are a stop criterion for dopamine, which causes more arrhythmias than norepinephrine, the first-line agent in septic shock. Beta-blocking a septic patient on a failing pressor risks collapse.
q1qfviqd: A 72-year-old has symptomatic bradycardia at 36 with BP 76/40 and confusion. Atropine has failed, and transcutaneous pacing gives only intermittent capture despite pad and output changes. What is the best next drug per ACLS?
A dopamine infusion titrated to HR and BP
Another 3 mg of atropine as a single bolus
Diltiazem to stabilize the conduction system
ACLS lists dopamine (or epinephrine) infusion when atropine fails and pacing is not effective. More atropine past the max adds little, and amiodarone or diltiazem would slow conduction further.
q1pf64uk: Three days after an MI, a 67-year-old has BP 98/64, HR 102, cool clammy skin, falling urine output and bibasilar crackles. MAP is 75. Which agent best addresses the main problem?

This is low-output cardiogenic shock with acceptable BP, so contractility is the target. Pure vasoconstrictors raise afterload on a failing ventricle, and nitroprusside with a borderline BP risks hypotension.
q1yxlgy2: Dobutamine is started for cardiogenic shock with an initial BP of 92/60. Ten minutes later, BP is 76/42 and HR 128. What is the best next step?
Add norepinephrine and reassess the dobutamine dose
Increase dobutamine to raise cardiac output
Stop all vasoactive drugs and observe the BP response for 10 minutes

Dobutamine can cause hypotension through beta-2 vasodilation, a stop criterion, so its dose is reassessed while a vasopressor such as norepinephrine restores MAP. Raising dobutamine worsens both the tachycardia and the vasodilation.
q1muqznt: A septic patient has reached MAP 68 on norepinephrine after adequate fluids. Lactate keeps rising, the skin stays mottled, and echo shows a severely depressed LV. Which addition best fits?
Add dobutamine to improve cardiac output
Raise norepinephrine until the MAP reaches about 85
Add vasopressin for more vascular tone
With the MAP at goal but low output, an inotrope addresses the real deficit. Pushing the MAP higher or adding pure vasoconstriction does not fix a weak pump.
q1ffqbrf: A 59-year-old with ischemic cardiomyopathy on high-dose home carvedilol is in low-output cardiogenic shock with BP 94/58. Dobutamine has had little effect. Which agent is most likely to work?
Milrinone raises contractility through PDE-3 inhibition, which bypasses beta receptors blocked by carvedilol. Increasing a beta agonist against a full blockade adds little inotropy.
qoph6a8: During an interfacility transfer, a patient on milrinone becomes hypotensive at 80/44 with new runs of ventricular ectopy. What is the best response?
Reduce or stop milrinone per orders and support MAP with a pressor
Increase milrinone to improve cardiac output
Give the loading dose again so the drug reaches steady state faster
Continue unchanged since ectopy is expected
Hypotension and ventricular dysrhythmias are stop criteria for milrinone. A vasopressor supports MAP while the effect fades; a repeat load or a higher rate makes both problems worse.
qar92f8: A 66-year-old with pneumonia and septic shock needs RSI. BP is 86/52 and HR 124 (shock index about 1.4) on low-dose norepinephrine. Ketamine is chosen. What is the best dosing approach?
Reduce the induction dose and give a full paralytic dose
Give the full induction dose and reduce the paralytic
Give a full induction dose and skip the paralytic to avoid apnea
Reduce both drugs to half their usual dose

In shock, a lower induction dose limits hemodynamic collapse, while a full (or higher) paralytic dose ensures good conditions because slow circulation delays onset. Cutting the paralytic invites a failed first pass.
q1h5mcre: A 52-year-old with a type A aortic dissection is in severe distress, hypoxic and needs intubation. BP is 192/110 and HR 112 despite an esmolol infusion. Which induction agent is LEAST appropriate?
Ketamine's sympathetic surge raises BP and HR, and severe hypertension is a stop criterion, which can extend a dissection. Agents that blunt or do not raise sympathetic tone fit better here.
qsj32xb: An intubated trauma patient on norepinephrine has BP 92/56 and needs sedation for a 90-minute flight. He was induced with ketamine and paralyzed with rocuronium. Which sedation plan best fits his hemodynamics?
A ketamine infusion with fentanyl as needed
A propofol infusion at standard dose
No sedation is needed because he is already paralyzed

Ketamine (per protocol infusion range) keeps sympathetic tone, so it suits a pressor-dependent patient. Propofol and large benzodiazepine boluses deepen hypotension, and a paralyzed patient always needs sedation and analgesia.
q101xe55: A septic patient has been on a propofol infusion at the referring facility. While on the transport ventilator, BP drifts from 104/60 to 82/48 and HR is 112. Sedation is deep (RASS -5). What is the best adjustment?
Lower the propofol and shift to analgesia-first sedation
Increase the propofol rate to blunt any sympathetic surges
Switch to midazolam boluses at a high dose
Hypotension and oversedation are stop criteria for propofol. Lowering it and using an analgesia-first approach (with pressor support as needed) protects BP; large benzodiazepine boluses also drop BP.
qc8ow79: Propofol is the only induction agent available for a 74-year-old with GI bleeding who needs intubation. BP is 88/56 after 2 units of blood. What is the best approach?
Give a reduced dose of 0.5-1 mg/kg with a pressor ready
Give the full 2.5 mg/kg dose for a smooth intubation
Avoid any induction agent and use paralytic only
Give propofol as a fast push followed by a fluid bolus
Propofol's labeled induction dose for unstable patients is 0.5-1 mg/kg, with vasopressor support at hand. A full dose risks arrest, and paralysis without sedation risks awareness.
q9py2xx: A 41-year-old with hypertriglyceridemia-induced acute pancreatitis is intubated for respiratory failure before transfer. Which sedation agent should be avoided for the infusion?

Propofol is a lipid emulsion that can raise triglycerides and cause pancreatitis (listed serious effects), so it is a poor choice in triglyceride-driven pancreatitis. The other agents lack that lipid load.
q11bf1pz: A 69-year-old in cardiogenic shock (BP 82/50, HR 108, crackles) needs RSI. Which induction choice best preserves hemodynamics?
Etomidate at the standard weight-based dose
Propofol at the full induction dose
Propofol with a full-dose fentanyl pretreatment for blunting

Etomidate has little effect on contractility or vascular tone, which suits a patient with a failing heart. Propofol, induction-dose midazolam and fentanyl pretreatment all lower BP in a patient with no reserve.
q14apdhc: Seconds after etomidate is pushed and before rocuronium takes effect, the patient has jerking movements of the arms. SpO2 is 96%. What is the most likely explanation and response?
Myoclonus from etomidate; proceed with the intubation
A seizure; give lorazepam and delay intubation
Malignant hyperthermia from etomidate; give dantrolene now

Myoclonus is a common effect of etomidate and resolves with paralysis. Treating it as a seizure delays the airway, and malignant hyperthermia is linked to succinylcholine and volatile agents, not etomidate.
qkf70xq: A 100-kg patient in cardiogenic shock with a low cardiac output needs RSI. Which rocuronium dose best ensures fast intubating conditions?

Low output slows drug delivery to muscles, so the upper RSI dose (1.2 mg/kg) gives faster onset. The lower doses are labeled for intubation but onset is slower, which matters most in a patient with little reserve.
q1h0ez3h: A 63-year-old dialysis patient with sepsis missed two sessions. He needs RSI for hypoxic respiratory failure. K is 6.6 mEq/L with peaked T waves. Which paralytic plan is best?
Use succinylcholine at a reduced dose

Known hyperkalemia is a contraindication to succinylcholine, which raises potassium further and can cause arrest. Rocuronium avoids that risk; calcium or a lower dose does not make succinylcholine safe here.
qzquksa: A 48-year-old has been bedbound in an ICU for 3 weeks after a stroke and now needs reintubation before transfer. Which paralytic consideration matters most?
Prolonged immobilization and stroke make succinylcholine unsafe
Succinylcholine is preferred for its short duration here
Rocuronium is unsafe after prolonged ICU stays
Either agent is fine as long as the K is normal on arrival

Stroke and immobilization over 48-72 hours upregulate receptors and can cause a severe potassium surge with succinylcholine, even with a normal baseline K. A nondepolarizing agent such as rocuronium avoids that.
qed8o9k: After intubation for ARDS, a 45-year-old is fighting the vent with HR 124 and BP 156/92. He is on a midazolam infusion only. What is the best next step?
Add analgesia with fentanyl, then reassess sedation
Add vecuronium to stop ventilator dyssynchrony
Increase midazolam until he stops moving
Give labetalol to control the HR and BP before anything else
An endotracheal tube is painful, and analgesia-first sedation treats the cause of the distress. Paralyzing him or raising only the benzodiazepine leaves pain untreated, and labetalol hides the signs.
q16ft5o3: A 71-year-old with septic shock has BP 84/50 and HR 126 before RSI. Your protocol lists fentanyl pretreatment as an option. What is the best decision?
Omit fentanyl pretreatment in this hypotensive patient
Give fentanyl pretreatment at the full dose
Give fentanyl pretreatment by rapid IV push
Give fentanyl and skip the induction agent to protect the BP
Fentanyl pretreatment blunts sympathetic tone, which this shock patient depends on; hypotension is a stop criterion. It suits hypertensive patients such as TBI or dissection, not septic shock.
qgu4t2j: An intubated patient in cardiogenic shock on norepinephrine becomes agitated during the flight. BP is 88/54. Which sedation choice is most likely to worsen his hemodynamics?
Small fentanyl doses titrated to effect
Checking tube position and analgesia first
Shock is a relative contraindication to midazolam, and large boluses cause hypotension in a patient without reserve. Small, titrated analgesic doses or ketamine better protect BP.
q1fed0a1: A post-arrest patient on norepinephrine (MAP 72) has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure on the transport ventilator. He has not received a paralytic since intubation. What is the best action?
Give midazolam IV titrated while watching BP
Give rocuronium to stop the motor activity
Withhold treatment since post-arrest seizures are expected
Give phenylephrine to protect cerebral pressure

Post-arrest seizures worsen brain injury and need treatment; a benzodiazepine is first-line, with close BP monitoring because of hypotension risk. A paralytic stops movement but not seizure activity in the brain.
q13bq5sa: A post-arrest patient on a dexmedetomidine infusion during transfer develops HR 42 in sinus rhythm with BP 82/50. What is the best first action?
Add a propofol infusion for deeper sedation
Bradycardia under 50 with hypotension is a stop criterion for dexmedetomidine. Raising the rate or giving a load (which can cause sinus arrest or hypertension then hypotension) worsens the problem.
q1ley7du: A patient with ARDS is on a rocuronium infusion for a long flight. The only sedation running is dexmedetomidine at a low rate. What is the main concern?
Sedation may be too light, risking awareness under paralysis
Dexmedetomidine causes malignant hyperthermia with rocuronium
There is no concern because dexmedetomidine is a complete anesthetic

Dexmedetomidine gives light, rousable sedation and does not reliably provide the deep sedation a paralyzed patient needs. Awareness under paralysis is a listed serious risk of rocuronium, so deep sedation and analgesia must be in place.
q1voh1fj: After ROSC from VF, a 70-year-old is in complete heart block with a ventricular rate of 38, BP 78/40 and occasional PVCs. The referring team asks about an amiodarone infusion. What is the best response?
Withhold amiodarone and treat the bradycardia with pacing
Start amiodarone to suppress the PVCs
Give amiodarone 150 mg as a slow bolus only
Give amiodarone together with atropine to offset any slowing
Third-degree AV block without a pacemaker is a contraindication to amiodarone, which could suppress the escape rhythm. The priority is rate support with pacing or a chronotrope.
q7lcnyv: A patient on an amiodarone infusion for recurrent VT has BP 82/50 and sinus rhythm at 50 during transport. Before the infusion, BP was 118/70 and HR 82. What is the best next step?
Stop the amiodarone and notify medical control
Speed up the infusion to finish the dose
Continue unchanged since the VT is now suppressed
Hypotension and bradycardia are stop criteria for amiodarone. Continuing or re-bolusing makes both worse; stop the drip and discuss next steps.
q8h294d: An 82-year-old with heart failure has been on a lidocaine infusion for 12 hours after VT. During transfer he reports perioral numbness and ringing in the ears, then becomes confused with muscle twitching. What is the best action?
Stop the lidocaine and prepare to treat seizures
Give a lidocaine bolus to treat the twitching
Continue the infusion and recheck in an hour
Switch to a higher lidocaine infusion rate
These are lidocaine toxicity signs, and heart failure plus older age reduce clearance. Stopping the drug and being ready for seizures is correct; more lidocaine would worsen CNS toxicity.
q7ruzb4: An intubated septic patient has pH 7.08, PaCO2 64 and HCO3 18. The ventilator is set to a low minute ventilation from the referring hospital. The referring physician suggests sodium bicarbonate. What should happen first?
Increase minute ventilation to clear CO2
Give bicarbonate now and leave the vent alone
Give bicarbonate and lower the respiratory rate
Inadequate ventilation is a contraindication to bicarbonate, which makes CO2 that must be exhaled. The acidosis here is largely respiratory, so fixing ventilation comes first.
q1vpe30j: A patient with acute pulmonary edema is on a nitroglycerin infusion. During transport, BP falls from 168/96 to 86/50, HR rises to 118, the skin becomes cool and mottled, and crackles persist. What is the best change?
Stop the nitroglycerin and start inotropic or pressor support
Keep the nitroglycerin and give furosemide
Increase the nitroglycerin to reduce preload and congestion further
An SBP under 90 is a stop criterion for nitroglycerin. With poor perfusion and crackles, this has turned into cardiogenic shock and needs support of BP and output, not more preload reduction.
q1ouywx1: A septic patient has received several liters of fluid. MAP is 58 on low-dose norepinephrine, SpO2 is 90% and new crackles are present. The referring team suggests furosemide. What is the best response?
Hold furosemide and titrate the vasopressor up
Give furosemide now to treat the crackles
Give furosemide and another fluid bolus together
Give furosemide and stop the norepinephrine
Furosemide is held in hypotension because diuresis worsens perfusion. Raising the pressor supports MAP without more fluid; any diuresis can wait until the shock improves.
q13jh07z: A septic patient has sinus tachycardia at 138 with MAP 62 on norepinephrine and a lactate of 5. A crewmember suggests esmolol to slow the HR. What is the best decision?
Withhold esmolol; the tachycardia is compensatory
Start esmolol to reduce myocardial oxygen use
Give esmolol as a bolus only with no infusion
Start esmolol and add phenylephrine to cover any BP drop
Sinus tachycardia in shock maintains cardiac output, and esmolol causes hypotension, a stop criterion. Treat the shock, not the heart rate.
qqx193g: A 76-year-old with a spontaneous ICH has SBP 186. The transfer orders call for a nicardipine infusion. Her chart shows advanced aortic stenosis. What is the best action?
Clarify the order since advanced AS is a contraindication
Start nicardipine at the maximum rate
Start nicardipine with a fluid bolus
Give nicardipine and add phenylephrine if the BP drops too low
Advanced aortic stenosis is a listed contraindication to nicardipine because fixed outflow cannot compensate for the drop in afterload. Clarify and pick an agent that fits her physiology.
qc1pbq6: A 66-year-old with NSTEMI is on a heparin infusion during transfer. Mid-flight he reports a sudden severe headache and then develops left arm weakness. What is the best first action?
Stop the heparin and notify the receiving team
Bolus heparin to treat a possible new clot
Lower heparin by half and keep watching
Give aspirin for a possible embolic stroke and continue heparin
A new neuro change on heparin suggests intracranial bleeding, which is a stop criterion. More anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy could be fatal.
qp4g8ak: A teenager in DKA is on an insulin infusion during transfer. A repeat potassium mid-flight is 3.1 mEq/L, and the patient has new PVCs. What is the best action?
Hold insulin and replace potassium per protocol
Keep insulin running and recheck in 2 hours
Double the insulin to close the gap faster
Give sodium bicarbonate to raise potassium
Potassium under 3.3 is a stop criterion for insulin, which drives potassium into cells and can cause dysrhythmias. Replace potassium first, then resume insulin.
qqk1kod: A post-arrest patient with GCS 3 starts bucking the ventilator with HR 132 and BP 172/96. The crew gives vecuronium only, saying he is comatose and needs no sedation. What is the main problem?
He may be aware under paralysis without sedation
Vecuronium is unsafe in post-arrest patients
Vecuronium will raise his potassium sharply
Bucking proves he has no meaningful brain function left
A rising HR and BP while bucking suggest arousal, and paralysis hides both comfort and seizure signs. Awareness under paralysis is a listed serious risk, so sedation and analgesia must be given.
q1fj06l0: A dialysis patient has ROSC after a brief arrest. During transfer, the QRS widens to 160 ms with peaked T waves. K is 7.4 mEq/L, and a central line is in place. What is the best first drug?
Calcium chloride slowly via the central line
Sodium bicarbonate alone with no calcium given first
Calcium stabilizes the heart in hyperkalemia within minutes, and a central line suits calcium chloride, which can cause necrosis if it leaks. Antiarrhythmics do not address the cause.
qpf1zjl: A 4-year-old with septic shock gets a second dose of succinylcholine after a failed first attempt. HR drops from 140 to 66 with delayed capillary refill. SpO2 is 97% with good BVM ventilation. What is the best next step?
Give atropine IV per PALS dosing
Give amiodarone for the slow rhythm
Give more succinylcholine to finish the attempt

A repeat succinylcholine dose in a child commonly causes vagal bradycardia, and with oxygenation and ventilation confirmed, atropine treats it. Compressions are indicated only if HR falls below 60 with poor perfusion despite effective ventilation.
qdbxa8m: A 32-year-old ejected from a vehicle 50 minutes ago has HR 128, BP 84/52 and a positive FAST. The ground crew gave TXA 1 g IV over 10 minutes just before handoff. What should the flight crew do with TXA now?
Start the second 1 g as an infusion over 8 hours
Push a second 1 g bolus now because he is still hypotensive
Stop TXA because the BP did not improve after the bolus
Hold further TXA until a fibrinogen level is available

Per CRASH-2 based protocols the 1 g load over 10 minutes is followed by 1 g over 8 hours. TXA is antifibrinolytic, not a pressor, so persistent hypotension is not a reason to stop it or to push another rapid bolus (rapid push causes hypotension).
q1mrtcr2: A 54-year-old with a sudden worst-ever headache has GCS 13 and BP 168/94. CT at the sending hospital shows a nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage. A resident asks the crew to start TXA in flight to prevent rebleeding. What is the best response?
Withhold TXA; SAH is a contraindication
Give 1 g over 10 minutes since he is within 3 hours of onset
Give 2 g as a single bolus per the trauma protocol
Give TXA only if the BP rises above 180 systolic
Subarachnoid hemorrhage is a contraindication to TXA, and the 3-hour window applies to trauma, not to this indication. BP control and rapid transport to neurosurgery are the priorities.
qzwcrks: A 25-kg 7-year-old struck by a car 40 minutes ago has HR 150, BP 78/40 and capillary refill of 4 seconds. Your pediatric trauma protocol includes TXA. Which loading dose fits?
375 mg IV over 10 minutes, then 2 mg/kg/h
1 g IV over 10 minutes, the same as an adult
250 mg IV push over 1 minute, then stop
2 g IV single bolus per the adult alternative
Pediatric trauma protocols use 15 mg/kg over 10 minutes (max 1 g), here 375 mg, followed by 2 mg/kg/h. The adult 1 g or 2 g doses overshoot a 25-kg child, and a rapid push risks hypotension.
q17lfwk5: Forty-five minutes into a TXA maintenance infusion, a trauma patient without head injury has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Glucose is 112 and SpO2 is 97%. What is the best interpretation and action?
A known TXA adverse effect; stop it and treat the seizure
This is expected with TXA; continue the infusion and observe
The seizure means occult head injury; double the TXA rate
Seizures signal under-dosing; give an extra 1 g bolus

Seizures are a listed serious adverse effect of TXA, so the infusion is stopped, the seizure treated, and medical control informed. Assuming it is unrelated and continuing, or giving more TXA, ignores a known drug toxicity.
q12pezfc: A dialysis patient with K 7.2 had a QRS of 160 ms. After calcium gluconate the QRS narrows to 110 ms and peaked T waves persist. What is the most important next step?
Shift potassium into cells with insulin and dextrose
Stop treatment because the ECG has improved
Repeat calcium until the T waves normalize
Give furosemide to remove the potassium through the kidneys

Calcium only stabilizes the cardiac membrane for a short time and does not lower potassium, so a shifting agent such as insulin with dextrose is next. Furosemide is not useful in an anuric dialysis patient.
q18dxm3f: A 20-kg child with renal failure has K 7.4, peaked T waves and a widening QRS. Per PALS, which calcium gluconate dose is appropriate?
3 g IV push regardless of weight

PALS calcium gluconate for hyperkalemia is 60 mg/kg (max 3 g), 1.2 g for 20 kg. The tempting 20 mg/kg figure is the calcium chloride dose, which contains about three times more elemental calcium per gram.
qlqo24s: A 41-year-old industrial worker splashed hydrofluoric acid on two fingers. The skin looks almost normal, but he reports severe pain out of proportion to the findings. After copious irrigation, what is the best next treatment?
Apply calcium gluconate topically to the burn
Apply silver-based burn dressing and reassess later
Give morphine only, since the skin is intact
Neutralize the area with sodium bicarbonate
Fluoride ions bind calcium and cause deep tissue injury with pain out of proportion; topical calcium gluconate binds fluoride. Opioids alone treat the symptom but not the ongoing chemical injury.
q18jmjnf: A 66-year-old with K 7.3 and a QRS of 150 ms is getting calcium chloride 1 g by slow push through a forearm IV. Halfway through, the site becomes swollen, pale and painful. The QRS has narrowed to 124 ms. What is the best action?
Stop the push at that site and give the rest through new access
Finish the push quickly since the QRS is improving
Flush the IV briskly with saline to dilute the calcium
Give the remaining calcium chloride IM in the thigh

Extravasation is a stop point for calcium chloride, which causes tissue necrosis, but the hyperkalemia still needs membrane stabilization, so the dose is completed through a new, reliable large vein. Pushing more drug or fluid into the infiltrated site worsens the injury, and calcium chloride is not given IM.
qosr0j8: A 60-year-old with a verapamil overdose has HR 40 and BP 72/40. After calcium chloride 1 g IV the BP rises to 90/56, then falls back to 74/42 fifteen minutes later. What is the best next step?
Repeat calcium chloride; its effect is often brief
Conclude calcium has failed and do not give more
Give a fluid bolus only and recheck in 30 minutes
Switch to calcium gluconate because chloride failed

In calcium channel blocker overdose, calcium is given as 1-2 g every 10-20 minutes because the response is often transient. A temporary response shows benefit, not failure, and switching salts adds nothing.
q19ipjv6: A 34-week preeclamptic patient is on magnesium 2 g/h for transfer. Which new finding should prompt the crew to stop the infusion first?
Patellar reflexes that were present are now absent
Facial flushing and a sensation of warmth after the bolus
BP 152/98, unchanged from the last reading
Loss of deep tendon reflexes is an early sign of magnesium toxicity and appears before respiratory depression; it is a listed stop point. Flushing, warmth and nausea are common expected effects.
q15iy5h3: A 30-week patient with severe preeclampsia has been on magnesium 2 g/h for 3 hours after a full load. Mid-flight she has a second eclamptic seizure. Reflexes were present and RR was 16 just before. What is the best next action?
Protect the airway; give another magnesium bolus per protocol
Stop magnesium since it has clearly failed, and give phenytoin instead
Give hydralazine first, then reassess the seizure
Double the magnesium infusion and wait 1 hour

Recurrent eclamptic seizures on maintenance therapy are treated with an additional magnesium bolus per protocol while supporting the airway, with toxicity checks afterward. Magnesium is not abandoned for phenytoin, and an antihypertensive does not stop a seizure.
qphv5d0: A 30-kg 9-year-old with severe asthma has poor air movement and SpO2 89% despite continuous albuterol, ipratropium and steroids. Which magnesium dose is appropriate?
Pediatric magnesium for asthma is 25-50 mg/kg IV over 15-30 minutes (max 2 g), here 750-1,500 mg. The 4 g dose is an eclampsia load, and a rapid push risks hypotension and bradycardia.
qvjxclc: A 36-week patient with severe preeclampsia is about to receive magnesium for seizure prophylaxis. Which history finding most changes the plan?
Known third-degree heart block without a pacemaker
Prior cesarean section two years ago
Mild intermittent asthma with no attacks in the last several years

Heart block is a listed contraindication to magnesium, which slows AV conduction, so this needs a different plan with medical control. Diabetes, prior surgery and asthma do not contraindicate magnesium.
q50nwa0: After a field delivery of one infant, the mother's abdomen stays distended, the fundus is well above the umbilicus and fetal parts are palpable. Bleeding is moderate and the placenta has not delivered. A partner draws up oxytocin 10 units IM. What is the best action?
Withhold oxytocin until a second fetus is ruled out
Give it now since bleeding is the top priority
Give it IV instead of IM for a faster effect
Give half the dose to reduce the uterine response and the bleeding

A possible second twin is a listed contraindication; oxytocin could contract the uterus around an undelivered infant. A fundus well above the umbilicus with palpable fetal parts after one birth suggests another fetus, so it must be excluded first.
q1mfahd7: A patient with postpartum hemorrhage has a boggy uterus after placental delivery. HR is 122 and BP 92/58. Two IV attempts have failed and the IO is not yet placed. What is the best oxytocin decision?
Give 10 units IM now while vascular access continues
Wait for IO access and then push 10 units IV
Hold oxytocin until a second IV line is placed
Give 40 units IM so it matches the amount placed in an IV infusion bag

Oxytocin 10 units IM is an accepted PPH route and should not be delayed for access. An IV push risks hypotension and tachycardia, and 40 units is the amount mixed into an infusion bag, not an IM dose.
qqf8yuq: Ten minutes after carboprost 250 mcg IM for atony, a patient with no known asthma develops wheezing, RR 30 and SpO2 dropping from 97% to 88%. What is the best next action?
Stop further carboprost and treat the bronchospasm
Give the next carboprost dose now since bleeding control comes first
Give oxytocin IV push to replace carboprost
Assume amniotic fluid embolism and start CPR
Bronchospasm and hypoxemia are listed stop points for carboprost, even without an asthma history. Treating the airway takes priority over repeating a drug that is causing it.
q19uio3d: Twenty minutes after methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM for atony, a postpartum patient has crushing chest pain and BP 174/110. HR is 96. What is the best next action?
Stop further doses; treat as coronary vasospasm
Repeat the dose because bleeding has slowed
Give oxytocin IV push to reverse the effect
Reassure her; this is expected uterine cramping
Chest pain and severe hypertension are listed stop criteria; methylergonovine can cause coronary vasospasm. Repeating the dose or dismissing the pain as cramping misses a serious adverse effect.
q1rppcnq: A patient with PPH from atony is vomiting repeatedly and cannot hold anything in her mouth. Oxytocin is running. Which misoprostol route fits best per ACOG/WHO?
250 mcg deep IM, repeat in 15 minutes
Rectal misoprostol 800-1,000 mcg avoids the oral route in a vomiting patient. Misoprostol has no IV form, 200 mcg QID is the ulcer dose, and 250 mcg IM is carboprost.
q16wzqsm: A 66-year-old being transferred for a large PE has HR 112 and BP 118/76. The chart notes heparin-induced thrombocytopenia 18 months ago. The sending order is a heparin bolus and infusion. What is the best action?
Withhold heparin and request a non-heparin anticoagulant
Give heparin since HIT more than a year ago no longer matters
Give a half-dose heparin bolus and watch platelets
Give heparin SQ instead of IV to lower the risk
A history of HIT is a listed contraindication to heparin, and a lower dose or a different route does not remove that risk. Medical control should order an alternative anticoagulant.
q1n754ik: Two hours after a femoral cardiac catheterization, a patient on a heparin infusion during transfer develops a firm, enlarging groin swelling. HR has risen from 78 to 112 and BP has fallen from 132/80 to 96/60. What is the best first action?
Stop the heparin and hold firm pressure above the puncture site
Increase the heparin to prevent a clot at the puncture site
Give a fluid bolus and keep the heparin running unchanged
Apply ice to the groin and recheck the vitals in 30 minutes

An expanding hematoma with rising HR and falling BP is active bleeding, a stop point for heparin, and manual pressure just above the arterial puncture controls the source. Giving fluid while the anticoagulant keeps running treats the numbers, not the bleed.
q1obz691: A 90-kg patient with NSTEMI needs heparin started for transfer per the ACC/AHA ACS regimen. What initial dosing is correct?
The ACS regimen is 60 units/kg (max 4,000) then 12 units/kg/h (max 1,000/h), so both values are capped for a 90-kg patient. 5,400 units ignores the caps, and 7,200 units uses the VTE nomogram.
q5blabv: Forty minutes into an alteplase infusion for ischemic stroke, the patient reports a sudden severe headache, vomits, and her NIHSS rises by 6 points. What is the best immediate action?
Stop the infusion; treat as intracranial hemorrhage
Give ondansetron and continue the infusion
Slow the infusion rate by half and recheck in 15 minutes
Finish the infusion since only 20 minutes remain
