Opioids should be secured and disposed of through take-back programs to prevent misuse and accidental ingestion.
q11sgiul: How should the nurse teach a client to take an ondansetron orally disintegrating tablet?
With dry hands, place it on the tongue to dissolve
Push it through the foil and swallow it whole with water
Crush it and mix it into a full glass of juice
Chew it well and follow it with an antacid
Peel back the foil with dry hands and let the tablet dissolve on the tongue, then swallow.
qfv2rat: A client going home on lactulose asks how to tell if the dose is right. The nurse explains that the usual goal is:
Two to three soft stools each day
One firm stool every 2 to 3 days
Six or more liquid stools every day
No stools until any confusion clears
Lactulose is titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools daily to lower ammonia without dehydration.
q1ufv92h: A client receiving cyclophosphamide should be taught to:
Drink plenty of fluids and empty the bladder often
Limit fluids to prevent swelling in the legs
Take the dose at bedtime and hold urine overnight
Avoid all fruit juices for the length of treatment
Hydration and frequent voiding help prevent hemorrhagic cystitis.
qr4dm94: A client receiving chemotherapy asks about handling body fluids at home for 48 hours after treatment. The nurse teaches:
Wear gloves for cleanup and flush twice with the lid down
Wash soiled laundry with the family's clothes in cold water
Clean the toilet with bleach once a week during treatment
No special precautions are needed once the client is home
Chemotherapy is excreted in body fluids; gloves, closed-lid double flushing, and separate laundry reduce exposure.
q1tefowx: A client with gestational diabetes receives betamethasone for preterm labor. The nurse teaches that she should expect:
Higher blood glucose for several days
Low blood glucose for a week, needing extra snacks
No change in blood glucose from this medication
Contractions to stop within 24 hours of the dose
Corticosteroids raise blood glucose for several days, so more frequent checks and insulin changes may be needed.
qvum1w6: A client is discharged on oral vancomycin for C. difficile infection. The nurse teaches:
It acts in the gut, so finish the full course even if stools improve
It is well absorbed, so kidney levels must be checked each week
Take it only on the days when the stools are still loose or watery
Take loperamide along with each dose to stop the diarrhea much faster
Oral vancomycin is poorly absorbed and works in the colon; antidiarrheals are avoided with C. difficile.
q1c4wtfp: Which instruction should the nurse give a client discharged on oral methylergonovine?
Report chest pain, headache, or cold, numb fingers
Expect bright red bleeding to increase each day
Take an extra dose whenever cramping feels strong
Stop the medication if the uterus feels firm
Methylergonovine causes vasoconstriction; chest pain, severe headache, or numb fingers suggest serious toxicity.
q1n1a21p: A client is starting haloperidol decanoate IM injections. Which teaching is correct?
It is given about every 4 weeks, so keep each appointment
It acts only on the day it is given and must be given daily
It must be stopped as soon as any thirst occurs
It can be stopped by skipping shots when feeling well
The decanoate form is a long-acting depot usually given every 4 weeks.
q1d5b5pc: A client discharged on lorazepam for anxiety should be taught to:
Avoid alcohol and not stop the drug suddenly
Take an extra dose before driving long distances
Stop the drug abruptly once the anxiety improves
Drink a glass of wine at night to help it work
Alcohol adds to CNS depression, and abrupt stopping can cause withdrawal and seizures.
q10d5xbd: Before starting infliximab, a client asks why a tuberculosis test was done. The nurse explains:
The drug can reactivate latent tuberculosis
The drug is used to cure latent tuberculosis
TB testing is required before all IV drugs
The test checks for an allergy to the drug
TNF blockers suppress immunity and can reactivate latent TB, so screening is required.
q1bn99mr: A client taking ciprofloxacin also takes a calcium supplement and antacids. The nurse teaches the client to:
Take ciprofloxacin 2 hours before or 6 hours after them
Take all of them together with breakfast each morning
Stop the calcium supplement permanently and switch to vitamin D
Take ciprofloxacin with a glass of milk
Calcium, magnesium, aluminum, and iron bind fluoroquinolones and reduce absorption.
q1bozgxv: A client taking lithium is newly prescribed hydrochlorothiazide. The nurse anticipates:
Closer monitoring of lithium levels for toxicity
A need to raise the lithium dose to keep it working
No effect, since they act on different organs
A fall in lithium levels below the target range
Thiazides reduce lithium clearance and can raise levels into the toxic range.
q1frpit3: A client taking warfarin is prescribed metronidazole. The nurse expects:
Closer INR checks, because bleeding risk rises
A lower INR, needing a larger warfarin dose each day
No interaction between these two drugs
The warfarin to be stopped permanently
Metronidazole inhibits warfarin metabolism and raises the INR.
q9j819e: A client taking sertraline asks about adding St. John's wort for mood. The nurse explains the combination may cause:
St. John's wort has serotonergic activity and adds to the effects of SSRIs.
qt2i0vx: A client taking phenelzine asks about a cold medicine that contains pseudoephedrine. The nurse explains:
It may cause a dangerous rise in blood pressure
It is safe if it is taken with plenty of water
It will make the phenelzine work faster
It is safe as long as it is taken at bedtime
Sympathomimetic decongestants can trigger hypertensive crisis with MAO inhibitors.
qm7f5uz: A client taking oxycodone asks about also taking lorazepam for sleep. The nurse knows this combination increases the risk of:
Severe hypertension and pounding morning headaches
Kidney damage and high serum potassium
Opioids with benzodiazepines carry a boxed warning for respiratory depression and death.
q1vjgnsf: A woman taking phenytoin also uses an oral contraceptive. The nurse reinforces that phenytoin may:
Make the birth control less effective
Make the birth control work much better
Cause the pill to raise phenytoin to toxic levels
Have no effect at all on birth control pills
Phenytoin induces liver enzymes and lowers hormone levels, so a backup or alternate method is advised.
qo08puo: An older adult taking promethazine is also ordered oxycodone. The nurse should monitor for:
Increased pain from a weaker opioid effect
Promethazine adds to opioid CNS and respiratory depression.
q7p31yr: For which client should the nurse question an order for IV ceftriaxone with an IV calcium-containing solution?
A neonate, because of fatal precipitates
An adult, because calcium inactivates it
An older adult, because of heart block
A client who had a penicillin rash as a child
Ceftriaxone and calcium can form fatal precipitates in neonates and must not be given together to them.
q108l0wu: A client receiving gentamicin is ordered IV furosemide. The nurse should monitor closely for:
Lower gentamicin levels and treatment failure
Loop diuretics add to aminoglycoside ear and kidney toxicity.
q1i7gx60: A client stable on valproic acid is started on IV meropenem. The nurse should anticipate:
A sharp drop in valproate levels and a seizure risk
A toxic rise in valproate levels within a day
Increased meropenem levels causing acute kidney injury
No interaction between these two medications
Carbapenems rapidly lower valproate levels, and the combination is generally avoided.
q1gqrv4x: A client taking escitalopram is ordered IV linezolid. The nurse should monitor for:
Linezolid is a weak MAO inhibitor and can cause serotonin syndrome with SSRIs.
q1lqmvo2: A client is ordered IV ondansetron and IV haloperidol. The nurse is most concerned about:
A weaker antiemetic effect from both
A higher risk of serious hypoglycemia
Both drugs prolong the QT interval; ECG and electrolytes are monitored.
qhksz1w: A client taking clozapine stops smoking during hospitalization. The nurse should monitor for:
Rising clozapine levels with sedation or seizures
Falling clozapine levels and return of psychosis
Nicotine withdrawal causing low blood pressure
No change, as smoking does not affect clozapine levels
Smoking induces CYP1A2; quitting can raise clozapine levels sharply.
q1tkej3a: A transplant client taking tacrolimus is started on fluconazole. The nurse anticipates:
Higher tacrolimus levels needing closer checks
Lower tacrolimus levels and a higher rejection risk
No interaction that requires any monitoring
A need to stop fluconazole after the first dose
Azole antifungals inhibit CYP3A4 and raise tacrolimus levels, increasing kidney and nerve toxicity.
qztduno: Which finding in a client taking quetiapine should the nurse report to the provider?
New fainting spells when standing up
Mild dry mouth in the morning hours
Mild drowsiness after the bedtime dose
A slight increase in appetite at meals
Fainting suggests significant orthostatic hypotension and fall risk; the others are common and expected.
qqlukcc: A client took about 15 grams of acetaminophen 8 hours ago and feels fine, with normal vital signs. What should the nurse report to the provider?
The time and amount taken, since injury appears later
That no treatment is needed because she has no symptoms
That a stomach washout should be arranged before labs
That she should be watched at home and seen in a week

Acetaminophen overdose has a quiet first day, with enzyme rises and jaundice appearing 24 to 72 hours later. Acetylcysteine works best within 8 to 10 hours, so the history and a 4-hour level drive care, not how she looks.
q15xa1ha: Which finding should a client taking metronidazole report to the provider promptly?
Numbness or tingling in the hands or feet
A metallic taste in the mouth after doses
Urine that looks darker than usual
Mild nausea after taking the tablets
Metronidazole can cause peripheral neuropathy and other neurotoxicity; dark urine and metallic taste are harmless.
qptmgsd: Ten minutes after an IM ceftriaxone injection, a client develops hives and wheezing. The nurse should first:
Call for help and start the anaphylaxis protocol
Apply ice to the injection site and observe
Give oral diphenhydramine and recheck in an hour
Document it as an expected reaction to the drug
Hives with wheezing suggest anaphylaxis, which requires emergency response and provider notification.
qd9idts: Which finding in a client taking phenytoin should be reported right away?
A new widespread rash with blisters
Mild gum overgrowth noticed at a dental visit
Slight drowsiness during the first week
A blistering rash may signal Stevens-Johnson syndrome; phenytoin can harmlessly tint urine.
q13753nk: Four clients have ketorolac ordered after surgery. Which client's order should the nurse report to the provider before giving it?
A client 2 days after coronary artery bypass surgery
A client who is 68 years old and weighs about 62 kilograms
A client who takes pantoprazole 40 mg every morning
A client 1 day after a total knee replacement

Ketorolac is contraindicated after coronary artery bypass surgery, because NSAIDs raise the risk of thrombotic events and bleeding in that setting. Age, a proton pump inhibitor and orthopedic surgery do not bar its use.
q1hi0p5n: A client on clozapine reports no bowel movement for 5 days with abdominal pain and distention. Why does the nurse report this at once?
Clozapine slows the gut and can cause a fatal ileus
Clozapine is held whenever any constipation is present
Constipation means the clozapine level has become toxic
Constipation is an early sign of clozapine neutropenia
Clozapine has strong anticholinergic effects on gut motility, and severe constipation can progress to ileus, bowel ischemia and death, so it is treated as urgent rather than routine.
q9u37nw: A client in septic shock on norepinephrine has MAP 68, cold mottled toes, lactate risen from 2.8 to 4.6, and urine output 15 mL/hr. What should the nurse report?
That perfusion is poor though the MAP is at goal
That the MAP goal should be raised to 85 mm Hg instead
That the mottling is the expected effect of the drug
That the urine output needs a dose of furosemide now
A MAP at target does not prove the tissues are perfused, and a rising lactate with mottling and oliguria suggests the client needs volume or another intervention rather than only a higher pressure.
qygwaig: A client on magnesium sulfate has absent reflexes and a respiratory rate of 9, and the infusion has been stopped. What should the nurse have ready?
Calcium gluconate 1 g IV over 10 minutes
Calcium chloride 1 g by rapid IV push now
Potassium chloride 10 mEq IV over 1 hour
Sodium bicarbonate 50 mEq by IV push now

Calcium directly antagonizes magnesium at the neuromuscular junction, and 1 g of calcium gluconate given slowly IV is the usual reversal order. Calcium chloride is far more irritating peripherally and is kept for codes.
q16e2ze9: After delivery, a client on an oxytocin infusion has a boggy uterus that does not firm with massage and soaks a pad every 15 minutes. The nurse should:
Notify the provider and prepare other uterotonic drugs
Stop the oxytocin and offer oral fluids
Let the client rest and recheck in 1 hour
Place the client in high Fowler position and keep her on bed rest
Persistent atony with heavy bleeding is postpartum hemorrhage; drugs such as methylergonovine or carboprost may be needed.
q2bz57a: A client receiving IV levofloxacin suddenly reports severe chest pain radiating to the back. The nurse notifies the provider immediately because this drug is linked with:
Fluoroquinolones increase the risk of aortic aneurysm and dissection.
qybdcho: A client on weekly methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis has a new prescription. Which one should the nurse report before it is filled?
Calcium carbonate 500 mg twice daily with meals
Loratadine 10 mg daily for seasonal allergies
Levothyroxine 75 mcg each morning before food
Trimethoprim is itself an antifolate and also slows methotrexate clearance, so the pair can cause severe bone marrow suppression and mucositis. The other three do not interact with methotrexate.
qrfe9v7: A client's first fentanyl patch was applied 4 hours ago, and he reports the pain is no better. What should the nurse report and expect?
That the patch needs 12 to 24 hours for full effect
That the patch has failed and a second one is needed now
That a heating pad over the patch will speed absorption
That the patch should be cut in half to adjust the dose
Transdermal fentanyl forms a depot in the skin, so analgesia builds over 12 to 24 hours and short-acting opioids cover the gap. Heat raises absorption unpredictably, and patches are not cut.
qkl5w4b: A client on a nitroglycerin infusion still has chest pain of 6/10 at the maximum ordered rate. The nurse should:
Notify the provider of the ongoing chest pain
Stop the infusion and give oral acetaminophen
Keep titrating above the ordered maximum rate
Document the pain and reassess in 2 hours
Unrelieved chest pain may signal ongoing ischemia and needs prompt evaluation.
q1w1n677: A client on IV vancomycin for cellulitis has a new order for piperacillin-tazobactam. What should the nurse monitor and report?
A rising creatinine, since this pair injures kidneys
A falling platelet count from marrow suppression by the two drugs
A prolonged QT interval from the combined antibiotic effect
A rising serum potassium from tubular blockade by the pair
Vancomycin with piperacillin-tazobactam carries a higher rate of acute kidney injury than vancomycin with cefepime or meropenem, so daily creatinine and drug levels are followed closely.
q1div73r: A resident takes furosemide every morning. Which change should the CNA report to the nurse?
A weight gain of 3 pounds since yesterday
That the resident ate all of breakfast
That the resident watched television all morning
Furosemide is a water pill. A sudden weight gain can mean fluid is building up, which the nurse needs to know about.
qep4wjr: A resident's furosemide is ordered twice a day, and the second dose is given at bedtime. She is up all night to the bathroom. What should the CNA report?
That the bedtime dose has her up all night
That she should drink nothing after her evening meal
That the dose should be moved to the early morning
That she needs a bedpan instead of walking at night

Furosemide starts working within an hour and keeps working about 6 hours, so a late dose breaks up sleep and raises the fall risk. The CNA describes what is happening; changing the schedule is a provider decision.
q1j776ve: A resident takes levothyroxine. When is it usually given?
On an empty stomach in the morning, before breakfast
Crushed into applesauce at bedtime with her other pills
With her biggest meal of the day at dinner time
Only on the days the resident feels tired
Levothyroxine is absorbed best on an empty stomach, usually 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast.
qaw5rna: A resident on warfarin has started eating a large spinach salad every day. What should the CNA tell the nurse?
The new daily salad, since greens affect warfarin
That the resident should stop eating all green vegetables now
That the salad is a healthy choice and needs no comment
That the resident needs a double portion of her warfarin
Vitamin K in leafy greens works against warfarin, so a big change in how much is eaten moves the INR. A steady amount is the goal, which is why the change is reported rather than the food banned.
q14qg3id: A resident gets insulin glargine at 2100 each night and insulin lispro with meals. She refuses her dinner tray. Which insulin should the CNA ask the nurse about?
The mealtime lispro, since she is not eating the meal
The bedtime glargine, since she is not eating the meal
Both insulins, since neither is given without a meal
Neither insulin, since one refused meal does not matter
Lispro is given to cover the carbohydrate in a meal, so a refused tray changes that dose. Glargine is a background insulin with no peak and is given on its own schedule whether or not she eats.
queuo82: A resident on metformin is going for a scan with contrast dye tomorrow. What should the CNA do with this information?
Make sure the nurse knows about the scan
Nothing; scans do not affect medications
Tell the resident to skip breakfast
Metformin and contrast dye can interact. The CNA passes along the information; the nurse and provider decide.
q7b6p2e: A resident takes docusate daily. What should the CNA record and report?
Bowel movements and any abdominal discomfort
A blood pressure reading every hour of the shift
How much television the resident watches
Only the resident's weight each morning
Docusate is a stool softener. Tracking bowel movements tells the nurse whether it is working.
q1wiwg88: A resident has been on 3 liters of oxygen by nasal cannula for a week. Which finding should the CNA report to the nurse?
Raw, broken skin over the tops of both ears
A fine dry crust inside one nostril in the morning
The tubing lying across the resident's lap
A faint hissing sound from the cannula prongs

Tubing pressure behind the ears causes real skin breakdown that needs padding and a treatment plan. Dry nares, tubing position and the normal hiss of flowing oxygen are expected and handled in routine care.
qaaw36l: A resident asks the CNA for Tylenol for a headache at 1400. What information will the nurse most need from the CNA?
What time the resident last had a dose of Tylenol
Whether the resident prefers tablets or the liquid form
Whether a family member has brought any Tylenol in
What the resident ate for lunch earlier that day

Acetaminophen has both a dosing interval and a daily ceiling near 4,000 mg, so the nurse needs to know when the last dose was given before another can be given. Food and tablet form do not change that.
qzd0inu: A resident takes low-dose aspirin daily. Which finding should the CNA report?
Black tarry stool can mean bleeding in the stomach, which aspirin makes more likely.
q1yzzz65: Four residents take lisinopril. Which finding should the CNA tell the nurse about first?
Swelling of the lips and tongue since breakfast
A dry tickly cough that started about a week ago
Dizziness for a moment when standing up quickly
A metallic taste noticed with the morning meal
Lip and tongue swelling can be angioedema, which can close the airway and is an emergency. The cough, brief dizziness and taste change are known effects that are reported but are not urgent.
qzs3i9w: A resident who takes a daily senna tablet now has frequent small liquid stools and a hard, distended abdomen. What should the CNA report?
The liquid stools with the hard abdomen
That the senna dose is working well at last
That the resident needs an extra senna tablet
That a bedside commode should be set up now

Liquid stool leaking around a hard mass of stool is a sign of impaction, not of a laxative working, and more stimulant laxative can be harmful. The CNA describes both findings so the nurse can assess.
qgmi6ig: A resident takes omeprazole. What is it usually for?
Omeprazole reduces stomach acid and is used for reflux and ulcers.
q1o9kkeu: A resident on atorvastatin reports muscle aches. Which added detail most needs to reach the nurse?
Her urine has looked dark brown since yesterday
The aching is worse after her physical therapy
The aching is in her right shoulder joint only
She takes the pill at night and not in the morning

Dark brown urine with muscle pain suggests rhabdomyolysis, where muscle breakdown products reach the kidneys, and it needs a CK and creatinine the same day. Exercise soreness, joint pain and evening dosing are not that picture.
qsaqro0: The nurse asks the CNA for a pulse before a resident's metoprolol. Which report is most useful to the nurse?
A radial pulse of 48, counted a full minute, regular
A pulse of about 50, counted 15 seconds and timed four
A pulse that felt slow but was hard to count exactly
A pulse of 48 taken 2 hours ago before she walked

Metoprolol is usually held for a rate under 50 to 60, so the nurse needs a rate counted for a full minute and taken now. A 15-second count magnifies error, and an old or vague number cannot support the decision.
q2szeel: A resident had her mealtime insulin lispro at 0800 with breakfast. When should the CNA watch most closely for signs of low blood sugar?
Right at 0800 as it is injected
Only if a meal is skipped entirely
Lispro starts in about 15 minutes and peaks around 1 to 2 hours, so the risk window is mid-morning. A low sugar can happen even when the resident ate, which is why that window is watched.
qt5gil1: A resident on a water pill is weighed daily. Why?
Weight changes show whether fluid is building up or being lost
It is required for the facility's monthly billing and audit records
It tracks how much food the resident is eating each day
It helps staff choose the right size of wheelchair
Daily weights are the simplest way to follow fluid changes on a diuretic.
q1jim9y2: A resident takes a potassium supplement. Which finding should the CNA report?
New muscle weakness or an irregular pulse
A normal appetite at every meal
Clear pale yellow urine all day
Potassium problems show up as muscle weakness and heart rhythm changes.
qgg1glj: A resident with dementia takes donepezil. What should the CNA watch for and report?
Nausea, vomiting or a slow pulse
A rash on the soles of the feet
A gain in her standing height
Donepezil commonly causes stomach upset and can slow the heart rate.
q166srd6: A resident on an antipsychotic develops stiffness and a shuffling walk. The CNA should:
Report the new stiffness and walking change
Withhold the resident's meals until it settles
Encourage her to walk faster each day
Assume it is a normal part of aging
Movement changes on antipsychotics are reported promptly; they can become permanent.
q1jolrg9: A resident started allopurinol 3 weeks ago and now has a spreading rash, sore spots in her mouth, and a fever. Why is this urgent?
A rash with mouth sores and fever can be dangerous
Allopurinol rashes are always caused by an allergy to dye
A rash means the gout has spread into the skin
A fever with a rash means the dose is too low
Allopurinol is a common cause of severe skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and mouth involvement with fever marks the dangerous form. The drug is stopped, so the nurse is told at once.
qnbmymp: A resident takes prednisone daily. Which finding should the CNA report?
A new fever or any sign of infection
A good night of sleep every night
Steroids suppress the immune system, so signs of infection matter and may be subtle.
q138kryl: A resident on warfarin is scheduled for a dental cleaning. What should the CNA do?
Make sure the nurse knows about the appointment
Tell the dental office that it is fine
Hold the warfarin dose that morning
Bleeding risk with dental work is a nursing and provider decision; the CNA passes the information along.
q1n8ddfb: A resident uses oxygen at home from a concentrator. Which thing in his room should the CNA report as unsafe?
A petroleum jelly jar at the bedside for his lips
A cotton blanket folded at the foot of the bed
Water in the humidifier bottle on the concentrator
The concentrator placed about 2 feet away from the wall
Petroleum products on the face near oxygen are a fire hazard, and a water-based lubricant is used instead. A cotton blanket, humidifier water and clearance around the unit are all normal.
q1mzaf5v: A resident takes digoxin and furosemide. Which group of findings should the CNA bring to the nurse first?
Dry mouth, thirst, and pale colored urine
A sore throat, a stuffy nose, and sneezing
Mild ankle swelling by the end of the day

Nausea, loss of appetite and yellow-green visual changes are classic digoxin toxicity, and furosemide makes it more likely by lowering potassium. The other groups are common complaints and not signs of toxicity.
q5lqe4f: A resident with Parkinson disease takes her medicine on a strict schedule. Why does timing matter?
Late doses can leave her unable to move or swallow safely
It helps the kitchen plan her meal trays around the dose times
It reduces the monthly cost of her medicine at the pharmacy
It keeps the medicine from tasting bitter when she takes it
Parkinson medicines wear off, and a late dose can leave a resident frozen and at risk when eating or walking.
q1hdlgjh: A resident has two insulin pens in the refrigerator. One looks clear and one looks milky white. What should the CNA do?
Tell the nurse how each pen looks and give neither
Shake the milky pen until the liquid looks clear again
Throw out the milky pen because insulin should be clear
Warm the milky pen in her hands until it turns clear

NPH is a suspension and is normally cloudy, while glargine and the rapid-acting insulins are clear, so cloudiness alone does not mean a spoiled pen. Preparing insulin is a licensed task, so the CNA reports what is seen.
q1lp26r7: A resident on clopidogrel has bleeding gums after brushing. The CNA should:
Report it and use a soft toothbrush
Give the resident extra vitamin C
Brush harder to toughen the gums
Stop oral care entirely for now
Clopidogrel increases bleeding. Gentle oral care and reporting is the right approach.
q1jg0dxl: A resident takes alendronate for her bones. After the dose she should:
Stay upright for at least 30 minutes with a full glass of water
Take it with a large glass of milk at bedtime instead
Lie down flat for at least 30 minutes after the dose
Take it with all of her other pills at lunch time
Alendronate can injure the esophagus. Staying upright with plain water afterward is the key instruction.
qr6hoxd: A resident starting tamsulosin is at risk for what?
Dizziness and falls when standing up
Steady weight gain over several weeks
A rise in her blood sugar readings
Gradual hearing loss in both ears
Tamsulosin relaxes blood vessels as well as the prostate and commonly causes a drop in blood pressure on standing.
q1govjcu: The LVN is asked to give subcutaneous enoxaparin. Which technique is correct?
Give it in the abdominal fat, without expelling the air bubble from a prefilled syringe
Expel the air bubble from the prefilled syringe first, then inject into the abdominal fat
Inject it into the deltoid muscle at a 90-degree angle to the skin surface
Massage the injection site firmly afterward to help spread the dose
The air bubble in a prefilled enoxaparin syringe is intentional. The abdomen is the usual site, and rubbing increases bruising.
qvul3mg: An LVN notices a patient on long-term phenytoin has swollen, overgrown gums. This is:
A known effect of phenytoin that should be reported
A sign of an allergic reaction requiring epinephrine
A reason to double the dose
Gingival hyperplasia is a classic long-term effect of phenytoin and prompts dental care and a conversation with the provider.
q16yn0yf: A patient on lithium has been vomiting with diarrhea for two days. What is the concern?
Lithium levels can rise dangerously with fluid and sodium losses
The patient needs an extra lithium dose to make up for the losses
Nothing, since lithium levels are unaffected by hydration
Lithium will stop working entirely until she rehydrates
Lithium is handled by the kidney alongside sodium. Dehydration and sodium loss raise levels into the toxic range.
q1nw3v8c: What should the LVN reinforce with a patient starting metronidazole?
Avoid alcohol during treatment and for several days afterward
Stop taking it as soon as the symptoms start to improve a little
Take each dose with a full glass of grapefruit juice
Double the next dose if a dose is missed by mistake
Metronidazole with alcohol can cause a severe flushing, vomiting reaction.
qhgtpg4: Which instruction is correct for a patient taking oral iron?
It is absorbed better on an empty stomach, and stools may turn black
Black stool means internal bleeding and the drug should be stopped
Take it with a glass of milk for the best possible absorption
Take it with an antacid each time to protect the stomach
Iron absorbs best without food, though it may be taken with food if it upsets the stomach. Black stool is expected.
q1jvsi8u: A patient takes methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis. How is it usually dosed?
Once a week, not once a day
Daily dosing of weekly methotrexate is a well-known fatal medication error.
q52fgst: Which instruction fits a patient starting spironolactone?
Avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes unless the provider says otherwise
Use as much salt substitute on her food as she likes, since it holds no potassium at all
Take a daily potassium supplement alongside this new medicine to be safe
Avoid all green leafy vegetables and bananas while taking this medicine
Spironolactone keeps potassium in the body, and salt substitutes are usually potassium chloride.
qqkgoxe: An EMT is treating a 58-year-old with crushing chest pain. Which aspirin instruction is correct?
Have the patient chew 162 to 324 mg of non-enteric aspirin
Have the patient swallow one enteric-coated 81 mg tablet whole
Hold aspirin until a 12-lead is obtained
Chewing non-enteric aspirin gets it into the bloodstream fastest. Enteric coating delays absorption when minutes matter.
q110ef0i: Which patient with chest pain should an EMT not give aspirin to?
One with an active gastrointestinal bleed
One who takes a daily low-dose aspirin at home
One whose pain started three hours ago
Active bleeding is the contraindication. Age, prior aspirin use and symptom duration are not.
q1p3kmvh: An EMT finds a patient breathing 4 times a minute with pinpoint pupils. What comes first?
Open the airway and ventilate, then give naloxone
Give naloxone and wait for it to work
Place the patient in the recovery position and monitor
Opioid overdose kills through hypoventilation. Ventilation fixes the problem that is killing the patient; naloxone follows.
qcgk94s: After intranasal naloxone, a patient is awake and refusing transport. Which fact best supports the need to be seen at a hospital?
Naloxone lasts 30 to 90 minutes, less than most opioids
Naloxone has no effect at all on long-acting opioids
A second naloxone dose cannot be given outside the hospital
Naloxone causes a rebound overdose about an hour later
Naloxone wears off sooner than most opioids do, so breathing can slow again after the patient looks fine. It does work on long-acting opioids; it simply wears off well before they do.
q8tj3br: An EMT gives an epinephrine auto-injector for anaphylaxis. Where is it placed?
The outer mid-thigh, through clothing if needed
The upper arm muscle, with the sleeve rolled up first
The upper outer buttock, as for other injections
Under the tongue, held in place for a minute
The anterolateral thigh gives the fastest absorption and is the standard site.
qmvjb8i: A 10-year-old weighing 22 kg needs an epinephrine auto-injector for anaphylaxis. Which strength fits?
The junior auto-injector covers roughly 15 to 30 kg.
q1go942m: An EMT assists a patient with her own albuterol inhaler. What should be checked first?
That it is her prescription, it is in date, and she has not exceeded her prescribed doses
Her serum potassium level, because albuterol shifts potassium into the cells and lowers it
Her insurance details and whether the inhaler prescription was refilled this month
When she last ate, because the inhaler is absorbed through the stomach
Assisting with a patient's own medication means confirming it is theirs, current, and not already overused.
qrg4a3t: A patient with asthma has used her inhaler six times in an hour and is now quiet with little air movement. What does the quiet chest mean?
She is moving too little air to wheeze, which is worse than wheezing
She is exaggerating the severity, since no wheeze means no obstruction
The inhaler is working well and her airways are now fully open
Her asthma attack has resolved and the inhaler finally worked
A silent chest in asthma is an ominous sign of severe obstruction, not improvement.
q2o3lpa: An EMT has a conscious hypoglycemic patient who can swallow and protect her airway. What is appropriate?
Oral glucose gel or another oral sugar source
Intravenous dextrose through a large-bore line
Glucagon intramuscularly into the outer thigh
Nothing by mouth until a paramedic arrives
Oral glucose is within EMT scope when the patient can swallow safely.
qrla6zn: Why should oral glucose not be given to an unresponsive hypoglycemic patient?
It can be aspirated into the lungs
It raises the blood sugar far too much
It works too slowly to be useful
An unresponsive patient cannot protect the airway, so anything placed in the mouth risks aspiration.
q52j4d2: An EMT is asked to assist a chest pain patient with his own nitroglycerin. Which finding makes this unsafe?
He has a history of high blood pressure
Phosphodiesterase inhibitors with nitrates can cause profound hypotension.
q1r1ahhh: Before assisting with nitroglycerin, an EMT should confirm what?
A systolic blood pressure above the protocol's minimum
A 12-lead tracing that already shows an acute STEMI pattern
That the patient has eaten within the last hour
A normal temperature taken before the first dose
Nitroglycerin drops blood pressure, so a minimum systolic is the standard check.
qbtqln5: A COPD patient is breathless with a saturation of 86 percent. What should the EMT do?
Give oxygen titrated toward the target range in protocol
Give the highest flow available whatever the saturation
Withhold oxygen entirely because of the COPD
Hypoxia is treated. The old fear of giving any oxygen in COPD has been replaced by titration to a target.
qr0natn: For which ingestion is activated charcoal least useful?
A large ingestion of an antidepressant
Charcoal does not bind caustics, and it obscures the view for endoscopy while risking a dangerous vomit.
q1n67a94: A patient with a known bee allergy is stung and has only localized swelling with no other symptoms. What is appropriate?
Monitor closely and treat symptoms; epinephrine is for systemic reactions
Give the epinephrine auto-injector immediately into the outer thigh muscle
Give oral diphenhydramine and release the patient at the scene
Apply a venous tourniquet above the sting to slow absorption
Epinephrine is for anaphylaxis, meaning systemic involvement, not for a local reaction alone.
q1g1cuij: An AEMT establishes an IV on an unresponsive patient with a glucose of 38 mg/dL. What is appropriate?
Intravenous dextrose, with the concentration and volume per protocol
Intramuscular glucagon only, keeping the dextrose in reserve for later
Oral glucose gel placed between the cheek and the gum to absorb
Waiting for a paramedic to arrive before giving any sugar at all
With intravenous access and an unresponsive patient, IV dextrose is the AEMT-level treatment.
q1w6vxza: Why is dextrose given through a well-running, well-secured line?
Infiltration of concentrated dextrose can cause severe tissue injury
Concentrated dextrose irritates the vein and burns if it refluxes upward
It cannot be given through standard plastic infusion tubing
It has to be given together with food to avoid severe nausea
Concentrated dextrose is a vesicant, and extravasation causes significant local damage.
q1kjwhpl: When is glucagon the better choice for hypoglycemia?
When no intravenous or intraosseous access can be obtained
When the blood glucose is only slightly below normal
When the patient is alert and able to swallow safely
When the patient has eaten a meal within the hour
Glucagon is the route-of-last-resort option when access cannot be obtained.
q1msh4ph: What limits how well glucagon works?
It needs glycogen stores, which are depleted in starvation and alcoholism
It works only in children, because adult liver glycogen stores are too small
It requires a patent intravenous line, so it cannot be given into muscle
It must be given together with a small dose of insulin to work
Glucagon mobilizes stored glycogen. With no stores, it does little.
qinxmef: An AEMT has intravenous access on an apneic opioid overdose. How should naloxone be titrated?
In small increments, to restore adequate breathing rather than full alertness
As one large intravenous push given quickly, to wake the patient fully and at once
Only intranasally, because the intravenous route is not approved for this
Only after the patient has been intubated and placed on a ventilator
Titrating to breathing avoids precipitating severe withdrawal and agitation.
qe1cm2n: A patient with severe asthma has had three albuterol treatments with little improvement. What else is commonly added at this level?
Combining ipratropium with albuterol improves bronchodilation in severe exacerbations.
q13zxbbp: An inferior wall infarct patient becomes profoundly hypotensive after nitroglycerin. What is the likely explanation?
A right ventricular infarct, which depends on preload that nitroglycerin removes
The dose given was too small, so a reflex tachycardia dropped the pressure further
An immediate allergic reaction to the nitroglycerin tablet he was given
Nitroglycerin always drops the pressure this much during an infarct
Right ventricular infarction is preload dependent, and nitrates can drop the pressure sharply.
q1f6di4f: In anaphylaxis with hypotension that persists after two intramuscular epinephrine doses, what is the next step at an advanced level?
Fluid resuscitation with crystalloid alongside further epinephrine
Oral antihistamines plus a steroid tablet, holding further epinephrine
A third auto-injector into the same thigh site as the first two
Lying the patient on the left side only, with the legs kept flat
Anaphylactic shock is distributive, and volume is a key part of the treatment.
qtq9qig: A patient has vomiting after a head injury. What is the main reason to treat it?
Vomiting raises intracranial pressure and threatens the airway
It causes hypertension, which is the main danger in head injury
It is unpleasant for the crew to manage in a moving ambulance
It stops the patient from eating or drinking before arrival
Controlling vomiting in head injury protects the airway and avoids pressure spikes.
q9utagu: A flight nurse transports a patient on a norepinephrine infusion. What is the most important preparation before lift-off?
Confirm pump battery charge, line security and a backup plan for infusion failure
Switch to a gravity drip for the whole flight so that no infusion pump is needed at all
Disconnect the infusion during takeoff and reconnect it once at altitude
Increase the infusion rate ahead of time to cover the whole transport
Pump failure in flight with no backup is a known and preventable critical event.
q1xwhjg4: Why is a central line preferred for norepinephrine in transport?
Extravasation from a peripheral line causes tissue necrosis, and a moving aircraft makes dislodgement more likely
Peripheral lines cannot carry vasopressors at all, so central access must be established before any transport flight
It allows a much faster maximum infusion rate than any peripheral line can safely carry
It lowers the drug cost, because less norepinephrine is wasted in the long infusion tubing
Vasopressor extravasation is a serious injury, and transport increases the risk of line problems.
qfjii6l: A ventilated patient on rocuronium becomes tachycardic and hypertensive during flight. What should the flight nurse consider first?
Inadequate sedation and analgesia under paralysis
That the rocuronium dose has fully worn off
A normal physiologic response to altitude
A paralyzed patient cannot show distress except through vital signs. Awareness under paralysis is the first thing to exclude.
q165gjz0: Which transport patient makes succinylcholine a poor choice?
A patient several days after a major burn or spinal cord injury
A patient with a full stomach and a short fasting time
A patient with asthma that is controlled on an inhaler
A patient who is hypertensive on the crew's arrival
Up-regulated receptors after burns, denervation and prolonged immobility cause a dangerous potassium release.
q16bcnvf: Why is ketamine often favored for induction in transport?
It tends to preserve blood pressure and respiratory drive compared with other agents
It provides deep muscle relaxation, so a separate paralytic is not needed for intubation
It has no cardiovascular effects at all, which is unique among induction agents
It reverses hypoxia directly by improving oxygen carriage in the blood
Hemodynamic stability is the main reason it is chosen in an unstable transport patient.
q1ddk814: A ventilated transport patient is on a fentanyl infusion. What is the altitude-related concern?
Expanding gas can change cuff pressure and pneumothorax size, so the whole picture changes, not the drug
Fentanyl infusion doses must be halved once in flight, because hepatic clearance falls with cabin altitude
Fentanyl lowers the seizure threshold at altitude, so a benzodiazepine is added
Fentanyl becomes chemically inactive above about 5,000 feet of cabin altitude in flight
The drug behaves normally. Boyle's law effects on trapped gas are what change with altitude.
qbzab30: A flight nurse is transporting a hemorrhaging trauma patient 90 minutes by air. What is the preferred resuscitation?
Blood products rather than crystalloid, with tranexamic acid if within the window
Three liters of warmed crystalloid given before any blood product is considered at all
Colloid solution alone, since it stays in the vascular space much longer
Vasopressors instead of volume, to keep the pressure up during flight
Crystalloid dilutes clotting factors. Blood is the resuscitation fluid for hemorrhage.
qtb6mtr: What is the key timing point for tranexamic acid in trauma?
Benefit is greatest when given early, within about three hours of injury
It should be withheld until arrival at the receiving trauma center
It works only once a blood transfusion has already been started
It can be given at any time after injury with the same benefit
Early administration is what drives the mortality benefit; later administration loses it.
q15kl81n: A head-injured patient shows a blown pupil in flight. What does hypertonic saline do?
Draws water out of brain tissue to reduce intracranial pressure as a temporizing measure
Reverses the underlying brain injury itself, so the dilated pupil returns to normal size quickly
Removes the need for any ventilation adjustment during the rest of the flight
Lowers the systemic blood pressure in order to protect the injured brain tissue
Osmotic therapy buys time to definitive care; it does not treat the lesion.
qpyroxk: A hypotensive patient needs sedation in flight. Why is propofol often avoided?
It causes vasodilation and myocardial depression, worsening hypotension
It raises the blood pressure and causes a marked tachycardia in unstable shock
It cannot be run safely on a standard transport infusion pump
It loses most of its sedative effect once at cabin altitude
Propofol's hemodynamic effects are the limiting factor in an unstable patient.
qzzw4w9: A flight nurse transports a patient on a heparin infusion who develops a falling platelet count. What is the concern?
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which causes clotting rather than bleeding
A laboratory artifact, since heparin has no effect at all on the platelet count
Simple dilution of the platelet count from the crystalloid she received
The normal expected response to any therapeutic heparin infusion
HIT is a prothrombotic state despite the low platelets, and heparin must be stopped.
q16g4kq4: A DKA patient is transported on an insulin infusion. What must the flight nurse monitor most closely?
Potassium and glucose, since insulin drives potassium into cells
The sodium and the arterial pH, since insulin corrects the acidosis
The blood glucose only, rechecked every hour during the flight
The blood pressure and the heart rate trend only
Insulin-driven hypokalemia is the dangerous and preventable event in DKA transport.
q6ll221: A pre-eclamptic patient on magnesium loses her patellar reflexes in flight. What does that indicate?
Rising magnesium toxicity, which precedes respiratory depression
A normal effect of magnesium that needs no further action
An unrecognized spinal cord injury during the transfer
That the magnesium dose is too low to be effective
Loss of deep tendon reflexes is the early warning sign of magnesium toxicity, and calcium gluconate is the antidote.
q1lq4485: A massively transfused patient becomes hypotensive with a prolonged QT in flight. What should be considered?
Hypercalcemia from the stored blood products
Hypernatremia from the saline carrier fluid
Hyperglycemia from the citrate in the blood
Citrate in stored blood binds calcium, and the resulting hypocalcemia impairs contractility and coagulation.
qsl730k: A flight nurse transports a patient with acute pulmonary edema on a nitroglycerin infusion. What is the main benefit?
Reduced preload and afterload, which unloads the failing left ventricle
An increase in heart rate and contractility that raises the cardiac output
Direct clearance of alveolar fluid from the flooded lung units
Bronchodilation, which lowers the work of breathing in flight
Nitroglycerin works by unloading the ventricle, which is why it helps before any diuretic does.
q1jmffzc: A flight nurse is asked to start a peripheral epinephrine infusion for refractory shock. What is the practical concern?
Extravasation risk and the need for frequent site checks and a plan for central access
That epinephrine cannot be given peripherally at all, so central access is required first
That the infusion requires an in-line filter that is not stocked on the aircraft
That it has to run through the same line as the blood products in flight
Peripheral vasopressors are used in transport with close monitoring and a plan to convert to central access.
q19uwmau: A client on a weight-based heparin infusion has an aPTT of 128 seconds (goal 60-85 per the nomogram) and new oozing from the gums. Vital signs are stable. What should the nurse do first?
Hold the infusion for the time the nomogram specifies, then restart at the lower rate
Give protamine sulfate IV now and discontinue heparin for the rest of the stay
Continue the current rate and redraw the aPTT in 6 hours to confirm the value
Cut the rate in half without stopping it and report the aPTT result at the morning rounds
A supratherapeutic aPTT with minor bleeding is handled by the nomogram hold and rate decrease with close monitoring. Protamine is reserved for serious bleeding or overdose.
q1l0gx07: A client on a heparin infusion has a platelet count fall from 240,000 to 105,000/mm3. Which added detail most supports heparin-induced thrombocytopenia?
It began on day 6 and the left calf is swollen
It began within 6 hours of the first heparin bolus
There is new oozing from the gums and the IV sites
The count fell while the aPTT stayed below the goal
HIT is an antibody reaction that appears on about day 5 to 10, with a fall of more than 50 percent and new clot rather than bleeding. A drop within hours is usually nonimmune and transient.
q1c97xnx: A client in DKA has glucose 486 mg/dL, potassium 3.0 mEq/L, and bicarbonate 8 mEq/L. Why does the insulin infusion wait?
Insulin drives potassium into the cells
Insulin cannot work in a low potassium state
The bicarbonate must be corrected first
The glucose must be lowered with fluid first

Per ADA guidance insulin is delayed until potassium is at least 3.3 mEq/L, because insulin shifts potassium intracellularly and can cause a fatal arrhythmia. Fluid and potassium replacement come first.
qkj6t3x: Four hours into a DKA insulin infusion, glucose is 212 mg/dL and the anion gap is still 19. What does the nurse anticipate per the DKA protocol?
Add dextrose to the IV fluids and continue the insulin infusion
Stop the insulin infusion and give the first dose of basal insulin
Hold insulin until glucose rises above 250 mg/dL, then restart it
Increase the insulin rate because the anion gap has not closed yet
Insulin is what clears the ketones, so once glucose falls below about 250 mg/dL dextrose is added and insulin continues until the gap closes. Stopping insulin early lets the ketoacidosis rebound.
q48w4sl: A client whose DKA has resolved is to change from the IV insulin infusion to subcutaneous Lantus. Which plan is safest?
Give the glargine, then stop the infusion about 2 hours later
Stop the infusion first, then give glargine once the client eats
Stop the infusion and give the glargine at the very same moment
Give glargine and keep the infusion running for another 24 hours
IV insulin has a half-life of minutes, so basal insulin must overlap the drip by 1-2 hours to prevent rebound hyperglycemia and ketosis. Stopping the drip first leaves a gap with no insulin on board.
qfqqm2r: A client is on insulin lispro with meals and insulin glargine at bedtime. Breakfast trays will be 45 minutes late. Which dose does the delay change?
The lispro, because it acts in about 15 minutes
The glargine, because it peaks at the morning meal
Both doses, because each is matched to food intake
Neither dose, since glucose is checked before both
Lispro starts within about 15 minutes and peaks in 1 to 2 hours, so it is timed within 15 minutes of food. Glargine is a peakless basal insulin given on a fixed schedule regardless of meals.
qfyliic: Which statement by a client starting Lantus shows a need for more teaching?
I can draw up my Lantus and NovoLog together to save an injection
I give the Lantus at about the same time every day, even on sick days
I do not need to roll or shake the Lantus pen before I inject it
I keep the pen I am using at room temperature and date it when opened

Glargine must never be mixed with another insulin because mixing changes its acidic solution and its long action. It is clear, so it needs no rolling, and basal insulin usually continues on sick days.
q1mlaq2d: A client received NPH and regular insulin at 0730, ate half of breakfast, and refused lunch. When is this client at greatest risk for hypoglycemia?
Mid-afternoon, when the NPH effect peaks
Within 15 minutes of the morning injection
Around 0300, when the regular insulin peaks
Only right before lunch, when regular peaks
NPH peaks about 4-12 hours after injection, so a missed lunch puts the risk in the afternoon. Regular insulin peaks in 2-4 hours and is long gone by 0300.
q18ftty9: An order reads: potassium chloride 40 mEq in 100 mL IV over 1 hour via the forearm peripheral IV on a med-surg unit. What should the nurse do?
Clarify the order, because the rate exceeds the usual peripheral limit
Give it as ordered on an infusion pump, checking the IV site every 15 minutes
Run it by gravity with a roller clamp so it can be stopped quickly
Give it as a slow IV push over 5 minutes through the same catheter
Most policies cap peripheral potassium at about 10 mEq/h outside monitored units, and 40 mEq/h risks arrhythmia and vein injury. Potassium is never given by IV push or by gravity.
q4debvr: Four clients each have potassium chloride 10 mEq IV ordered for a potassium of 3.2 mEq/L. Which order should the nurse question first?
Urine output 12 mL/h, creatinine risen to 2.1 mg/dL
Taking furosemide 40 mg daily with a magnesium of 1.9
Taking metoprolol with a heart rate of 58 beats a minute
Vomiting for 2 days with a bicarbonate of 32 mEq/L

Potassium leaves the body almost entirely through the kidneys, so new oliguria with a doubled creatinine turns replacement into hyperkalemia. The other three have ordinary reasons to run low and need the dose.
qfnpv5: A monitored client has potassium 6.4 mEq/L with tall peaked T waves. The rider is stopped and three more orders arrive. Which one protects the heart fastest?

Calcium does not lower the potassium at all; it restores the gap between resting and threshold potential in the myocardium within minutes. Insulin with dextrose shifts potassium in 15 to 30 minutes, and polystyrene and diuresis remove it slowly.
qihlpie: A client on magnesium sulfate for preeclampsia has a serum magnesium of 9.5 mg/dL. Which finding fits that level?
Patellar reflexes that can no longer be elicited
A respiratory rate that has fallen to 8 per minute
Complete heart block on the cardiac monitor
Flushing and warmth with mild drowsiness only

Reflexes disappear around 8 to 10 mg/dL, which is why they are the hourly bedside check. Respiratory depression comes near 12, cardiac arrest above 25, and flushing with drowsiness fits the therapeutic 4 to 7 range.
qroi8i1: A client on a magnesium sulfate infusion has these findings. Which one places her at greatest risk of magnesium toxicity?
Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL with falling urine output
Patellar reflexes 2+ and equal on both sides
Flushing and warmth during the loading dose
A serum magnesium of 5.8 mg/dL per protocol
Magnesium is cleared only by the kidneys, so renal impairment lets it build up. Flushing during the bolus is expected, and 2+ reflexes and a level of 5.8 mg/dL are within usual targets.
qalgyta: A client on magnesium sulfate for severe preeclampsia has an emergency cesarean under general anesthesia with rocuronium. What should the PACU nurse watch for most closely?
Prolonged weakness and hypoventilation from potentiated blockade
Malignant hyperthermia triggered by the two drugs used together
Rebound hypertension as the paralytic wears off in the first hour
Seizure activity caused by rocuronium lowering seizure threshold

Magnesium reduces acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction and potentiates nondepolarizing blockers, so residual paralysis and respiratory depression are the risk. Rocuronium does not trigger malignant hyperthermia.
q13vew5d: A post-op client on IV morphine has SpO2 95 percent on 2 L oxygen and a respiratory rate of 12. Which finding most predicts respiratory depression?
A pain score that has dropped from 8 to 3
Pupils that are 2 mm and equally reactive
Itching across the chest and upper arms

On the Pasero sedation scale, unintended sleepiness during conversation is the point at which the opioid is reduced, because sedation precedes respiratory depression. Miosis, itching and pain relief are expected effects.
q5ysmoz: An opioid-naive 80-year-old's order reads Dilaudid 4 mg IV every 4 hours PRN pain. Yesterday she received morphine 4 mg IV. What should the nurse do?
Question the order, as the dose is far above opioid-naive starting doses
Give it as ordered, since it matches the morphine dose she tolerated
Give it as ordered but over 5 minutes with an oxygen saturation probe
Give 2 mg now and the other 2 mg in an hour if pain is not relieved
Hydromorphone is roughly 5-7 times as potent as morphine, and the labeled IV starting range for opioid-naive adults is 0.2-1 mg. A milligram-for-milligram swap is a classic fatal error.
q1ocs637: A client with renal failure on IV morphine received naloxone for RR 6/min and became alert. Ninety minutes later the RR is again 6/min. What best explains this?
Naloxone wore off before the opioid and its active metabolite did
The client developed tolerance to naloxone after a single dose
A new problem such as a stroke is the most likely cause of this
The naloxone dose was too high and caused rebound sedation
Naloxone acts for about 30-90 minutes, shorter than many opioids, and morphine's active metabolite builds up in renal failure. Repeat doses or an infusion may be needed.
qmqfkwa: A hospice client on high-dose opioids for bone cancer pain is arousable only to pain with RR 7/min. Per your protocol, how should naloxone be given?
Dilute it and give small increments, titrated to the breathing rate
Give 2 mg IV push rapidly, repeating every 2 minutes until fully alert
Give 4 mg intranasally, then hold all opioids for the next 24 hours
Do not give naloxone at all, because the client is receiving hospice

In opioid-tolerant clients, small titrated doses reverse respiratory depression without causing severe withdrawal and a pain crisis. Hospice status alone does not forbid treating an unintended overdose.
qyf76h4: A client with a fentanyl 50 mcg/h patch has several new orders. Which one should the nurse question first?
Docusate sodium 100 mg PO twice daily
Famotidine 20 mg PO twice daily now
Clarithromycin strongly inhibits CYP3A4, which can raise fentanyl levels and cause fatal respiratory depression (boxed warning). The other drugs do not affect fentanyl metabolism.
qvolm9j: A client wearing a Duragesic patch develops a temperature of 39.6 C (103.3 F) and becomes hard to arouse with RR 9/min. What is the most likely explanation?
Fever increased drug absorption through the skin
Sepsis is causing encephalopathy without opioid effect
The patch was worn past 72 hours and began to leak
The fever lowered the opioid's protein binding
Heat and fever increase transdermal fentanyl absorption and can cause overdose. The patch is removed, the client stimulated, and the provider notified.
q1v84jug: A client on methadone 120 mg daily is admitted with pneumonia. QTc 498 ms, K 3.2 mEq/L, Mg 1.5 mg/dL. Levofloxacin and ondansetron are ordered. What is the priority action?
Report the QT risk and request electrolyte replacement before the doses
Give both drugs and recheck the ECG in the morning per the routine unit protocol
Hold the methadone dose today to make room for the new medications
Give the ondansetron but hold levofloxacin until the next ECG is done
Methadone, levofloxacin and ondansetron all prolong QT, and low potassium and magnesium add to torsades risk. Abruptly holding methadone causes withdrawal and does not quickly shorten the QT.
q1ofcvgu: Which statement by a client discharged on OxyContin shows that teaching was NOT effective?
If it is hard to swallow, I can crush it into some applesauce
I will not drink any alcohol while I am taking this medicine
I will keep it locked up and away from my grandchildren at home
I will add fiber and a stool softener while I take this medicine
Crushing an extended-release tablet releases the whole dose at once and can cause a fatal overdose.
qv5x8wn: A client who uses illicit fentanyl wants to begin buprenorphine-naloxone in the ED. Before the first dose, which finding matters most?
Objective signs of moderate withdrawal on the COWS scale
A urine drug screen that is negative for fentanyl now
At least 72 hours since the last use of any fentanyl
A normal liver panel drawn earlier during the visit

Buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial agonist that displaces full agonists, so it precipitates withdrawal unless the client is already in moderate withdrawal. A fixed 72-hour wait or a negative screen is not required.
qlrg2rb: A client on warfarin has an INR of 11.4 and no signs of bleeding. What does the nurse anticipate per current guidelines?
Hold warfarin and give oral vitamin K
IV vitamin K 10 mg plus 4-factor PCC
Hold one dose, then resume the same dose
Transfuse 2 units of fresh frozen plasma
With an INR above 10 and no bleeding, guidelines advise holding warfarin and giving low-dose oral vitamin K. IV vitamin K with PCC is reserved for major bleeding.
q18odv84: A client with a stable INR on warfarin is prescribed an antibiotic for a UTI. Which choice should prompt the nurse to request closer INR monitoring?
Fosfomycin 3 g as a single oral dose sachet
Sulfamethoxazole inhibits CYP2C9, the main pathway for S-warfarin, and can sharply raise the INR. The others have little effect on warfarin.
qkrag9w: A 72 kg client has enoxaparin 70 mg subcut every 12 hours ordered for DVT. Creatinine clearance is 24 mL/min. What should the nurse do?
Clarify the order, as the label calls for once-daily dosing at this CrCl
Give it as ordered, since weight-based dosing already accounts for kidneys
Give it as ordered and request an anti-Xa level after the fourth dose
Hold it and ask for heparin, since enoxaparin is contraindicated now
With CrCl below 30 mL/min, the labeled treatment dose is 1 mg/kg once daily because enoxaparin accumulates. It is not contraindicated, so a switch is not required.
qai1idj: A client with an epidural catheter received enoxaparin 40 mg subcut at 2100. Anesthesia asks when the catheter may be removed. What should the nurse say?
At 0100, about 4 hours after the dose
At 2130, once the site stops oozing
At 0300, about 6 hours after the dose
The label calls for at least 12 hours between a prophylactic dose and catheter removal, and at least 4 hours after removal before the next dose, to limit the risk of spinal hematoma and paralysis.
q1rxfjiq: A client is 40 minutes into an alteplase infusion for stroke. Which finding means the infusion is stopped and an emergent head CT is obtained?
Headache, vomiting, and a GCS fall of 3 points
Oozing from the antecubital venipuncture site
A blood pressure that has risen to 176/98 mm Hg
A transient nausea with no change in the neuro exam

Sudden headache, vomiting and neurologic decline during thrombolysis suggest intracranial hemorrhage, the feared complication. Minor oozing, nausea and a pressure under 180/105 are managed without stopping the drug.
qa2m5rb: Two stroke clients both have a BP of 196/108. One received alteplase an hour ago and one did not. How do their targets differ?
The treated client is kept at or below 180/105
The treated client is kept at or below 220/120 instead
Both clients are kept at or below 185/110
Neither client has the pressure lowered at all

AHA guidance keeps BP at or below 180/105 for 24 hours after a lytic to limit hemorrhage, and allows up to 220/120 when no lytic was given. The 185/110 figure is the threshold before the lytic is started.
q1155ou5: During alteplase for stroke, a client develops swelling of the tongue and lip on one side. Which home medication most increases the risk of this reaction?
Orolingual angioedema during alteplase is more common in clients on ACE inhibitors, because both raise bradykinin activity.
qrql272: A norepinephrine infusion has extravasated into the forearm, which is pale and cool. Which antidote does the nurse expect to infiltrate into the site?
Hyaluronidase, which spreads the drug out in tissue
Sodium thiosulfate, which binds the drug locally
Dexrazoxane, which protects the tissue from injury

Phentolamine reverses the alpha-mediated vasoconstriction that is starving the tissue of blood. Hyaluronidase is used for vinca and nutrition extravasation, thiosulfate for mechlorethamine, and dexrazoxane for anthracyclines.
qqnkx3l: A client on norepinephrine titrated to MAP 65 or higher has an arterial line reading 76/42 (MAP 53) with a flattened waveform. Cuff BP is 112/66 and mentation is unchanged. What should the nurse do first?
Troubleshoot the line: flush, level and zero it
Increase the norepinephrine to bring MAP above 65
Add vasopressin and report refractory shock now
Give a 1 L crystalloid bolus while awaiting orders
A damped arterial waveform underreads systolic pressure, and titrating to a false reading causes harmful vasoconstriction. Correlate with the cuff and fix the line first.
q1dvkiry: A client has received Nipride for 3 days. New findings: confusion, lactate 7.2 mmol/L, falling bicarbonate, and venous blood that looks bright red. What should the nurse suspect?
Thiocyanate retention from mild renal impairment
Methemoglobinemia from the nitrite ions released
Septic shock that has gone unrecognized for days
Cyanide blocks cellular oxygen use, causing lactic acidosis and high venous oxygen content. The infusion is stopped and hydroxocobalamin or sodium thiosulfate given.
qtvo882: A client with chest pain took a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor last night. How long are nitrates withheld?
48 hours for tadalafil and 24 for sildenafil
24 hours for either drug, since both are short acting
48 hours for either drug, since both are long acting
12 hours for tadalafil and 48 for sildenafil

Tadalafil has a half-life near 17.5 hours against roughly 4 hours for sildenafil, so the nitrate-free interval is 48 hours after tadalafil and 24 hours after sildenafil. A nitrate inside that window can cause profound hypotension.
q1g4dgmb: A client with an inferior STEMI has BP 92/58, clear lungs, JVD, and ST elevation in lead V4R. Why is nitroglycerin a problem here?
A right ventricular infarct needs preload
Nitrates block conduction through the AV node
Nitrates raise oxygen demand in the right heart
A right ventricular infarct causes pulmonary edema

ST elevation in V4R with clear lungs and raised neck veins points to right ventricular infarction, which fills by volume, so a venodilator drops cardiac output sharply. A fluid bolus is given instead.
qj47ugh: A client in atrial fibrillation with a rate of 152 has a Cardizem bolus and drip ordered. Which finding should make the nurse question the order?
Heart failure with an ejection fraction of 20 percent
An irregularly irregular rhythm on the cardiac monitor
BP of 118/76 mmHg with brisk capillary refill
Taking apixaban daily for stroke prevention at home
Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers depress contractility and can cause decompensation in HFrEF; amiodarone or digoxin is usually chosen instead.
q1g26op: An amiodarone maintenance infusion arrives mixed at 3.6 mg/mL. The client has only a 20-gauge forearm IV. What should the nurse do?
Clarify it, because this concentration needs central access
Give it, since amiodarone is safe through any peripheral catheter
Give it through the forearm IV and check the site every 4 hours
Give it through the forearm IV after removing the in-line filter
The label calls for a central line when concentrations exceed 2 mg/mL because of phlebitis risk, and amiodarone infusions use an in-line filter.
q1pp4fwt: A client on digoxin reports nausea and yellow-tinged vision. Apical HR 54. Digoxin level 1.4 ng/mL, K 2.9 mEq/L. What should the nurse do?
Hold digoxin and report possible toxicity from the low potassium
Give the digoxin, since the level is within the reference range
Give digoxin and an antiemetic, then recheck the level in 6 hours
Hold digoxin and request a level drawn 2 hours after the next dose
Hypokalemia increases digoxin binding to the sodium-potassium pump, so toxicity can occur with a normal level. Levels are drawn at least 6 hours after a dose.
q1l169vi: Four hours after DigiFab for digoxin toxicity, the HR and potassium have normalized, but the total digoxin level rose from 4.1 to 9.8 ng/mL. What does this mean?
It is expected, since the assay also counts Fab-bound drug
Fab failed, so a second full dose is needed right away
The sample was drawn from the line used to infuse the Fab
Toxicity is worsening and the client now needs dialysis
Most assays measure total digoxin, including drug bound to Fab, so levels rise after treatment and are unreliable. The clinical response guides care.
q19rbck6: An 86-year-old on digoxin 0.25 mg daily has a creatinine clearance that has fallen to 28 mL/min. Which new findings most suggest toxicity?
A heart rate of 64 and a dry mouth
A dry cough with new ankle swelling
Thirst with frequent urination at night

In older adults digoxin toxicity often shows first as anorexia, nausea and confusion, well before bradycardia, and reduced renal clearance lets the drug build up. A heart rate above 60 does not rule it out.
qg8kod4: A client in SVT takes dipyridamole. Adenosine is about to be given. What should the nurse anticipate per ACLS?
A smaller first dose, since dipyridamole boosts its effect
A larger first dose, since dipyridamole blocks its effect
The usual dose, since there is no interaction between them
Avoiding adenosine, since the pair is fully contraindicated
Dipyridamole blocks adenosine reuptake and potentiates it, so ACLS suggests a reduced first dose of 3 mg. Caffeine and theophylline have the opposite effect.
q18q4die: A client with BP 214/124 and an acute asthma flare with diffuse wheezes has IV labetalol ordered. What should the nurse do?
Question the order because of the bronchospasm
Give it, since labetalol is cardioselective
Give it right after an albuterol treatment
Give half the dose and recheck in 10 minutes
Labetalol blocks beta-2 receptors and can worsen bronchospasm; agents such as nicardipine or clevidipine avoid this. Labetalol is not cardioselective.
q156lipi: A client on Diprivan at 70 mcg/kg/min for 4 days has new findings: lactate 6.1, CK 9,400, K 6.0, and a new RBBB pattern. What should the nurse suspect?
Prolonged high-dose propofol can cause metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, arrhythmias and heart failure. The infusion is stopped and the provider notified.
q19efdd2: A propofol bottle and its tubing were spiked 14 hours ago and 40 mL remain. What should the nurse do?
Replace the bottle and the tubing
Let it run until the bottle is empty
Replace the bottle but keep the tubing
Add a new filter and keep it running
Propofol is a lipid emulsion that supports bacterial growth, so the label requires discarding the bottle and tubing 12 hours after spiking.
q1fkvxfb: A client needs sedation but has borderline hypotension and a heart rate of 50. Which difference between dexmedetomidine and propofol matters most here?
Dexmedetomidine slows the heart rate further
Dexmedetomidine has no effect on heart rate

As an alpha-2 agonist, dexmedetomidine causes bradycardia and hypotension but little respiratory depression, which is why it can sedate an unintubated client. With a rate of 50 already, that bradycardia is the limiting problem.
qrjostw: A client is scheduled for sedation with IV midazolam. Which home medication should the nurse report to the anesthesia team?
Ritonavir, taken as part of an HIV regimen
Levetiracetam, taken twice daily for seizures
Metformin, taken twice daily with the meals
Rosuvastatin, taken each evening at bedtime
Ritonavir strongly inhibits CYP3A4, the main pathway for midazolam, so sedation becomes deep and prolonged and the plan has to change. The other three do not inhibit that pathway.
qqewsz4: A client who took an unknown number of pills is sedated. The QRS is 140 ms, and the family says she takes alprazolam daily. Flumazenil is ordered. What should the nurse do?
Question the order because of seizure risk
Give it, since a benzodiazepine is likely
Give it slowly over 30 seconds with suction
Give it, then prepare activated charcoal
A wide QRS suggests a tricyclic co-ingestion, and both TCAs and chronic benzodiazepine use make flumazenil-induced seizures likely.
q11j9zcd: A client on a Nimbex infusion has HR 128, BP 172/98, and tears on the cheeks. Train-of-four is 1/4. What do these findings suggest?
Paralytics provide no sedation or analgesia, so tachycardia, hypertension and tearing in a paralyzed client suggest awareness or pain. A TOF of 1/4 shows the blockade is adequate.
q1ruvqpk: A 28-year-old who takes oral contraceptives received Bridion at the end of surgery. What should the nurse teach?
Use a backup birth control method for 7 days
No change is needed with the contraceptive pill
Stop taking the contraceptive pill for a week
Take two contraceptive pills tomorrow morning
Sugammadex can bind progestogen, so the label treats it like a missed pill and advises a nonhormonal backup method for 7 days.
qbax38h: During surgery with sevoflurane and succinylcholine, which finding is often the earliest sign that dantrolene will be needed?
Temperature of 40 C (104 F) with heavy sweating
Dark brown urine in the Foley drainage bag
Malignant hyperthermia raises CO2 production first. Hyperthermia and myoglobinuria are later findings.
q1evv8w3: Vancomycin 1 g IV is run over 30 minutes. The client develops flushing of the face and neck and itching. BP is 108/68 with no wheezing. What should the nurse do?
Stop it, notify, then resume at a slower rate
Give epinephrine IM for suspected anaphylaxis
Stop it and chart vancomycin as an allergy
Continue it and give acetaminophen for comfort
This is the vancomycin infusion reaction from histamine release at fast rates; the label calls for infusion over at least 60 minutes. It is not a true allergy.
q11yo0i7: A 10-day-old infant receiving calcium-containing parenteral nutrition is ordered ceftriaxone. What should the nurse do?
Question the order because of the calcium
Give it through a separate IV line instead
Flush with saline between the two infusions
Give it, since neonates tolerate ceftriaxone
In neonates, ceftriaxone with calcium-containing IV solutions can form fatal precipitates in the lungs and kidneys even through separate lines, so the label contraindicates it.
q40tczu: A client on sertraline is started on Zyvox. Two days later the client is agitated and sweaty, with temperature 39.2 C (102.6 F) and inducible clonus. What is most likely?
Linezolid is a weak MAO inhibitor that, with SSRIs, can cause serotonin syndrome. Clonus and hyperreflexia separate it from NMS, which causes rigidity.
q1jcinek: A client with eGFR 38 on metformin is scheduled for a CT with IV iodinated contrast. What does the nurse anticipate?
Hold metformin at the scan, then recheck eGFR in 48 h
Continue metformin, since it does not affect the kidneys
Stop metformin permanently because of this eGFR level
Hold it only on the morning of the scan, then resume it
With eGFR 30-60, the label says stop metformin at or before the contrast study and restart 48 hours later if renal function is stable, because AKI can lead to lactic acidosis.
q34ryx9: An 82-year-old taking glyburide has recurrent hypoglycemia overnight after D50 at midnight. CrCl is 35 mL/min. What should the nurse expect?
Prolonged monitoring and a dextrose infusion
One more dose of D50, then discharge home
Glucagon IM to prevent another low tonight
A glucose recheck only at 0600 with breakfast
Glyburide has active metabolites that build up in renal impairment, causing prolonged hypoglycemia that outlasts a D50 bolus. The Beers criteria advise avoiding it in older adults.
q1uo5evr: A client on Jardiance, NPO 2 days after surgery, has glucose 178 mg/dL, pH 7.19, bicarbonate 11, and anion gap 22. What does the nurse suspect?
SGLT2 inhibitors can cause DKA with near-normal glucose, especially with fasting or surgery; the label advises holding it 3 days before surgery.
q1j9rclk: A client's stable lithium level was 0.8 mEq/L. After starting a new medication, a week later the client has coarse tremor, vomiting and confusion with a level of 1.9. Which new medication most likely caused it?
Amlodipine 5 mg daily for blood pressure
NSAIDs reduce renal lithium clearance and can push levels into the toxic range, as can thiazides and ACE inhibitors.
q6520r6: Which statement by a client taking lithium shows that teaching was NOT effective?
I will cut way back on salt to protect my heart
I will drink about 2 to 3 liters of fluid each day
I will call the clinic if I have vomiting or diarrhea
I will get my lithium level checked when I am told
Low sodium intake makes the kidneys hold onto lithium and can cause toxicity. Sodium intake should stay consistent.
q1dooota: A client on phenytoin has nystagmus and ataxia. The total level is 9 mcg/mL (range 10-20) and albumin is 2.0 g/dL. A dose increase is ordered. What should the nurse do?
Report the toxicity signs and ask about a free level
Give the higher dose, since the level is below range
Give the higher dose and recheck the total level tomorrow
Hold all phenytoin until albumin is replaced IV
With low albumin, more phenytoin is unbound, so the total level underestimates active drug. The clinical signs of toxicity matter more than the number.
q6d5k08: IV phenytoin is to be given piggyback into a running line of D5W. What should the nurse do?
Flush with saline before and after the dose
Give it through the D5W line very slowly
Mix the phenytoin into the D5W bag first
Give it through the D5W line quickly
Phenytoin precipitates in dextrose solutions, so it is given only with normal saline and the line is flushed before and after.
q46ju3j: A client who was seizure-free on valproic acid is started on meropenem for pneumonia and has a seizure two days later. What is the most likely cause?
The valproate level rose too high
Carbapenems sharply reduce valproate levels, and raising the valproate dose does not overcome this; a different antibiotic or antiseizure drug is needed.
qimg18i: A client on haloperidol has a temperature of 40.1 C (104.2 F), rigidity, labile BP, and a CK of 12,000. Which finding separates this from serotonin syndrome?
A temperature above 40 C with sweating
A creatine kinase level in the thousands

Both syndromes cause fever, rigidity and autonomic instability, but neuroleptic malignant syndrome gives lead-pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia, while serotonin syndrome gives clonus and hyperreflexia. Fever and a high CK occur in both.
qmeb3ws: A 3-year-old weighing 14 kg has IV acetaminophen 210 mg every 4 hours ordered. What should the nurse do?
Clarify, since the daily total exceeds the label maximum
Give it as ordered, since 15 mg/kg is a normal dose
Give it as ordered but only overnight while awake
Give it orally instead at the same dose and interval
For ages 2-12 the label gives 15 mg/kg every 6 hours or 12.5 mg/kg every 4 hours, maximum 75 mg/kg/day. 210 mg every 4 hours is 90 mg/kg/day.
qn518w2: Four discharge prescriptions are being reviewed. For which client does the label contraindicate tramadol?
A 7-year-old going home after a tonsillectomy
A 70-year-old with a creatinine clearance of 45
A 55-year-old with a history of kidney stones

Tramadol is contraindicated under age 12, and after tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy under 18, because ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizers convert it to a large opioid load. Renal impairment and an SSRI call for caution, not a ban.
q1qoae9y: A parent of a 1-year-old says: When the children's ibuprofen runs out, I will give the same 5 mL using the infant drops. How should the nurse respond?
