Graviola has only laboratory and animal data; the FTC has acted against sellers making cancer cure claims.
q9pvc3c: A client develops an itchy blistering rash around the mouth after peeling a mango with their teeth. Which history is most relevant?
Mango peel contains urushiol-like compounds; mango is in the same family as poison ivy, so sensitized people can develop contact dermatitis.
qnwcxxg: A client on glipizide adds a mango extract supplement marketed for blood sugar. Which concern is most relevant?
Laboratory and animal data suggest glucose-lowering effects, so additive effects with sulfonylureas are a theoretical concern.
qrv0kpi: Mango shares its plant family with which group?
Mango, poison ivy, cashew and pistachio are in the Anacardiaceae family.
qk2hy22: Phlorizin, from apple tree bark, causes glucosuria by inhibiting which transporters?
Phlorizin is a nonselective competitive SGLT1 and SGLT2 inhibitor; it was the starting point for gliflozins.
qvahadc: Why was phlorizin not developed as an oral diabetes drug?
It was far too expensive to extract from bark
It blocked insulin receptors in the liver
Phlorizin is hydrolyzed in the intestine by lactase-phlorizin hydrolase and poorly absorbed, and SGLT1 inhibition causes GI effects.
q9u5aml: Phlorizin is the natural parent of which drug class?
Gliflozins are hydrolysis-resistant, SGLT2-selective C-glucosides designed from the O-glucoside phlorizin.
q1nwjdjw: Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) is an essential structural component of which molecule?
Pantothenate kinase phosphorylates B5 in the first step of coenzyme A synthesis; 4'-phosphopantetheine also forms the arm of acyl carrier protein in fatty acid synthase.
ql9nc9m: A client asks about a vitamin B5 supplement. Which statement about B5 status is accurate?
Deficiency is rare because most foods contain it
Deficiency is common in all older adults
It is found only in animal foods
It is made in large amounts by the skin in sunlight
Pantothenic acid is present in almost every food, so deficiency is rare and mainly seen with severe malnutrition; the classic historical picture is burning feet syndrome.
qwd8t01: Which effect is most often reported with very high intake of pantothenic acid?
No upper intake level has been set for pantothenic acid; diarrhea and GI upset are the main effects reported at very high intake.
q1moqx46: Choline deficiency in controlled depletion studies most classically produces which finding?
Phosphatidylcholine is needed to package triglyceride into VLDL for export from the liver, so low choline intake leads to hepatic steatosis (and muscle damage in some studies).
q16e05p6: A client taking a high-intake choline product reports a fishy body odor. Which explanation fits?
Gut bacteria make trimethylamine from choline
Choline causes a fungal skin infection
Choline is excreted unchanged through the lungs
Gut bacteria convert choline to trimethylamine (TMA), which has a fishy odor; the liver enzyme FMO3 oxidizes TMA to odorless TMAO, and people with FMO3 deficiency are especially affected.
q1ujhmbx: A pregnant client asks about choline in her prenatal vitamin. Which statement is accurate?
Many prenatal vitamins have little or no choline
All prenatal vitamins contain full daily choline
Choline is not needed during pregnancy
Choline intake should drop in pregnancy
Choline needs rise during pregnancy and breastfeeding, and NIH ODS notes that many prenatal supplements contain little or no choline.
q13os2ke: A client on warfarin has a newly low INR after starting a bone health supplement. Which ingredient is most likely involved?
Vitamin K2, like K1, supports gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors and opposes warfarin; MK-7 has a long half-life, so the INR effect can persist for days.
qun1fk3: Vitamin K forms such as menaquinone-7 serve as the cofactor for which enzyme?

Reduced vitamin K is the cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which forms Gla residues on factors II, VII, IX and X, proteins C and S, osteocalcin and matrix Gla protein; warfarin blocks VKORC1, which recycles vitamin K.
q1g6y4vs: Which lab is most relevant when a client taking warfarin reports a new vitamin K2 supplement?
Vitamin K intake lowers the INR in warfarin users, raising clotting risk; MK-7 is cleared more slowly than K1.
qk8u1je: Methylcobalamin is the cofactor for which enzyme?
Methylcobalamin is the cofactor for methionine synthase; adenosylcobalamin is the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, so B12 deficiency raises both homocysteine and methylmalonic acid.
q1ovj0nc: A client with type 2 diabetes reports numbness in both feet after years of treatment. Which medication is linked to low B12 levels?
Long-term metformin use reduces B12 absorption, and B12 deficiency can cause neuropathy that may be mistaken for diabetic neuropathy.
q1bjfju: A young adult with frequent recreational nitrous oxide use has leg numbness and an unsteady gait. What mechanism best explains this?
Nitrous oxide oxidizes the cobalt in cobalamin and inactivates methionine synthase, which can cause subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts.
qoc17s1: Which enzyme step does L-methylfolate bypass compared with folic acid?
L-methylfolate is 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, the product of MTHFR, and does not need DHFR either; it still needs B12-dependent methionine synthase to release tetrahydrofolate.
q1m2tw51: A client with macrocytic anemia takes an L-methylfolate product. Which lab is most important to also review?
Folate, including L-methylfolate, can correct the anemia of B12 deficiency while neurologic damage continues, so B12 status matters in macrocytic anemia.
q130fgii: A client asks whether Deplin (L-methylfolate) is an FDA-approved prescription drug. Which answer is accurate?
It is a medical food, not an approved drug
It is approved as a first-choice antidepressant
It is approved only for seizures
Medical foods such as Deplin are intended for use under physician supervision but are not FDA-approved drugs; they are not reviewed for effectiveness like prescription medicines.
q1f3110n: After conversion to thiamine pyrophosphate, benfotiamine supplies the cofactor for which enzyme?

Thiamine pyrophosphate is the cofactor for transketolase, pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase; red cell transketolase activity is a classic functional test.
q7p49kf: A malnourished client who drinks heavily and takes benfotiamine at home arrives confused with nystagmus and ataxia. Which statement is accurate?
These findings are expected benfotiamine effects
The supplement has caused vitamin B1 toxicity
An oral thiamine supplement does not rule out deficiency; confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia in at-risk patients suggest Wernicke encephalopathy, which is treated in hospital with IV thiamine.
q6jvyht: A client with diabetes asks why they take benfotiamine. Which use is it most often marketed for?
Benfotiamine is mainly marketed for diabetic neuropathy; trial results are mixed and it is not FDA approved.
qr0x0jb: Why does nicotinamide riboside not cause the flushing seen with nicotinic acid (niacin)?
Niacin flushing is mediated by GPR109A (HCA2) activation and prostaglandin D2 release; nicotinamide riboside and nicotinamide do not activate this receptor.
Nicotinamide Riboside (NAD+ precursor, vitamin B3 form)
qbwg4lc: A client asks whether nicotinamide riboside has been proven to slow aging. Which response is accurate?
It raises NAD+, but human benefit is unproven
It is FDA approved to slow aging
It reverses heart disease in most adults
It lowers LDL as much as statins
Nicotinamide riboside raises blood NAD+ in human studies, but anti-aging and clinical benefits in people have not been established; it is a dietary supplement.
Nicotinamide Riboside (NAD+ precursor, vitamin B3 form)
q1ov93dt: Nicotinamide riboside is converted in the body to which coenzyme?
Nicotinamide riboside kinases convert NR to NMN, which is then converted to NAD+.
Nicotinamide Riboside (NAD+ precursor, vitamin B3 form)
q894toy: Why do statins lower coenzyme Q10 levels?
Statins bind and destroy CoQ10 in blood
Statins block CoQ10 absorption in the gut
CoQ10 is made from LDL particles
Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase upstream of farnesyl pyrophosphate, which supplies both cholesterol and the isoprenoid tail of coenzyme Q10.
qz0ez4d: A client taking warfarin started coenzyme Q10. Which change has been reported?
Coenzyme Q10 is structurally similar to vitamin K, and case reports describe reduced warfarin effect with a lower INR.
q1shm4bq: A client on a statin who takes CoQ10 reports severe muscle pain and dark urine. Which concern is most relevant?
Severe muscle pain with dark urine in a patient on a statin raises concern for rhabdomyolysis; CoQ10 has not been shown to reliably prevent statin muscle injury.
qxzw9mq: Arsenic poisoning inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase by binding which cofactor?
Arsenite binds the dithiol of lipoic acid, inhibiting PDH and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase; the PDH cofactors are thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD and NAD+.
q18gfnjf: A client with type 2 diabetes on a sulfonylurea starts alpha-lipoic acid. Which effect is most relevant?
Added risk of low blood glucose
Alpha-lipoic acid may lower blood glucose and add to insulin or sulfonylureas; it has also been linked in case reports to insulin autoimmune syndrome with recurrent hypoglycemia.
q85zggi: A toddler swallowed many alpha-lipoic acid capsules from a parent's supply. Which findings are reported in case reports?
Case reports describe seizures, metabolic acidosis and severe multi-organ toxicity after large ingestions of alpha-lipoic acid by young children.
q1gr20mt: A 62-year-old woman cannot void 2 days after abdominal surgery. A bladder scan shows 700 mL, and there is no outlet obstruction. Which receptor should a drug directly activate to relieve her retention?
Muscarinic M3 receptor on the detrusor muscle
Nicotinic NN receptor at autonomic ganglia
Alpha-1 receptor on the internal sphincter
Beta-3 receptor on detrusor smooth muscle
Bethanechol is a cholinesterase-resistant muscarinic agonist that contracts the detrusor; it is used for nonobstructive urinary retention.
q2aibj2: A 58-year-old woman with Sjogren syndrome has a severely dry mouth that impairs eating. She is prescribed an oral drug that increases saliva and also causes sweating. What is its mechanism of action?
Pilocarpine directly stimulates muscarinic receptors on exocrine glands, increasing salivation, lacrimation and sweating.
qq27ywq: A 28-year-old woman has ptosis and diplopia that worsen toward evening. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are positive. The oral drug started for symptom control works by which mechanism?
Direct stimulation of muscle nicotinic receptors
Pyridostigmine reversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase, raising ACh at the neuromuscular junction; as a quaternary amine it does not enter the CNS.
q1voq8pr: A 4-year-old boy has flushed, dry skin, dilated pupils, fever, urinary retention and agitated delirium after eating jimsonweed seeds. Which drug reverses both his central and peripheral toxicity?
Physostigmine is a tertiary amine cholinesterase inhibitor that crosses the blood-brain barrier and reverses anticholinergic delirium.
q1cdm3m1: A farmer has miosis, bronchorrhea, bradycardia and muscle fasciculations after spraying an organophosphate insecticide. After atropine, which drug should be given early to regenerate acetylcholinesterase before aging occurs?
Pralidoxime removes the phosphate group from acetylcholinesterase if given before the enzyme-inhibitor bond ages; it helps nicotinic weakness that atropine cannot reverse.
q1x8i2sn: A 40-year-old man with organophosphate poisoning receives repeated doses of IV atropine until his secretions dry. Which finding will persist despite adequate atropinization?
Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors only; nicotinic effects at the neuromuscular junction need pralidoxime.
q1t77og8: At the end of surgery, an anesthesiologist reverses rocuronium with neostigmine and gives glycopyrrolate at the same time. What is the main purpose of the glycopyrrolate?
Prolong neostigmine action at the endplate
Block nicotinic receptors at the ganglia
Reverse residual sedation from volatile agents
Glycopyrrolate is a quaternary antimuscarinic that blocks the muscarinic effects of neostigmine without entering the CNS.
qms225w: A 24-year-old man started on haloperidol 2 weeks ago develops cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia and a shuffling gait. Which drug is most appropriate, and how does it work?
Bromocriptine, a dopamine D2 receptor agonist
Antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism responds to centrally acting antimuscarinics such as benztropine, which restore dopamine-acetylcholine balance in the striatum.
q119od45: A healthy volunteer receives a continuous IV infusion of isoproterenol. Which combination of hemodynamic changes is expected?
Increased heart rate and decreased diastolic pressure
Decreased heart rate and increased diastolic pressure
Increased heart rate and increased diastolic pressure
Decreased heart rate and decreased systolic pressure
Isoproterenol is a nonselective beta agonist: beta-1 raises heart rate and contractility while beta-2 vasodilation lowers diastolic pressure.
q1em7h0p: A volunteer receives IV phenylephrine. Mean arterial pressure rises and heart rate falls from 72 to 54 beats per minute. What best explains the fall in heart rate?
Direct blockade of cardiac beta-1 receptors
Direct stimulation of cardiac muscarinic receptors
Inhibition of the SA node funny current
Phenylephrine is a selective alpha-1 agonist; the rise in pressure triggers a baroreceptor-mediated reflex bradycardia.
qe20xxs: In an experiment, an animal pretreated with phentolamine is given IV epinephrine, and mean arterial pressure falls instead of rising. Which receptor mediates this fall?
Beta-2 receptors in skeletal muscle arterioles
Alpha-2 receptors on presynaptic nerve endings
Dopamine D1 receptors in the renal vasculature
Epinephrine reversal: with alpha receptors blocked, unopposed beta-2 vasodilation lowers blood pressure.
qm23oi5: A 66-year-old woman with septic shock remains hypotensive after fluids and is started on norepinephrine. Which receptor profile best explains its effects?
Alpha-1 and beta-1 agonism with little beta-2 effect
Beta-1 and beta-2 agonism with little alpha effect
Alpha-1 agonism with no beta receptor activity
Dopamine D1 and beta-1 agonism at low doses
Norepinephrine stimulates alpha-1 and beta-1 but has weak beta-2 activity, so it raises SVR and pressure; heart rate may fall reflexively.
q1ynlrfs: A 45-year-old man taking phenelzine eats aged cheese and develops a pounding headache and blood pressure of 232/128. Which drug is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
Clonidine, a central alpha-2 receptor agonist
Tyramine releases norepinephrine when MAO is inhibited; IV phentolamine rapidly reverses the alpha-mediated hypertensive crisis.
q1tkn82o: A 40-year-old woman has episodic headaches, palpitations and sweating. Plasma metanephrines are high and CT shows a 4-cm adrenal mass. Which drug should be started first to prepare her for surgery?
Irreversible alpha blockade must come before any beta blocker so that unopposed alpha vasoconstriction does not cause a hypertensive crisis.
q1rcmbq8: A 68-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia faints when he stands up a few hours after the first dose of a new medication. Which mechanism caused this?
Central alpha-2 agonism lowering sympathetic outflow
Alpha-1 antagonists such as prazosin cause first-dose orthostatic hypotension; start at bedtime with a low dose.
q1fakd3l: A 50-year-old man runs out of an antihypertensive and within 24 hours develops headache, tremor, tachycardia and blood pressure of 210/120. The drug he stopped most likely acts by which mechanism?
Central alpha-2 agonism reducing sympathetic outflow
Nonselective beta antagonism reducing renin release
Direct arteriolar dilation by opening K+ channels
Abrupt clonidine withdrawal causes rebound sympathetic overactivity and severe hypertension; taper the dose.
q1ekr7ce: A 29-year-old pregnant woman is treated for chronic hypertension. Later in pregnancy she develops anemia with a positive direct Coombs test. Which drug most likely caused this?
Methyldopa, a central alpha-2 agonist prodrug safe in pregnancy, can cause a positive Coombs test and autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
qi0idbh: A 70-year-old man with autonomic failure from Parkinson disease is prescribed midodrine for orthostatic hypotension. Which adverse effect is most characteristic of this drug?
Midodrine is an alpha-1 agonist prodrug; supine hypertension is its key adverse effect, so doses are not given near bedtime.
q8027at: A 61-year-old man in cardiogenic shock receives a drug that increases contractility and cardiac output with a mild decrease in systemic vascular resistance. Which receptor does this drug primarily stimulate?
Dobutamine is mainly a beta-1 agonist, raising contractility; minor beta-2 effects mildly lower SVR.
q4z9w4l: A 57-year-old man taking long-term carvedilol is admitted with low-output heart failure. An inotrope is chosen that does not depend on beta receptors. What is its mechanism?
Stimulation of beta-1 receptors, raising cAMP
Inhibition of Na/K-ATPase, raising intracellular calcium
Sensitization of troponin C to calcium ions
Milrinone inhibits PDE-3, increasing cAMP in myocardium (inotropy) and vascular smooth muscle (vasodilation); it bypasses blocked beta receptors.
q1f0ob53: A 60-year-old man in shock is started on dopamine and titrated to 15 mcg/kg/min. At this dose, the rise in systemic vascular resistance is due to stimulation of which receptors?
Dopamine is dose dependent: D1 at low doses, beta-1 at moderate doses and alpha-1 vasoconstriction at high doses.
q1f46hyq: A 30-year-old woman with mild asthma takes propranolol before a recital for stage fright and develops wheezing within an hour. What is the mechanism?
Blockade of beta-1 receptors in airway glands
Stimulation of M3 receptors in the airways
Increased leukotriene synthesis in mast cells
Nonselective beta blockers block beta-2-mediated bronchodilation and can provoke bronchospasm in asthma.
q1lj6lv5: A 55-year-old man with type 1 diabetes starts metoprolol after a myocardial infarction. Which warning symptom of hypoglycemia is least likely to be blunted by this drug?
Sweating is mediated by sympathetic cholinergic fibers, so it persists on beta blockers, while tachycardia and palpitations are masked.
q1z0cush: A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks of gestation has a blood pressure of 172/112 and is given IV labetalol. Which pharmacologic action does this drug have?
Selective beta-1 blockade with partial agonism
Direct arteriolar dilation by releasing nitric oxide
Central alpha-2 agonism reducing sympathetic tone
Labetalol blocks alpha-1, beta-1 and beta-2 receptors and is a first-line agent for severe hypertension in pregnancy.
qxl5nb2: A 63-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is started on carvedilol instead of metoprolol. Which additional property distinguishes carvedilol?
Selective blockade of beta-1 receptors only
Inhibition of the cardiac funny sodium current
Carvedilol is a nonselective beta blocker that also blocks alpha-1 receptors, producing vasodilation; it reduces mortality in HFrEF.
qyzcad5: A 58-year-old man with acute aortic dissection is given an esmolol infusion for rate control, and its effect wears off within 15 minutes of stopping it. What explains this short duration?
Hydrolysis by red blood cell esterases
Rapid renal excretion of unchanged drug
Redistribution from the heart into fat tissue
Esmolol has an ester linkage cleaved by RBC esterases, giving a half-life of about 9 minutes.
qfsq4my: A 52-year-old woman develops a persistent dry cough 3 weeks after starting a new antihypertensive. Her chest radiograph is normal. Accumulation of which substance is responsible?
ACE (kininase II) breaks down bradykinin; ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin, causing cough and angioedema.
q17n9ev7: A 52-year-old woman with an ACE inhibitor cough is switched to losartan and her cough resolves while her blood pressure remains controlled. Why does losartan avoid this effect?
It blocks AT1 receptors and spares bradykinin breakdown
It inhibits renin and lowers angiotensin I production
It inhibits ACE but spares substance P breakdown
It blocks mineralocorticoid receptors in the kidney
ARBs block the AT1 receptor without inhibiting ACE, so bradykinin is still degraded.
qfrh2a6: A 70-year-old man with bilateral renal artery stenosis starts enalapril. One week later his serum creatinine has risen by 60 percent. What is the mechanism?
Loss of angiotensin II efferent arteriolar constriction
Direct tubular toxicity from the active metabolite
With poor renal perfusion, GFR depends on angiotensin II constriction of the efferent arteriole; ACE inhibitors remove it and GFR falls.
q1rmkjz2: A 64-year-old woman with HFrEF is switched from enalapril to sacubitril-valsartan after a 36-hour washout. Sacubitril increases the levels of which substances?
Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin, which degrades natriuretic peptides; the washout after stopping the ACE inhibitor prevents angioedema from excess bradykinin.
qm4w3cg: A 58-year-old man with cirrhotic ascites develops painful bilateral breast enlargement 3 months after starting a diuretic. Which drug action causes this adverse effect?
Blockade of ENaC in collecting ducts
Spironolactone also blocks androgen receptors and affects steroidogenesis, causing gynecomastia; eplerenone is more selective.
qajtedi: A 66-year-old man taking eplerenone after a myocardial infarction is given clarithromycin for pneumonia. Three days later his potassium is 6.8 mEq/L. What is the mechanism?
Eplerenone is a CYP3A4 substrate; strong inhibitors such as clarithromycin raise levels and cause hyperkalemia.
qpsyzn6: A 70-year-old woman with acute pulmonary edema receives IV furosemide and has a brisk diuresis. Which transporter does this drug inhibit?
Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule
Epithelial sodium channel in the collecting duct
Carbonic anhydrase in the proximal convoluted tubule
Loop diuretics inhibit NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, the most potent site of sodium reabsorption.
q77fjj: A 59-year-old man with heart failure and a documented severe sulfonamide allergy (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) needs a loop diuretic. Which agent is preferred?
Ethacrynic acid is the only loop diuretic that is not a sulfonamide; however, it is more ototoxic.
qp3xdf6: A 66-year-old man started on hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension later has a gout flare. Which set of laboratory changes is expected with this drug?
Thiazides cause hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, hyperuricemia, hyperglycemia and hyperlipidemia.
qp9g0ym: A 45-year-old man has recurrent calcium oxalate kidney stones caused by idiopathic hypercalciuria. Which diuretic will lower his urinary calcium excretion?
Thiazide-type diuretics increase calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule, lowering urinary calcium; loop diuretics increase calcium excretion.
q1m24n6s: A 30-year-old climber takes acetazolamide before ascending to 4,500 meters. Which acid-base disturbance does this drug produce?
Carbonic anhydrase inhibition causes bicarbonate loss in urine and a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis, which stimulates ventilation at altitude.
qczsqsj: A 35-year-old man with a traumatic brain injury and rising intracranial pressure is considered for IV mannitol. Which condition is a contraindication to this drug?
Mannitol expands extracellular volume before it is excreted; in anuria or heart failure it can precipitate pulmonary edema.
q4h2rsp: A 40-year-old woman taking lithium for bipolar disorder has polyuria. Urine osmolality does not rise after desmopressin. Which drug is preferred to treat her polyuria?
Amiloride blocks ENaC, preventing lithium entry into collecting duct cells and treating lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
q71evpy: A 68-year-old man with small cell lung cancer has euvolemic hyponatremia with a sodium of 121 mEq/L and concentrated urine. Which drug antagonizes vasopressin V2 receptors in the collecting duct?
Tolvaptan is an oral V2 receptor antagonist used for SIADH; correct sodium slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination.
qa5kfnc: A 74-year-old woman with heart failure and atrial fibrillation is started on digoxin. By which mechanism does digoxin increase myocardial contractility?
Opening L-type channels, raising calcium entry
Digoxin inhibits the Na/K-ATPase; higher intracellular sodium slows the Na/Ca exchanger, so more calcium is stored and released.
q1f3260y: A 79-year-old woman taking digoxin has nausea, yellow-tinted vision and bidirectional ventricular tachycardia. Her potassium is 6.1 mEq/L. What is the most appropriate treatment?
Digoxin immune Fab binds digoxin and is indicated for life-threatening arrhythmias or hyperkalemia above 5 mEq/L in digoxin toxicity.
q1ysw5yl: A 72-year-old man has stable serum digoxin levels for atrial fibrillation. A new drug is added, and 2 weeks later his digoxin level has nearly doubled. Which added drug is most likely responsible?
Amiodarone (like verapamil and quinidine) inhibits P-glycoprotein and reduces digoxin clearance; halve the digoxin dose.
q175omme: A 60-year-old man who is a slow acetylator takes a class IA antiarrhythmic and develops arthralgias, pleuritic chest pain and anti-histone antibodies. Which drug is responsible?
Procainamide is acetylated in the liver; slow acetylators are prone to drug-induced lupus with anti-histone antibodies.
qzdxh33: A 55-year-old woman on an antiarrhythmic develops tinnitus, headache, blurred vision and diarrhea, along with a prolonged QT interval. Which drug most likely caused these findings?
Quinidine causes cinchonism (tinnitus, headache, vertigo, visual changes) and diarrhea, and its class IA effect prolongs QT.
q4amku2: A 61-year-old man has recurrent ventricular tachycardia during an acute myocardial infarction and is given IV lidocaine. Why are class IB agents most effective in ischemic tissue?
They block potassium channels and prolong QT
They slow conduction through the AV node
They dissociate slowly from resting channels
Class IB drugs preferentially block open and inactivated sodium channels, which are abundant in depolarized ischemic myocardium.
q1xmurda: A 66-year-old man with a prior myocardial infarction and frequent premature ventricular complexes is being treated. Which antiarrhythmic is contraindicated because it increases mortality in this setting?
In the CAST trial, class IC agents increased mortality after MI; avoid them in structural heart disease.
qj3o0h4: A 68-year-old man taking a long-term antiarrhythmic develops dyspnea with reticular lung infiltrates, an elevated TSH and blue-gray skin on his face. Which monitoring should accompany this drug?
Pulmonary, thyroid and liver function tests
Serum drug levels and complete blood counts
Fasting glucose and a fasting lipid panel
Amiodarone causes pulmonary fibrosis, hypo- or hyperthyroidism, hepatotoxicity, corneal deposits and skin discoloration.
q185jl52: A 59-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation starts an antiarrhythmic that has both beta-blocking and potassium channel-blocking activity. Her QT lengthens to 540 ms. Which drug was started?
Sotalol is a class III agent with nonselective beta blockade; it is renally cleared and can cause torsades de pointes.
q8fhj6m: A 25-year-old woman with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia receives IV adenosine, but the arrhythmia does not convert even at higher doses. She drinks large amounts of coffee. Which drug also reduces adenosine efficacy?
Methylxanthines such as caffeine and theophylline block adenosine receptors; dipyridamole and carbamazepine enhance its effect.
qwiu2p1: A 67-year-old woman takes verapamil to control the rate of atrial fibrillation. Which adverse effect is most characteristic of this drug?
Verapamil commonly causes constipation and can cause bradycardia and AV block; nondihydropyridines do not cause reflex tachycardia.
q1ihp58n: A 60-year-old woman starts nifedipine for hypertension and develops ankle edema and a faster heart rate. What explains the edema?
Precapillary arteriolar dilation raising capillary pressure
Lymphatic obstruction from tissue drug deposits
Dihydropyridines dilate arterioles but not venules, raising capillary hydrostatic pressure; diuretics do not help this edema.
q1x6pve7: A 59-year-old man with HFrEF in sinus rhythm has a resting heart rate of 78 despite maximal beta blocker therapy. He starts a drug that inhibits the funny sodium current in the SA node. Which adverse effect is characteristic?
Ivabradine blocks If channels in the SA node and similar HCN channels in the retina, causing phosphenes; it also causes bradycardia.
q1iz2nmq: A 70-year-old man has chronic stable angina despite a beta blocker and nitrate. He starts ranolazine, which does not change his heart rate or blood pressure. What is its mechanism?
Inhibition of the late sodium current
Release of nitric oxide in venous beds
Inhibition of the funny current in the SA node
Ranolazine blocks the late inward sodium current, reducing calcium overload and oxygen demand; it can prolong QT.
q1k7jext: A 63-year-old man takes sublingual nitroglycerin for chest pain 2 hours after taking sildenafil and becomes profoundly hypotensive. What is the mechanism?
Additive increase in smooth muscle cGMP
Additive increase in cardiac myocyte cAMP
Additive alpha-1 blockade in venous smooth muscle
Nitrates raise cGMP via nitric oxide and PDE-5 inhibitors block cGMP breakdown, causing severe vasodilation.
q16ukwr7: A 64-year-old woman with stable angina finds that her long-acting nitrate seems to work less well after a few weeks. Which regimen best prevents this problem?
A daily nitrate-free interval of 10 to 12 hours
Doubling the nitrate dose every two weeks
Nitrate tolerance develops with continuous exposure; a daily nitrate-free period restores responsiveness.
qr3c77k: A 58-year-old man is treated with an IV nitroprusside infusion for 3 days. He becomes confused and develops lactic acidosis with a high mixed venous oxygen saturation. Which antidote is most appropriate?
Nitroprusside releases cyanide, which blocks cytochrome oxidase; hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin.
q1n5mxpt: A 48-year-old man with hypertension is given hydralazine. His physician adds a beta blocker and a diuretic. Which effects of hydralazine are these drugs meant to counteract?
Bradycardia with heart block and hyperkalemia
Hydralazine directly dilates arterioles, triggering reflex sympathetic activation and renin-mediated fluid retention.
q1bwjm1w: A 50-year-old man with refractory hypertension develops excessive hair growth on his face and arms after starting a new oral antihypertensive. What is the mechanism of this drug?
Blocking L-type calcium channels in arterioles
Minoxidil opens K-ATP channels, hyperpolarizing arteriolar smooth muscle; hypertrichosis and pericardial effusion are adverse effects.
q1jj8jx9: A 35-year-old woman with pulmonary arterial hypertension starts an oral drug that requires monthly liver tests and pregnancy tests because it is teratogenic. What is the mechanism?
Bosentan blocks ETA and ETB receptors, reducing pulmonary vasoconstriction; it is hepatotoxic and teratogenic.
q1m4hz41: A 62-year-old man taking simvastatin is given clarithromycin for pneumonia. Five days later he has diffuse muscle pain and a creatine kinase of 12,000 U/L. What is the mechanism of this interaction?
Displacement of the statin from albumin
Inhibition of renal tubular statin excretion
Simvastatin is metabolized by CYP3A4; strong inhibitors raise its levels and the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis.
q1jh1koo: A 55-year-old woman with an LDL of 190 mg/dL starts atorvastatin. Which enzyme, which catalyzes the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis, does this drug inhibit?
Statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, which converts HMG-CoA to mevalonate; hepatocytes then upregulate LDL receptors.
qmlpd8q: A 50-year-old man started on niacin for low HDL complains of intense facial flushing and warmth after each dose. Which measure best reduces this effect?
Taking each dose on an empty stomach
Niacin flushing is mediated by prostaglandins (PGD2); aspirin taken beforehand blocks their synthesis.
qwt7vyz: A 50-year-old man has fasting triglycerides of 1,100 mg/dL and a history of pancreatitis. He starts fenofibrate. What is its mechanism?
Inhibition of intestinal NPC1L1 cholesterol uptake
Inhibition of hepatic HMG-CoA reductase activity
Fibrates activate PPAR-alpha, upregulating lipoprotein lipase and lowering triglycerides; they increase gallstone risk.
q1ipgm1o: A 60-year-old man cannot reach his LDL target on a maximal statin dose, so ezetimibe is added. Which protein does ezetimibe inhibit?
NPC1L1 sterol transporter in the intestine
Ezetimibe blocks NPC1L1 at the brush border, reducing intestinal cholesterol absorption.
q1f0l5uj: A 45-year-old woman with high LDL starts cholestyramine. Six weeks later her LDL is lower, but another lipid value has worsened. Which adverse effect is most likely?
Bile acid sequestrants can raise triglycerides; they also cause GI upset and reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamins and many drugs.
qzcelsq: A 38-year-old man with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia remains above his LDL goal on a statin and ezetimibe. He starts a subcutaneous monoclonal antibody every 2 weeks. What is its target?
Evolocumab binds PCSK9, preventing LDL receptor degradation and increasing LDL clearance.
q1ogjtfe: A 22-year-old man with secondary syphilis receives IM benzathine penicillin G. Which bacterial process does this drug inhibit?
Polymerization of peptidoglycan by binding D-Ala-D-Ala
Synthesis of mycolic acids in the cell envelope
Penicillins bind penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases), blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking.
q1m5vxhm: A 30-year-old man who injects drugs has methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia, and the isolate produces penicillinase. Why is nafcillin effective against this organism?
Its bulky side chain blocks beta-lactamase access
It binds altered PBP2a with high affinity
It binds D-Ala-D-Ala termini of cell wall precursors
Nafcillin and oxacillin have bulky R groups that protect the beta-lactam ring from penicillinase; they do not cover MRSA.
qwcnr9n: A 6-year-old boy with acute otitis media fails amoxicillin therapy because of a beta-lactamase-producing Moraxella. He is switched to amoxicillin-clavulanate. What is the role of clavulanate?
Blocks renal tubular secretion of amoxicillin
Clavulanate is a suicide inhibitor of many beta-lactamases, protecting amoxicillin; probenecid is the drug that blocks tubular secretion.
q10c7ch: A 70-year-old man has enterococcal bacteremia that is resistant to vancomycin. What is the molecular basis of this resistance?
Production of an altered PBP2a transpeptidase
Vancomycin binds D-Ala-D-Ala; VRE replaces it with D-Ala-D-Lac, which vancomycin binds poorly.
q1k6hus1: A 45-year-old woman receiving her first dose of IV vancomycin develops flushing and pruritus of the face, neck and upper chest. Her blood pressure is stable. Which measure is most appropriate?
Slow the infusion and give an antihistamine
Stop the drug permanently and give epinephrine
Switch to IV nafcillin for the full course
The vancomycin infusion reaction is caused by non-IgE histamine release from mast cells; it is not a true allergy and responds to slower infusion and antihistamines.
q1a32pac: A 5-day-old neonate with suspected bacterial sepsis has significant jaundice. The team chooses cefotaxime rather than ceftriaxone. What is the main reason?
Ceftriaxone does not cross the blood-brain barrier
Ceftriaxone lacks activity against group B streptococci
Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin (risk of kernicterus) and precipitates with IV calcium in neonates.
q1i27wx: A 64-year-old woman has a skin and soft tissue infection with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. She receives the only cephalosporin with reliable MRSA activity. Why does it work?
It binds PBP2a with high affinity
It binds the D-Ala-D-Ala cell wall terminus
Ceftaroline, a fifth-generation cephalosporin, binds the altered PBP2a of MRSA.
qpgp6ay: A 54-year-old man with a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin has Pseudomonas aeruginosa pneumonia. Which beta-lactam can most safely be given?
Aztreonam is a monobactam with minimal cross-reactivity with penicillins; it covers only gram-negative rods, including Pseudomonas.
q1drhb0v: A 72-year-old man with renal impairment is treated for a polymicrobial abdominal abscess with imipenem-cilastatin and has a generalized seizure. What is the role of cilastatin?
Blocks renal tubular secretion of imipenem
Prevents the seizures caused by imipenem
Cilastatin inhibits renal dehydropeptidase I, preventing imipenem inactivation; carbapenems lower the seizure threshold.
q162p8o8: A 52-year-old woman has a liver abscess with Bacteroides fragilis. Why would gentamicin alone be ineffective?
Its uptake into bacteria requires oxygen
It cannot penetrate the abscess capsule
Aminoglycoside uptake requires oxygen-dependent transport, so anaerobes are intrinsically resistant.
qwbkr52: A 76-year-old man with enterococcal endocarditis receives ampicillin and gentamicin. During treatment he is also given high-dose IV furosemide. Which toxicity is now of greatest concern?
Aminoglycosides and loop diuretics both damage the inner ear; combined use increases ototoxicity and also nephrotoxicity.
q1bof6u4: A 24-year-old woman with Lyme disease takes doxycycline with her daily calcium carbonate and iron supplement, and her infection responds poorly. What is the mechanism of this interaction?
Chelation by divalent cations reducing absorption
Induction of CYP3A4 increasing drug clearance
Raised gastric pH preventing tablet dissolution
Increased renal tubular secretion of the drug
Tetracyclines chelate calcium, magnesium, aluminum and iron, sharply reducing oral absorption.
q1fca1eo: A 30-year-old woman with Rocky Mountain spotted fever is treated with doxycycline. How does this drug stop bacterial protein synthesis?
Blocks aminoacyl-tRNA binding at the 30S A site
Blocks peptidyl transferase on the 50S subunit
Causes misreading of mRNA codons at the 30S
Tetracyclines bind the 30S subunit and prevent aminoacyl-tRNA from attaching to the acceptor (A) site.
q1vt3pe: A 68-year-old man with community-acquired pneumonia is given azithromycin. Which molecular target does this drug bind?
Macrolides bind 23S rRNA on the 50S subunit and block translocation; they can prolong the QT interval.
q13lyj53: A 52-year-old woman with diabetic gastroparesis is given low-dose erythromycin to improve gastric emptying. Which mechanism explains this effect?
Macrolides, especially erythromycin, stimulate motilin receptors and increase GI motility.
qg4y11x: A 66-year-old woman treated with an antibiotic for an aspiration lung abscess develops profuse watery diarrhea and a positive toxin assay. The antibiotic binds the 50S subunit and has good anaerobic coverage. Which drug was it?
Clindamycin binds the 50S subunit, covers anaerobes above the diaphragm and is strongly associated with C. difficile infection.
q12l6faj: A 45-year-old man taking sertraline is given linezolid for vancomycin-resistant enterococcal bacteremia. Two days later he has agitation, hyperthermia, clonus and diarrhea. What property of linezolid explains this?
Inhibition of CYP2D6 raising sertraline levels
Linezolid is a weak MAO inhibitor and can cause serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs; it also causes thrombocytopenia.
q90whz6: A premature infant treated with an antibiotic for meningitis develops vomiting, an ashen-gray color, hypotension and cardiovascular collapse. The infant lacks adequate UDP-glucuronyltransferase. Which drug was given?
Gray baby syndrome results when neonates cannot glucuronidate chloramphenicol, a 50S peptidyltransferase inhibitor.
q1pwhexp: A 70-year-old man with MRSA bacteremia improves on daptomycin, but he later develops MRSA pneumonia that does not respond to this drug. Why is daptomycin ineffective here?
It is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant
It does not penetrate into lung tissue
MRSA in the lung loses its lipid membrane
It is rapidly cleared by alveolar macrophages
Daptomycin, a lipopeptide that depolarizes the bacterial membrane, is inactivated by surfactant; monitor CK for myopathy.
q19867ys: A 72-year-old woman taking prednisone for COPD is treated with ciprofloxacin for pyelonephritis and feels a pop with sudden pain at the back of her ankle. What is the mechanism of the drug, and what happened?
DNA gyrase inhibitor causing tendon rupture
Cell wall synthesis inhibitor causing tendinitis
Folate synthesis inhibitor causing a fracture
Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; tendon rupture risk rises with age and corticosteroids.
q1g0fkep: A 66-year-old man taking theophylline for COPD is treated with ciprofloxacin. Four days later he has nausea, tachycardia and a seizure. What explains this interaction?
Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2, the main enzyme metabolizing theophylline and tizanidine, raising their levels.
qg5n7f8: A 40-year-old man with HIV takes TMP-SMX for Pneumocystis prophylaxis. Which pair of enzymes in folate synthesis does this combination block?
Sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase and trimethoprim inhibits bacterial DHFR, a sequential blockade.
qndu4c3: A 70-year-old man taking lisinopril is treated with TMP-SMX for a urinary tract infection. His potassium rises from 4.6 to 6.2 mEq/L. Which mechanism of trimethoprim explains this?
Blockade of ENaC in the collecting duct
Inhibition of renin release from the kidney
Shift of potassium out of cells
Trimethoprim blocks the epithelial sodium channel like amiloride, reducing potassium secretion.
qduxo5z: A 36-year-old woman treated for bacterial vaginosis drinks wine at a party and develops flushing, headache, nausea and palpitations. Which enzyme does the drug inhibit to cause this?
Metronidazole causes a disulfiram-like reaction by inhibiting aldehyde dehydrogenase, allowing acetaldehyde to build up.
q1kmzc3r: An 82-year-old woman has taken nitrofurantoin for recurrent urinary tract infections for 2 years. She now has progressive dyspnea and bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Which drug toxicity is most likely?
Long-term nitrofurantoin can cause chronic pulmonary fibrosis; acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis also occurs.
q18kdqdf: A 38-year-old man with HIV starts dapsone for Pneumocystis prophylaxis. He becomes cyanotic with a pulse oximetry reading of 85 percent that does not improve with oxygen, and his blood is chocolate-brown. What is the treatment?
Dapsone causes methemoglobinemia; methylene blue reduces ferric to ferrous iron (avoid in G6PD deficiency).
q1x7xlyz: A 34-year-old man has active tuberculosis resistant to isoniazid. Sequencing shows a mutation in katG. How does this mutation cause resistance?
Loss of the enzyme that activates the prodrug
Increased drug efflux from the bacterial cell
Overexpression of the mycolic acid synthase
Altered RNA polymerase beta subunit binding
Isoniazid is a prodrug activated by catalase-peroxidase (KatG); it then inhibits mycolic acid synthesis (InhA).
q5wooad: A 26-year-old woman taking combined oral contraceptives starts treatment for latent tuberculosis and becomes pregnant 3 months later. She also noticed orange urine. Which mechanism explains the contraceptive failure?
Chelation of estrogen in the gut
Rifampin is a potent CYP450 inducer that lowers levels of estrogens, warfarin, protease inhibitors and many other drugs.
qhqnk7s: A 50-year-old man with active tuberculosis is treated with a 4-drug regimen. One drug inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Which mutation causes resistance to it?
rpoB mutation altering the RNA polymerase
pncA mutation preventing activation to pyrazinoic acid
Rifampin binds the beta subunit of RNA polymerase encoded by rpoB; resistance develops quickly if used alone.
q1g5jom0: A 45-year-old man receiving 4-drug therapy for pulmonary tuberculosis develops a painful, swollen great toe in the second month. Which drug is most likely responsible?
Pyrazinamide decreases renal urate excretion, causing hyperuricemia and gout; it is also hepatotoxic.
qqyk37o: A 52-year-old man on treatment for tuberculosis has blurred vision and cannot distinguish red from green. Which enzyme does the responsible drug inhibit?
Ethambutol inhibits arabinosyltransferase (arabinogalactan synthesis) and causes optic neuritis with red-green color blindness.
q1dymmx6: A 40-year-old man with cryptococcal meningitis is treated with amphotericin B. Which mechanism and laboratory toxicity are expected?
Amphotericin binds ergosterol and forms membrane pores; it causes nephrotoxicity with potassium and magnesium wasting.
qg0nsy1: A 65-year-old woman stable on warfarin is prescribed fluconazole for esophageal candidiasis. Her INR rises from 2.5 to 6.1. What is the mechanism?
Reduced synthesis of vitamin K by gut flora
Azoles inhibit fungal 14-alpha-demethylase and human CYP enzymes; fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9, which clears S-warfarin.
q1rqwpni: A 58-year-old woman in the ICU has candidemia with Candida glabrata. She is treated with caspofungin. What is its target?
Echinocandins inhibit beta-1,3-D-glucan synthesis in the fungal cell wall; they cause little toxicity.
qafowx: A 50-year-old man has thick, discolored toenails with dermatophytes on culture. He starts a 12-week oral course of terbinafine. Which enzyme does it inhibit?
Terbinafine inhibits squalene epoxidase, causing toxic squalene to build up; monitor for hepatotoxicity.
qi5h8mm: A 35-year-old man with cryptococcal meningitis receives amphotericin B with a second agent. He later develops pancytopenia. The second agent is converted within fungi by which enzyme?
Flucytosine is converted to 5-fluorouracil by fungal cytosine deaminase, inhibiting DNA and RNA synthesis; bone marrow suppression occurs.
qajqqby: A 55-year-old man with leukemia and invasive aspergillosis starts voriconazole. Two days later he reports altered color perception and blurry vision. Which statement about this effect is most accurate?
It is a common and usually transient effect
It reflects optic neuritis from the drug
It indicates fungal spread to the eye
Transient visual disturbances are common with voriconazole; photosensitivity and hepatotoxicity also occur.
q1nvszju: A 66-year-old woman receiving unfractionated heparin after knee replacement has a platelet count that falls from 250,000 to 90,000 on day 7, with a new leg DVT. What is the most appropriate anticoagulant?
HIT is caused by antibodies to heparin-platelet factor 4; stop all heparins and use a direct thrombin inhibitor such as argatroban.
q120a9hv: A 55-year-old man develops bleeding after receiving too much unfractionated heparin during cardiac catheterization. Which antidote is most appropriate, and how does it act?
Protamine, a basic protein binding heparin
Vitamin K, restoring clotting factor synthesis
Andexanet, a decoy factor Xa protein
Protamine is positively charged and binds negatively charged heparin, neutralizing it.
q9rkv78: A 70-year-old man on warfarin has an INR of 9.5 and active GI bleeding. Which treatment provides the fastest reversal?
Holding warfarin and giving oral vitamin K
Four-factor PCC replaces factors II, VII, IX and X immediately; IV vitamin K is also given for sustained reversal.
qgabuq7: A 76-year-old woman taking dabigatran for atrial fibrillation has a subdural hematoma needing emergency surgery. Which agent specifically reverses this drug?
Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor.
qwpka2a: A 58-year-old man has a stent thrombosis despite taking clopidogrel. Genetic testing shows he is a CYP2C19 poor metabolizer. Why did the drug fail?
It is a prodrug needing CYP2C19 activation
It is inactivated faster by CYP2C19
It requires CYP2C19 for intestinal uptake
Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by CYP2C19 to irreversibly block the P2Y12 ADP receptor; ticagrelor does not need activation.
q1m5ok9d: A 62-year-old man takes low-dose aspirin daily to prevent heart attacks. Why does a single dose inhibit platelet function for the life of the platelet?
It irreversibly blocks platelet P2Y12 receptors
Platelets lack a nucleus and cannot make new COX-1, so irreversible acetylation lasts 7 to 10 days.
q10259ht: A 68-year-old woman with an acute ischemic stroke arrives 2 hours after symptom onset and receives alteplase. Which mechanism and major risk does this drug have?
Tissue plasminogen activators convert plasminogen to plasmin to lyse fibrin; intracranial bleeding is the major risk.
q1vc06wr: A drug is given by continuous IV infusion. It has first-order elimination and a half-life of 6 hours. How long will it take to reach approximately 94 percent of steady-state concentration?
Time to steady state depends only on half-life: about 50, 75, 88 and 94 percent are reached after 1, 2, 3 and 4 half-lives.
q6lrrs4: A drug has a volume of distribution of 40 L and bioavailability of 1. The target plasma concentration is 10 mg/L. What loading dose is needed?
Loading dose equals target concentration times volume of distribution divided by bioavailability: 10 times 40 = 400 mg.
qvo46cw: A drug has a clearance of 5 L/h and an oral bioavailability of 0.5. The target steady-state concentration is 2 mg/L, given every 12 hours. What maintenance dose is needed?
Maintenance dose equals Css times CL times dosing interval divided by F: 2 times 5 times 12 divided by 0.5 = 240 mg.
qilfawg: A drug has a volume of distribution of 70 L and a clearance of 7 L/h. What is its approximate elimination half-life?
Half-life equals 0.7 times Vd divided by CL: 0.7 times 70 divided by 7 = 7 hours.
q1gdr42g: A 500 mg IV dose of a drug produces an initial plasma concentration of 2 mg/L. Which statement best describes this drug?
It is confined mostly to the plasma
It distributes mainly in extracellular fluid
It is highly bound to plasma proteins
Vd equals dose divided by concentration (250 L), far above total body water, so the drug is sequestered in tissues.
q55w0ly: In a phase 1 study, a drug has an ED50 of 10 mg and a TD50 of 200 mg. What is its therapeutic index?
Therapeutic index equals TD50 divided by ED50; a higher value means a safer drug.
q1lnnixv: In an isolated tissue experiment, adding a fixed concentration of an antagonist shifts the agonist dose-response curve to the right, but the maximal response is still reached at high agonist doses. What type of antagonist is this?
A competitive (surmountable) antagonist raises EC50 without lowering Emax; potency falls but efficacy does not.
q1ozkbde: Two opioids are compared. Drug A produces a maximal analgesic effect of 100 percent at 10 mg. Drug B produces a maximal effect of 60 percent at 1 mg. Which statement is correct?
The two drugs have equal efficacy
Efficacy is the maximal effect (Emax); potency relates to the dose needed (EC50). Drug A is more efficacious, and Drug B is more potent.
qedr7zn: A 34-year-old man with HSV encephalitis receives high-dose IV acyclovir as a rapid infusion. On day 3 his creatinine rises from 0.9 to 2.4 mg/dL and urine microscopy shows needle-shaped crystals. What is the mechanism of his kidney injury?
Drug precipitation within the renal tubules
Afferent arteriolar constriction from loss of prostaglandins
Acyclovir is poorly soluble in urine and can crystallize in tubules, causing obstructive nephropathy; IV hydration and slower infusion prevent it.
q6t28r1: A 38-year-old man with AIDS has HSV lesions that progress despite acyclovir, and the isolate lacks thymidine kinase activity. He is switched to a drug that does not need viral phosphorylation. Which laboratory abnormalities should be monitored most closely?
Foscarnet is a pyrophosphate analog that binds viral DNA polymerase directly; it chelates divalent cations (risk of seizures) and is nephrotoxic.
q4h4dt3: A 52-year-old kidney transplant recipient develops CMV colitis and is treated with IV ganciclovir. Two weeks later his absolute neutrophil count is 600/uL. Which statement best explains the drug's activation and main toxicity?
Activated by viral UL97 kinase; suppresses bone marrow
Pyrophosphate analog; chelates calcium and magnesium
Activated by host thymidine kinase; causes nephrolithiasis
Blocks viral uncoating; directly destroys neutrophils
Ganciclovir is monophosphorylated by the CMV UL97 kinase and then inhibits viral DNA polymerase; myelosuppression is its dose-limiting toxicity.
q7ccjoa: A 70-year-old woman develops fever, myalgia and cough during a winter outbreak, and a rapid test is positive for influenza A. She starts an oral drug within 48 hours of symptom onset. Which viral step does it inhibit?
Release of new virions from infected cells
Fusion of the viral envelope with the endosome
Uncoating of the virus through the M2 channel
Cap-snatching by the polymerase acidic endonuclease
Oseltamivir inhibits neuraminidase, so progeny virions cannot cleave sialic acid and be released; baloxavir inhibits the cap-dependent endonuclease.
q1gm4xny: A 29-year-old woman with HIV takes a regimen that includes zidovudine. Routine labs show hemoglobin of 8.9 g/dL with an MCV of 112 fL. Which mechanism underlies the antiviral effect of this drug?
Chain termination of viral DNA after phosphorylation
Allosteric inhibition of reverse transcriptase without activation
Blockade of strand transfer by the viral integrase
Inhibition of the protease that cleaves the gag-pol protein
NRTIs such as zidovudine are phosphorylated by host kinases and lack a 3' hydroxyl, terminating DNA chains; zidovudine causes macrocytic anemia and marrow suppression.
q186i840: A 26-year-old man starting HIV therapy has vivid dreams, insomnia and dizziness in the first weeks. The responsible drug binds reverse transcriptase at a pocket distant from the active site. How does it differ from nucleoside analogs?
It does not require intracellular phosphorylation
It requires activation by a viral thymidine kinase
It competes with natural nucleotides at the catalytic site
It acts only after viral DNA has integrated into the host genome
NNRTIs such as efavirenz bind an allosteric site and need no phosphorylation; CNS effects are characteristic.
q166a0g4: A 33-year-old woman with well-controlled HIV takes dolutegravir. Her viral load rises after she begins taking an aluminum-magnesium antacid at the same time as her morning pills. What explains the treatment failure?
Chelation by polyvalent cations lowering absorption
Induction of hepatic CYP3A4 increasing drug clearance
Higher gastric pH preventing tablet dissolution
Competition for renal tubular secretion of the drug
Integrase inhibitors bind metal ions in the integrase active site and also chelate Mg, Al, Ca and Fe in the gut; doses must be separated.
q1xkqhiq: A 36-year-old man's HIV regimen includes darunavir with a low dose of ritonavir. The ritonavir dose is too low to have meaningful antiviral activity on its own. What is its purpose?
Inhibition of CYP3A4 to raise darunavir levels
Induction of P-glycoprotein to improve CNS penetration
Inhibition of renal secretion to prolong darunavir action
Blockade of a second binding site on HIV protease
Low-dose ritonavir strongly inhibits CYP3A4, boosting levels of other protease inhibitors; this causes many drug interactions.
q11p53jk: Before starting a new HIV regimen, a 30-year-old man is tested for HLA-B*57:01 and the result is positive. Which drug must be avoided because of the risk of a severe hypersensitivity reaction?
Abacavir hypersensitivity (fever, rash, GI and respiratory symptoms) is strongly linked to HLA-B*57:01, and rechallenge can be fatal.
qvnj5sd: A 45-year-old treatment-experienced man with HIV has a tropism assay showing only CCR5-using virus. He starts a drug that blocks viral entry by binding a host cell protein. What is the drug's target?
Host CD4 receptor on helper T cells
Maraviroc binds host CCR5 and prevents its interaction with gp120; enfuvirtide binds gp41 and blocks membrane fusion.
q16zusmv: A 50-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C genotype 1 is cured after 12 weeks of an oral combination that contains sofosbuvir. Which viral protein does sofosbuvir inhibit?
Sofosbuvir is a nucleotide analog inhibitor of NS5B; drugs ending in -previr inhibit NS3/4A and those ending in -asvir inhibit NS5A.
qg0li7x: A 24-year-old soldier returning from Southeast Asia is treated for Plasmodium vivax malaria. Before a second drug is added to prevent relapse, his G6PD activity is measured. What does that second drug target, and what is the risk?
Primaquine eradicates dormant liver hypnozoites of P. vivax and P. ovale but causes oxidative hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
qifhrax: A 35-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has taken hydroxychloroquine for 6 years. Which screening test should she have regularly because of this drug?
Hydroxychloroquine can cause irreversible bull's-eye maculopathy, so annual retinal screening is recommended after 5 years of use.
q1snfmyb: A 6-year-old girl has perianal itching at night, and a tape test shows Enterobius eggs. She receives a single oral dose that is repeated in 2 weeks. What is the mechanism of this drug?
Mebendazole binds parasite beta-tubulin and blocks microtubule formation, impairing glucose uptake; pyrantel is a depolarizing nicotinic agonist.
qv4d7v8: A 40-year-old man from Sierra Leone has itchy skin nodules and microfilariae in skin snips, consistent with onchocerciasis. Which drug and mechanism are most appropriate?
Pyrantel; causes spastic paralysis via nicotinic agonism
Ivermectin activates invertebrate glutamate-gated chloride channels, causing hyperpolarization and paralysis of microfilariae.
q1grgza9: A 30-year-old woman returns from Nigeria with fever and uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria and receives artemether-lumefantrine. How does the artemisinin component kill the parasite?
Prevention of heme polymerization to hemozoin
Heme iron cleaves the endoperoxide bridge of artemisinins, producing free radicals that damage parasite proteins.
qok5d5y: A 9-year-old boy has tinea capitis and starts oral griseofulvin, which his mother is told to give with a fatty meal. Which mechanism and drug interaction are characteristic of this drug?
Griseofulvin deposits in keratin and disrupts the mitotic spindle; it induces CYP450, lowering warfarin and oral contraceptive levels, and is teratogenic.
q1uysm7p: A 28-year-old woman from rural Mexico has new-onset seizures, and MRI shows multiple cystic brain lesions containing scolices. In addition to corticosteroids, which drug is given?
Neurocysticercosis is treated with albendazole (sometimes with praziquantel), with steroids to limit inflammation as cysts die.
q1trz8ur: A 19-year-old student with pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly is given ampicillin. Three days later she develops a diffuse maculopapular rash. What is the most likely explanation?
Nonallergic rash associated with EBV infection
Toxin-mediated scarlet fever from group A streptococci
Serum sickness from immune complex deposition
Aminopenicillins given during infectious mononucleosis commonly cause a nonallergic morbilliform rash that does not predict true penicillin allergy.
qk2uao2: A 45-year-old woman with epilepsy controlled on valproic acid is treated with meropenem for a resistant gram-negative infection. Two days later she has a generalized seizure. What is the most likely cause?
Direct carbapenem agonism at GABA-A receptors
Carbapenems block hydrolysis of valproate glucuronide, so valproate levels drop sharply within days; the combination should be avoided.
q144gh5: A 78-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease receives full-dose cefepime for Pseudomonas pneumonia. Three days later she is confused with myoclonus, and EEG shows nonconvulsive status epilepticus. What best explains this toxicity?
Drug accumulation with central GABA-A antagonism
Thiamine depletion from altered gut flora
Hypoprothrombinemia from its N-methylthiotetrazole side chain
Disulfiram-like reaction to its side chain group
Cefepime accumulates when renal dosing is not adjusted and antagonizes GABA-A receptors, causing encephalopathy and seizures.
q1yq63ht: A 60-year-old man has pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae that is resistant to levofloxacin. Which mechanism most likely produced this resistance?
Mutations in DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
Fluoroquinolone resistance arises mainly from chromosomal mutations in gyrA and parC, plus efflux pumps.
q1gu7opw: A 55-year-old man in the ICU has pneumonia caused by carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter and is treated with colistin. Which toxicity profile is most characteristic of this drug class?
Polymyxins act as cationic detergents on bacterial membranes and cause dose-related nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity, including neuromuscular blockade.
qeldksl: A 70-year-old woman has a second recurrence of Clostridioides difficile colitis. She is treated with a narrow-spectrum macrocyclic antibiotic that is minimally absorbed and spares normal colonic flora. What is its target?
Fidaxomicin inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase and has lower recurrence rates than vancomycin.
qvqg5hr: A 30-year-old man with neurosyphilis declines IV therapy and is treated with IM procaine penicillin G plus oral probenecid. How does probenecid improve therapy?
Inhibits renal tubular secretion of penicillin
Increases penicillin entry across the blood-brain barrier
Probenecid blocks organic anion transporters in the proximal tubule, raising and prolonging penicillin levels.
qcu9nmm: A 12-year-old boy with osteosarcoma receives high-dose methotrexate. Twenty-four hours later he is given a reduced folate that rescues normal cells without needing the enzyme that methotrexate blocks. Which enzyme does methotrexate inhibit?
Methotrexate inhibits DHFR; leucovorin (folinic acid) bypasses the block and rescues normal cells.
qgq7an: A 60-year-old man with colon cancer receives fluorouracil with leucovorin. Here leucovorin is given to increase cytotoxicity rather than to rescue normal cells. What is the target of fluorouracil?
5-FdUMP forms a covalent complex with thymidylate synthase and methylene-THF; leucovorin stabilizes this complex.
q108nitw: A 42-year-old woman with lupus nephritis receives IV cyclophosphamide and is given mesna with each dose. Which toxicity is mesna preventing?
Acute tubular necrosis from cast formation
The metabolite acrolein injures bladder urothelium; mesna is a thiol that binds and inactivates acrolein in the urine.
q916ipe: A 58-year-old man receiving cisplatin for bladder cancer develops high-frequency hearing loss, a rising creatinine and hypomagnesemia. How does cisplatin kill tumor cells?
Crosslinks DNA by forming platinum adducts
Stabilizes microtubules and blocks mitotic exit
Inhibits topoisomerase II and causes DNA breaks
Intercalates in DNA and generates oxygen free radicals
Cisplatin forms intrastrand and interstrand DNA crosslinks; it causes nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity and neuropathy, reduced by hydration and amifostine.
q1jqyn4w: A 50-year-old woman develops dyspnea, edema and an ejection fraction of 30 percent a year after breast cancer chemotherapy. Her cumulative dose of one agent exceeded recommended limits. Which drug could have been given with it to reduce this toxicity?
Doxorubicin causes cumulative dose-dependent dilated cardiomyopathy through free radicals; the iron chelator dexrazoxane is protective.
q185wvgc: A 28-year-old man treated for testicular cancer with a three-drug regimen develops progressive dyspnea and bibasilar crackles, with a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function testing. Which drug most likely caused this?
Bleomycin causes pulmonary fibrosis because the lung lacks bleomycin hydrolase; it acts by generating free radicals that break DNA.
qp7dou1: A 6-year-old boy with acute lymphoblastic leukemia develops constipation, tingling in his hands and foot drop during induction chemotherapy. Which mechanism explains the responsible drug's activity?
Depletes asparagine needed by leukemic cells
Inhibits topoisomerase II during the S and G2 phases
Vincristine binds tubulin and blocks microtubule assembly, arresting cells in M phase; peripheral and autonomic neuropathy are dose-limiting.
q164x1b1: A 25-year-old man with testicular cancer receives a podophyllotoxin derivative. Years later he develops acute myeloid leukemia with an 11q23 rearrangement. What is this drug's mechanism?
Etoposide stabilizes the topoisomerase II-DNA complex, causing double-strand breaks; secondary leukemias with MLL rearrangement can follow.
q12q9806: A 48-year-old man with fatigue, splenomegaly and a WBC of 120,000/uL has a t(9;22) translocation. He starts an oral drug and achieves remission. What does the drug inhibit?
Imatinib blocks the ATP-binding site of the constitutively active BCR-ABL kinase in chronic myeloid leukemia.
qhyuirl: A 47-year-old woman with HER2-positive breast cancer receives trastuzumab, and echocardiograms are scheduled every 3 months. Which statement best describes its cardiotoxicity compared with that of anthracyclines?
Trastuzumab cardiac dysfunction is usually reversible after stopping the drug and is not related to cumulative dose, unlike anthracycline cardiomyopathy.
q1itbgov: A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman has taken tamoxifen for 3 years for estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer and now has vaginal bleeding. Which property of the drug explains this finding?
Partial estrogen agonism in the endometrium
Complete estrogen antagonism in the uterus
Tamoxifen is a SERM that blocks estrogen in breast tissue but acts as an agonist in the endometrium (hyperplasia, cancer) and raises VTE risk.
q7rbxn7: A 9-year-old boy on maintenance mercaptopurine for ALL is started on allopurinol for hyperuricemia without a dose change, and he develops severe pancytopenia. What explains this?
Xanthine oxidase inhibition raises drug levels
Allopurinol directly suppresses the bone marrow
Competition for renal secretion of the drug
Xanthine oxidase inactivates mercaptopurine and azathioprine; with allopurinol or febuxostat their doses must be reduced by about 75 percent.
q1dvrsw9: A 62-year-old man treated for metastatic melanoma develops fatigue, weight gain and a TSH of 24 mU/L after 3 months of an intravenous antibody. Which target of this drug best explains the adverse effect?
PD-1 inhibitors release T-cell checkpoints and can cause immune-related thyroiditis, colitis, hepatitis and pneumonitis.
q1vawfst: A 45-year-old kidney transplant recipient has gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism and hypertension, and his creatinine has risen slowly. By which mechanism does his immunosuppressant work?
Inhibits calcineurin and lowers IL-2 transcription
Inhibits mTOR and blocks IL-2 signal transduction
Blocks the alpha chain of the IL-2 receptor on T cells
Cyclosporine binds cyclophilin, and the complex inhibits calcineurin, preventing NFAT activation and IL-2 transcription.
q1nxcoc7: A 38-year-old liver transplant recipient taking tacrolimus develops new-onset diabetes and a fine tremor. To which intracellular protein does tacrolimus bind before inhibiting its target?
Tacrolimus binds FKBP12, and the complex inhibits calcineurin; it is more diabetogenic and neurotoxic than cyclosporine.
q3xyxo4: A 30-year-old woman with lupus nephritis is maintained on mycophenolate mofetil. Which enzyme does it inhibit, and why are lymphocytes most affected?
IMP dehydrogenase; lymphocytes lack a salvage pathway
Calcineurin; lymphocytes depend on IL-2 transcription
Xanthine oxidase; lymphocytes accumulate toxic purine bases
Mycophenolate inhibits IMP dehydrogenase in de novo guanine synthesis, which lymphocytes rely on because they lack a purine salvage pathway.
q121tf22: A 34-year-old man with Crohn disease is about to start azathioprine. Which test should be done first to estimate his risk of severe myelosuppression?
Low TPMT activity shunts azathioprine toward toxic thioguanine nucleotides and severe marrow suppression.
q11f16zu: A 40-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is about to start infliximab. Which test must be completed before the first dose?
Serum IgA level for anaphylaxis risk
Antinuclear antibody titer to predict drug-induced lupus
TNF-alpha maintains granulomas, so TNF inhibitors can reactivate latent tuberculosis; screening is required first.
q1tv8x4c: A 25-year-old woman with severe allergic asthma and a high serum IgE has exacerbations despite high-dose inhaled steroids and a LABA. She starts a monthly injection. What does the drug bind?
Free IgE at its Fc region
Omalizumab binds the Fc portion of free IgE, preventing it from binding FcER1 on mast cells and basophils.
q1d50d0n: A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and an eGFR of 25 mL/min has his metformin stopped. Which adverse effect is being avoided, and what is the drug's main action?
Metformin reduces hepatic glucose output (in part via AMPK); accumulation in renal failure can cause lactic acidosis, and it rarely causes hypoglycemia alone.
qeij0nu: A 78-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and reduced kidney function is found confused with a glucose of 38 mg/dL. Her drug closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels on beta cells and has active metabolites cleared by the kidney. Which drug is she taking?
Sulfonylureas depolarize beta cells to release insulin; long-acting glyburide is especially likely to cause prolonged hypoglycemia in older adults with CKD.
qh5s6x4: A 64-year-old man with type 2 diabetes develops weight gain, ankle edema and worsening dyspnea after a new drug is added. The drug acts on a nuclear receptor that is highly expressed in adipose tissue. What is its mechanism?
Thiazolidinediones activate PPAR-gamma to improve insulin sensitivity but cause fluid retention and can worsen heart failure.
q1nb8tic: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes presents with nausea, a glucose of 190 mg/dL and an anion gap metabolic acidosis with positive serum ketones. Where does her diabetes drug act?
Intestinal alpha-glucosidase in the brush border
SGLT2 inhibitors cause glucosuria and can produce euglycemic DKA; they also increase the risk of genital mycotic infections.
q10rad8y: A 45-year-old woman with obesity and type 2 diabetes wants to start weekly semaglutide injections. Which history would be a contraindication?
GLP-1 agonists caused thyroid C-cell tumors in rodents and are contraindicated with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2.
qjc4827: A 26-year-old woman at 8 weeks of gestation has Graves disease and is given an antithyroid drug for the first trimester only. Which property is unique to this drug compared with the alternative thionamide?
Inhibits peripheral T4 to T3 conversion
Blocks iodide uptake through the NIS symporter
Carries a lower risk of liver failure
PTU inhibits thyroid peroxidase and peripheral 5'-deiodinase; it is used in the first trimester because methimazole is teratogenic, but it carries more hepatotoxicity.
q1j8gny5: A 40-year-old woman with Graves disease started methimazole 6 weeks ago and now has a fever and severe sore throat. What should be checked immediately?
Thionamides can cause agranulocytosis; the drug should be stopped and the neutrophil count checked when fever or sore throat develops.
q1un13i5: A 55-year-old man who has taken prednisone 20 mg daily for 6 months for polymyalgia rheumatica stops it abruptly. He develops weakness, vomiting, hypotension and hypoglycemia. What best explains this?
Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex
Hemorrhagic infarction of both adrenal glands
Exogenous glucocorticoids suppress CRH and ACTH, causing adrenal atrophy; stopping abruptly causes secondary adrenal insufficiency.
qsdxa6h: A 30-year-old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency takes hydrocortisone but still has salt craving, orthostatic hypotension and hyperkalemia. Which drug and receptor would correct these findings?
Desmopressin at the vasopressin V2 receptor
Midodrine at the alpha-1 adrenergic receptor
Primary adrenal insufficiency causes aldosterone deficiency; fludrocortisone replaces mineralocorticoid activity.
q1yszts6: A 25-year-old man has polyuria after a head injury. His urine osmolality rises from 150 to 600 mOsm/kg after he receives a synthetic hormone. Which receptor and second messenger does this drug use?
V2 receptor via Gs and cAMP
V1 receptor via Gq and IP3
V2 receptor via Gi and lower cAMP
Oxytocin receptor via Gq and calcium
Desmopressin is a selective V2 agonist; Gs-cAMP signaling inserts aquaporin-2 into collecting duct membranes in central diabetes insipidus.
qyjoc9t: A 29-year-old woman with amenorrhea, galactorrhea and a prolactin of 180 ng/mL has a 7-mm pituitary adenoma. What is the mechanism of the preferred drug?
Dopamine tonically inhibits lactotrophs; D2 agonists such as cabergoline lower prolactin and shrink prolactinomas.
q1fwkh93: A 28-year-old woman with polycystic ovary syndrome wants to conceive and is treated with clomiphene. How does this drug induce ovulation?
Blocks estrogen negative feedback on the hypothalamus
Inhibits ovarian aromatase and lowers estradiol
Mimics LH to trigger rupture of the dominant follicle
Directly stimulates FSH receptors on granulosa cells
Clomiphene is a SERM that blocks hypothalamic estrogen receptors, raising GnRH, FSH and LH release.
q1fjuy28: A 70-year-old woman with severe osteoporosis and vertebral fractures starts daily subcutaneous teriparatide. Why does intermittent dosing build bone?
Pulsatile PTH directly inhibits osteoclast activity
Pulsatile PTH blocks RANKL binding to RANK
Intermittent PTH analogs favor osteoblast bone formation, whereas continuous PTH promotes resorption; osteosarcoma was seen in rats.
q132cg1d: A 30-year-old woman receives a prolonged high-dose oxytocin infusion in dilute dextrose during labor and later has a seizure with a serum sodium of 118 mEq/L. Which property of oxytocin explains this?
Structural similarity to ADH causing antidiuresis
Direct stimulation of adrenal aldosterone release
Inhibition of atrial natriuretic peptide secretion
Oxytocin resembles vasopressin and at high doses activates V2 receptors, causing water retention and hyponatremia.
q3p7ihp: A 68-year-old woman who has taken omeprazole for 5 years develops muscle cramps, tremor and a prolonged QT interval. Which electrolyte abnormality is most likely?
Long-term PPI use impairs intestinal magnesium absorption; other risks include C. difficile, B12 deficiency and fractures.
qmk6g1k: A 50-year-old man taking warfarin and phenytoin starts an over-the-counter H2 blocker for dyspepsia, and his INR rises. Which H2 blocker most likely caused this, and how?
Cimetidine, by displacing warfarin from albumin
Nizatidine, by blocking vitamin K absorption
Cimetidine inhibits several CYP450 enzymes and has antiandrogenic effects; famotidine has few interactions.
q1ioeqau: A 60-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis taking long-term NSAIDs is given a drug to prevent gastric ulcers that increases bicarbonate and mucus secretion. What is the drug, and which warning applies?
Proton pump inhibitor; frequently causes diarrhea
Misoprostol replaces protective prostaglandins; it stimulates uterine contraction and is an abortifacient, and diarrhea is common.
qmho88d: A 45-year-old woman receiving cisplatin is given ondansetron to prevent nausea. Which receptor does it block, and which ECG change can it cause?
Ondansetron blocks 5-HT3 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone and vagal afferents; it can prolong QT and cause constipation and headache.
q1nqucwx: A 74-year-old man with diabetic gastroparesis has taken metoclopramide for 2 years and develops involuntary lip-smacking and tongue movements. Which mechanism caused this?
Muscarinic receptor antagonism in the gut
Motilin receptor agonism in the gastric antrum
Metoclopramide is a D2 antagonist that crosses the blood-brain barrier; long-term use can cause irreversible tardive dyskinesia.
q1wxcqj6: A 35-year-old man with chronic diarrhea takes loperamide. Why does this mu-opioid agonist have little central effect at usual doses?
P-glycoprotein efflux at the blood-brain barrier
Selective agonism of kappa receptors in the gut
Complete first-pass sulfation in the liver
Inability to bind central mu receptors
Loperamide is pumped out of the CNS by P-glycoprotein; massive doses or P-gp inhibitors can cause QT prolongation and CNS effects.
qk2v0ig: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis is confused and has asterixis. He is started on lactulose. How does this drug lower blood ammonia?
Colonic acidification traps ammonia as ammonium
Increased activity of hepatic urea cycle enzymes
Colonic bacteria metabolize lactulose to acids, converting NH3 to NH4+, which is trapped and excreted; it also acts as an osmotic laxative.
qx06iq6: A 22-year-old woman with an asthma exacerbation receives repeated albuterol nebulizer treatments and develops tremor and palpitations. Which laboratory change is expected?
Beta-2 stimulation activates Na/K-ATPase and shifts potassium into cells; it also raises glucose and lactate.
q1nuym08: A 66-year-old man with COPD starts a once-daily inhaled bronchodilator whose long duration comes from slow dissociation from its receptor. Which receptor does it act on, and how?
Tiotropium is a long-acting muscarinic antagonist that blocks M3-mediated bronchoconstriction; dry mouth is common.
q7xoqit: A 14-year-old boy with asthma and allergic rhinitis takes a nightly oral tablet. His parents notice nightmares and mood changes. What is the drug's mechanism?
Montelukast blocks CysLT1 receptors; it carries a boxed warning for neuropsychiatric events. Zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase.
q3ikn42: A 30-year-old woman with persistent asthma starts an inhaled corticosteroid and develops white plaques on her tongue and palate. Which measure most effectively prevents this?
Rinsing the mouth after each use
Taking the inhaler only at bedtime
Oropharyngeal candidiasis from steroid deposition is reduced by rinsing and spitting after each dose and by using a spacer.
q1q3dkb7: A 19-year-old man with moderate persistent asthma is prescribed salmeterol as his only controller medication. Why is this regimen unsafe?
LABAs cause bronchospasm via M3 stimulation
LABAs act too briefly to control persistent asthma
LABAs cause adrenal suppression unless paired with steroids
LABAs do not treat airway inflammation; used without an inhaled corticosteroid they increase severe exacerbations and asthma deaths.
q1ezau5u: A 45-year-old woman stable on lithium starts hydrochlorothiazide and develops coarse tremor, confusion and ataxia. What is the mechanism of this interaction?
Displacement of lithium from plasma proteins
Reduced lithium distribution into the brain
Thiazides cause volume contraction, increasing proximal reabsorption of sodium and lithium; ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs also raise levels.
qbbhr8s: A 35-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia starts clozapine. Which laboratory value must be monitored regularly?
Clozapine can cause agranulocytosis, so ANC is monitored; it also causes seizures, myocarditis and weight gain.
