Prochlorperazine and lorazepam as needed after each chemotherapy infusion
Highly emetogenic chemotherapy such as cisplatin warrants four-drug prophylaxis per ASCO and NCCN: an NK1 antagonist, a 5-HT3 antagonist, dexamethasone, and olanzapine.
q5543zy: A 54-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer has a temperature of 38.6 C (101.5 F). ANC is 200/mm3. BP is 122/76 mm Hg, she has no catheter site infection, and lungs are clear. Which is the most appropriate empiric therapy?
High-risk febrile neutropenia requires prompt IV monotherapy with an antipseudomonal beta-lactam. Vancomycin is added only for specific indications such as instability or catheter infection.
q1ftmqzp: A 16-year-old boy with osteosarcoma receives high-dose methotrexate. Which medication is given 24 hours later to protect normal cells?
Leucovorin (folinic acid) bypasses dihydrofolate reductase to rescue normal cells after high-dose methotrexate. Hydration, urine alkalinization, and level monitoring are also used.
qlskjyq: A 45-year-old woman with lupus nephritis is receiving IV cyclophosphamide. Which medication reduces her risk of hemorrhagic cystitis?
Acrolein, a cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide metabolite, injures the bladder. Mesna binds acrolein in the urine; hydration also helps.
qxfbs61: A 64-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer has new back pain, bilateral leg weakness, and urinary retention. Which is the most appropriate immediate step while arranging urgent MRI of the spine?
Suspected malignant spinal cord compression is treated with high-dose dexamethasone immediately, then urgent MRI of the whole spine and radiation or surgery.
q1lpqyq9: A 72-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer starts scheduled oxycodone for pain. Which is the most appropriate bowel regimen to start at the same time?

Opioid-induced constipation should be prevented when opioids are started, using a stimulant laxative such as senna, with or without an osmotic laxative. Fiber can worsen it, and docusate alone is ineffective.
q3cvz1x: A 68-year-old man with stage 4 CKD (eGFR 22 mL/min) has an acutely painful, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint. Joint aspiration shows negatively birefringent crystals. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
Oral prednisone 30 to 40 mg daily for 5 days
Colchicine 1.2 mg then 0.6 mg every hour until diarrhea
Glucocorticoids are preferred for acute gout in advanced CKD. NSAIDs worsen kidney function, and colchicine requires dose reduction in CKD; hourly high-dose colchicine is no longer used.
qo9w51t: A 58-year-old man of Korean descent with CKD stage 3 has recurrent gout and tophi. Urate-lowering therapy is planned. Which test is recommended before starting allopurinol?

ACR recommends HLA-B*5801 testing before allopurinol in people of Korean descent with CKD 3 or worse and in those of Han Chinese, Thai, or African ancestry, because the allele predicts severe cutaneous reactions.
q19mdqdg: A 45-year-old woman has newly diagnosed rheumatoid arthritis with high disease activity. Liver enzymes, creatinine, and CBC are normal. She does not drink alcohol. Which is the most appropriate initial DMARD?
ACR recommends methotrexate monotherapy as the first DMARD in RA with moderate to high disease activity, with folic acid to reduce adverse effects. Long-term glucocorticoids should be avoided.
qxjdxp8: A 72-year-old woman has new temporal headache, jaw claudication, and 1 day of blurred vision in the left eye. ESR is 98 mm/h. Temporal artery biopsy is scheduled for next week. Which is the most appropriate next step?
Start high-dose glucocorticoids now, before biopsy
Wait for biopsy results before starting any therapy
Giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms requires immediate high-dose glucocorticoids (often IV methylprednisolone) to prevent permanent vision loss. Biopsy remains diagnostic for 2 weeks or more.
q1k9w66q: A 70-year-old woman has 2 months of bilateral shoulder and hip girdle aching with morning stiffness lasting 2 hours. ESR is 62 mm/h and CK is normal. She has no headache, jaw claudication, or visual symptoms. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
Oral naproxen 500 mg twice daily alone
Polymyalgia rheumatica responds rapidly to low-dose prednisone 12.5 to 25 mg daily with a slow taper. High doses are used for giant cell arteritis.
q1fze8fc: A 26-year-old woman with SLE has hematuria, proteinuria of 2.5 g/day, and rising creatinine. Kidney biopsy shows class IV lupus nephritis. Which is the most appropriate induction therapy with glucocorticoids?
Mycophenolate or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide with glucocorticoids is used to induce remission in proliferative lupus nephritis. Belimumab or a calcineurin inhibitor may be added.
q1ckspfo: A 48-year-old woman has a duodenal ulcer and a positive H. pylori stool antigen. She received clarithromycin for sinusitis last year. She has no drug allergies. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
PPI, clarithromycin, and amoxicillin for 7 days

ACG prefers bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI, bismuth, tetracycline, metronidazole) for 14 days for treatment-naive H. pylori infection, especially with prior macrolide exposure, because clarithromycin resistance is common.
q1qm3h0a: A 55-year-old man with cirrhosis has hematemesis. BP is 92/58 mm Hg and pulse 116/min. He is given blood transfusions with a hemoglobin target of 7 g/dL. Which is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy before endoscopy?
Vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma to correct the INR

Suspected variceal bleeding is treated with a vasoactive agent such as octreotide and antibiotic prophylaxis with ceftriaxone, followed by endoscopy within 12 hours. Nonselective beta blockers are avoided acutely.
q1v5m1sj: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis has a second episode of overt hepatic encephalopathy despite adherence to lactulose with 2 to 3 soft stools daily. Which is the most appropriate addition?
Add long-term metronidazole three times daily
Add lorazepam at night for agitation

Rifaximin added to lactulose reduces recurrent hepatic encephalopathy and hospitalization. Long-term metronidazole is neurotoxic, protein restriction is not recommended, and benzodiazepines precipitate encephalopathy.
qrcupmt: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis and ascites has abdominal pain and fever. Ascitic fluid has 640 neutrophils/mm3. Creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL and bilirubin is 4.2 mg/dL. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
IV cefotaxime plus albumin on days 1 and 3

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is treated with a third-generation cephalosporin. With creatinine above 1 mg/dL or bilirubin above 4 mg/dL, albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 reduces kidney failure and death.
q1k7h44e: A 32-year-old woman has mildly to moderately active ulcerative colitis extending to the splenic flexure with 4 bloody stools daily. Which is the most appropriate initial therapy?
Oral prednisone 40 mg daily for 3 months
Oral 5-ASA (2 g or more daily) combined with rectal mesalamine is first-line for mild to moderate left-sided ulcerative colitis. Steroids are for induction only and antibiotics have no role.
q4h7lrv: A 45-year-old woman with heavy alcohol use has jaundice, fever, and tender hepatomegaly. Bilirubin is 14 mg/dL, AST 220 U/L, and ALT 90 U/L. Maddrey discriminant function is 48. Infection and GI bleeding are excluded. Which is the most appropriate treatment?

Prednisolone improves short-term survival in severe alcohol-associated hepatitis (discriminant function 32 or more or MELD above 20). Prednisolone is used rather than prednisone because it does not require hepatic activation.
q15loe9: A woman on metoclopramide for 18 months develops lip smacking and tongue movements. Which mechanism underlies this?
Upregulated D2 receptors after chronic blockade
Peripheral 5-HT4 receptor agonism in the gut wall
Direct toxicity to cerebellar Purkinje cells

Tardive dyskinesia is attributed to supersensitivity of striatal D2 receptors upregulated during months of blockade, which is why risk climbs after about 12 weeks and why anticholinergics do not relieve it. The 5-HT4 agonism is what gives metoclopramide its prokinetic action.
q1h5h3c3: A 70-year-old man with CKD has weakness. Potassium is 7.4 mEq/L and ECG shows peaked T waves and a widened QRS. Which is the most appropriate first medication?
Patiromer orally with a recheck in 6 hours
Calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes in hyperkalemia with ECG changes. Insulin with glucose and albuterol shift potassium into cells, and binders, diuretics, or dialysis remove it.
qv77vd6: A 66-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is confused and dehydrated. Calcium is 14.6 mg/dL, PTH is suppressed, and creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
IV saline, calcitonin, and zoledronic acid
IV furosemide 80 mg before any fluids
Oral alendronate and increased fluid intake

Severe hypercalcemia of malignancy is treated with IV isotonic saline, calcitonin for rapid effect, and a bisphosphonate such as zoledronic acid or denosumab for sustained control. Thiazides raise calcium.
qzv064p: A 62-year-old man on long-term omeprazole and furosemide has potassium 2.9 mEq/L despite 3 days of oral potassium chloride. Magnesium is 1.0 mg/dL. Which is the most appropriate next step?
Hypomagnesemia causes renal potassium wasting through ROMK, making hypokalemia refractory until magnesium is replaced. PPIs and loop diuretics both cause hypomagnesemia.
q13mk10n: A 58-year-old man on hemodialysis has phosphate 7.2 mg/dL and calcium 10.4 mg/dL despite dietary counseling. Which is the most appropriate phosphate binder?
Non-calcium binders such as sevelamer or lanthanum are preferred when calcium is high. Aluminum is avoided long term because of bone disease and encephalopathy.
q17ullf1: A 64-year-old woman with CKD stage 4 has fatigue. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL, ferritin 60 ng/mL, and transferrin saturation 12 percent. Which is the most appropriate next step?
Iron repletion before considering an ESA
Epoetin alfa targeting hemoglobin above 13 g/dL
Iron deficiency should be corrected first in CKD anemia; ESAs are less effective without adequate iron. Hemoglobin targets above 11.5 g/dL with ESAs increase stroke and cardiovascular events.
q19fr1a8: A 45-year-old man has recurrent calcium oxalate stones. A 24-hour urine collection shows high urinary calcium with normal serum calcium and PTH. He drinks 3 L of fluid daily. Which is the most appropriate medication?

Thiazide diuretics increase distal calcium reabsorption and reduce hypercalciuria and stone recurrence. Loop diuretics increase urinary calcium, and dietary calcium restriction increases oxalate absorption.
q5lmhx7: A 74-year-old woman with untreated hypothyroidism is found lethargic. Temperature is 34.2 C (93.6 F), BP 84/50 mm Hg, pulse 48/min, and sodium 124 mEq/L. TSH is 85 mU/L and free T4 is undetectable. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
Oral levothyroxine 25 mcg daily, recheck TSH in 6 weeks
Active external rewarming with heating blankets only
Myxedema coma requires IV levothyroxine, with stress-dose hydrocortisone given first until adrenal insufficiency is excluded. Active rewarming can cause vasodilation and shock.
qzfujxw: A 68-year-old woman has received denosumab every 6 months for 5 years for osteoporosis. She wants to stop treatment. Which is the most appropriate plan?
Stop denosumab with no further therapy
Delay the next dose by 1 year as a drug holiday
Switch to calcium and vitamin D supplements only
Stopping denosumab causes rapid bone loss and rebound multiple vertebral fractures. Doses should not be delayed, and a bisphosphonate should follow discontinuation.
q1mw91c5: A 28-year-old woman has amenorrhea and galactorrhea. Prolactin is 180 ng/mL, pregnancy test is negative, and MRI shows an 8-mm pituitary adenoma without visual field defects. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
Dopamine agonists are first-line for prolactinomas; cabergoline is more effective and better tolerated than bromocriptine. Surgery is for intolerance or resistance.
qa4rfbi: A 42-year-old woman has episodic headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis. BP is 172/104 mm Hg. Plasma metanephrines are markedly elevated and CT shows a 4-cm adrenal mass. Surgery is planned. Which medication should be started first?

Preoperative alpha blockade for 10 to 14 days precedes beta blockade in pheochromocytoma. Starting a beta blocker first leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can cause hypertensive crisis.
q1mwwtk7: A 60-year-old man has taken prednisone 20 mg daily for 6 months for interstitial lung disease. He is scheduled for an open colectomy. Which is the most appropriate perioperative steroid plan?
Give dexamethasone only if hypotension develops
Long-term glucocorticoid use at 20 mg or more for 3 weeks or more suppresses the HPA axis. Major surgery warrants stress-dose hydrocortisone (100 mg IV then 50 mg every 8 hours) with a taper.
q1bw0ei2: A 38-year-old woman has 2 weeks of anterior neck pain, palpitations, and tremor after a viral illness. The thyroid is tender. TSH is suppressed, free T4 is high, ESR is 70 mm/h, and radioactive iodine uptake is low. Which is the most appropriate treatment?

Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis is self-limited thyrotoxicosis from hormone release, not synthesis. Treatment is beta blockade and NSAIDs, with prednisone if severe. Thionamides and RAI are ineffective.
q10u4r0l: A 19-year-old woman ingested an unknown amount of acetaminophen 4 hours ago. She is asymptomatic. The 4-hour acetaminophen level is 220 mcg/mL, above the treatment line. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
An acetaminophen level above the treatment line on the nomogram requires NAC, which replenishes glutathione. It is most effective within 8 hours of ingestion.
q1mdejx8: A 45-year-old man ingested a large amount of aspirin. He is confused and has tinnitus. Salicylate level is 105 mg/dL, pH 7.30, and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. Sodium bicarbonate is infusing. Which is the most appropriate next step?

Hemodialysis is indicated for salicylate poisoning with altered mental status, a level above 90 to 100 mg/dL, kidney failure, or pulmonary edema. Intubation is dangerous because loss of respiratory compensation worsens acidosis.
q1d994g3: A 40-year-old man is confused after drinking antifreeze. pH is 7.12, anion gap 28, and osmolal gap 30 mOsm/kg. Urine shows calcium oxalate crystals. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
Fomepizole inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase to block formation of toxic metabolites of ethylene glycol and methanol. Hemodialysis is added for severe acidosis or kidney failure.
qlq81g2: A 78-year-old woman on digoxin for AF has nausea and yellow-tinted vision. Pulse is 40/min with runs of bidirectional ventricular tachycardia. Potassium is 6.1 mEq/L and the digoxin level is 4.2 ng/mL. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
Life-threatening dysrhythmias, potassium above 5 to 6 mEq/L, or end-organ toxicity are indications for digoxin-specific antibody fragments. Dialysis does not remove digoxin.
qy62fgc: A 35-year-old farmer has vomiting, diarrhea, miosis, bronchorrhea, wheezing, bradycardia, and fasciculations after spraying pesticide. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
Atropine alone without any other antidote
Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Atropine treats muscarinic effects, titrated to drying of secretions, and pralidoxime regenerates the enzyme to reverse nicotinic weakness before aging.
q1wynpwv: A 40-year-old man is rescued from a house fire. He is confused and hypotensive with soot in the oropharynx. Lactate is 12 mmol/L and SpO2 is normal. Which is the most appropriate antidote in addition to 100 percent oxygen?

Smoke inhalation with lactate above 8 suggests cyanide poisoning. Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin. Nitrites induce methemoglobinemia, worsening oxygen delivery with coexisting carbon monoxide.
q17bf8il: A 24-year-old man has cyanosis and dyspnea after receiving topical benzocaine spray before endoscopy. SpO2 is 85 percent despite oxygen, and PaO2 is 210 mm Hg. Methemoglobin is 32 percent. Which is the most appropriate treatment?

Methylene blue reduces methemoglobin to hemoglobin via NADPH methemoglobin reductase. It is ineffective and may cause hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, and it can cause serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs.
q16o883p: A 55-year-old woman who has taken alprazolam daily for years is found unresponsive next to empty bottles of alprazolam and amitriptyline. Respiratory rate is 8/min and ECG shows a QRS duration of 120 ms. Which medication should be avoided?
Flumazenil can precipitate seizures in chronic benzodiazepine users and in coingestion of proconvulsants such as TCAs. Airway support is preferred.
q1j6j7fw: A 22-year-old woman who recently started treatment for latent TB took an overdose of her medication. She has recurrent seizures not responding to lorazepam and a severe anion gap metabolic acidosis. Which is the most appropriate antidote?
Isoniazid overdose depletes pyridoxine and GABA, causing refractory seizures and lactic acidosis. IV pyridoxine, 1 g per g of isoniazid or 5 g empirically, is the antidote; phenytoin is ineffective.
q1hs5n2s: A 17-year-old boy has inflammatory papules and pustules on the face, chest, and back with scattered comedones, unresponsive to topical benzoyl peroxide. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
Topical retinoid, benzoyl peroxide, and oral doxycycline
Oral isotretinoin as first-line without other trials

Moderate inflammatory acne is treated with a topical retinoid and benzoyl peroxide plus an oral tetracycline for about 3 months. Benzoyl peroxide limits resistance and antibiotics should not be used alone.
q70ovyb: A 7-year-old boy has a scaly patch of alopecia with broken hairs and posterior cervical adenopathy. KOH prep shows hyphae within the hair shaft. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
Tinea capitis requires systemic therapy because topical agents do not penetrate hair follicles. Terbinafine and griseofulvin are first-line; selenium sulfide shampoo reduces spread.
q1w1rzcj: An 84-year-old nursing home resident has thick, crusted, scaling plaques on the hands and trunk. Several staff members have itching. Scraping shows numerous mites. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
Crusted scabies has a very high mite burden and requires combined oral ivermectin with topical permethrin. Contacts and staff are treated simultaneously.
q1d73xf8: You are cross-covering an 80-year-old man on warfarin with a stable INR of 2.4. He is started on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for cystitis. Which is the most appropriate plan?
Choose a different antibiotic or recheck the INR within 3-5 days
Double the warfarin dose for the full length of the antibiotic course
Stop warfarin until the antibiotic course is fully finished
Continue both drugs unchanged and recheck the INR in 1 month
TMP-SMX inhibits CYP2C9 and markedly raises the INR; avoid it or monitor closely.
qkzw1eh: A 92-kg man with MRSA bacteremia is admitted. Which approach to vancomycin monitoring do current national guidelines recommend?
Adjust dosing to an AUC/MIC target of about 400-600
Adjust dosing to keep every trough between 25 and 30
Give a fixed dose of 1 g every 12 hours without drug levels
Check a peak level after the first dose and target 40
The 2020 ASHP/IDSA consensus favors AUC-guided dosing (AUC/MIC 400-600) over trough-only monitoring to limit nephrotoxicity.
q1466lfm: A 100-kg woman with septic shock and suspected MRSA pneumonia has normal renal function. Which initial vancomycin order is most appropriate?
Loading dose of about 20-35 mg/kg of actual body weight, maximum 3 g
Loading dose of 5 mg/kg of ideal body weight, then check levels
Flat dose of 500 mg IV every 6 hours without any loading dose
Loading dose of 50 mg/kg of actual body weight with no maximum
Per ASHP/IDSA guidelines (off-label; the label lists 2 g/day), critically ill patients get a 20-35 mg/kg loading dose capped near 3 g.
qzkzvaa: A patient on once-daily (extended-interval) gentamicin 7 mg/kg has a random level drawn 10 hours after the dose. How is this level used?
Plotted on a nomogram to choose the dosing interval
Compared with a target peak of 20-30 mcg/mL for efficacy
Ignored, since only troughs matter for extended dosing
Used to calculate a new loading dose for the next day
With extended-interval dosing, a single random level (6-14 hours post-dose) is plotted on a nomogram such as the Hartford nomogram to set a q24h, q36h, or q48h interval.
qd2zcev: A patient is on gentamicin 1 mg/kg q8h for enterococcal synergy. Which peak and trough pair is the target for that indication?
Peak 3 to 4 mcg/mL with a trough under 1 mcg/mL
Peak 16 to 24 mcg/mL with a trough under 1 mcg/mL
Peak 3 to 4 mcg/mL with a trough of 5 to 10 mcg/mL
Peak 8 to 10 mcg/mL with a trough of 2 to 4 mcg/mL

Synergy dosing aims only for a peak near 3 to 4 mcg/mL, because the role is to help a cell-wall agent rather than to kill on its own. Troughs are kept under 1 mcg/mL since sustained exposure drives nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity; peaks of 16 to 24 belong to extended-interval dosing for gram-negative infection.
q1m3t6w3: A 70-kg man with type 2 diabetes on metformin is admitted for cellulitis. He is eating normally, and his glucose readings are 220-280 mg/dL. Which regimen is preferred?
Basal-bolus insulin of about 0.4-0.5 units/kg/day total
Sliding-scale regular insulin alone before each meal
Continue metformin and add glipizide for the stay
Glargine 1 unit/kg once daily with no prandial or correction insulin
ADA guidance favors basal-bolus (or basal plus correction) insulin over sliding-scale insulin alone, with half of the total daily dose given as basal and half as prandial insulin.
q132ej9p: An 84-year-old woman with an eGFR of 25 mL/min is starting inpatient insulin. How should the weight-based total daily dose be chosen?
Use a lower dose, about 0.2-0.3 units/kg/day
Use the standard dose of 0.5 units/kg/day
Use a higher dose, about 0.8 units/kg/day, to avoid DKA
Use 1 unit/kg/day split into four injections
Older adults and those with renal impairment are at higher hypoglycemia risk, so start insulin at about 0.2-0.3 units/kg/day.
q8juwsq: What is the generally recommended glucose target for most non-critically ill hospitalized patients on insulin?
ADA recommends 140-180 mg/dL for most hospitalized patients; tighter targets of 80-110 mg/dL increase hypoglycemia without benefit.
q1axkci2: A woman with type 1 diabetes is made NPO for a morning procedure. The night-float nurse asks whether to hold her bedtime glargine. What do you order?
Give glargine at about 75-80% of the usual dose
Hold all glargine until she is eating again
Give the full glargine dose plus extra prandial insulin
Replace glargine with sliding-scale insulin only
Patients with type 1 diabetes always need basal insulin to prevent DKA; a modest dose reduction (about 20-25%) limits fasting hypoglycemia.
q1kin07: A 75-kg patient with a new pulmonary embolism is started on an unfractionated heparin weight-based nomogram. What is the usual initial order?
60 units/kg bolus, then 12 units/kg/hr with a 1000 units/hr cap
The standard VTE nomogram is an 80 units/kg bolus and 18 units/kg/hr; 60/12 is the lower-dose ACS nomogram.
q3p9n17: After a heparin infusion rate change, when should the next aPTT or anti-Xa level be drawn?
Only at the next morning labs
After 3 full days at the new rate
Heparin reaches a new steady state in about 6 hours, so levels are checked about 6 hours after each change.
qdg45yp: On day 7 of heparin therapy, a patient's platelet count has fallen from 240,000 to 95,000/mm3, and a new DVT is found. The 4T score is high. What is the next step?
Stop all heparin and start a non-heparin agent such as argatroban
Switch to enoxaparin and continue full-dose anticoagulation as before
Stop heparin and start warfarin immediately at full dose
Transfuse platelets and continue the heparin infusion
Suspected HIT requires stopping all heparin including LMWH and starting a non-heparin anticoagulant; warfarin is delayed until platelets recover.
qfgvqo9: A patient on telemetry has a potassium of 3.0 mEq/L and has only a peripheral IV. What is a safe maximum infusion rate for IV potassium chloride?
Peripheral KCl is usually limited to about 10 mEq/hr (up to 20 mEq/hr via central line with monitoring); it is never given by IV push.
q1nrl27b: Roughly how much will 40 mEq of potassium chloride raise serum potassium in a patient with normal renal function?
A common rule is that each 10 mEq raises serum potassium by about 0.1 mEq/L, though total body deficits vary.
qqjv15u: A patient with diarrhea has received 120 mEq of potassium over 2 days, but potassium remains 3.1 mEq/L. Which laboratory test is most useful to check next?
Hypomagnesemia increases renal potassium wasting; hypokalemia will be refractory until magnesium is replaced.
qjg5zqt: A patient on telemetry develops polymorphic VT with a prolonged QT but still has a pulse and a normal blood pressure. Which drug should be given first?
Torsades de pointes is treated with IV magnesium 2 g; amiodarone and procainamide further prolong the QT.
qcnur5w: A malnourished patient restarted on tube feeds has muscle weakness and a phosphorus level of 0.9 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate step?
Give IV phosphate and slow the feeding advance
Give oral phosphate only and advance feeds to goal now
Hold phosphate, since levels rebound on their own within 1-2 days
Give IV calcium chloride to raise the phosphorus
Severe (below 1 mg/dL) symptomatic hypophosphatemia from refeeding needs IV phosphate and a slower feeding advance.
qgt0btg: A patient has ionized hypocalcemia with perioral tingling after thyroidectomy and has only a peripheral IV. Which order is preferred?
IV calcium chloride by rapid push
Calcium gluconate is preferred peripherally; calcium chloride has three times the elemental calcium but causes severe tissue injury if it extravasates.
q58mgd7: A patient has total calcium 7.6 mg/dL and albumin 2.0 g/dL. What is the corrected calcium?
Corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.8 x (4 - albumin) = 7.6 + 1.6 = 9.2 mg/dL.
q67s8r7: A patient with chronic hyponatremia (sodium 112 mEq/L) is mildly confused. What is a generally accepted maximum correction in the first 24 hours?
Limit correction to about 8 mEq/L per 24 hours in high-risk chronic hyponatremia to avoid osmotic demyelination.
qoxnnon: A woman with a sodium of 116 mEq/L is now having a seizure. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
100 mL of 3% saline IV, repeated if symptoms persist
1 L of 0.9% saline wide open over 30 minutes
Fluid restriction to 800 mL per day and recheck sodium in the morning
Oral tolvaptan 15 mg and recheck in 24 hours
Severe symptomatic hyponatremia is treated with 100-mL boluses of 3% saline (up to three), aiming for a 4-6 mEq/L rise.
q1qj899o: Twelve hours into treatment of hyponatremia, the sodium has risen from 114 to 125 mEq/L. Which action is appropriate?
Give D5W and consider desmopressin to re-lower sodium
Continue the 3% saline at the same infusion rate
Switch to 0.9% saline at a higher rate to slow the rise in sodium
Add oral salt tablets and fluid restriction
An 11 mEq/L rise in 12 hours exceeds limits; re-lowering with free water and desmopressin reduces osmotic demyelination risk.
q4mvuru: Which patient is the least appropriate candidate for tolvaptan for hyponatremia?
A patient with cirrhosis and SIADH-range sodium
A patient with SIADH from small cell lung cancer
A patient with euvolemic SIADH and normal liver tests
A patient with heart failure and Na 124 mEq/L
Tolvaptan can cause serious liver injury and should be avoided in liver disease; it must also be started in the hospital.
q1ckvvh0: An 82-year-old woman has taken omeprazole for 6 years after a single episode of dyspepsia and has no history of Barrett esophagus, ulcer, or GI bleeding. What is the best plan?
Taper omeprazole, with an on-demand H2 blocker for symptoms
Continue omeprazole indefinitely and add a second PPI
Stop omeprazole and start sucralfate four times daily
Double the omeprazole dose to prevent rebound symptoms
Beers criteria advise against PPIs beyond 8 weeks without a clear indication; deprescribe by tapering to limit rebound acid.
q1uwefg0: A 79-year-old woman has taken lorazepam 1 mg nightly for 10 years and has fallen twice. What is the best deprescribing approach?
Taper gradually by about 10-25% every 2-4 weeks
Stop it tonight and start diphenhydramine for sleep
Switch to diazepam 10 mg nightly for long-term use
Continue it, since stopping at her age is unsafe
Benzodiazepines are on the Beers list for falls and cognition; long-term users need a slow taper, often with CBT-I.
qgum4vo: Which sleep aid is the most appropriate to remove from the medication list of an 85-year-old man with BPH and mild cognitive impairment?
Melatonin 3 mg at bedtime as needed
First-generation antihistamines are strongly anticholinergic (confusion, urinary retention) and are on the Beers list.
qdhsndd: A 78-year-old man with an eGFR of 40 mL/min has recurrent morning hypoglycemia. Which home medication is the most likely culprit and should be stopped?
Glyburide has active renally cleared metabolites and a long duration; Beers advises avoiding it in older adults.
q1lhhb9d: An 81-year-old woman with no vascular disease takes aspirin 81 mg daily for primary prevention. What is the best recommendation?
Discuss stopping it, since bleeding risk outweighs benefit
Increase aspirin to 325 mg for better protection
Add clopidogrel for dual antiplatelet prevention
Continue aspirin and add a daily NSAID for her arthritis pain
Beers and USPSTF guidance advise against starting aspirin for primary prevention in older adults; consider deprescribing.
q1tyf9xz: An 88-year-old woman with CrCl 22 mL/min has uncomplicated cystitis. Which agent is least appropriate?
Nitrofurantoin is less effective and more toxic at low CrCl; Beers advises avoiding it below CrCl 30.
qwdv1v0: A man on simvastatin 40 mg is prescribed clarithromycin for pneumonia. Two days later he has myalgias and dark urine. What is the mechanism?
Clarithromycin strongly inhibits CYP3A4, raising simvastatin levels and causing rhabdomyolysis; the combination is contraindicated.
qzecnl8: A patient on simvastatin is started on amlodipine 10 mg daily. What does the simvastatin label direct?
Make no change to the simvastatin

The simvastatin label caps the dose at 20 mg daily with amlodipine and at 10 mg daily with verapamil or diltiazem, because those drugs inhibit CYP3A4 and raise simvastatin exposure and myopathy risk. Strong 3A4 inhibitors such as clarithromycin are contraindicated outright.
q1792vmr: A patient on amiodarone needs a statin. What is the maximum recommended simvastatin dose?
Amiodarone inhibits simvastatin metabolism; FDA labeling limits simvastatin to 20 mg daily with amiodarone or amlodipine.
q144o63d: A kidney transplant patient on tacrolimus is started on voriconazole for invasive aspergillosis. What is the expected adjustment?
Reduce tacrolimus to about one-third and follow levels
Increase tacrolimus threefold to offset enzyme induction by the azole
Keep tacrolimus unchanged and check levels in a month
Stop tacrolimus entirely while on voriconazole
Voriconazole inhibits CYP3A4, sharply raising tacrolimus levels; labeling suggests a one-third dose with close trough monitoring.
q1ampdc7: A patient on warfarin with an INR of 2.5 is started on fluconazole for esophageal candidiasis. What is the expected effect?
The INR will rise, so monitor closely and consider a dose reduction
The INR will fall because fluconazole induces CYP2C9
No change, since azoles affect only CYP3A4 substrates
The INR will fall, so increase the warfarin dose by half for the course
Fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9 and CYP3A4, increasing warfarin effect and bleeding risk.
qyoi8wj: A patient stable on warfarin is started on rifampin for latent TB. What should you anticipate?
A falling INR that requires a higher warfarin dose
A rising INR that requires a lower warfarin dose for the whole course
No effect on the INR at any point in therapy
Bleeding that requires immediate vitamin K
Rifampin is a strong CYP inducer and can reduce warfarin effect dramatically; warfarin doses often need to increase.
q1hunaqj: An inpatient on methadone, IV haloperidol, and levofloxacin has a QTc of 520 ms. Nausea develops. Which antiemetic plan is best?
Avoid ondansetron, review QT drugs, and check K and Mg
Give ondansetron 8 mg IV and recheck the ECG in a week
Give droperidol since it does not affect the QT interval
Give ondansetron with promethazine and no ECG monitoring
Ondansetron, haloperidol, methadone, and fluoroquinolones all prolong the QT; with a QTc over 500 ms, remove offenders and replete electrolytes.
qzdg0da: Before giving IV haloperidol to a delirious patient, which test is most important?
IV haloperidol prolongs the QTc and can cause torsades; check a baseline ECG and electrolytes.
q1udjkwt: A patient on sertraline is started on linezolid for VRE. Two days later he has tremor, clonus, diarrhea, and fever. What is the most likely cause?
Serotonin syndrome from linezolid MAO inhibition
Linezolid is a weak MAO inhibitor; with SSRIs it can cause serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperthermia, GI symptoms).
qsek7id: What is the most appropriate treatment for moderate serotonin syndrome after stopping the offending drugs?
Dantrolene and bromocriptine given together, plus cooling
Haloperidol for agitation and a cooling blanket
Physostigmine and a repeat dose of the SSRI
Management is stopping serotonergic drugs, benzodiazepines, supportive care, and the 5-HT2A antagonist cyproheptadine.
qea5qvi: A patient on high-dose venlafaxine needs post-op pain control. Which opioid is most important to avoid?
Tramadol has serotonergic activity and lowers the seizure threshold, so it can precipitate serotonin syndrome with SNRIs.
qmmqllt: A patient on fluoxetine develops vasoplegia after cardiac surgery and the team considers methylene blue. What is the main concern?
Methylene blue is a potent MAO inhibitor; serotonin syndrome risk is high with SSRIs.
q1nslvt5: A 29-year-old woman on lisinopril for chronic hypertension tells you she is 7 weeks pregnant. What is the best plan?
Stop lisinopril and start labetalol or nifedipine
Continue lisinopril, since risk is in the first trimester
Switch to losartan for safer blood pressure control
Stop all antihypertensives for the rest of pregnancy
ACE inhibitors and ARBs are fetotoxic (renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios); labetalol, nifedipine, or methyldopa are used in pregnancy.
q6btpnz: A woman on warfarin for recurrent DVT learns that she is 6 weeks pregnant. Which anticoagulant should replace warfarin?
Rivaroxaban 20 mg daily with the evening meal
Warfarin causes embryopathy; LMWH does not cross the placenta and is preferred. DOACs are not recommended in pregnancy.
q1nqsd89: A woman at 24 weeks gestation has asymptomatic bacteriuria with pansensitive E. coli. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
Asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated in pregnancy; beta-lactams such as cephalexin are safe, while fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines are avoided.
qmohxmr: A breastfeeding mother with postpartum depression needs an antidepressant. Which is a commonly preferred choice?
Sertraline has very low milk transfer and is among the preferred antidepressants during lactation.
qmqm0h4: A breastfeeding mother needs short-term analgesia after a cesarean. Which opioid is specifically warned against in lactation?
FDA warns against codeine (and tramadol) in breastfeeding because ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizers can pass toxic morphine to infants.
q1vdorrs: A woman with Graves disease is 8 weeks pregnant. Which antithyroid drug is preferred now?
PTU is preferred in the first trimester because methimazole is teratogenic; switch to methimazole after the first trimester because of PTU hepatotoxicity.
qo6g0at: A 23-year-old woman with epilepsy who is planning a pregnancy asks about her medication. Which drug carries the greatest teratogenic risk?
Valproate has the highest rates of neural tube defects and cognitive harm; lamotrigine and levetiracetam are preferred.
ql3kwev: A patient with decompensated cirrhosis needs a benzodiazepine for alcohol withdrawal. Which is preferred?
Lorazepam (with oxazepam and temazepam) undergoes glucuronidation only, so it does not accumulate in liver failure.
qm7nwxj: A patient with compensated cirrhosis who does not drink asks about acetaminophen. What is a commonly recommended daily maximum?
Acetaminophen at up to 2 g/day is considered safe and preferred over NSAIDs in cirrhosis.
qptsfne: Why should NSAIDs be avoided in a patient with cirrhosis and ascites?
They can precipitate renal failure and GI bleeding
They raise the INR by inhibiting vitamin K
They cause rebound ascites and hyponatremia when they are stopped
NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandins, precipitating AKI and diuretic resistance, and raise GI bleeding risk in cirrhosis.
qpli0ef: A patient on hemodialysis needs IV opioid analgesia. Which opioid is the least appropriate?
Morphine metabolites (M3G, M6G) accumulate in renal failure, causing sedation, myoclonus, and respiratory depression.
qiqqt1f: A patient on metformin for 8 years has new distal paresthesias and a macrocytic anemia. Which effect of the drug fits?
Reduced ileal absorption of vitamin B12
Reduced intrinsic factor output by the stomach

Metformin interferes with calcium-dependent uptake of the B12-intrinsic factor complex in the terminal ileum, and deficiency appears in roughly 5 to 10 percent of long-term users, so B12 is checked when anemia or neuropathy shows up. Intrinsic factor production itself is unaffected.
q6norg5: A 70-kg patient with CrCl 22 mL/min has a new DVT. Which enoxaparin dose is appropriate?
For CrCl under 30, therapeutic enoxaparin is reduced to 1 mg/kg once daily because it is renally cleared.
qn127ds: A medical inpatient with CrCl 25 mL/min needs VTE prophylaxis. Which enoxaparin order is correct?
Prophylactic enoxaparin is 40 mg daily, reduced to 30 mg daily when CrCl is below 30 mL/min.
qkpa8tq: An 82-year-old woman weighing 55 kg with creatinine 1.1 mg/dL is starting apixaban for atrial fibrillation. What dose is correct?
Apixaban is reduced to 2.5 mg twice daily when at least two of three criteria are present: age 80 years or older, weight 60 kg or less, or creatinine 1.5 mg/dL or higher.
q1i91mh: A patient on dabigatran with severe GI bleeding needs reversal. Which agent is specific for dabigatran?
Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran; andexanet reverses factor Xa inhibitors.
q1wpd869: A patient on apixaban presents with an intracranial hemorrhage. Which reversal option is appropriate in the US?
Factor Xa inhibitor bleeding is treated with 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate; andexanet alfa was withdrawn from the US market in 2025.
q1bt2axd: A patient on warfarin has an INR of 11 and no bleeding. What is the recommended management?
Hold warfarin and give oral vitamin K 2.5-5 mg
Hold warfarin and give 4-factor PCC immediately
Continue warfarin and recheck the INR in a week
Give IV vitamin K 10 mg plus fresh frozen plasma
For INR above 10 without bleeding, hold warfarin and give oral vitamin K; PCC is reserved for major bleeding.
qom62n0: An intern is ordering vitamin K for warfarin reversal. Which statement about the route is correct?
IV vitamin K carries a risk of anaphylactoid reaction
Subcutaneous dosing acts faster than the oral route
Oral vitamin K needs a bile-independent carrier
Intramuscular dosing is preferred during anticoagulation

IV phytonadione carries a boxed warning for hypersensitivity including fatal anaphylactoid reactions, so it is diluted and infused over at least 20 minutes. Subcutaneous absorption is erratic and slower than oral, and IM injection risks hematoma in an anticoagulated patient.
q1h1hgyx: A patient on warfarin has a major GI bleed with INR 4.8. What is the best combination for reversal?
4-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K 10 mg
Oral vitamin K 2.5 mg alone and observation
Major warfarin bleeding requires rapid reversal with 4-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K to sustain the effect.
q1ik6797: A patient taking oral morphine 60 mg per day is now NPO. What is the equianalgesic IV morphine dose per day?
Oral morphine 30 mg is roughly equivalent to IV morphine 10 mg (3:1), so 60 mg oral is about 20 mg IV.
q1aovqvz: A patient uses oxycodone 10 mg every 4 hours (60 mg/day). What is the equianalgesic daily oral morphine dose before any cross-tolerance reduction?
Oral oxycodone 20 mg is about oral morphine 30 mg (1:1.5), so 60 mg oxycodone is about 90 mg oral morphine.
q1xgnhh6: A patient receives IV hydromorphone 1.5 mg. Roughly how much IV morphine is this equivalent to?
Conventional tables equate IV hydromorphone 1.5 mg with IV morphine 10 mg.
q10u17j6: When switching a patient from one opioid to another, how should the calculated equianalgesic dose usually be adjusted?
Reduce it by about 25-50% for incomplete cross-tolerance
Increase it by about 50% to avoid withdrawal
Give the exact calculated dose without changes
Reduce it by 90% and then titrate up slowly every week
Incomplete cross-tolerance means the new opioid is usually started at 25-50% less than the calculated equivalent.
q15zc1bu: A cancer patient takes long-acting oxycodone totaling 120 mg/day. What is an appropriate breakthrough dose of immediate-release oxycodone?
About 10-20 mg every 2-4 hours as needed
About 60 mg every 2 hours as needed
About 2.5 mg every 12 hours as needed for pain
About 120 mg once daily as needed
Breakthrough doses are typically 10-20% of the total daily opioid dose.
qr0zmjf: An opioid-naive post-op patient has severe pain. A colleague suggests a fentanyl 25 mcg/hr patch. What is the main problem?
Fentanyl patches are for opioid-tolerant patients only
The patch dose is far too low to have any effect
Fentanyl patches are contraindicated in renal disease
Patches work within 15 minutes and then wear off very quickly
Transdermal fentanyl has a slow onset and long duration and is contraindicated in opioid-naive patients and for acute pain.
q1hicwz3: An opioid-naive post-op patient is being started on morphine PCA. Which setting is generally avoided?
A lockout interval of about 10 minutes
Basal infusions in opioid-naive patients increase respiratory depression without improving analgesia.
qyx3d25: A post-op patient on opioids is somnolent with a respiratory rate of 7/min but has a pulse and a good airway. What naloxone approach is preferred?
Dilute 0.4 mg and give 0.04-0.08 mg in IV increments
Give 2 mg IV push all at once and repeat
Give 10 mg IM and transfer to the ICU
Withhold naloxone and start a flumazenil infusion instead
Small titrated naloxone doses reverse respiratory depression without causing abrupt severe pain, withdrawal, or pulmonary edema.
q1mnbekp: Why is rotation from high-dose morphine to methadone considered too risky for an intern to do alone?
Its conversion ratio is nonlinear and its half-life is long
Methadone has no oral form and is IV only
Methadone has no effect on the QT interval
Methadone is cleared within a few hours of each dose, so it needs q2h dosing
Methadone has a variable, dose-dependent conversion ratio and a long half-life, which can cause delayed toxicity; involve pain or palliative care specialists.
q1s219av: A patient on sublingual buprenorphine for opioid use disorder is admitted for elective surgery with moderate pain expected. What does current guidance generally favor?
Continue buprenorphine and add multimodal analgesia
Stop buprenorphine 2 weeks before every surgery
Switch to methadone the night before surgery
Give naltrexone the night before surgery to block opioid cravings
Most guidance now recommends continuing buprenorphine perioperatively, with added non-opioid and short-acting opioid analgesia as needed.
qboj624: An 82-year-old man is agitated with delirium and is pulling at lines after nonpharmacologic measures failed. Which treatment is reasonable?
Lorazepam 2 mg IV every hour as needed
Haloperidol 10 mg IV every 30 minutes until calm
If medication is needed, use the lowest effective antipsychotic dose briefly; benzodiazepines and anticholinergics worsen delirium.
qyzbgf9: A man with Parkinson disease is acutely delirious and agitated. Which antipsychotic is preferred if one is needed?
High-potency D2 blockers worsen parkinsonism; low-dose quetiapine is preferred in Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia.
q148h77s: In which delirious patient is a benzodiazepine the treatment of choice?
A patient in alcohol withdrawal delirium
A patient with delirium from a UTI
Benzodiazepines worsen most delirium but are the treatment of choice for alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.
qt0tyfq: A malnourished patient with alcohol use disorder is hypoglycemic and confused. Which order is correct?
Give thiamine before or with dextrose
Give dextrose only, then thiamine next week
Give thiamine only and hold all glucose
Thiamine should be given before or with glucose to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy, but glucose should not be delayed.
q1fqscen: A ventilated ICU patient needs sedation and the team wants to reduce delirium. Which agent is generally preferred over benzodiazepines?
Guidelines favor propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines for ICU sedation to reduce delirium and ventilator days.
q1jzm1e9: A patient with atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc 3) on warfarin is scheduled for an elective colectomy. What is the usual plan?
Stop warfarin 5 days before without bridging
Stop warfarin 1 day before and bridge with heparin
Continue warfarin through surgery at full dose
Stop warfarin 2 weeks before and bridge with enoxaparin
Warfarin is held 5 days pre-op; the BRIDGE trial showed bridging in most AF patients increases bleeding without reducing stroke.
qu3kxxz: Which patient on warfarin most clearly needs heparin bridging before major surgery?
A patient with a mechanical mitral valve
A patient with AF and CHA2DS2-VASc of 2
A patient with a DVT 2 years ago
A patient with a bioprosthetic aortic valve
Mechanical mitral valves carry high thrombotic risk and typically require bridging.
q7uzcox: A patient with normal renal function on apixaban needs a high-bleeding-risk surgery. When should the last dose be given?
For apixaban with normal renal function, hold it about 48 hours before high-bleeding-risk procedures (24 hours for low-risk procedures); bridging is not needed.
q38daqm: A patient on metformin is having elective surgery and will likely receive IV contrast. What is a common instruction?
Hold metformin on the day of surgery
Double the dose the night before surgery
Hold it for 1 month after surgery
Continue it even when made NPO
Metformin is usually held the day of surgery and resumed once the patient is eating and renal function is stable.
q1uqr6xk: A patient on empagliflozin is scheduled for elective surgery. Per FDA labeling, when should it be stopped?
It does not need to be stopped
SGLT2 inhibitors are held at least 3 days before surgery (4 days for ertugliflozin) to reduce euglycemic DKA risk.
qzht4uo: A post-op patient on dapagliflozin is vomiting, with glucose 165 mg/dL, bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, and an anion gap of 22. What is the likely diagnosis?
SGLT2 inhibitors can cause DKA with near-normal glucose, especially with surgery, fasting, or illness.
q2s8cmu: A patient on prednisone 20 mg daily for 1 year is undergoing major abdominal surgery. Which stress-dose plan is appropriate?
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction, then 50 mg q8h
No steroid on the day of surgery, then resume later
Dexamethasone 0.5 mg orally on the day of surgery
Fludrocortisone 0.1 mg orally alone at anesthesia induction
Patients with HPA suppression need stress-dose hydrocortisone for major surgery, tapered over 1-2 days.
q1pew93j: A patient on lisinopril for hypertension is having major surgery. What is a common perioperative approach?
Hold it about 24 hours before surgery
Double the dose on the morning of surgery
Stop it 3 weeks before and switch to clonidine
Give it IV during surgery to prevent swings
ACE inhibitors and ARBs are often held 24 hours pre-op to reduce intraoperative hypotension.
q1oicxqa: A patient on long-term metoprolol for coronary disease is having surgery. What is recommended?
Stop it the morning of surgery
Switch to high-dose IV atenolol on the day of surgery
Chronic beta blockers should be continued to avoid rebound tachycardia and ischemia.
q1bqpnay: A patient with MRSA bacteremia is on vancomycin. Which monitoring target do current consensus guidelines recommend?

The 2020 consensus guideline recommends AUC-guided dosing with an AUC to MIC ratio of 400 to 600 for serious MRSA infection, because troughs pushed to 15 to 20 raise nephrotoxicity without improving outcomes. Peak levels are not used for vancomycin.
q1nvxbvq: Blood cultures grow methicillin-susceptible S. aureus in a patient on vancomycin with no beta-lactam allergy. What is the best change?
Continue vancomycin since it covers MSSA
Beta-lactams are superior to vancomycin for MSSA bacteremia.
qqflzuj: A patient has uncomplicated MSSA bacteremia with negative repeat cultures and no endocarditis. What is the minimum IV duration?
14 days from the first negative culture
5 days from the first positive culture
7 days from the start of therapy
6 weeks from the start of IV therapy
Uncomplicated S. aureus bacteremia needs at least 14 days of IV therapy from clearance; complicated cases need 4-6 weeks.
qrna6n6: An adult with community-acquired pneumonia is improving and afebrile for 48 hours. What is the usual total antibiotic duration?
Most CAP patients need at least 5 days, stopping once clinically stable for about 48 hours.
q1ylcs0r: A woman with uncomplicated pyelonephritis caused by ciprofloxacin-susceptible E. coli is being discharged. What duration is appropriate?
IDSA supports 7 days of ciprofloxacin for uncomplicated pyelonephritis; TMP-SMX requires 14 days.
q1t1bzh7: A patient has uncomplicated E. coli bacteremia from a urinary source and is clinically improving. What is the commonly accepted duration?
Trials show 7 days is noninferior to 14 days for uncomplicated gram-negative bacteremia.
q1j1j46p: A patient with perforated appendicitis had adequate source control. How long should antibiotics continue after source control?
The STOP-IT trial showed about 4 days after source control is as effective as longer courses.
qmvkvj: An 80-year-old nursing home resident has a positive urine culture but no urinary symptoms or fever. What is the appropriate management?
Asymptomatic bacteriuria should not be treated except in pregnancy or before urologic procedures.
q1gex9fp: A patient has a first episode of non-severe C. difficile infection. Which regimen is appropriate?
Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days
IV vancomycin 1 g every 12 hours for 10 days
Oral metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 3 days
Oral vancomycin 2 g once as a single dose, then observe for relapse
Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily or fidaxomicin for 10 days is recommended; IV vancomycin does not reach the colon.
q1o7wge4: A patient with ESRD receiving full-dose cefepime becomes confused and has myoclonus. What is the likely cause?
Serotonin syndrome from cefepime and his home medications
Cefepime accumulates in renal failure and causes encephalopathy, myoclonus, and nonconvulsive seizures.
q1ccxytz: Which antibiotic combination is associated with a higher AKI risk than alternatives?
Observational studies show more AKI with vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam than vancomycin plus cefepime.
q1r5g4uk: A 68-year-old medical inpatient with pneumonia and normal renal function is immobile. What is the standard VTE prophylaxis?
Warfarin to an INR of 2-3 during the stay
Enoxaparin 40 mg daily or SC heparin is standard VTE prophylaxis in at-risk medical inpatients.
q13pkel4: Which inpatient most clearly meets criteria for stress ulcer prophylaxis?
A ventilated ICU patient with a coagulopathy
A ward patient with pneumonia who is eating
A post-op patient walking the halls on day 2
A ward patient on prophylactic enoxaparin and aspirin
Stress ulcer prophylaxis is indicated in critically ill patients with risk factors such as mechanical ventilation or coagulopathy.
q1081q0o: A patient with cirrhosis presents with an upper GI bleed. Which antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended?
Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily for up to 7 days
Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily
No antibiotics are needed in this setting
Metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours for 10 days
Cirrhotic patients with GI bleeding have high infection risk; ceftriaxone for up to 7 days reduces infections and mortality.
q150cwr9: A patient with cirrhosis has recovered from an episode of SBP. Which long-term prophylaxis is appropriate?
Patients with prior SBP need long-term secondary prophylaxis, such as ciprofloxacin or TMP-SMX.
q1n6zw2j: A patient taking cyclophosphamide has also been on prednisone 30 mg daily for 6 weeks. Which prophylaxis should be added?
Prolonged prednisone at 20 mg or more per day combined with another immunosuppressant warrants PCP prophylaxis with TMP-SMX.
qsj3ast: A patient with HIV and a CD4 count of 150 cells/mm3 has a severe sulfa allergy. Which PCP prophylaxis is reasonable after G6PD testing?
Dapsone is an alternative to TMP-SMX for PCP prophylaxis but causes hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
q1vrm54p: A patient develops hives, wheezing, and a BP of 78/40 mm Hg after IV ceftriaxone. Which drug should be given first?
IM epinephrine (1 mg/mL) in the thigh is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis.
q1ehfmgz: A patient on metoprolol has anaphylaxis that is refractory to repeated epinephrine. Which drug may help?
Glucagon acts independently of beta receptors and can help in anaphylaxis in patients on beta blockers.
qpxqowl: Thirty minutes into a PRBC unit a patient has a temperature rise of 1.5 C with chills and no other findings. Haptoglobin and LDH are normal. Which reaction is this?
Acute hemolytic reaction from an ABO mismatch

Febrile nonhemolytic reactions come from cytokines accumulated in the stored unit and from recipient antibodies against donor leukocytes; normal haptoglobin and LDH argue against hemolysis. Prestorage leukoreduction lowers the recurrence rate.
q4zvz56: During a transfusion, a patient's temperature rises 1.2 degrees C with no other symptoms. What is the best management?
Stop it, rule out hemolysis, and give acetaminophen
Continue it and give IV methylprednisolone
Stop it and give IM epinephrine right away
Speed up the transfusion to finish the unit quickly and observe
Febrile nonhemolytic reactions are common, but hemolysis must be excluded before considering further transfusion.
qdoporx: During a platelet transfusion, a patient develops mild urticaria only, with stable vital signs. What is appropriate?
Pause it, give an antihistamine, and resume if better
Stop it permanently and start an epinephrine infusion
Give IV furosemide and stop all future transfusions permanently
Continue it with no other change needed
Mild allergic reactions (hives only) may be treated with antihistamines and the transfusion resumed.
q1yoqr0k: An elderly patient with heart failure receiving 2 units of PRBCs has dyspnea, hypertension, and an elevated BNP. Which treatment is most appropriate?
TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload) is treated with diuretics, unlike TRALI, which is managed supportively.
q1bf3tcd: A hospitalized patient has a glucose of 42 mg/dL is confused, and has IV access. What is the first treatment?
Hypoglycemia with altered mental status and IV access is treated with IV dextrose; glucagon is used without IV access.
q1cfbqt3: A dialysis patient has a potassium of 7.2 mEq/L with peaked T waves and a widened QRS. What should be given first?
IV calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane immediately; insulin with dextrose, beta-agonists, and dialysis follow.
qyluif: A stable patient has a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 180/min that persists after vagal maneuvers. Which drug should be given first?
Adenosine 6 mg rapid push (then 12 mg) is first-line for stable SVT.
qkwv3zf: A patient has symptomatic sinus bradycardia with a heart rate of 38/min and a BP of 80/50 mm Hg. What is the first drug and dose?
Current ACLS recommends atropine 1 mg IV every 3-5 minutes (max 3 mg) for symptomatic bradycardia.
q11okapb: A patient with IV access is having a generalized tonic-clonic seizure that has lasted 6 minutes. Which drug should be given first?
Lorazepam 4 mg IV, may repeat once
Benzodiazepines are first-line for status epilepticus; second-line agents include fosphenytoin, levetiracetam, or valproate.
qybv9w6: After lorazepam, seizures continue. Which second-line loading dose is appropriate?
Fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg, levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, or valproate 40 mg/kg are second-line options.
q1hnpz1l: A patient has a hypertensive emergency with a BP of 220/130 mm Hg and encephalopathy. What is the initial blood pressure goal?
Lower MAP by no more than 25% in the first hour
Lower BP to 120/80 within the first hour
Avoid any blood pressure lowering for 24 hours
Rapid overcorrection risks ischemia; reduce MAP by no more than 25% in the first hour, then gradually.
qz4k7gy: A patient on lithium is started on lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide. What is the main concern?
ACE inhibitors, thiazides, and NSAIDs reduce lithium clearance and increase toxicity risk.
qcm1ewd: When should a lithium level be drawn after a dose change?
A 12-hour trough about 5 days after the change
One hour after the first new dose, same day
Randomly at any time of day, with other labs
Only once yearly at the annual physical exam
Lithium levels are drawn 12 hours post-dose at steady state, about 5 days after a dose change.
q73za7c: Which labs should be monitored periodically in a patient on long-term lithium?
CBC and lipase only, every 3 months
Lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, CKD, hypothyroidism, and hyperparathyroidism.
q12o8nxz: A patient is starting amiodarone. What baseline monitoring is recommended?
TSH, LFTs, chest x-ray, and PFTs
Lipase, uric acid, and CK only
Urine drug screen and lipid panel only
Amiodarone causes thyroid, liver, and lung toxicity; baseline and periodic monitoring is required.
q15ehdsp: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis is started on weekly methotrexate. Which supplement and monitoring are standard?
Folic acid, CBC, LFTs, and creatinine
Vitamin K, INR, and lipase monthly
Vitamin D, calcium, and CK every visit
Folic acid reduces toxicity; methotrexate needs CBC, liver, and renal monitoring.
q1c4cfwv: A patient on methotrexate is prescribed TMP-SMX. What is the main risk?
TMP-SMX inhibits folate metabolism and reduces methotrexate clearance, causing pancytopenia.
qcsxkil: A patient is being started on clozapine. What is the minimum ANC required to start it in the general population?
Clozapine requires an ANC of 1500 or more to start (1000 for benign ethnic neutropenia) because of agranulocytosis risk.
q1ch94ma: Three weeks into clozapine, a patient has fever, tachycardia, and chest pain. What should be checked?
Clozapine-induced myocarditis usually occurs in the first 4-8 weeks; troponin and CRP screen for it.
qrq0b93: A patient started on atorvastatin develops mild muscle aches. What is the best next step?
Check CK and consider dose change or another statin
Double the dose to improve tolerance
Ignore it, since statins rarely cause any muscle symptoms at all
Statin-associated muscle symptoms are evaluated with CK; mild cases can be managed by dose reduction or switching.
qringix: A patient with heart failure on lisinopril is started on spironolactone. What should be monitored?
Spironolactone with ACE inhibitors increases hyperkalemia risk; check K and creatinine in a few days and periodically.
q6w8w84: A patient on digoxin is started on amiodarone. What adjustment is recommended?
Reduce the digoxin dose by about 50%
No change is necessary for either drug
Amiodarone raises digoxin levels; reduce digoxin and monitor levels.
qha05dw: A patient on azathioprine is started on allopurinol for gout. What is the main concern?
Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, which metabolizes azathioprine, causing toxicity; reduce the azathioprine dose substantially or avoid the combination.
qax9eb3: A patient on dialysis is prescribed gabapentin 600 mg three times daily and becomes sedated. What is the problem?
Gabapentin accumulates and needs renal dosing
Gabapentin is removed completely by each dialysis session
Gabapentin is renally cleared and requires dose reduction in renal impairment.
q1ap8tvp: A patient ingested a large amount of acetaminophen 4 hours ago. When should NAC be started?
If the 4-hour level is above the treatment line
Only if LFTs are already elevated
Never, since activated charcoal alone is enough treatment
The 4-hour acetaminophen level is plotted on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram to guide NAC therapy.
q1mxeccx: A transplant patient on tacrolimus is started on rifampin. What is the expected effect?
Tacrolimus levels fall and rejection risk rises
Rifampin induces CYP3A4, reducing tacrolimus levels.
qfebueq: A structural analog of amiodarone was designed to reduce thyroid toxicity and shorten tissue accumulation. Which structural change most directly explains its lower thyroid toxicity?
Removal of the iodine atoms from the molecule
Addition of a beta-lactam ring to the benzofuran core
Conversion to a prodrug activated by esterases in plasma
Replacement of the benzofuran with a piperazine ring
Dronedarone lacks iodine and has a methanesulfonyl group that reduces lipophilicity, giving less thyroid toxicity and a much shorter half-life than amiodarone.
q1mgin8x: A 74-year-old man with atrial fibrillation for 3 years has failed two cardioversions and is now managed with rate control only. His cardiologist plans no further rhythm attempts. Why is dronedarone inappropriate for him?
It increases death and stroke in permanent atrial fibrillation
It is ineffective unless combined with a class Ic antiarrhythmic
It must be loaded intravenously before oral maintenance
It causes hypothyroidism in most patients within 1 year
In PALLAS, dronedarone increased stroke, HF, and CV death in permanent AF, which is now a boxed-warning contraindication.
qrkghpn: A client is switched from amiodarone to dronedarone. Which monitoring need is reduced by that change?
Periodic thyroid studies and lung imaging
Periodic ECG review of the QT interval on telemetry

Dronedarone was built without the iodine moiety of amiodarone, so thyroid dysfunction and pulmonary fibrosis are far less common. Liver injury, an early creatinine rise and QT prolongation still occur and are still followed.
q1rp2eoq: An IV class III antiarrhythmic converts atrial flutter to sinus rhythm. In addition to blocking the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current, it has a second distinctive ionic action. Which action is it?
Enhancement of the slow inward late sodium current
Activation of the ATP-sensitive potassium channel
Blockade of the funny current in the sinoatrial node
Stimulation of the cardiac sodium-potassium ATPase
Ibutilide blocks IKr and activates the slow inward plateau sodium current, both of which prolong the action potential and QT interval.
q1cm6iph: A 58-year-old woman with atrial flutter of 12 hours' duration receives IV ibutilide and converts to sinus rhythm. Twenty minutes later she becomes unresponsive. Which rhythm is most likely?
Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with QT prolongation
Complete heart block with a narrow junctional escape
Monomorphic VT from a scar-mediated reentry circuit
Ibutilide causes torsades de pointes in about 2% of patients, usually within an hour of infusion and more often in women.
q1dqrhli: A client with recent-onset atrial fibrillation is ordered IV ibutilide. Which laboratory values should the nurse confirm are within normal limits before starting the infusion?
Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia increase the risk of torsades de pointes with ibutilide and should be corrected before the infusion.
q18si2yu: A class Ia antiarrhythmic is chosen for a patient with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy to reduce the outflow tract gradient. Which property of this drug produces that benefit?
Negative inotropic effect on ventricular myocardium
Selective blockade of the IKs potassium current
Stimulation of cardiac beta-1 adrenergic receptors
Inhibition of the sodium-calcium exchanger pump
Disopyramide strongly reduces contractility, which lessens dynamic LVOT obstruction in HCM; the same property worsens HFrEF.
q18c0fd7: A 71-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia is started on disopyramide. Two days later he has suprapubic fullness and cannot void. What property of the drug best explains this?
Antimuscarinic blockade of the bladder detrusor
Alpha-1 agonist contraction of the prostate
Direct nephrotoxicity causing acute tubular necrosis
Disopyramide has prominent anticholinergic effects that cause urinary retention, dry mouth, constipation, and may precipitate angle-closure glaucoma.
qzp66cg: A client receiving disopyramide has a QRS that increased from 0.09 to 0.13 seconds since the drug was started. What should the nurse do?
Hold the dose and report the QRS change to the provider
Give the dose because the QRS remains under 0.20 seconds
Give the dose with milk to lessen the conduction effect
Hold the dose for 1 hour and then give it as scheduled
A QRS widening of more than 25% from baseline suggests sodium channel toxicity, so the dose is held and the provider notified.
q15qdqpp: A patient with acute decompensated heart failure receives a recombinant peptide that binds natriuretic peptide receptor-A. Which second messenger mediates its vasodilating effect?
Increased cyclic GMP from particulate guanylate cyclase
Increased cyclic AMP from Gs-coupled adenylyl cyclase
Increased IP3 and calcium release from Gq signaling
Decreased cyclic GMP from phosphodiesterase activation
Nesiritide is recombinant BNP; NPR-A is a membrane-bound guanylate cyclase that raises cGMP, relaxing vascular smooth muscle.
qokjeg0: A 66-year-old woman with acute decompensated heart failure is started on nesiritide. Which adverse effect is most common and most likely to limit the infusion?
Hypotension is the most frequent adverse effect of nesiritide; it is contraindicated in cardiogenic shock and when SBP is below 100 mmHg.
q1dw6faz: A client is to begin a nesiritide bolus and infusion. Current vital signs are BP 94/58 mmHg, HR 92/min, and RR 24/min. What is the nurse's best action?
Withhold the drug and notify the provider of the BP
Give the bolus and begin the infusion as ordered
Give the bolus only and hold the infusion for 1 hour
Begin the infusion at a double rate to skip the bolus
Nesiritide should not be started when systolic BP is below 100 mmHg because it can cause significant, prolonged hypotension.
q1m7hajq: A patient with a hypertensive emergency and acute kidney injury receives an IV agent that dilates renal arterioles and increases sodium excretion. Which receptor does this drug activate?
Fenoldopam is a selective peripheral D1 agonist that raises cAMP in vascular smooth muscle, dilating renal and mesenteric arterioles.
q15kw1dw: A 60-year-old man with a hypertensive emergency is treated with a fenoldopam infusion. Which adverse effect is a recognized dose-related consequence of this drug?
Fenoldopam can raise intraocular pressure and cause hypokalemia and reflex tachycardia; cyanide toxicity is associated with nitroprusside.
q18jy4bo: A client has been receiving a fenoldopam infusion for 6 hours for severe hypertension. Which laboratory value is most important for the nurse to monitor?
Fenoldopam commonly lowers serum potassium, often within the first 6 hours, so potassium should be checked and replaced as ordered.
q1jp2hos: A 45-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and an LVOT gradient of 80 mmHg is started on a drug that reduces actin-myosin cross-bridge formation. What is its molecular target?
Mavacamten is an allosteric, reversible inhibitor of cardiac myosin ATPase that reduces hypercontractility and LVOT obstruction.
qmg30bl: A patient with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is being considered for mavacamten. Which finding must be confirmed before therapy begins?
Left ventricular ejection fraction of at least 55%
Resting heart rate of at least 70/min in sinus rhythm
Serum potassium above 5.0 mEq/L before the first dose
Absence of prior septal myectomy on surgical history
The boxed warning requires echocardiographic LVEF of at least 55% before starting because mavacamten can cause HF from systolic dysfunction.
q19fhaj8: A client on mavacamten for obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy comes for the scheduled echocardiogram. Which result requires the drug to be interrupted?
A left atrial size of 42 mm

Mavacamten reduces contractility by inhibiting cardiac myosin ATPase, so its REMS program requires serial echocardiograms and the drug is interrupted when LVEF falls below 50 percent. Atrial size and septal thickness are features of the disease, not stopping rules.
q1qsetls: An oral heart failure drug increases cyclic GMP by directly stimulating the nitric oxide receptor, even when nitric oxide levels are low. Which enzyme does it act on?
Vericiguat stimulates soluble guanylate cyclase independently of NO and sensitizes it to endogenous NO, increasing cGMP.
qv0vaa6: A 62-year-old man with HFrEF who was recently hospitalized is being started on vericiguat. Which of his current medications is contraindicated with it?
Vericiguat is contraindicated with other soluble guanylate cyclase stimulators such as riociguat because of additive hypotension.
q5v28lh: A woman of reproductive age is starting vericiguat. Which teaching point is the priority for the nurse to include?
Avoid pregnancy and use effective contraception
Take each dose on an empty stomach at bedtime
Avoid foods high in potassium such as bananas
Expect orange urine during the first week of use
Vericiguat carries a boxed warning for embryo-fetal toxicity, so pregnancy must be excluded and effective contraception used.
qe5r7w3: A 54-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis and ascites develops hepatorenal syndrome with acute kidney injury. He is treated with albumin plus a vasopressin analog. Which receptor mediates the main therapeutic effect of this drug?
V1 receptor on splanchnic vascular smooth muscle
V2 receptor on renal collecting duct principal cells
Alpha-1 receptor on systemic arteriolar smooth muscle
SSTR2 receptor on splanchnic endothelial cells
Terlipressin is a V1-selective vasopressin analog; splanchnic vasoconstriction raises effective arterial volume and improves renal perfusion in hepatorenal syndrome.
q13fzc8f: A 60-year-old woman with cirrhosis and hepatorenal syndrome-AKI is being considered for terlipressin. Which finding is a contraindication to starting it?
Oxygen saturation of 88% on room air
Terlipressin carries a boxed warning for serious or fatal respiratory failure and should not be started in patients with SpO2 below 90% or worsening respiratory symptoms.
q3e6mxb: A client is starting terlipressin for hepatorenal syndrome. Which baseline assessment does the boxed warning drive?
A twelve-lead ECG with QT interval
A fasting lipid panel with an A1c and TSH

Terlipressin carries a boxed warning for serious or fatal respiratory failure, so oxygenation and volume status are assessed before the first dose and the drug is avoided in patients who are hypoxic or fluid overloaded. Its V1 receptor action causes ischemic complications rather than QT change.
q1xhy1ib: A 68-year-old hospitalized woman with SIADH and a serum sodium of 118 mEq/L is started on an IV drug that blocks vasopressin receptors. What is the mechanism by which this drug raises the serum sodium?
Reduced aquaporin-2 insertion in the collecting duct
Inhibition of the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the loop
Increased aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex
Blockade of the epithelial sodium channel in the tubule
Conivaptan blocks V2 receptors, preventing cAMP-driven aquaporin-2 insertion and producing free water excretion (aquaresis); it also blocks V1a receptors.
q1rxiit3: A 72-year-old man is admitted with a serum sodium of 121 mEq/L. Which clinical situation is a contraindication to treatment with IV conivaptan?
Vomiting with dry mucosa and orthostasis
Conivaptan is contraindicated in hypovolemic hyponatremia; it is used for euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia.
q50kfbp: A client with euvolemic hyponatremia receives an IV conivaptan infusion. Which effect accounts for the rise in serum sodium?
Loss of free water without loss of sodium
Loss of sodium and water in about equal amounts
Movement of sodium out of the cells

Conivaptan blocks the V2 receptor in the collecting duct, so aquaporin-2 channels are withdrawn and solute-free water is excreted. That is an aquaresis rather than a diuresis, which is why fluid restriction is relaxed during the infusion to keep the sodium from climbing too fast.
q1o74etx: A 47-year-old man with acromegaly has persistent elevation of IGF-1 after transsphenoidal surgery. He is started on a monthly deep subcutaneous injection that inhibits growth hormone release. Which receptor does this drug activate?
GHRH receptor on anterior pituitary cells
Lanreotide is a long-acting somatostatin analog that acts mainly at SSTR2 and SSTR5, a Gi-coupled receptor that suppresses GH secretion.
qa5nj83: A 58-year-old woman with metastatic small bowel neuroendocrine tumor and carcinoid syndrome has received lanreotide every 4 weeks for 1 year. Which adverse effect is most likely to develop with long-term use?
Somatostatin analogs reduce gallbladder contractility and cholecystokinin release, causing gallbladder sludge and gallstones.
q98yx8g: A nurse is preparing to give lanreotide 120 mg to a client with a neuroendocrine tumor. Which administration technique is correct?
Deep subcutaneous injection in the upper outer buttock
IV push over 2 minutes through a saline lock
Intramuscular injection into the deltoid muscle
Subcutaneous injection into the abdomen with massage
Lanreotide is given by deep subcutaneous injection in the superior external quadrant of the buttock, alternating sides; the site is not massaged.
qnsjn9j: A 35-year-old woman has fasting hypoglycemia with inappropriately high insulin and C-peptide levels from an unresectable insulinoma. She is started on an oral drug that prevents insulin release. Which action describes this drug?
Opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels in beta cells
Closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels in beta cells
Blocks GLP-1 receptors on pancreatic beta cells
Activates SSTR5 receptors on pancreatic delta cells
Diazoxide binds the SUR1 subunit and opens K-ATP channels, hyperpolarizing beta cells and blocking insulin release, the opposite of sulfonylureas.
q9x0cxw: A 6-month-old infant with congenital hyperinsulinism has been treated with oral diazoxide for 4 months. Which adverse effect is most characteristic of this therapy?
Diazoxide commonly causes hypertrichosis and also fluid retention; infants are at risk for pulmonary hypertension.
q1uz3cnz: A nurse is teaching the parents of an infant started on diazoxide oral suspension for congenital hyperinsulinism. Which statement by a parent shows correct understanding?
I will report fast breathing or swelling right away
I will stop it if my baby grows extra body hair
I can measure the dose with a kitchen teaspoon
I will give it only when the sugar reading is low
Diazoxide can cause fluid retention and pulmonary hypertension in infants; respiratory distress or swelling must be reported promptly, and doses are measured with the dropper on a schedule.
q12llgfo: A 3-year-old boy has recurrent hypoketotic hypoglycemia during fasting, muscle weakness, and cardiomyopathy. Plasma carnitine is very low. Supplementation corrects his defect in which process?
Transport of long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria
Transport of pyruvate into the mitochondrial matrix
Conversion of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA in cytosol
Transfer of reducing equivalents by the malate shuttle
Carnitine is required to carry long-chain fatty acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane for beta-oxidation; deficiency causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia and myopathy.
qow46lb: A 24-year-old woman with epilepsy takes a large intentional overdose of valproic acid. She is lethargic, and her ammonia level is markedly elevated. Which therapy is most appropriate for the hyperammonemia?
Valproate depletes carnitine and impairs urea cycle function; IV levocarnitine is used for valproate-induced hyperammonemia and hepatotoxicity.
q1gxq750: A client on hemodialysis is prescribed IV levocarnitine. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
Give it as a slow IV bolus after the dialysis session
Give it before dialysis so the filter clears the excess
Mix it with the client's oral phosphate binder dose
Give it by rapid IV push during the first hour of dialysis
In end-stage renal disease, levocarnitine is given as a slow IV bolus over 2-3 minutes at the end of each dialysis session, since dialysis removes carnitine.
q1kw5461: A 16-year-old with osteosarcoma develops acute kidney injury after high-dose methotrexate and has a markedly elevated plasma methotrexate level. He receives an IV enzyme. What is the mechanism of this drug?
Cleaves the terminal glutamate from methotrexate
Bypasses dihydrofolate reductase by providing folate
Enhances renal tubular secretion of methotrexate
Inhibits thymidylate synthase in normal tissues
Glucarpidase (carboxypeptidase G2) hydrolyzes methotrexate to inactive DAMPA and glutamate; leucovorin, by contrast, bypasses the DHFR block.
q1spgrtw: A 45-year-old man with lymphoma receives glucarpidase for toxic methotrexate levels and impaired renal function. Which statement about subsequent management is correct?
Leucovorin is continued but not within 2 hours of the dose
Leucovorin should be stopped once glucarpidase is given
Immunoassay methotrexate levels are reliable right away
Hemodialysis should be started at the same time as dosing
Glucarpidase degrades leucovorin, so leucovorin is separated by 2 hours but continued; immunoassays overestimate methotrexate for 48 hours due to DAMPA.
q12cgpk4: A nurse is giving glucarpidase to a client with methotrexate toxicity. The client is also scheduled for IV leucovorin. When should the leucovorin be given?
At least 2 hours after the glucarpidase dose
Mixed with glucarpidase in the same syringe
Immediately before glucarpidase in the same line
Only after levels are undetectable on immunoassay
Leucovorin is a substrate for glucarpidase, so it should not be given within 2 hours before or after the glucarpidase dose.
q1rguvq9: A 64-year-old man on a continuous 5-fluorouracil infusion receives the full 4-day dose in 4 hours due to a pump error. He is given an oral antidote. What is its mechanism?
Uridine competes with fluorouridine triphosphate for RNA
It restores thymidylate synthase activity by binding 5-FU
It supplies reduced folate to stabilize thymidylate synthase
Uridine triacetate is converted to uridine, and the resulting UTP competitively limits incorporation of the 5-FU metabolite FUTP into RNA of normal cells.
q1fkrvn6: A 59-year-old woman taking capecitabine develops severe diarrhea, mucositis, and neutropenia within 2 days of starting therapy. Genetic testing later shows dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency. Which is the most appropriate antidote?
