Uridine triacetate treats early-onset severe toxicity from 5-FU or capecitabine within 96 hours; leucovorin potentiates 5-FU, and glucarpidase is for methotrexate.
q1q8mq1u: A client receiving uridine triacetate every 6 hours vomits 45 minutes after taking a dose. What should the nurse do?
Give another full dose as soon as possible
Wait and give the next dose on schedule
Give half a dose mixed with water instead
Hold all remaining doses and notify pharmacy
The label directs that if vomiting occurs within 2 hours of a dose, a complete dose should be repeated as soon as possible, then the schedule continues.
qen03hk: A 78-year-old woman taking apixaban has a large intracerebral hemorrhage. She receives a recombinant protein that lacks the Gla domain and has an inactivated active site. How does this agent restore hemostasis?
It acts as a decoy that binds and sequesters the factor Xa inhibitor
It directly activates factor X to generate thrombin at the bleeding site
It replaces vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX and X in plasma
It binds the drug with a monoclonal antibody fragment and is renally cleared
Andexanet alfa is a catalytically inactive factor Xa decoy that binds apixaban and rivaroxaban, freeing native factor Xa to function.
q10tk49u: A 70-year-old man on rivaroxaban receives andexanet alfa for a life-threatening GI bleed and hemostasis is achieved. Which complication carries a boxed warning for this agent?
Thromboembolic events, ischemic events and cardiac arrest
Acute interstitial nephritis progressing to renal failure
Hepatic necrosis with marked transaminase elevation
Andexanet alfa has a boxed warning for thromboembolic and ischemic events, cardiac arrest and sudden death; anticoagulation should resume when appropriate.
qvo949p: A 60-year-old man has persistent oozing after cardiac surgery with laboratory evidence of hyperfibrinolysis. He is given a lysine analog. What is its mechanism?
Blocks plasminogen binding to fibrin, preventing plasmin formation
Directly inhibits thrombin and fibrin-bound thrombin
Replaces fibrinogen and factor XIII consumed during bypass surgery
Activates glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors on platelets
Aminocaproic acid occupies the lysine-binding sites of plasminogen, preventing its binding to fibrin and its activation to plasmin.
q1w7k5y5: A patient with severe hemophilia A is treated with aminocaproic acid for a prolonged dental bleed. Which condition is a contraindication to this drug unless heparin is also given?
Disseminated intravascular coagulation with active clotting
Stable stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a normal serum potassium
A history of seasonal allergic rhinitis and asthma
Antifibrinolytics can cause dangerous thrombosis in active intravascular clotting such as DIC unless heparin is given concurrently.
qo6xrxm: A patient has received continuous aminocaproic acid for several days. Which laboratory value should the nurse monitor for a characteristic adverse effect?
Prolonged aminocaproic acid can cause skeletal muscle weakness with necrosis and rhabdomyolysis, so CK should be monitored.
q106lzaw: During PCI, a patient receives an IV antiplatelet agent with a half-life of 3 to 6 minutes that does not need hepatic activation. Which statement best describes this drug?
A direct, reversible antagonist of the platelet P2Y12 receptor
An irreversible prodrug inhibitor of the platelet P2Y12 receptor
A reversible antagonist of the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor
An irreversible inhibitor of platelet cyclooxygenase-1
Cangrelor is an ATP analog that directly and reversibly blocks P2Y12 without metabolic activation, so platelet function returns within about 1 hour.
q1d4q3mi: A patient finishing PCI on a cangrelor infusion needs to start oral clopidogrel. When should the clopidogrel 600 mg load be given to achieve platelet inhibition?
Immediately after the cangrelor infusion is stopped
Thirty minutes before the cangrelor bolus is given
Only after a 24-hour washout of cangrelor
Cangrelor blocks binding of the clopidogrel and prasugrel active metabolites, so those loads are given right after the infusion ends; ticagrelor may be given during it.
qtg3iqp: A nurse is caring for a patient receiving a cangrelor infusion after femoral PCI. Which assessment finding requires immediate notification of the provider?
A rapidly expanding hematoma at the groin access site
Mild bruising near a peripheral IV site in the forearm
Heart rate of 78 beats per minute and regular rhythm
Blood pressure of 128/76 mmHg with no symptoms
Bleeding is the main adverse effect of cangrelor; an expanding hematoma suggests significant access site bleeding and needs urgent evaluation.
qcy4hm9: A 6-year-old boy with severe hemophilia A has high-titer factor VIII inhibitors. He starts a SC antibody that prevents bleeding. What is its mechanism?
Bridges factors IXa and X to replace the cofactor role of factor VIIIa
Directly activates prothrombin to thrombin at sites of tissue injury
Inhibits tissue factor pathway inhibitor to increase thrombin generation
Binds and neutralizes the factor VIII inhibitor antibodies in plasma
Emicizumab is a bispecific antibody that binds factor IXa and factor X, mimicking factor VIIIa; it is not affected by factor VIII inhibitors.
q94rno0: A patient with hemophilia A and inhibitors on emicizumab prophylaxis has a breakthrough joint bleed. Which treatment carries a boxed warning in combination with emicizumab?
Activated prothrombin complex concentrate at high cumulative doses
Recombinant activated factor VII given at standard labeled doses
Tranexamic acid given orally for a mucosal bleed
Acetaminophen for joint pain after the bleed
Thrombotic microangiopathy and thromboembolism occurred when aPCC averaging more than 100 U/kg per 24 hours was given for 24 hours or more.
q12xglvf: A patient on emicizumab has a preoperative aPTT that is shorter than normal. What is the best interpretation by the nurse?
The drug interferes with aPTT, so the result does not reflect hemostasis
The patient has developed a clot and needs heparin started
The patient no longer has hemophilia and needs no further factor therapy
The specimen was hemolyzed and must be redrawn at once
Emicizumab falsely shortens the aPTT and affects one-stage factor VIII assays; chromogenic assays with bovine reagents are used instead.
qutoyhl: A patient in refractory septic shock is started on a synthetic peptide vasopressor. Which receptor mediates its pressor effect?
Angiotensin II type 1 receptor on vascular smooth muscle
Alpha-1 adrenergic receptor on vascular smooth muscle
Vasopressin V1a receptor on vascular smooth muscle
Beta-1 adrenergic receptor on cardiac myocytes
Angiotensin II activates Gq-coupled AT1 receptors, causing vasoconstriction and aldosterone release, a mechanism distinct from catecholamines and vasopressin.
q1o1hu8h: A 64-year-old man in septic shock remains hypotensive despite norepinephrine and vasopressin and is started on angiotensin II. Which order should accompany this drug?
Daily scheduled IV loop diuretic therapy to prevent edema
Continuous IV insulin regardless of glucose
Thrombosis occurred more often with angiotensin II than placebo, so the label requires concurrent VTE prophylaxis.
q166etps: A nurse is titrating an angiotensin II infusion for distributive shock. Which finding is most important to report as a drug-related adverse effect?
Cool, mottled fingers with weak radial pulses
Mean arterial pressure of 68 mmHg on the infusion
Urine output of 45 mL per hour for 2 hours
Heart rate of 92 beats per minute and regular rhythm
Angiotensin II can cause peripheral ischemia and thrombosis; signs of poor distal perfusion must be reported promptly.
qlrd93z: A 38-year-old woman with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension starts a continuous SC infusion. Which intracellular change mediates the drug's vasodilation?
Increased cAMP after prostacyclin IP receptor activation
Increased cGMP after soluble guanylate cyclase stimulation
Decreased endothelin-1 binding at ETA receptors
Treprostinil is a prostacyclin analog that activates Gs-coupled IP receptors, raising cAMP to cause vasodilation and platelet inhibition.
q3ka2wh: A patient with PAH on continuous IV treprostinil arrives with a disconnected pump that stopped 2 hours ago. What is the most important risk?
Rebound pulmonary hypertension with acute right heart failure
Severe systemic hypertensive crisis from unopposed vasoconstriction
Acute hypoglycemia from loss of prostacyclin effect
Delayed allergic reaction once the infusion is restarted
Abrupt withdrawal or interruption of prostacyclin therapy can cause rebound PAH and right ventricular failure; the infusion should be restored promptly.
qdg00if: A nurse is caring for a patient receiving SC treprostinil by home pump. Which teaching point is most accurate?
Pain and redness at the infusion site are common and should be reported
The pump may be turned off overnight to rest the infusion site
The catheter should be flushed rapidly whenever the alarm sounds
Missed doses should be made up by doubling the next pump rate
Infusion site pain is the most common adverse effect of SC treprostinil; the infusion must never be interrupted, flushed or bolused.
q1pnyn2e: A 55-year-old man with inoperable chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension starts an oral drug that works even when nitric oxide is low. What is its target?
Riociguat sensitizes soluble guanylate cyclase to NO and stimulates it directly, increasing cGMP; it is approved for CTEPH and PAH.
qz3gx9d: A woman with CTEPH is stable on riociguat. Which medication is contraindicated with riociguat because of severe hypotension?
Riociguat is contraindicated with PDE5 inhibitors and nitrates because combined cGMP elevation causes profound hypotension.
q32x0k6: A nurse reviews the plan for a 30-year-old woman starting riociguat. Which action must be confirmed before the first dose?
Riociguat has a boxed warning for embryo-fetal toxicity; pregnancy must be excluded before starting and effective contraception used.
q3izq6c: A 41-year-old woman with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension begins an oral once-daily agent that selectively blocks one receptor subtype for a potent vasoconstrictor peptide. Which receptor is targeted?
Ambrisentan is ETA-selective, blocking endothelin-1 mediated vasoconstriction and proliferation while largely sparing ETB.
qpmgcen: A 66-year-old man with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has pulmonary hypertension on right heart catheterization. Which drug is contraindicated in this patient?
Ambrisentan is contraindicated in IPF, including IPF with pulmonary hypertension, because it increased disease progression and hospitalization in a trial.
q7xkwxv: A client with pulmonary arterial hypertension started ambrisentan 2 weeks ago. Which finding is most important for the nurse to report?
Bilateral ankle edema with a 2-kg weight gain
Mild nasal congestion since starting the drug
Occasional flushing after taking the tablet
Fatigue that improves after a short afternoon rest period
Peripheral edema and fluid retention are common with ambrisentan and may signal heart failure or pulmonary edema requiring evaluation.
q1ma2our: A 52-year-old woman with pulmonary arterial hypertension starts a once-daily dual endothelin receptor antagonist. Which enzyme converts it to its active metabolite and mediates its key drug interactions?
Macitentan is metabolized by CYP3A4 to an active metabolite, so strong CYP3A4 inducers and inhibitors should be avoided.
q1txhnf3: A 34-year-old woman with pulmonary arterial hypertension is starting macitentan. Which laboratory test must be obtained before the first dose?
Macitentan carries a boxed warning for embryo-fetal toxicity, so pregnancy must be excluded before starting therapy.
q18m749y: A client taking macitentan for pulmonary arterial hypertension is prescribed rifampin for latent tuberculosis. What is the nurse's best action?
Contact the prescriber about the interaction
Give both drugs at least 2 hours apart
Give rifampin and hold macitentan for the next week
Administer both drugs as ordered with food
Rifampin is a strong CYP3A4 inducer that markedly lowers macitentan levels, and the combination should be avoided.
q10wve2e: A 47-year-old woman with pulmonary arterial hypertension on an endothelin receptor antagonist and a PDE-5 inhibitor starts an oral nonprostanoid agent. Which intracellular change mediates its vasodilator effect?
Increased cAMP via a Gs-coupled IP receptor
Increased cGMP via soluble guanylate cyclase
Decreased IP3 via Gq-coupled receptor blockade
Decreased calcium entry via L-type channel block
Selexipag activates the Gs-coupled prostacyclin IP receptor, raising cAMP in pulmonary vascular smooth muscle.
qtdfeta: A 58-year-old man with pulmonary arterial hypertension takes selexipag. His physician plans to treat his hypertriglyceridemia. Which drug is contraindicated with selexipag?
Gemfibrozil is a strong CYP2C8 inhibitor that greatly increases exposure to the active selexipag metabolite.
q1ls1474: A client on selexipag for pulmonary arterial hypertension is prescribed gemfibrozil for high triglycerides. What does the selexipag label say?
The selexipag dose should be doubled
The two should be given 2 hours apart
No change is needed with this pair

Gemfibrozil is a strong CYP2C8 inhibitor and roughly doubles selexipag exposure while raising the active metabolite several-fold, so the label contraindicates concomitant use. Selexipag is an oral agonist at the prostacyclin IP receptor, not a prostacyclin analog.
q17jide3: A 62-year-old man with coronary artery disease receives a subcutaneous drug every 6 months that is taken up by hepatocytes via the asialoglycoprotein receptor. What is its mechanism?
RNA interference that degrades PCSK9 mRNA
Inclisiran is a GalNAc-conjugated siRNA that directs RISC-mediated cleavage of PCSK9 mRNA in hepatocytes.
qhy31yx: A 59-year-old woman with prior MI has an LDL of 104 mg/dL on maximally tolerated statin and ezetimibe. She prefers the fewest injections. Which regimen fits best?
Inclisiran at day 0, month 3, then every 6 months
Alirocumab every 2 weeks indefinitely by self-injection
Evolocumab every 2 weeks or monthly by self-injection
After the initial doses, inclisiran is given every 6 months, the least frequent schedule among LDL-lowering injectables.
q1mo6mq: A client received the first dose of inclisiran today. When should the nurse schedule the next dose?
Inclisiran is given at day 0, again at 3 months, and then every 6 months.
q1abcz4q: A 45-year-old man with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia starts alirocumab. By which mechanism does it lower LDL?
Prevents degradation of hepatic LDL receptors
Alirocumab binds PCSK9 so LDL receptors recycle to the hepatocyte surface instead of being degraded.
q1nsea5v: A 64-year-old man is evaluated 2 months after an acute coronary syndrome. His LDL is 92 mg/dL on high-intensity statin and ezetimibe. Which addition has been shown to reduce cardiovascular events after recent ACS?
ODYSSEY OUTCOMES showed alirocumab reduced major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with recent ACS on statins.
q194af1b: A client is learning to self-inject alirocumab with a prefilled pen stored in the refrigerator. Which instruction is correct?
Let it warm to room temperature for 30 to 40 minutes
Shake the pen well to mix it before each injection
Warm the pen in the microwave for a few seconds
Inject into the same spot each time for consistency
Allowing the pen to reach room temperature reduces injection discomfort; it should not be shaken or heated, and sites should be rotated.
qnxnpb0: A 68-year-old woman develops myalgias on several statins and starts an oral lipid-lowering prodrug. Its activating enzyme is absent in skeletal muscle. Which enzyme does the active drug inhibit?
Bempedoic acid is activated by ACSVL1 in liver and inhibits ATP-citrate lyase, upstream of HMG-CoA reductase.
q3g0k9n: A 70-year-old man with statin intolerance starts bempedoic acid. Three months later he has an acutely painful, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint. What is the most likely explanation?
Bempedoic acid inhibits renal OAT2 and raises serum uric acid, which can precipitate gout.
q15g53pf: A client who stopped statins because of muscle aches is started on bempedoic acid. Why is muscle pain less likely with it?
The prodrug is activated only in the liver
It does not lower LDL cholesterol at all
It is given every other day instead of daily
It is not absorbed from the small intestine

Bempedoic acid is a prodrug activated by ACSVL1, an enzyme present in liver but not in skeletal muscle, so no active drug forms in muscle. It inhibits ATP-citrate lyase upstream of HMG-CoA reductase and does lower LDL, and it raises uric acid.
q10d5r9t: A 60-year-old man with diabetes and triglycerides of 210 mg/dL on atorvastatin starts a prescription omega-3 product. Which statement describes this product?
It contains purified EPA without DHA
It inhibits PCSK9 messenger RNA synthesis
It contains both EPA and DHA in equal amounts
Icosapent ethyl is purified eicosapentaenoic acid ethyl ester; it lacks DHA and does not significantly raise LDL.
q1rt05r3: A 67-year-old woman with prior MI starts icosapent ethyl 2 g twice daily for elevated triglycerides on a statin. Which adverse effect occurred more often with this drug in its outcome trial?
In REDUCE-IT, icosapent ethyl increased hospitalization for atrial fibrillation or flutter and showed a trend toward more bleeding.
q1y3bpk4: A client starting icosapent ethyl also takes apixaban. Which finding should the nurse teach the client to report?
Icosapent ethyl can increase bleeding risk, especially with anticoagulants, so bleeding should be reported.
q9nx5ng: A 78-year-old woman (64 kg) has a new proximal DVT. Her creatinine clearance is 22 mL/min, and she has no active bleeding. Which enoxaparin order is correct for treatment?
1 mg/kg (64 mg) subcutaneously once every 24 hours
1 mg/kg (64 mg) subcutaneously every 12 hours, unchanged
40 mg subcutaneously once daily, the standard prophylaxis dose
1.5 mg/kg (96 mg) subcutaneously every 12 hours for the first week

Per the label, CrCl below 30 mL/min calls for 1 mg/kg once daily for treatment because enoxaparin accumulates. Keeping q12h dosing raises bleeding risk, and 40 mg daily is a prophylaxis dose that undertreats a DVT.
q1m85fo1: A 74-year-old man on dabigatran for atrial fibrillation arrives with an acute subdural hematoma and a GCS of 11. His last dose was 5 hours ago and his CrCl is 48 mL/min. Which reversal order is best?
Andexanet alfa high-dose bolus then infusion
Protamine sulfate 50 mg slow IV push
Vitamin K 10 mg IV with fresh frozen plasma
Idarucizumab is an antibody fragment that binds dabigatran; the labeled dose is 5 g IV. Andexanet reverses factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban and rivaroxaban, not a direct thrombin inhibitor.
q17e31jb: A 66-year-old man on apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc 3, CrCl 85 mL/min) is scheduled for an elective total knee replacement, a high bleeding-risk procedure. What is the best periprocedural plan?
Hold apixaban 2 days before surgery with no heparin bridging
Hold apixaban 5 days before surgery and bridge with enoxaparin
Continue apixaban without any interruption through the surgery
Hold apixaban the morning of surgery only and resume that night

Per the PAUSE approach, apixaban is held 2 days before a high bleeding-risk procedure (1 day for low risk) with normal renal function, and bridging is unnecessary given its short half-life. Bridging only adds bleeding.
q3jfst8: A 58-year-old woman with a mechanical mitral valve on warfarin (INR goal 3.0) needs an elective colonoscopy with likely polypectomy. Which plan is most appropriate?
Stop warfarin 5 days prior and bridge with therapeutic enoxaparin
Stop warfarin 5 days prior with no bridging, as in the BRIDGE trial
Switch warfarin to apixaban for the week around the procedure
Continue warfarin and give vitamin K only if bleeding occurs

A mechanical mitral valve is a high thrombotic risk, so bridging with LMWH or UFH is indicated. BRIDGE studied atrial fibrillation, not mechanical valves, and DOACs are contraindicated with mechanical valves.
q1qi4v64: A 71-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation has an INR of 6.8 on routine testing. He has no bleeding and no planned procedures. What is the best management per CHEST guidelines?
Hold 1-2 doses, then resume at a lower dose and recheck the INR
Give vitamin K 10 mg IV now and recheck the INR in 6 hours
Give 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate and hold all warfarin
Stop warfarin permanently and switch to dabigatran the same day

For INR 4.5-10 without bleeding, CHEST guidance is to hold warfarin and resume at a lower dose; routine vitamin K is not needed. IV vitamin K 10 mg overshoots and causes warfarin resistance on restarting.
q1nu2u40: An 80-year-old woman on warfarin presents with a spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage; her INR is 3.4. Which reversal strategy is best?
4-factor PCC plus vitamin K 10 mg by slow IV infusion
Vitamin K 10 mg orally and repeat the INR in 24 hours
Fresh frozen plasma alone, 2 units, without any vitamin K
Protamine sulfate IV followed by recombinant factor VIIa
Guidelines favor 4F-PCC for rapid factor replacement plus IV vitamin K to sustain reversal after the PCC wears off. FFP alone is slow and volume-heavy, and protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin.
q1atpryf: A 70-year-old man on prednisone starts levofloxacin and 3 days later has posterior ankle pain and cannot push off. Which drug effect is this?
Myopathy from direct skeletal muscle toxicity
Arthropathy from loss of cartilage glycosaminoglycan

Fluoroquinolones carry a boxed warning for tendinitis and tendon rupture, most often Achilles, through degradation of collagen and the tenocyte matrix; risk is highest over age 60 and with concurrent corticosteroids. The cartilage effect is the separate pediatric concern.
qkkri6n: A man on chronic colchicine for gout is started on clarithromycin. Which toxicity is he now at risk for?
Colchicine toxicity with pancytopenia and myopathy
Clarithromycin toxicity with irreversible hearing loss
Colchicine failure with a rebound gout flare

Colchicine is a substrate of both CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein and clarithromycin inhibits both, so levels climb and fatal colchicine toxicity with diarrhea, myelosuppression and myopathy has been reported. Azithromycin lacks meaningful CYP3A4 inhibition.
q1evh29m: A 55-year-old man with Child-Pugh B cirrhosis (no active drinking) has knee osteoarthritis pain. Which analgesic plan is safest?
Acetaminophen at a reduced ceiling of about 2 g per day
Ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours with food
Naproxen 500 mg twice daily with a daily PPI for GI protection
Tramadol 100 mg every 4 hours as needed for pain

Expert guidance favors acetaminophen up to about 2 g/day in cirrhosis. NSAIDs precipitate renal failure, GI bleeding, and diuretic resistance in cirrhosis, and tramadol accumulates and lowers the seizure threshold.
qtml1y4: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and HFrEF takes Jardiance. He is scheduled for an elective colectomy next week. What is the correct perioperative order?
Hold it for at least 3 days before surgery
Hold it only on the morning of surgery
Continue it, since it rarely causes hypoglycemia
Hold it 2 weeks before and restart once discharged

The label advises stopping empagliflozin at least 3 days before scheduled surgery because of euglycemic DKA risk with fasting and surgical stress. Its low hypoglycemia risk is irrelevant; ketoacidosis is the danger.
q1w677pf: A 70-year-old woman on metformin with an eGFR of 38 mL/min/1.73 m2 needs a CT with IV iodinated contrast. What is the correct metformin order?
Hold it at the scan, recheck eGFR, and restart at 48 hours
Continue it without interruption, since her eGFR is above 30
Stop it permanently, since her eGFR is now below 45 mL/min
Hold it 1 week before the scan and restart it 1 week after

Per the label, metformin is held at or before iodinated contrast when eGFR is 30-60 and restarted 48 hours later if renal function is stable. An eGFR of 30-45 does not mandate permanent discontinuation.
q6ifgg5: A 61-year-old man had a drug-eluting stent placed 2 months ago for stable angina and takes aspirin plus Plavix. He is referred for an elective inguinal hernia repair. What is the best recommendation?
Defer the elective surgery until DAPT can safely be interrupted
Stop both antiplatelets 7 days before and proceed as planned
Stop clopidogrel 5 days before and bridge with enoxaparin
Switch clopidogrel to warfarin for the perioperative period

Elective noncardiac surgery should be delayed after DES (ideally 6 months for stable disease) because stopping a P2Y12 inhibitor early markedly raises stent thrombosis risk. Heparin bridging does not protect against stent thrombosis.
q1p8nftx: A 72-year-old man on Tikosyn for atrial fibrillation develops cystitis. Which antibiotic is contraindicated with his antiarrhythmic?
Trimethoprim inhibits renal cationic secretion of dofetilide, raising levels and torsades risk; the label lists it as contraindicated. The other agents do not interact this way.
q1wwsmp2: On day 7 of heparin prophylaxis after hip surgery, a 68-year-old woman's platelets fall from 260,000 to 95,000 and she has a new DVT. CrCl is 20 mL/min; liver tests are normal. What is the best order?
Stop all heparin and start an argatroban infusion
Switch to enoxaparin at a renally adjusted dose
Stop heparin and start warfarin 5 mg daily now
Continue heparin and transfuse platelets as needed

Suspected HIT requires stopping all heparin, including LMWH, and starting a non-heparin anticoagulant; argatroban is hepatically cleared, suiting renal failure. Starting warfarin during acute HIT can cause venous limb gangrene.
q142qsvd: A 52-year-old man with septic shock from a central line infection was started on vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam. Blood cultures on day 2 grow methicillin-susceptible S. aureus. What is the best antibiotic change?

For MSSA bacteremia, a beta-lactam such as cefazolin or nafcillin is superior to vancomycin, which kills more slowly and fails more often. Keeping broad Gram-negative coverage adds toxicity and resistance without benefit.
qfyg1uv: A 67-year-old woman with pyelonephritis and bacteremia is on Zosyn. Cultures grow ESBL-producing E. coli that tests susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam. What is the best definitive therapy?

In the MERINO trial, piperacillin-tazobactam had higher mortality than meropenem for ESBL bloodstream infection, so a carbapenem is preferred despite in-vitro susceptibility. Third- and fourth-generation cephalosporins are hydrolyzed by ESBLs.
qer2h6z: Twenty minutes into a vancomycin infusion a patient has flushing of the face and trunk with itching and a brief fall in BP. Which mechanism is this?
Direct mast cell degranulation by the drug
IgE antibody formed at a prior exposure

Vancomycin infusion reaction is a non-immune, rate-dependent release of histamine from mast cells through the MRGPRX2 receptor, so it responds to slowing the infusion and to antihistamine premedication rather than requiring avoidance. True IgE-mediated anaphylaxis to vancomycin is rare.
q1fc51zl: A 64-year-old woman with urosepsis has a MAP of 57 mmHg after 30 mL/kg of crystalloid; lactate is 4.6 mmol/L. She has only peripheral IV access. What is the best next step?
Start Levophed through a proximal peripheral IV
Give another 3 liters of crystalloid before any vasopressor
Delay vasopressors until a central line is placed
Start dopamine as the first-line vasopressor

Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidance supports starting norepinephrine peripherally rather than delaying for central access. Dopamine causes more arrhythmias, and excess fluid beyond initial resuscitation worsens outcomes.
qrm046l: A 76-year-old woman has 9 watery stools daily, WBC 19,000, and creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (baseline 0.9) with positive C. difficile toxin. She is not hypotensive and has no ileus. Which treatment is best?
Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days
Oral metronidazole 500 mg three times daily
Oral vancomycin 500 mg four times daily plus IV metronidazole

Per IDSA, an initial severe episode (WBC above 15,000 or creatinine above 1.5) is treated with oral vancomycin 125 mg QID or fidaxomicin. IV vancomycin does not reach the colon, and 500 mg plus IV metronidazole is for fulminant disease.
q1wbw3a2: A 64-year-old man presents with fever, neck stiffness, and confusion. CSF shows 1,800 WBC with neutrophil predominance. Besides dexamethasone, which empiric antibiotic regimen is best?
Adults over 50 need ampicillin for Listeria added to vancomycin plus ceftriaxone. Omitting vancomycin misses resistant pneumococcus, and acyclovir does not replace Listeria coverage.
qr6luse: A 58-year-old man has MRSA pneumonia with concurrent MRSA bacteremia. A colleague suggests daptomycin to cover both sites. What is the best response?
Use linezolid or vancomycin, since daptomycin fails in the lung
Use daptomycin, since its rapid bactericidal killing covers both sites
Use daptomycin at double the usual dose for the lung
Use cefazolin, since it covers MRSA in the lung
Daptomycin is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant and should not be used for pneumonia. Cefazolin does not cover MRSA.
q1hmvros: A patient in DKA on an insulin drip has glucose down to 220 mg/dL but the anion gap is still 18. What is the appropriate change?
Add dextrose to the fluids and keep the insulin drip
Stop the insulin drip and give subcutaneous insulin
Halve the insulin rate and recheck the gap in 6 hours
Switch to subcutaneous insulin since glucose is under 250

The insulin infusion continues until the anion gap closes and bicarbonate recovers, because insulin is what suppresses ketogenesis; dextrose is added near a glucose of 200 mg/dL so that can happen without hypoglycemia. Stopping at a normal glucose with an open gap lets ketoacidosis return.
q1p2gz22: A man with DKA on an insulin infusion now has a glucose of 220 mg/dL, but his anion gap remains 19. What is the best next step?
Add dextrose to the fluids and continue the insulin infusion
Stop the insulin infusion and start a correction scale
Stop the infusion and give glargine subcutaneously now
Double the insulin infusion rate to close the anion gap faster

Insulin is needed to clear ketones, so once glucose reaches about 250 mg/dL, dextrose is added (often with a lower rate) while insulin continues until the gap closes. Stopping insulin early causes rebound ketosis.
q1a9kgrp: A patient with type 1 diabetes recovering from DKA has a closed anion gap and is eating. How should the transition off the insulin infusion be ordered?
Give subcutaneous Lantus 2 hours before stopping the drip
Stop the drip and give Lantus 2 hours later
Stop the drip and use a correction scale only
Stop the drip once the glucose is below 150 mg/dL
Basal insulin must overlap the infusion by about 2 hours because IV regular insulin has a half-life of minutes; a gap leads to recurrent DKA. Correction scale alone is inadequate in type 1 diabetes.
qsca74y: A 74-year-old man with HHS has glucose 1,020 mg/dL, measured sodium 131 mEq/L, and severe dehydration with BP 92/58. Which initial management is best?
Isotonic saline first, adding insulin once fluids alone plateau
An insulin bolus of 0.1 units/kg plus an infusion before any IV fluids
Hypotonic 0.45% saline as the first liter given his sodium
Insulin infusion at 0.14 units/kg/h with free water flushes

In HHS, isotonic fluid is the priority; insulin given before volume repletion shifts water into cells and worsens hypotension. His corrected sodium is high, but hypotonic fluid is not the first choice in shock.
qo8fcdt: A 90-kg woman with type 2 diabetes (A1c 9.4%) is admitted with pneumonia, eating well, with glucoses of 250-320 mg/dL on correction insulin alone. Using about 0.5 units/kg/day per guidelines, which regimen is best?
Glargine 22 units daily plus lispro 7 units with meals, plus correction
Lispro correction every 6 hours only, switching to a more aggressive scale
Glargine 45 units daily alone with no prandial or correction insulin
NPH 45 units twice daily before meals with no correction scale

A total daily dose of about 45 units is split half basal and half prandial (divided over 3 meals), plus correction insulin. Sliding scale alone is reactive and discouraged, and 90 units of NPH doubles the needed dose.
q1sxcx2a: A 34-year-old man with type 1 diabetes on glargine 30 units nightly is NPO for an elective morning surgery. What is the best order for the night before?
Give about 75-80% of the glargine dose (about 24 units)
Hold glargine entirely while he remains NPO
Give the full 30 units plus a dose of lispro
Switch the glargine to a correction scale only
Guidelines suggest about 75-80% of basal insulin the evening before surgery. Holding basal insulin in type 1 diabetes risks DKA, since he makes no endogenous insulin.
q1h52aws: A 56-year-old woman on empagliflozin and metformin has vomited for 2 days. Glucose 188 mg/dL, bicarbonate 11 mEq/L, anion gap 24, beta-hydroxybutyrate 6.1 mmol/L. What is the best management?
Insulin infusion with dextrose-containing fluids; stop empagliflozin
Withhold insulin because the glucose is under 250 mg/dL
IV fluids alone without insulin until glucose exceeds 250
Sodium bicarbonate infusion, then resume empagliflozin at discharge
This is euglycemic DKA from an SGLT2 inhibitor; insulin suppresses ketogenesis and dextrose prevents hypoglycemia. A near-normal glucose does not mean insulin is unnecessary.
q2q0l7h: An 82-year-old woman with CKD stage 4 on glyburide is found with glucose 38 mg/dL. She improves with D50 but becomes hypoglycemic twice more in 4 hours despite a dextrose infusion. What is the best addition?
Glucagon 1 mg IM every hour as needed
Oral diazoxide, then discharge her home

Sulfonylureas drive ongoing insulin secretion that dextrose further provokes; octreotide suppresses this and prevents rebound hypoglycemia. Glucagon also stimulates insulin release and wears off quickly.
qrf4852: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is started on prednisone 60 mg each morning for a COPD flare. Fasting glucose is 130 mg/dL, but afternoon readings exceed 300 mg/dL. Which insulin strategy best matches the steroid effect?
Add morning NPH dosed by weight and steroid dose
Add bedtime NPH titrated to target the fasting glucose
Add a correction scale at bedtime only

Morning prednisone causes afternoon and evening hyperglycemia that matches the NPH profile when given with the steroid. Raising bedtime basal insulin risks overnight hypoglycemia as the steroid wears off.
q6sjwxu: An anuric 60-year-old man on hemodialysis missed two sessions. K is 7.4 mEq/L with a widened QRS. He received calcium gluconate, insulin with dextrose, and albuterol, and the QRS has narrowed. What is the definitive next step?
Calcium stabilizes membranes and insulin and albuterol shift K into cells for only a few hours; an anuric patient needs dialysis to remove potassium. Furosemide requires urine output.
q139v753: A 46-year-old woman with Na 113 mEq/L has a generalized seizure. Which treatment is most appropriate per expert hyponatremia guidelines?
100 mL bolus of 3% saline, repeated up to twice if needed
Fluid restriction to 800 mL per day
Tolvaptan 15 mg orally now with hourly sodium checks
1 liter of 0.9% saline over 1 hour, then recheck the sodium

Severe symptomatic hyponatremia needs a 3% saline bolus (about 100 mL, repeatable) to raise Na 4-6 mEq/L and stop seizures. Tolvaptan acts too slowly for emergencies, and normal saline can worsen Na in SIADH.
q6m37zh: A 52-year-old man with alcohol use disorder and K 2.9 mEq/L had Na 112 mEq/L. Twelve hours later his Na is 123 mEq/L and he is making 400 mL/hour of dilute urine. What is the best next step?
Give D5W and IV desmopressin to re-lower the sodium
Continue current management and recheck in 12 hours
Start 3% saline to maintain the current trajectory
Restrict all fluids to slow the water diuresis

He has exceeded the safe correction limit (about 8 mEq/L per 24 hours in high-risk patients such as alcoholism and hypokalemia), so relowering with free water and desmopressin reduces osmotic demyelination risk. Fluid restriction accelerates the rise.
qiguoob: A 66-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer has calcium 14.6 mg/dL and creatinine 3.4 mg/dL from AKI that persists after fluids. He has received calcitonin. Which agent is preferred for durable calcium lowering?

Bisphosphonates are nephrotoxic and need dose reduction or avoidance in severe renal dysfunction, while denosumab is not renally cleared (watch for hypocalcemia). High-dose loop diuretics are no longer recommended.
q13xre8q: A 71-year-old woman with SIADH (Na 121 mEq/L, asymptomatic) is started on tolvaptan in the hospital. Which order is inappropriate and should be removed?
Fluid restriction to 1 liter per day
Free access to water when thirsty
Plan to stop the drug within 30 days
The label warns against fluid restriction in the first 24 hours because it risks overly rapid correction and osmotic demyelination. Use is limited to 30 days because of hepatotoxicity.
q1liq4mz: A 50-year-old woman has K 3.0 mEq/L, normal renal function, and is tolerating a diet. A peripheral IV order reads KCl 40 mEq IV over 1 hour. What is the best action?
Change to oral KCl, or IV at no more than 10 mEq/h
Approve it, since 40 mEq/h is safe for K above 2.5
Give it as a 40 mEq IV push for faster correction
Infuse at 40 mEq/h in 50 mL via the peripheral IV

Per the KCl label, when K exceeds 2.5 mEq/L the rate should generally not exceed 10 mEq/h; faster rates risk arrhythmia and peripheral vein injury. The oral route is preferred when the patient can eat.
q1rkwol6: A 77-year-old man on lisinopril and spironolactone for HFrEF is given Bactrim for a UTI. Three days later his K is 6.6 mEq/L. Which mechanism explains the antibiotic's contribution?
Trimethoprim blocks ENaC in the collecting duct, like amiloride
Trimethoprim inhibits aldosterone synthase in the adrenal gland
Sulfamethoxazole causes acute interstitial nephritis alone
Trimethoprim acts like a potassium-sparing diuretic by blocking epithelial sodium channels, compounding ACE inhibitor and spironolactone effects. Hemolysis is not the main mechanism.
q1hk9i9c: A 68-year-old woman 1 day after hip surgery on a morphine PCA is arousable only to sternal rub, RR 7, pinpoint pupils, SpO2 88% on 2 L. What is the best Narcan order?
0.1-0.2 mg IV every 2-3 minutes titrated to breathing
2 mg IV push now, repeated every 2 minutes
4 mg intranasal, then restart the PCA later
0.4 mg IM once, then resume the PCA at once

For postoperative opioid depression, the label uses small IV increments (0.1-0.2 mg) titrated to ventilation to avoid abrupt pain, hypertension, arrhythmia, and pulmonary edema. A full 2 mg push reverses analgesia abruptly. Stop the PCA in any case.
q8fvb5o: A 72-kg man develops wheezing, hypotension, and hives 10 minutes into a cefazolin infusion. The infusion is stopped. What is the next drug to give?
Epinephrine 0.5 mg IM into the lateral thigh
Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV push, then reassess
Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV with an H2 blocker

IM epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg in adults) is first-line for anaphylaxis. Antihistamines and steroids do not treat airway obstruction or shock, and a 1 mg IV push is a cardiac arrest dose that can cause arrhythmia.
q3tyaeg: An 81-year-old man with Parkinson disease on carbidopa-levodopa becomes agitated and hallucinating overnight, pulling at his lines. Nonpharmacologic measures fail. Which drug is safest if one is needed?
Reglan 10 mg IV for nausea and sedation
Haloperidol and metoclopramide (Reglan) block D2 receptors and can severely worsen parkinsonism, while low-dose quetiapine has little D2 blockade. Benzodiazepines worsen delirium in the elderly.
q1keigcl: A 54-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis on day 2 of admission has tremor, diaphoresis, HR 128, and visual hallucinations from alcohol withdrawal. Which benzodiazepine is preferred?

Lorazepam is conjugated by glucuronidation without active metabolites, so it does not accumulate in severe liver disease. Diazepam and chlordiazepoxide have long-acting active metabolites that accumulate in cirrhosis.
q1bgzq8a: A 73-year-old woman with HFrEF (EF 20%) has new atrial fibrillation with HR 150, BP 96/58, and crackles. Cardioversion is not immediately available. Which rate-control drug is most appropriate?

Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are negatively inotropic and are avoided in decompensated HFrEF, and beta-blocker boluses can worsen acute heart failure. Amiodarone or digoxin is preferred.
q17mc8jw: At 2 a.m. a 66-year-old man admitted for pneumonia has BP 188/104. He is asymptomatic with normal labs and no chest pain or neurologic deficits. He missed his evening amlodipine. What is the best order?
Give his home amlodipine and recheck later
Hydralazine 10 mg IV now, repeated as needed
Labetalol 20 mg IV now and every 10 minutes
Start a nicardipine infusion in the step-down unit

Asymptomatic inpatient hypertension without end-organ damage is not an emergency; IV hydralazine or labetalol causes unpredictable drops and is linked to harm. Resume oral home therapy and address pain or anxiety.
q9fizna: A 70-kg man with epilepsy is still seizing after two doses of lorazepam 4 mg IV. Which second-line order is correctly written?
Fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV at up to 150 mg PE/min
Fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IM over 1 hour
Phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV in 5% dextrose over 20 minutes

Per the labels, fosphenytoin may run up to 150 mg PE/min, but phenytoin must not exceed 50 mg/min because of hypotension and arrhythmia, and phenytoin precipitates in dextrose. IM routes are too slow for status epilepticus.
q1p7eh5: A 31-year-old woman at 20 weeks' gestation has an acute proximal DVT. Which anticoagulant is preferred?
Warfarin with an INR goal of 2-3
LMWH does not cross the placenta and is preferred in pregnancy. Warfarin is teratogenic and causes fetal bleeding, and DOACs lack safety data and cross the placenta.
qhcnw9a: A 29-year-old at 34 weeks with preeclampsia has BP 168/112 sustained over 15 minutes. Which treatment does ACOG recommend?

Severe-range BP in pregnancy is treated within 30-60 minutes with IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or immediate-release oral nifedipine. ACE inhibitors are fetotoxic, and nitroprusside risks fetal cyanide toxicity.
q1mfzoju: A 35-year-old woman with chronic hypertension on lisinopril has a positive pregnancy test at 6 weeks. What is the best plan?
Stop lisinopril and start labetalol or nifedipine
Continue lisinopril until the second trimester
Switch to losartan for the rest of the pregnancy
Stop all antihypertensives and recheck at 20 weeks
ACE inhibitors and ARBs cause fetal renal damage, oligohydramnios, and skull hypoplasia, mostly in the second and third trimesters; switch to labetalol or nifedipine. Losartan carries the same risk.
q20ftzi: A 26-year-old at 10 weeks' gestation has asymptomatic bacteriuria with E. coli susceptible to all tested agents. Which treatment is best?

Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated to prevent pyelonephritis, and beta-lactams are safe. Fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines are avoided, and TMP-SMX is generally avoided in the first trimester.
q1br1v19: A patient with magnesium toxicity needs IV calcium through a peripheral line. Why is calcium gluconate 1 g chosen over calcium chloride 1 g?
It delivers less elemental calcium and is less sclerosing
It antagonizes magnesium at the motor end plate much better
It is absorbed more completely from a peripheral vein
It does not need the liver to release the free calcium

Calcium gluconate 1 g contains about 93 mg of elemental calcium against 273 mg in calcium chloride, and it is far less irritating to veins, so gluconate is the peripheral choice while chloride goes centrally in arrest. Both antagonize magnesium at the motor end plate once the calcium is free.
qki1c4g: A 28-year-old woman with epilepsy well controlled on Lamictal is 14 weeks pregnant and has new breakthrough seizures. What is the most likely cause and step?
Rising lamotrigine clearance; check a level and adjust
Teratogenic effect; switch to valproic acid now
Normal pregnancy change; no action is needed
Folate interaction; stop her folic acid supplement
Estrogen induces lamotrigine glucuronidation, so levels can fall substantially in pregnancy; monitor levels and increase the dose. Valproate has the highest teratogenic risk and is avoided.
qm1xq69: A 27-year-old at 8 weeks' gestation has Graves hyperthyroidism needing a thionamide. Which plan is preferred?
PTU now, then consider methimazole after the first trimester
Methimazole now, continued through the entire pregnancy and delivery
Radioactive iodine ablation in the first trimester

Methimazole carries first-trimester embryopathy risk, so PTU is preferred until about 16 weeks, then switching to methimazole is considered because of PTU hepatotoxicity. Radioiodine is contraindicated in pregnancy.
qqas1nv: A woman with severe preeclampsia and moderate persistent asthma has postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony despite oxytocin and massage. Which uterotonic is most appropriate next?

Methylergonovine is contraindicated in hypertension and preeclampsia, and carboprost (a PGF2-alpha analog) can trigger bronchospasm in asthma. Terbutaline relaxes the uterus and would worsen bleeding.
qea01z4: A 12-kg toddler with fever has an order for Tylenol 1,800 mg PO every 6 hours. What is the correct dose?
The pediatric dose is 10-15 mg/kg per dose, so the order is a tenfold decimal error. 30 mg/kg per dose is a double dose and risks hepatotoxicity with repeated dosing.
q1r7ueey: A 44-lb child has acute otitis media. A resident orders high-dose amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day by multiplying by 44, giving 3,960 mg/day. What should the order be?
44 lb is 20 kg, so the AAP high-dose regimen of 90 mg/kg/day is 1,800 mg/day divided twice daily. The resident used pounds instead of kilograms, more than doubling the dose.
q5xa1wv: Which analgesic plan is best for a 6-year-old after tonsillectomy?
Acetaminophen plus codeine at night only

Codeine and tramadol are contraindicated under 12 and after tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy under 18 because ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizers can develop fatal respiratory depression. Ibuprofen does not meaningfully raise post-tonsillectomy bleeding.
q1c6yt1q: A 10-day-old neonate with suspected sepsis is receiving IV calcium gluconate for hypocalcemia. Which antibiotic order is contraindicated?

Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in neonates receiving IV calcium because of fatal ceftriaxone-calcium precipitates, and in hyperbilirubinemic neonates because it displaces bilirubin. Ampicillin plus gentamicin is standard.
q1fd1rvt: A 15-kg child develops anaphylaxis. Which order is correct?
0.15 mg of 0.1 mg/mL epinephrine IV push
IM epinephrine is 0.01 mg/kg, so 0.15 mg (0.15 mL of 1 mg/mL). 1.5 mg is a tenfold error, and IV push is reserved for arrest or refractory shock.
qy7s2x1: An 83-year-old woman with two falls has taken Xanax 1 mg nightly for 12 years and asks to stop. What is the best plan?
Slow taper over weeks to months with CBT for insomnia
Stop it today, since falls outweigh any withdrawal risk
Switch to diphenhydramine 50 mg at bedtime

Long-term benzodiazepine users need gradual tapering (about 10-25% every 2-4 weeks) to avoid withdrawal and seizures. Zolpidem and diphenhydramine are Beers list drugs that also raise fall and delirium risk.
q1wgrk2y: An older man with CKD stage 3b has prolonged nocturnal hypoglycemia on glyburide. Which property of glyburide explains that?
It has renally cleared active metabolites
It has the shortest half-life of its class
It blocks hepatic glucose output directly

Glyburide produces active metabolites cleared by the kidney, so they accumulate in renal impairment and prolong hypoglycemia; that is why it is on the Beers list and glipizide, whose metabolites are inactive, is preferred. Sulfonylureas work by closing the beta cell KATP channel.
q256nr4: A 78-year-old man with Alzheimer dementia on donepezil was started on oxybutynin for urge incontinence that began after donepezil was started. His cognition has worsened. What is the best interpretation?
A prescribing cascade with opposing drugs
The oxybutynin dose is too low
Donepezil should be stopped for the incontinence
Cholinesterase inhibitors can cause urinary urgency, and treating it with an anticholinergic both worsens cognition and cancels the donepezil. Reassess and remove the cascade.
q1lkp8ef: A woman has ankle edema from amlodipine 10 mg and furosemide is added with no benefit. Why does a loop diuretic fail against this edema?
The edema comes from precapillary arteriolar dilation
The edema comes from a loss of plasma oncotic pressure
Amlodipine blocks the Na-K-2Cl transporter directly
Furosemide needs an intact RAAS in order to work

Dihydropyridines dilate precapillary arterioles while postcapillary tone is preserved, so capillary hydrostatic pressure rises and fluid is pushed into the interstitium even though total body volume is normal. Diuresis only produces volume depletion and hypokalemia, the cascade seen here.
q1lmb7m7: A patient on linezolid for 4 weeks for VRE osteomyelitis now has platelets of 68,000 and hemoglobin of 8.9 g/dL. Which mechanism fits?
Immune destruction of platelets by drug antibody
Direct binding of linezolid to the platelet surface
Suppression of erythropoietin by the kidney

Linezolid binds the bacterial 23S ribosomal subunit, and because human mitochondrial ribosomes resemble it the drug also inhibits mitochondrial protein synthesis, giving reversible myelosuppression, lactic acidosis and optic neuropathy after about 2 weeks. Counts recover once it is stopped.
qqqynq5: A 35-year-old man given Haldol in the ED 3 days ago has temperature 40.1 C (104.2 F), lead-pipe rigidity, labile BP, confusion, and CK 14,000 U/L. Reflexes are diminished without clonus. Besides stopping the drug and cooling, which drug is a reasonable addition?
Slow onset, lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, and very high CK indicate NMS from D2 blockade; bromocriptine (a D2 agonist) and dantrolene are used. Cyproheptadine treats serotonin syndrome.
q1ysl2se: An 84-year-old woman on digoxin develops AKI with nausea, yellow vision, HR 38 in a junctional rhythm, and K 5.9 mEq/L. Her digoxin level is 3.6 ng/mL. What is the best treatment?
Calcium gluconate 3 g IV for the potassium
Atropine, then a dopamine infusion only

Hyperkalemia with a symptomatic bradyarrhythmia marks life-threatening toxicity and is an indication for DigiFab, which also corrects the potassium. Digoxin has a large volume of distribution and is not dialyzable.
q12drj1d: A 72-year-old man with CrCl 18 mL/min receiving cefepime 2 g every 8 hours for pneumonia develops confusion and myoclonus on day 4. EEG shows triphasic waves with nonconvulsive features. What is the most likely cause?
Cefepime neurotoxicity from lack of renal dosing
Hepatic encephalopathy from sepsis-related liver injury

Cefepime enters the CNS and antagonizes GABA-A; accumulation in renal failure causes encephalopathy, myoclonus, and nonconvulsive status. The label requires dose reduction for CrCl of 60 mL/min or less.
q4fni0c: A 44-year-old has dyspnea after benzocaine spray for endoscopy. SpO2 is 85% despite 100% oxygen, PaO2 is 410 mmHg, and methemoglobin is 32%. He has no G6PD deficiency and takes no serotonergic drugs. What is the best treatment?
Symptomatic methemoglobinemia is treated with methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV per the label, which reduces methemoglobin via NADPH. Hydroxocobalamin and thiosulfate are cyanide antidotes.
qty8qtu: During laparoscopy with sevoflurane and succinylcholine, a patient develops rising end-tidal CO2 despite increased ventilation, masseter rigidity, and temperature 39.5 C (103.1 F). Besides stopping the volatile agent, which order is correct?
Dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV, repeated until signs resolve
Acetaminophen 1 g IV with external cooling as the only therapy
Per MHAUS, malignant hyperthermia is treated with dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV repeated as needed (label cumulative up to 10 mg/kg). 0.25 mg/kg is a tenfold underdose.
q196y8ca: A 19-year-old ingested diphenhydramine. She is agitated and mumbling, with mydriasis, dry flushed skin, urinary retention, and HR 128. QRS is 92 ms. Which drug can both diagnose and treat her delirium?

Physostigmine crosses into the CNS and reverses antimuscarinic delirium; a narrow QRS lowers the risk from diphenhydramine sodium-channel blockade. Haloperidol worsens anticholinergic toxicity and lowers the seizure threshold.
qj1m72z: A man had tongue swelling without urticaria on lisinopril. Which replacement carries the lowest risk of the same event?
An angiotensin receptor blocker such as losartan
Another ACE inhibitor such as enalapril
A neprilysin inhibitor plus an ARB such as sacubitril
A direct renin inhibitor added to an ACE inhibitor

ACE inhibitor angioedema is bradykinin-mediated because ACE is the main enzyme degrading bradykinin, so every ACE inhibitor carries the risk. ARBs do not block bradykinin breakdown and recurrence is much lower, while sacubitril adds neprilysin inhibition and raises bradykinin further.
q13owl13: A patient on methadone and haloperidol has runs of polymorphic VT preceded by a long QT; between runs he is awake with a pulse and BP 118/70. What is the first drug?
Torsades with a pulse is treated with IV magnesium (2 g per ACLS) regardless of serum level. Amiodarone and procainamide further prolong the QT.
q1jlnx0w: Two minutes after IV iohexol, an adult develops diffuse hives, wheezing and a BP of 78/40. Which drug and route should be given first?
Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM in the lateral thigh
This is anaphylaxis with hypotension and bronchospasm; IM epinephrine 0.3 mg (1 mg/mL) is first-line per ACR. Antihistamines and steroids do not reverse shock or airway swelling.
q1lzrill: Which epinephrine concentration is used for the 0.3 mg intramuscular dose in an adult contrast reaction?
IM epinephrine uses the 1 mg/mL concentration (0.3 mL = 0.3 mg). The 0.1 mg/mL concentration is for slow IV dosing under physician direction; confusing them causes serious errors.
qofdfgt: A 20 kg child has throat tightness and stridor after contrast. What IM epinephrine dose is appropriate?
Pediatric IM epinephrine is 0.01 mg/kg up to a maximum of 0.3 mg; a 0.15 mg autoinjector is used for smaller children.
q1eakuak: Ten minutes after CT contrast, a patient has a few scattered hives, normal vital signs and no breathing complaints. Which treatment is most appropriate if one is needed?
Atropine 0.6 mg IV with the legs elevated
Mild limited hives may need only observation or an H1 antihistamine; epinephrine is reserved for diffuse or progressive symptoms, airway involvement or hypotension.
qrni7n4: After IV contrast, a patient becomes pale and sweaty with HR 44 and BP 76/40, but no hives or wheeze. Besides leg elevation, oxygen and IV fluid, which drug is indicated?
Bradycardia with hypotension is a vasovagal reaction. ACR treatment is leg elevation, oxygen, IV fluids and atropine 0.6-1 mg IV, repeated to 3 mg total.
q14rw6ga: A patient develops isolated mild wheezing after gadolinium with normal BP and SpO2. Per ACR, what is the initial bronchodilator dose?
Albuterol 2 puffs, repeated up to 3 times
Albuterol 10 puffs at once, then no more doses
Albuterol 0.3 mg IM in the lateral thigh
ACR recommends albuterol 2 puffs by MDI, repeatable up to 3 times, for mild bronchospasm; worsening bronchospasm calls for epinephrine.
q176h4ly: After a contrast reaction, a patient has BP 230/130 with chest pain. Which ACR regimen addresses this hypertensive crisis?
Labetalol 20 mg IV, doubled every 10 minutes
Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM, repeated every 5 minutes
Furosemide 80 mg IV followed by IV fluids
Atropine 1 mg IV, repeated to 3 mg
ACR lists labetalol 20 mg IV over 2 minutes, then 40 and 80 mg every 10 minutes, with nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL as an alternative.
qobftbg: A patient with heart failure develops crackles, pink frothy sputum and low SpO2 after IV contrast. Which drug is part of ACR management?
Normal saline 1 L bolus over 10 minutes
Pulmonary edema is managed with the head elevated, oxygen, and furosemide 20-40 mg IV slowly per ACR, with emergency response activated.
qocgvq: In a MAG3 diuretic renogram, why is furosemide given?
To tell true obstruction from dilation without obstruction
To block thyroid uptake of free pertechnetate
To lower the radiation dose to the bone marrow and gonads
To reverse side effects of the radiotracer
Washout after furosemide separates mechanical obstruction (retained tracer) from a dilated but nonobstructed collecting system.
q1pxbsme: Which is an ACR elective oral premedication regimen for a patient with a prior allergic-like reaction to iodinated contrast?
Methylprednisolone 32 mg PO 12 and 2 hours before
Methylprednisolone 4 mg PO the morning of the scan
Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV right before injection
ACR lists methylprednisolone 32 mg PO at 12 and 2 hours before contrast, with or without diphenhydramine 50 mg 1 hour before. Steroids need hours to be effective.
qd25c41: What is the ACR prednisone-based premedication schedule?
50 mg PO at 13, 7 and 1 hour before contrast
20 mg PO once, 1 hour before contrast
50 mg PO once, the night before contrast
50 mg PO at 1 hour and 6 hours after contrast
ACR premedication uses prednisone 50 mg at 13, 7 and 1 hour before contrast plus diphenhydramine 50 mg 1 hour before.
qnixnpt: An inpatient with a prior moderate contrast reaction needs urgent CT and cannot take oral medicine. Which accelerated ACR regimen fits?
Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV every 4 hours until contrast
Hydrocortisone 20 mg PO 30 minutes before contrast
Hydrocortisone cream applied to the IV site
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV only after the scan is complete
ACR accelerated regimens use methylprednisolone 40 mg IV or hydrocortisone 200 mg IV every 4 hours until contrast, plus diphenhydramine 50 mg 1 hour before.
qgrysvm: A patient reports a severe shellfish allergy but no prior contrast exposure. What is the correct approach for IV iohexol?
No premedication is needed for this history alone
Cancel the exam because iodine allergy is absolute
Use barium instead of IV contrast for the CT
Shellfish or iodine allergy is not a specific contrast risk factor; any atopy raises risk only slightly. ACR does not recommend premedication for it.
qe5josp: What is the strongest risk factor for an allergic-like reaction to IV iodinated contrast?
A prior allergic-like reaction to iodinated contrast
A history of seafood or iodine allergy
A history of skin reaction to topical povidone-iodine
A prior allergic-like reaction to the same class of contrast is the single strongest predictor of a future reaction.
q1iwscry: A power injection extravasates into the forearm. Which finding most often prompts surgical consultation under ACR guidance?
A tense compartment with altered sensation
An extravasated volume above about 10 mL
Swelling still present at the 1 hour recheck
Mild erythema over the puncture site

Most extravasations, including large ones, settle with elevation and cold packs. The ACR manual lists progressive pain or swelling, altered perfusion or sensation, and skin blistering as the signs prompting surgical assessment for compartment syndrome; volume alone predicts poorly.
q1uy2svo: Which finding after a contrast extravasation requires urgent surgical consultation?
Worsening pain, altered sensation or poor capillary refill
Mild swelling that improves with elevation
Slight redness that fades within an hour of a warm compress
Coolness of the skin after a cold compress
Progressive swelling or pain, altered perfusion, changed sensation, or skin blistering or ulceration suggest compartment syndrome or tissue injury and need surgical evaluation.
q1hnrh07: Which iodinated contrast product family is specifically labeled for intrathecal myelography at selected concentrations?
Only contrast products and concentrations labeled for intrathecal use, such as Omnipaque 180, 240 and 300 or Isovue-M, may be given intrathecally; inadvertent intrathecal ionic contrast can be fatal.
qktuhoo: Per FDA labeling, what follow-up is recommended for a child age 0-3 years after iodinated contrast?
Thyroid function monitoring within about 3 weeks
Serum creatinine every day for one week
The FDA added a recommendation to monitor thyroid function in children 0-3 years after iodinated contrast because of hypothyroidism risk.
q1knx7a8: Per ACR, which patient group is generally considered for IV hydration prophylaxis before iodinated contrast?
eGFR below 30 not on dialysis, or AKI
Any patient over 60 years of age
Patients with a history of hypertension
ACR suggests prophylaxis for patients with AKI or eGFR below 30 not on dialysis; eGFR 30-44 is case by case.
q3x52tn: Why is high-concentration iopamidol warmed to 37 C (98.6 F) before CT angiography?
It lowers viscosity, easing injection at high rates
It raises the iodine concentration in each mL
It prevents the drug from crystallizing in the IV line
It increases renal clearance after the scan
Warming reduces viscosity, lowering injection pressure and potentially extravasation and reactions, especially for high-concentration agents.
q1z0qz6v: Nonionic iso-osmolar dimer with high viscosity
Ionic high-osmolar monomer for oral use only
Nonionic monomer with about 5 times plasma osmolality
Iodixanol is a nonionic dimer with osmolality similar to blood (about 290 mOsm/kg) and relatively high viscosity, so warming helps.
q1b04mws: A patient with eGFR 58 and no AKI takes metformin and will get IV contrast. What does ACR recommend?
Continue metformin; no hold is needed
Hold metformin for 48 hours after contrast
ACR says patients with eGFR 30 or more and no AKI do not need to stop metformin.
q1oerx86: A patient with AKI who takes metformin needs IV iodinated contrast. What is the ACR guidance?
Hold it 48 hours; restart once renal function is stable
Continue metformin because contrast is excreted by the liver
Double the next metformin dose after the scan
With AKI or eGFR below 30, metformin is held at or before contrast for 48 hours and restarted only after renal function is reevaluated and stable.
qecl7jp: A diabetic patient on metformin with eGFR 22 is scheduled for a gadobutrol-enhanced MRI. What metformin change is needed for the GBCA?
None; standard GBCA doses do not require a hold
Hold metformin for 48 hours after the MRI
Stop metformin 1 week before the MRI
Give insulin in place of metformin for the next 48 hours
ACR states no metformin change is needed for standard GBCA doses; the metformin guidance applies to iodinated contrast.
qonxcyv: Which statement about ACR group II gadolinium agents is correct?
NSF risk is so low that eGFR screening is optional
They cause NSF in about 1 in 10 dialysis patients
They are contraindicated for all patients on dialysis
They require dialysis within 2 hours of every injection
ACR notes the risk of NSF with group II agents is so low that eGFR screening before administration is optional.
qugr68v: Which patient is at highest risk for nephrogenic systemic fibrosis after a GBCA?
A dialysis patient given a group I agent
An adult with eGFR 75 given a group II agent
A child with normal kidneys given gadoterate
A patient with diabetes and normal creatinine
NSF has been linked mostly to group I agents in patients on dialysis, with eGFR below 30 or with AKI.
qnc9g3q: Which pair of GBCAs are both macrocyclic agents in ACR group II?
Gadoterate and gadobutrol are macrocyclic group II agents; gadodiamide, gadopentetate and gadoversetamide are linear group I agents.
q1iee08d: A patient has a severe reaction to gadolinium in the MRI scanner room (Zone IV). What should be done first?
Remove the patient from Zone IV, then resuscitate
Bring the crash cart into the magnet room
Start CPR on the scanner table inside the bore
Use a standard laryngoscope inside the room
Most resuscitation equipment is MR unsafe; the patient is moved out of Zone IV to a safe area where the code team can work.
q4vftft: Per ACR, what is the advice for a breastfeeding mother who received a GBCA?
Discard breast milk for one full week
Pump and discard milk for 30 days
Very little GBCA enters breast milk and even less is absorbed; ACR says interruption is not necessary.
qccxpqw: Which GBCA is hepatocyte-specific, with roughly half excreted in bile and a hepatobiliary phase at about 20 minutes?
Gadoxetate is taken up by hepatocytes and about 50 percent is excreted in bile, allowing hepatobiliary-phase imaging about 20 minutes after injection.
q1cie6ja: Gadobenate (MultiHance) is a linear agent. Which ACR group is it in?
Gadobenate is linear but has low reported NSF risk and is placed in ACR group II.
q1vtcc2: What makes gadopiclenol (Elucirem, Vueway) dosing different from most GBCAs?
Its high relaxivity allows half the usual gadolinium dose
It must be given as a slow 60-minute infusion through a filter
It is dosed by body surface area, not weight
It is given orally 1 hour before scanning
Gadopiclenol has about twice the relaxivity of other macrocyclics, so it is dosed at 0.05 mmol/kg.
q1cc6pzx: Ferumoxytol is ordered off-label as MRI contrast for a dialysis patient. How should it be given per its boxed warning?
Diluted IV infusion over at least 15 minutes
Rapid undiluted IV push over 10 seconds, then flush
Because of fatal anaphylaxis risk, ferumoxytol is given as a diluted infusion over at least 15 minutes with BP and pulse monitoring for at least 30 minutes after.
q15ufqf9: A patient has free air on a chest x-ray and suspected gastric perforation. Which oral contrast is appropriate?
Barium leaking into the peritoneum causes severe peritonitis, so suspected perforation calls for water-soluble iodinated contrast.
q75yh31: A patient is scheduled for abdominal CT, upper GI barium study and a gallbladder ultrasound on the same day. What is the best order?
Ultrasound and CT first, then the barium study
Barium study first, then CT, then ultrasound
Barium study first, then ultrasound, then CT
Any order works since barium is invisible on CT
Barium residue causes streak artifact on CT and acoustic shadowing on ultrasound, so those studies should be done before barium.
q14rizn1: A frail elderly patient with poor swallowing needs an esophagram for possible leak. Why is Gastrografin a poor choice?
Aspirated hyperosmolar contrast can cause pulmonary edema
It is too dense to show a small leak
It is not labeled for oral use in adults or older children
It is absorbed and causes NSF
Aspirated hyperosmolar diatrizoate draws fluid into the lungs and can cause severe pulmonary edema; nonionic low-osmolar contrast is preferred.
qb1spps: Which allergy is a contraindication to Definity and Lumason?
Both Definity and Lumason contain PEG components; known PEG hypersensitivity is a contraindication.
qj4bjfw: Which pediatric use is FDA-approved for sulfur hexafluoride microspheres (Lumason)?
Lumason is approved for intravesical use in children for ultrasonographic evaluation of suspected or known vesicoureteral reflux, avoiding fluoroscopic radiation.
q1emos08: A diabetic patient arrives for an oncologic FDG PET study. Which fingerstick glucose is the usual upper limit for proceeding?

Protocols generally proceed below roughly 150 to 200 mg/dL, because glucose competes with FDG for GLUT transport and hexokinase, lowering tumor uptake and raising background. Rapid insulin given shortly before injection drives FDG into skeletal muscle and is avoided.
q1dxkpak: How long are methylxanthines withheld before a regadenoson myocardial perfusion study?

The regadenoson label directs avoiding caffeine, tea, chocolate and theophylline for at least 12 hours, because they are adenosine receptor antagonists that blunt coronary vasodilation and produce a false negative study. Aminophylline stays on the cart to reverse a prolonged reaction.
q19j1sd3: What patient instruction helps image quality and lowers radiation dose after Tc-99m MDP injection?
Drink fluids and void often before imaging
Fast and avoid all fluids until imaging is done
Lie still in a cold room for 2 hours
Hydration and frequent voiding clear unbound tracer, reduce bladder dose and prevent bladder activity from obscuring the pelvis.
q1xrv6q9: A bone scan shows activity in the thyroid and stomach. What does this most likely indicate?
Free Tc-99m pertechnetate from poor labeling
Widespread metastases to the skull and ribs
Normal renal excretion of the MDP tracer
Residual barium from a recent GI study
Thyroid, salivary and gastric activity indicates free pertechnetate, a radiochemical purity problem, not bone disease.
qa51502: How is regadenoson given for pharmacologic stress?
0.4 mg IV bolus, saline flush, then tracer
0.4 mg IM in the deltoid, then exercise
Oral tablet 1 hour before the tracer
Regadenoson is a fixed 0.4 mg dose given over about 10 seconds, followed by a 5 mL flush and the radiotracer 10-20 seconds later.
q17hmbr2: A patient has a seizure after regadenoson. Which drug should be avoided for treating it?
Regadenoson labeling advises that methylxanthines such as aminophylline not be used for regadenoson-associated seizures because they lower the seizure threshold.
q1o3ry54: During dipyridamole stress, a patient has chest pain and ST depression. Which drug reverses dipyridamole's effects?
Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV with flush
Aminophylline blocks adenosine receptors and reverses dipyridamole, whose effects last longer than adenosine's; it is ideally given after the tracer has circulated.
quz0n7q: Which feature makes adenosine side effects usually resolve within about a minute of stopping the infusion?
It is cleared rapidly by the kidneys
It is reversed by the radiotracer
Adenosine is rapidly taken up and metabolized by red cells and endothelium, giving a half-life of seconds.
q1i9vodx: A patient takes oral dipyridamole for stroke prevention and is scheduled for adenosine stress. Why does this matter?
Dipyridamole blocks adenosine reuptake, boosting effects
Dipyridamole blocks the radiotracer from reaching the heart
Dipyridamole raises blood glucose and ruins the images
Dipyridamole reverses adenosine and makes it ineffective
Dipyridamole inhibits adenosine reuptake, increasing adenosine levels and side effects; it is typically held about 48 hours before adenosine stress.
qc0jaqn: Which patient is the best candidate for dobutamine stress instead of a vasodilator?
Severe bronchospasm and unable to exercise
Recent caffeine intake and able to exercise
Second-degree heart block without a pacemaker
Dobutamine is used when patients cannot exercise and cannot receive vasodilators, as in active bronchospasm; aortic stenosis and arrhythmias are cautions.
q1o4cx1k: Before coronary CT angiography, why is metoprolol often given?
To lower heart rate and reduce motion artifact
To dilate the coronary arteries before the scan starts
A heart rate below about 60-65 bpm reduces cardiac motion and improves CCTA image quality; nitroglycerin is what dilates the coronaries.
q1xm67yf: Before coronary CTA, which history is a contraindication to sublingual nitroglycerin?
Nitrates with PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil or vardenafil within 24 hours, tadalafil within 48 hours) can cause profound hypotension.
q1tlu28u: Why is potassium iodide given before I-123 MIBG (iobenguane) imaging?
To block thyroid uptake of free radioiodine
To enhance tumor uptake of the tracer
To reverse nausea from the tracer
To speed renal excretion of the tracer after imaging
Stable iodide saturates the thyroid so free radioiodine released from the agent is not trapped, protecting the thyroid.
qm5qtwn: For which study would potassium iodide pretreatment be inappropriate?
An I-123 thyroid uptake and scan
An I-123 MIBG scan for neuroblastoma
An I-131 MIBG therapy for pheochromocytoma
Blocking the thyroid before a thyroid uptake or radioiodine thyroid study would prevent the uptake the study measures.
q2638s0: During HIDA imaging, sincalide is given to measure gallbladder ejection fraction. How is it best given to reduce cramping?
A slow infusion (label: 0.12 mcg/kg over 50 minutes; SNMMI GBEF protocol: 0.02 mcg/kg over 60 minutes) causes less cramping and nausea than rapid injection.
q15nbp0s: During secretin-enhanced MRCP, what does secretin do?
Stimulates pancreatic juice, distending the duct
Contracts the gallbladder to empty bile into the duodenum
Blocks thyroid uptake of free iodine
Secretin stimulates pancreatic ductal fluid and bicarbonate secretion, distending the pancreatic duct and filling the duodenum for evaluation.
q1jdc44f: Glucagon is ordered as a hypotonic agent for MR enterography. Which history is a contraindication?
Glucagon can release catecholamines from a pheochromocytoma and cause a hypertensive crisis; insulinoma is also a contraindication.
q12gxpty: During IR moderate sedation with midazolam, the patient's SpO2 falls and capnography shows a flat waveform. After stimulating and opening the airway, which reversal agent is used for midazolam?
Flumazenil 0.2 mg IV, repeat each minute to 1 mg
Naloxone 2 mg IV push, repeated in 1 hour if needed
Atropine 1 mg IV, repeat to 3 mg
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines; airway support comes first. Monitor for resedation since flumazenil is shorter-acting than midazolam.
q1gpii5f: In which patient is flumazenil most likely to cause seizures?
A healthy adult after a single midazolam dose
A child sedated for a short MRI scan
An adult given fentanyl only for a biopsy
Flumazenil can precipitate withdrawal seizures in chronic benzodiazepine users and in tricyclic overdose.
q1rdqay6: A patient given fentanyl for a biopsy is reversed with naloxone and is awake. Why is continued monitoring needed?
Naloxone can wear off before the opioid, causing resedation
Naloxone causes delayed anaphylaxis after 4 hours
Naloxone raises blood glucose for several hours
Naloxone causes seizures in all patients
Naloxone acts for about 30-90 minutes, so the opioid effect can return; monitor for resedation before discharge.
qqfzlg6: Rapid IV administration of a large fentanyl dose during sedation can cause which specific complication?
Prolonged bleeding from the arterial access site
High-dose rapid fentanyl can cause chest wall rigidity; slow titration in small increments with capnography reduces risk.
q10ndn3w: During IR access-site infiltration, a patient reports perioral numbness, metallic taste and ringing ears. What is the most likely cause?
A vasovagal reaction to the needle
These are early signs of LAST; stop injecting, call for help and prepare for seizures, arrhythmias and lipid emulsion.
q1vhce7f: Which statement about bupivacaine toxicity is correct?
It can cause refractory cardiac arrest; lipid is used
It is reversed by naloxone in standard doses
It is safe to give intravenously for pain
Its toxicity is limited to minor skin reactions at the site
Bupivacaine is especially cardiotoxic; LAST management includes airway support, seizure control and 20 percent lipid emulsion.
q39yvrm: An IR patient with a history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia needs catheter flushes. What should be used?
Non-heparin flush per protocol, such as plain saline
Heparinized saline at half the usual strength
Any heparin exposure, including flushes and LMWH, is avoided in HIT; plain saline or a non-heparin anticoagulant is used.
qdk3kb0: Which patient has a higher risk of reaction to protamine after an IR procedure?
A patient with a penicillin allergy
A patient who had CT contrast last year
A patient with a latex allergy only
Prior protamine exposure, such as NPH insulin, fish allergy and vasectomy increase protamine reaction risk; give slowly and monitor.
qwhprp0: During catheter-directed alteplase thrombolysis the fibrinogen level falls to 95 mg/dL. Why is fibrinogen tracked during the infusion?
A low level signals systemic lysis and bleeding risk
It confirms the catheter still sits inside the thrombus
It shows the clot is dissolving as intended
It predicts how long the infusion will run

Alteplase converts plasminogen to plasmin, which digests circulating fibrinogen as well as clot, so a fibrinogen under about 100 to 150 mg/dL marks systemic fibrinolysis and rising hemorrhage risk; the rate is cut or held on that result. Catheter position is confirmed by imaging.
q7gb9pv: Why is verapamil added to a radial artery access cocktail in IR?
To raise blood pressure during sedation
To speed clearance of contrast by the kidneys
Intra-arterial verapamil, with nitroglycerin and heparin, prevents spasm and occlusion of the radial artery.
q948xjk: For IR port placement, when should prophylactic cefazolin be given?
Within 60 minutes before the skin incision
Only if the patient develops a fever later
After the port is accessed for the first time
Surgical prophylaxis is timed within 60 minutes before incision so tissue levels are adequate during the procedure.
q19danmr: Which adverse effect should be watched most closely when dexmedetomidine is used for pediatric MRI sedation?
Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-2 agonist that causes relatively little respiratory depression but commonly causes bradycardia and hypotension.
q1oet39o: Before a Tc-99m pertechnetate Meckel scan, why might famotidine be given?
To increase tracer retention in gastric mucosa
To block thyroid uptake of pertechnetate
To speed gastric emptying of the tracer
To prevent an allergic reaction to the injected tracer
H2 blockers reduce release of pertechnetate from gastric mucosa, improving detection of ectopic gastric mucosa in a Meckel diverticulum.
q1omk3ds: Ondansetron is ordered for nausea after IR sedation. Which history requires caution?
Ondansetron can prolong the QT interval; caution in congenital long QT, electrolyte problems and other QT-prolonging drugs.
q2u60v4: An outpatient who must drive home has a few mild hives after contrast. Which antihistamine might a protocol favor because it is less sedating?
A second-generation antihistamine such as cetirizine or fexofenadine causes less sedation than first-generation agents.
q1p7ndax: A patient scheduled for contrast-enhanced CT reports a prior reaction of hives after iodinated contrast. What is the usual approach?
Premedication with a corticosteroid and antihistamine on a timed schedule, per department protocol
Proceed without any change, since hives are a mild reaction that almost never recurs on a repeat study
Substitute a gadolinium-based agent for the CT so the iodinated agent is avoided
Cancel contrast imaging permanently and use only non-contrast studies from now on
A prior mild reaction raises the risk of another, and timed premedication is the standard mitigation.
q15t25nj: Which patient history most increases the risk of contrast-associated kidney injury?
Chronic kidney disease with a reduced eGFR
A prior CT with contrast that was normal
Baseline renal impairment is the dominant risk factor. Shellfish allergy is not a contrast risk factor.
q86kukj: A 40 mL contrast extravasation in the forearm is comfortable with a good radial pulse. What is the usual initial care?
Elevate the limb and apply a cold pack
Elevate the limb and apply a heat pack
Aspirate the fluid through the IV catheter
Inject hyaluronidase into the swollen area
