Standard care for an uncomplicated extravasation is elevation of the limb above the heart to aid resorption plus cold packs for symptom relief, with documentation and a recheck before discharge. Aspiration and hyaluronidase are not part of routine ACR practice.
q13wdwgh: Which sign after extravasation suggests a serious complication rather than a routine one?
Increasing pain with a tense compartment, skin blistering or altered sensation
Transient coolness and pallor of the skin that improve once the cold pack comes off
Mild local swelling that is comfortable and settles over a few hours
A small bruise at the puncture site with no swelling or pain beyond it
Compartment syndrome and skin ulceration are the complications that need surgical assessment.
qydwbgu: For which patient is metformin typically withheld around iodinated contrast?
One with significantly reduced kidney function or acute kidney injury
Every patient who takes metformin, regardless of kidney function or dose
Only patients having an MRI with a gadolinium-based agent
Only patients younger than 40 who take more than one tablet daily
Current guidance individualizes this by renal function rather than holding it for everyone.
qeinwmf: Which patient group is at risk for nephrogenic systemic fibrosis with gadolinium agents?
Those with severe kidney impairment, especially on dialysis
Those with a documented penicillin allergy and a prior drug rash
Those with well-controlled asthma on an inhaled steroid
Those over 65 years old with normal kidney function
Severe renal impairment is the risk factor, and newer agent groups carry much lower risk.
ql5u4u6: A patient asks whether gadolinium stays in the body. What is accurate?
Small amounts can be retained in tissue including brain, with no proven clinical harm to date
It is completely eliminated within an hour of the scan, so no retention in any tissue occurs at all
Retained gadolinium causes progressive dementia in most patients within a few years
Tissue retention occurs only with iodinated contrast agents, never with gadolinium
Retention is documented; clinical significance remains unestablished, and that is the honest answer.
q3fqvu7: During a contrast reaction, a patient has wheezing and hives but a normal blood pressure. What is the usual treatment?
Epinephrine intramuscularly if bronchospasm is significant, with a bronchodilator and oxygen
Diphenhydramine alone, since the hives show this is a purely cutaneous reaction that will settle
Intravenous corticosteroids alone, which reverse bronchospasm within minutes
Observation only, because a normal blood pressure rules out a serious reaction
Significant bronchospasm during a contrast reaction is treated with epinephrine; antihistamines treat the skin only.
qee7kme: What is diphenhydramine's role in a contrast reaction?
It treats urticaria and itching; it does not treat airway or circulatory compromise
It is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis and should be given before epinephrine
It reverses bronchospasm directly by relaxing the airway smooth muscle
It raises the blood pressure by causing peripheral vasoconstriction
Antihistamines address the cutaneous component only, which is why they never substitute for epinephrine.
qdzg83p: A patient develops isolated mild wheezing after contrast, with normal vital signs. A reasonable first step is:
An inhaled beta agonist with oxygen and close monitoring
Intravenous corticosteroids alone, with no inhaler
Immediate intramuscular epinephrine in every case
Discharge from the department with no treatment
Mild isolated bronchospasm can be treated with a bronchodilator, with escalation if it does not settle.
q18zxshd: A patient becomes bradycardic and hypotensive after contrast, with warm dry skin and no urticaria. What does this suggest?
A vasovagal reaction rather than anaphylaxis
Anaphylactic shock from the contrast injection
Acute pulmonary embolism during the scan
Bradycardia with hypotension points to a vagal reaction. Anaphylaxis is typically tachycardic with skin findings.
qqpjsy: How does the management of a vasovagal reaction differ from anaphylaxis?
Elevate the legs, give fluids, and use atropine for persistent bradycardia rather than epinephrine
Give intramuscular epinephrine first in both situations, then add fluids and atropine if they are needed
Withhold fluids in a vagal reaction and raise the head of the table instead of the legs
Treat both with antihistamines and oxygen only, reserving other drugs for arrest
Mistaking one for the other leads to the wrong first drug, which is why the distinction matters.
q14mpqqt: What instruction matters most before a myocardial perfusion study with a pharmacologic stress agent?
Avoid caffeine and methylxanthines for the period specified by protocol
Fast for a full 24 hours before the appointment, taking only sips of water
Drink several liters of water immediately before the tracer injection
Stop all cardiac medications for one week before the study
Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors and can invalidate the stress portion of the study.
qzfijju: A patient becomes severely bronchospastic after regadenoson. What is the specific reversal agent?
Aminophylline is a competitive antagonist at the adenosine receptor and reverses regadenoson effects.
qn561uj: Which patient history is a concern before a regadenoson stress study?
Significant reactive airway disease or high-grade atrioventricular block
Well-controlled hypothyroidism on a stable levothyroxine dose for several years
Mild seasonal allergic rhinitis treated with an antihistamine
A prior pharmacologic stress test read as normal two years ago
Adenosine receptor agonists can cause bronchospasm and conduction block.
q18uhz3k: A patient is receiving therapeutic radioiodine. Which instruction is part of the standard discharge guidance?
Time and distance precautions from others, especially children and pregnant people
Complete isolation in a lead-lined hospital room for one month after the treatment dose
Avoid all oral fluids for 48 hours so the dose stays concentrated in the thyroid
No precautions are needed at all once the patient leaves the department
Time, distance and simple hygiene measures are the practical radiation protection instructions.
q14xhzbc: Why is blood glucose checked before an FDG PET study?
High glucose competes with the tracer and degrades image quality
The glucose level determines the radiation dose that is administered
The glucose level identifies patients with a contrast allergy
A high glucose predicts extravasation at the injection site
FDG is a glucose analog, so hyperglycemia reduces tumor uptake and study quality.
q1amqhwj: Before an MRI with contrast, which screening question is essential?
Renal function and any implanted or embedded metal
Daily caffeine intake and the time of the last cup of tea
Any recent dental cleaning or scaling visit
The time of the last meal and what it held
Renal function governs gadolinium safety, and metal screening governs MRI safety itself.
qyoxjn7: A patient on hemodialysis with no residual renal function needs contrast CT. What is generally true?
Contrast can usually be given, because there is no remaining renal function to protect
Urgent dialysis must be arranged immediately after the scan in every case to clear the contrast
Only gadolinium-based agents may be used once a patient has started dialysis
Iodinated contrast is absolutely contraindicated in any patient on maintenance dialysis
With no residual function there is nothing left to injure; routine urgent dialysis afterward is not required.
q1f8wtew: What is the limitation of corticosteroid premedication before contrast?
It needs hours to work, so it does not help in an emergency scan
It prevents contrast reactions completely when the schedule is followed
It takes full effect within about five minutes of the first dose
It can be given only by the intravenous route in the department
The timed schedule exists because steroids take hours; urgent studies use alternative strategies.
qqvximg: A patient asks whether a shellfish allergy means they are allergic to contrast. What is accurate?
There is no specific link; the iodine in shellfish is not what causes allergy
A shellfish allergy means a reaction to iodinated contrast is essentially certain
All iodine-containing foods and antiseptics must be avoided for life
Only gadolinium agents are safe for a patient with shellfish allergy
This is a persistent myth. Any atopic history raises general reaction risk slightly, but shellfish is not special.
qvsvavk: When should a water-soluble contrast agent be used instead of barium?
When perforation of the bowel is suspected
For every fluoroscopic study of the bowel
Only in pediatric and neonatal patients
When the patient has a contrast allergy
Barium in the peritoneum causes a severe inflammatory reaction, so suspected perforation calls for a water-soluble agent.
q1disi8j: Why is glucagon sometimes given during a gastrointestinal imaging study?
It relaxes smooth muscle and reduces bowel motion artifact
It raises the blood pressure during a long fluoroscopic study
It enhances the contrast signal in the bowel wall directly
It prevents allergic reactions to the barium suspension
Glucagon's smooth muscle relaxation is used to reduce peristalsis.
qlu5h1b: Which patient history warrants caution before giving glucagon for imaging?
Glucagon can precipitate a hypertensive crisis in pheochromocytoma and hypoglycemia in insulinoma.
q3nvr8o: In a contrast reaction with hypotension and airway swelling, what dose and route of epinephrine is standard for an adult?
0.3 mg of the 1 mg/mL concentration intramuscularly in the lateral thigh
1 mg of the 1 mg/mL concentration given intravenously over about one minute
3 mg of the 1 mg/mL concentration intramuscularly in the lateral thigh
0.3 mg of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration intravenously as a slow push
Confusing the concentrations is a well-known fatal error. The intramuscular dose uses the 1 mg/mL product.
q7sxyl2: What is the role of oxygen in managing a moderate contrast reaction?
It is given early alongside the specific drug treatment
It replaces the need for epinephrine in most reactions
It is used only during cardiac arrest in the scanner
It is withheld until the reaction fully resolves
Oxygen is a standard early measure in any significant reaction.
q4zn4rk: Which response during an iodinated contrast injection is a physiologic effect rather than a hypersensitivity reaction?
Warm flushing with a metallic taste
Scattered hives on the chest and arms
Sneezing with itching of the eyes

Warmth, flushing, metallic taste and nausea are osmotic and chemotoxic effects of the contrast itself and do not predict a later allergic-like reaction, so the injection continues. Urticaria, sneezing with itch and laryngeal symptoms are allergic-like and treated as hypersensitivity.
q73n0va: A technologist is pregnant and asks about working with radiopharmaceuticals. What is the correct approach?
Declare the pregnancy so dose limits and monitoring are applied, following facility policy
Stop all work with radiopharmaceuticals at once, without discussing it with the safety officer
Continue working with no changes at all, since the fetal dose is always negligible
Rely on the lead apron alone, since it shields the fetus from all exposure
Declared pregnancy triggers specific dose limits and monitoring under radiation safety regulations.
q1q21bef: A patient reports a metallic taste and a warm flushing sensation during contrast injection. What is this?
A common physiologic effect, not an allergic reaction
An early warning sign of a developing anaphylactic reaction
A sign that the contrast is extravasating at the site
Evidence of early contrast-induced kidney injury
These sensations are expected and are not a reaction. Recognizing that avoids unnecessary stopping of a study.
q1rh5ajf: Why does MRI require screening even for staff entering the magnet room?
The static field is always on and attracts ferromagnetic objects with lethal force
Screening applies to patients only, because staff never go inside the bore of the magnet
The magnetic field is switched on only while a scan is actually in progress
The field affects only electronic devices and never plain metal objects
The magnet is never off, and projectile injuries are a known cause of death in MRI suites.
q1adqx6u: A 58-year-old man is found unresponsive with snoring respirations at 6 breaths/min and pinpoint pupils. After opening the airway, what should you do next?
Ventilate with a BVM attached to high-flow oxygen
Apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min and closely monitor his breathing
Give naloxone before performing any airway intervention
Place him in the recovery position and reassess in 5 minutes
A respiratory rate of 6 with snoring is inadequate breathing, so assisted ventilation with oxygen comes first; naloxone may follow but never replaces ventilation.
q1nd2j9t: You are ventilating an apneic 45-year-old man who has a strong carotid pulse. No advanced airway is in place. How often should you deliver a breath?
For an adult in respiratory arrest with a pulse, current AHA guidance is 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 breaths/min), each over about 1 second with visible chest rise.
qy2k6u0: A 4-year-old girl is apneic but has a pulse of 96/min. How often should you ventilate her with a BVM?
Infants and children with a pulse but absent or inadequate breathing should receive 1 breath every 2-3 seconds (20-30 breaths/min).
qs26zfq: How should you select the correct size oropharyngeal airway for an adult?
Corner of the mouth to the earlobe
Tip of the nose to the sternal notch
Width of the patient's little finger
Center of the lips to the bottom of the chin
An OPA is sized from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe or angle of the jaw; an incorrect size can push the tongue back or fail to open the airway.
qqbd2bp: Which finding would make a nasopharyngeal airway inappropriate for an unresponsive patient?
Clear fluid draining from the nose after a head injury
An intact gag reflex with clenched teeth
Snoring respirations at a rate of 10 per minute
The patient is over 70 years old with dentures in place
Clear fluid from the nose after head trauma suggests a basilar skull fracture, a contraindication to an NPA; a gag reflex or clenched teeth are actually reasons to choose an NPA over an OPA.
qlqp527: When suctioning the oropharynx of an adult, what is the maximum duration of each suction attempt?
As long as secretions are still visible
Adults should be suctioned for no more than 15 seconds at a time (less for children and infants) because the patient is not being oxygenated during suctioning.
qmgqzut: Before placing a nonrebreather mask on a patient, what should you do?
Fill the reservoir bag with oxygen
Set the flow rate to 4 L/min
Remove the one-way valves from the mask
Ask the patient to exhale fully first
The reservoir bag should be prefilled and stay at least partly inflated during inhalation, using 10-15 L/min; otherwise the patient may rebreathe exhaled air.
q5s2kst: A 5-year-old boy has a sudden high fever, is drooling, sits leaning forward on his hands, and speaks in a muffled voice. What is the most appropriate approach?
Keep him calm in a position of comfort and avoid looking in his throat
Lay him supine and use a tongue depressor to inspect the throat
Insert an oropharyngeal airway to keep the swollen tissues open
Separate him from his parent so you can examine him more easily
These findings suggest epiglottitis; agitating the child or placing anything in the mouth can trigger complete obstruction, so give oxygen as tolerated and transport promptly.
q16vo7pq: A 9-month-old infant is choking, cannot cry, and is turning blue but remains responsive. What should you do?
Give 5 back slaps followed by 5 chest thrusts
Give abdominal thrusts until the object comes out
Perform a blind finger sweep of the mouth
Give 2 rescue breaths and then check a pulse
For a responsive infant with severe obstruction, alternate 5 back slaps and 5 chest thrusts; abdominal thrusts and blind finger sweeps are not used in infants.
q16ir4er: A woman in her third trimester of pregnancy is choking and cannot speak or cough. What maneuver should you use?
Chest thrusts are used in visibly pregnant or obese patients because abdominal thrusts are ineffective or may harm the fetus.
q1p1a6o3: An adult choking patient you have been treating becomes unresponsive. After lowering him to the ground and calling for help, what should you do?
Begin CPR, looking in the mouth for the object before each set of breaths
Continue abdominal thrusts while he lies supine until the object is seen
Perform repeated blind finger sweeps until the obstruction is removed
Check a carotid pulse for a full 30 seconds before starting anything
An unresponsive choking victim gets CPR; compressions may dislodge the object, and you look in the mouth and remove only a visible object before ventilating.
q10ly281: A 16-year-old with asthma was wheezing loudly 10 minutes ago. She is now drowsy, her chest is nearly silent, and air movement is minimal. What does this indicate?
The bronchospasm is resolving on its own and she can rest
She is hyperventilating from anxiety and needs coaching
Her airway is clear, so oxygen can be reduced
A quiet chest with decreasing mental status means too little air is moving to produce wheezes, an ominous sign of respiratory failure that requires BVM ventilation and rapid transport.
qlxxf9h: A 70-year-old man with COPD is in respiratory distress, speaking in short phrases, with an SpO2 of 84%. How should you manage oxygen?
Give oxygen and titrate to relieve hypoxia
Withhold oxygen because it will suppress his hypoxic drive
Give no oxygen until the hospital checks a blood gas
Only use room air and coach pursed-lip breathing
Oxygen should never be withheld from a hypoxic COPD patient; give it, titrate to the target saturation in your protocol, and monitor mental status and breathing.
q1tlrpb7: A 3-year-old with labored breathing has been crying and agitated. Which change suggests he is progressing toward respiratory arrest?
Sleepiness and a falling heart rate
Louder crying and kicking during your exam
A respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute
Nasal flaring that started on the drive to the hospital
Decreasing level of consciousness and bradycardia are late signs of hypoxia in children and signal impending arrest; begin assisted ventilation.
q1y2v4ax: A 22-year-old woman has rapid breathing, tingling hands, and numbness around her mouth after an argument. Her lung sounds are clear. What is the best approach?
Coach her to slow her breathing while assessing for medical causes
Have her breathe into a paper bag to raise her carbon dioxide level
Assume it is anxiety and release her without further assessment
Restrict all oxygen because it will worsen her symptoms
Hyperventilation may be anxiety-related but can also stem from serious conditions such as PE or DKA; coach slower breathing and do not use a paper bag, which can cause hypoxia.
qefgmq8: An unresponsive motorcyclist with suspected spinal injury has snoring respirations. Which technique should you use first to open the airway?
The jaw thrust opens the airway with minimal neck movement; if it fails to open the airway, head-tilt chin-lift is used because the airway takes priority.
qgtilix: An adult patient is breathing 36 times per minute with very shallow chest movement. Why is this a concern?
Minute volume is likely inadequate, so assist ventilations
The fast rate guarantees good oxygenation, so no action is needed
Rapid breathing always means anxiety and should be coached down
Shallow breaths are normal when the respiratory rate is that high
Minute volume equals rate times tidal volume; very shallow breaths move mostly dead-space air, so a fast shallow pattern can be inadequate and needs BVM assistance.
qne7jnk: A 74-year-old woman with heart failure is sitting upright, coughing pink frothy sputum, with crackles in both lungs. She is alert, BP 168/98, SpO2 86%. Which treatment is most appropriate within EMT scope?
Lay her supine with legs raised
This is acute pulmonary edema in an alert patient with good blood pressure, a classic indication for CPAP, which improves oxygenation and reduces work of breathing.
q17hksv6: While you ventilate an apneic patient, the upper abdomen becomes increasingly distended. What is the most likely cause?
Ventilations that are too forceful or too fast
An oropharyngeal airway that is slightly too small
Chest compressions that are too shallow
Excess ventilation volume or rate forces air into the stomach, increasing vomiting risk; reposition the airway and give only enough volume for visible chest rise.
q84mvs7: What compression rate should you use when performing CPR on an adult?
At least 140 per minute, as fast as possible
AHA guidelines call for a compression rate of 100-120/min for patients of all ages; faster rates reduce depth and filling time.
q9834sv: What is the correct compression depth for an adult in cardiac arrest?
At least 2 inches but not more than 2.4 inches
About 1 inch, just enough to see the chest move
At least 3 inches to maximize blood flow
One-quarter of the depth of the chest
Adult compressions should be at least 2 inches (5 cm) and no more than about 2.4 inches (6 cm), with full recoil after each one.
q1ybmg8u: You are performing CPR on a 3-month-old infant. How deep should compressions be?
One-half the depth of the chest
Infant compressions should be at least one-third of the chest depth, about 1.5 inches (4 cm).
q1dlomak: Two EMTs are performing CPR on a 6-year-old with no advanced airway. What compression-to-ventilation ratio should they use?
Two-rescuer CPR for infants and children uses 15:2; single rescuers use 30:2, and 3:1 is reserved for newborns.
q104ewdt: You are about to use an AED on a pulseless 5-year-old, but only adult pads are available. What should you do?
Use the adult pads, placing them front and back if they would overlap
Withhold the AED until pediatric pads arrive
Cut the adult pads in half so they fit the small chest
Use one adult pad only on the center of the chest
If pediatric pads or an attenuator are not available, adult pads should be used; anterior-posterior placement prevents the pads from touching.
qiafkpn: The AED has just delivered a shock to an adult in cardiac arrest. What should you do next?
Resume CPR with compressions right away
Check a carotid pulse for 10 seconds
Give 2 breaths and then check for breathing
After a shock, immediately resume compressions for about 2 minutes before the next rhythm analysis; pausing for a pulse check delays perfusion.
q1ifmiwy: Paramedics have placed an advanced airway in an adult in cardiac arrest. How should you now provide ventilations?
1 breath every 6 seconds during continuous compressions
2 breaths after every 30 compressions with pauses
1 breath every 2 seconds without pausing compressions
1 breath every 15 seconds to avoid hyperventilation
With an advanced airway in place, compressions are continuous and ventilations are given at 1 breath every 6 seconds (10/min).
qt8g2xj: A 62-year-old man collapses. He is unresponsive, has no pulse, and takes occasional gasping breaths. What should you do?
Start CPR and apply the AED
Place him in the recovery position
Assist ventilations and recheck in 2 minutes
Agonal gasps are not effective breathing and are a sign of cardiac arrest; start compressions and attach the AED immediately.
qhco9uu: When checking for a pulse in an unresponsive adult, what is the maximum time you should spend?
However long it takes to be certain
Pulse and breathing checks should take no more than 10 seconds so that compressions are not delayed when the patient is in arrest.
q1iizg84: A 78-year-old woman with diabetes reports weakness, nausea, and mild shortness of breath for 2 hours. She denies chest pain. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
Suspect a possible heart attack and treat accordingly
Chest pain is absent, so a heart problem is ruled out
These are common age-related symptoms needing no treatment
This is most likely a stomach virus with dehydration
Older adults, women, and diabetics often have atypical ACS presentations without chest pain, so these symptoms should be treated as a possible heart attack.
q1afyt1q: A 69-year-old man has new right-sided weakness and slurred speech. Which piece of history is most important to obtain?
The time he was last known well
Whether he has had a recent flu shot
The name of his primary care doctor
Stroke treatment eligibility depends on time from onset, which is defined as the last time the patient was known to be at baseline.
q3fhyqp: An 80-year-old man has confusion and weakness on one side of his body. Which assessment should you perform because its result can mimic a stroke?
Hypoglycemia can produce stroke-like deficits, so the blood glucose should be checked in any patient with suspected stroke.
q1hz0n7x: A patient with suspected stroke asks for a glass of water. What should you do?
Withhold food and drink because swallowing may be impaired
Give small sips of water to keep her mouth moist
Allow water but not food until the hospital
Give a sugary drink to protect her brain
Stroke patients frequently have difficulty swallowing, so they should receive nothing by mouth to prevent aspiration.
q1lxxfjk: A 72-year-old man has sudden severe abdominal pain radiating to his back, a pulsating mass near the umbilicus, and pale skin. What should you suspect?
Sudden abdominal or back pain with a pulsatile mass in an older man suggests an AAA; handle the abdomen gently, treat for shock, and transport rapidly.
q1aiudbs: A 1-year-old has a heart rate of 52/min, pale mottled skin, and poor responsiveness despite effective BVM ventilation with oxygen. What should you do?
Place the child in a car seat for transport
In infants and children, a heart rate below 60/min with poor perfusion despite adequate oxygenation and ventilation requires CPR.
qrtbefe: After defibrillation, an adult regains a pulse but remains unresponsive and is not breathing adequately. How should you ventilate?
As fast as possible to clear CO2
After ROSC, ventilate at about 10 breaths/min and avoid hyperventilation, which raises intrathoracic pressure and lowers cardiac output.
qrri5qi: A 28-year-old with a suspected opioid overdose is unresponsive, apneic, and pulseless. What is your priority?
Searching the scene for the drug used
A pulseless patient is in cardiac arrest; CPR and defibrillation take priority, and naloxone, if given, must not delay them.
q6xp79: A woman who is 34 weeks pregnant is in cardiac arrest. Along with high-quality CPR, what should be done?
Place her on her right side for CPR
Manually displacing the uterus to the left relieves compression of the vena cava and improves blood return during CPR.
q1ii34tj: A 59-year-old man had chest pressure begin while shoveling snow. It has continued for 30 minutes despite rest. How should this be interpreted?
Possible heart attack, because the pain is not relieved by rest
Stable angina that will resolve if he keeps resting
Muscle strain because it started during physical work
Indigestion because it has lasted longer than 15 minutes
Angina typically resolves within minutes of rest; chest pain persisting despite rest suggests an acute MI and should be treated as ACS.
q1vkcyb: An 81-year-old woman fainted while sitting at the dinner table and is now alert. What is the most concerning possible cause?
Syncope that occurs while seated or without warning in an older adult raises concern for a cardiac rhythm problem and needs evaluation.
qar9tlb: Two EMTs are performing CPR on an infant. Which compression technique is preferred?
Two thumbs with hands encircling the chest
Heel of both hands stacked on the sternum
Three fingers placed below the nipple line
One thumb pressing on the lower sternum
For two-rescuer infant CPR, the two thumb-encircling hands technique is recommended because it produces better depth and blood pressure.
q1k4gdex: A man has bright red blood spurting from a deep wound to his mid-thigh. What should you do?
Apply a tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above the wound
Elevate the leg and apply a cold pack
Apply a loose dressing and check distal pulses
Apply a tourniquet directly over the knee joint
Life-threatening extremity bleeding is controlled with a tourniquet placed 2-3 inches proximal to the wound, not over a joint, and tightened until bleeding stops.
q4k01be: A tourniquet has been tightened fully on a patient's thigh, but bright red bleeding continues. What should you do next?
Apply a second tourniquet just above the first
Remove the tourniquet and use direct pressure
Loosen the tourniquet to let the limb reperfuse
Place it lower, directly over the wound
If one correctly applied tourniquet does not stop the bleeding, a second tourniquet is placed proximal to the first.
q1n0uepu: A stab wound to the groin is bleeding heavily. A tourniquet cannot be applied. What should you do?
Pack the wound and hold firm direct pressure
Elevate the legs and apply an ice pack
Apply a loose bandage and transport quickly
Wait for ALS to arrive and place a tourniquet at the hip
Junctional wounds such as the groin are controlled by packing the wound tightly with gauze, ideally hemostatic, and holding firm direct pressure.
qjqa4ie: After you seal an open chest wound with an occlusive dressing, the patient becomes more short of breath and hypotensive. What should you do?
Briefly lift a corner of the dressing to release air
Add a second occlusive dressing over the first
Pack the chest wound with gauze
Increase BVM pressure to force the lung open
Worsening distress after sealing a chest wound suggests developing tension pneumothorax; briefly lifting the dressing lets trapped air escape.
q1lhf7yn: A man has a knife impaled in his abdomen. He is alert and his airway is clear. How should you manage the knife?
Stabilize it in place with bulky dressings
Remove it and apply direct pressure
Pull it out partway to reduce bleeding
Cut it off at skin level so it fits under a dressing
Impaled objects are stabilized in place because removal can cause uncontrolled bleeding; they are removed only if they obstruct the airway or prevent CPR.
q7g5xrl: A patient has abdominal organs protruding through a laceration. How should you treat the wound?
Cover it with a moist sterile dressing and then an occlusive layer
Gently push the organs back into the abdomen
Apply a dry gauze dressing held with firm pressure
Leave the organs uncovered so they can be watched
Eviscerated organs are covered with a moist sterile dressing and occlusive layer to keep them moist and warm; never try to replace them.
qb9qbsp: A 40-year-old man has lost a large amount of blood. Which sign indicates his shock has become decompensated?
Hypotension is a late sign of shock that appears after compensatory mechanisms fail; anxiety, tachycardia, and pale cool skin are earlier signs.
q1wptrs2: A 6-year-old struck by a bicycle has a heart rate of 150, capillary refill of 4 seconds, cool skin, and a normal blood pressure. How should you interpret this?
No shock because blood pressure is normal
Normal vital signs for this age
Children maintain blood pressure until late; tachycardia and poor perfusion with a normal BP indicate compensated shock needing rapid treatment and transport.
qfmzjvo: Using the rule of nines, estimate the burned area for an adult with full-thickness burns to the entire right arm and the entire front of the torso.
In an adult each arm is 9% and the anterior trunk is 18%, totaling 27% of body surface area.
qr09e70: A worker is covered with a dry chemical powder that is burning his skin. What should you do first?
Brush off the powder, then flush with large amounts of water
Immediately pour water over the powder
Cover the area with a dry sterile dressing
Dry chemicals should be brushed away before irrigation, because some react with water; then flush with copious water.
qyb9jkn: A man with a head injury has a blood pressure of 188/100, a pulse of 48, and irregular respirations. What do these findings suggest?
Hemorrhagic shock from a scalp wound
An anxiety reaction to the crash and injury
Rising blood pressure, falling pulse, and irregular breathing (Cushing's triad) indicate increasing intracranial pressure and possible brain herniation.
qy9mst5: Which finding is a contraindication to using a traction splint for a suspected femur fracture?
Traction splints pull against the pelvis and are contraindicated with pelvic, hip, knee, or lower leg injuries on the same side; a closed midshaft femur fracture is the indication.
q10xyus1: A woman struck by a car has pelvic pain, instability, and signs of shock. What is the best action?
Apply a pelvic binder and avoid rocking the pelvis
Compress and rock the pelvis to confirm instability
Elevate her legs and roll her to check her back
Apply a traction splint to both legs
An unstable pelvis can bleed heavily; a pelvic binder or sheet wrap stabilizes it, and repeated manipulation may worsen bleeding.
q1756zst: How should you care for a finger that was completely amputated?
Wrap it in moist sterile gauze, seal it in a bag, and keep it cool
Submerge the finger directly in a cup of ice water
Pack the finger in dry ice for the trip
Rinse it in tap water and wrap it in a towel
The part should be wrapped in moist sterile gauze, placed in a sealed bag, and kept cool without direct contact with ice to avoid tissue damage.
qaww2d3: An 82-year-old woman on a blood thinner fell from standing and bumped her head. She is alert with a small bruise on her forehead. What is your main concern?
A minor bruise that only needs an ice pack
Dehydration that caused her to fall
Older adults on anticoagulants have a high risk of intracranial bleeding even after minor head trauma, and symptoms may be delayed, so they should be transported.
qy2br9l: A 52-year-old diabetic is confused but can follow commands and swallow. Her blood glucose is 48 mg/dL. What should you do?
Have her lie flat and rest
A hypoglycemic patient who can swallow and protect the airway should receive oral glucose, then be reassessed.
q1ljj9dc: A diabetic man is unresponsive with snoring respirations and a glucose of 32 mg/dL. Which action is inappropriate?
Placing oral glucose between his cheek and gum
Opening the airway and providing ventilation as needed
Positioning him to protect the airway
Oral glucose should not be given to a patient who cannot swallow or protect the airway because of aspiration risk; manage the airway and request ALS.
qb7bhwy: An 18-month-old with a fever had a seizure that stopped after 1 minute. He is now drowsy but breathing adequately. What is appropriate?
Place him in a cold-water bath to lower the fever quickly
Place a bite block in his mouth in case of another seizure
Febrile seizures are managed by protecting the airway, removing excess clothing, and transport; cold baths and alcohol can cause hypothermia or toxicity.
q1hbe4h2: A 2-year-old may have swallowed some of her grandmother's pills. What information is most important to obtain?
What was taken, how much, and when
Whether the child has been vaccinated
The color of the child's last stool
The substance, amount, and time of ingestion guide treatment; bring the containers and contact poison control per protocol.
q5ig676: On a cold winter night, a family of four has headaches, nausea, and dizziness. Their furnace was recently repaired. What should you do?
Remove them from the home and give high-flow oxygen
Have them rest in bed and recheck in an hour
Give oxygen only if their SpO2 is below 94%
Open one window and treat them inside
Multiple people with the same symptoms indoors suggests carbon monoxide poisoning; remove them from the environment and give high-flow oxygen, as pulse oximetry can be falsely normal.
qeilvld: A marathon runner collapsed on a hot day. He is confused with hot skin and a rapid pulse. What is the priority?
Let him rest in the shade
Heat stroke is life-threatening; altered mental status with hyperthermia requires immediate, aggressive cooling and rapid transport.
q719wfj: Which finding most reliably separates heat stroke from heat exhaustion?
Painful muscle cramps in the legs
Heat stroke is defined by central nervous system dysfunction such as confusion or seizures; sweating may be present in either condition.
q13r5js8: A severely hypothermic patient is found outdoors with a slow pulse. Why should you handle him gently?
Rough movement can trigger ventricular fibrillation
Rough movement will make him shiver less
His skin is too cold to feel pain
Fast movement improves blood flow to the heart
The cold heart is very irritable, and rough handling can cause ventricular fibrillation; move patients gently and prevent further heat loss.
q6tylze: A hiker has frozen, hard, white toes. Transport will take 2 hours over snowy terrain. What should you do?
Protect the area and avoid rewarming if refreezing is possible
Rub the toes vigorously with snow
Massage the toes until color returns
Apply a heating pad set to high
Frostbitten tissue should not be rubbed and should not be thawed if refreezing could occur; protect the area and transport.
q12jo0ts: A child is pulled from a pool. She is apneic but has a pulse. What should you do first?
Perform abdominal thrusts to remove water
Turn her on her side to drain water
Wrap her in blankets and recheck
Hypoxia is the main problem in drowning; ventilation with oxygen is the priority, and abdominal thrusts to remove water are not recommended.
q1bp1ytg: A man was bitten on the leg by a rattlesnake. What is appropriate care?
Keep him calm, limit movement, and remove tight items
Apply ice directly to the bite
Apply a tight tourniquet above the bite
Cut the wound and suction the venom
Keep the patient calm, immobilize the limb, and remove rings or constricting items before swelling; ice, tourniquets, and cutting can cause harm.
q1t8hw5g: A woman in labor has the urge to push and you see the baby's head at the vaginal opening during contractions. What should you do?
Prepare to deliver the baby on scene
Tell her to hold her breath
Push the head back to slow labor
Crowning with the urge to push indicates imminent delivery; prepare for birth on scene rather than attempting transport.
q1ceo53s: During delivery, you find the umbilical cord wrapped loosely around the infant's neck. What should you do?
Gently slip the cord over the head
Pull hard on the cord to free it
Push the baby back into the birth canal
A loose nuchal cord should be slipped over the head; if it is too tight, clamp it in two places and cut between the clamps.
qs3fdos: During labor, you see the umbilical cord protruding from the vagina before the baby. What should you do?
Raise her hips and lift the baby's head off the cord
Gently push the cord back into the vagina
Pull the cord to speed up delivery
Have her push hard with each contraction
A prolapsed cord is compressed by the presenting part; elevate the hips, lift the presenting part off the cord with gloved fingers, keep the cord moist, and transport rapidly.
q184jpkm: During delivery, a single arm protrudes from the vagina. What should you do?
Wait for contractions to deliver the baby
A limb presentation cannot be delivered in the field; place the mother in a position of comfort, give oxygen, and transport immediately.
q15yt7m4: After 30 seconds of effective BVM ventilation, a newborn's heart rate remains 50/min. What should you do?
Begin chest compressions at a 3:1 ratio
Continue ventilation only and recheck in 5 minutes
A newborn heart rate below 60 despite 30 seconds of effective ventilation requires compressions coordinated with ventilations at a 3:1 ratio.
qhzz5jb: A newborn is apneic with a heart rate of 80/min after drying and stimulation. What should you do?
Begin BVM ventilation with room air or oxygen
Continue drying and rubbing the back for 2 more minutes
Apnea or a heart rate below 100 after initial steps requires positive pressure ventilation.
q1kiucgi: A baby has just been born. What are the first steps in caring for the newborn?
Suction the stomach and give oxygen
Give 2 breaths and check a pulse
Clamp the cord and weigh the baby
Initial newborn care includes drying, warming, positioning the airway, clearing secretions as needed, and stimulating breathing.
qf4cuoa: A woman 36 weeks pregnant becomes dizzy and hypotensive while lying flat on her back. What should you do?
Place her on her left side
Keep her supine and raise the head of the stretcher
Supine hypotensive syndrome occurs when the uterus compresses the vena cava; placing her on her left side relieves it.
qqqh0al: A woman 34 weeks pregnant has a severe headache, blurred vision, swelling of her hands and face, and a BP of 168/110. What complication is she at risk for?
These findings suggest preeclampsia, which can progress to eclampsia with seizures; keep her calm, minimize stimulation, and transport.
q10hjohw: A 26-year-old woman has sudden lower abdominal pain, a missed period, dizziness, and a rapid pulse. What should you suspect?
Abdominal pain with a missed period and signs of shock in a woman of childbearing age suggests a ruptured ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise.
q1jlx0wr: You arrive at a scene where a patient says he wants to die and is holding a knife. What should you do first?
Retreat to safety and wait for police
Scene safety comes first; retreat and wait for law enforcement to secure the scene.
q1ktwi8a: A combative patient must be physically restrained for transport. How should he be positioned?
Supine or on his side with continuous monitoring
Face down with his wrists tied to his ankles
Face down with a responder kneeling on his back
Seated upright with a towel over his face
Restraining a patient face down can cause positional asphyxia and death; restrain supine or on the side and monitor airway and breathing continuously.
q1v4phw9: A 64-year-old man vomited dark material resembling coffee grounds. What does this suggest?
Bleeding from hemorrhoids in the rectum
Coffee-ground emesis indicates partially digested blood from the upper GI tract, such as from an ulcer.
q1mfag3d: A 76-year-old man taking a beta blocker has a GI bleed. His heart rate is 68. How should you interpret this?
The beta blocker may be hiding a fast heart rate
His bleeding is minor because his heart rate is normal
The heart rate shows he is not in shock
Beta blockers can blunt the expected tachycardia of shock, so older adults may be in shock despite a normal heart rate.
q1xxhqxk: What are the three components of the Pediatric Assessment Triangle?
Appearance, work of breathing, circulation to skin
The Pediatric Assessment Triangle is a quick visual assessment of appearance, work of breathing, and skin circulation.
q13hwt0f: A dialysis patient has an AV fistula in the left arm. Where should you take a blood pressure?
Blood pressure should not be taken on an arm with a fistula because cuff pressure can damage it.
qu66upd: A college student has fever, headache, a stiff neck, and a purple rash. What should you suspect?
Fever, headache, stiff neck, and petechial rash suggest meningitis; use droplet precautions including a mask.
q1vzfkdj: A 45-year-old woman suddenly develops the worst headache of her life and vomits. What should you suspect?
A sinus infection with pressure behind the eyes
A sudden, severe headache suggests a subarachnoid hemorrhage, a type of hemorrhagic stroke requiring rapid transport.
q1w3obia: You are dispatched to a shooting. Police have not yet arrived. What should you do?
Stage nearby until the scene is secured
Enter quickly to treat the patient
Park in front of the house
Ask bystanders whether the shooter has left, then enter
Responders should stage at a safe distance until law enforcement secures a violent scene.
q13wbemx: At an MCI using START triage, an adult is breathing 34 times per minute. How should this patient be triaged?
Delayed, because the patient is still breathing
In START, a respiratory rate over 30 indicates immediate (red) priority.
qmaqrex: At an MCI, a 5-year-old is apneic but has a pulse. Using JumpSTART, what should you do?
JumpSTART calls for 5 rescue breaths for an apneic child with a pulse; if breathing resumes, the child is tagged immediate.
q1eiwg1b: When lifting a stretcher, what is the correct technique?
Keep the weight close and lift with your legs
Bend at the waist and lift with your back
Twist your torso while lifting to face the ambulance
Hold the weight far from your body
The power lift keeps the back straight and the weight close, using the legs to lift and reducing back injury.
q9pwrzz: A patient is in a car that is on fire. What type of move should you use?
An emergency move along the long axis of the body
A full spinal immobilization before moving
An emergency move is used when there is immediate danger; pull along the long axis of the body to limit spinal movement.
q1p8mcf6: A physician gives you an order over the radio. What should you do?
Repeat the order back to confirm it
Ask your partner to write it down for the report later
The echo technique confirms the order and prevents errors.
q14y7mpi: You discover an error in a patient care report. How should you correct it?
Draw a single line through it, initial, and date
Erase or white out the error
Rewrite the entire report and throw away the original copy
Errors are corrected with a single line, initials, and date so the original remains readable; never erase or obliterate.
qiwz7n4: Which action would be considered abandonment?
Transferring care to a lower-level provider
Giving a report to a nurse
Abandonment is terminating care without ensuring continued care at an equal or higher level.
q1fu3qkh: A hospice patient with a valid DNR is short of breath but has a pulse. What should you do?
Give comfort care such as oxygen and positioning
A DNR applies to resuscitation, not to comfort care; patients with a pulse should still receive appropriate treatment.
q4239xc: You suspect a patient has tuberculosis. What PPE should you use?
Tuberculosis is airborne; responders should wear an N95 respirator and place a surgical mask on the patient if tolerated.
q1cfzr2t: You approach an overturned tanker with a hazmat placard. Where should you stage?
Upwind and uphill at a safe distance
Downhill near the spill so you can see the product
Stage upwind and uphill at a safe distance, identify the hazard with binoculars and the ERG, and wait for a hazmat team.
q1ma9auc: Where do most ambulance crashes occur?
Intersections are the most common location of ambulance crashes; slow down and ensure all lanes have stopped.
qop0jg4: You placed a supraglottic airway in a 55-year-old apneic man who still has a strong carotid pulse. How often should you deliver ventilations through the device?
One breath every 2 to 3 seconds as fast as the bag refills
One breath every 12 to 15 seconds to limit gastric inflation
Two breaths after every 30 chest compressions

An adult who is apneic but has a pulse receives about 10 breaths per minute, one every 6 seconds, whether ventilated by mask or advanced airway. Faster rates cause hyperventilation, raise intrathoracic pressure and reduce venous return.
qes9se: After inserting a supraglottic airway and making one attempt to reposition it, you see no chest rise, hear no lung sounds and get no capnography waveform. What should you do?
Remove it and ventilate with a BVM and basic adjunct
Inflate the cuff with an additional 30 mL of air and keep ventilating
Increase the ventilation rate until lung sounds become audible
Leave it in place and let the hospital team confirm placement

A device that still cannot ventilate after adjustment must be removed so oxygenation is not delayed. BVM ventilation with an oral or nasal airway is the fallback while you prepare a further attempt or transport.
qfsgbd5: Which patient is the most appropriate candidate for a supraglottic airway?
Adult in cardiac arrest with no gag reflex
Responsive overdose patient who gags when an oral airway is inserted
Adult who drank drain cleaner and is now drooling and anxious
Alert asthmatic who is tiring but still speaking in short phrases
Supraglottic airways are for unresponsive patients without a gag reflex who need ventilation. An intact gag reflex, caustic ingestion and known esophageal disease are contraindications.
qpga27b: A 30-year-old motorcyclist is unresponsive with snoring respirations after striking a guardrail. What is the best way to open the airway?
Jaw-thrust maneuver with manual spinal stabilization
Head-tilt chin-lift maneuver with the head turned to the side
Insert a nasopharyngeal airway before any manual maneuver
Place the patient in the recovery position and observe

Snoring signals partial obstruction by the tongue, and the jaw-thrust opens the airway without moving the cervical spine. If the jaw-thrust fails to open the airway, a head-tilt chin-lift is still used because the airway takes priority.
q7oropy: You hear gurgling while ventilating an unresponsive adult. What is the longest you should apply suction in a single attempt?
5 seconds in adults and 15 seconds in infants
30 seconds or until the airway is clear
Until the oxygen saturation drops below 90 percent

Adult suctioning is limited to 15 seconds per attempt because suction removes oxygen along with secretions. Shorter limits apply to children and infants, and the patient is reoxygenated between attempts.
qkfynmh: A 4-year-old is sitting upright and leaning forward, drooling, with a muffled voice, high fever and soft stridor. What is the most appropriate management?
Keep her calm in a position of comfort and transport
Lay her supine and inspect the throat with a tongue depressor
Insert an oral airway to prevent the tongue from obstructing
Have her lie flat so you can start an IV before moving her

This picture suggests epiglottitis, where agitation or throat manipulation can trigger complete obstruction. Give oxygen as tolerated, avoid examining the pharynx, keep the child with a caregiver and transport.
q4m5gsi: A firefighter removed a 40-year-old woman from a house fire. She has a headache and nausea, and her pulse oximeter reads 99 percent. Which action is most appropriate?
Nasal cannula at 2 L/min because the saturation is normal
No oxygen, since a normal reading rules out poisoning
Room air with a repeat pulse oximetry reading in 15 minutes

Standard pulse oximeters cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so readings stay falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning. High-concentration oxygen shortens the half-life of carbon monoxide.
q1bgvpwp: A 70-year-old woman is breathing 6 times per minute with shallow breaths, and her waveform capnography reads 62 mmHg. What does this reading most likely indicate?
Hyperventilation with excessive carbon dioxide loss
Normal ventilation for a patient of her age
Poor pulmonary blood flow from a large pulmonary embolism
A normal ETCO2 is roughly 35 to 45 mmHg, and a high value with slow shallow breathing shows the patient is retaining carbon dioxide. She needs assisted ventilation.
q7azphz: A 19-year-old with a history of asthma has a capnography waveform with a slanted, shark-fin upstroke. What does this pattern suggest?
An esophageal placement of the sensor tubing
Cardiac arrest with absent pulmonary perfusion
Normal respiratory pattern in a young adult
A sloped upstroke shows slow, obstructed exhalation from narrowed lower airways, as in asthma or COPD. The shape often improves as the bronchospasm is treated.
qo023xu: A 68-year-old woman found on the floor next to opioid pills is breathing 6 times per minute with pinpoint pupils and an SpO2 of 82 percent. What should you do first?
Ventilate with a BVM and oxygen
Give naloxone and wait to see whether her breathing improves
Apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min and reassess
Insert a supraglottic airway while she still has a gag reflex
Inadequate breathing is corrected right away with assisted ventilation, which treats the hypoxia while naloxone is being prepared. Naloxone is then titrated to restore adequate breathing.
q1sk8bic: You are considering CPAP for a patient in respiratory distress. Which finding is a contraindication?
Crackles in both lung bases with an SpO2 of 88 percent
Respiratory rate of 28 with accessory muscle use
An alert patient who can follow commands and hold the mask

CPAP raises intrathoracic pressure and lowers venous return, so it can worsen hypotension. Other contraindications include an inability to protect the airway, unresponsiveness, suspected pneumothorax and vomiting.
qo3ym1w: While you ventilate a patient with a BVM, the abdomen becomes increasingly distended. Which change in technique best reduces this problem?
Give each breath over 1 second with just enough volume to make the chest rise
Squeeze the bag faster and harder so the air reaches the lungs first
Stop ventilating and switch to a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
Push firmly on the upper abdomen during each ventilation

Gastric inflation happens when ventilation pressure exceeds esophageal opening pressure, usually from breaths that are too large or too fast. Slow, modest breaths lower the risk of regurgitation and aspiration.
q1rgufgo: You are opening the airway of an unresponsive 3-month-old infant on a flat surface. What helps keep the airway in a neutral position?
A folded towel under the shoulders
A pillow under the back of the head
Hyperextending the neck as far as possible
Placing the infant face down with the head turned
An infant's large occiput bends the neck forward when the infant lies flat, which can close off the airway. Padding under the shoulders aligns the airway in a neutral or sniffing position.
q133wh5g: A 12-year-old with a tracheostomy has noisy breathing, retractions and a falling SpO2. His mother says the tube has not been cleaned today. What should you do first?
Apply a nonrebreather mask over the mouth and nose
Insert a supraglottic airway through the mouth
Start an IV and give a fluid bolus

Mucus plugging is the most common cause of distress in a tracheostomy patient, and suctioning the tube often fixes it right away. If suctioning fails, the tube may need to be replaced or the patient ventilated through the stoma.
q1fi4sn3: A 9-year-old having an asthma attack has become drowsy, and her wheezing is getting quieter while her breath sounds fade. How should you interpret this?
Improving bronchospasm because the wheezing is resolving
An anxiety reaction that is ending
A normal response to the albuterol she took at home
Quieter wheezing with fading breath sounds and drowsiness means little air is moving and the child is tiring. Prepare to assist ventilation and transport urgently.
qic4g6f: At what rate should chest compressions be performed on an adult in cardiac arrest?
60 per minute with long pauses for recoil
Current AHA guidelines call for 100 to 120 compressions per minute. Slower rates decrease blood flow, and faster rates reduce depth and filling time.
qwq9r98: How deep should chest compressions be for an average-sized adult?
At least 2 inches but no more than 2.4 inches
About 1 inch, or one-quarter of the chest depth
At least 3 inches, regardless of patient size
Adult compressions should be at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep and not more than 2.4 inches (6 cm). Compressions that are too shallow fail to circulate blood, and excessive depth increases injury.
q1n9g88f: Two rescuers are performing CPR on a pulseless 6-month-old infant without an advanced airway. What compression-to-ventilation ratio should they use?
Two-rescuer CPR for infants and children uses 15 compressions to 2 breaths, with the two-thumb encircling-hands technique for infants. A single rescuer uses 30:2.
qylcw: The AED has just delivered a shock to a 60-year-old man in cardiac arrest. What should you do next?
Check for a carotid pulse for up to 30 seconds
Press analyze again to confirm the rhythm
Give two rescue breaths and then check for breathing

Compressions resume immediately after a shock and continue for 2 minutes before the next rhythm check. Even when defibrillation works, the heart usually needs perfusion support before a pulse can be felt.
qv9lzzi: A supraglottic airway has been placed in an adult in cardiac arrest. How should compressions and ventilations now be coordinated?
Continuous compressions and 1 breath every 6 seconds
Pauses after every 30 compressions to give 2 breaths
Continuous compressions with a breath every 2 seconds
Compressions paused for 1 breath every 15 compressions
With an advanced airway in place, compressions are continuous and ventilations are given asynchronously at 10 per minute. This keeps compressions going while avoiding hyperventilation.
qkakqs2: You are about to use an AED on a pulseless 5-year-old, but only adult pads are available. What should you do?
Use the adult pads, placing them front and back if they would touch
Withhold defibrillation until pediatric pads arrive
Cut the adult pads in half to fit the small chest
Use one adult pad on the chest and skip the second pad
If pediatric pads or an attenuator are unavailable, a standard AED with adult pads should be used. Pads must not touch or overlap, so anterior-posterior placement is used on a small chest.
q1n766kp: A 66-year-old diabetic woman complains of sudden fatigue, nausea and shortness of breath but denies chest pain. Her skin is cool and diaphoretic. What should you suspect?
Gastroenteritis, because she has no chest pain
A panic attack brought on by the stress of the call
Hyperglycemia from missing her morning insulin

Women, older adults and diabetics often have ACS without classic chest pain, presenting instead with dyspnea, weakness or nausea. Treat as a possible cardiac event and transport to an appropriate facility.
q1artgsz: A 58-year-old man has substernal chest pressure and a BP of 146/90. He says he took sildenafil for erectile dysfunction about 12 hours ago. What is the correct approach to nitroglycerin?
Give half the usual dose and recheck the BP
Give it as normal since the BP is above 100
Give it only after a fluid bolus
Nitroglycerin given within 24 hours of sildenafil (48 hours for tadalafil) can cause profound hypotension. Continue other ACS care and tell the receiving facility.
q1eouz1z: A 71-year-old man with crushing chest pain is pale and cool with a BP of 78/50, HR of 112 and crackles throughout both lungs. Which action is most appropriate?
Expedite transport to a PCI center without nitroglycerin
Infuse 2 liters of normal saline wide open to raise the BP
Give nitroglycerin to relieve the chest pain and pulmonary edema
Apply CPAP at high pressure to clear the crackles quickly

Hypotension with pulmonary edema after an MI suggests cardiogenic shock, where nitroglycerin and CPAP can worsen hypotension and large fluid boluses worsen pulmonary edema. Rapid transport for reperfusion is the priority.
qz7nlv6: A 74-year-old woman has a new facial droop and slurred speech. Which piece of information is most important for the receiving stroke center?
Time she was last known to be well
Her blood pressure readings from last month
The name of her primary care physician
Whether she has had a flu vaccine this year
Eligibility for clot-dissolving drugs and clot removal depends on the time since the patient was last known well. Get this time from witnesses and report it early.
qfaibce: A 62-year-old man has sudden confusion and weakness on one side. Before you call a stroke alert, which assessment helps rule out a common stroke mimic?
Hypoglycemia can cause focal weakness and confusion that look exactly like a stroke. A glucose check takes moments and changes management.
qdv9bct: An 80-year-old woman is sitting bolt upright with severe dyspnea, crackles to the mid-lung fields, BP of 184/102 and an SpO2 of 86 percent. She is alert and following commands. Which intervention will most improve her oxygenation?
Laying her flat to rest the heart
CPAP pushes fluid out of the alveoli, improves gas exchange and reduces the work of breathing in acute pulmonary edema. She is hypertensive and alert, so she is a good candidate.
q8tmkmc: A 67-year-old man with a history of hypertension has sudden, tearing chest pain that radiates to his back. His BP is 190/100 in the right arm and 140/84 in the left. What is the most likely cause?
Abrupt tearing pain radiating to the back with a significant BP difference between the arms suggests aortic dissection. Transport rapidly and notify the receiving facility.
qpioqhu: A 1-year-old has a heart rate of 50, mottled skin and poor responsiveness despite effective oxygenation and ventilation. What should you do next?
Continue ventilating and recheck in 10 minutes
Apply the AED and deliver a shock

In children, a heart rate below 60 with signs of poor perfusion despite adequate ventilation calls for CPR. Bradycardia in children is usually caused by hypoxia and is a sign of arrest about to happen.
qpd91ts: After defibrillation and 4 minutes of CPR, a 59-year-old man has a pulse. He remains unresponsive with a BP of 74/40 and clear lung sounds. Which intervention is appropriate?
Removing the AED pads to prevent burns

After return of spontaneous circulation, hypotension is treated to keep systolic pressure at least 90 mmHg, and a crystalloid bolus is a first step when the lungs are clear. Keep the pads on in case of re-arrest.
qqjno0x: An AED analyzes the rhythm of a pulseless, apneic 70-year-old woman and advises no shock. What should you do?
Turn off the AED and start transport without CPR
Check for a pulse for 1 full minute
Reposition the pads and analyze again right away
A no-shock message means the rhythm is not shockable, such as asystole or PEA, but the patient is still in arrest. Resume high-quality CPR and reanalyze every 2 minutes.
q3oc65h: A bystander is doing CPR on a pulseless 25-year-old found with a syringe in his arm. What is your highest priority?
High-quality CPR and early AED use
Placing an IV for drug administration
Searching the scene for the substance used
Once an opioid overdose patient is pulseless, CPR and defibrillation take priority. Naloxone may be given but must not delay or interrupt compressions.
qotae6g: A 22-year-old has bright red blood spurting from a deep laceration on his upper thigh that continues despite firm direct pressure. What should you do next?
Apply a tourniquet proximal to the wound
Elevate the leg and add more gauze on top
Apply pressure to the femoral artery at the groin
Apply a cold pack and loosen the dressing

Life-threatening extremity bleeding that is not controlled by direct pressure requires a tourniquet placed 2 to 3 inches above the wound. Elevation and pressure points are not reliable for hemorrhage control.
q15dord8: A 28-year-old man was stabbed in the abdomen. He is anxious with a weak radial pulse and a BP of 80/50, and there is no head injury. Transport will take 20 minutes. What is the best fluid strategy?
Small boluses to keep a radial pulse
Two liters wide open through two large-bore lines
No IV access until arrival at the trauma center
Dextrose infusion to provide energy to tissues

In penetrating torso trauma without head injury, permissive hypotension aims for a palpable radial pulse or a systolic pressure around 80 to 90 mmHg. Large volumes can raise pressure enough to disrupt clots and dilute clotting factors.
q1ml9eus: A 35-year-old has a severe head injury with a GCS of 7 and a BP of 84/50. What is the blood pressure goal for this patient?
Systolic pressure of at least 90 mmHg
Systolic pressure of 70 mmHg to limit brain swelling
The lowest pressure that keeps a radial pulse present
Systolic pressure above 200 mmHg to force perfusion
Even one episode of hypotension worsens outcomes after a traumatic brain injury, so permissive hypotension is not used. Give fluids to keep the systolic pressure at or above 90 mmHg in adults.
qc97r50: A patient with a head injury develops a BP of 196/110, a pulse of 48 and irregular breathing. What do these findings indicate?
Hypovolemic shock that is still compensated
Neurogenic shock from a spinal injury

Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respirations make up Cushing's triad, a late sign of rising intracranial pressure and possible herniation. Manage the airway, avoid hypoxia and transport rapidly.
qehtekw: You sealed a gunshot wound to the chest with an occlusive dressing. The patient now has worsening dyspnea, absent breath sounds on that side and a falling BP. What should you do?
Briefly lift the dressing to release trapped air
Add a second occlusive dressing over the first
Place the patient supine with legs elevated
These signs suggest a developing tension pneumothorax, and briefly unsealing the dressing lets trapped air escape. Reseal it afterward and transport rapidly to ALS or a trauma center.
q9jv2gc: A 45-year-old was ejected from a vehicle. She has pelvic pain, instability and signs of shock. Which intervention is most appropriate?
Apply a pelvic binder over the greater trochanters
Rock the pelvis repeatedly to check for instability
Apply the binder around the waist at the iliac crests
Flex both hips and knees and tie the legs together
A binder centered over the greater trochanters closes an open pelvic ring and reduces bleeding. Repeated manipulation can disrupt clots, and a binder placed too high is ineffective.
qyeqigo: An 82-year-old who takes a blood thinner fell from standing and hit her head. She is alert with a small forehead bruise and wants to stay home. What is your main concern?
Hip fracture from a minor fall
Anticoagulants and age-related brain atrophy raise the risk of a slowly expanding brain bleed after minor head trauma. These patients need hospital evaluation even when they appear well.
q1ta8xet: An adult has partial-thickness burns covering the entire anterior chest and abdomen and the entire right arm. Using the rule of nines, estimate the burned body surface area.
In adults, the anterior trunk is 18 percent and each arm is 9 percent, giving 27 percent. Superficial burns are not counted in this total.
qehme5x: A 1-year-old has partial-thickness burns covering the entire head and the entire anterior trunk. Using the pediatric rule of nines, estimate the burned body surface area.
In infants, the head is about 18 percent because it is larger in proportion, and the anterior trunk is 18 percent. Children lose heat and fluid quickly from burns, so prevent hypothermia.
qwyapk6: A 24-year-old diver hit his head in shallow water. He cannot move his legs and has a BP of 78/48, pulse of 54, and warm, dry skin below the nipple line. What is the most likely cause?
Spinal cord injury cuts off sympathetic tone, causing vasodilation, hypotension and a slow heart rate with warm, dry skin. Hemorrhagic shock usually produces tachycardia with cool, clammy skin.
q157vbkc: You have made two unsuccessful IV attempts in a 30-year-old with hemorrhagic shock who has an altered mental status. What is the most appropriate next step for vascular access?
Keep attempting IVs in the hands until one succeeds
Abandon vascular access and give fluids orally
Place an IV in the foot of the injured leg
IO access is fast and reliable when peripheral IVs fail in a critically ill patient, and AEMTs can place it. An injured extremity should not be used for vascular access.
qcr0yls: A 54-year-old diabetic man is unresponsive with a blood glucose of 36 mg/dL, and you have a patent IV. Which treatment is most appropriate?
Oral glucose gel between the cheek and gum
A rapid bolus of normal saline only
Waiting for him to wake up enough to drink juice
An unresponsive hypoglycemic patient cannot protect the airway, so oral glucose is unsafe. IV dextrose, such as D10 titrated to response, raises the glucose quickly.
qpr742s: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes has deep, rapid respirations, a fruity breath odor, a glucose reading of HI, a pulse of 124 and dry mucous membranes. Which intervention is most appropriate?
Oral glucose to correct the imbalance
Encouraging him to slow his breathing

Diabetic ketoacidosis causes severe dehydration from osmotic diuresis, so isotonic fluid replacement is the key prehospital treatment. The deep, rapid breathing compensates for acidosis and should not be suppressed.
qsf7bz6: A 70-year-old woman is unresponsive with a blood glucose of 30 mg/dL. Two IV attempts have failed. What is a reasonable alternative within AEMT scope?
Oral glucose solution poured into the mouth
Repeated IV attempts for 20 more minutes
Glucagon given IM mobilizes stored glycogen when IV access cannot be obtained. It works more slowly than IV dextrose and depends on liver glycogen stores.
q1d8ilki: An 18-month-old had a 2-minute generalized seizure that has stopped. He has a temperature of 39.6 C (103.3 F) and is becoming more alert. What is appropriate care?
Remove excess clothing and monitor during transport
Put the child in an ice water bath
Sponge the child with rubbing alcohol to cool the skin
Restrain the child to prevent another seizure
Simple febrile seizures are common in this age group and are managed with airway support, passive cooling and transport. Ice baths and alcohol can cause shivering, hypothermia or toxicity.
q1auqumc: A 12-kg 2-year-old with vomiting and diarrhea is lethargic, with a capillary refill of 4 seconds and a heart rate of 180. Protocol calls for a 20 mL/kg isotonic bolus. What volume should you give?
20 mL/kg multiplied by 12 kg equals 240 mL. Reassess perfusion, mental status and lung sounds after each bolus.
qdzigfd: A woman who is 34 weeks pregnant becomes dizzy and pale while lying supine on a stretcher. What should you do?
Position her on her left side
Elevate her legs and keep her supine
Place her in a seated position with her legs dangling

In late pregnancy, the uterus can compress the inferior vena cava when the patient lies supine, decreasing venous return. Left lateral positioning or manually moving the uterus to the left restores blood flow.
q3jonp5: A woman who is 35 weeks pregnant has a severe headache, visual disturbances, swelling of the hands and face, and a BP of 172/112. What is the most likely condition?
Hypertension with headache and visual changes after 20 weeks of gestation suggests severe preeclampsia, which can progress to seizures (eclampsia). Keep the environment calm and transport.
q1u2bgxm: A newborn was dried and stimulated and has received 30 seconds of effective ventilation, but the heart rate is 50. What should you do?
Continue ventilations and recheck in 5 minutes
Stop ventilating and give blow-by oxygen
Increase stimulation by flicking the feet
Newborn resuscitation calls for chest compressions when the heart rate remains below 60 despite 30 seconds of effective ventilation. The ratio is 3 compressions to 1 breath.
q18k9nd4: Ten minutes after delivering the placenta, a woman continues to bleed heavily and her uterus feels soft and boggy. What should you do first?
Pull gently on the umbilical cord
Fundal massage stimulates uterine contraction, the main way bleeding is controlled after delivery. Breastfeeding also helps, and signs of shock call for IV fluids and rapid transport.
qcbv3bx: A 24-year-old woman has sudden, severe lower abdominal pain, a missed period and dizziness. Her pulse is 128 and BP is 86/56. What should you suspect?
A woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain, a missed period and shock should be assumed to have a ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Treat for hemorrhagic shock and transport rapidly.
q1py0rac: After a small dose of naloxone, a patient who overdosed on opioids is breathing 14 times per minute with good tidal volume but remains drowsy. What should you do?
Continue to monitor without additional naloxone
Give more naloxone until he is fully awake
Restrain him before giving another dose
Naloxone is titrated to adequate breathing, not to a full return of consciousness. Large doses can cause abrupt withdrawal, vomiting and agitation.
q1hhhexy: A 21-year-old runner collapsed in a race on a hot day. She is confused with hot skin and a rectal temperature of 41.2 C (106.2 F). What is the priority?
Transport without cooling to avoid delay
Exertional heat stroke is a true emergency, and outcomes depend on how fast the core temperature drops. Cold water immersion or aggressive ice and water cooling should begin as soon as possible.
q1uokzs9: A 7-year-old was pulled from a pool. She is unresponsive and apneic with a slow pulse. What is your first priority?
Drowning causes death by hypoxia, so ventilation is the priority. Abdominal thrusts delay ventilation and increase the risk of vomiting.
qhr5ihw: After a bee sting, a 40-year-old has widespread hives, wheezing, a swollen tongue and a BP of 76/44. Which medication is the first-line treatment?
Anaphylaxis with airway involvement and hypotension requires epinephrine IM in the lateral thigh. Albuterol can help with wheezing but does not reverse the systemic reaction.
q6bvpiu: A 35-year-old man says he wants to kill himself and has a plan, but he refuses transport. He is calm and alert. What is the most appropriate action?
Stay with him and involve law enforcement as needed
Leave after he signs a refusal form
Agree to leave if he promises not to hurt himself
Leave him with a family member and depart

A patient with active suicidal intent and a plan lacks the capacity to refuse care for this condition and must not be left alone. Follow local protocols, which often require law enforcement assistance.
q1yamwuc: A 64-year-old dialysis patient with an AV fistula in his left arm needs IV access and a blood pressure reading. Which arm should you use?
The left arm, above the fistula
The left arm, below the fistula
Cuffs and IVs on the fistula arm can damage or clot the dialysis access. Use the opposite extremity.
qdaw64a: An 84-year-old nursing home resident with a urinary catheter is newly confused, with a temperature of 38.9 C (102 F), a pulse of 118, a respiratory rate of 26 and a BP of 84/50. Lung sounds are clear. What is the most appropriate care?
This presentation suggests septic shock from a urinary source. Isotonic fluids are given while lung sounds are reassessed frequently, especially in older patients.
quld07h: During a fluid bolus, a 79-year-old with a history of heart failure develops crackles, worsening dyspnea and a falling SpO2. What should you do?
Slow the infusion and raise the head
Increase the flow rate to finish the bolus
Switch to a second large-bore IV
New crackles and worsening oxygenation during fluid administration suggest fluid overload. Reduce the rate to keep the vein open, sit the patient up, give oxygen and notify medical direction.
q1dl4q10: You notice cool, pale, swollen skin around an IV site, and the infusion has slowed. What is the most likely problem?
Infiltration occurs when fluid leaks into the surrounding tissue, causing swelling and coolness. Stop the infusion, remove the catheter and restart in another site.
q1ez8ci0: You need to infuse 600 mL over 1 hour using a 10 gtt/mL set. What drip rate should you use?
600 mL over 60 minutes is 10 mL/min, and 10 mL/min times 10 gtt/mL equals 100 gtt/min. Check the drip chamber against a watch and reassess.
qw4jnr5: You arrive at a tanker rollover with a placard on the truck. Where should you stage?
Close to the vehicle to start care quickly
Downhill so runoff is easy to see
Staging upwind and uphill at a safe distance keeps responders away from vapors and runoff. Use the Emergency Response Guidebook to identify the hazard and set isolation distances.
q1u432zx: Using START triage, how would you categorize an adult who cannot walk and has a respiratory rate of 36?
In START triage, a respiratory rate above 30 places the patient in the immediate category. No further assessment is needed for categorization.
q8r9tv8: Which intervention is one of the lifesaving interventions allowed during SALT triage?

SALT allows only quick lifesaving interventions such as controlling major hemorrhage, opening the airway, chest decompression, antidote autoinjectors, and 2 rescue breaths for children. Longer treatments wait until triage is complete.
qzyks27: A diabetic man is alert and oriented after receiving IV dextrose, and he refuses transport. What must happen before you leave?
He makes an informed refusal and you document it
He must accept transport because he received medication
You must leave immediately when he refuses
You must call the police to force transport
A competent adult may refuse care after being told the risks, benefits and alternatives. Recommend that he eat and have someone with him, and document thoroughly.
q12gmcxg: You arrive to find a pulseless, apneic patient whose family shows you a valid, signed DNR order. What should you do?
Start CPR until a physician arrives
Ask the family to vote on care
A valid DNR order directs EMS not to start resuscitation. Follow local protocol for verifying the order and confirming death.
qphxc2r: While you treat a 3-year-old, you notice bruises in different stages of healing and an explanation that does not match the injuries. What is your obligation?
Report your concerns per mandatory reporting laws
Ignore the bruises because they are old
Wait for the child to tell you what happened
EMS providers are mandatory reporters of suspected child abuse in most states. Document objective findings and report to the appropriate authority.
q19v6ldq: Your service's written protocols allow you to give certain treatments without calling a physician. What type of medical direction is this?
Offline (indirect) medical direction includes protocols and standing orders written ahead of time. Online medical direction is real-time contact with a physician.
qim4vct: You discover an error on a patient care report you have already completed. How should you correct it?
Draw a single line through it and initial it
Use correction fluid to cover it
Create a new report and destroy the old one
A single line keeps the original entry readable and initialing it shows who made the correction. Follow agency policy for electronic reports.
qenxznr: A patient has a chronic cough, night sweats, weight loss and blood-tinged sputum. What personal protection should you use?
These symptoms suggest tuberculosis, which spreads by airborne droplets. Wear an N95 respirator and put a surgical mask on the patient if possible.
qmwd6hi: You are ventilating an intubated adult whose continuous capnography waveform has been normal at 38 mmHg. While moving him to the stretcher the waveform suddenly becomes a flat line at zero, although his SpO2 still reads 97 percent. What is the most likely cause?
Hypoventilation from a slow bagging rate

A sudden loss of the waveform after patient movement means the tube is out of the trachea (or the circuit is disconnected) until proven otherwise. SpO2 lags behind, so it cannot be used to rule out displacement.
q1hl1858: A 24-year-old with a severe asthma attack is being assisted with a bag-valve mask. The capnography waveform has a slanted, rounded upstroke with no flat plateau, giving a shark-fin shape. What does this pattern indicate?
A shark-fin waveform reflects slow, uneven emptying of narrowed lower airways, as in bronchospasm. Esophageal placement gives no sustained waveform at all.
q19xk3oq: A 30-year-old with an isolated severe head injury is intubated. BP 138/82, HR 88, SpO2 99 percent, ETCO2 27 mmHg with no signs of herniation. What should you do?
Increase the rate to 20 breaths per minute
Routine hyperventilation lowers cerebral blood flow and worsens outcomes in TBI. Ventilation should be slowed to bring ETCO2 back to 35 to 45 mmHg.
