Impaled objects in the eye are stabilized, not removed; covering both eyes reduces sympathetic eye movement that could worsen the injury.
q1ttxb3c: A 36-year-old worker splashed a cleaning chemical into his left eye. How should you irrigate it?
With water flowing from the inner corner outward
With water flowing from the outer corner toward the nose
With a few drops of saline every few minutes
Only after you identify the exact chemical
Irrigate immediately and continuously, directing the flow from the inner corner outward so contaminated fluid does not wash into the other eye; do not delay to identify the chemical.
qkdso1p: A 23-year-old was struck across the front of the neck by a wire while riding a motorcycle. He is hoarse, and you feel a crackling sensation under the skin of his neck. What does this suggest?
Possible laryngeal or tracheal injury that may compromise the airway
A minor abrasion that needs only a dressing
A cervical spine injury with spinal cord damage
Normal swelling expected after any neck trauma
Hoarseness and subcutaneous air after a blow to the neck suggest injury to the larynx or trachea, which can rapidly obstruct the airway.
q1k9xtbl: A 31-year-old man was in a low-speed crash. He is alert, sober, has no neck pain or midline tenderness, no numbness or weakness, and no other painful injuries. Based on current national guidance, what is the most appropriate approach to spinal motion restriction?
It is not needed for this patient
Apply a cervical collar and long backboard because he was in a crash
Apply a cervical collar only, since the mechanism alone requires it
Have him lie on the floor while you call for a backboard
Current joint guidance supports selective spinal motion restriction; an alert, sober patient with no spinal pain, tenderness, neurologic deficit, or distracting injury does not need it.
q138qrow: You are placing a 2-year-old on a firm, flat device for spinal motion restriction. What should you do to keep the spine in a neutral position?
Pad beneath the shoulders and torso
Place a folded towel under the back of the head
Tilt the head forward with the chin on the chest
Leave the child flat on the device with no padding
A young child's large head flexes the neck forward when lying flat, so padding under the shoulders and torso keeps the airway open and the spine neutral.
q8ou9pu: A 29-year-old motorcyclist wearing a full-face helmet is vomiting and you cannot clear his airway with the helmet on. What should you do?
Remove the helmet with two rescuers while keeping the head stable
Leave the helmet on and suction through the face opening only
Cut the chin strap and tilt the head back to drain the vomit
Have him remove the helmet himself while you hold suction ready
A helmet must be removed if it prevents airway management; two rescuers work together, one stabilizing the head and neck while the other removes the helmet.
q1u21g3u: An 86-year-old woman with a severely curved upper spine (kyphosis) needs spinal motion restriction after a fall. How should you position her?
Pad behind her head and shoulders to support her natural curve
Force her head back against the board so it lies flat
Place her prone on the stretcher to protect her airway
Secure her flat without padding to keep the spine straight
Older adults with kyphosis cannot lie flat without forcing the spine out of its normal position, so padding fills the gaps and keeps them in a neutral, comfortable position.
qbchsjp: A 21-year-old man dove into a shallow pool. His chest wall does not move as he breathes, but his abdomen rises and falls with each breath. What should you be prepared to do?
Place him in the recovery position
Abdominal breathing without chest movement suggests a cervical spinal cord injury that paralyzes the intercostal muscles; breathing may quickly become inadequate.
q1wf6bdf: A 64-year-old driver struck the steering wheel. A section of his right chest moves inward when he inhales and outward when he exhales. His breathing is shallow at 32 per minute with an SpO2 of 86 percent. What is the best treatment?
Assist ventilations with a BVM and oxygen
Tape a heavy sandbag over the moving segment
Wrap a bandage tightly around the entire chest
Place him on his left side and give oxygen by nasal cannula
Paradoxical movement means a flail segment, and the underlying lung injury causes poor oxygenation; positive-pressure ventilation with a BVM supports breathing and stabilizes the segment from inside.
q1fh4v0s: A 30-year-old man has a stab wound to the right chest. Air bubbles from the wound each time he breathes. What should you do first?
Cover the wound with a gloved hand
Look for an exit wound on his back
Place him supine and elevate his legs
Apply a bulky gauze dressing with tape
An open chest wound should be sealed immediately, first with a gloved hand and then with an occlusive dressing, to stop air from entering the chest.
q10qumua: A 55-year-old man fell onto a railing and has no open wounds. He is increasingly short of breath with absent breath sounds on the left, distended neck veins, and falling blood pressure. What is the most appropriate EMT care?
High-flow oxygen, assisted ventilations as needed, and rapid transport with ALS intercept
Insert a needle into the second intercostal space on the left side
Seal the left chest with an occlusive dressing
Keep him on scene until his breath sounds return
These findings suggest a tension pneumothorax; needle decompression is outside EMT scope, so EMTs support oxygenation and ventilation and get the patient to definitive care quickly.
q11zk144: After a fall, a 42-year-old man has diminished breath sounds on the right and signs of shock. Which finding suggests massive hemothorax rather than tension pneumothorax?
Absent breath sounds on the injured side
Both can cause decreased breath sounds and shock, but blood loss into the chest usually leaves the neck veins flat, while tension pneumothorax often distends them.
q969t7r: A 14-year-old baseball catcher is struck in the chest by a pitch and immediately collapses. He is unresponsive, not breathing, and pulseless. What should you do?
Start CPR and apply an AED as soon as possible
Apply high-flow oxygen and check for rib fractures
Assess for a tension pneumothorax and transport
Place him in the recovery position and monitor
A blow directly over the heart at a vulnerable moment can trigger ventricular fibrillation (commotio cordis); immediate CPR and early defibrillation are lifesaving.
q1c9u80x: A 38-year-old man was pinned under a car for several minutes with heavy pressure on his chest. His face and neck are purple and swollen, with small red spots on the skin and bloodshot eyes. What injury does this suggest?
Sudden severe chest compression forces blood back into the head and neck, producing the purple face, petechiae, and bloodshot eyes of traumatic asphyxia; associated chest injuries are common.
q9khzow: A 33-year-old restrained driver has a red, bruised band across her lower abdomen from the lap belt. Her vital signs are normal and she says she feels fine. How should you interpret this?
Suspect an internal abdominal injury despite normal vital signs
A seat belt mark is expected and not concerning in a stable patient
Normal vital signs rule out internal bleeding
The injury is limited to the skin and needs only a cold pack
A seat belt sign is associated with injuries to the bowel, other abdominal organs, and the lumbar spine; patients can look stable early before shock develops.
q1ftavet: Where should a pelvic binder be positioned to stabilize a suspected unstable pelvic fracture?
Around the waist at the level of the navel
Around the upper thighs above the knees
A pelvic binder centered over the greater trochanters (the bony points of the hips) best closes the pelvic ring; placing it too high is a common error.
q1v6kb2s: A 13-year-old fell off a skateboard and has a painful, deformed midshaft forearm. When splinting, which joints must be immobilized?
For a long bone fracture, splint the joint above and the joint below; for a midforearm fracture, that is the wrist and elbow.
q1o5qtfq: A 25-year-old basketball player has a deformed, painful elbow after a fall. He has a strong radial pulse and normal sensation in his fingers. How should you splint it?
Straighten the arm fully before splinting
Pull firmly on the forearm to reduce the joint
Apply a traction splint to the arm
Joint injuries with intact distal circulation are splinted in the position found because manipulation could injure nearby nerves and vessels.
q1v6pxk7: A 47-year-old man has a severely angulated midshaft fracture of the lower leg. His foot is cool and pale with no pulse. What should you do?
Apply gentle manual traction to align the limb, then splint
Splint in the angulated position and transport immediately
Wrap the foot in a heat pack and recheck in 15 minutes
Elevate the leg and apply a tourniquet above the fracture
A long bone with absent distal circulation should be gently realigned to restore blood flow; stop if resistance or a large increase in pain occurs, then splint and reassess pulses.
q56sqeu: A 22-year-old fell on his outstretched arm. He holds his arm away from his body and will not let it move; the shoulder looks squared off. How should you splint it?
Place a pillow between the arm and chest and secure with a sling and swathe
Pull the arm down and in until it pops back into place
Straighten the arm against his side and tape it there
Apply a rigid splint from wrist to shoulder with the arm extended overhead
An anterior shoulder dislocation is splinted in the position of comfort, often with a pillow filling the gap between arm and chest, then a sling and swathe.
q6amhjw: A 10-month-old infant was scalded over the entire head and the entire front of the torso. Using the pediatric rule of nines, what percentage of body surface area is burned?
In infants the head is about 18 percent and the front of the torso is 18 percent, totaling 36 percent; the infant head is proportionally larger than an adult head.
qzwgurv: A 45-year-old man has partial- and full-thickness burns over 40 percent of his body. The burning process has been stopped. Which dressing is most appropriate?
Dry, sterile dressings and blankets to keep him warm
Wet, cold towels over all burned areas for the entire transport
Burn ointment applied under occlusive plastic wrap
Ice packs placed directly on the burned skin
Large burns destroy the skin's ability to hold heat, so after cooling briefly, cover with dry sterile dressings and prevent hypothermia; ice and prolonged wet dressings over large areas cause harm.
qm09gz1: A 52-year-old woman was rescued from a house fire. Which finding is most concerning for an airway burn that could rapidly obstruct her airway?
Burns to the backs of both hands
Hoarseness, along with soot in the mouth, singed nasal hair, and stridor, signals swelling of the upper airway that can progress quickly; early ALS and rapid transport are needed.
qkm2beo: A utility worker is still in contact with a downed power line and appears unresponsive. What should you do?
Stay clear until the power company confirms the line is de-energized
Use a dry wooden broom handle to push the wire away
Grab him by his clothing and pull him away quickly
Approach with rubber gloves and boots to assess his pulse
Never approach a patient in contact with an electrical source until trained personnel have confirmed it is safe; improvised tools and standard gloves do not protect from high voltage.
qnh4ski: A 30-year-old electrician received a high-voltage shock. He has small burns on his hand and foot and says he feels fine. What is your main concern?
Hidden internal injury and abnormal heart rhythms
Infection of the small skin burns
A sprained wrist from the fall
Electrical current can damage deep tissues and the heart even when surface burns are small, so these patients need transport and monitoring for dysrhythmias.
q7nmyy2: Lightning strikes a group of hikers. Several are injured; one is pulseless and apneic while others are awake and moving. How should triage differ from a typical MCI?
Treat the patient in cardiac arrest first
Tag the pulseless patient as deceased and move on
Treat the awake and moving patients first
Wait for police before treating anyone
Lightning victims in arrest often have a good chance of recovery with prompt CPR and ventilation, and those still conscious are likely to survive, so lightning triage reverses the usual priority.
qibfby8: A 2-year-old has sharply outlined burns covering both feet and ankles like socks, with no splash marks. The caregiver says the child stepped into a hot bath. What should you suspect?
An accidental scald from a spilled cup
A chemical burn from bath products
A contact burn from a heater
Burns with sharp, uniform borders in a stocking or glove pattern without splash marks suggest forced immersion; document carefully and report suspected abuse as required.
qff6afj: A 44-year-old man has been stabbed in the back and is now in cardiac arrest. The knife is still in place and prevents you from placing him supine for compressions. What should you do?
Remove the knife and begin CPR
Perform CPR with him lying on his side
Stabilize the knife and delay CPR until arrival
Pad around the knife and compress with him prone
Impaled objects are normally stabilized, but one that prevents CPR may be removed, followed by bleeding control and high-quality compressions.
q1cfu56h: A 37-year-old man caught his hand in a machine. The hand is nearly severed and remains attached only by a strip of skin. What should you do?
Keep it attached, align it, and splint it
Complete the amputation and place the part on ice
Leave it hanging and apply a tourniquet to the forearm
Pull the hand into its normal position firmly
A partial amputation should never be completed in the field; keep the part attached, align it in normal position, dress it, and splint it.
qlsuc4j: A 50-year-old construction worker's leg has been pinned under a concrete slab for 5 hours. He is alert with stable vital signs. Before the slab is lifted, what should you do?
Request ALS so treatment can begin before release
Lift the slab as quickly as possible and transport
Apply ice to the leg and wait another hour
Massage the leg to restore circulation
Prolonged crush injury can release potassium and toxins into the circulation when pressure is removed, causing cardiac arrest; ALS care should begin before the release.
q1kapndt: Ten minutes after you applied a pressure bandage to a forearm laceration, the patient says his fingers are numb, cool, and tingling. What should you do?
Loosen the bandage and reassess circulation
Tighten the bandage further to stop any residual bleeding
Apply a tourniquet above the bandage
Ignore it, since numbness is expected after a laceration
New numbness, coolness, or tingling distal to a bandage suggests it is too tight; loosen it enough to restore circulation while maintaining bleeding control.
qf9fuoh: A 34-week pregnant woman is secured supine to a long backboard after a crash. She becomes dizzy and her blood pressure falls to 86/54. What should you do?
Tilt the board to her left or manually displace the uterus to the left
Raise her legs and lower her head
Remove her from the board and have her stand
Place her prone to take pressure off the uterus
The pregnant uterus can compress the inferior vena cava when the patient is supine, reducing blood return to the heart; tilting the board left or displacing the uterus relieves the pressure.
qmihlqc: A 30-week pregnant woman was in a crash. She has a rigid, painful abdomen, dark vaginal bleeding, and signs of shock. What does this suggest?
Separation of the placenta from the uterine wall causes abdominal pain, a rigid uterus, dark bleeding, and maternal shock; the fetus is at high risk.
q120cihy: A 26-week pregnant woman was the restrained driver in a minor crash. She has no pain and normal vital signs and wants to go home. What is the most appropriate advice?
She should be evaluated at the hospital because the fetus may be injured
She can safely stay home since her vital signs are normal
She should only seek care if she notices bleeding in the next week
She should lie on her back at home and rest for 24 hours
Pregnancy beyond 20 weeks is a special consideration in field triage; placental and fetal injury can occur without maternal symptoms, so she should be evaluated with fetal monitoring.
qlzr40m: A 6-year-old was struck in the chest by a car's mirror. His ribs feel intact, but he is tachypneic and anxious. What is important to remember about children with chest trauma?
Serious lung or heart injury can occur without rib fractures
Children rarely injure internal organs if the ribs are intact
Children compensate poorly, so vital signs drop immediately with injury
Rib fractures are more common in children than in adults
A child's ribs are flexible and transmit force to the organs beneath without breaking, so significant internal injury can be present with an intact chest wall.
q12hk4xy: What is the lowest acceptable systolic blood pressure for a 4-year-old child?
For children 1 to 10 years, the minimum systolic pressure is about 70 plus twice the age in years, which is 78 mmHg for a 4-year-old.
q1eu5qm7: A 74-year-old man was in a car crash. He is alert with a blood pressure of 104/70 and a pulse of 92. Under the 2021 field triage guideline, how should his blood pressure be interpreted?
It meets high-risk criteria because it is below 110 in an older adult
It is normal and does not affect destination
It only matters if his pulse is over 120
It meets criteria only if he becomes unresponsive
The 2021 guideline uses a systolic pressure below 110 mmHg as a high-risk criterion for adults 65 and older, since older adults may be in shock at pressures that look normal.
qboavf8: A 31-year-old was near an explosion at a factory. He has no visible injuries but complains of ringing in his ears and shortness of breath. Which injury should you be most concerned about?
The pressure wave of a blast damages air-filled organs such as the ears, lungs, and bowel; ear injury suggests the patient was exposed to enough pressure to injure the lungs.
q12q8wpg: A 28-year-old was struck in the face with a bat. His left eye has been forced out of the socket and is hanging on the cheek. How should you manage it?
Cover it with a moist dressing and a protective cup without pushing it back
Gently push the eye back into the socket before covering it
Apply a firm pressure dressing over the eye
Leave it uncovered and have him keep both eyes open
Never try to replace an extruded eye; protect it with a moist sterile dressing and a cup, and cover the other eye to reduce movement.
q1kh0bjq: A 16-year-old was hit in the nose by a soccer ball. His nose is bleeding steadily, he is alert, and there is no concern for spinal injury. How should you position him?
Sitting up and leaning forward while pinching the nostrils
Lying flat on his back with his head tilted back
Sitting with his head tilted back while pinching the bridge of the nose
Lying on his stomach with his face turned down
Leaning forward keeps blood from running down the throat, where it can be aspirated or cause vomiting; pinch the soft part of the nose with steady pressure.
q67vzfw: A 20-year-old man sustained a single gunshot wound to the thigh. A tourniquet controls the bleeding. His pulse is 132, his skin is cool and pale, and he is anxious. What should you do next?
Begin rapid transport while keeping him warm
Loosen the tourniquet to see if bleeding has stopped
Wait on scene for ALS to start an IV
Give him water for his thirst
After bleeding control, a patient showing signs of shock needs rapid transport to a trauma center, warmth, oxygen as needed, and ongoing reassessment.
q1es8ja1: You are dispatched to a reported domestic dispute. While you are assessing the patient, another person becomes increasingly agitated and picks up a kitchen knife. What should you do?
Leave the scene and wait for law enforcement
Continue care quickly and ask the person to calm down
Try to take the knife from the person
Move the patient into another room and lock the door
If a scene becomes unsafe, retreat to a safe location and request law enforcement; EMS providers should not attempt to disarm anyone.
qy4pwpr: You respond to a home where a family of four all complain of headaches and nausea. It is winter and a furnace is running. What should you do first?
Get everyone, including your crew, out of the house
Place everyone on nasal cannula oxygen inside the home
Open a window and continue the assessment inside
Multiple patients with similar symptoms in a heated home suggest carbon monoxide poisoning; remove everyone from the environment before providing care.
qajw3s1: Which principle is the basis of standard precautions?
Treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious
Use protective equipment only for patients with known infections
Wear gloves only when blood is visible
Ask each patient about infectious diseases before giving care
Standard precautions assume every patient's blood and body fluids may carry infection, so protective equipment is chosen based on the expected exposure, not the diagnosis.
qjzpwl7: After caring for a patient with diarrhea caused by Clostridioides difficile, how should you clean your hands?
Wipe them with a disinfectant towel
Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores, so hands must be washed with soap and running water to remove them mechanically.
q1pzgupn: You are removing personal protective equipment after a call. Which item is generally removed first?
Gloves are the most contaminated and are removed first, followed by eye protection and gown, with the mask or respirator removed last after leaving the patient area.
quyw6n2: While recapping a needle after a call, your partner sticks himself. What should he do first?
Wash the site with soap and water and report it immediately
Squeeze the wound hard and finish the shift before reporting
Wait to see if the patient tests positive before taking action
Apply bleach directly to the puncture
After a needlestick, wash the area with soap and water and report the exposure right away so testing and preventive treatment can start promptly; needles should never be recapped.
qpep3yu: A patient you transported two days ago has been diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. How would you normally be notified of the exposure?
Through your agency's designated infection control officer
You will not be notified, so you must track down the diagnosis yourself
Federal law requires hospitals to notify EMS agencies of exposures to certain diseases through a designated officer, who then informs the exposed providers.
q1risl23: An alert 70-year-old man with no suspected spinal injury needs to be moved down three narrow flights of stairs. Which device is most appropriate?
A stair chair is designed for alert patients who can sit upright on stairs and narrow hallways; it is safer than carrying a stretcher down tight stairways.
q1mkv7x5: A 25-year-old driver is sitting in her car after a crash. She is becoming less responsive and her breathing is getting worse. There are no hazards at the scene. How should she be removed?
Rapid extrication with manual spinal stabilization
Emergency drag by her clothing without regard to the spine
Wait for a fully padded vest-type device to be applied first
Ask her to get out and walk to the stretcher
A deteriorating patient needs an urgent move; rapid extrication removes her quickly while still limiting spinal movement.
q1lu0z02: You arrive to transport a 590-pound patient who has fallen. Your stretcher is rated for 500 pounds. What should you do?
Request additional personnel and bariatric equipment
Use the stretcher anyway, since ratings allow a margin of safety
Have the patient walk to the ambulance
Use a long backboard and six bystanders to carry him
Exceeding equipment weight limits risks injury to the patient and crew; request bariatric equipment and enough trained personnel for a safe move.
qezmax3: A 34-year-old man smells of alcohol, has slurred speech and a large bruise on his forehead after a fall, and insists he does not want to go to the hospital. What should you do?
Do not accept the refusal, and involve medical control or police per protocol
Have him sign a refusal form and leave
Leave without a refusal form because he is intoxicated
Accept the refusal once a friend agrees to watch him
An intoxicated patient with a possible head injury lacks decision-making capacity, so his refusal is not valid; follow protocol to obtain help in getting him evaluated.
q182phlv: A 15-year-old girl injured her ankle at soccer practice. She does not want to go to the hospital, but her mother, who is present, wants her transported. Who can give consent for care?
A minor generally cannot give or refuse consent for care; a parent or legal guardian makes the decision unless the minor is emancipated or a state exception applies.
qs8fh9u: You ask an alert 50-year-old man if you can check his blood pressure, and he rolls up his sleeve and holds out his arm. What type of consent is this?
Expressed consent can be verbal or nonverbal; holding out his arm after being asked indicates he agrees to the procedure.
q1liqnzy: An alert adult with decision-making capacity clearly refuses care. An EMT holds him down and transports him anyway. Which legal problem could this create?
Touching or treating a competent adult without consent can be considered battery; capable adults have the right to refuse care.
qo6zc1c: An EMT posts a photo from a dramatic call on social media with the patient's face blurred. The photo shows the street sign and the vehicle. How should this be viewed?
It may still violate patient privacy
It is acceptable because the face is blurred
It is acceptable if the EMT is off duty when posting
It is acceptable as long as no names are given
Location, vehicle, and other details can identify a patient even with the face hidden; posting call photos can violate HIPAA and agency policy.
q1wbh2la: You are treating a 3-year-old with bruises on the back, buttocks, and upper arms in different stages of healing. The parent says the child is clumsy. What is your responsibility?
Report your suspicion to the appropriate authority as required by law
Confront the parent and demand an explanation
Report only if the child tells you someone hurt them
Document only and take no further action
EMTs are mandatory reporters in most states; you report reasonable suspicion of abuse and do not need proof, and you should avoid confronting the caregiver.
q1uqe5c5: A 79-year-old man is in cardiac arrest. His daughter says he has a DNR order but she cannot find it. What should you do?
Withhold resuscitation based on her statement
Wait while the family searches for the document
Call his physician before doing anything
Without a valid DNR order or other legally recognized document present, start resuscitation; if valid documentation is produced later, care can be stopped per protocol.
q1tqama2: Which statement in a patient care report is written most appropriately?
Odor of alcohol on breath, speech slurred
Patient appeared to be a typical alcoholic
Documentation should record objective observations rather than opinions or labels, which can be inaccurate and create legal risk.
q1jswdwy: After a busy call, you realize you forgot to take a second set of vital signs. What should you document?
Only the vital signs you actually obtained
An estimate of the second set based on the first
A copy of the first set with a later time
The vital signs the hospital recorded, as if you took them
Falsifying a report is illegal and unethical; document only what you actually did and observed, even when something was missed.
qob8phy: A physician orders you over the radio to assist a patient with a medication to which the patient has told you he is allergic. What should you do?
Question the order and tell the physician about the allergy
Refuse silently and document the refusal
Give half of the ordered amount
When an order seems unsafe or inappropriate, clarify it with the physician and share the relevant information rather than following it blindly or ignoring it.
q1wc2a3u: You are the first unit arriving at a bus crash with many injured patients. What should you do first?
Establish command, size up the scene, and request resources
Begin treating the most seriously injured patient
Start loading the walking wounded into your ambulance
Wait for a supervisor before taking any action
The first arriving unit establishes command and gives a size-up report so resources can be requested; starting patient care immediately leaves the incident unmanaged.
qo2rehk: At an MCI, which position is responsible for coordinating ambulances, assigning patients to hospitals, and tracking where patients go?
The transportation officer coordinates with hospitals, assigns patients to ambulances, and tracks every patient who leaves the scene.
q7iein0: Using START triage, an adult has a respiratory rate of 22 and a radial pulse, but he cannot follow simple commands. How should he be tagged?
In START, an adult who breathes under 30 and has adequate perfusion but cannot follow simple commands is tagged immediate.
q1rwh5n7: Using START triage, an adult has a respiratory rate of 24 and follows commands, but you cannot feel a radial pulse. How should he be tagged?
An absent radial pulse (or capillary refill over 2 seconds) indicates inadequate perfusion, so the patient is tagged immediate.
qd79cp9: Using JumpSTART triage, a 3-year-old who cannot walk is breathing at 48 breaths per minute. How should she be tagged?
In JumpSTART, a respiratory rate under 15 or over 45 is a sign of serious injury, so this child is tagged immediate.
qebntwt: At an MCI using SALT triage, you ask everyone who can walk to move to a designated area and those who cannot walk to wave. Who should be assessed first?
Those who remain still or have obvious life threats
Those who walk to the designated area
Those who wave an arm or leg
Children before adults regardless of their response
In SALT global sorting, patients who are still or have obvious life threats are assessed first, those who wave are next, and those who walk are last.
q49m8l5: At a hazardous materials incident, in which zone should EMS normally treat patients?
The hot zone, where the release occurred
Any zone, if EMS is wearing gloves
EMS providers without specialized training and protective equipment treat patients in the cold zone after they have been decontaminated in the warm zone.
q1w1juy0: You see a placard with a four-digit UN number on a leaking truck. Which section of the Emergency Response Guidebook should you use first to look up that number?
The yellow pages list materials by ID number and refer you to a guide; blue pages list materials by name, orange pages contain the guides, and green pages give isolation distances.
qx2f6st: At a chemical spill, a contaminated worker walks out of the warm zone toward your ambulance asking for help. What should you do?
Direct him back to the decontamination area before you treat him
Put him in the ambulance and treat him there
Remove his shirt and transport him immediately
Give him water to rinse his mouth and transport
Contaminated patients must be decontaminated before treatment and transport to protect EMS providers, the ambulance, and the hospital.
qs6717t: You are driving an ambulance with lights and siren activated. Which statement about other vehicles is correct?
You must drive with due regard for the safety of all others
Other drivers are required to stop immediately when they see you
You may proceed through red lights without slowing
Lights and siren give you the right of way in all situations
Warning devices request the right of way but do not guarantee it; drivers of emergency vehicles must use due regard and are held responsible for crashes they cause.
q1y6ydqa: You are responding with lights and siren and approach a school bus with its red lights flashing. What should you do?
Stop and wait until the bus turns off its red lights
Pass the bus slowly on the left
Pass the bus quickly to reduce the time near children
Use the air horn and continue
Most states require all vehicles, including ambulances, to stop for a school bus with flashing red lights; proceed only when the bus driver signals or the lights are off.
q245sm6: A medical helicopter has landed with the rotor still turning. How should you approach it?
From the front, in view of the pilot, after the crew signals you
From the rear, to stay out of the pilot's way
From the uphill side so you stay level with the aircraft
Immediately after it lands, as fast as possible
Approach only when the flight crew signals, from the front where the pilot can see you, and never near the tail rotor; on a slope, approach from the downhill side.
q5n1bvn: A 22-year-old woman reports she was sexually assaulted. She is alert with minor injuries. What should you advise her?
Not to shower, urinate if avoidable, or change clothes before evaluation
To shower and change clothes so she feels more comfortable
To wash any wounds thoroughly with soap at home before transport
That evidence is collected only if she reports it within a week
Showering, changing clothes, and urinating can destroy evidence; if clothing must be removed, place items in separate paper bags.
q1f7qaok: After a call involving the death of an infant, your partner has trouble sleeping, is irritable, and is avoiding work. What is the best response?
Encourage your partner to use available professional resources
Tell your partner it is part of the job and to move on
Report your partner for disciplinary action
Suggest alcohol to help with sleep
Stress reactions after difficult calls are common; peer support, employee assistance programs, and mental health professionals help, and untreated stress can lead to burnout or PTSD.
qjfdcd0: Your stretcher has visible blood on it after a call. How should you clean it?
Remove the blood, then use an EPA-registered disinfectant per label directions
Wipe it with a dry towel until it looks clean
Spray it with water and let it air dry
Sterilize it in an autoclave before the next call

Surfaces with blood should be cleaned to remove visible material and then disinfected with an approved disinfectant for the required contact time; sterilization is for items that enter sterile tissue.
q1hofmwt: A combative patient must be restrained per protocol for safe transport. Which practice is correct?
Restrain the patient face up and continually monitor breathing
Restrain the patient face down with hands and feet tied together
Tighten restraints across the chest to prevent all movement
Leave the patient unattended once restraints are secure
Prone hobble restraint and chest compression can cause positional asphyxia and death; restrain supine or on the side, avoid chest compression, and continuously monitor the airway and breathing.
q5chrbp: An 80-year-old woman is lying supine on a narrow bathroom floor after a fall and needs to be lifted with minimal body movement. Which device separates into two halves that slide beneath her from each side?
A scoop (orthopedic) stretcher splits lengthwise so each half slides under the patient from the sides, lifting her with very little rolling or movement.
q12mc4yw: You arrive at a house where a man has been shot. Police tell you the scene is secure. As you enter, you notice a firearm on the floor near the patient. What should you do?
Tell police about it and avoid touching it unless needed for safety
Pick it up and unload it before treating the patient
Kick it under a couch so no one can reach it
Place it in the ambulance for safekeeping
Notify law enforcement of any weapon and leave it alone if possible; if it must be moved for safety, tell police exactly what you did.
ql3pknw: Which single action is most effective at preventing the spread of infection between patients and EMS providers?
Wearing a surgical mask on every call
Cleaning hands before and after patient contact and after removing gloves is the most effective way to prevent infection transmission.
q13wwn5w: A 41-year-old man has upper abdominal pain. You ask him, "Does the pain move or spread anywhere else?" Which part of OPQRST are you assessing?
Time and duration of the pain
The R in OPQRST covers where the pain is located and whether it radiates to another area.
q1iaklja: A 29-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes tells you she took her usual morning insulin but skipped lunch because she was busy. In the SAMPLE history, this information falls under which component?
The L in SAMPLE is last oral intake, which is especially relevant for diabetic patients because missed meals after insulin can cause hypoglycemia.
q1igq1du: A 73-year-old man lying in bed does not respond when you speak loudly to him but moans and opens his eyes when you squeeze his trapezius muscle. How should you document his mental status on the AVPU scale?
Alert but disoriented to time and place
Unresponsive to all forms of stimulus
A patient who reacts only to a painful stimulus, not to voice, is documented as P on the AVPU scale.
qkclnch: A 56-year-old woman opens her eyes when you speak to her, answers questions but is confused about where she is, and follows your commands to squeeze your hand. What is her Glasgow Coma Scale score?
Eye opening to voice scores 3, confused speech scores 4, and obeying commands scores 6, for a total of 13.
q1o0ni65: A 58-year-old woman has vomited for 3 days. Lying down, her BP is 116/74 and pulse 86. When she sits up, she becomes lightheaded and her pulse rises to 118. How should you interpret this?
She likely has significant volume loss
This is a normal response to changing position
It shows that she is having an allergic reaction
It confirms that her dizziness is from an inner ear disorder
A marked rise in heart rate with dizziness on sitting or standing suggests a low circulating volume, as seen with prolonged vomiting or bleeding.
q1kltyy: From the doorway you see a 3-year-old boy who is limp and not interacting with his mother. His breathing appears quiet and unlabored, but his skin is pale and mottled. What does this general impression suggest?
He is critically ill, likely in shock
He has respiratory distress that is well compensated
He has an isolated breathing problem from a partial airway obstruction
He is stable, so a slower, detailed assessment is acceptable
Abnormal appearance combined with abnormal circulation to the skin on the Pediatric Assessment Triangle indicates shock and a critically ill child.
q1suxuh1: A 4-year-old girl is drowsy and not tracking your movements. Her breathing is quiet and unlabored, and her skin color is normal. Using the Pediatric Assessment Triangle, which problem is most likely?
A brain dysfunction such as a toxin, low glucose, or head injury
Upper airway obstruction from a foreign body
Lower airway disease such as asthma or bronchiolitis
Abnormal appearance with normal work of breathing and normal circulation points to a primary brain or metabolic problem, such as hypoglycemia, poisoning, or head injury.
qcpbzvs: A calm, content 6-month-old has a resting heart rate of 140/min and a respiratory rate of 40/min. How should you interpret these vital signs?
They are within normal limits for an infant
The heart rate is normal but the respiratory rate shows distress
Both are too slow and suggest hypoxia
Normal infant heart rates are roughly 100-160/min and respiratory rates roughly 30-60/min, so these values are expected.
q170wy0d: A 47-year-old woman with a medical complaint is awake and able to answer questions. After the primary assessment, what is usually the next step?
Obtain the history of the present illness and SAMPLE history
Perform a rapid head-to-toe trauma assessment before speaking with her
Obtain a full set of baseline vital signs before asking any questions
Transport immediately and defer all history to the hospital staff
For a responsive medical patient, the history guides the exam, so the history of present illness and SAMPLE history come before the focused secondary assessment.
q4hom16: You find a 60-year-old man unresponsive on his kitchen floor with no signs of trauma. His airway is open and breathing is adequate. What is the most appropriate approach to the secondary assessment?
Rapid full-body exam, then history from bystanders
Focused exam of only the chest and abdomen, guided by his chief complaint
Wait until he wakes up, then obtain a SAMPLE history from him directly
Skip the physical exam and transport, since unresponsive patients cannot be assessed
An unresponsive medical patient cannot give a history, so a rapid full-body exam is done first, followed by information from family, bystanders, and the scene.
q1opaaza: In which patient is capillary refill time most useful as an indicator of perfusion?
An 82-year-old found on a cold porch
Capillary refill is most reliable in young children; cold exposure, age, smoking, and some medications reduce its accuracy in adults.
qf8zneg: A 71-year-old woman with dementia is more confused than usual, has a temperature of 100.9 F, and her caregiver reports new incontinence and foul-smelling urine. What should you suspect?
An infection that may be developing into sepsis
Normal progression of her dementia over time
Simple dehydration from not drinking enough fluids
Acute worsening of mental status with fever and urinary symptoms in an older adult suggests infection, such as a urinary tract infection, which can lead to sepsis.
q1fxu13q: A 52-year-old man smelling strongly of alcohol is confused, has slurred speech, and is staggering. What is the main danger of assuming he is simply intoxicated?
Missing low glucose, head injury, or other serious causes
Embarrassing him in front of bystanders and family
Delaying the police response to the scene
Failing to document the odor of alcohol on the report
Alcohol odor does not explain all altered mental status; hypoglycemia, head injury, stroke, infection, and other poisonings can coexist and must be considered.
qz4zcm: A 34-year-old man with epilepsy has two generalized seizures in a row without regaining consciousness between them. What is this condition called?
Continuous seizure activity, or repeated seizures without return to consciousness between them, is status epilepticus, a life-threatening emergency.
qpmxv7: A 38-year-old woman has been seizing continuously for 7 minutes. She is cyanotic and her mouth is full of secretions. What should you do?
Suction, give high-flow oxygen, request ALS, and transport
Insert a bite block between her teeth to protect her tongue
Hold her arms and legs down firmly to stop the movements
Wait until the seizure stops before beginning any care
Prolonged seizures need airway clearance, oxygenation, ventilation as needed, ALS support for medications, and prompt transport; restraint and objects in the mouth cause injury.
q1sv74lm: A 25-year-old man is drowsy and confused after a witnessed seizure that has stopped. He is breathing adequately with gurgling sounds. How should you position him?
On his side in the recovery position
Prone with his face turned to one side
Sitting upright with his head tilted back
The recovery position lets secretions drain and protects the airway of a postictal patient who is breathing adequately; suction should be ready.
q1hzrw69: A 79-year-old man suddenly passed out while seated at dinner, with no warning symptoms. He is now alert with normal vital signs. Why is transport important?
Sudden syncope in an older adult may indicate a dysrhythmia
Syncope while seated is always caused by low blood sugar
He needs observation for a likely postictal period
Fainting in an older adult always means he has had a stroke
Syncope without a warning period, especially while seated or in an older adult, raises concern for a cardiac rhythm problem that may recur.
q1c8dzlc: A 22-year-old fainted when she saw blood during a lab draw. She is now alert, with normal vital signs. What is the most likely mechanism?
A vagal response that slowed her heart and dilated vessels
A seizure triggered by a sudden emotional shock
A sudden drop in her blood glucose level
An allergic reaction to the needle or skin cleanser
Vasovagal syncope occurs when a trigger such as fear or pain stimulates the vagus nerve, slowing the heart rate and dilating blood vessels so that brain blood flow briefly falls.
q6c1zzv: A 16-year-old with type 1 diabetes has had flu symptoms and vomiting for 2 days. She now has abdominal pain and deep, rapid breathing. Why is she breathing this way?
Her body is compensating for acid buildup
She is anxious and having a panic attack
She has inhaled vomit into her lungs
Her blood sugar has dropped dangerously low
In diabetic ketoacidosis, deep rapid respirations blow off carbon dioxide to offset the metabolic acidosis caused by ketones.
qn06erp: A 67-year-old man was hypoglycemic, received oral glucose, and is now alert. He takes a long-acting oral diabetes medication and wants to refuse transport. What is the main concern?
Oral glucose may cause high blood sugar later
He may have an allergic reaction to the glucose
He will need insulin within the next hour
Some diabetes medications last many hours, so hypoglycemia can recur after a temporary improvement; this should be explained during any refusal discussion.
qvdc1lv: A 68-year-old woman has new right-sided weakness and slurred speech. Her blood glucose is 38 mg/dL. What should you keep in mind?
The low glucose confirms she has had a stroke
Glucose readings are unreliable in stroke patients
She should be given nothing and reassessed in an hour
Low blood glucose can cause focal weakness and speech changes that look like a stroke, so it must be identified and treated, with reassessment of the neurologic findings.
q1ddz1j9: An 81-year-old with type 2 diabetes has become confused over the past week. She is very dehydrated, has no fruity breath odor, and breathes normally. Her glucose meter reads "HI." What condition is most likely?
Older type 2 diabetics can develop extremely high glucose and severe dehydration over days without significant ketone production, so Kussmaul breathing and fruity odor are often absent.
qtoox81: A 30-year-old man has itchy hives on his arms after eating shrimp. He has no history of severe reactions, no breathing difficulty, no swelling of the face or throat, and normal vital signs. What is appropriate?
Monitor closely for progression during transport
Administer an epinephrine auto-injector right away
Insert an oral airway to prevent swelling
Place him supine with legs elevated and give nothing else
Isolated skin findings without respiratory, circulatory, or other systemic signs indicate a mild allergic reaction, but it can progress, so close monitoring is essential.
qylbpap: A 10-year-old with a peanut allergy ate a cookie at a party. She has stridor, a hoarse voice, and hives, and has her prescribed epinephrine auto-injector. What is the most important action?
Have her drink water to rinse the allergen down
Give high-flow oxygen and wait to see if it resolves
Transport first and let the hospital decide on treatment
Airway involvement with known allergen exposure is anaphylaxis, and early epinephrine is the treatment that reverses airway swelling and shock.
qz5virf: A 26-year-old's breathing and blood pressure improved after his epinephrine auto-injector. He now feels fine and wants to go home. Why should he be transported?
Symptoms can return as the epinephrine wears off
The epinephrine will cause a dangerously high blood sugar
He needs a second injection given at the hospital
He is at risk for low blood pressure from the injection itself
Epinephrine acts for a short time, and anaphylaxis can recur or a second phase can develop hours later, so observation at a hospital is needed.
q10qkrk2: A 2-year-old swallowed liquid drain cleaner. There are burns around his mouth and he is drooling. What should you do?
Do not induce vomiting; transport and contact poison control
Make him vomit to empty the stomach quickly
Give him milk to neutralize the chemical
Give him a large glass of water to dilute the chemical
Vomiting re-exposes the esophagus and airway to a corrosive, so it is never induced; giving anything by mouth should be guided by medical direction or poison control.
q1e22fjq: A 50-year-old man is removed from a closed garage where a car was running. He has a headache and nausea, and his SpO2 reads 99%. How should you interpret the SpO2?
It may be falsely normal; give high-flow oxygen
It confirms that he has no carbon monoxide exposure
It shows that he needs no supplemental oxygen
It means his headache must have another cause
Standard pulse oximeters read carbon monoxide-bound hemoglobin as oxygenated, so the reading can be falsely high; treat suspected CO exposure with high-flow oxygen.
qmaiym6: You arrive at a farm where two workers have collapsed inside a manure storage tank. A third worker climbed in to help and also collapsed. What should you do?
Stay out and request specialized rescue
Enter quickly while holding your breath
Lower a rope into the tank and climb in after it
Enter wearing a surgical mask over your face
Multiple collapses in a confined space suggest a toxic or oxygen-deficient atmosphere; only rescuers with proper training and supplied-air equipment should enter.
qw9smoc: A landscaper has a dry chemical powder on his arms and clothing. The label says it reacts with water. What should you do first?
Brush off the powder and remove contaminated clothing
Flush the area immediately with large amounts of water
Wipe the skin with an alcohol pad to remove it
Cover the area with a dressing and leave it in place
Dry chemicals should be brushed off and contaminated clothing removed before any flushing, especially when the product reacts with water.
qgb1wsz: A worker got a liquid industrial chemical splashed in both eyes. Which action is most important?
Flush the eyes with clean water for at least 20 minutes
Patch both eyes and transport without flushing them
Rinse briefly with saline and stop when the pain eases
Have the patient rub his eyes to clear the chemical
Prolonged irrigation is the key treatment for chemical eye exposure and should continue during transport when possible.
q1vq3jr2: After naloxone, a 33-year-old who overdosed on an opioid is awake and breathing well. He wants to leave. What is the main risk of refusal?
The naloxone may wear off before the opioid
He will become hypoglycemic within minutes
The naloxone will cause delayed anaphylaxis
He is likely to develop dangerously high blood pressure
Many opioids act longer than naloxone, so respiratory depression can return after the antidote wears off.
q2pz9mg: A 24-year-old who used cocaine is agitated and sweating heavily, with a heart rate of 142, a temperature of 104 F, and dilated pupils. Which toxidrome does this represent?
Stimulants such as cocaine and methamphetamine cause agitation, tachycardia, hyperthermia, diaphoresis, and dilated pupils.
qqhtaw1: A 15-year-old took a large amount of an over-the-counter antihistamine. Which findings would you expect?
Hot, dry, flushed skin with dilated pupils
Cool, sweaty skin with pinpoint pupils
Heavy drooling, tearing, and frequent urination
Slow breathing with pinpoint pupils and no agitation
Anticholinergic poisoning causes dry, hot, red skin, dilated pupils, rapid heart rate, and confusion, the opposite of the wet cholinergic picture.
qtgcbxe: A 55-year-old who drinks heavily every day stopped 2 days ago. He is tremulous, sweating, and seeing insects on the wall. Why is this serious?
Severe alcohol withdrawal can cause seizures and death
Withdrawal symptoms are mild and fade within an hour
It shows that he is intoxicated again and needs only rest
Hallucinations confirm a primary psychiatric illness
Alcohol withdrawal can progress to seizures and delirium tremens, which carries significant mortality and needs medical care.
qitseqt: A 72-year-old man has sudden, severe abdominal pain radiating to his back. You feel a pulsating mass above his navel. His BP is 90/58. What should you do?
Treat for shock and transport promptly
Palpate the mass firmly to estimate its size
Have him walk to the stretcher to save time
Give him water to ease his discomfort
These findings suggest a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm; avoid vigorous palpation, treat for shock, and transport rapidly to an appropriate facility.
qff0iaz: A 44-year-old woman has right upper quadrant abdominal pain that began after a fatty meal and spreads to her right shoulder. Which organ is most likely involved?
Gallbladder inflammation often follows fatty meals and refers pain to the right shoulder or scapula.
q1pi2jj3: A 19-year-old has pain that began around his navel and over several hours moved to the right lower quadrant. He has nausea and a low-grade fever. What should you suspect?
Pain that starts near the umbilicus and migrates to the right lower quadrant, with nausea and fever, is classic for appendicitis.
q8h8r7l: A 61-year-old has had black, tarry, foul-smelling stools for 2 days and feels dizzy when standing. What does this suggest?
Bleeding in the upper digestive tract
Black, tarry stool (melena) is digested blood, usually from the stomach or upper intestine, and dizziness on standing suggests significant blood loss.
q1m46r5f: A 58-year-old man with a long history of heavy drinking is vomiting large amounts of bright red blood. What is your first priority?
Keep the airway clear with suction and positioning
Give him water to rinse his mouth between episodes
Lay him flat on his back and elevate his legs
Collect the vomit to measure its volume
Massive upper GI bleeding, such as from esophageal varices, threatens the airway first; position and suction to prevent aspiration while treating for shock.
q1d3jlux: A 66-year-old dialysis patient missed his last two treatments. He is weak, and his pulse is 46 and irregular. What is the greatest concern?
A high potassium level causing a dangerous rhythm
Low blood sugar from skipping meals
Dehydration from too much fluid removal
Infection of his dialysis access site
Missed dialysis allows potassium to build up, which can slow the heart and cause life-threatening dysrhythmias.
qc2ls2v: A 59-year-old just left her dialysis center and is bleeding steadily from her AV fistula needle site. What should you do first?
Apply firm direct pressure to the site
Apply a tourniquet before trying anything else
Clamp the fistula shut with a hemostat
Elevate the arm and wait for clotting
Direct pressure controls most fistula bleeding; escalate per bleeding control guidelines if pressure fails, but avoid clamping the fistula.
q1su5p1c: A 70-year-old dialysis patient who missed treatment is short of breath, with crackles in both lungs and swollen ankles. What should you do?
Sit him upright and support his breathing
Lay him flat with his legs raised
Give him fluids by mouth to restore volume
Apply cold packs to his chest and legs
Missed dialysis can cause fluid overload and pulmonary edema; an upright position, oxygen, ventilatory support as needed, and transport are appropriate.
q18kymou: A 35-year-old man is pacing and cannot get comfortable. He has severe left flank pain radiating to his groin and blood in his urine. What is the most likely cause?
Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with restlessness and hematuria is typical of a kidney stone.
qt8zgy2: An 84-year-old nursing home resident has a temperature of 96.2 F, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 26, BP 94/58, and new confusion. What should you suspect?
Normal aging changes in vital signs
Older adults with serious infections may have low or normal temperatures; tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, and altered mentation point to sepsis.
q12epvcl: You suspect sepsis in a 58-year-old woman who is hypotensive and confused. Which action most improves her care?
Notify the hospital early of possible sepsis
Delay transport to obtain repeated vital signs
Allow her to walk to the ambulance
Give her large amounts of water by mouth
Sepsis outcomes depend on early antibiotics and fluids, so prompt transport and early hospital notification matter, along with oxygen and warmth as needed.
q197s8zx: A 30-year-old man was extremely agitated, sweating, and fighting with police. He is now physically restrained and suddenly becomes quiet and still. What should you do?
Immediately check his breathing and pulse
Assume he has calmed down and continue transport
Tighten the restraints to prevent further struggle
Leave him alone so he does not become agitated again
Sudden quiet in a severely agitated, restrained patient can signal respiratory or cardiac arrest, so assess breathing and circulation immediately.
qbhg3rd: You are called for a 40-year-old man who is anxious and agitated but not violent. How should you position yourself while talking with him?
With a clear path to the exit
Between him and the only door in the room
Directly face to face within arm's reach
Behind him, out of his line of sight
Keeping your exit route clear lets you leave if the situation escalates; do not let the patient come between you and the door.
q1avq8wt: A 27-year-old woman is breathing rapidly after an argument and has tingling around her mouth and in her hands. What should you do?
Reassure her and coach her breathing
Have her breathe into a paper bag
Tell her the symptoms are all in her head
Restrain her until her breathing slows
Coaching slower breathing and reassurance help anxiety-related hyperventilation; paper bag rebreathing is unsafe because serious medical causes of rapid breathing may be missed.
q1sd56y3: A 17-year-old is withdrawn and tearful after a breakup. What is the best approach?
Ask her directly if she is thinking of suicide
Avoid the topic because asking may put the idea in her head
Tell her she will feel better soon and change the subject
Ask her parents but not her about suicidal thoughts
Asking directly about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk and is the only way to find out whether she is in danger.
q1vrqzpr: A 36-year-old man says he took a bottle of pills to end his life. He is alert and refuses transport. What should you do?
Stay with him and involve law enforcement and medical direction
Have him sign a refusal form and leave
Leave a crisis hotline number and clear the scene
Wait outside until he changes his mind
A patient with a suicide attempt and possible overdose lacks capacity to refuse; do not leave him, and use law enforcement and medical direction per local protocol.
q1hj7kd: A 32-year-old hiker is shivering, alert, and talking clearly after falling into a cold stream. What is the best care?
Remove wet clothing and warm her in a heated area
Rub her arms and legs briskly to restore circulation
Give her a drink of alcohol to warm her up
Have her walk quickly to generate body heat
Mild hypothermia is treated by removing wet clothing, insulating, and passive or external rewarming in a warm environment.
qgeka6z: A 74-year-old was found in an unheated house. He is unresponsive, with very cold skin. How should you check his pulse?
Feel for a pulse longer than usual
Check briefly and start CPR if none is felt immediately
Skip the pulse check and begin CPR at once
In severe hypothermia, the pulse may be very slow and faint, so it should be checked for longer than usual before deciding on CPR.
q1js2v4: A skier's cheeks are pale and numb, but the skin is soft and regains color when warmed. What condition is this?
Frostnip is superficial cold injury with blanched, numb skin that remains soft and recovers with warming.
qma25vj: A 46-year-old roofer working in the heat has painful cramps in his legs. He is alert and sweating. What should you do?
Move him to a cool place and give electrolyte fluid by mouth
Apply a tourniquet to his legs to relieve cramping
Immerse him immediately in an ice water bath
Have him continue working to stretch the muscles
Heat cramps from salt and fluid loss respond to rest, cooling, and oral electrolyte replacement in an alert patient.
q1jzvux8: A 38-year-old is dizzy and nauseated after working in the heat. Her skin is pale and sweaty, her heart rate is 110, and she is fully alert and oriented. What is most likely?
Heat exhaustion causes weakness, dizziness, sweating, and tachycardia with normal mental status; altered mental status indicates heat stroke.
qccheqx: An 11-year-old was pulled from a pool. She coughed up water and is now alert and breathing normally. Her parents want no transport. What is your concern?
Breathing problems can develop hours later
She has a high risk of hypothermia from the warm pool
She may have swallowed too much chlorine
She may become dehydrated from swallowing water
Aspiration of water can cause delayed respiratory compromise, so evaluation after a submersion event is important even when the patient looks well.
q54don8: A 16-year-old dove into the shallow end of a lake and is floating face down. What should you suspect?
Diving into shallow water causes cervical spine injuries; remove the patient from the water with in-line stabilization while maintaining the airway.
q4sswxh: A 9-year-old is pulled from a lake. She is unresponsive, apneic, and pulseless. What should you do?
Begin CPR with emphasis on effective ventilations
Drain water from her lungs before starting CPR
Perform abdominal thrusts to remove water
Do not attempt CPR because she was submerged
Drowning arrest is caused by hypoxia, so ventilations are especially important; attempts to drain water delay care.
q1wsc54h: Lightning struck a group of hikers. One is screaming in pain, one is confused, and one is apneic and pulseless. Whom should you treat first?
The hiker who is screaming in pain
All are equal, so treat whoever is closest
In lightning strikes, those in respiratory or cardiac arrest often survive with prompt care, so reverse triage puts them first.
q10czqvr: A 39-year-old was bitten while moving wood. She now has severe abdominal cramping and a rigid abdomen. Which bite is most likely?
Black widow venom acts on nerves and causes muscle cramping and abdominal rigidity, while brown recluse bites cause local tissue damage.
q1ujw2an: A 23-year-old was stung by a bee and the stinger is still in his skin. What should you do?
Remove it quickly, such as by scraping with a card
Leave it in place for removal at the hospital
Squeeze it out between your fingers slowly
Cover it with a tight dressing to trap the venom
Prompt removal limits venom delivery; the method matters less than speed, and scraping is a common technique.
q1w0uw3v: A 30-year-old stepped on a stingray. She has severe foot pain and a small wound. What is appropriate?
Immerse the foot in hot water as tolerated
Apply a tight tourniquet above the ankle
Rub sand into the wound to remove venom
Hot water immersion, without causing burns, helps relieve pain from many marine venoms.
qrbq8q8: A 42-year-old scuba diver has joint pain and tingling in his arms 2 hours after surfacing. What should you suspect?
Nitrogen bubbles forming after a dive cause joint pain, skin changes, and neurologic symptoms; high-flow oxygen and transport to a facility able to provide hyperbaric care are needed.
q1056nus: A 28-year-old diver ascended quickly and, within a minute of surfacing, became unresponsive with one-sided weakness. What is most likely?
Rapid ascent can force air into the arterial circulation, causing stroke-like signs immediately after surfacing.
q1a7mexs: During a delivery, the baby's head has delivered and you have checked for a cord. What is the next step?
Support the head and guide it gently downward to deliver the upper shoulder
Pull firmly on the head to deliver the body quickly
Push the head back up to slow down the delivery
Wait until the next day for the mother to deliver the shoulders
Gentle downward guidance helps the upper shoulder deliver, then upward guidance for the lower shoulder; never pull hard on the head.
qblj00a: When should you suction a newborn's mouth and nose after delivery?
Only if secretions block the airway
Routine suctioning is not recommended for newborns; suction the mouth before the nose only when secretions obstruct breathing or ventilation is needed.
qcny6c3: A healthy term newborn is crying with good tone. When should the umbilical cord be clamped?
Delayed cord clamping for at least 30 to 60 seconds is recommended for vigorous newborns.
q1ia46u1: After delivery of the baby, the placenta has not yet delivered. What should you do?
Allow it to deliver naturally and bring it to the hospital
Pull firmly on the cord to speed it up
Push on the uterus forcefully to expel it
Cut the cord close to the vagina and leave the placenta
Pulling on the cord can tear it or invert the uterus; the placenta should deliver naturally and be bagged for examination.
qaswbn3: During delivery, the umbilical cord is wrapped tightly around the baby's neck and cannot be slipped over the head. What should you do?
Clamp the cord in two places and cut between them
Pull the baby out quickly to loosen the cord
Push the baby's head back in
Leave it and continue the delivery
A tight nuchal cord that cannot be loosened must be clamped and cut so delivery can continue safely.
qe2x0ke: During a breech delivery, the body has delivered but the head has not after 3 minutes. What should you do?
Place gloved fingers to form an airway for the baby
Pull firmly on the legs to deliver the head
Push the body back into the vagina
Wait until the mother can be transported
Creating an airway by placing fingers alongside the baby's face allows breathing while transport continues.
q1it220z: After the baby's head delivers, it pulls back tightly against the mother's perineum and the shoulders do not deliver. What should you do?
Have her pull her knees back toward her chest
Pull hard on the baby's head
Push on the top of the uterus
Push the head back into the vagina
This is shoulder dystocia; flexing the mother's hips by drawing her knees to her chest widens the pelvis and can free the shoulder.
qmxl4o9: A 37-weeks-pregnant woman is having a seizure. Her BP is 172/112. What is appropriate?
Place her on her left side, give oxygen, and transport rapidly
Give her oral glucose and wait
Put her flat on her back and elevate her legs
Place a bite block in her mouth
Eclampsia is life-threatening; protect the airway, position on the left side, give oxygen, minimize stimulation, and transport rapidly.
qovvqcp: A woman who gave birth 10 days ago has a seizure. Her BP is 170/110. What should you suspect?
Epilepsy that she has always had
Preeclampsia and eclampsia can occur up to several weeks after delivery, so new seizures and hypertension postpartum are concerning.
q1et52af: A woman 33 weeks pregnant has sudden painless bright red vaginal bleeding. What should you suspect?
Placenta previa causes painless bright red bleeding late in pregnancy; never perform a vaginal exam.
q1ij0him: A 27-year-old woman who is 9 weeks pregnant has heavy vaginal bleeding with cramping and has passed clots and tissue. Her pulse is 116. What should you do?
Treat for shock and bring the passed tissue to the hospital
Discard the tissue in a biohazard bag to reduce infection risk
Pack gauze into the vagina to stop the bleeding
Reassure her that early pregnancy bleeding is normal and suggest she follow up with her doctor
A likely miscarriage with tachycardia needs shock care and transport; place a pad over the vaginal opening, never pack it, and bring tissue for examination.
q1vnwd6x: You have just delivered a baby at home. The mother's abdomen remains about as large as before, and strong contractions begin again a few minutes later. What should you suspect?
A second baby is about to deliver
The placenta is delivering and nothing else is expected
She has a uterine rupture and needs immediate surgery
This is normal and she can be transported without further preparation
A uterus that stays large with renewed contractions after the first birth suggests multiple gestation; prepare for a second delivery and additional newborn care.
q1y5vpv4: A term baby is born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid. He is crying vigorously with good muscle tone. What should you do?
Suction deeply below the vocal cords before stimulating him
Begin positive pressure ventilation at once
Withhold drying until the meconium is suctioned
A vigorous newborn needs routine care (warm, dry, stimulate, clear the airway only if needed) whether or not meconium is present.
q9vp75p: At 1 minute, a newborn has a pink body with blue hands and feet, a heart rate of 110/min, a grimace to stimulation, some flexion of the arms and legs, and a weak, slow cry. What is the APGAR score?
Appearance 1, pulse 2, grimace 1, activity 1, and respiration 1 total 6.
qnvj5jr: A newborn is limp and not breathing immediately after birth. How should the APGAR score affect your initial care?
Do not wait for it to begin resuscitation
Wait for the 1-minute score to decide whether to ventilate
Begin compressions only if the 1-minute score is below 7
Delay ventilation until both the 1-minute and 5-minute scores are known
The APGAR score describes the newborn's condition at 1 and 5 minutes but is not used to decide whether to start resuscitation; breathing and heart rate guide care.
q1pgvsws: Despite effective ventilation, a newborn's heart rate remains below 60/min and you begin chest compressions. What compression-to-ventilation ratio should you use?
Neonatal resuscitation uses a 3:1 ratio, giving about 90 compressions and 30 breaths per minute.
q197lmyu: Two minutes after birth, a crying newborn has a pink trunk and lips but bluish hands and feet. How should you interpret this?
It indicates severe hypoxia that requires chest compressions
It is a sign of shock that requires immediate fluid replacement
It suggests a heart defect and requires high-flow oxygen by mask
Acrocyanosis, bluish extremities with a pink central body, is common in the first minutes of life and does not require treatment.
q1htgial: Which method gives the most accurate heart rate in a newborn who needs resuscitation in the field?
Palpating the radial pulse at the wrist
Palpating the carotid pulse in the neck
Auscultation of the chest is more reliable than palpation in newborns, whose peripheral pulses are difficult to feel.
qm4nfn0: You are providing positive pressure ventilation to an apneic newborn with a heart rate of 90/min. At what rate should you ventilate?
Newborn positive pressure ventilation is given at 40 to 60 breaths per minute, watching for chest rise and a rising heart rate.
q1qsp2ph: An 8-month-old has had diarrhea for 3 days. She is lethargic, with a heart rate of 190/min, capillary refill of 4 seconds, and cool, mottled extremities. What does this indicate?
Mild dehydration that can be managed at home
Normal findings for an infant who has been sleeping
A fever that has broken and is resolving
Lethargy, marked tachycardia, delayed capillary refill, and cool, mottled skin indicate shock; give oxygen, keep her warm, and transport rapidly.
q7kdt7l: A 2-month-old is found unresponsive in his crib. He is warm, has no lividity or rigor mortis, and has no pulse. What should you do?
Pronounce death on scene and call the medical examiner
Interview the parents in detail before touching the infant
Wait for law enforcement to photograph the scene first
Without obvious signs of death, an infant in cardiac arrest should receive immediate resuscitation; questions about the cause come later.
q1x5gdnq: A 3-month-old briefly stopped breathing, turned blue, and went limp, then recovered within a minute. She now looks well. The parents ask whether transport is needed. What should you advise?
No care is needed because she looks normal now
Watch her closely at home and call again only if it recurs
Give her a bottle and recheck her in an hour
A brief resolved unexplained event can be caused by serious problems such as infection, seizures, heart rhythm problems, or abuse, so evaluation is recommended even when the infant appears well.
qbu0lau: You suspect that a 5-year-old's injuries were caused by abuse. The caregiver is present. What should you do?
Report your concerns as required by law
Confront the caregiver about your suspicions
Leave the child at home to avoid conflict
Ask the child repeatedly until he admits what happened
Suspected abuse must be reported according to state law and agency policy; avoid confrontation, care for the child, and document objectively.
qvxtniu: A 4-month-old is lethargic and has been vomiting, with no visible injuries. The caregiver says the baby was "fine an hour ago" and gives a vague story. What should you suspect?
Colic that will resolve on its own
Normal infant sleepiness after a feeding
Unexplained lethargy and vomiting in an infant, with an inconsistent history, can be signs of abusive head trauma even without external injury.
qh7b8q4: An 82-year-old takes nine medications. Her family says she became confused and fell twice since a new medication was added last week. What should you consider?
An adverse drug effect or interaction
Normal aging that requires no further evaluation
Long-standing dementia that has not changed
Too little sleep, with no other cause to consider
Polypharmacy is a common cause of new confusion and falls in older adults; bring the medications or a list to the hospital.
q4kuv0g: A 78-year-old woman fell in her bathroom and has hip pain. Why is it important to ask what happened just before the fall?
A medical problem may have caused it
To decide who is legally responsible
To determine which hospital she prefers
To confirm whether she needs a walker
Falls in older adults are often caused by syncope, dysrhythmias, stroke, hypoglycemia, or medications, and these must be identified along with the injury.
q1jklsvq: An 85-year-old has mild abdominal discomfort, normal vital signs, and no fever. Why is transport still recommended?
Serious problems may present subtly in older adults
Older adults usually exaggerate their pain
Abdominal pain in older adults is almost always minor
Normal vital signs rule out serious illness in older adults
Older adults often have blunted pain, fever, and heart rate responses, so serious conditions can present with mild symptoms and normal vital signs.
q191sxgc: A 76-year-old with known dementia has become much more confused and agitated over the past day. What does this suggest?
Delirium from an acute medical problem
A normal change in older adults
A sudden change in mental status is delirium, which often signals infection, dehydration, medication effects, or another acute medical problem.
q5mpgzi: A 54-year-old on a home ventilator is in respiratory distress and the ventilator alarm is sounding. What should you do?
Disconnect and ventilate with a BVM
Silence the alarm and continue to watch him
Increase the ventilator rate and wait
Call the equipment company before any care
When a ventilator-dependent patient is in distress, remove the ventilator from the equation and ventilate manually while looking for the cause.
q1eimxd7: A 64-year-old with a left ventricular assist device (LVAD) is alert and talking. You cannot feel a radial pulse or hear a blood pressure. How should you interpret this?
It may be normal with this device
Many LVADs produce continuous flow with little or no pulse; assess mental status and skin perfusion, and contact the device coordinator listed on the equipment.
q1b9oaln: A 70-year-old with a gastrostomy feeding tube develops coughing and difficulty breathing right after a feeding. What should you suspect?
An allergic reaction to the formula
Patients with feeding tubes can aspirate stomach contents; position them upright, suction as needed, and support breathing.
qe5j8ke: A 45-year-old receiving long-term treatment through a central venous catheter has a fever, chills, and a heart rate of 118. What should you suspect?
A normal reaction to the catheter
A blood clot in the leg
Central lines provide a direct route for infection into the blood, so fever and tachycardia in these patients raise concern for sepsis.
q1lrp738: A 7-year-old with a shunt for hydrocephalus has a headache, vomiting, and increasing sleepiness. What should you suspect?
Shunt blockage or infection causes rising pressure in the skull, with headache, vomiting, and decreasing mental status, and requires prompt transport.
qwprw7k: A 9-year-old with autism spectrum disorder becomes very agitated in the ambulance. What should you do?
Reduce stimulation and involve the caregiver
Restrain the child before he becomes violent
Turn on more lights so you can see him better
Ignore the behavior and continue with your questions
Reducing noise, lights, and touch, and using the caregiver's knowledge of the child, help keep patients with autism calm.
q1ujhucg: You are preparing to insert a supraglottic airway in an unresponsive adult in cardiac arrest. How should you choose the device size?
Follow the manufacturer's height or weight guide for that device
Measure from the corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw
Measure from the tip of the nose to the earlobe
Match the diameter of the patient's little finger to the outside of the tube
Supraglottic airways are sized by the manufacturer's height or weight chart for that specific product. The mouth-to-jaw and nose-to-earlobe measurements are used to size oral and nasal airways.
q1em9nck: A 61-year-old man with a pulse is being ventilated through a supraglottic airway. His capnography waveform has been normal at 38 mmHg, but after he is moved down a flight of stairs the waveform is a flat line, there is no chest rise and his SpO2 is falling. What is the most likely cause?
The oxygen saturation probe has slipped off

A sudden loss of the capnography waveform with no chest rise after moving the patient points to a dislodged airway. Bronchospasm produces a sloped waveform rather than a flat line, and a loose oximeter probe would not stop chest rise.
q1kadxj3: During transport, the SpO2 of a patient ventilated through a supraglottic airway drifts from 96 to 85 percent. Chest rise is good, breath sounds are equal and the capnography waveform is unchanged. What should you check next?
The oxygen tubing connection and the cylinder pressure
Whether the cuff needs an additional 20 mL of air
Whether the device should be exchanged for a larger size
Whether the ventilation rate should be doubled

With good chest rise, equal breath sounds and a normal waveform, the airway is working, so equipment failure such as a disconnected oxygen line or empty tank is the likely problem. Thinking through displacement, obstruction, pneumothorax and equipment keeps troubleshooting organized.
qwcu7ne: A 35-year-old crash victim with chest wall bruising is being ventilated through a supraglottic airway. Bagging becomes progressively harder, breath sounds disappear on the right, his neck veins distend and his BP falls to 74/40. What is the most likely cause?
Displacement of the device into the esophagus
Mucus plugging of the airway tube

Rising resistance to ventilation, unilateral absent breath sounds, distended neck veins and hypotension after chest trauma indicate tension pneumothorax, which positive pressure ventilation can worsen. Request ALS for decompression and expedite transport.
qw0w60a: You are ventilating an adult through a supraglottic airway when frothy secretions begin bubbling up into the tube and resistance to bagging increases. Chest rise and capnography were confirmed earlier. What should you do?
Suction the airway tube with a soft catheter, then reassess
Add air to the cuff until the secretions stop rising
