Very preterm newborns lose heat rapidly. Placing the body in plastic wrap or a bag without drying it, plus a hat and a warm environment, reduces heat loss.
q1qzjqnm: At 1 minute, a newborn has a pink body with blue hands and feet, a heart rate of 110, grimaces when stimulated, some flexion of the arms and legs and a weak cry. What is the APGAR score?
Appearance 1, pulse 2, grimace 1, activity 1 and respiration 1 total 6.
qaoi65p: A woman about 10 weeks pregnant has heavy vaginal bleeding and cramping. Her pulse is 118. What is the most appropriate care?
Treat for shock and bring any passed tissue
Pack the vagina with gauze to stop the bleeding
Have her walk to the ambulance
Wait on scene until the bleeding stops
Early pregnancy loss can cause heavy bleeding and shock. Treat for shock, bring passed tissue to the hospital and provide emotional support.
qbmbbi9: After delivering a healthy baby, the placenta has not delivered after 30 minutes. What should you do?
Transport without pulling on the cord
Reach inside the uterus to remove the placenta
Cut the cord at the vagina and push it back in
Pulling on the cord can tear it or invert the uterus. The mother is transported with monitoring for bleeding.
qjml4r: A 67-year-old found outdoors in winter is confused and no longer shivering, with a core temperature of 29 C (84 F) and a pulse of 42. Why should you move him gently and keep him horizontal?
Rough handling can trigger ventricular fibrillation
Gentle handling allows his muscles to resume shivering
Moving him upright helps blood return to the brain faster
Rough handling causes the skin to rewarm too quickly
A severely cold heart is irritable, and jarring movement can trigger ventricular fibrillation. Remove wet clothing, insulate him and keep him horizontal during transport.
q16zswfu: A hiker has frozen, waxy toes and must walk out through deep snow for several more hours before reaching transport. What should you do about the toes?
Leave them frozen until refreezing can be prevented
Rub them vigorously with snow to restore circulation
Rewarm them beside the campfire before the hike out
Thaw them in warm water, then continue the walk out
Thawing followed by refreezing causes much worse tissue damage than leaving the part frozen until definitive rewarming. Protect the area, pad it and never rub frostbitten tissue.
q6ewthj: Lightning strikes a group of hikers. Several are down. Which patients should receive care first?
Those who are pulseless and apneic
Those who are awake and talking with burns
Those with confusion and ringing in the ears
Those who are walking with minor injuries

Unlike standard triage, lightning patients in cardiac or respiratory arrest are treated first because they often recover with prompt CPR and ventilation. Conscious patients usually survive, so this is called reverse triage.
qri6ww1: A 35-year-old finished a marathon after drinking water at every station. She is confused with a headache and vomiting, a normal temperature and a glucose of 94 mg/dL. What should you suspect?

Drinking excess water during endurance events dilutes blood sodium, causing headache, confusion, vomiting and seizures. Giving large volumes of fluid can make it worse, so she needs prompt hospital evaluation.
q11i1i5l: A scuba diver made a rapid ascent and within 2 minutes of surfacing developed chest pain and weakness of one arm. What is the most likely cause?
Delayed decompression sickness from long bottom time

Gas forced into the arterial circulation during rapid ascent causes stroke-like and cardiac symptoms within minutes of surfacing. Give high-concentration oxygen, keep the patient supine and transport toward recompression.
qkvg96b: A 40-year-old was bitten on the ankle by a rattlesnake 10 minutes ago. Swelling is spreading. What is appropriate care?
Immobilize the leg and mark the swelling edge
Apply a tight tourniquet above the bite to trap the venom
Make a small incision and suction out the venom
Pit viper bites are managed by keeping the patient calm, immobilizing the limb, removing rings or tight items and marking the advancing swelling. Tourniquets, ice, cutting and suction cause harm.
q1d5cevf: A 31-year-old with suspected hyperactive delirium, sometimes called excited delirium, was hot, sweaty and fighting restraints. He suddenly becomes quiet and still. What should you do?
Check breathing and pulse at once
Let him rest since he has finally calmed down
Tighten the restraints before he becomes agitated again
Turn him prone so he cannot strike the crew
Sudden quiet in a severely agitated, hyperthermic patient may mean respiratory or cardiac arrest. Check immediately and start resuscitation if needed.
qz8j74k: How should a combative patient be positioned once physical restraint is required?
Supine or on the side, continuously monitored
Prone with wrists and ankles tied together behind him
Prone with a long backboard strapped over his back
Seated with a blanket held over his face to calm him

Prone and hobble positions, and any weight on the back, can cause positional asphyxia and death. Restrained patients are placed supine or on their side with continuous monitoring of breathing and mental status.
qvx473f: You are dispatched to a man who is waving a knife and threatening his neighbors. What should you do?
Stage until law enforcement secures the scene
Approach calmly and try to talk him into putting it down
Enter with your partner and restrain him together
Cancel the call because it is a law enforcement matter
Responder safety comes first. EMS stages at a safe distance and enters only after police have secured the scene, then provides care.
q3h24v2: A 74-year-old with COPD is newly combative and confused. Her SpO2 is 82 percent and her glucose is 110 mg/dL. What is the most likely cause of the behavior?
Hypoxia commonly causes confusion, restlessness and combativeness. Medical causes of behavior change are identified and treated before assuming a psychiatric cause.
qttunwy: A 40-year-old says he feels hopeless and has been giving away his belongings. What is the best way to assess suicide risk?
Ask directly whether he is thinking of suicide
Avoid the topic because asking may plant the idea
Change the subject to something more positive
Reassure him that things will get better soon
Asking directly about suicidal thoughts and plans does not increase risk and is the best way to identify patients who need emergency evaluation. Giving away belongings is a warning sign.
q1p79wf2: A 23-year-old has right lower abdominal pain that began near the umbilicus, with fever, nausea and pain when the ambulance hits bumps. What should you suspect?

Appendicitis classically begins with pain around the umbilicus that moves to the right lower quadrant, often with fever, nausea and pain on movement. Transport in a position of comfort and give nothing by mouth.
qli292o: A 2-year-old with vomiting received a 20 mL/kg isotonic bolus. He is still listless with a capillary refill of 4 seconds and a heart rate of 170, and his lungs are clear. What should you do next?
Repeat the isotonic bolus and reassess perfusion
Stop fluids because one bolus is the limit for children
Switch to oral fluids now that one bolus is in
Give dextrose 50 percent for the poor perfusion
Persistent signs of poor perfusion after one bolus in a child without signs of fluid overload call for another isotonic bolus with reassessment after each one.
q17x4uzj: A 38-year-old man has sudden severe left flank pain that radiates to his groin. He is restless and cannot find a comfortable position, and he has blood in his urine. What is the most likely cause?
Kidney stones cause colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, restlessness and blood in the urine. In an older patient, an abdominal aortic aneurysm must also be considered.
q1aevt0l: You are assessing a 48-year-old man before intubation. Using the 3-3-2 approach, you find only one fingerbreadth between the hyoid bone and the top of the thyroid cartilage. What does this suggest?
A high, anterior larynx that is hard to visualize
Mouth opening too narrow to insert a laryngoscope blade
Probable difficulty obtaining a bag-valve-mask seal
Restricted neck extension from cervical arthritis
Fewer than two fingerbreadths from hyoid to thyroid cartilage means the larynx sits high and anterior, so the glottis is harder to bring into the line of sight.
q6puevn: A 55-year-old woman sitting upright opens her mouth and protrudes her tongue. You can see only her hard palate; the soft palate and uvula are hidden. What does this predict?
An easy view with a curved blade
A high risk of aspiration during bag-valve-mask ventilation
A normal airway needing no special preparation
Seeing only the hard palate (Mallampati class IV) predicts a poor laryngoscopic view, so a bougie, video laryngoscope, supraglottic airway and surgical backup should be ready.
qkp4z9p: A 62-year-old alert man needs rapid sequence intubation for worsening pneumonia. SpO2 is 95 percent on a nonrebreather mask. Which preoxygenation approach best fills his lungs with oxygen before induction?
At least 3 minutes of high-flow oxygen with tidal breathing
One minute of nasal cannula oxygen at 4 L/min
Rapid bag-valve-mask ventilation at 30 breaths/min for 1 minute
Room air until induction so the oximeter shows his true baseline
Several minutes of tidal breathing on high-flow oxygen washes nitrogen out of the lungs, creating an oxygen reservoir that lengthens safe apnea time.
q1pe3yma: A 160-kg woman needs to be intubated. How should she be positioned to improve both preoxygenation and the laryngoscopic view?
Ramped, ear canal level with the sternal notch
Flat supine with a rolled towel under her shoulders
Head-down tilt to improve venous return to the heart
Left lateral recumbent with the neck flexed forward
Ramping an obese patient so the external ear canal lines up with the sternal notch improves the glottic view and reduces the abdominal pressure that speeds desaturation.
q1tkdexy: During your first intubation attempt on a 50-year-old man, his SpO2 falls from 99 to 89 percent and you still cannot see the vocal cords. What should you do?
Stop and reoxygenate with a bag-valve mask
Keep going until the cords are seen, since the oximeter reading lags
Pass the tube blindly and check it with capnography
Have your partner apply cricoid pressure and continue looking
Falling saturation means the attempt should end; reoxygenate with a bag-valve mask and change something (position, device or operator) before the next attempt.
q1e90rcb: A 67-year-old septic patient needs intubation for a worsening mental status. BP is 74/40 and HR is 128. What should be addressed before induction drugs are given?
Hypotension, with fluids or vasopressors per protocol
Hypothermia, by warming the patient compartment first
Hyperventilation, by bagging at a slower rate beforehand
Agitation, by applying soft restraints to both arms and legs
Induction drugs and positive pressure ventilation commonly drop blood pressure further, so resuscitating the hypotension first reduces the risk of peri-intubation cardiac arrest.
q1nifb85: A 24-year-old in severe diabetic ketoacidosis is breathing deeply at 34/min with an ETCO2 of 16 mmHg. After he is intubated, how should his ventilation be managed?
Match his high pre-intubation minute ventilation
Ventilate at 10 breaths/min to prevent barotrauma
Let the ETCO2 rise to 40 mmHg so it is normal
Ventilate only when the SpO2 falls below 90 percent
His low CO2 is compensation for a severe metabolic acidosis; ventilating at a normal rate lets CO2 rise, the pH falls sharply and cardiac arrest can follow.
ql7p8li: On laryngoscopy of a 44-year-old man you can see the epiglottis but none of the glottic opening. Which device is most helpful for passing the tube?
With an epiglottis-only view a bougie can be steered under the epiglottis; clicks against the tracheal rings or hold-up in a small airway confirm placement before the tube is passed over it.
q1bqfvcz: During laryngoscopy you can see only the posterior part of the vocal cords. Which maneuver may improve your view?
Backward, upward and rightward pressure on the thyroid cartilage
Firm pressure on the cricoid cartilage throughout the attempt
Turning the patient's head toward the left shoulder
Pressing downward on the forehead while lifting the patient's chin
External laryngeal manipulation, such as backward, upward and rightward pressure on the thyroid cartilage, moves the larynx into view; cricoid pressure can actually worsen the view.
qhde8xu: After intubating an adult you check the endotracheal tube cuff with a manometer. Which cuff pressure range is generally recommended?
A cuff pressure of about 20 to 30 cm H2O seals the airway while limiting injury to the tracheal lining; cuffs inflated by feel are often far too tight.
q8i8ao8: After intubating a 5-foot-2-inch woman, you hear breath sounds only on the right. The tube is at 27 cm at the teeth and the ETCO2 waveform is normal. What should you do?
Deflate the cuff and pull back slightly while listening
Remove the tube completely and reintubate with a smaller size
Perform needle decompression of the left side of the chest
Advance the tube 2 cm further and then reassess breath sounds
A normal waveform with right-only breath sounds and a deep tube suggests a right mainstem intubation; withdrawing the tube a short distance usually restores left-sided ventilation.
qfgjoz2: A ventilated 30-year-old after a fall from height has rising airway pressures, absent breath sounds on the left, BP 70/40 and distended neck veins. What should you do?
Perform needle decompression on the left
Increase the PEEP to reinflate the left lung
Withdraw the tube 2 cm and recheck
Increase the tidal volume to improve oxygenation
Positive pressure ventilation can rapidly turn a pneumothorax into a tension pneumothorax; hypotension with distended neck veins and absent breath sounds needs immediate decompression.
qtstbuh: The transport ventilator on an intubated patient sounds a low-pressure alarm and the exhaled tidal volumes have dropped sharply. What is the most likely cause?
A leak or disconnection in the circuit
A mucus plug in the tube

Low pressure with loss of returned volume points to a leak, such as a disconnected circuit, a deflated cuff or a tube pulled above the cords; obstruction, bronchospasm and pneumothorax raise pressures.
qif372c: You hear air escaping from the mouth of an intubated patient with each breath, and the pilot balloon is flat. Tube depth is unchanged and the ETCO2 waveform persists but is smaller. What is the first step?
Reinflate the cuff and see if it holds
Remove the tube immediately and insert a supraglottic airway instead
Increase the tidal volume to make up for the lost volume
Advance the tube 3 cm so the cuff sits deeper in the trachea
A deflated cuff with the tube still in place is first managed by reinflating it; if the cuff will not hold air, the tube needs to be exchanged.
qhcri2w: An intubated, sedated 52-year-old has a normal square ETCO2 waveform, but over 20 minutes his ETCO2 has risen from 38 to 56 mmHg. SpO2 is 97 percent and BP is stable. What is the most appropriate adjustment?
A rising ETCO2 with a normal waveform means CO2 is not being removed fast enough; increasing the rate or tidal volume increases CO2 elimination.
qajqrbn: The capnography waveform of a patient being bagged no longer returns to zero between breaths; the baseline now sits at 8 mmHg. What does this indicate?
An elevated baseline means the inhaled gas contains CO2, as with a faulty exhalation valve, inadequate fresh gas flow or a contaminated sensor, so the equipment should be checked.
qf70bqo: You intubate a 40-year-old with a pulse who had been drinking soda shortly before he became unresponsive. Capnography shows small waveforms for 4 breaths that steadily fade to zero. What is the most likely explanation?
The tube is in the esophagus
The tube is in the right mainstem bronchus
His cardiac output has suddenly improved
CO2 from stomach contents can produce a few waveforms after an esophageal intubation, but they fade within several breaths; a sustained waveform is required to confirm tracheal placement.
q1az0q8m: An intubated patient's capnogram shows a regular plateau with a small notch dipping into it on each breath. What does this notch most likely mean?
The patient is starting to breathe on his own
The tube has migrated into the esophagus
CO2 is being rebreathed from the circuit
The patient has gone into cardiac arrest
A cleft in the plateau appears when the patient makes spontaneous respiratory efforts, often as paralysis or sedation wears off, and may signal the need for more sedation.
qbdfpsv: A ventilated 58-year-old who had hip surgery 3 days ago suddenly has his ETCO2 drop from 36 to 18 mmHg with an unchanged waveform shape. SpO2 falls to 85 percent and BP to 78/50. What is the most likely cause?

An abrupt ETCO2 drop with a preserved waveform plus hypotension and hypoxia suggests a sudden loss of pulmonary blood flow, such as a massive PE; extubation gives a flat line and a kink raises pressures.
q5d4q16: During CPR on an intubated 63-year-old, ETCO2 has been 14 mmHg. It suddenly jumps to 42 mmHg with no change in ventilation. What does this most likely indicate?
Displacement of the tube into the esophagus
Fatigue of the person doing compressions
An abrupt, sustained rise in ETCO2 during CPR is an early sign of ROSC because restored blood flow delivers more CO2 to the lungs; confirm with a pulse check.
q18re1f6: During CPR you intubate an adult. Capnography shows a consistent waveform with every breath and a value of 12 mmHg. How should you interpret this?
Tracheal placement with low blood flow
The tube is in the esophagus and must be removed now
The tube has entered the right mainstem bronchus
The capnography sensor is faulty and should be replaced
A persistent waveform confirms the tube is in the trachea even during arrest; the low number reflects limited pulmonary blood flow, not misplacement.
q4fl9ef: A 66-year-old on a transport ventilator for acute pulmonary edema has an SpO2 of 86 percent on 100 percent oxygen with PEEP of 5 cm H2O. BP is 148/90 and tube position is confirmed. Which change is most likely to improve oxygenation?
Lower the tidal volume to 4 mL/kg
PEEP holds fluid-filled alveoli open and improves oxygenation; with an adequate blood pressure, raising PEEP is the usual next step when oxygen is already at 100 percent.
q1tvgict: An intubated 26-year-old asthmatic on a ventilator has high peak pressures, and the expiratory flow does not return to zero before the next breath starts. Which change best reduces air trapping?
Slow the rate to allow longer exhalation
Raise the respiratory rate to clear CO2 faster
Increase the PEEP to 15 cm H2O
In severe asthma the lungs need a long time to empty; a slower rate lengthens exhalation, reducing trapped air (auto-PEEP), even if CO2 rises somewhat.
q1r62562: During a critical care transfer of a patient with ARDS, which ventilator goal reflects a lung-protective strategy?
Plateau pressure at or below 30 cm H2O
Tidal volumes of 12 mL/kg to recruit alveoli
PEEP of zero to avoid barotrauma
Lung-protective ventilation in ARDS uses small tidal volumes and limits plateau pressure to about 30 cm H2O or less to reduce further lung injury.
q16fcgx6: A 45-year-old admitted 2 days ago with severe pancreatitis is being transferred. He has worsening hypoxia despite high-flow oxygen, bilateral infiltrates on chest x-ray, flat neck veins and no cardiac history. What condition is most likely?
ARDS is an inflammatory, noncardiogenic lung injury triggered by conditions such as sepsis, pancreatitis or major trauma, causing refractory hypoxia with bilateral infiltrates.
q1x4klw0: How does CPAP improve oxygenation in a patient with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
It keeps alveoli open and reduces preload
It increases heart rate and contractility
It removes fluid from the alveoli by suction
CPAP splints alveoli open to improve gas exchange and raises intrathoracic pressure, which reduces venous return (preload) to the failing heart.
q19y1kgl: Compared with CPAP, what does BiPAP add for a patient with a COPD exacerbation and CO2 retention?
A guaranteed higher delivered oxygen concentration
Built-in protection of the airway from aspiration
A lower risk of hypotension because chest pressure is lower
BiPAP delivers a higher inspiratory pressure above the expiratory pressure, increasing tidal volume and helping clear CO2, whereas CPAP holds one constant pressure.
q1ekz4b9: A 71-year-old with COPD has been on CPAP for 15 minutes. He is now hard to arouse, respirations are shallow at 8/min and ETCO2 has climbed to 74 mmHg. What should you do?
Remove CPAP and ventilate with a bag-valve mask
Continue CPAP and recheck in 10 minutes
A falling mental status with rising CO2 means noninvasive ventilation is failing; he needs assisted ventilation and likely an advanced airway.
q1chr4rj: You must perform a surgical cricothyrotomy on a 40-year-old. Where is the incision through the membrane made?
Between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages
Between the hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage
Between the first and second tracheal rings
The cricothyroid membrane lies between the thyroid cartilage above and the cricoid ring below; it is superficial and relatively avascular.
q17w20h8: A 6-year-old with an obstructed upper airway is being oxygenated through a needle cricothyrotomy. Which problem limits how long this technique can be relied on?
A needle cricothyrotomy can oxygenate but allows poor exhalation, so CO2 accumulates; it is only a temporary bridge to a definitive airway.
qkd91b7: A 68-year-old who had a total laryngectomy is apneic. A stoma is visible at the base of his neck. How should you ventilate him?
Through the stoma with a small mask
With a standard adult mask sealed over the mouth and nose
Through the mouth after placing an oropharyngeal airway
With a nasal cannula running at 15 L/min
After a total laryngectomy the trachea no longer connects to the mouth or nose, so ventilation must be delivered through the stoma, often with an infant or pediatric mask.
qljpu8a: A 3-year-old's tracheostomy tube came out at home and the parents could not replace it. The child is cyanotic. You have a same-size tube and one a half size smaller. What should you do first?
Insert a replacement tube into the stoma
Ventilate with a mask over the mouth and nose only
Intubate orally with a tube two sizes larger
Reinserting a tube into the existing stoma, trying the smaller size if needed, is the fastest way to restore the airway; if that fails, ventilate through the stoma or by mouth with the stoma covered.
q1tdhuit: A 50-year-old choked on steak and became unresponsive. You cannot ventilate him despite several cycles of CPR. Which advanced technique should you use?
Repeated blind finger sweeps of the posterior pharynx
Abdominal thrusts with the patient supine
Insert a supraglottic airway and ventilate through it
Paramedics can look directly into the upper airway with a laryngoscope and remove a visible obstruction with Magill forceps; blind sweeps can push the object deeper.
qkkzg8b: You are opening the airway of an unresponsive 4-month-old lying supine on the stretcher. His head flexes forward. What should you do?
Place a folded towel under the shoulders
Hyperextend the neck as for an adult
Place a pillow under the head
Turn the head to one side
An infant's large occiput flexes the neck when supine; padding under the shoulders brings the airway into a neutral position.
qf2je1e: Using the age-based formula for cuffed tubes, which endotracheal tube size is appropriate for a 6-year-old?
For cuffed tubes the size is about age divided by 4 plus 3.5, so a 6-year-old needs roughly 5.0 mm; a half size larger and smaller should be ready.
q1g279lk: During intubation of a 2-year-old, the heart rate falls from 140 to 70/min and the SpO2 to 80 percent. What should you do?
Stop and ventilate with oxygen by bag-valve mask
Give atropine and continue the attempt
Pass the tube as quickly as possible
Bradycardia during pediatric intubation is usually caused by hypoxia; stopping to oxygenate usually reverses it.
qxb14km: An unvaccinated 5-year-old is sitting upright and drooling, with a muffled voice, a temperature of 39.8 C (103.6 F) and soft inspiratory stridor. What is the best approach?
Keep him calm in a position of comfort
Examine the throat with a tongue blade to confirm the cause
Place him supine and insert an oropharyngeal airway
Attempt intubation now before he gets worse
These signs suggest epiglottitis; agitating the child or instrumenting the throat can cause complete obstruction, so keep him calm, give oxygen as tolerated and transport with airway equipment ready.
q1qzgdfb: A 15-year-old with asthma has been wheezing for hours. Now he is drowsy, his chest is nearly silent and SpO2 is 86 percent. What does the silent chest indicate?
Minimal air movement and impending arrest
The bronchospasm is resolving and airflow is improving
Pneumonia has developed and replaced the wheezing
Hyperventilation from anxiety that will settle with coaching
A silent chest in a tiring asthmatic means too little air is moving to produce a wheeze; with drowsiness it signals impending respiratory arrest and the need for assisted ventilation.
qzve2ej: A 34-year-old rescued from a house fire has singed nasal hair, soot in his sputum and a hoarse voice that is getting worse. SpO2 is 96 percent. What is the key airway concern?
Swelling that may close the airway
Carbon monoxide causing a falsely low SpO2 reading
Bronchospasm that should be managed with CPAP
Aspiration of gastric contents during transport
Progressive hoarseness after inhalation injury signals upper airway edema; early definitive airway management may be needed before swelling makes intubation impossible.
q1m65b4c: What is an advantage of a second-generation supraglottic airway with a gastric channel?
It allows the stomach to be decompressed
It completely protects the lungs from aspiration
It can be inserted in patients with an intact gag reflex
It provides confirmation that the tube is in the trachea
The gastric channel lets air and fluid vent from the stomach or a gastric tube be passed, reducing the risk of regurgitation, although it does not fully protect against aspiration.
q1jvbmo6: A 58-year-old has rapidly progressing tongue and lip swelling with a muffled voice, and you decide he needs an advanced airway. How should you prepare?
Be ready for a surgical airway if intubation fails
Plan blind nasal intubation as the only option
Use a supraglottic airway as the primary device
Wait until he becomes apneic before intervening
With upper airway swelling, intubation can fail and supraglottic devices may not seal, so a double setup with the neck prepared for cricothyrotomy is essential.
q1y1smxg: A septic 70-year-old has an ABG of pH 7.24, PaCO2 26 mmHg and HCO3 11 mEq/L. How should it be interpreted?
Mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic alkalosis together
A low pH with a low bicarbonate is a metabolic acidosis; the low PaCO2 reflects the lungs blowing off CO2 to compensate.
q36dcv3: A 22-year-old with severe anxiety, tingling fingers and carpopedal spasm has an ABG of pH 7.53, PaCO2 27 mmHg and HCO3 24 mEq/L. What is the acid-base disorder?
A high pH with a low PaCO2 and a normal bicarbonate is an acute respiratory alkalosis; serious causes such as pulmonary embolism should still be considered before blaming anxiety.
q1w4y3jg: A 40-year-old has vomited repeatedly for 4 days. His ABG shows pH 7.51, PaCO2 47 mmHg and HCO3 35 mEq/L. Which disorder is present?
Losing stomach acid raises bicarbonate; a high pH and high HCO3 identify metabolic alkalosis, and the slightly raised PaCO2 is compensatory hypoventilation.
q57vkgl: A 74-year-old with long-standing COPD who is at his baseline has an ABG of pH 7.36, PaCO2 62 mmHg and HCO3 34 mEq/L. How should it be interpreted?
Acute respiratory acidosis requiring immediate intubation
A near-normal pH with high PaCO2 and high bicarbonate shows the kidneys have retained bicarbonate over time to offset chronic CO2 retention.
q1tzxxuf: A 69-year-old is dizzy. The rhythm strip shows regular P waves at 84/min, with every other P wave followed by a narrow QRS. The PR interval of the conducted beats is constant. What is the rhythm?
Second-degree AV block with 2 to 1 conduction

When every second P wave is blocked, the block cannot be firmly classified as type I or type II; it is described as 2 to 1 second-degree AV block, and a wide QRS makes an infranodal (more dangerous) block more likely.
qbbohse: A rhythm strip shows regular P waves at 80/min and regular narrow QRS complexes at 44/min, with no consistent relationship between them; the P waves march through the QRS complexes. What is the rhythm?
Third-degree AV block with a junctional escape
Atria and ventricles beating independently is complete heart block; a narrow escape rhythm in the 40s to 50s arises from the AV junction and is usually more stable than a wide ventricular escape.
qpwx1kw: A 54-year-old on methadone collapses. The monitor shows a wide-complex tachycardia whose QRS amplitude repeatedly grows and shrinks, appearing to twist around the baseline. What is this rhythm?
Torsades de pointes is a polymorphic VT with twisting amplitude linked to a prolonged QT interval, which methadone and many other drugs can cause.
q170a7as: A 73-year-old has had palpitations for an unknown number of days. The monitor shows an irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm at 128/min. He is alert with BP 132/80. Why is elective cardioversion avoided in the field?
It may dislodge a clot from the atria
It will convert the rhythm into asystole
It is ineffective for atrial rhythms
It requires general anesthesia in all patients
Atrial fibrillation lasting more than about 48 hours, or of unknown duration, may have formed atrial clots that can embolize when sinus rhythm returns, causing a stroke.
qdky28b: A 22-year-old with palpitations has an irregular wide-complex tachycardia at 240/min with QRS complexes that vary in width. He has a history of an accessory pathway. BP is 118/72. Which treatment approach must be avoided?
In atrial fibrillation with an accessory pathway (pre-excitation), blocking the AV node can push more impulses down the accessory pathway and trigger ventricular fibrillation.
q1olox9v: During CPR on a 66-year-old, the rhythm check shows a flat line in lead II. What should you do?
Confirm in another lead and check the gain
Defibrillate in case it is fine VF
Stop CPR, since asystole is not survivable
Before treating as asystole, confirm the leads are connected, the gain is adequate and the flat line persists in another lead, so fine VF is not missed; CPR continues meanwhile.
q1cc39s6: A 67-year-old on a ventilator for COPD loses his pulse. The monitor shows a narrow-complex rhythm at 130/min. Breath sounds are absent on the right and his neck veins are distended. Which cause of PEA is most likely?
A fast, narrow PEA suggests a mechanical problem; absent breath sounds and distended neck veins in a ventilated COPD patient point to tension pneumothorax, which needs decompression.
q10ldwds: A 58-year-old dialysis patient who has missed two treatments is pulseless. The monitor shows slow, very wide, bizarre complexes at 30/min. Which reversible cause is most likely?
Slow, wide PEA in a patient who has missed dialysis strongly suggests hyperkalemia, which needs specific treatment along with high-quality CPR.
q1la9ao3: A 77-year-old with several days of black, tarry stools becomes pulseless. The monitor shows a narrow-complex rhythm at 120/min. Which treatment addresses the most likely cause?
A fast, narrow PEA after GI bleeding points to hypovolemia; restoring volume, ideally with blood where available, treats the cause while CPR continues.
qwx14f3: A 61-year-old has chest pain with ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6 and ST depression in III. Which coronary artery is most likely involved?
ST elevation limited to the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6) usually reflects occlusion of the circumflex artery or one of its branches.
qrkjqrh: A 64-year-old has chest pain. His 12-lead shows ST depression in III and aVF and subtle ST elevation in I and aVL. How should this be interpreted?
High lateral STEMI with inferior reciprocal changes
Inferior ischemia only, not a STEMI
A normal variant in an older adult
ST depression in the inferior leads can be the mirror image of a high lateral infarction; subtle elevation in I and aVL with reciprocal inferior depression should be treated as STEMI.
qugttku: A 59-year-old with an inferior STEMI has more ST elevation in lead III than in lead II, with ST depression in lead I. Which artery is most likely occluded?
In an inferior STEMI, ST elevation greater in III than II with depression in lead I points to the right coronary artery, which also raises concern for right ventricular involvement.
q1w1v4h9: A 70-year-old with crushing chest pain and BP 92/60 has ST elevation in aVR and widespread ST depression in most other leads. What does this pattern suggest?
ST elevation in aVR with diffuse ST depression suggests severe ischemia from left main or three-vessel disease, a high-risk pattern needing rapid transport to a PCI-capable center.
q1ltt7eq: A 51-year-old had chest pain yesterday that has now resolved. His 12-lead shows deep, symmetric T-wave inversions in V2 and V3 with no ST elevation. What is the concern?
Critical narrowing of the proximal LAD
A healed old infarction needing no action
Normal T waves for a middle-aged adult
This Wellens pattern indicates a critical proximal LAD stenosis with a high risk of a large anterior MI in the coming days, so the patient needs cardiology evaluation even though pain-free.
q18uuttk: A 48-year-old with ongoing chest pain has upsloping ST depression at the J point with tall, symmetric T waves across V1 to V6 and no ST elevation. How should this be handled?
As a STEMI equivalent from LAD occlusion
As nonspecific changes needing no special action
This de Winter pattern signals acute proximal LAD occlusion without classic ST elevation and should prompt activation of the STEMI system per protocol.
q14slkvs: A 75-year-old with a known left bundle branch block has chest pain. Which finding on his 12-lead most strongly suggests an acute MI?
ST elevation in the same direction as the QRS
ST elevation opposite to a deep negative QRS in V1
T waves opposite to the main QRS direction
In LBBB, ST segments normally go opposite the QRS; ST elevation of at least 1 mm in the same direction as the QRS (concordant) is a specific sign of acute infarction.
q8zvhbw: A healthy 23-year-old athlete has a 12-lead done after a minor injury. It shows concave ST elevation in V2 to V4 with a notched J point, no reciprocal depression, and no symptoms. What is the most likely explanation?
Concave ST elevation with J-point notching and no reciprocal changes in a young, asymptomatic person is typical of early repolarization, a common STEMI mimic.
qwombvz: A 31-year-old has sharp chest pain and diffuse ST elevation. Which additional ECG finding favors pericarditis over STEMI?
ST depression in leads opposite to the elevation
ST elevation confined to II, III and aVF
New Q waves in the anterior leads
Pericarditis typically causes widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal ST depression except in aVR; localized elevation with reciprocal depression favors STEMI.
q1mr1uv1: A 33-year-old fainted at rest. His ECG shows a right bundle branch-like pattern with coved ST elevation in V1 and V2. Why is this important?
It indicates a risk of sudden cardiac death
It is a normal finding in young men
It indicates an old septal infarction
It shows that the faint was vasovagal
Coved ST elevation in V1 and V2 with syncope suggests Brugada syndrome, which predisposes to ventricular fibrillation and requires hospital evaluation.
q2t3zp1: A 25-year-old marathon runner has a heart rate of 42/min in sinus rhythm during a screening exam. He is alert, BP is 118/70 and he has no complaints. What is the appropriate treatment?
No treatment for the slow rate
Bradycardia is treated only when it causes symptoms or poor perfusion; well-conditioned athletes often have resting rates in the 40s.
qdymlet: You are pacing a 74-year-old with complete heart block. Each pacer spike is followed by a wide QRS on the monitor. How should you confirm mechanical capture?
Palpate a femoral pulse that matches the paced rate
Palpate a carotid pulse during pacing
See that the pacer spikes appear on the screen
Watch for chest wall muscle twitching
Electrical capture on the monitor does not prove the heart is pumping; a femoral pulse matching the paced rate confirms mechanical capture, and carotid checks are confused by muscle twitching.
q1mgapp6: A 72-year-old has second-degree AV block type II with a wide QRS at 54/min. He is alert, BP 118/70, with no chest pain or dizziness. What is the most appropriate action?
Apply pacing pads and monitor closely
No monitoring is needed since he is stable
Type II block can suddenly progress to complete heart block, so pads should be on and ready for pacing even in a stable patient.
q1vw8lym: A 60-year-old who had a heart transplant 5 years ago has symptomatic bradycardia at 38/min with BP 78/44. Why is atropine unlikely to help?
The transplanted heart lacks vagal innervation
Transplant patients are allergic to atropine
Atropine only works for wide-complex rhythms
Atropine is used only in children
A transplanted heart is denervated, so blocking vagal tone has little effect; pacing or an adrenergic infusion is usually needed.
q1yphu3c: A 34-year-old with 2 days of fever and vomiting has a regular narrow-complex rhythm at 142/min with visible P waves before each QRS. The rate varies slightly with movement. BP is 104/66. What is the best management?
Vagal maneuvers to break the rhythm
Sinus tachycardia is a response to an underlying problem, such as fever, pain or hypovolemia; treating the cause is correct, and cardioversion or vagal maneuvers are not.
qwe4wx5: You deliver a synchronized shock to a hypotensive 66-year-old in atrial fibrillation with rapid response, but the rhythm does not change. Before delivering the next synchronized shock, what must you check?
That the sync mode is still selected
That the pads have been moved to the back
That the monitor is in pacing mode
That the patient's pulse is absent
Many monitors return to unsynchronized mode after each shock, so sync must be confirmed before every shock to avoid delivering it on the T wave.
q1l7nw79: A 29-year-old with stable SVT at 188/min is alert and normotensive. Which vagal technique is most likely to convert the rhythm?
Carotid massage on both sides at once

The modified Valsalva maneuver, a strain against resistance followed immediately by lying flat with legs raised, converts SVT more often than a standard Valsalva; eyeball pressure and bilateral carotid massage are dangerous.
q103jrj6: A 48-year-old had a witnessed collapse with immediate bystander CPR. He remains in VF after three shocks. A mechanical CPR device is in place and your system has an ECPR center 15 minutes away. What is the most appropriate step?
Early transport to the ECPR center per protocol
Continue on scene for 60 minutes before moving
Stop resuscitation after the third failed shock
Transport to the nearest non-ECPR hospital

Refractory VF in a young patient with a witnessed arrest and good bystander CPR is the classic ECPR candidate; early transport with mechanical CPR is needed because outcomes depend on the time to bypass.
q1ic3olm: You are ventilating an intubated 59-year-old after ROSC. Which ETCO2 range is generally targeted?
Post-arrest ventilation aims for normal CO2 levels; hyperventilation lowers CO2 and reduces cerebral blood flow, while hypoventilation worsens acidosis.
q1ui26n5: A 57-year-old has ROSC after a VF arrest. His post-ROSC 12-lead shows ST elevation in V1 to V4. Where should he be transported?
The closest emergency department regardless of capability
Post-arrest patients with STEMI benefit from emergency coronary angiography, so they should go to a PCI-capable center, ideally a designated cardiac arrest center.
q1h3ivcb: A comatose 62-year-old has ROSC after a cardiac arrest. Which temperature-related practice is not recommended in the prehospital setting?
Rapid infusion of cold IV fluids
Routine prehospital cooling with rapid cold IV fluid infusion has not improved outcomes and has caused pulmonary edema and re-arrest; preventing fever remains part of post-arrest care.
qe7v8v3: A 3-month-old has a heart rate of 270/min with a narrow QRS, no visible P waves and no beat-to-beat variation. The parents say he was feeding normally an hour ago. What is the most likely rhythm?
In infants, SVT is usually above 220/min with absent P waves, a fixed rate and abrupt onset; sinus tachycardia is usually lower, varies with activity and follows a cause such as fever or dehydration.
q1u6nrea: A 6-month-old has a narrow-complex tachycardia at 280/min. He is lethargic and mottled with weak pulses. No vascular access has been obtained yet. What is the appropriate treatment?
Wait for IO access before any treatment
Unstable SVT with poor perfusion needs immediate synchronized cardioversion when vascular access is not available; delaying for access worsens shock.
qir257c: A 20-kg child is in ventricular fibrillation. What energy should be used for the first defibrillation?
The initial pediatric defibrillation dose is 2 J/kg, so 40 J for a 20-kg child; later shocks are increased to 4 J/kg or more.
qav0i6l: You are preparing to defibrillate a 5-month-old in VF, but the adult-size pads would touch each other on the front of the chest. What should you do?
Place one pad on the front and one on the back
Overlap the pads slightly on the front of the chest
Cut the pads to a smaller size
Place both pads on the back
Pads must not touch; when the chest is too small, anterior-posterior placement allows the current to pass through the heart without arcing between pads.
q3oi8xh: A 10-month-old with bronchiolitis is limp, with a heart rate of 58/min, SpO2 of 70 percent and poor perfusion. No ventilation has been given yet. What is the first priority?
Ventilate with oxygen by bag-valve mask
Bradycardia in children is most often caused by hypoxia; oxygenation and ventilation come first, and compressions start if the rate stays below 60 with poor perfusion despite effective ventilation.
qd90791: A 66-year-old dialysis patient has weakness. The 12-lead shows tall, narrow, peaked T waves with otherwise normal intervals. What do these findings suggest?
Peaked T waves are usually the first ECG sign of rising potassium; with further rises the P wave flattens, the QRS widens and a sine-wave pattern can precede arrest.
q1u249c9: A 79-year-old found outdoors in winter has a core temperature of 30 C (86 F). The ECG shows sinus bradycardia with a distinct hump at the end of each QRS complex. What is this finding?
Osborn waves, an extra deflection at the J point, are characteristic of hypothermia and tend to grow as the temperature falls.
q9t8yca: A 68-year-old woman is sitting bolt upright with pink, frothy sputum, crackles throughout, BP 222/124 and SpO2 84 percent. She is alert and follows commands. Which intervention should be started first?
Hypertensive acute pulmonary edema responds rapidly to CPAP, usually combined with nitrates per protocol; fluids and lying flat worsen the congestion.
qamee6e: A 64-year-old with an anterior STEMI is cool and clammy, with BP 76/48, crackles to the mid-lung fields and SpO2 89 percent. What should be avoided?
Rapid transport to a PCI-capable center
Oxygen to keep SpO2 above 90 percent
This is cardiogenic shock; nitrates worsen hypotension and large fluid volumes worsen pulmonary edema, so management focuses on careful hemodynamic support and rapid reperfusion.
q1pdaui6: A 71-year-old with severe COPD has distended neck veins, swollen ankles and an enlarged, tender liver. His lungs have scattered wheezes but no crackles. Which condition do these findings suggest?
Right heart failure, often from chronic lung disease, causes systemic venous congestion such as JVD, edema and liver enlargement, without the pulmonary crackles of left-sided failure.
qzovhys: A 63-year-old has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to his back, a weak left radial pulse and ST elevation in II, III and aVF. What is the key concern?
A dissection extending into the right coronary artery
A routine inferior STEMI needing standard treatment only
Acute pericarditis from a viral illness
Gastroesophageal reflux with a nonspecific ECG
An aortic dissection can involve a coronary artery and cause STEMI; recognizing it matters because antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy can be catastrophic, so the receiving center must be told.
qo3pmqq: A 72-year-old man suddenly developed severe low back and flank pain, then fainted. He has a pulsatile abdominal mass and BP 84/50. What is the most appropriate approach?
Rapid transport to a center with vascular surgery
Large fluid boluses to bring the systolic BP to 140 mmHg
Transport to the nearest clinic for imaging
A suspected ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm needs surgery; limit scene time, avoid raising the BP to normal, and transport to a facility that can repair it.
qlrunlg: A 69-year-old has left arm weakness, right gaze deviation and neglect starting 50 minutes ago. Your regional plan allows bypassing a primary stroke center 10 minutes away for a thrombectomy-capable center 25 minutes away when an LVO is suspected. Where should she go?
The primary stroke center 10 minutes away
With a positive LVO screen and modest added time, direct transport to a thrombectomy-capable center speeds clot retrieval, as regional stroke plans allow.
qot8iax: A 58-year-old suddenly develops right-sided weakness. Which feature most suggests a hemorrhagic rather than an ischemic stroke?
Severe headache, vomiting and falling LOC
Slurred speech that began on waking
Sudden severe headache with vomiting and a declining level of consciousness suggests raised intracranial pressure from bleeding, although only imaging can confirm the stroke type.
q1dpxace: A 35-year-old with epilepsy had a witnessed generalized seizure 20 minutes ago and now has right arm weakness. Glucose is 112 mg/dL. Which condition can mimic a stroke in this patient?
Temporary weakness after a seizure (Todd paralysis) is a common stroke mimic, though a stroke cannot be ruled out in the field and the history should be clearly reported.
q15z14o9: A 74-year-old with an acute ischemic stroke 1 hour ago has BP 196/104. She is alert with stable vital signs otherwise. What is the appropriate field management of her blood pressure?
Monitor it without trying to lower it
Give a large fluid bolus to protect the brain
Lay her flat with legs raised
Elevated blood pressure helps perfuse threatened brain tissue, so it is not lowered in the field unless directed by medical control; the hospital manages it according to treatment plans.
qtuwh9o: A 61-year-old has sudden vertigo, vomiting, double vision and cannot walk without falling. His face, arm drift and speech are normal. What should you suspect?
Posterior circulation strokes often spare the face, arms and speech, so screening tools that include balance and eye findings help detect them.
qws35k8: A 57-year-old with lung cancer is short of breath and hypotensive. The 12-lead shows low voltage, and the QRS height alternates from beat to beat. What does this suggest?
Low voltage with electrical alternans, the heart swinging within a large fluid-filled pericardium, suggests a large effusion and possible tamponade.
q1vb34qo: A 63-year-old with a left ventricular assist device is alert and talking. You cannot palpate a radial pulse and the automatic BP cuff gives no reading. What is the best interpretation?
This can be normal with a continuous-flow device
He is in cardiac arrest and needs compressions
The device has failed and must be switched off
He is in hypovolemic shock and needs fluids
Continuous-flow LVADs often produce no palpable pulse or measurable cuff pressure; perfusion is judged by mental status, skin signs and device alarms, and an alert patient is not in arrest.
q1cr445d: A rhythm strip shows a regular narrow-complex rhythm at 50/min. In lead II the P waves are inverted and appear just before each QRS with a very short PR interval. What is the rhythm?
Impulses from the AV junction spread backward through the atria, producing inverted P waves just before, during or after the QRS, at a rate of about 40 to 60.
qznixdx: A 76-year-old with a COPD exacerbation and SpO2 of 84 percent has an irregular narrow-complex rhythm at 118/min with at least three different P wave shapes. What is the best approach to this rhythm?
Treat the hypoxia and lung disease
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is driven by underlying illness, especially lung disease and hypoxia; it does not respond to cardioversion and improves when the cause is treated.
qe86q34: After reperfusion of an inferior STEMI, a 62-year-old's monitor shows a regular wide-complex rhythm at 72/min. He has a strong pulse and BP 124/76. What is this rhythm most likely to be?
Third-degree AV block with slow escape
A wide ventricular rhythm at 40 to 100 after reperfusion is usually accelerated idioventricular rhythm; it is generally benign and should not be suppressed with antiarrhythmics.
q6mbote: A newborn's heart rate remains 50/min after 30 seconds of positive pressure ventilation that moves the chest. What is the next step?
Start compressions at a 3 to 1 ratio
Continue ventilation alone for 2 more minutes
Start compressions at a 15 to 2 ratio
NRP calls for chest compressions coordinated with ventilations at 3 to 1, with increased oxygen, when the heart rate stays below 60 despite effective ventilation.
qjwjgij: A 29-year-old construction worker has a near-amputation of the left lower leg with massive bleeding. He has snoring respirations and a GCS of 10. Using the MARCH sequence, what do you address first?
Apply a tourniquet high and tight on the leg
Insert a nasopharyngeal airway to relieve the snoring
Expose the chest and look for an open pneumothorax
Obtain a blood glucose and a full set of vital signs
MARCH puts massive hemorrhage before the airway because a person can bleed to death from a severed leg artery within minutes. The airway is managed right after the bleeding is controlled.
qd7u990: You have controlled bleeding, managed the airway, sealed a chest wound and started an IV on a 40-year-old gunshot victim lying on wet pavement on a cold night. Under MARCH, what should you do next?
Remove wet clothing and cover him to prevent heat loss
Start a second IV and give a large crystalloid bolus
Complete a detailed secondary exam before covering him
The H in MARCH covers hypothermia and head injury. Even mild hypothermia worsens bleeding by impairing clotting, so heat loss must be prevented early.
q1bz9utm: A 25-year-old has a gunshot wound to the right groin with steady bright red bleeding. There is no room above the wound for a limb tourniquet. What should you do?
Pack the wound tightly with hemostatic gauze and hold firm pressure
Apply a limb tourniquet just below the wound
Elevate the leg and place a bulky dressing over the wound surface
Apply a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters

Groin wounds are junctional and cannot be controlled with a limb tourniquet. Packing the wound cavity onto the bleeding vessel and holding direct pressure, or using a junctional device, is the correct approach.
q1vmwp9i: A 32-year-old with a tourniquet on his thigh for an arterial bleed asks you to loosen it because the pain is severe. Bleeding is controlled and transport time is 25 minutes. What should you do?
Leave it in place and treat his pain
Loosen it briefly every 10 minutes to reduce pain
Remove it and replace it with a pressure dressing
Move it lower on the leg to a less painful spot
A properly applied tourniquet is painful, and loosening it can restart life-threatening bleeding. It should stay in place, the time should be noted, and pain should be managed per protocol.
q43bo4l: A 70-kg man was crushed between two vehicles. He is confused and anxious, HR 128, BP 84/58, RR 32, with pale cool skin. Which class of hemorrhagic shock best fits these findings?
Class III, about 30 to 40 percent blood loss
Class I, under 15 percent blood loss
Class II, about 15 to 30 percent blood loss
Class IV, more than 40 percent with lethargy and no measurable pressure

Class III blood loss is the point where systolic pressure falls, with marked tachycardia and confusion. Class II usually keeps a normal systolic pressure, and class IV brings profound hypotension and lethargy.
q1nvyvj0: A 30-year-old fell from a ladder and is anxious, with HR 112, BP 124/100, RR 22 and capillary refill of 3 seconds. What does his blood pressure reading most likely reflect?
Normal perfusion with no blood loss
Neurogenic shock from a spinal injury

A rising diastolic pressure with a normal systolic gives a narrow pulse pressure, an early sign that the body is compensating for blood loss with vasoconstriction. A normal systolic pressure does not rule out shock.
qm7yfjs: A 34-year-old with a severe head injury has a GCS of 5, a fixed dilated right pupil and new extensor posturing. He is intubated and the BP is 142/80. What ETCO2 should you target while signs of herniation persist?

With active signs of herniation, brief controlled hyperventilation to an ETCO2 of about 30 to 35 mmHg is recommended. Driving it lower causes cerebral vasoconstriction severe enough to cause ischemia.
q6yr41y: You have been mildly hyperventilating an intubated head-injured adult with a blown pupil. After 10 minutes the pupil begins to react and his posturing stops. What should you do now?
Return to a normal rate targeting an ETCO2 of 35 to 40
Continue hyperventilating until arrival at the hospital
Increase the rate further to keep improving the pupil
Stop ventilating briefly to let the ETCO2 rise above 50
Hyperventilation is a temporary bridge only while signs of herniation are present. Once they resolve, ventilation returns to normal to avoid the cerebral ischemia caused by prolonged low CO2.
qdnk5c9: In a patient with a severe traumatic brain injury, which pair of secondary insults most strongly worsens outcome and must be prevented in the field?
Even a single episode of hypoxia or hypotension is linked to markedly higher death rates after TBI. Field care focuses on keeping SpO2 at least 90 percent and avoiding low blood pressure.
q18sic3j: A 19-year-old was hit in the temple with a baseball and was knocked out briefly. He then talked normally for 30 minutes but is now vomiting, with a GCS of 10 and a dilated right pupil. What is the most likely injury?
A brief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval and then rapid decline after a blow to the temple is the classic picture of an arterial epidural hematoma. This needs rapid transport for surgery.
q1i1243d: After a fall, a 50-year-old has bruising around both eyes and clear fluid draining from the nose. Which airway adjunct should you avoid?
Raccoon eyes and CSF rhinorrhea suggest a basilar skull fracture, and a nasal airway could pass through the fractured cribriform plate into the cranial vault. Oral routes are preferred.
q1kqf096: A head-injured patient opens his eyes only to pain, says inappropriate words and withdraws from a painful stimulus. What is his GCS?
Eye opening to pain scores 2, inappropriate words score 3, and withdrawal from pain scores 4, for a total of 9.
qsxgml4: A 22-year-old with a stab wound to the right chest had a vented chest seal placed. He is now more short of breath, SpO2 has dropped to 86 percent, HR is 132 and BP 84/52. What should you do first?
Lift a corner of the seal to release trapped air
Add a second occlusive dressing over the first one
Increase oxygen and reassess in 5 minutes
Place him on his left side and start a fluid bolus
A chest seal can clog or fail and allow a tension pneumothorax to build. Burping or briefly removing the dressing is the first step, followed by needle decompression if signs persist.
qugas5j: You need to perform needle decompression on an adult with a tension pneumothorax but cannot use the second intercostal space at the midclavicular line. Which alternate site is accepted?
Fourth or fifth intercostal space at the anterior axillary line
Second intercostal space right beside the sternum
Sixth intercostal space at the midclavicular line
Third intercostal space just medial to the nipple

The lateral site at the fourth or fifth intercostal space in the anterior axillary line often has a thinner chest wall. Sites next to the sternum risk the internal mammary vessels, and low anterior sites risk the heart, liver or spleen.
q1a4am6: A 40-year-old crushed under a vehicle has absent breath sounds on the right, dullness to percussion on that side, flat neck veins and BP 78/50. What is the most likely cause?
Dullness with absent breath sounds and flat neck veins point to a chest filling with blood. Tension pneumothorax gives hyperresonance and usually distended neck veins.
qrdv228: A patient has a suspected massive hemothorax with hypotension, dullness on the left and flat neck veins. What is the best prehospital management?
Oxygen, rapid transport and fluids to a radial pulse
Needle decompression of the left chest
Supine position with legs raised and a 2-liter bolus
An occlusive dressing over the left chest wall

Needle decompression does not drain blood and will not help a hemothorax. Care is focused on oxygenation, hemorrhage-focused resuscitation that avoids overloading with fluids, and fast transport to surgery.
qvd39kg: A 28-year-old with a stab wound to the left chest is hypotensive. On the monitor the QRS amplitude alternates from tall to short with every beat. What does this suggest?
Electrical alternans comes from the heart swinging within a fluid-filled pericardial sac. In a penetrating chest injury with hypotension, it strongly suggests tamponade.
qsfzrip: A 68-year-old driver struck the steering wheel. A segment of his right chest moves inward when he inhales. RR 30 and shallow, SpO2 88 percent. What is the most serious underlying problem?
The bruised lung under the flail segment
The flail segment collapsing the lung completely
Rib ends lacerating the heart muscle
The paradoxical movement is dramatic, but the main cause of hypoxia is the pulmonary contusion beneath the flail segment. Pain also limits ventilation and adds to the problem.
q1w0fmmg: A patient with a flail chest has RR 36 with very shallow breaths and SpO2 84 percent on a nonrebreather. What should you do?
Assist ventilations with a bag-valve mask
Splint the segment with a sandbag
Wrap the chest tightly with tape
Continue the nonrebreather and recheck in 10 minutes
Positive pressure ventilation supports gas exchange and splints the flail segment from the inside. Sandbags and tight wrapping restrict chest movement and worsen ventilation.
q12i64xn: An unrestrained driver's chest struck the steering wheel. He has sternal bruising, HR 118 with frequent PVCs and BP 128/80. What injury should you suspect?
Blunt cardiac injury commonly presents with unexplained tachycardia and dysrhythmias after a blow to the sternum. Cardiac monitoring and a 12-lead ECG are indicated.
qp5c075: After a high-speed frontal crash, a 45-year-old has pain between the shoulder blades and a BP of 150/90 in the right arm but 112/70 in the left. What injury is most likely?
Sudden deceleration can tear the aorta near the ligamentum arteriosum. Interscapular pain and a blood pressure difference between the arms are warning signs.
q1ne58mr: A 24-year-old snowboarder fell onto his left side. He now has left upper quadrant tenderness, left shoulder pain without shoulder injury, HR 118 and BP 104/70. Which organ is most likely injured?
Pain referred to the left shoulder, called Kehr's sign, comes from blood irritating the diaphragm. With left upper quadrant tenderness it suggests a splenic injury.
q1fpmnub: A 9-year-old restrained only by a lap belt has a band of bruising across the lower abdomen after a crash. Which injuries should you suspect?
A seatbelt sign raises concern for hollow organ injury and a flexion-distraction fracture of the lumbar spine. Children riding in lap belts without proper boosters are at particular risk.
q113u5i: A 30-year-old with a knife wound to the abdomen has a loop of bowel protruding from the wound. What is the correct care?
Cover it with a moist sterile dressing
Gently push the bowel back inside
Tape a dry gauze pad tightly over it
Irrigate and leave it uncovered for inspection
An evisceration is covered with a moist sterile dressing and then an occlusive or dry layer to keep it moist and warm. Replacing the organs risks contamination and further injury.
qx34fxo: A motorcyclist has pelvic pain, leg length discrepancy and BP 86/50. How should you assess and handle his pelvis?
Avoid rocking it and apply a binder
Rock the iliac crests firmly to confirm instability
Log roll him fully to inspect the back first
Flex his hips to relieve the pelvic pain
Repeated pelvic compression or rocking can disrupt clots and worsen bleeding. When a fracture is suspected, a binder is applied and movement of the pelvis is kept to a minimum.
q8jve66: Why is a pelvic binder applied to a hypotensive patient with a suspected open-book pelvic fracture?
It reduces pelvic volume and stabilizes fragments
It raises the blood pressure by compressing the aorta
It prevents spinal cord injury in the lumbar spine
It allows the legs to be elevated safely
Closing the widened pelvic ring decreases the space for blood to collect and limits fragment movement. This mostly slows venous and bone bleeding while the patient is moved to surgery.
qvtc7oj: A 74-year-old fell forward and struck her chin. She has burning pain in her hands and much more weakness in her arms than in her legs. What spinal cord syndrome is most likely?
Hyperextension of an arthritic neck in older adults damages the center of the cord, where the arm fibers lie. Weakness is greater in the arms than the legs.
q1g89n0q: A 26-year-old was stabbed in the back. His right leg is weak with poor position sense, and he cannot feel pain or temperature in his left leg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Damage to one side of the cord causes loss of motor function and position sense on the same side, and loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side.
q1iuegy5: A 31-year-old ejected from a vehicle has a suspected cervical cord injury with no movement below the shoulders. He is pale, cool and clammy with HR 128 and BP 82/50. How should you interpret this?
Neurogenic shock alone fully explains these findings
This is spinal shock and no treatment is needed
These are signs of a normal stress response
Neurogenic shock typically causes warm dry skin and a normal or slow heart rate. Tachycardia with cool, clammy skin suggests blood loss, which must be found and treated.
qmelyt5: After a diving injury, a 20-year-old is quadriplegic with abdominal breathing, RR 28 and shallow, and a falling SpO2. Why is he at high risk for respiratory failure?
Intercostal paralysis leaves only the diaphragm
The phrenic nerve is unaffected by neck injuries
His airway is blocked by the tongue
Cervical cord injuries paralyze the intercostal muscles, leaving the diaphragm, supplied by C3 to C5, to do all the work. Injuries at or above that level can stop breathing entirely.
q1scn3y1: A 40-year-old was burned at 1400 hours and you reach the hospital at 1530. When does the first 8-hour period of the Parkland formula begin?
At the time of the burn
When the first IV is started
When the burn size is calculated
Half of the 24-hour Parkland volume is given in the first 8 hours counted from the time of injury. Delays in starting fluids mean the remaining volume must be given faster.
q12cljrv: An 80-kg man has partial- and full-thickness burns over 25 percent of his body. Using the Parkland formula of 4 mL x kg x percent TBSA, how much fluid is planned for the first 8 hours?
The 24-hour total is 4 x 80 x 25, or 8,000 mL, and half of it, 4,000 mL, is planned for the first 8 hours from the burn. Many systems now start with a lower rate and adjust to urine output.
qef0tqi: A 30-year-old has superficial, red, unblistered burns on 20 percent of his body and partial-thickness blistered burns on 10 percent. What burn size is used for fluid calculations?
Superficial burns are not counted in the TBSA used for fluid resuscitation. Only partial- and full-thickness burns are included.
qex961l: A 2-year-old has partial-thickness burns to the entire head and both entire arms. Using the pediatric rule of nines, what is the burned surface area?
In young children the head is about 18 percent and each arm about 9 percent, giving 36 percent. The larger head proportion is the key difference from the adult chart.
q13pjfnx: A 45-year-old has full-thickness circumferential burns around the chest. He is becoming harder to ventilate with a bag-valve mask despite a patent airway. What is the most likely cause?
Stiff eschar restricting chest wall movement
Leathery eschar does not stretch, so a circumferential chest burn can restrict ventilation. It may need surgical escharotomy at the hospital.
qlmkbr7: A lineman contacted a 10,000-volt line. He has a small burn on his hand and another on his foot and is alert with stable vital signs. What is the most important concern?
Hidden deep tissue and cardiac injury
The burns are minor and need only dressings
He can be released if the ECG is normal on scene
Treat only the visible surface burns
High-voltage current travels through deep tissue, so small skin wounds hide extensive muscle damage and the risk of dysrhythmias. Cardiac monitoring and transport to a burn center are needed.
qmwtbdj: A 35-year-old has partial- and full-thickness burns over 45 percent of his body. The fire was put out 10 minutes ago. How should you dress the burns?
Clean dry dressings or sheets, keeping him warm
Wet sheets for the whole transport
Ice packs on the deepest burns
Large burns lose heat rapidly, and prolonged cooling causes hypothermia. After the burning process is stopped, cover with clean dry dressings and prevent heat loss.
q1dud73g: A family of four has headaches, nausea and confusion after running a generator in the garage. The father's SpO2 reads 99 percent. How should you interpret this?
Standard pulse oximetry can't detect carbon monoxide
His oxygenation is normal, so oxygen is not needed
The reading proves this is a viral illness
Standard pulse oximeters read carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin, giving falsely normal values. High-flow oxygen is needed, and CO oximetry should be used if available.
qzy6t0h: A man pulled from a house fire is unresponsive with seizures, BP 72/40 and a normal SpO2. Cyanide toxicity is suspected along with carbon monoxide. Which antidote approach is preferred?
Nitrites work by creating methemoglobin, which further reduces oxygen delivery in a patient already poisoned with CO. Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide without that harm.
q14qzlmz: A 38-year-old pulled from a burning building has singed nasal hair and soot in his mouth. Over 15 minutes his voice becomes hoarse and soft stridor develops. What is the priority?
Wait until stridor becomes severe before acting
Give oral fluids to soothe the throat
Place a nasal cannula at 2 L/min
Progressive hoarseness and stridor signal airway swelling that can close the airway within minutes. Early definitive airway management is safer than waiting.
q161ma0o: A 50-year-old's legs have been pinned under a concrete slab for 4 hours. Rescuers are ready to lift it. What should you do before the slab is lifted?
Start IV fluids and apply the cardiac monitor
Apply tourniquets to both legs and leave them for transport
Lift the slab right away and assess afterward
Elevate his head and apply ice to his legs
Release of a prolonged crush sends potassium, acid and myoglobin into the circulation. Fluids before release and cardiac monitoring help prevent sudden dysrhythmias and kidney injury.
qb0fqnm: Minutes after a crushed leg is freed, the patient's ECG shows tall peaked T waves and a widening QRS. What is the most likely cause?
Potassium released from damaged muscle causes peaked T waves and QRS widening and can lead to cardiac arrest. Treatment follows protocol for hyperkalemia.
qr1a05l: A 28-year-old with a splinted tibia fracture has worsening leg pain out of proportion to the injury and severe pain when you gently move his toes. Pedal pulses are present. What is the most likely problem?
Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are early signs of compartment syndrome. Pulses are often present until very late, so a pulse does not rule it out.
qqorqn2: After a bomb blast, a woman has multiple penetrating wounds from flying glass. What category of blast injury is this?
Secondary blast injuries come from debris and fragments driven by the explosion. Primary is the pressure wave, tertiary is the body being thrown, and quaternary includes burns and other effects.
q1y4piow: A woman 34 weeks pregnant was in a car crash. She is supine on a long board and complains of dizziness, BP 88/50, HR 110. What should you do first?
Manually displace the uterus to the left
Raise her legs and start a large fluid bolus
In late pregnancy the uterus compresses the vena cava when the patient is supine. Moving the uterus to the left or tilting the board improves venous return.
qleo03g: A pregnant trauma patient seems stable, but her fetus may be in danger. What is the most effective way to protect the fetus in the field?
Focus on fetal heart tones before maternal care
Keep the mother supine for close monitoring
Withhold fluids to avoid placental swelling

The body diverts blood away from the uterus to protect the mother, so the fetus may be in shock before maternal vital signs change. Supporting the mother's oxygenation and circulation is the best fetal care.
qx85h21: A woman 30 weeks pregnant had a car crash. She has steady abdominal pain, a rigid tender uterus and only slight vaginal bleeding. What should you suspect?
A painful, rigid uterus after trauma suggests the placenta has separated. Bleeding may be concealed behind the placenta, so the amount seen does not reflect blood loss.
q1t1aqw4: An 8-year-old was run over by a car. You feel no rib fractures, but she has crackles, RR 34 and SpO2 89 percent. Why is lung injury likely despite intact ribs?
Pliable ribs pass the force to the lungs
Children's lungs are larger than adults'
Rib fractures in children are always hidden
Hypoxia in children is normal after trauma
A child's flexible chest wall bends without breaking and transfers energy to the lungs. Pulmonary contusion without rib fractures is common.
q1jc9lev: You place a 3-year-old supine on a firm surface for spinal motion restriction. His neck flexes forward because of his large head. What should you do?
Pad under the shoulders and torso
Place a folded towel under the head
Tape the forehead down more tightly
Elevate the head of the board 30 degrees
A young child's large occiput flexes the neck when lying flat. Padding under the torso brings the spine into a neutral position.
qekn1on: What systolic blood pressure indicates hypotension in a 5-year-old trauma patient?
Hypotension in children 1 to 10 years is a systolic pressure below 70 plus twice the age in years, so below 80 for a 5-year-old. Hypotension is a late sign in children.
q1nmb4z5: Under the 2021 National Guideline for Field Triage, which systolic pressure meets a red criterion in a trauma patient 65 or older?

The 2021 guideline uses a systolic pressure below 110 in patients 65 and older because older adults may be in shock at pressures that look normal. A heart rate greater than the systolic pressure is also a criterion.
q96xuza: A 30-year-old fell 14 feet from scaffolding. He is alert with normal vital signs and only a sprained wrist. Under the 2021 field triage guideline, what is the right destination?
A trauma center, not necessarily the highest level
The closest emergency department regardless of level
A fall from more than 10 feet is a yellow mechanism criterion that calls for a trauma center. Without red criteria, it need not be the highest level.
q9shoib: A 26-year-old shot in the left chest has just lost his pulse in front of you, with PEA on the monitor. Which intervention is most likely to help?
Repeated epinephrine with CPR on scene
A prolonged search for medical causes
In traumatic arrest, outcomes depend on correcting the cause, such as tension pneumothorax, bleeding or hypoxia. Decompressing the chest addresses a reversible cause quickly.
q13lgac0: A 36-year-old has a laceration on the side of the neck with dark blood flowing and sucking sounds from the wound. What should you apply?
A dry, loosely taped gauze pad
An open neck vein can draw in air and cause a fatal air embolism. An occlusive dressing with careful pressure seals the wound without obstructing the airway.
q16qaj8a: A 79-year-old on metoprolol fell down stairs. He is pale with a firm, distended abdomen. HR 74, BP 112/70. How should you interpret his heart rate?
Beta blockers may mask tachycardia from bleeding
A normal heart rate rules out significant bleeding
His blood pressure proves he is stable
Beta blockers blunt the heart rate response to blood loss, and older adults may be in shock with pressures that look normal. Rely on other findings such as the abdomen and skin.
q1quiifv: An 84-year-old on an anticoagulant fell yesterday and hit her head. Today she is more confused and has a headache. What injury is most likely?
Brain atrophy stretches the bridging veins in older adults, and anticoagulants make them bleed more. Subdural bleeding often causes delayed decline hours to days later.
q4v7lu4: You call a physician by radio for permission to give a treatment not covered by your standing orders. What type of medical direction is this?
Online medical direction is real-time contact with a physician. Offline direction includes protocols, standing orders, training and quality review.
qbngmvp: Online medical direction orders a medication dose that you believe is ten times too high. What should you do?
Repeat the order back and question it
Give it as ordered because the physician is responsible
Give half the dose without telling anyone
Give the dose you think is correct
Repeating orders back is a safety step. If an order seems wrong, ask for clarification, and do not carry out an order you believe would harm the patient; document the exchange.
qy8uszd: A 45-year-old diabetic has a glucose of 38 mg/dL. He is confused and refuses care. What is true about his refusal?
He lacks capacity, so treat under implied consent
His refusal must be honored because he is an adult
You must wait for police before giving any care
You must get written consent from his spouse first
Hypoglycemia with confusion impairs the ability to understand and weigh choices. Without capacity, emergency treatment proceeds under implied consent per protocol.
qbjsiom: A married 17-year-old with a minor ankle injury declines transport. She is alert and understands the risks. How should you proceed?
Treat her as an adult who may refuse
Transport her against her will because she is a minor
Call her parents to consent for her
Have police place her in custody
Minors who are married or otherwise emancipated can usually consent to or refuse their own care. Local law defines emancipation, so follow protocol.
q9nrxft: A 70-year-old with a POLST marked do not resuscitate and selective treatment is in respiratory distress from pneumonia with a pulse. Which care fits his orders?
No treatment because a DNR is in place
Comfort care only, with no transport
Selective treatment allows noninvasive care such as CPAP, IV fluids and hospital transport, but not intubation. A DNR applies to cardiac arrest, while the POLST guides care when a pulse is present.
q1cmyy2j: A patient with a valid DNR order develops a narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 with chest pain and is still awake. How should you proceed?
Withhold all treatment because of the DNR
A DNR applies to resuscitation after cardiac arrest. Conditions with a pulse are treated normally unless another order limits care.
q1mhvpbm: An 88-year-old is found in cardiac arrest. The family says she has a DNR, but no one can find the document. What should you do?
Begin resuscitation and contact medical direction
Withhold resuscitation based on the family's word
Wait until the document is found
Without valid documentation, most protocols require resuscitation. Medical direction can help while the family searches.
qs27hju: Which statement is an example of a pertinent negative in a chest pain report?
Patient was found sitting in a recliner
A pertinent negative documents an important finding that is absent, such as no shortness of breath with chest pain. It shows the finding was checked.
qp8h7ka: You smell alcohol on a patient's breath. Which narrative entry is most appropriate?
Odor of an alcoholic beverage on the breath
Documentation should be objective and describe what you observed. Labels and opinions can be used against you and may be libelous.
qbtenyh: Your partner asks you to record a medication on the report that was never given, to match the narcotic count. What should you do?
Refuse, document accurately and report it
Record it as given to keep things simple
Leave the medication off the report
Record it with a note that you are unsure
Falsifying a medical record is illegal and dishonest. Accurate records and reporting a narcotic discrepancy through proper channels are required.
q6tv27d: An alert adult with capacity refuses care, but a paramedic threatens to restrain her if she does not comply. What has the paramedic committed?
Assault is causing a person to fear immediate bodily harm. Battery is unlawful touching without consent.
q5aga5v: You arrive at a hospital emergency department with a patient. The charge nurse asks you to take her to another hospital without being seen. What applies?
EMTALA requires a medical screening exam
The hospital may refuse any patient it chooses
You must leave right away for the other hospital
Only HIPAA applies to this situation

Once a patient arrives on hospital property seeking emergency care, EMTALA requires a medical screening exam and stabilization. Hospitals cannot turn patients away for financial or capacity reasons alone.
q1twlnij: An 85-year-old who depends on her son has pressure sores, soiled bedding and unexplained bruises. What must you do?
Report suspected elder abuse per state law
Leave it to the family to manage
Report it only if the patient asks you to
EMS providers are mandated reporters of suspected elder abuse and neglect in most states. Report as required and document objective findings.
q1ta54ej: You honor an alert, capable patient's decision to decline a treatment you recommend. Which ethical principle are you following?
Autonomy is the right of capable people to make their own decisions. Beneficence is doing good, nonmaleficence is avoiding harm, and justice is fairness.
qqoez7i: You are asked to transfer a patient with an infusion outside your scope of practice. What should you do?
Request a qualified provider to accompany the patient
Transport and manage the infusion yourself
Stop the infusion yourself without asking
