Paramedics cannot manage care beyond their scope. A qualified provider can accompany the patient, or the sending physician can change the treatment.
q1tzi4at: A large incident involves fire, police and EMS from several jurisdictions. What ICS structure should be used?
A separate command for each agency
Unified command lets agencies with responsibility share decisions and set common objectives. Separate commands lead to conflicts.
qj4ccjm: What is the recommended span of control for a supervisor in ICS?
As many as the situation demands
A span of control of three to seven, with five ideal, keeps supervisors effective. Larger groups should be divided into more units.
qrmu5nu: At a mass casualty incident, which officer manages arriving ambulances and assigns them when needed?
The staging officer tracks and releases resources as requested. This prevents vehicle congestion at the scene.
qhn14ff: At a mass casualty incident, who coordinates patient destinations so the nearest hospital is not overwhelmed?
The transport officer works with hospitals to distribute patients. This prevents a single facility from being overloaded.
q1gy31nf: In SALT triage, which patients are assessed first after the global sort?
Those who are still or have an obvious life threat
Those who walk to the designated area
Those who wave or move purposefully
SALT asks walking patients to move and others to wave. Patients who do neither are assessed first.
q1kfldiw: Under START triage, an adult who cannot walk has RR 22 and a radial pulse but cannot follow simple commands. What category is assigned?
START checks respirations, perfusion and mental status. Failure to follow simple commands puts the patient in the immediate category.
q30aloa: During JumpSTART triage, a 6-year-old who cannot walk has a respiratory rate of 48. What category is assigned?
In JumpSTART, a respiratory rate below 15 or above 45 is immediate. The child's range differs from the adult threshold.
qv4wdwv: At an MCI, a 7-month-old cannot walk because of her age. How is she triaged with JumpSTART?
Assign minor because she cannot walk
Assign immediate due to her age
Infants who cannot walk because of development are evaluated with the rest of the algorithm. They are not automatically assigned minor.
q11z2aid: You are approaching a tanker rollover with a placard on the tank. What is the safest approach?
Approach from uphill and upwind, using binoculars
Approach downwind for a closer look
Approach from downhill to stay low
Approach directly to read the placard up close
Staying uphill and upwind keeps vapors and runoff away. Placards and the ERG can be read from a distance.
qnqkgv6: Patients from a chemical release are arriving at your location. Which single action removes the largest share of contamination?
Removing clothing removes much of the contaminant. Washing with water follows for liquid exposures.
qjtgg2b: After a subway vapor release, several commuters have runny noses and pinpoint pupils but no breathing problems. What exposure should you suspect?
Miosis is the most consistent sign of nerve agent vapor exposure, often with rhinorrhea. More severe exposures add secretions, bronchospasm and seizures.
q19lyzra: Several patients have a fever and a rash, with all lesions at the same stage and concentrated on the face and limbs. What should you suspect?
Smallpox lesions are at the same stage and concentrated on the face and limbs. Chickenpox lesions vary in stage and appear mostly on the trunk.
qj7dh55: At an active shooter incident, you reach a victim with severe leg bleeding while the shooter is still active nearby. What should you do?
Apply a tourniquet and move to cover
Perform a full primary survey on the spot
Insert an airway and start an IV
Leave the victim because it is unsafe
In direct threat care, only massive bleeding is treated with a tourniquet before moving to cover. Other care waits for a safer zone.
qz980is: At an active shooter incident, where does a rescue task force operate?
The warm zone, with police protection
The hot zone, before police arrive
Rescue task forces work in areas that have been cleared but are not fully secured. Police provide protection while EMS treats and removes victims.
qdzcsm7: A helicopter has landed at your scene. How should you approach it?
From the front, only when signaled by the crew
From the tail to stay out of the pilot's sight
From uphill so you are close to the rotor
As soon as it lands to save time
Approach in view of the pilot and only after signaling. Tail rotors and uphill approaches risk serious injury.
q1secdek: During air transport, what happens to an untreated pneumothorax as altitude increases?
Gas expands as pressure decreases, by Boyle's law. Air in the chest or a tube cuff expands with altitude.
q40k9tq: You stick yourself with a used needle. What should you do first?
Wash with soap and water and report right away
Wait until the end of your shift to report
Squeeze the wound and apply bleach
Ignore it if the patient seems healthy
Wash the area immediately and report so testing and prophylaxis can start quickly. Prophylaxis works best when started within hours.
q1w31pq3: After caring for a patient with C. difficile diarrhea, how should you clean your hands?
Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores. Washing with soap and water removes them.
q1lxktoz: When removing PPE after caring for a patient on airborne precautions, which item is removed last?
The respirator is removed last, after leaving the room, and then hands are cleaned.
qae488i: Your partner says "give 1 mg of epinephrine," and you reply "giving 1 mg of epinephrine" before giving it, then confirm "1 mg given." What practice is this?
Closed-loop communication confirms the order and its completion, reducing errors.
q16035hg: You are working on a highway crash. How should the fire apparatus be positioned?
On the opposite side of the road
Parked as close to the patient as possible
Positioning apparatus upstream protects workers from oncoming traffic. Responders should also wear high-visibility vests.
q1cayldn: A colleague says he feels hopeless and has been thinking about not being here after a series of bad calls. What should you do?
Ask directly about suicide and connect him to help
Tell him to take a few days off and see
Avoid the topic so it does not upset him
Asking directly about suicide does not increase risk and allows you to connect the person with help.
q1dwxjdq: Which type of study provides the strongest evidence for a treatment?
Systematic review of randomized controlled trials
Systematic reviews of well-designed randomized trials give the highest level of evidence.
q17aid9q: What does high sensitivity in a diagnostic test mean?
It correctly identifies most people with the condition
It correctly identifies most people without the condition
It works only in large populations
Sensitivity is the ability to detect people who have the condition. Specificity is the ability to identify those who do not.
q1xdg9r2: Why are patients randomized in a clinical trial?
To make sure patients choose their treatment
To avoid the need for consent
Randomization balances known and unknown factors so differences in outcome can be attributed to the treatment.
q1tyf1f2: A 29-year-old in status epilepticus stops seizing after a benzodiazepine. He remains unresponsive with snoring respirations at 6 per minute and SpO2 86 percent. What should you do next?
Open the airway and assist ventilations
Give a second benzodiazepine dose to prevent a recurrence
Place him in the recovery position and observe him
Give naloxone to reverse the respiratory depression
Benzodiazepines and the postictal state can both depress breathing. A rate of 6 with snoring and hypoxia is inadequate, so the airway must be opened and ventilations assisted with a bag-valve mask.
q19gpu0z: A 52-year-old's generalized seizure stopped 20 minutes ago, but she is still unresponsive, with rhythmic twitching of the right eyelid and fingers and her eyes deviated to the right. What should you suspect?
Failure to wake combined with subtle rhythmic movements or gaze deviation suggests nonconvulsive status epilepticus, which needs treatment just like a visible convulsion.
q1mcyfxk: A 67-year-old with diabetes is found with new right-sided weakness and slurred speech. Which assessment is most important to complete before activating a stroke alert?
A 12-lead ECG to look for atrial fibrillation
A check of the deep tendon reflexes
Hypoglycemia is a common, quickly reversible stroke mimic that can produce focal deficits. A glucose check should precede stroke activation and destination decisions.
q1g6dehk: A 74-year-old developed symptoms 40 minutes ago. She has dense left-sided weakness, her eyes are deviated to the right, and she ignores people standing on her left. What do these findings suggest?
A small lacunar stroke deep in the brain
A transient ischemic attack that will resolve

Cortical signs such as gaze deviation, neglect and aphasia with dense hemiparesis suggest a large vessel occlusion, which may benefit from transport to a thrombectomy-capable center under local destination protocols.
q175w5pw: A 62-year-old went to bed at 22:00 acting normally. His wife found him unable to speak when he woke at 06:30. What is his last known well time?
The time the 911 call was placed
Midnight, at the start of the new day
Last known well is the last time the patient was confirmed to be at baseline. For wake-up strokes that is the time he went to sleep, not the time the deficit was discovered.
q53ihsa: A 40-year-old has a new facial droop. Which finding most suggests Bell palsy rather than a stroke?
Loss of forehead wrinkling on the affected side
Slurred speech with drift of the arm on the same side
Sudden onset of the droop within the last hour
Drooping at the corner of the mouth on smiling
The forehead has nerve supply from both sides of the brain, so a central (stroke) lesion usually spares it. Inability to raise the brow on the affected side points to a peripheral facial nerve palsy.
q1fg2y3s: A 2-month-old has a temperature of 38.6 C (101.5 F), poor feeding and irritability that worsens when his mother picks him up. His anterior fontanelle is bulging. What is the most concerning possibility?
Young infants with meningitis rarely show a stiff neck. Fever with paradoxical irritability, poor feeding and a bulging fontanelle should be treated as meningitis until proven otherwise.
qe3f4ib: A 58-year-old with myasthenia gravis has worsening ptosis, double vision, a nasal voice and trouble clearing secretions. RR 28 and shallow, SpO2 95 percent on room air, ETCO2 56 mmHg. How should you interpret these findings?
She is stable, because her oxygen saturation is normal
Hyperventilation from anxiety about her illness

Myasthenic crisis weakens the breathing muscles, so CO2 builds up while SpO2 may stay normal, especially early. Rising ETCO2 with shallow breathing and pooled secretions means she may soon need ventilatory support.
q1vgueh2: A 30-year-old with a complete T4 spinal cord injury has a pounding headache, BP 210/118, HR 52, and flushing and sweating above the level of injury. What should you do first?
Sit him up and look for a trigger such as a blocked catheter
Lay him flat, raise his legs and recheck the pressure in 15 minutes
Apply a cooling blanket to his trunk
Begin transcutaneous pacing for the bradycardia

Autonomic dysreflexia is a dangerous hypertensive response to a stimulus below the injury, most often a full bladder or kinked catheter. Sitting upright lowers pressure, and removing the trigger usually resolves it.
qv94gwr: A 7-year-old with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt has had worsening headache, vomiting and sleepiness over the day. She has no fever. What is the most likely cause?
Headache, vomiting and decreasing level of consciousness in a child with a shunt suggest obstruction and rising intracranial pressure, which needs prompt evaluation.
qo2aiqh: A 22-year-old in DKA has been breathing deeply at 34 per minute with an ETCO2 of 18 mmHg. He becomes obtunded and is intubated. How should he be ventilated?
Keep a high rate that matches his own compensation
Ventilate at 10 per minute as for any adult patient
Ventilate to bring ETCO2 up to 35 to 45 mmHg as quickly as possible
Ventilate at 6 per minute to rest his respiratory muscles
His rapid deep breathing was blowing off CO2 to offset a severe metabolic acidosis. Slowing ventilation after intubation lets CO2 rise and can cause a dangerous fall in pH and cardiac arrest.
qr3h0mt: A 9-year-old in DKA is receiving IV fluids. During transport he develops a headache, becomes confused, and his HR falls from 130 to 64 while his BP rises. What should you suspect?
Cerebral edema is a leading cause of death in pediatric DKA. Headache, declining mental status, bradycardia and rising BP are warning signs of rising intracranial pressure.
q1w7mc4j: A 76-year-old taking glipizide was found with a glucose of 38 mg/dL. After IV dextrose he is alert with a glucose of 112 and wants to stay home. What should you advise?
Transport, because hypoglycemia is likely to recur
He can stay home since his glucose is now normal
Eat a meal and stay home with no further follow-up needed
Take a second dose of dextrose before you leave the scene
Sulfonylureas act for many hours, so hypoglycemia often recurs after dextrose wears off. These patients usually need observation and should be strongly encouraged to accept transport.
q1gk37ms: A malnourished 50-year-old with chronic heavy alcohol use has a glucose of 32 mg/dL. No IV could be started, and IM glucagon 15 minutes ago has not helped. What is the most likely reason?
Depleted glycogen stores in the liver
IM absorption takes at least an hour
Glucagon works only when given by the IV route
Glucagon raises glucose by releasing liver glycogen. Malnourished and chronically alcoholic patients have little glycogen, so they need dextrose by IV or IO access.
q9r1h5z: A 45-year-old has taken prednisone daily for years but stopped 3 days ago because of vomiting. He is lethargic with BP 74/40 despite 2 liters of fluid and a glucose of 58 mg/dL. What is the most likely cause?

Long-term steroid use suppresses the adrenal glands, and stopping suddenly can cause adrenal crisis with refractory hypotension and hypoglycemia. Treatment requires stress-dose steroids in addition to fluids.
q14xczad: An 81-year-old is found in a cold house in winter with a temperature of 33.8 C (92.8 F), HR 44, RR 8, a puffy face and coarse dry skin. She has not taken her levothyroxine in months. What is the most likely condition?
Myxedema coma is severe hypothyroidism with hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation and altered mental status, often triggered by cold or illness. Expect hypoglycemia and support ventilation.
qxtugri: A 38-year-old took an overdose of amitriptyline. QRS is 150 ms, HR 128, BP 82/50. Which intervention most directly treats the wide QRS?
Tricyclics block cardiac sodium channels. Sodium bicarbonate supplies sodium and alkalinizes the blood, narrowing the QRS; class IA and IC antidysrhythmics worsen sodium channel blockade.
q1stw0mr: A 60-year-old took an overdose of his blood pressure medicine. HR 38, BP 70/40, glucose 290 mg/dL. Which drug class is most likely?

Both beta blockers and calcium channel blockers cause bradycardia and hypotension. Calcium channel blockers also impair insulin release and cause hyperglycemia, while beta blocker overdose tends to cause hypoglycemia.
q1qpzq0j: A 2-year-old may have swallowed one of his grandmother's extended-release verapamil tablets an hour ago. He is alert with normal vital signs. What is the best plan?
Transport, since toxicity from extended-release tablets can be delayed
Leave him home with his parents, since one tablet cannot harm a toddler
Observe on scene for 30 minutes and release him if well
Induce vomiting before leaving the scene
A single tablet of some cardiac drugs can be dangerous to a toddler, and extended-release forms may not cause symptoms for many hours. The child needs transport and observation.
qh3rmwh: A farm worker was sprayed with an organophosphate pesticide and has heavy secretions and vomiting. What is the priority before you provide care?
Starting an IV in the contaminated arm
Giving atropine through his wet clothing
Organophosphates are absorbed through skin, so responders must protect themselves and remove the patient's contaminated clothing and decontaminate before or alongside treatment.
qonu62v: You are giving repeated doses of atropine to a patient with organophosphate poisoning. Which finding is the main endpoint for atropine?
Dilation of the pupils to normal size or larger
A heart rate that rises above 120 per minute
Return to a normal level of consciousness
Atropine is titrated to dry the bronchial secretions and ease breathing. Pupil size and heart rate are unreliable endpoints and may lag behind or mislead.
qlhb5ja: A 17-year-old says she swallowed 30 acetaminophen tablets 2 hours ago. She feels fine and her vital signs are normal. How should you interpret this?
Liver injury may still develop, and the antidote works best early
Normal vitals 2 hours after ingestion show the dose was not toxic
Liver damage occurs only if she vomits blood within 4 hours
She can be safely monitored at home by her parents
Acetaminophen toxicity often causes no symptoms for the first day, while liver injury silently develops. The antidote is most effective when started within about 8 hours, so early transport matters.
qd1fp0t: A 48-year-old drank windshield washer fluid yesterday. He now has blurred vision he describes as like a snowstorm, and deep rapid respirations. Which substance most likely caused this?
Methanol is metabolized to formic acid, which damages the optic nerve and causes a severe metabolic acidosis. Visual changes after a delay are a hallmark.
q1ha30n3: A 55-year-old heavy daily drinker stopped drinking 3 days ago. He is confused and hallucinating, tremulous and sweating, with HR 138 and a temperature of 38.6 C (101.5 F). What is the most likely diagnosis?
Delirium tremens typically starts 2 to 4 days after the last drink, with autonomic hyperactivity, hallucinations and confusion. It is life-threatening and needs aggressive treatment.
q1yne8nl: A man pulled from an enclosed house fire is unresponsive with BP 78/40, SpO2 98 percent and SpCO 8 percent. Which treatment targets the most likely additional poison?
Smoke from burning plastics contains cyanide. Coma and hypotension that are out of proportion to a modest carboxyhemoglobin level suggest cyanide toxicity, treated with hydroxocobalamin.
q1kqvii7: A 32-year-old taking sertraline started tramadol 2 days ago. He is agitated and sweating, with a temperature of 39.0 C (102.2 F), HR 124, diarrhea, and sustained clonus and brisk reflexes in his legs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Combining serotonergic drugs can cause serotonin syndrome, which comes on quickly and features clonus and hyperreflexia, most marked in the legs.
qiys0ql: A 44-year-old started haloperidol a week ago. He is confused, with a temperature of 40.2 C (104.4 F), rigid lead-pipe muscles, slow reflexes and a fluctuating blood pressure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome develops over days after starting antipsychotics, with hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, decreased reflexes and autonomic instability.
q87crmk: A 24-year-old used a stimulant at a party. He is agitated with HR 140, BP 176/100, temperature 38.8 C (101.8 F) and dilated pupils. Which finding best separates a sympathomimetic toxidrome from an anticholinergic one?
Both toxidromes cause agitation, tachycardia, hyperthermia and mydriasis. Sympathomimetics cause diaphoresis, while anticholinergics cause hot, dry skin.
qish7wt: You are ventilating a 40-year-old with an opioid overdose and a respiratory rate of 4. What is the goal of naloxone?
Full wakefulness so he can refuse care
Pupils that return to normal size
A heart rate above 100 per minute
Naloxone is titrated to restore adequate breathing. Pushing for full arousal can cause abrupt withdrawal, vomiting and agitation.
q1oh6bku: After naloxone, a 33-year-old who injected fentanyl now breathes 14 times a minute with SpO2 96 percent but remains deeply sedated, with HR 52 and chronic wounds on his forearms. What is the best approach?
Supportive care, as a non-opioid sedative such as xylazine may be present
Keep repeating naloxone doses until he is fully awake
Give flumazenil to reverse the remaining sedation
Begin transcutaneous pacing for the heart rate

Xylazine is a common adulterant that causes sedation, bradycardia and chronic wounds and does not respond to naloxone. Once breathing is adequate, support the airway and monitor rather than giving more naloxone.
qe99kfi: You find a person unresponsive in a closed car with a note on the window warning of toxic gas, and you notice a rotten egg odor. What should you do?
Back away, isolate the area and request hazmat
Open the doors and rapidly remove the patient
Hold your breath and reach in to check a pulse
Break a window to air out the car, then enter
Chemical suicide with hydrogen sulfide can kill rescuers quickly. Scene safety comes first, and rescue requires proper respiratory protection.
q7nduls: A 70-year-old in septic shock has received 30 mL/kg of IV fluid. Her lungs remain clear, HR 118, MAP 56 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step under sepsis guidelines?
Give a diuretic to mobilize the fluid
Accept the pressure, since a MAP above 50 is adequate
Give a steroid in place of a vasopressor
When hypotension persists after initial fluid resuscitation, a vasopressor such as norepinephrine is started to reach a MAP of at least 65 mmHg.
quhfokr: A 66-year-old with pneumonia has HR 122, RR 30, BP 100/62 and an ETCO2 of 22 mmHg by nasal cannula. How should you interpret the low ETCO2?
A sign of metabolic acidosis with likely high lactate
Hypoventilation with CO2 retention that needs a bag-valve mask
A faulty sensor, since sick patients always have high CO2
A normal value for a patient with pneumonia
In sepsis, a low ETCO2 reflects compensatory hyperventilation for metabolic acidosis and correlates with elevated lactate and poor perfusion.
qqrskh8: A 57-year-old received chemotherapy 9 days ago. She has a temperature of 38.4 C (101.1 F), HR 112 and BP 104/66 but says she feels okay. What is the best approach?
Treat it as possible sepsis and transport promptly
Take a rectal temperature to confirm the fever
Advise acetaminophen and a call to her oncologist in the morning
Delay transport unless her fever rises above 39 C (102.2 F)
Chemotherapy can lower the white cell count around 7 to 14 days after treatment. Fever in that window can signal sepsis that progresses quickly, and rectal procedures should be avoided.
qdkuz3o: An 88-year-old with dementia is more confused than usual. Temperature 35.6 C (96.1 F), HR 104, RR 24, BP 96/58, and her urine is cloudy. How should you interpret these findings?
Sepsis is still likely despite the low temperature
Infection is unlikely because she has no fever
She is simply having a bad day with her dementia
Her findings are explained by a cool room
Older adults often have no fever with sepsis and may even become hypothermic. New confusion, tachycardia and tachypnea with a likely source should be treated as sepsis.
qtudltx: A 74-year-old dialysis patient with suspected sepsis has BP 84/50 and clear lungs. How should IV fluid be given?
Small boluses with frequent lung reassessment
Withhold all fluid because he receives dialysis
Give 30 mL/kg as fast as possible without reassessing
Give oral fluids only and avoid IV access
Patients with kidney failure or heart failure still need fluid for septic hypotension, but they are prone to pulmonary edema, so fluid is given in smaller amounts with frequent reassessment.
qpkhu7u: A dialysis patient with hyperkalemia has a wide QRS. What is the main purpose of giving IV calcium?
Stabilize the heart muscle cell membranes
Move potassium out of the blood into the cells
Calcium protects the heart from dysrhythmias within minutes but does not lower potassium. Other treatments are needed to shift or remove potassium.
q15h8va: A 34-year-old finished a marathon after drinking water at every station. She has nausea, headache and confusion, then has a seizure. Her glucose is normal and she has gained weight. What is the most likely cause?
Drinking more water than is lost can dilute the blood sodium, causing brain swelling with confusion and seizures. Giving more hypotonic fluid makes it worse.
qkartcd: A 66-year-old is bleeding briskly from the puncture site of his dialysis fistula at home. What should you do first?
Firm direct pressure over the bleeding site
Apply a tourniquet above the fistula before anything else
Elevate the arm and apply an ice pack without pressure
Clamp the fistula with a hemostat
Fistula bleeding usually stops with steady direct pressure. A tourniquet is reserved for life-threatening bleeding that pressure cannot control.
q1qppeeb: A 61-year-old missed two dialysis sessions. She is in severe respiratory distress with crackles throughout, BP 196/104 and SpO2 84 percent. Which intervention is most helpful prehospital?
CPAP with the patient sitting upright
Fluid overload from missed dialysis causes pulmonary edema. CPAP and upright positioning improve oxygenation and reduce the work of breathing while she is transported for dialysis.
q1c7mrex: A 46-year-old had thyroid surgery 2 days ago. She has tingling around her mouth and fingers, spasm of her hands and a prolonged QT interval. What is the most likely cause?
The parathyroid glands can be injured during thyroid surgery, causing low calcium with paresthesias, carpopedal spasm and QT prolongation.
q1pdhl5m: An 81-year-old was found on the floor after about 2 days. His urine is dark brown. What is the most immediately dangerous complication?
Prolonged immobility can cause rhabdomyolysis, releasing potassium from damaged muscle. Hyperkalemia can cause lethal dysrhythmias, and myoglobin can injure the kidneys.
q1ih839c: A 58-year-old with cirrhosis is vomiting large amounts of bright red blood. GCS 10, HR 132, BP 78/44. What is the first priority?
Suction and position to protect the airway
Start bilateral large-bore IVs before anything else
Insert an orogastric tube to empty the stomach
Massive hematemesis with a depressed level of consciousness puts the patient at high risk of aspiration. Airway protection comes first, then vascular access and resuscitation.
qw6n2ta: A 74-year-old taking metoprolol and an anticoagulant has had black stools for 2 days. He is pale and dizzy when standing. HR 76, BP 96/58. How should you interpret his heart rate?
His medication may hide the tachycardia of blood loss
A normal heart rate proves the blood loss is minor
His low pressure is from his BP medicine, not bleeding
His heart rate shows he is fully compensating
Beta blockers blunt the heart rate response to hemorrhage, so a normal rate does not rule out significant blood loss in an anticoagulated patient with orthostatic symptoms.
qcjvoho: A 70-year-old with several prior abdominal surgeries has crampy diffuse pain, a distended abdomen, foul brown vomit and no stool or gas for 2 days. What is the most likely cause?
Adhesions from earlier surgery are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction, which causes crampy pain, distension, vomiting and absent stool or flatus.
q14rg8f8: A 42-year-old heavy drinker has severe constant upper abdominal pain boring through to his back, with vomiting. HR 118, BP 100/64. What is the most likely cause?
Pancreatitis causes severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and can cause large fluid shifts and shock. Alcohol and gallstones are the main causes.
q1dh3tx5: A 79-year-old with atrial fibrillation who is not anticoagulated has sudden severe abdominal pain, yet his abdomen is soft and barely tender. What should you be most concerned about?
Pain out of proportion to the exam in an older patient with atrial fibrillation suggests an embolus to the mesenteric arteries, a time-critical emergency.
q1o78dec: A 30-year-old was stung by a bee 10 minutes ago. She is dizzy with BP 76/42 and HR 128. She has no hives. How should you interpret this?
Not anaphylaxis, because hives are required
A vasovagal reaction to the pain of the sting
A local reaction that needs only ice
Hypotension soon after exposure to a known or likely allergen meets the criteria for anaphylaxis even without skin involvement. Give IM epinephrine promptly.
q1u21ci8: A 22-year-old's food-related anaphylaxis resolved completely after one IM epinephrine dose. She wants to go home. What should you tell her?
Resolution after epinephrine means the reaction is over for good
An oral antihistamine taken now fully prevents any recurrence
A recurrence is only possible if she eats the food again
A biphasic reaction can recur hours later without re-exposure, and epinephrine wears off within minutes to hours. Patients should be observed after anaphylaxis.
q1wvpwhk: A 64-year-old who has taken lisinopril for years has had swelling of the tongue and lips over 2 hours, without hives, itching or wheezing. What is the most likely cause?
ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin levels and can cause angioedema at any time, even after years of use. It often responds poorly to epinephrine and antihistamines.
q14znyld: The same patient now has drooling, stridor and cannot swallow. What is the most important airway consideration?
Expect a difficult airway with a surgical backup ready
Insert a supraglottic airway as the first choice
Lay him flat to improve airway alignment
Wait for the swelling to respond to antihistamines
Angioedema distorts the upper airway. Plan for a difficult intubation by the most experienced provider and prepare for a surgical airway. A supraglottic device does not bypass the swelling.
qleanlc: A 16-year-old with sickle cell disease has chest pain, a temperature of 38.7 C (101.7 F), cough, RR 30 and SpO2 89 percent. What is the most concerning diagnosis?
Acute chest syndrome is a leading cause of death in sickle cell disease, with chest pain, fever, respiratory symptoms and hypoxia. It needs oxygen and prompt transport.
q1x3lxu1: A 2-year-old with sickle cell disease is pale and lethargic, with HR 180, capillary refill of 4 seconds and an enlarging mass in the left upper abdomen. What is the most likely cause?
In young children, sickled cells can pool in the spleen, enlarging it rapidly and causing anemia and hypovolemic shock.
q1u9fgo6: A 24-year-old is in a sickle cell pain crisis with severe leg and back pain. SpO2 97 percent and vital signs are stable. What is the most appropriate care?
Withhold pain medication until the hospital confirms the crisis
High-flow oxygen for everyone with sickle cell, whatever the SpO2
Cold packs on the painful areas
Vaso-occlusive crisis needs early, adequate pain control and fluids if dehydrated. Oxygen is given for hypoxia, and cold can worsen sickling.
q2rvmef: A 12-year-old with hemophilia A hit his head on a door 2 hours ago. He has a mild headache and GCS 15. What is the best plan?
Transport, as bleeding inside the skull is a real risk
Release him because his neurologic exam is normal
Apply ice and have his parents watch him at home
Wait on scene for 1 hour to see if he gets worse
Patients with clotting disorders can develop delayed intracranial bleeding after minor trauma and need evaluation and often factor replacement.
q17lp2f: A 52-year-old kidney transplant recipient on immunosuppressants has fatigue, a cough and a temperature of 37.9 C (100.2 F). How should you interpret this?
Serious infection may be present despite mild signs
A low-grade fever means only a minor infection
He should stop his immunosuppressants on scene
His new kidney protects him from infection
Immunosuppression blunts fever and inflammation, so serious infections can look mild. These patients should be evaluated promptly.
qc53bb6: An agitated 28-year-old with hyperactive delirium has been chemically sedated after physical restraint. What monitoring is required?
Continuous ETCO2, SpO2 and ECG monitoring
A single set of vital signs before transport
Visual checks only, to avoid agitating him
Hourly vital signs as with any stable patient
Sedated patients with hyperactive delirium are at risk of respiratory depression and sudden cardiac arrest. Continuous capnography and cardiac monitoring detect deterioration early.
q1rzzsvg: A restrained, combative, hyperthermic man suddenly becomes quiet and still during transport. What does this most likely mean?
A possible arrest that needs immediate assessment
He has calmed down and no longer needs monitoring
His sedation is working as expected
He is tired from the struggle and is sleeping
Sudden calm after severe agitation can mean respiratory or cardiac arrest. Check breathing and pulse immediately.
q8qcx5c: A 42-year-old is tearful after a breakup and says she feels hopeless. How should you ask about suicide?
Ask directly if she is thinking about killing herself
Avoid the topic, since asking may plant the idea
Ask her family privately instead, so as not to upset her
Wait for her to bring up the subject herself
Asking directly about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk and is the only way to assess it accurately.
qcn7w1j: A 30-year-old took a handful of pills to end his life and now refuses transport. He is alert and oriented. What is the correct approach?
He cannot make a valid refusal
He may refuse because he is alert and oriented
He may refuse if he signs in front of a witness
He may refuse if a family member stays with him
A patient at immediate risk of self-harm lacks the capacity to refuse care. Follow local law and protocol, which may involve law enforcement.
q1fr6dut: You are cooling a patient with exertional heat stroke by cold water immersion. At about what core temperature should active cooling stop?
Cooling is usually stopped at about 38.5 to 39 C (101.3-102.2 F) to avoid overshooting into hypothermia.
q2o71ow: A 35-year-old was pulled from an icy lake after 25 minutes. He is pulseless and in asystole with a core temperature of 26 C (78.8 F) and no lethal injuries. What is the best approach?
Begin CPR and transport for active internal rewarming
Pronounce death because asystole at 26 C (78.8 F) is unsurvivable
Delay CPR until he has been rewarmed above 30 C (86 F)
Give rescue breaths only, since compressions cause VF
Hypothermia protects the brain, and people have survived long arrests after rewarming. Continue CPR and transport to a center capable of extracorporeal rewarming.
qv0f42i: A hiker has frostbitten feet and must walk 3 hours to reach the trailhead. What should you do about rewarming?
Do not thaw the feet if they could refreeze
Rub the feet with snow to restore circulation
Thaw the feet with dry heat from a campfire
Thaw the feet in hot water before walking out
Thawing and refreezing causes more tissue damage than delaying rewarming. Walking on frozen feet is preferable to thawing them before a long walk out.
qj4ev3b: For a drowning victim in cardiac arrest, what is emphasized compared with a typical adult cardiac arrest?
Hands-only CPR so compressions are not delayed
Defibrillation before any breaths are given
Full spinal motion restriction before CPR
Drowning causes a hypoxic arrest, so early ventilation is key. Spinal precautions are not routine unless there is a diving or trauma mechanism.
q1jrkmvy: A climber at 4,200 meters has a headache, confusion and cannot walk heel to toe. What is the most important treatment?
Rest at the same altitude for 24 hours
Fluids and sleep, deciding in the morning
Continued ascent to finish the climb quickly
Ataxia and altered mental status at altitude suggest high-altitude cerebral edema, which can be fatal. Immediate descent is the definitive treatment.
q1xsn94b: After 2 days at 3,800 meters, a hiker has shortness of breath at rest, a cough with pink frothy sputum, crackles and SpO2 70 percent. What is the most likely condition?
High-altitude pulmonary edema causes dyspnea at rest, cough and hypoxia. It is treated with oxygen and descent.
qfmfe2t: A diver ran out of air and ascended rapidly. Within 3 minutes of surfacing, he became confused with weakness on one side. What is the most likely cause?
Rapid ascent can rupture alveoli and send gas bubbles into the arteries, causing stroke-like signs within minutes. Treat with 100 percent oxygen and arrange hyperbaric therapy.
q1llio1i: Six hours after a deep dive, a diver has deep aching pain in his shoulder and fatigue. He plans to fly home tonight. What is the best advice?
100 percent oxygen and evaluation for recompression
Fly home and see a doctor afterward
Massage and heat for the sore shoulder
Return to depth to recompress in the water
Joint pain hours after diving suggests decompression sickness. Flying lowers ambient pressure and worsens bubbles, so he needs oxygen and evaluation for hyperbaric treatment.
q1apqe9e: A 30-year-old was bitten on the ankle by a rattlesnake and swelling is spreading up his leg. Which treatment is appropriate?
Keep the limb still and mark the edge of the swelling
Apply a tight arterial tourniquet above the bite to stop the venom
Cut over the fang marks and suction out the venom
Pack the leg in ice to slow venom absorption
Pit viper bites are managed by immobilizing the limb, marking swelling progression and rapid transport for antivenom. Tourniquets, incisions and ice cause harm.
q1usyr9d: A 22-year-old at 37 weeks has a generalized seizure. BP 172/110. What is the first-line medication to stop and prevent eclamptic seizures?
Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for eclampsia. A benzodiazepine may be used if magnesium is not available.
q19y7ngl: A 29-year-old delivered a baby 10 days ago. She has a severe headache, BP 166/104 and is seeing spots. What is the most likely condition?
Preeclampsia can develop up to 6 weeks after delivery and carries the same risk of seizures and stroke.
q2hcias: A 30-year-old in active labor who had a prior cesarean section has sudden tearing abdominal pain, her contractions stop, and fetal parts are easily felt through the abdomen. HR 130, BP 84/50. What is the most likely cause?
A previous uterine scar increases the risk of rupture, which causes sudden pain, loss of contractions, palpable fetal parts and maternal shock.
q1u6f4bk: During a breech delivery the body and arms have delivered, but the head has not delivered after 3 minutes. What should you do?
Make an airway with a gloved hand and transport
Pull firmly on the baby's legs to deliver the head
Push the baby's body back into the vagina
Apply firm pressure to the top of the uterus
If the head does not deliver, place gloved fingers to hold the vaginal wall away from the baby's face to create an airway, and transport rapidly.
q18mx6us: You have placed the mother in the McRoberts position for a shoulder dystocia, but the shoulders still do not deliver. What should you do next?
Firm pressure on the top of the uterus
Strong downward traction on the head
Push the head back into the vagina
Suprapubic pressure helps dislodge the anterior shoulder from behind the pubic bone. Fundal pressure worsens impaction.
q19mcepm: The baby's head delivers with the cord wrapped tightly around the neck twice, and it cannot be slipped over the head. What should you do?
Clamp the cord in two places and cut between the clamps
Pull firmly on the head so the shoulders deliver more quickly
Push the head back and wait for the next contraction
Leave the cord in place and continue the delivery
A cord too tight to slip over the head must be clamped and cut to allow delivery.
q1fqyg3r: During labor, a 35-year-old suddenly becomes severely short of breath and hypoxic, then hypotensive, then has a seizure and arrests. After resuscitation she bleeds from her IV sites. What is the most likely cause?
Amniotic fluid embolism causes sudden hypoxia, shock and arrest during labor or just after delivery, often followed by a bleeding disorder.
qlo27hr: At what rate should positive-pressure ventilation be given to a newborn?
NRP recommends 40 to 60 breaths per minute during positive-pressure ventilation.
q12r3e52: You are starting chest compressions on a newborn. What oxygen concentration should be used?
NRP recommends increasing oxygen to 100 percent when compressions begin, then weaning it as soon as the heart rate recovers.
q10a18d4: A newborn born at 30 weeks needs PPV. What oxygen concentration should you start with?
For newborns under 35 weeks, NRP recommends starting at 21 to 30 percent and adjusting to reach target saturations.
q1nd7ryv: A newborn delivered through thick meconium-stained fluid is limp and not breathing. What should you do?
Initial steps, then PPV if still apneic
Intubate and suction the trachea before any breaths
Suction the stomach before drying and warming
Routine tracheal suctioning is no longer recommended for non-vigorous newborns with meconium. Start the initial steps and ventilation without delay.
q1setx0n: A baby born at 28 weeks is delivered in the ambulance. How should you keep the baby warm?
Place the body in plastic wrap without drying first
Dry vigorously and leave the skin uncovered for assessment
Bathe the baby with warm water to remove the vernix
Place the baby on a cool surface to prevent overheating
Very premature newborns lose heat rapidly. Covering them up to the neck in plastic wrap without drying, along with a hat and a warm environment, reduces heat loss.
qpu4u55: During newborn resuscitation with chest compressions, which method gives the most accurate heart rate?
A cardiac monitor with ECG leads
NRP recommends an electronic cardiac monitor during compressions, since palpation and pulse oximetry can be inaccurate.
qa3z1ay: A newborn is apneic at birth. When should you calculate the 1-minute Apgar score before starting resuscitation?
Do not wait for the Apgar score
Apgar scores describe the newborn's condition but are not used to decide whether to resuscitate.
qhysfs3: A 3-month-old has had a runny nose for 3 days and now has wheezing, retractions, poor feeding and SpO2 91 percent. What is the most helpful first step?
A routine albuterol nebulizer for the wheezing
An oral steroid dose for the inflammation

Infants breathe mainly through the nose, and secretions from bronchiolitis can block the airway. Suctioning improves breathing and feeding, while bronchodilators and steroids are not routinely helpful.
qyidl8v: A 2-year-old has croup. Which finding indicates severe croup?
A loud barking cough that is worse at night
Low-grade fever with a runny nose
Stridor at rest, especially with retractions or agitation, means significant airway narrowing that needs treatment.
q1n7q2x6: Which feature makes a febrile seizure complex rather than simple?
Complex febrile seizures last longer than 15 minutes, are focal or recur within 24 hours. Simple seizures are brief and generalized.
q1uzoki5: A 20-month-old had a 2-minute generalized seizure with a temperature of 39.4 C (102.9 F). He is now drowsy but improving, with a patent airway. What is the best plan?
Remove excess clothing, monitor and transport
Place the child in a cold bath to bring the fever down quickly
Sponge the child with rubbing alcohol
Place a bite block to protect the tongue
Simple febrile seizures are usually harmless, but children need evaluation. Cold baths, alcohol and objects in the mouth are dangerous.
q11dkoiy: Which bruising pattern in a 2-year-old is most concerning for abuse?
Bruising on the ears, neck or torso
Scrapes on the knees and elbows
Bruises on protected areas such as the ears, neck and torso are rarely accidental in young children. Shins, forehead and knees are common sites for accidental injuries.
q1q2x6d: A 4-month-old has irritability, vomiting, lethargy and an episode of apnea, without fever or visible injury. What should you suspect?
Shaken infants may have no external injury. Unexplained lethargy, vomiting and apnea in an infant should raise concern for abusive head trauma.
qycxmli: You suspect a child has been abused. What is your responsibility?
Document objectively and report as required by law
Confront the caregivers about your suspicion on scene
Report only if you are certain abuse occurred
Leave reporting to the hospital without telling staff
EMS providers are mandated reporters in most states. Reasonable suspicion is enough, and the report should be objective without accusations.
qheq57r: A 10-month-old has bouts of inconsolable crying with his knees drawn up every 15 to 20 minutes, is lethargic between episodes and has passed red jelly-like stool. What is the most likely cause?
In intussusception the bowel telescopes into itself, causing intermittent severe pain, lethargy and currant jelly stool.
q1psrpc5: A 6-week-old briefly turned pale and limp for 20 seconds, then recovered. She now looks normal. What is the best plan?
Transport for evaluation despite the normal exam
Release her, since she now looks completely normal
Advise the parents to follow up within a week
Release her if her pulse oximetry is normal
A brief resolved unexplained event can signal serious illness, such as infection, abuse or a cardiac problem, and needs medical evaluation.
q1qz5erv: An 82-year-old has new confusion, dry mouth and urinary retention after starting an over-the-counter sleep aid containing diphenhydramine. What is the most likely cause?
Older adults are very sensitive to anticholinergic drugs, which can cause delirium, urinary retention and constipation.
q150p9u7: A 79-year-old hospice patient with a POLST for comfort measures only has new pauses in breathing and gurgling. She appears comfortable. What is the best approach?
Follow the comfort-care plan and contact hospice
Begin aggressive suctioning and assist with a BVM
Start CPR if her breathing stops for 20 seconds
These are normal changes near death. Follow the patient's wishes and support the family.
q1luq61x: What is the best way to manage noisy upper airway secretions in a dying patient receiving comfort care?
Turn the patient onto the side
Deep nasotracheal suctioning every few minutes
A large IV fluid bolus to thin secretions
Repositioning helps secretions drain. Deep suction is uncomfortable and usually ineffective at this stage.
q1dy2880: An 85-year-old with a valid do-not-resuscitate order has a pulse and acute respiratory distress. What should you do?
Treat her distress within the limits of her orders
Provide no treatment because she has a DNR
Intubate, since a DNR applies only to cardiac arrest
Call her family before any care is given
A DNR order does not mean no treatment. Provide oxygen, positioning and other care allowed by her orders and local protocol.
q1huoij6: Which three findings make up the Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale?
Facial droop, arm drift and abnormal speech
Facial droop, grip strength and gaze deviation
Arm drift, leg drift and level of consciousness
The CPSS checks a smile for facial droop, 10 seconds of arm drift with eyes closed, and repeating a sentence.
q1h7c2vb: How many abnormal Cincinnati findings are needed to suspect a stroke?
At least two plus a headache
Any single abnormal CPSS finding is a positive screen. With one finding the chance of stroke is about 72%; with all three it is over 85%.
qli7c62: A positive Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale tells you what?
That this could be a stroke
That there is a large vessel occlusion
That the patient qualifies for thrombolysis
The CPSS is a screen. It does not measure severity or predict an LVO; a severity scale or the hospital exam does that.
quafatu: How is arm drift tested in the Cincinnati scale?
Eyes closed, both arms out with palms up for 10 seconds
Squeeze both of your hands as hard as possible
Lift each leg off the stretcher for 5 seconds
Touch the finger to the nose with eyes open
Closing the eyes removes visual correction, so a weak arm drifts down or pronates.
qnmxj2z: What do the B and E in BE-FAST add to FAST?
Balance and eyes, to catch posterior circulation strokes
Breathing and EKG, to catch cardiac causes
Blood glucose and eyes, to rule out mimics
Bleeding and edema, to spot hemorrhagic strokes
Strokes in the back of the brain (posterior circulation) often cause imbalance, vertigo or vision loss with a normal face, arm and speech exam.
q8ods46: A 62-year-old has sudden vertigo, cannot walk straight and has double vision. Face, arms and speech are normal. With BE-FAST this patient is:
Positive, because of the balance and eye findings
Negative, because face, arm and speech are normal
Positive only if a headache is present
Negative until the symptoms last 24 hours
Any one sudden BE-FAST finding is positive. This is the posterior stroke picture FAST alone would miss.
q1wywttg: What does the T in BE-FAST stand for?
Time: note the last known well and move quickly
Every stroke treatment window is measured from the last known well time.
qsfielv: Which glucose range is required for a positive LAPSS?
LAPSS requires a glucose of 60 to 400 to help screen out hypoglycemia and severe hyperglycemia as mimics.
q1jfyhhc: A patient has a negative LAPSS but a clear story of sudden one-sided numbness and confusion. What is the best approach?
Treat it as a possible stroke anyway
Document a negative stroke screen and transport routinely
Obtain a refusal since the screen is negative
A negative LAPSS does not rule out stroke. Clinical suspicion wins.
qarxsgk: What is the Los Angeles Motor Scale total that suggests a large vessel occlusion?
LAMS scores facial droop 0 to 1, arm drift 0 to 2 and grip 0 to 2. A total of 4 or 5 suggests an LVO.
q1g0e79r: Which three items are scored in LAMS?
Facial droop, arm drift and grip strength
Facial droop, speech and leg drift
Level of consciousness, gaze and arm drift
LAMS is a pure motor scale built from the LAPSS motor items.
qndgp0w: A patient has facial droop, an arm that falls rapidly and no grip on that side. What is the LAMS?
Facial droop 1 + arm falls rapidly 2 + no grip 2 = 5, which suggests an LVO.
qzrs2kz: What RACE score suggests a large vessel occlusion?
RACE runs 0 to 9; a score of 5 or more suggests an LVO.
qhukiig: In RACE, when do you score agnosia instead of aphasia?
When the left side is weak
When the right side is weak
Left-sided weakness means a right-brain stroke, which causes neglect or agnosia. Right-sided weakness means a left-brain stroke, which causes aphasia.
q1eqbn0q: How many points does conjugate gaze deviation earn on C-STAT?
It is not part of C-STAT
Gaze deviation is worth 2 points, so it alone reaches the LVO cutoff of 2.
q1takkbw: What C-STAT total suggests a large vessel occlusion?
C-STAT runs 0 to 4; 2 or more suggests an LVO.
qvh6wsk: A patient cannot hold the left arm up for 10 seconds, knows their age and the month, and follows commands. Gaze is midline. What is the C-STAT?
1, which is below the LVO cutoff
0, because the arm is not scored
Only arm weakness scores (1 point). The LOC point needs a wrong answer AND a failed command.
q7i3930: What FAST-ED score suggests a large vessel occlusion?
FAST-ED runs 0 to 9; 4 or more suggests an LVO.
q1r43p5y: What do the E and D in FAST-ED stand for?
Eye deviation and denial or neglect
Eye deviation and denial or neglect are cortical signs that point to a large clot.
q1hp2nij: Facial palsy (1), arm falls (2), mild aphasia (1), no eye deviation, no neglect. What is the FAST-ED and what does it suggest?
3, which does not suggest an LVO
qysfwe2: What must be present before the rest of the VAN assessment counts?
VAN starts with arm weakness. No weakness means VAN negative.
q1s9l8yz: A patient has right arm drift and cannot name objects. Vision and attention are normal. The VAN is:
Negative, because only one cortical sign is present
VAN positive = arm weakness plus any one of vision, aphasia or neglect.
quoodqd: A patient has left arm weakness only. Speech, vision and attention are normal. The VAN is:
Indeterminate until a glucose is checked
Positive if the weakness is severe
Weakness alone, without a vision, aphasia or neglect finding, is VAN negative.
q1yp464a: What are the three parts of the MEND exam?
Mental status, cranial nerves and limbs
MEND checks mental status, cranial nerves (face, fields, gaze) and limbs (drift, sensation, coordination).
qkw7kyv: Which scale is built into the MEND exam?
MEND includes facial droop, arm drift and speech, so it also answers the CPSS.
qemohuo: How is the MEND exam scored?
Any abnormal finding is a positive exam
A total of 4 or more is positive
MEND is a checklist rather than a point score.
q4bgg8p: What is the range of the NIH Stroke Scale?
q1bbb3lr: What NIHSS is the usual minimum for thrombectomy of an anterior LVO?
The 2026 guideline uses NIHSS 6 or more for anterior LVO thrombectomy (10 or more for basilar occlusion).
qzpxs7c: A patient has NIHSS 3 from isolated severe aphasia that keeps them from working or communicating. Under the 2026 guideline, are they a thrombolysis candidate within 4.5 hours?
Yes, because the deficit is disabling
No, because the NIHSS is under 6
Only if a perfusion scan is done first
Thrombolysis is for disabling deficits regardless of the NIHSS number.
qau417k: What is the key difference between a TIA and a stroke?
A TIA leaves no infarct on imaging; a stroke does
A TIA is always under 5 minutes
A TIA is a brief blockage without dead tissue. You cannot tell them apart in the field, so active symptoms are treated as a stroke.
q1sox06a: A 70-year-old had 20 minutes of right arm weakness that has fully resolved. Now he wants to stay home. What is the best response?
Explain that stroke risk is highest in the next 48 hours and encourage transport
Have him follow up with his doctor next week
Transport only if the blood pressure is high
A TIA is a warning sign; urgent evaluation lowers the risk of a disabling stroke.
qk1l8e7: A woman went to bed at 22:00 normal and woke at 06:00 with left-sided weakness. What is her last known well?
Unknown, so no time is recorded
Wake-up stroke: LKW is when she was last seen normal, not when symptoms were found.
qq58qbf: Symptoms started at 13:00, fully resolved at 13:30, then returned at 15:00. What is the last known well?
A complete return to baseline resets the clock to the time they were last fully normal.
q17x1625: Symptoms started at 09:00 and partly improved at 09:40 but never fully cleared. What is the last known well?
Only a full return to baseline resets the clock. Partial improvement does not.
qh1q7bk: What is the single most important stroke mimic to rule out in the field?
Low glucose can cause any focal deficit and is quickly reversible. Check a glucose on every suspected stroke.
ql66yck: Which finding points to Bell's palsy rather than a stroke?
The forehead on the affected side cannot wrinkle
Arm drift on the same side
Bell's palsy weakens the whole side of the face, forehead included. A stroke usually spares the forehead.
qcq4ple: Why can dropping the blood pressure worsen a swelling ischemic brain?
CPP = MAP - ICP, so a lower MAP with a high ICP cuts perfusion to the penumbra
Lower pressure increases bleeding into the clot
Low pressure raises intracranial pressure directly
Autoregulation is lost around the stroke, so flow follows pressure. Less flow turns penumbra into core and worsens swelling.
q9laka9: Stunned but still living brain around the dead core
The dead core of the infarct
Blood that has leaked into the brain
The swelling seen 3 days after a stroke
Saving the penumbra is the whole point of reperfusion and of protecting blood pressure.
qc4l2ez: In many EMS systems, when is the blood pressure of a suspected ischemic stroke treated in the field?
Only when it is over 220/120 (or per medical control)
Permissive hypertension protects the penumbra. The hospital lowers it to under 185/110 only if thrombolysis is planned.
q1p00jq7: What blood pressure must be reached before IV thrombolysis for stroke?
After thrombolysis it is kept under 180/105 for 24 hours.
q1gs9rd7: After a successful thrombectomy, what does the 2026 guideline say about lowering systolic BP below 140?
It is harmful and not recommended
It is recommended only for large-core strokes
Intensive lowering below 140 after recanalization worsened outcomes in trials.
qgvf8od: Under the 2026 AHA/ASA guideline, what is the standard window for IV thrombolysis for stroke?
Within 4.5 hours of last known well
Within 6 hours of last known well
Within 24 hours of last known well
0 to 4.5 hours from LKW for eligible patients with disabling deficits.
q2ugiy: A wake-up stroke patient was last seen normal 8 hours ago. Under the 2026 guideline, can thrombolysis still be considered?
Yes, if advanced imaging shows salvageable brain (for example DWI-FLAIR mismatch)
No, the window is 4.5 hours with no exceptions
Only if the NIHSS is over 20
Extended-window thrombolysis (about 4.5 to 9 hours or unknown onset) may be considered with imaging selection.
q1m8c9md: Which statement about tenecteplase versus alteplase for stroke is correct under the 2026 guideline?
Either may be used within 4.5 hours; tenecteplase is a single IV push
Tenecteplase is only for patients over 80
The 2026 guideline endorses both. Tenecteplase's single bolus makes transfers simpler than alteplase's 60-minute infusion.
q1a6zz0g: Why can tenecteplase be given as one push while alteplase needs an infusion?
Tenecteplase has a longer half-life and more fibrin specificity
Tenecteplase is a smaller dose of the same drug
Tenecteplase does not need to reach the clot
Tenecteplase was engineered from alteplase to last longer and bind fibrin more selectively.
q9g4k3d: What does the 2026 guideline say about the higher tenecteplase dose used in some trials?
It is not recommended because it did not help and may cause harm
It is preferred for basilar occlusion
It is preferred for patients over 100 kg
Only the standard stroke dose is recommended.
q95h320: A patient has a mild, non-disabling stroke 2 hours after onset. What does the 2026 guideline prefer?
Dual antiplatelet therapy rather than thrombolysis
Thrombolysis has not been shown to help non-disabling deficits; DAPT is preferred.
q18f6gjl: Which hospitals can perform endovascular thrombectomy?
Any emergency department with a CT
Primary Stroke Centers and Acute Stroke Ready Hospitals can give thrombolysis but not thrombectomy.
q12lsnof: Which findings most strongly suggest a large vessel occlusion?
Gaze deviation, aphasia or neglect with dense one-sided weakness
Cortical signs plus dense weakness are the classic LVO picture, which is what the severity scales measure.
q1nsfo8n: Your severity scale is positive for LVO, LKW was 2 hours ago, and a thrombectomy center is 20 minutes farther than the nearest primary stroke center. Under the AHA Mission: Lifeline routing algorithm, where should most systems go?
Suspected LVO goes to a CSC or TSC when the extra time is about 30 minutes or less and thrombolysis eligibility is not lost. Local protocols set exact minutes.
q198rbim: When does a suspected LVO patient go to the nearest stroke center instead of bypassing to a thrombectomy center?
When the bypass would push a thrombolysis-eligible patient past their window
Whenever the blood pressure is high
When the patient is on aspirin
Getting thrombolysis started (drip and ship) can come first when the bypass costs the window.
qfxcl4: What is the standard time window for thrombectomy of an anterior LVO without advanced imaging selection?
0 to 6 hours from last known well
Up to 6 hours is the early window; 6 to 24 hours needs imaging selection.
q1tcew89: Up to how long after last known well can selected anterior LVO patients get a thrombectomy?
From 6 to 24 hours, patients are selected by imaging; the 2026 guideline now includes some large-core strokes.
qovh8l4: For basilar artery occlusion, the 2026 guideline supports thrombectomy within 24 hours for patients with which NIHSS?
Benefit for NIHSS 6 to 9 in basilar occlusion is not well established.
qwaw6ew: What is the field scene-time goal for a suspected stroke?
No target; take as long as needed
Short scene times and pre-notification shorten door-to-needle and door-to-puncture times.
qg31dqg: What SpO2 is the usual threshold for giving oxygen to a stroke patient?
Oxygen for everyone regardless of SpO2
Routine oxygen for a normal saturation does not help stroke outcomes.
q1df1fry: Why should a stroke patient have nothing by mouth?
Swallowing may be impaired and aspiration is common
Dysphagia is common after stroke; the hospital screens the swallow first.
q16drb0p: How soon after first medical contact should a 12-lead be obtained in suspected ACS?
Only if the pain is severe
Early 12-leads let EMS activate the cath lab from the field.
qfw3e2f: What is the ST elevation threshold for V2 and V3 in a woman?
In V2-V3: 1.5 mm in women, 2 mm in men 40 and over, 2.5 mm in men under 40. Other leads: 1 mm.
qg3urp7: ST elevation in II, III and aVF points to which territory?
Inferior, usually the right coronary artery
Inferior STEMI: check right-sided V4R for right ventricular involvement.
qm4xdd0: Inferior STEMI with 1 mm ST elevation in V4R and a BP of 92/60. Which drug is most likely to drop the pressure dangerously?
Right ventricular infarcts are preload-dependent; nitrates reduce preload and can crash the pressure.
qpguz99: ST depression in V1 to V3 with tall R waves suggests what?
Confirm with posterior leads V7 to V9: 0.5 mm of elevation.
q1gkmegh: What is the elevation threshold in posterior leads V7 to V9?
Posterior leads are far from the heart, so the cutoff is lower.
q1xrw7re: Upsloping ST depression with tall symmetric T waves across V1 to V6 in chest pain suggests what?
De Winter T waves, a proximal LAD occlusion
De Winter is a STEMI equivalent that deserves cath lab activation per protocol.
q19vwf4i: A pain-free patient has deep biphasic T waves in V2 and V3 after chest pain yesterday. What is this, and why does it matter?
Wellens pattern: critical LAD narrowing at risk of closing
Wellens is not a STEMI, but these patients need urgent cardiology and should not get stress testing.
qby6od9: Which criteria help find an MI in a patient with left bundle branch block or a paced rhythm?
Concordant ST elevation of 1 mm or more, concordant ST depression of 1 mm or more in V1 to V3, or excessively discordant elevation.
q1671mys: ST elevation in aVR with widespread ST depression suggests what?
High-risk pattern; follow your protocol on activation.
qee66nx: EMS takes a STEMI patient directly to a PCI-capable center. What is the first-medical-contact-to-device goal?
Direct transport: FMC to device within 90 minutes.
q1lbkrvy: When is fibrinolysis chosen over transfer for PCI in STEMI?
When FMC to device would exceed 120 minutes, within 12 hours of onset
Whenever the pain is under 1 hour
If PCI cannot happen within 120 minutes, fibrinolysis (door to needle within 30 minutes) is the alternative.
q1jw19a: What is the door-in-door-out goal at a non-PCI hospital transferring a STEMI?
DIDO of 30 minutes keeps FMC to device near 120 minutes.
q1uqo975: When is oxygen indicated in suspected ACS?
Only if the patient is over 65
Extra oxygen does not help a normal saturation.
q1u927xd: Why are defibrillation pads placed early on a STEMI patient?
Ventricular fibrillation is most common in the first hours
Early VF is the most common cause of sudden death in STEMI.
q13pkl18: Life-threatening organ dysfunction from the body's response to infection
Infection with a fast heart rate
q15ci8hu: Which qSOFA finding is NOT one of the three criteria?
qSOFA is respiratory rate, mentation and systolic BP. The 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign advises against using it alone as a screen.
q41bjib: A low end-tidal CO2 in a suspected sepsis patient often correlates with what?
EtCO2 of about 25 mmHg or less tracks with elevated lactate and poor perfusion.
qu9j95k: Vasopressors needed for MAP 65 or more and lactate over 2 despite fluids
Septic shock carries a much higher mortality than sepsis alone.
qcz1f2u: What is the antibiotic time goal for septic shock?
Each hour of delay raises mortality; a field sepsis alert speeds this up.
q1m4orbh: During fluid resuscitation in sepsis, what should be reassessed between boluses?
Fluids help until they cause pulmonary edema; reassess each time.
q196fy0v: In the 2021 field triage guideline, which vital sign is a red criterion for an adult aged 10 to 64?
Heart rate greater than systolic BP
For 10 to 64: SBP under 90 or HR greater than SBP. For 65 and over: SBP under 110 or HR greater than SBP.
qrm2srw: What systolic BP is a red criterion for a patient 65 or older?
Older adults decompensate at higher pressures.
q1gsga6t: A fall from what height is a yellow (mechanism) criterion for all ages?
The 2021 guideline uses 10 feet for all ages.
qcli70r: What are the parts of the trauma lethal triad?
Each worsens the others; keep trauma patients warm from the start.
qhv7uid: Which patient should NOT get permissive hypotension?
A patient with a traumatic brain injury
A stab wound to the abdomen with no head injury
A patient with a pelvic fracture and no head injury
The injured brain needs a normal blood pressure for perfusion.
qntgpw7: Tranexamic acid for trauma bleeding is not started after how long from injury?
Benefit is greatest within 1 hour; after 3 hours it may cause harm.
q11a6fho: After ROSC, what SpO2 range is targeted?
q1lxrsu: After ROSC, what end-tidal CO2 range is targeted?
Hyperventilation lowers CO2 and constricts cerebral vessels.
q1q9pkpo: After ROSC, what blood pressure goals are typical?
Systolic 90 or more and MAP 65 or more
Treat hypotension with fluids and vasopressors per protocol.
q131sqxf: During post-ROSC care, the end-tidal CO2 suddenly falls from 38 to 12. What is the most likely cause?
Check a pulse and resume CPR if absent.
q3h9qi7: Why is a 12-lead obtained soon after ROSC?
To find a STEMI that needs the cath lab
Post-arrest STEMI goes to a PCI center.
q1q9vw74: In Care Under Fire, where does TCCC describe placing a limb tourniquet when the bleeding site is not obvious?
High and tight on the injured limb, over the uniform
Directly over the wound on bare skin
Two inches below the nearest joint
On the uninjured limb for comparison
When the bleeding site cannot be seen under fire, TCCC describes applying the tourniquet high and tight on the injured limb, over the uniform, and reassessing it later in Tactical Field Care.
q1yp8s6n: Which form documents casualty care in TCCC?
The DD 1380 TCCC Card records injuries, treatments and times so the next level of care knows exactly what was done.
q1touylb: Why does TCCC start hypothermia prevention even in a warm climate?
Cold blood clots poorly, so heat loss worsens bleeding
Shivering prevents the casualty from walking
Hypothermia raises blood pressure too high
Hypothermia, acidosis and clotting problems feed each other in bleeding casualties. Even in heat, a casualty in shock loses body heat quickly.
q5vj7ec: A casualty has an open chest wound. What does TCCC list for it?
A vented or non-vented chest seal
TCCC treats open and sucking chest wounds with a vented or non-vented chest seal, then monitors for a developing tension pneumothorax.
q1t9kj1n: When does TCCC describe converting a tourniquet to a hemostatic or pressure dressing?
When the casualty is not in shock, can be closely watched, and the tourniquet has been on less than 2 hours
Whenever the bleeding seems to have stopped
Only at surgery; tourniquets stay on until then
Conversion is considered only when the casualty is not in shock, can be monitored, the wound is not an amputation, and the tourniquet has been in place under 2 hours.
q1mh77bp: Which oral antibiotic is first-line for an open combat wound in the 2026 TCCC Guidelines?
The 2026 update replaced moxifloxacin with cefadroxil as the oral first-line choice, with cephalexin as the alternative.
q1ovd3c0: A casualty with a forearm wound can still fight. Which pain option fits TCCC?
Casualties who can stay in the fight use the oral Combat Wound Medication Pack (acetaminophen, meloxicam and, since 2026, suzetrigine), which does not sedate.
q1d53kfw: TCCC lists TXA as soon as possible, but no later than how long after injury?
The benefit of TXA falls with time and may reverse after 3 hours, which is why TCCC sets that limit.
q1vgeehn: Which blood product does TCCC rank first for hemorrhagic shock?
Whole blood replaces red cells, plasma and platelets at once. Components follow, and crystalloid is not the TCCC fluid for hemorrhagic shock.
qii6x5p: When does TCCC list calcium during resuscitation?
After the first transfused blood product
Citrate in stored blood binds calcium, so calcium follows the first product to support clotting and heart contraction.
qd30h1l: Which finding prompts hypertonic saline in a head-injured casualty?
Unequal or fixed and dilated pupils, or posturing
TCCC lists hypertonic saline for herniation signs only, not to prevent herniation ahead of time.
q1qlqbpr: What endpoint does TCCC describe for ketamine pain control?
The goal is tolerable pain that preserves airway, breathing and mentation, not complete pain relief or unconsciousness.
qtuo1qf: During tactical evacuation, what airway may a trained provider consider instead of a cricothyroidotomy?
Bag-valve-mask alone for the whole flight
TCCC notes that endotracheal intubation may be considered in TACEVAC by trained providers, a Tier 4 skill.
qitszqr: What oxygen saturation does TCCC target in a casualty with moderate or severe head injury?
Low oxygen worsens brain injury. TCCC lists a target of at least 92% for head-injured casualties.
q18171z9: Which monitoring tool is added at Tier 4?
Tier 4 adds capnography, point-of-care lactate, Foley catheters and urine output monitoring to the earlier tiers' vital signs.
q1ud8qaa: Why is 23.4% sodium chloride attractive to special operations medics?
It gives a similar osmotic load to 3% or 5% saline in a much smaller volume
It needs no IV or IO access
It prevents herniation when given early
The concentrated solution weighs and takes up far less space. Like other hypertonic saline, it is for herniation signs, followed by a flush.
q1s0vngo: A pulseless combat casualty with torso trauma is found during TACEVAC. What does TCCC list before considering CPR?
An immediate shock with an AED
In traumatic arrest, TCCC lists bilateral needle decompression. CPR may be attempted only if there are no obviously fatal wounds and surgical care is close.
qnbfkxy: A diver who breathed compressed gas surfaces and becomes unconscious within minutes. What does the U.S. Navy Diving Manual say to assume?
Any diver who breathed compressed gas and surfaces unconscious or with neurological symptoms within 10 minutes is assumed to have arterial gas embolism.
q6135gl: A diver has a deep, dull shoulder ache a few hours after a dive, with a normal full neurological exam. Which category fits?
Joint pain with a dull, aching quality and no neurological findings is the classic Type I picture. Without a complete neurological exam, it is treated as Type II.
q1ll2ce2: After a dive, a diver has a band of pain wrapping around the trunk. How does the Navy Diving Manual classify it?
As Type II DCS, a sign of spinal cord involvement
Pain in the chest, abdomen or hips, and girdle pain wrapping around the body, suggest spinal cord involvement and are treated as Type II.
qnqfiog: Why does the Navy Diving Manual advise against giving pain medicine to make a DCS patient comfortable?
Pain may be the only way to localize the problem and track the treatment
Divers cannot take pain medicine for 24 hours
It is not allowed in a chamber
The pain marks where bubbles are and shows whether recompression is working, so masking it can hide the response.
q1yl03pb: Why does prolonged care guidance run each sedation drug in its own bag?
Mixing drugs in one bag is untested and can form unsafe compounds
It makes the drip run faster
One bag cannot hold two drugs
Each medicine runs separately so it can be adjusted or stopped on its own and to avoid untested mixtures.
q3wg6cl: During a long hold, what does hourly urine output from a Foley mainly show?
Whether the kidneys are being perfused, a sign of adequate resuscitation
How much pain the casualty has
Urine output is one of the most useful trends in prolonged care, because it reflects blood flow to the kidneys.
q12rl3l4: Why might famotidine be given during prolonged casualty care?
To help prevent stress ulcers in a critically ill casualty
Critically ill casualties are at risk of stomach bleeding from stress ulcers. Acid reducers like famotidine help prevent them.
q1xmta51: After several units of stored blood, which i-STAT change is expected?
Citrate in stored blood binds calcium, so ionized calcium falls. Potassium often rises.
qnxdens: A casualty with a high above-knee amputation is in hemorrhagic shock 40 minutes after injury. The tourniquet is controlling the bleeding. Which medication is the priority now?
Tranexamic acid as soon as possible
Enoxaparin to prevent clots in the limb

TCCC gives TXA as early as possible, within 3 hours of injury, to casualties expected to need significant transfusion. Ketorolac impairs platelets, enoxaparin is an anticoagulant, and hetastarch worsens coagulopathy.
q12yxaay: You reach a casualty with ongoing hemorrhagic shock 4 hours after his injury. No TXA has been given. What is the correct approach to TXA?
Withhold it, as the 3-hour window has passed
Give it now, then repeat it after an hour
Give it now, since late doses still reduce bleeding
Give it only after the second unit of blood
In CRASH-2, TXA started more than 3 hours after injury was linked to higher death from bleeding, so TCCC limits it to the first 3 hours. Late dosing is not a catch-up step.
qr5q94e: What is the mechanism of action of tranexamic acid?
It blocks plasminogen binding to fibrin, slowing clot breakdown
It activates platelets directly at the site of vessel injury
It replaces fibrinogen consumed during massive bleeding
It reverses the anticoagulant effect of citrate in stored blood
TXA is a lysine analog that blocks the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen, inhibiting fibrinolysis. It adds no factors or platelets and does not affect citrate.
qnix953: A medic pushes tranexamic acid rapidly through an IO line. Which adverse effect is the FDA label warning most associated with rapid IV injection?
The TXA label notes hypotension with rapid intravenous injection, which is why TCCC directs a slow IV or IO push. Seizures and thrombosis are other labeled risks.
qlks0zd: A casualty with a blunt head injury from a blast has a GCS of 10, no major external bleeding, and was injured 1 hour ago. Per current TCCC, which statement about TXA is correct?
Significant TBI is an indication for TXA within 3 hours
TXA is reserved for casualties with a tourniquet in place
TXA is contraindicated in any casualty with a head injury
TXA is given only after a CT scan excludes brain bleeding
TCCC includes signs of significant TBI or altered mental status after blast or blunt trauma as an indication for TXA within 3 hours, supported by CRASH-3. Imaging is not required first.
q3voh9s: A casualty is about to receive his first unit of cold-stored low-titer O whole blood. Per TCCC, when is calcium given?
During or immediately after the first unit
Only after the fourth unit has been given
Only if ionized calcium is measured as low
Only when the casualty develops tetany
TCCC gives calcium during or right after the first blood product because citrate binds calcium and many casualties are hypocalcemic on arrival. Waiting for labs or symptoms delays care.
q1r0qlvs: Why do transfused blood products lower the recipient's ionized calcium?
Citrate anticoagulant in the bag binds calcium
Stored red cells absorb calcium from the plasma
Cold blood drives calcium into skeletal muscle
Plasma proteins in the unit excrete calcium
Citrate prevents clotting in the bag by chelating calcium, and it does the same in the casualty until the liver metabolizes it. Shock, hypothermia, and liver injury slow that clearance.
qxekv0r: Compared with calcium gluconate, what is the key practical difference of calcium chloride?
About three times the elemental calcium and more vein irritation
Less elemental calcium per volume and safer in small fragile veins
No risk of tissue injury if it leaks out of the vein
It requires refrigeration and cannot be carried in the aid bag
Calcium chloride delivers roughly three times as much elemental calcium per volume but is caustic, so a large vein, central line, or IO is preferred. Extravasation of either can injure tissue.
qam2iy: After several units of blood, a casualty becomes more hypotensive despite ongoing transfusion, and the monitor shows a prolonged QT interval. What is the most likely cause?
Citrate-induced low ionized calcium reduces cardiac contractility and vascular tone and prolongs the QT interval. It is treated with calcium.
q1w80dbq: Which group of findings makes up the lethal diamond of trauma?
The lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy was expanded to a diamond by adding hypocalcemia, which worsens clotting and cardiac function. Each component feeds the others.
qn4f4io: Per current TCCC, what is the preferred fluid for a casualty in hemorrhagic shock?
TCCC lists cold-stored low-titer O whole blood first because it replaces red cells, plasma, and platelets together. Crystalloid and colloid dilute clotting factors, and red cells alone lack them.
qfy2w42: Cold-stored whole blood is not available. Per the TCCC resuscitation order, what comes next?
Prescreened low-titer O fresh whole blood
Plasma and red cells given in a 1:1 ratio

After cold-stored low-titer O whole blood, TCCC lists prescreened low-titer O fresh whole blood, then plasma, red cells, and platelets 1:1:1, then plasma and red cells 1:1, then plasma or red cells alone.
q1rxxg12: No whole blood of any kind is available, but components are. Which combination best follows the TCCC order?
Red cells alone until whole blood arrives
Balanced component therapy approximates whole blood. Plasma and red cells 1:1 is the next step down, and single components are the last blood option.
q8ktsjn: A casualty in hemorrhagic shock without a head injury is receiving whole blood. Which finding is a TCCC endpoint for slowing resuscitation?
A palpable radial pulse with improved mentation
Heart rate below 60 beats per minute on the monitor
TCCC resuscitates until a palpable radial pulse, improved mental status, or a systolic pressure of 100 mmHg. Pushing pressure higher risks disrupting clot and wasting scarce blood.
qx8iz8: A casualty with suspected moderate TBI is in hemorrhagic shock. Which blood pressure target does TCCC set when monitoring is available?
Systolic pressure of 160 mmHg or higher
Hypotension worsens secondary brain injury, so TCCC sets a systolic target of 100 to 110 mmHg in TBI rather than the permissive targets used for torso hemorrhage.
q4j2j8u: Why is permissive hypotension used for a casualty with uncontrolled torso hemorrhage and no head injury?
Higher pressures can dislodge clot and dilute factors
Low pressure lowers the need for calcium replacement
Raising pressure before surgical control can blow off fragile clot and, if achieved with crystalloid, dilutes clotting factors. TBI is the main exception because the brain needs perfusion pressure.
qqqd4px: Why is large-volume crystalloid avoided in hemorrhagic shock?
It dilutes clotting factors and worsens acidosis and cooling
It contains citrate that binds the casualty's calcium
It carries a high risk of acute hemolytic reaction
It raises hemoglobin too quickly and makes the blood too thick
