TCCC and JTS guidance targets normocapnia at 35-40 mmHg; hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction and ischemia, and hypercapnia raises intracranial pressure.
q1shvn6w: A ventilated TBI casualty develops a unilateral dilated pupil and extensor posturing. Along with hyperosmolar therapy, which ventilation change is a reasonable brief temporizing step?
Lower the rate to raise EtCO2 above 45
Remove PEEP and cut FiO2 to room air
Brief, monitored hyperventilation lowers intracranial pressure as a bridge for impending herniation; prolonged or deep hypocapnia under 30 risks cerebral ischemia, and hypercapnia raises ICP.
q4gzto2: Which positioning measure helps lower intracranial pressure in an intubated TBI casualty without spinal concerns?
Head of the litter raised about 30 degrees
Lateral position with the neck flexed
Elevating the head about 30 degrees with the neck midline improves venous drainage; head-down positions and neck flexion or tight collars raise ICP.
q2izqms: In a TBI casualty, which pair of secondary insults most worsens outcome and is the focus of prolonged care?
Even single episodes of hypotension or hypoxia markedly raise TBI mortality, so oxygenation and perfusion are the priorities; an EtCO2 of 38 is within target.
q1qx6xhw: On the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS), what score describes a casualty who is alert and calm?
RASS runs from +4 (combative) to -5 (unarousable), with 0 meaning alert and calm; -3 is moderate sedation with movement to voice but no eye contact.
qycr48j: A ventilated casualty opens his eyes and makes eye contact for more than 10 seconds to voice, then drifts off. What is his RASS score?
Sustained awakening to voice with eye contact over 10 seconds is -1 (drowsy); -2 is under 10 seconds, -3 is movement without eye contact, and -4 needs physical stimulation.
q1j5hthh: For most ventilated casualties without severe ARDS or paralysis, what sedation target is preferred?
No sedation goal, titrated to vital signs
Light sedation reduces ventilator days, delirium and hypotension; deep sedation is reserved for specific needs such as neuromuscular blockade or severe dyssynchrony.
qidch2j: What is the analgesia-first approach to sedation in ventilated casualties?
Treat pain first, then add sedatives only as needed
Give sedatives first and pain medication later
Avoid analgesics to allow neurologic exams
Use a paralytic in place of sedation
Pain drives much of the agitation and ventilator dyssynchrony in trauma, so analgesia comes first and lowers sedative needs; paralysis without sedation risks awareness.
qq5vnz0: A ventilated casualty receives rocuronium for transport. What is the key safety requirement?
Adequate sedation and analgesia before and during paralysis
Stopping all sedation so the exam is reliable
Removing the EtCO2 monitor to save battery
Neuromuscular blockers provide no sedation or pain relief, so a paralyzed casualty without them is awake and in pain; paralysis also hides seizures and agitation, making monitoring more important.
q1wqmksp: A hypotensive, intubated casualty in hemorrhagic shock needs ongoing sedation. Which agent best preserves blood pressure?
Ketamine supports sympathetic tone and is favored for sedation and analgesia in shock; propofol and dexmedetomidine commonly cause hypotension and benzodiazepines add hypotension in shock states.
qoai9nw: Which feature makes dexmedetomidine useful in a ventilated casualty being prepared for extubation?
Arousable sedation with little respiratory depression
Strong analgesia that replaces all opioids
Rapid blood pressure support in shock
Dexmedetomidine, an alpha-2 agonist, gives cooperative sedation without much respiratory depression; its common effects are bradycardia and hypotension, and it is not suited to deep sedation.
q1e9qb1h: A ventilated casualty has received prolonged high-rate propofol and develops unexplained metabolic acidosis, rising potassium and dark urine. What is suspected?
Propofol infusion syndrome brings metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, arrhythmias and cardiac failure with prolonged or high-rate use; stopping the infusion is the key step.
q1yu2epx: A casualty on a fentanyl infusion has worsening sedation, pinpoint pupils and a falling respiratory rate after extubation. Which medication reverses this effect?
Naloxone reverses opioid effects, titrated to breathing rather than full wakefulness; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and can provoke seizures.
qi194th: A casualty on day 3 of prolonged care has a temperature of 39.2 C (102.6 F), heart rate 124, respiratory rate 26, confusion and SBP 92. Which qSOFA criteria are met?
All three: RR 22 or higher, altered mentation, SBP 100 or lower
Only the fever and the heart rate
None, because the SBP is above 90
qSOFA uses respiratory rate of 22 or more, altered mentation and SBP of 100 or less; temperature and heart rate are not part of it, and two or more criteria flag high risk.
q1e233gy: In suspected septic shock, when are antibiotics given relative to recognition?
As soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour
After culture results return in 48 hours
Only after fluids fail to correct the BP
Once the fever has lasted 24 hours
Each hour of delay in septic shock is linked to higher mortality, so broad-spectrum antibiotics are given within 1 hour; cultures are drawn first only if that causes no delay.
ql55ykp: A wounded casualty becomes septic on day 2 with a contaminated open fracture. Which TCCC/JTS-supported IV option covers broad gram-negative and anaerobic organisms?
Ertapenem covers gram-negative, gram-positive and anaerobic organisms and is a TCCC wound antibiotic; oral first-generation cephalosporins and metronidazole alone are too narrow for this.
q1xpa7z1: A septic casualty remains hypotensive after adequate fluid resuscitation. Which vasopressor is first-line?
Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor in septic shock; dopamine causes more arrhythmias, and vasopressin is usually added rather than used alone.
q1of6gkf: A casualty in prolonged care has a red, warm, tender wound with purulent drainage and fever on day 3. What is the most important step besides antibiotics?
Source control by opening and draining the wound
Closing the wound tightly to keep bacteria out
Applying a tourniquet above the wound
Covering it with an occlusive dressing for a week
Antibiotics penetrate pus poorly, so drainage, debridement and irrigation are the definitive source control; closing an infected wound traps the infection.
q173f9nx: A casualty with spreading skin discoloration, crepitus and pain out of proportion around a wound on day 2 is suspected of having which condition?
Crepitus, rapid spread and pain out of proportion suggest necrotizing infection, a surgical emergency needing early teleconsult, broad antibiotics and urgent evacuation.
q1xluo1h: For a casualty in hemorrhagic shock, which resuscitation fluid does TCCC prefer?
TCCC prefers whole blood, then blood components; crystalloids and colloids dilute clotting factors and worsen coagulopathy, so they are not the fluids for bleeding.
q2mycij: Using the USAISR Rule of Ten, what initial fluid rate is calculated for a 70 kg casualty with a 40% TBSA burn?
The Rule of Ten multiplies %TBSA by 10 for casualties 40-80 kg, so 40 x 10 = 400 mL/hr; 100 mL/hr is added for every 10 kg above 80 kg.
q1evay84: Using the Rule of Ten, what initial burn fluid rate is calculated for a 100 kg casualty with a 30% TBSA burn?
30 x 10 = 300 mL/hr, plus 100 mL/hr for each 10 kg above 80 kg (2 x 100), totaling 500 mL/hr.
qj9weg3: Using the rule of nines, what TBSA percentage is burned in an adult with full-thickness burns of the entire front of the torso and the entire left arm?
The anterior trunk is 18% and one entire arm is 9%, totaling 27%; superficial (first-degree) burns are not counted in TBSA.
q1nre8vv: In an adult burn casualty, what urine output target guides adjustment of burn resuscitation fluids?
JTS burn guidance titrates fluids to 30-50 mL/hr of urine in adults; low output signals under-resuscitation, and far higher output signals over-resuscitation and edema.
qn8r5io: In a casualty with suspected rhabdomyolysis from crush injury, which finding supports the diagnosis?
Dark tea-colored urine with high potassium
Clear dilute urine with low potassium
Low creatine kinase with normal urine
Muscle breakdown releases myoglobin (dark urine), potassium and CK; treatment centers on early, generous fluids and watching for hyperkalemia.
q1tit257: An i-STAT shows Na 140, Cl 104 and HCO3 12. What is the anion gap?
Anion gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3) = 140 - 116 = 24, which is elevated (normal about 8-12) and points to causes such as lactic acidosis or ketoacidosis.
q5b8hl1: An i-STAT shows pH 7.22, PaCO2 28 and HCO3 11. What is the primary disorder?
A low pH with low bicarbonate is metabolic acidosis, and the low PaCO2 is the expected compensation; Winter's formula (1.5 x 11 + 8, about 24-26) checks whether it is adequate.
q12vv9ih: Using Winter's formula, a casualty with HCO3 of 14 has an expected PaCO2 of about 27-31. The measured PaCO2 is 45. What does this indicate?
Expected PaCO2 = 1.5 x 14 + 8 = 29 (plus or minus 2); a PaCO2 well above that means ventilation is failing to compensate, a warning sign of fatigue or oversedation.
q29axqc: An i-STAT on a ventilated casualty shows pH 7.28, PaCO2 58 and HCO3 26. What is the disorder?
Low pH with high PaCO2 and a near-normal bicarbonate is acute respiratory acidosis, which suggests inadequate minute ventilation; increasing the rate is the usual correction.
q16es4g0: After several whole blood transfusions, a casualty's i-STAT ionized calcium is 0.88 mmol/L. What is the cause and response?
Citrate in stored blood binds calcium, and low ionized calcium (normal about 1.12-1.32) weakens clotting and cardiac contraction; TCCC calls for calcium with transfusion.
q1rzm0z0: A crush casualty's i-STAT shows potassium 7.1 and the ECG shows peaked T waves and widening QRS. What is the first priority?
Calcium to stabilize the cardiac membrane
Repeat the i-STAT in an hour
Calcium does not lower potassium but protects the heart within minutes; insulin with dextrose, albuterol and bicarbonate then shift potassium into cells.
q1vq32rq: A casualty has an i-STAT sodium of 118 that developed over several days. What is the key risk of correcting it too quickly?
Chronic hyponatremia corrected faster than about 8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours can cause osmotic demyelination; severe symptoms such as seizures still warrant prompt partial correction.
qz5klfg: Which i-STAT finding is expected in a casualty with prolonged nasogastric suction?
Loss of gastric acid raises bicarbonate and causes potassium and chloride depletion; acidosis with high potassium fits renal failure or tissue breakdown instead.
q1qceedu: On day 4 a casualty starts tube feeds after several days without nutrition and develops weakness and arrhythmias. Which lab pattern is most likely?
Refeeding syndrome drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells when feeding restarts; feeds are started slowly and electrolytes checked and replaced.
q1rpi77h: A casualty is on a litter in prolonged care for 48 hours. How often is repositioning done to prevent pressure injury?
Pressure injuries on the sacrum, heels and occiput can develop within hours on a hard litter; turning about every 2 hours plus padding bony prominences prevents them.
qzihazu: A sedated, ventilated casualty has eyes that do not fully close. What eye care is indicated?
Lubricate and keep the lids closed with tape or film
Leave the eyes open to allow pupil checks
Apply firm pressure patches over both eyes
Irrigate the eyes hourly with tap water

Sedated casualties lose blink and lid closure, causing exposure keratopathy and corneal ulcers; lubricant and gentle closure protect the cornea. Pressure patches are avoided if globe injury is possible.
qqumhp2: Which measure is part of a ventilator-associated pneumonia prevention bundle?
Head of litter at 30 to 45 degrees
Head elevation, oral care, suctioning secretions and daily sedation review reduce aspiration and VAP; flat positioning increases aspiration, and frequent circuit changes add risk.
q15o5gfh: What urine output target is used for an adult non-burn casualty in prolonged care to judge perfusion?
Urine output of at least 0.5 mL/kg/hr reflects adequate kidney perfusion; trending it hourly with a Foley guides resuscitation.
q90zwin: Which Foley catheter practice reduces catheter-associated urinary tract infection?
A closed system with the bag below the bladder
Opening the system to empty the bag
Hanging the bag on the litter above the bladder
A closed system kept below the bladder prevents backflow and contamination; breaking the system or raising the bag pushes contaminated urine back.
q5djmtf: A ventilated casualty has controlled hemorrhage and stable hemoglobin on day 2. Which DVT prophylaxis approach fits?
Enoxaparin with mechanical compression if possible
Tourniquet placement to limit venous flow

Trauma casualties are at high VTE risk; once bleeding is controlled, a low molecular weight heparin such as enoxaparin is started, with mechanical compression added or used alone if bleeding risk remains.
qzqd3h5: Which situation makes chemical DVT prophylaxis with enoxaparin inappropriate at this time?
Major abdominal injury that is now stable
Anticoagulant prophylaxis is held while bleeding is active; immobility, ventilation and major trauma are risk factors that call for prophylaxis once bleeding is controlled.
qhwgd2k: A casualty ventilated for more than 48 hours with coagulopathy is in prolonged care. Which medication provides stress ulcer prophylaxis?
Mechanical ventilation over 48 hours and coagulopathy are major risks for stress-related GI bleeding; acid suppression with an H2 blocker or PPI lowers it. Ketorolac raises bleeding risk.
q1q4yyj3: When is enteral nutrition started for a stable casualty in prolonged care who cannot eat?
Only once evacuated to a hospital
Only if the casualty asks for food
Early enteral feeding supports gut integrity and immunity and lowers infection; it is delayed in unresolved shock with escalating vasopressors.
q1jd543x: What is the purpose of a daily sedation interruption or lightening in a ventilated casualty?
To assess neurologic status and readiness to wean
To allow the ventilator battery to recharge
Daily sedation lightening, paired with a breathing trial, shortens ventilation time and allows a neurologic exam; it is not done during paralysis or uncontrolled intracranial hypertension.
q11yaodw: A ventilated casualty on day 3 becomes inattentive, fluctuates between agitation and drowsiness, and pulls at lines. What is the likely diagnosis?
Acute fluctuating inattention with altered awareness is delirium, linked to worse outcomes; causes such as hypoxia, infection, pain and benzodiazepines are sought and treated.
q122tg1e: A contaminated blast wound is being managed in prolonged care. Which approach to closure is preferred?
Leave open with delayed primary closure
Close tightly with sutures in the field
Glue the skin edges after irrigation
Apply staples once the bleeding stops
Combat wounds are heavily contaminated, so they are irrigated, debrided and left open for delayed closure; early closure traps bacteria and leads to abscess.
q4k591c: For wound irrigation in an austere setting when sterile saline is unavailable, what is an acceptable alternative?
Potable water is as effective as sterile saline for wound irrigation; peroxide and bleach damage tissue, and seawater adds contamination.
qgqzt6y: On day 2, a casualty with a tibial fracture has pain out of proportion, pain on passive toe stretch and a tense calf. Distal pulses are present. What is suspected?
Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are early signs of compartment syndrome; pulses are often present until late, so their presence does not exclude it.
q8gvz5w: A casualty has a tourniquet that has been on for 3 hours and evacuation is delayed. What is the guidance regarding conversion?
Reassess now for conversion if not in shock or amputated
Leave it in place regardless of the duration
Loosen it every 30 minutes to rest the limb
Remove it at 6 hours even if bleeding resumes

TCCC directs reassessing tourniquets for conversion to a hemostatic or pressure dressing as soon as possible, within 2 hours if feasible, unless the casualty is in shock or the injury is an amputation; at 6 hours or more conversion is generally not attempted outside a facility.
q12t4agv: A casualty has a burned extremity with circumferential full-thickness burns and progressive loss of distal sensation. What does this suggest?
Expected burn swelling with no concern
Need for ice packs on the wound
Circumferential eschar is inelastic, and swelling under it compresses circulation like a compartment syndrome; escharotomy releases it, usually under teleconsult guidance.
qys1hn8: Which TCCC antibiotic is given orally to a casualty with an open combat wound who can swallow?
TCCC uses oral moxifloxacin for casualties able to take pills and IV or IM ertapenem or ceftriaxone for those who cannot.
qyx3esd: A casualty with a penetrating eye injury is in prolonged care. Which eye protection is correct?
A rigid shield without pressure on the globe
A tight pressure patch over the eye
A rigid shield protects the globe without pressure, which can extrude eye contents; oral moxifloxacin is also given per TCCC.
qz12ey5: What is ADVISOR in prolonged casualty care?
A 24/7 DoD virtual medical consult service
ADVISOR (Advanced Virtual Support for Operational Forces) connects medics with specialists by phone or data around the clock for real-time guidance on casualty care.
q9alku3: The TCCC Card that documents care and travels with the casualty
DD Form 1380 records injuries, tourniquets, vitals and treatments at the point of injury and accompanies the casualty; the PCC flowsheet tracks trends over hours.
q1ca58fb: In a prolonged care handoff, what does the MIST format cover?
MIST gives a fast structured summary of how the casualty was hurt, what injuries were found, vital signs and the care given.
q136n2hb: On a 9-line MEDEVAC request, what does Line 3 report?
Method of marking the pickup site
Line 3 lists patients by precedence (urgent, urgent-surgical, priority, routine, convenience); Line 1 is location, Line 4 is special equipment and Line 7 is marking.
q12bam6s: On a 9-line MEDEVAC request, which line notes that a ventilator is required?
Line 4 covers special equipment: none, hoist, extraction equipment or ventilator; Line 5 is litter versus ambulatory.
qfz9s5n: On a wartime 9-line MEDEVAC request, what does Line 6 report?
In wartime, Line 6 is security at the pickup zone (no enemy, possible enemy, enemy in area, armed escort required); terrain is described there only in peacetime.
q1g4ay1t: What is the normal rectal temperature range for a military working dog?
Dogs run warmer than people, about 101-102.5 F (38.3-39.2 C (100.9-102.6 F)); temperatures above about 105 F suggest heat injury.
qjjqphg: A military working dog collapses after exertion in heat with a rectal temperature of 107 F. When is active cooling stopped?
When the temperature reaches about 103 F
Only after evacuation to a veterinarian
After a set 5 minutes of active cooling
Cooling stops at about 103 F to avoid rebound hypothermia as the body continues to cool; delaying cooling until evacuation worsens heat injury.
qs2z9qw: A large military working dog has a distended, tight abdomen, retches without producing vomit, and is restless after eating. What is suspected?
Unproductive retching and abdominal distension in a large deep-chested dog suggest GDV, a life-threatening emergency needing decompression, fluids and urgent veterinary surgery.
q8u9any: A handler asks whether a human over-the-counter NSAID such as ibuprofen can be given to an injured military working dog. What is the concern?
Dogs are prone to GI ulceration and kidney injury from them
Dogs need higher human NSAID amounts to feel relief
Human NSAIDs have no effect in dogs
The only risk is a mild skin rash
Dogs are highly sensitive to human NSAIDs, which cause gastric ulceration, perforation and kidney failure; analgesia comes from veterinary-approved options.
q1dmktv2: A military working dog becomes sedated with slow breathing after sniffing a suspected fentanyl package. What is the treatment of choice?
Naloxone with airway and breathing support
Naloxone reverses opioid effects in dogs as in people, given with ventilation support; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids.
q1u4btjk: Why is an elastic tourniquet or improvised elastic wrap often used on a military working dog's limb instead of a standard windlass tourniquet?
The conical shape of the dog's limb lets windlass straps slip
Dogs have no arteries in the lower limb
Windlass tourniquets are toxic to dogs
Elastic tourniquets allow walking on the limb
A dog's limb tapers sharply, so wide straps slide down; elastic wraps conform and compress the vessels effectively.
q1q6mk3y: What is the normal resting heart rate range for a large-breed military working dog?
Large dogs at rest have heart rates of about 60-120; puppies and small dogs run faster, and tachycardia above the range suggests pain, shock or heat injury.
qm5l98u: Before treating an injured, conscious military working dog, which step protects the medic?
Muzzle the dog unless it is vomiting or struggling to breathe
Wait for the dog to fall asleep
Muzzle the dog even if it is vomiting
Injured dogs may bite even familiar people, so a muzzle is placed first; it is avoided in vomiting or respiratory distress because it can obstruct the airway.
q1p87utj: Which shock index value suggests significant hemorrhage in a casualty?
Shock index = heart rate / SBP; above 1.0 suggests significant blood loss and transfusion need, and normal is about 0.5-0.7.
qev4jb2: In TCCC, which fluid resuscitation endpoint is used for a casualty in hemorrhagic shock without TBI?
Improved mental status and a palpable radial pulse
Heart rate below 50 beats per minute
Permissive hypotension targets a radial pulse and improved mentation (about SBP 100) until bleeding is controlled; higher pressures increase bleeding, and TBI raises the targets.
q1yiavwy: In TCCC, when is calcium given to a casualty receiving blood products?
During or after the first blood product
Only if the casualty has seizures
TCCC calls for calcium during or after the first blood product because citrate binds calcium quickly and hypocalcemia worsens coagulopathy and cardiac function.
q1nu84x6: A casualty in prolonged care is on oxygen with limited supply. What is the best way to conserve oxygen?
Titrate to the lowest FiO2 keeping SpO2 at target
Keep FiO2 at 100% for the whole transport
Remove oxygen during each sleep period
Use only room air for all casualties
Oxygen is a finite resource in PCC, so titrating to the target saturation extends supply; unnecessary 100% FiO2 depletes it and adds toxicity.
q1cv0w40: A casualty on day 2 is being considered for extubation. Which finding supports readiness?
Tolerating a spontaneous breathing trial on minimal support
High FiO2 needs and frequent desaturation
Deep sedation with no cough reflex
Copious secretions needing suction every 15 minutes
Readiness depends on an intact drive, adequate oxygenation on low support, airway protection and cough; a spontaneous breathing trial tests this.
q16rgawr: A casualty on day 3 develops wheezing, hives and hypotension minutes after an IV antibiotic is started. What is the first medication?
Epinephrine is first-line for anaphylaxis, reversing bronchospasm and vasodilation; antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts and do not treat shock.
q1iyhnch: During prolonged care, the TCCC guidance on documentation priorities includes which practice?
Recording times of tourniquets, medications and changes
Writing notes on the casualty's skin only
Timed records of tourniquets, medications, fluids and vitals let receiving teams understand trends and avoid repeat dosing; memory and skin writing are unreliable.
qrntvss: A casualty in prolonged care has a blood glucose of 52 mg/dL and is confused. What is the immediate treatment?
Hypoglycemia causes confusion and seizures and is corrected quickly with dextrose; insulin lowers glucose further.
q8vmscf: Which normal resting rectal temperature range best fits a healthy dog?
Dogs normally run warmer than people, about 101 to 102.5 F. Working dogs can briefly reach about 106 F during hard work.
q1955gjn: Why is a respiratory rate count often unreliable in a working dog?
Panting is a normal cooling behavior that raises the count
Dogs breathe only through the mouth
Dogs hold their breath when handled
Dog chest movement cannot be seen
Panting is how dogs shed heat. Effort, noise and posture tell more about breathing difficulty than the raw count.
q12wqva3: A dog has black (pigmented) gums. Where else can mucous membrane color and capillary refill be assessed?
The inner lip, conjunctiva, prepuce or vulva
Pigmented gums hide color. Unpigmented mucous membranes, such as the inner lip, conjunctiva, prepuce or vulva, are alternatives.
q12pkxm5: Where is the femoral pulse felt on a dog?
On the inside of the thigh
On the outside of the hock
The femoral artery runs on the inside (medial) thigh. Its strength helps judge perfusion and shock.
q1v76mt9: In which situation is a muzzle contraindicated?
A dog in respiratory distress or vomiting
A calm dog with a paw cut
A dog with a tail wound
A dog being moved to a litter
The K9TCCC Guidelines describe muzzling unless there is airway obstruction or breathing difficulty. Vomiting and heat injury also make a closed muzzle dangerous.
q1wiumoy: Why do the K9TCCC Guidelines consider only elastic tourniquets for dog limbs?
Windlass tourniquets tend to slip down the cone-shaped dog limb
The canine limb tapers toward the paw, so rigid windlass tourniquets slide down and lose pressure. An elastic wrap acts as a tight circumferential pressure bandage.
q1o0yy46: How are junctional wounds of the axilla or groin managed in K9TCCC?
Hemostatic gauze packing with firm direct pressure
Junctional tourniquets and pelvic binders are not recommended for dogs. Packing with hemostatic gauze and direct pressure is the approach.
qlskl5p: Where is the surgical airway made in a dog per the K9TCCC Guidelines?
Between tracheal rings on the front of the neck
Through the side of the neck
The guidelines describe an incision between tracheal rings, such as rings 3 and 4 or 4 and 5, rather than through the cricothyroid membrane.
q258lpb: Which airway devices do the K9TCCC Guidelines describe as not used in dogs?
Nasopharyngeal airways, blind-insertion airways and extraglottic devices are not used. Orotracheal intubation under direct vision is the main advanced airway.
qesr5k0: Where is needle decompression performed on a dog in the K9TCCC Guidelines?
7th to 9th intercostal space on the side of the chest
2nd intercostal space, front of the chest
Just behind the last rib on the belly
Under the front leg at the armpit crease
The lateral chest at the 7th to 9th intercostal space, about midway up, angled toward the head, with the catheter fed off the needle. Both sides are often decompressed.
q6sjlsw: Why is a pneumothorax in a dog often bilateral?
The canine mediastinum is thin and often communicates between sides
The thin, often incomplete mediastinum lets air move between the two sides of the chest.
q50s56k: What is the most common IV site in a conscious dog?
Cephalic vein on the front of the forearm
The cephalic vein is the usual site. The jugular is avoided in head injury and bleeding disorders.
q10zkkb8: Which IO site do the K9TCCC Guidelines describe when IV access fails?
Proximal medial tibia just below the knee
The proximal medial tibia is the listed site; the proximal humerus is also described in the JTS MWD CPG.
q397hjf: Which blood product is NOT given to a dog?
Human low titer O whole blood
Human blood products carry a high risk of transfusion reaction in dogs. Only canine products are used.
q5lwqd6: Why might a dog tolerate its first mismatched transfusion but react to a later one?
Dogs generally lack strong naturally occurring antibodies but become sensitized after transfusion
Dogs make antibodies only to human blood
Dog red cells have no antigens
Dogs only have one blood type
Dogs usually lack strong preformed antibodies against DEA 1. After exposure they become sensitized, which is why prior transfusion more than 72 hours earlier calls for veterinary direction.
qg5zj4e: Per the JTS K9 heat injury CPG, at about what rectal temperature does active cooling stop?
Active cooling stops at about 103 to 103.5 F to avoid rebound hypothermia, followed by drying and close monitoring.
qa9qiap: Which cooling method does the JTS K9 heat injury CPG describe?
Soaking the coat to the skin with tepid water and using fans
Covering with wet towels left in place
Tepid water soaked through the coat plus airflow is the described method. Wet towels left in place and masks trap heat.
qppb12t: A German Shepherd is retching without producing anything and has a tight, swollen belly. What is the leading concern?
Unproductive retching with a distended abdomen in a large, deep-chested dog is classic for GDV, a surgical emergency.
q15g5797: Why does xylitol cause hypoglycemia in dogs?
It triggers a large, rapid insulin release in dogs
In dogs, unlike people, xylitol stimulates a strong insulin surge, dropping blood sugar within about 10 to 60 minutes. Liver failure can follow.
q1ptuid6: Which human pain reliever is a common cause of stomach ulcers and kidney injury in dogs?
Human NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen cause GI ulceration and kidney injury in dogs; naproxen lasts much longer in dogs than in people.
q3p80mu: A detection dog becomes suddenly sedated with slow breathing after a search. Naloxone produces little response. What else is considered?
Illicit drug supplies may contain xylazine, which naloxone does not reverse. Re-sedation after naloxone can also occur as it wears off.
q1s90jl7: Which side effect is commonly seen when dogs receive opioids such as hydromorphone?
Opioids commonly cause vomiting and hydromorphone causes heavy panting in dogs, which is why a muzzled dog is watched closely after opioid dosing.
q1cz7fvp: Why do the K9TCCC Guidelines prefer alternatives to ketamine in penetrating eye trauma?
Ketamine can cause nystagmus and raise intraocular pressure
Ketamine is not used in dogs
Ketamine can raise eye pressure and cause nystagmus, so alternatives are preferred with a penetrating eye injury.
q1h4hdg7: Which form travels with an injured MWD through each handoff?
The K9TCCC Card (DD Form 3073) stays with the dog and later goes to the veterinary record and the DoD MWD Trauma Registry.
q12ypty4: Under the JTS K9 Healthcare Provider Responsibilities CPG, when do human providers give emergency care to an MWD?
When the dog is too unstable to move, evacuation is not possible and veterinary staff are unavailable
For all routine and dental care
Only after a veterinarian arrives on scene
Human providers address threats to life, limb or eyesight and prepare the dog for evacuation, under veterinary guidance, when no veterinary personnel are available.
qa4ir70: A soldier in MOPP 4 notes dim vision, runny nose and chest tightness after an attack. He can still walk and talk. Army first aid doctrine describes which step?
Self-aid with one nerve agent kit
Buddy gives three nerve agent kits and the anticonvulsant at once
Mild signs in a casualty able to act are treated with self-aid of one nerve agent kit. Three kits plus the anticonvulsant are given by a buddy for severe signs.
qedahsl: What is the main endpoint for titrating atropine in nerve agent poisoning?
Drying of airway secretions and easier breathing
Atropine treats the muscarinic killer Bs. Pupils may stay small for days and heart rate is a poor guide.
qxs2wu9: Why does early pralidoxime matter most in soman exposure?
Soman ages the enzyme bond within minutes, after which oximes cannot reactivate it
Soman is not affected by atropine
Aging makes the agent-enzyme bond permanent; soman ages very quickly, which is also why PB pretreatment exists for it.
q1due15l: Pyridostigmine bromide (PB) tablets are FDA approved for which use?
Pretreatment against soman, taken on command order
Treatment after any nerve agent exposure
PB was approved in 2003 as military pretreatment against soman. After exposure it does not help and can add to toxicity.
q1068gdq: A soldier taking PB on order develops mild cramps and loose stools with normal pupils. This most likely reflects:
Mild GI effects are common with PB. Real exposure brings miosis, rhinorrhea and chest tightness.
q1c9furl: A casualty from a nerve agent attack begins seizing. What medication class is paired with the nerve agent kits in buddy aid?
Atropine and oximes do not stop established nerve agent seizures; the anticonvulsant autoinjector is a benzodiazepine.
q14bz3hb: Why did the DoD move from diazepam (CANA) to midazolam?
Midazolam is absorbed faster and more reliably from muscle
IM midazolam reaches effect faster than IM diazepam, which matters because seizure brain injury progresses within minutes.
q1c0a29l: Which statement about RSDL matches its FDA clearance?
It removes or neutralizes chemical warfare agents and T-2 toxin on intact skin
It is a barrier cream applied before exposure
RSDL is a 510(k)-cleared device for skin decon; it is not labeled for eyes, mouth or wounds.
q1qr58dj: A firefighter is pulled from an enclosed-space fire, confused with low blood pressure and high lactate. Which cyanide antidote is generally preferred here?
Nitrites create methemoglobin and worsen oxygen delivery when carbon monoxide is also present; hydroxocobalamin does not.
qtswds1: After hydroxocobalamin, a casualty's skin and urine turn red. This is:
An expected effect of the drug
The red color is expected and can interfere with lab tests and pulse oximetry.
qowqnt7: Which effect is a known risk of sodium nitrite?
Nitrite works by creating methemoglobin; too much reduces oxygen delivery and the drug can drop blood pressure.
q6yw86y: A soldier smelled fresh-cut hay, felt mild throat irritation, and now feels fine 1 hour later. What is the main concern?
Delayed pulmonary edema from phosgene over the next 2 to 24 hours
Nothing; he can return to duty
Phosgene causes delayed pulmonary edema; rest and observation are part of care. There is no antidote.
q411x4d: A casualty reports immediate burning pain on the skin after a liquid exposure, with blisters forming hours later. Which agent fits best?
Lewisite causes immediate pain; sulfur mustard is painless at the time of exposure.
q14r4xbg: Dimercaprol (BAL) is prepared in which oil, making which allergy a caution?
BAL in Oil uses peanut oil; peanut allergy is a labeled caution.
q1u68jv: Which statement about sulfur mustard is accurate?
There is no antidote; care is decon and supportive
No antidote exists for sulfur mustard. Decon, eye care, wound care and airway support are the mainstays.
qv263mm: Blister fluid from a mustard casualty is:
Not a source of active agent
Blister fluid does not contain active mustard. Surface contamination before decon is the hazard to staff.
q6ug05a: Potassium iodide protects against which hazard?
Radioactive iodine uptake by the thyroid
KI only fills the thyroid with stable iodine; it does nothing for external radiation or other isotopes.
q1hodw2e: After a dirty bomb containing cesium-137, which agent is FDA approved to increase elimination?
Prussian blue binds cesium and thallium in the gut. DTPA is for plutonium, americium and curium.
qqivmfc: Which DTPA form is labeled as the choice during pregnancy?
Ca-DTPA was linked to fetal harm in animal studies; Zn-DTPA is preferred in pregnancy.
qrwbkwe: Within the first 24 hours after plutonium contamination of a wound, the DTPA label favors:
Ca-DTPA is more effective in the first 24 hours; Zn-DTPA is used after that.
qvh9swd: A crowd collapses with pinpoint pupils, slow breathing and dry skin after an aerosol is sprayed into a theater. The leading consideration is:
Pinpoint pupils with dry skin and respiratory depression point to opioids, as in Moscow 2002. Nerve agents cause secretions and twitching.
q1pajow: After naloxone, a casualty exposed to a carfentanil aerosol wakes up, then becomes drowsy again 40 minutes later. This is most likely:
Potent, long-acting fentanyl analogs often outlast naloxone; repeat doses and observation are common.
q3h1tas: A soldier is delirious with dilated pupils, hot dry skin, fever and urinary retention after a suspected chemical release. Which agent fits best?
This is the anticholinergic toxidrome; BZ is a glycolate incapacitating agent.
q1b5i3si: Physostigmine use for anticholinergic delirium carries which main risk?
Cholinergic excess: slow heart rate, bronchospasm, seizures
Physostigmine is a cholinesterase inhibitor; atropine is kept at hand. It is contraindicated with tricyclic overdose.
q12csxkg: Compared with a nerve agent casualty, a farm worker with organophosphate pesticide poisoning typically needs:
Far more atropine over a longer time
Less atropine for a shorter time
Pesticide ingestion often produces long-lasting toxicity requiring large total atropine amounts; intermediate syndrome can follow.
qezzdl5: A mechanic splashed rust remover on his fingers and has severe pain with little visible injury. What does this suggest, and what topical agent is used?
Pain out of proportion is classic for HF. Calcium binds fluoride; large burns risk low calcium and dysrhythmias.
q779ufk: Which statement about riot control agents (CS, OC) is accurate?
There is no antidote; fresh air and decon are the care
Effects last for days in most cases
Effects usually fade within about 30 minutes of fresh air. Persistent symptoms point to another cause or heavy exposure.
q1nsn11j: Removing a casualty's clothing removes roughly how much contamination, per commonly cited guidance?
Most of it, around 80 to 90 percent
Clothing removal is the single most effective decon step; wet or dry decon follows.
quemf5p: What is the usual site for a nerve agent autoinjector through MOPP gear?
Autoinjectors fire through clothing into the lateral thigh, away from pocket contents and the inner thigh vessels.
qaii2md: A casualty from a VX attack received three kits and improved, but 4 hours later wheezing and secretions return. Why?
Ongoing absorption of persistent liquid agent from the skin as antidote effects wear off
V-agents are persistent and absorb slowly through skin; thorough decon and repeat atropine in medical channels address recurrence.
qh5y168: A previously healthy soldier has had two days of fever, cough and fatigue, then suddenly develops severe breathlessness and shock. The chest film shows a widened mediastinum with pleural effusions and no infiltrate. What fits best?
The two-phase course and a widened mediastinum from hemorrhagic mediastinitis, without a pneumonic infiltrate, is the classic picture of inhalational anthrax.
qpx05jo: Which precautions fit a patient with suspected pneumonic plague?
Droplet precautions until about 48 hours of effective antibiotics
Airborne precautions for the whole admission
No precautions, as plague is not contagious
Pneumonic plague spreads by respiratory droplets. Droplet precautions continue until roughly 48 hours of effective antibiotics with clinical improvement.
q1ko9m5e: How long is post-exposure prophylaxis for anthrax, and why?
60 days, because spores can persist in the lungs
10 days, as for most bacterial infections
Spores can germinate long after exposure, so a 60-day antibiotic course with vaccination is used; shortened courses have been followed by late cases.
q1vb7990: An alert, afebrile casualty has double vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech and trouble swallowing, with symmetric weakness spreading downward. Sensation is normal. What fits best?
Botulism produces a descending symmetric flaccid paralysis starting with bulbar muscles, with a clear mind, normal sensation and no fever.
q1q77gg8: What distinguishes nerve agent poisoning from botulism at the bedside?
Nerve agents cause tiny pupils, heavy secretions and twitching
Nerve agents cause descending paralysis and botulism causes ascending
Botulism causes fever and nerve agents do not
The cholinergic picture of wet secretions, pinpoint pupils and fasciculations is absent in botulism, which produces dry mouth and dilated pupils.
q1va2q9d: Botulinum antitoxin is given as early as possible because it
Neutralizes circulating toxin but does not reverse paralysis already present
Antitoxin halts further binding of toxin. Nerve endings that are already blocked recover only as they regrow, which takes weeks to months.
qnaqhve: Which feature separates smallpox from chickenpox?
Lesions on one area are all at the same stage, and palms and soles are involved
Lesions appear in several stages at once
The rash is heaviest on the trunk
Smallpox lesions progress together, are deep-seated and involve palms and soles; varicella shows mixed stages, is trunk-heavy and spares palms and soles.
qti02zt: A rash illness with fever also has prominently swollen lymph nodes. Which possibility does that favor?
Marked lymphadenopathy is a recognized feature of mpox and is not typical of smallpox, which helps separate the two.
qwwp9pi: Smallpox spreads by droplets, by airborne routes in some settings and by contact with lesion material, so airborne and contact precautions are used together.
q123jcty: Roughly 4 hours after a shared exposure, many people develop fever, chills, headache and a dry cough. Almost none become critically ill and none infect anyone else. What fits best?
A short incubation measured in hours, a large number of similar casualties, low mortality and no person-to-person spread is the SEB pattern.
q10a7uk9: Why do antibiotics not change the course of SEB illness?
It is caused by a preformed toxin rather than an infection
The organism is resistant to all antibiotics
Antibiotics are only withheld because of supply
SEB is a toxin-mediated illness. Antibiotics have no target, although they are often started before the cause is known.
q6a6ny1: About 12 hours after an inhalational exposure, casualties develop cough and worsening low oxygen with widespread pulmonary infiltrates. There is no spread to caregivers and no response to antibiotics. What fits best?
Inhaled ricin produces a progressive chemical-type pneumonitis over 12 to 24 hours with no transmission and no antibiotic response.
q129j0d9: What treatment exists for ricin poisoning?
Supportive care only, with no antidote or vaccine
There is no licensed antidote or vaccine for ricin; care centers on decontamination, oxygen and lung-protective ventilation when needed.
q417blj: Which agent on these lists causes burning skin and blistering within minutes of contact?
Trichothecenes injure skin, eyes and airways on contact, which is unlike the bacteria and viruses on these lists, where exposure causes no sensation.
q1krmq0c: Why is immediate decontamination especially important after T-2 exposure?
The toxin keeps injuring tissue while it remains on the skin
It stops the marrow suppression entirely
Soap and water inactivate the toxin in the bloodstream
T-2 continues to damage tissue on contact, so washing early limits injury. It does not pass between people.
q40q02f: A casualty who recovered from a T-2 exposure develops bleeding and infection two weeks later. What explains this?
Bone marrow suppression, as in radiation injury
Trichothecenes suppress rapidly dividing cells, so low white cells and platelets appear days to weeks after the exposure looks resolved.
qhz5m7u: Which statement about alcohol-based hand gel and anthrax spores is correct?
It does not kill spores, so soap, water and friction are used
It kills spores faster than soap and water
It is adequate when no water is available
It is preferred for decontaminating clothing
Alcohol does not kill anthrax spores. Removing clothing and washing with soap and water physically removes them.
q1ijrava: Which first-line options does CDC treatment guidance give for pneumonic plague?
No antibiotics, as care is supportive
Streptomycin or gentamicin, or a fluoroquinolone such as ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, are placed first for pneumonic and septicemic plague.
q1d89k9e: A cluster develops severe febrile illness with cough, the chest films look worse than the lungs sound, and nobody transmits it to anyone else. Mortality is low with treatment. What fits best?
Tularemia produces severe constitutional illness with modest examination findings, is not spread person to person, and has much lower mortality than plague or anthrax.
q1l7plmm: Why are two drugs used over several weeks for brucellosis?
Single short courses are followed by relapse
It is resistant to every single agent
To reduce the cost of treatment
Brucella survives inside cells, so combination therapy for at least six weeks is used; single agents and short courses relapse.
qus1tgp: Which incubation period fits Q fever after a shared exposure?
Q fever typically incubates 10 to 40 days, most often two to three weeks, which separates it from the agents that strike within days.
q14h4qgl: A pneumonia with abscesses and skin nodules fails standard antibiotics in a patient with heavy soil and water exposure. Which group fits?
These organisms form abscesses and resist many common antibiotics; ceftazidime or a carbapenem is used, followed by months of oral therapy.
qxfrq7w: Early in viral hemorrhagic fever, which finding is most common?
Fever with heavy vomiting and diarrhea
Bleeding is a late and inconsistent finding. The early illness looks like a severe febrile gastrointestinal illness, and that is when transmission risk is already present.
qk29cxg: Which measure has lowered mortality most in viral hemorrhagic fever?
Supportive care, especially careful replacement of large gastrointestinal losses, has done more for survival than any single specific agent.
qomqc44: Where are caregivers most often infected during care of a filovirus patient?
Through intact skin contact with the patient's clothing
By airborne spread across the ward
Doffing is the recognized high-risk step, which is why trained doffing with an observer is part of the protocol.
qxbeuvu: An explosive outbreak of fever and severe headache occurs where horses are dying of neurologic illness. A few patients develop seizures. What fits best?
Venezuelan, eastern and western equine encephalitis viruses cause disease in horses and people, and sick or dying horses are a classic clue.
qjs5wec: What treatment exists for the equine encephalitis viruses?
Supportive care, with no specific antiviral
No specific antiviral exists. Care is supportive, with seizure control and airway protection for patients who progress to encephalitis.
q18kjfc0: Which pattern most strongly suggests a toxin rather than an infection?
Symptoms within hours and no spread between people
Symptoms after several days with spread to caregivers
A rash appearing on day three
Toxins act in hours, do not spread between people and do not respond to antibiotics; infections incubate for days and several of them transmit.
q1fi7irv: When is a suspected biological agent reported?
At the end of the shift
Only if more than ten casualties are involved
Early reporting is what starts prophylaxis, protective measures and specimen handling for everyone else; waiting for confirmation costs that time.
qwhvseg: Why is the laboratory warned when one of these agents is suspected?
Several have infected laboratory workers handling routine cultures
It is needed to release antibiotics
Brucella, Francisella and Yersinia pestis in particular have caused laboratory-acquired infections, so advance notice lets staff handle specimens at the right containment level.
q92096x: A cluster of acute liver failure is traced to a shared grain supply with no viral cause found. Which agent fits?
Aflatoxins are fungal toxins of grain and nuts, weaponized by Iraq in the 1980s. A large dose causes acute liver failure; the characteristic harm, liver cancer, takes years.
q3o4x7i: A casualty with tetrodotoxin poisoning appears unresponsive with fixed dilated pupils. What is the key point?
They are conscious and aware, and sedation is part of the care
They are brain dead and care can be withdrawn
Tetrodotoxin blocks sodium channels without affecting consciousness. People have been declared dead while awake. Survivors recover completely if ventilated through it, usually over 24 to 72 hours.
qfjvx1o: What is the earliest warning of a Rift Valley fever outbreak in people?
Livestock abortion storms and an animal die-off
A rash in the first cases
A rise in mosquito trap counts alone
Vision loss in the index case

The veterinary picture precedes the human outbreak. Most human cases come from handling infected animal blood and tissue, so the slaughtering and animal-contact history is the question that separates it from other deployment fevers.
q10oqldh: What distinguishes pandemic influenza from most of the classic biological warfare agents?
It spreads efficiently from the casualty to the team and onward
It only affects the people present at the release
It is a toxin rather than an organism

Anthrax, ricin and most agents on these lists affect only those exposed to the release. Influenza keeps going, so the first few cases change the posture of the whole unit rather than just the treatment of those casualties.
q2zzmoc: Why is a neuraminidase inhibitor started before test confirmation in suspected pandemic influenza?
Its benefit falls off sharply after 48 hours from symptom onset
It is harmless so the threshold does not matter
Oseltamivir works best within 48 hours of symptoms. Waiting for confirmation commonly spends that window, so treatment is started on clinical suspicion in a suspected outbreak.
q1xxqzc2: A soldier has fever, severe calf pain and red eyes without discharge, a week after a river crossing. What fits best?

Conjunctival suffusion without discharge plus severe calf pain after fresh-water exposure is close to specific for leptospirosis. It responds to doxycycline, so presumptive treatment is low-cost and the untreated severe form kills.
qkfcsv: What is the most useful physical finding in suspected scrub typhus, and why is it missed?
A painless black eschar at the mite bite, usually hidden in a skin fold
A petechial rash on the palms
The eschar is painless and typically in the groin, axilla, waistband or under a breast, so it is only found if someone deliberately looks. Doxycycline usually breaks the fever within 48 hours.
qa1oply: How does typhoid fever differ from ordinary foodborne gastroenteritis?
Fever climbs stepwise over a week and the bowel can perforate in the third week
It causes profuse watery diarrhea immediately
It is not treatable with antibiotics

Typhoid is a systemic illness, not a gut infection. Constipation is as common as diarrhea, the pulse is slower than the fever predicts, and the lethal complication is intestinal perforation in the third week.
q1p2gg7m: Why does a hepatitis A cluster point to an exposure about a month earlier?
The incubation period is 15 to 50 days
The virus takes a month to become infectious
Jaundice is always a late sign of any illness
The long incubation hides the cause, so several people jaundiced in the same week shared an exposure weeks ago. Shedding also peaks before symptoms, so cases found late were infectious earlier.
q1oxg6dr: A soldier has had three weeks of pneumonia unresponsive to antibiotics after working in desert dust, with red tender nodules on the shins. What fits?

Coccidioides lives in desert soil, and disturbing it aerosolizes spores. Erythema nodosum with a respiratory illness in that setting is close to diagnostic, and it points away from more antibacterials rather than toward them.
qtxp6fu: In dengue, when does the dangerous phase begin?
As the fever falls, when plasma leak starts
In the first 24 hours of fever
Only after the rash fades completely

Defervescence marks the start of the critical phase. A casualty who looks better as the fever settles but has abdominal pain, persistent vomiting or a rising hematocrit with falling platelets is entering plasma leak.
q1x4jww0: Which analgesic is used in suspected dengue, and why?
Acetaminophen, because NSAIDs and aspirin worsen the bleeding risk
Ibuprofen, because it also reduces plasma leak
Ketorolac, because it is the most effective
Dengue causes thrombocytopenia and bleeding, which NSAIDs and salicylates worsen. Acetaminophen is the analgesic and antipyretic used throughout.
q7cjyn5: How is dengue distinguished from a viral hemorrhagic fever in posture terms?
Dengue does not spread between people, so isolation precautions differ

Dengue is mosquito-borne and not transmitted person to person, while Ebola, Marburg, Lassa and CCHF spread through fluids. A travel, mosquito and contact history is what separates them and determines the isolation posture.
qmlknzg: A casualty pulled from a bunker is drooling, tearing, wheezing and twitching, with pinpoint pupils. Which endpoint guides atropine dosing?
Drying of airway secretions and easier ventilation
Return of pupils to normal size
A fixed total dose of 6 mg
Pupils can stay small for hours after secretions clear, so they are a poor endpoint. Atropine is titrated to dry secretions and improved ventilation; large cumulative doses may be needed.
q166vxhi: What does the oxime component of a nerve-agent auto-injector add that atropine does not?
It reactivates acetylcholinesterase, which can help the muscle weakness
It blocks muscarinic receptors more completely
Atropine blocks muscarinic effects but does nothing at the neuromuscular junction. An oxime such as pralidoxime reactivates the enzyme before it ages, which is where nicotinic weakness improves.
q1ygie63: Which benzodiazepine role is specific to nerve-agent exposure?
Seizure control, which also limits nerve-agent brain injury

Nerve-agent seizures respond poorly to most anticonvulsants and cause ongoing brain injury. A benzodiazepine is given for seizures and, in doctrine, alongside multiple auto-injectors in severe exposure.
q1kh8f9m: A casualty has painless skin redness after a reported chemical attack, with blisters appearing hours later. Which agent fits?
Mustard exposure is typically painless at the time, with erythema in 2 to 24 hours and blistering later. Lewisite and phosgene oxime hurt immediately.
q1fg2iue: How does fluid resuscitation for a large mustard blister injury differ from a thermal burn of the same size?
Mustard injuries generally need less fluid than a thermal burn formula predicts
They need roughly twice the Parkland volume
They need no fluid at all
Mustard lesions are more superficial than they look and leak less. Applying a thermal burn formula unchanged tends to over-resuscitate, so fluids are titrated to perfusion and urine output.
q1438bzx: Which vesicant has a specific chelating antidote?
Lewisite is an arsenical, and dimercaprol chelates arsenic. There is no antidote for sulfur or nitrogen mustard or for phosgene oxime; care is decontamination and wound care.
q1s02s2y: A casualty from a fire in an enclosed space is comatose with a lactate of 14, normal-looking skin and no cyanosis. Which antidote is generally preferred?
In smoke inhalation, nitrites induce methemoglobinemia on top of possible carbon monoxide, further cutting oxygen carriage. Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide without that problem.
q9nzzmr: Why is the quiet interval after phosgene exposure a trap?
A casualty can look well for hours and then develop pulmonary edema, and exertion makes it worse
The quiet interval means the dose was trivial
Phosgene has an antidote that must be given during it
Phosgene injures the alveolar membrane slowly. A latent period of hours is common, exertion shortens and worsens it, so exposed casualties are kept at rest and observed even while well.
qxu3qey: What is the main difference in where chlorine and ammonia injure the airway?
Ammonia is highly water-soluble and hits the upper airway early, while chlorine reaches deeper
Chlorine hits the upper airway and ammonia the alveoli
Water solubility drives the level of injury. Ammonia dissolves in the upper airway, causing immediate pain and potential obstruction; chlorine is intermediate and reaches the lower airway as well.
q15zg54: Why can a small hydrofluoric acid burn be dangerous?
Fluoride is absorbed and binds calcium and magnesium, causing dysrhythmias
It converts to hydrochloric acid in the blood
Burn size predicts systemic risk poorly with hydrofluoric acid. Absorbed fluoride chelates calcium and magnesium, so monitoring and calcium are considerations even with a modest-looking burn.
q1nksc8s: A worker collapses instantly in a sewer, and the first responder to approach also collapses. Which agent fits best?
Hydrogen sulfide at high concentration causes immediate knockdown, and rescuers are classic secondary casualties. Its rotten-egg smell is lost at dangerous concentrations.
qztymq2: A casualty is hot, dry, flushed, confused and hallucinating, with dilated pupils and no sweating after a reported chemical release. Which picture is this?
This is the anticholinergic toxidrome, the opposite of the wet nerve-agent picture. Care is cooling, protection from injury and supportive sedation; physostigmine use is a medical direction decision.
qb13o7: Why are white phosphorus wounds kept wet during care?
Drying lets retained particles reignite in air
Retained particles can reignite when they dry and contact air. Dressings are kept wet while particles are removed, and the dressings themselves are handled as a hazard.
qxu6vys: A casualty exposed to arsine develops dark urine, jaundice and anemia over hours. What is the main threat?
Pulmonary edema from the gas itself
Arsine is a hemolytic gas. The danger is hemolysis and the pigment load on the kidneys, so care centers on supportive measures and renal protection, not blister care.
qjbztrc: No, chelation does not reverse the hemolysis
Yes, it is the first-line treatment
Yes, but only within one hour
Only when combined with an oxime
Although arsine is an arsenic compound, chelation does not address the hemolysis that causes the harm. Supportive care, transfusion as needed and renal protection are the mainstays.
qfc8gxg: How does an organophosphate pesticide poisoning differ in course from a military nerve agent?
Pesticide effects can last days and may relapse, so prolonged treatment is common
Lipophilic pesticides redistribute slowly, so cholinergic crisis can persist or relapse over days and infusions of antidote may be needed, while nerve-agent exposure tends to be shorter.
qrnm35m: Which decontamination step matters most for a liquid nerve-agent or mustard exposure?
Removing clothing and physically removing the agent from skin early
Giving the antidote before any decontamination
Waiting for a decontamination line at the hospital

Removing clothing takes away most of the agent, and physical removal from skin limits both the casualty's dose and the risk to the team. Antidote and decontamination proceed together in severe exposure.
qm4e2vk: Why is pyridostigmine a pretreatment rather than a treatment?
It reversibly occupies some cholinesterase so antidotes work better afterward, and it is stopped at exposure
It is an antidote given after exposure

Pyridostigmine bromide is taken before anticipated soman exposure to protect a reserve of enzyme. It is not a treatment, it does not replace antidotes, and it is stopped once exposure occurs and antidotes are given.
qphw9bo: A crowd-control agent exposure leaves a casualty with burning eyes and coughing that improves within 30 minutes outdoors. What is the usual care?
Fresh air, removing contaminated clothing and eye irrigation

Riot-control agents are irritants with short-lived effects. Care is removal from exposure, air, decontamination and eye irrigation; persisting or severe symptoms suggest a confined space, a different agent or asthma.
qwyc9d9: What makes the Novichok class a particular field problem?
Very low volatility and persistence, so contamination and secondary exposure last
They cause blistering rather than cholinergic signs
Standard antidotes have no role at all

These agents are persistent and have caused prolonged environmental contamination and secondary casualties. Care remains cholinergic management with high-dose atropine, oxime and benzodiazepine under medical direction.
q1b4ju59: A casualty exposed to aircraft hydrazine fuel is seizing despite repeated benzodiazepines. What is specifically indicated?

Hydrazines interfere with pyridoxine-dependent enzymes, the same mechanism as isoniazid overdose. High-dose vitamin B6 is the specific treatment, given with benzodiazepines rather than instead of them.
q1gtwhac: Which poisoning is made worse by routine supplemental oxygen?
Paraquat concentrates in the lung and kills by oxidative damage, so oxygen feeds the mechanism. It is withheld unless hypoxia is severe, which inverts the usual reflex.
qsrwjms: Workers opening a fumigated shipping container collapse with refractory shock and a garlic odor. Which agent fits?
Aluminum and zinc phosphide release phosphine on contact with moisture. It blocks mitochondrial energy production, and the characteristic death is refractory cardiogenic shock within the first day.
q59uoug: Why is gastric lavage with water avoided after metal phosphide ingestion?
Water releases more phosphine from the remaining tablet
It causes aspiration more than other lavage fluids
It raises the risk of seizures
The tablet releases phosphine gas on contact with moisture, so adding water to the stomach generates more of the toxic gas. Decontamination decisions here are made with poison center input.
q13c193i: What makes nitrogen dioxide exposure different from chlorine?
A second illness, bronchiolitis obliterans, appears two to six weeks later

Nitrogen dioxide has a two-phase course: delayed pulmonary edema, apparent recovery, then bronchiolitis obliterans weeks later. Discharging a well-looking casualty without a return instruction misses it.
qp9v3j0: A casualty exposed to a tear-gas-like agent has eyes that settle in fresh air, but the exposure was heavy. What is the concern with chloropicrin specifically?
Chloropicrin combines immediate irritant effects with the delayed deep-lung injury of a choking agent. Treating it as a simple riot-control exposure and releasing the casualty misses the second part.
q1fyaazb: How does diphosgene differ practically from phosgene?
It is a liquid, so it contaminates clothing and gear and keeps releasing phosgene
It causes blistering rather than lung injury

Diphosgene is a liquid that breaks down into phosgene. The clinical course is the same, but it persists on clothing and equipment, so decontamination matters here in a way it does not for the pure gas.
q1114sj1: A casualty exposed to a vomiting agent such as adamsite reports that symptoms got worse after leaving the cloud. What does this mean?
This is expected; effects continue to worsen for 20 to 30 minutes after exposure ends
The mask failed and they took a second dose
They have been exposed to a nerve agent instead
They are having an allergic reaction

The delayed onset and continued worsening after leaving the area is the characteristic feature, and it is what makes people remove their masks. Keeping the mask on through that window prevents a further dose.
qg4xf2n: Several people in a building have headache and nausea, and a pulse oximeter reads 98 percent on all of them. What should be considered?
Carbon monoxide, which a pulse oximeter cannot distinguish from oxygen
Nothing further; the saturation is reassuring

A pulse oximeter cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so it reads normal in significant poisoning. A co-oximeter or blood gas is what answers the question, and oxygen is started on suspicion.
q957kqs: A casualty from an enclosed-space fire has a severe lactic acidosis and did not improve on high-flow oxygen. What else is likely present?

Burning synthetics release cyanide alongside carbon monoxide. Hydroxocobalamin treats the part oxygen cannot, and it is preferred over nitrites here because nitrites would add methemoglobinemia on top of the carbon monoxide.
qgy1oix: What finding typically prompts the diagnosis of thallium poisoning, and why is that a problem?
Hair loss at around two weeks, by which point the treatment window has largely passed
Immediate blistering, which is easily confused with mustard

The painful ascending neuropathy comes first and is often read as Guillain-Barre. The hair loss that names it arrives around two weeks, so waiting for it loses the window when Prussian blue works best.
qqsgxdq: Several people become ill with seizures and severe acidosis after sharing a meal, and two arrest. What does the pattern suggest?
A deliberately contaminated food or water source that is still in use

Multiple casualties from a shared source means the source is still active. Agents like sodium fluoroacetate are odorless, tasteless and water-soluble, and there is no antidote, so recognizing the pattern is what protects everyone else.
q3kp89w: A casualty has whole-body extensor spasms triggered by noise and touch, and is fully conscious throughout. What does that consciousness change?
Sedation becomes part of the treatment, and stimulation is minimized
It confirms a seizure disorder rather than a poisoning
It means paralysis alone is sufficient

Strychnine blocks spinal inhibition without affecting consciousness, so the casualty experiences all of it. A dark, quiet space with minimal handling is an active treatment, and paralysis without sedation would leave an aware, paralyzed casualty.
q1bytm5b: A casualty received a significant whole-body dose from an external source and is not contaminated. What hazard do they pose to the team?
None. External irradiation does not make a person radioactive
They emit gamma radiation and need lead shielding
They are a contact hazard until washed

Irradiation and contamination are different things. A casualty exposed to external penetrating radiation is not a source, and delaying their care on that belief is the most common error in radiation events.
qlui15i: In a mass-casualty radiation event with no dosimetry, what single piece of information most helps triage?
The interval from exposure to the first episode of vomiting
The casualty's blood pressure on arrival
Whether their hair has started to fall out
The reading on a survey meter held to their chest
Time to vomiting correlates with dose: within an hour suggests a high dose, after six hours or not at all a low one. It can only be captured at the time, so it is recorded on every casualty.
qa1023: Why are serial lymphocyte counts used rather than a single count?
The first count is often normal, and the rate of fall carries the dose information
Lymphocytes rise with dose, so a trend is needed to see it
A single count is unreliable because of laboratory error
Lymphocytes are only affected above 10 Gy
Lymphocytes fall predictably with dose over the first 48 hours, but the initial count is frequently normal. The Andrews method uses counts every 6 to 12 hours to estimate dose from the slope.
q1ie8ojh: What does potassium iodide protect against?
Thyroid uptake of radioactive iodine only

It saturates the thyroid so radioiodine is not taken up. It does nothing for other isotopes or for external dose, and the belief that it is a general radiation antidote leads people to take it instead of evacuating.
q1100cs8: A contaminated casualty arrives with uncontrolled external hemorrhage. What comes first?
Hemorrhage control, with the team in standard precautions
A survey meter reading of the whole body

Contamination has not killed anyone in the first hour and hemorrhage does. Standard precautions with respiratory protection protect the team adequately while life-saving care is given; clothing removal then takes away most of the contamination.
qb0zzzg: Which countermeasure matches cesium-137 internal contamination?

Prussian blue binds cesium and thallium in the gut and interrupts their reabsorption, shortening the time the body is irradiated. The pharmaceutical-grade product is used; artists' pigment is not a substitute.
q8o0fjg: Which countermeasure matches inhaled plutonium or americium?
Pentetate calcium trisodium (Ca-DTPA), as early as possible
DTPA chelates transuranics. Ca-DTPA is first-line in the first 24 hours and works best in the first hours, so it is started before confirmatory bioassay rather than after it.
qjct0n8: Why are nasal swabs taken immediately on a contaminated casualty?
They estimate inhalation, and become useless once the face is washed
They are the only way to detect gamma emitters
They determine whether potassium iodide is needed
Nasal swabs give an early estimate of how much material was inhaled. Taken after facial decontamination they tell you nothing, so they are done on arrival.
q7zgql7: What makes a criticality accident different from other radiation exposures?
Neutron activation makes some of the casualty's own body and metal items briefly radioactive

The neutron component activates sodium in the casualty's blood and metal items they carry. Blood sodium-24 and activated rings, buckles and coins give a physical dose estimate, so those items are collected rather than discarded.
q58tea2: After a nuclear detonation, what is the best protective action for people downwind in the first hours?
Take potassium iodide and continue working
Drive upwind regardless of the route

Moving through fallout in the first hours usually delivers more dose than staying inside a substantial structure. Sheltering for roughly the first 12 to 24 hours, then evacuating on direction, blocks far more dose.
q15hf4gj: A casualty has marrow failure and hair loss, no known radiation exposure, and a normal gamma survey meter reading. What should be considered?
An alpha emitter such as polonium-210, which a gamma meter does not detect
Nothing further; the clean survey rules out radiation

Pure alpha emitters give no reading on a standard gamma survey meter while irradiating the body from within. A clean survey is not clearance, and alpha spectrometry of urine has to be requested specifically.
qh2cvxc: Why is early surgery favored in a casualty with combined radiation and traumatic injury?
The window closes as blood counts fall over the following days
Wounds heal faster in the first 48 hours after irradiation

An irradiated casualty's marrow is failing, so infection risk rises and healing worsens as the days pass. If surgery is going to happen it happens in roughly the first 48 hours, before the counts drop.
q1p5aqlq: What is the characteristic timing of a cutaneous radiation injury?
An early flush that fades, then the real injury at two to three weeks
Immediate blistering like a thermal burn
Pain at the time of exposure with no later changes

The early erythema settles and gives a false reassurance, then redness, blistering and breakdown appear at two to three weeks and evolve in waves for months. Treating it as a thermal burn underestimates the depth.
q5lxsek: Which statement about a radiological dispersal device is accurate?
The blast causes the deaths; radiation causes contamination, fear and a long cleanup
Most casualties develop acute radiation syndrome
Potassium iodide is given to everyone at the scene
The casualties are trauma casualties. Acute radiation syndrome is uncommon after a dispersal device, and the largest medical burden is screening and informing a very large number of uninjured people.
q2wh5s6: Which isotope behaves like calcium and lodges in bone?

Strontium follows the calcium pathway into bone, where it irradiates the adjacent marrow for decades. There is no effective chelator, so the useful actions are reducing gut absorption early and calcium loading under specialist direction.
q69wo2l: In the 9-line MEDEVAC request, which lines are needed to launch the asset?
Lines 1 to 5 (location, frequency and call sign, precedence, special equipment, patient type) are the minimum to launch; lines 6 to 9 can follow en route.
qpab73f: What does line 1 of the 9-line contain?
Line 1 is the grid location of the pickup site.
q18gdklk: Radio frequency, call sign and suffix
Line 2 is the frequency, call sign and suffix at the pickup site.
q161he7w: A is Urgent: evacuation as soon as possible, within a maximum of 1 hour, to save life, limb or eyesight.
q10k9zj1: B is Urgent-Surgical: within 1 hour to a facility for surgical intervention needed to save life and stabilize.
q1s6w3my: What time window is associated with Priority (line 3 C (37.4 F))?
Priority is within 4 hours, or when the condition could deteriorate to urgent.
q1at4zxo: What time window is associated with Routine (line 3 D)?
Routine is within 24 hours, for casualties not expected to deteriorate.
q1upk30i: Line 3 E, Convenience, is used when:
Evacuation is a matter of medical convenience rather than necessity
The casualty is urgent but the LZ is hot
The casualty is on a ventilator
Convenience covers movement for medical convenience, not medical necessity.
q16ml3fv: Line 4: A None, B Hoist, C Extraction equipment, D Ventilator.
qr1x42p: L for litter and A for ambulatory
Line 5 reports the number of patients by type: L litter, A ambulatory.
q1c6zc7r: In wartime, line 6 code P means:
Possible enemy troops in area, approach with caution
Enemy troops in area, armed escort required
P is possible enemy troops in the area; approach with caution.
q4dc2ov: In wartime, line 6 code X means:
Enemy troops in area, armed escort required
X is enemy troops in the area with an armed escort required.
q1mus3f: Number and type of wound, injury or illness
In peacetime, line 6 describes the number and type of wounds, injuries or illnesses.
qv000y7: Line 7: A Panels, B Pyrotechnic signal, C Smoke signal, D None, E Other.
q1tcjcya: Line 8: A U.S. military, B U.S. civilian, C Non-U.S. military, D Non-U.S. civilian, E EPW.
qndnudm: Wartime line 9 reports contamination: N nuclear, B biological, C chemical, with R radiological in current TCCC material.
q4zyfq6: Terrain description of the pickup site
In peacetime, line 9 is a terrain description of the pickup site.
q5zoism: In MIST, the S stands for:
MIST is Mechanism, Injuries, Signs and symptoms, Treatment.
qxjr216: The DD 1380 EVAC section offers which categories?
The card itself has three EVAC boxes: Urgent, Priority and Routine.
qbifmxm: On the DD 1380, tourniquet entries include:
Limb, tourniquet type and time applied
Each limb box on the front records the tourniquet type and the time applied.
q1n1d9xc: Which DD 1380 section records whole blood?
Blood product row with name, volume, route and time
Blood products have their own row: name, volume, route and time.
qh22ov: According to the JTS telemedicine CPG, ADVISOR is:
A synchronous teleconsult line for urgent and emergent consults
ADVISOR provides synchronous voice consults; it is not a route of MEDEVAC and does not arrange patient movement.
qzecq1w: In the prolonged care teleconsult script, what typically opens the call?
Caller identity, role and call-back number
The script opens with who is calling and how to be reached, followed by a pause to confirm contact details.
q2ndh4g: In SBAR, the R stands for:
SBAR is Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation (or request).
q179x7d7: What is the USP definition of controlled room temperature?
20-25 C (68-77 F) with excursions to 15-30 C (59-86 F)
USP controlled room temperature is 20-25 C (68-77 F), with excursions permitted to 15-30 C (59-86 F).
qgc4vfd: What temperature range defines refrigerated storage?
q199a8hu: What does mean kinetic temperature express?
The cumulative heat stress on a product, weighting hot periods more heavily
The average of the daily highs and lows
MKT is a calculated single temperature reflecting cumulative thermal stress; hot periods count more than an arithmetic average would suggest.
qjsaq88: In the 1999 prehospital study by Gottwald and colleagues, which drug lost about 75 percent of its concentration at 37 C (98.6 F) over 210 days?
Lorazepam lost about 75 percent at 37 C (98.6 F), while refrigerated lorazepam showed no loss.
q1xm9kjk: Per its label, how long can multi-dose succinylcholine vials stay at room temperature without significant loss of potency?
The succinylcholine label allows up to 14 days at room temperature for multi-dose vials.
q1g696cx: Per its label, how long can rocuronium be kept at room temperature after removal from refrigeration?
Rocuronium may be held up to 60 days at room temperature; opened vials are used within 30 days.
qxmuu16: In the USAISR TXA study, what was the main problem with storage at -20 C (-4 F)?
The drug degraded into toxic products
TXA itself remained stable, but glass ampules cracked during freezing.
q1su3l5o: Which visible sign indicates epinephrine has oxidized?
Pink, brown, or cloudy epinephrine has oxidized and is not used.
q1lngk6b: What does a strong vinegar smell from aspirin tablets indicate?
Hydrolysis into salicylic and acetic acid
Heat and moisture hydrolyze aspirin, releasing acetic acid with its vinegar smell.
qt8522r: Which of these is damaged by freezing and discarded even after thawing, per its label?
Frozen insulin is discarded per label even after it thaws.
q1mlczij: Why is a frozen propofol vial not used?
Freezing disrupts propofol's emulsion; a broken emulsion is not given.
qm5p4uq: What does the adenosine label say about refrigeration?
It is excluded because crystals can form
It extends shelf life to 5 years
Adenosine is not refrigerated because crystallization can occur; crystals are dissolved by warming to room temperature before use.
q15nnxjc: Which product label specifically describes tolerating 4 days of desert transport at 5-60 C (41-140 F)?
The Cyanokit label describes short-term transport tolerances, including desert transport and freeze-thaw cycles.
qvzg7ki: After reconstitution, how long does the Cyanokit label allow the solution to be kept?
6 hours at no more than 40 C (104 F)
Reconstituted hydroxocobalamin is kept up to 6 hours at no more than 40 C (104 F).
q144tc07: What is the upper storage limit for unmixed ertapenem powder?
The ertapenem label sets 25 C (77 F) as the upper limit for the powder.
qjlgc6u: Why is ceftriaxone not mixed with lactated Ringer's?
Calcium forms a precipitate with ceftriaxone
Ceftriaxone precipitates with calcium, which lactated Ringer's contains.
q1md8kte: What does the albuterol MDI label warn about temperatures above 49 C (120 F)?
The pressurized canister can burst at temperatures above 49 C (120 F).
q1t008ia: Which statement about the Shelf Life Extension Program is accurate?
It covers only specific lots tested and extended under the program
It extends every lot of a drug nationwide
It applies to any stock older than its label date
It is run by drug manufacturers alone
SLEP extensions are lot specific and apply only to lots tested under the DoD/FDA program.
qvxfp44: In the one-year Luxembourg ambulance study, which drug was the only one to fall below 90 percent of its starting concentration?
Succinylcholine reached about 89 percent at 12 months; the other drugs lost under 5 percent.
q1sdyn9j: What is the room-temperature allowance for Vasostrict vials after removal from refrigeration?
12 months within the original expiration date
Vasostrict vials may be held up to 12 months at room temperature, not beyond the original expiration date.
