qww2q8j: What color change in hydromorphone injection does the label describe as not indicating potency loss?
Per label, a slight yellowish discoloration can develop without loss of potency.
qb4zfai: Which IV product label states that brief exposure up to 40 C (104 F) does not adversely affect it?
Baxter IV fluid labels state that brief exposure up to 40 C (104 F) does not adversely affect the product.
q15kfv7b: Which is the most reliable way to know an aid bag exceeded its temperature limits?
A temperature data logger or indicator
Many degraded drugs look normal; only temperature monitoring shows actual exposure.
qe6gzws: Which drug crystallizes in the cold and is redissolved by warming, cooling to body temperature, and giving through an in-line filter, per its label?
Concentrated mannitol crystallizes when cold, and its label describes redissolving with warming and use of a filter.
qc6jeuy: How does the Narcan nasal spray OTC label describe its storage?
2-25 C (35.6-77 F), no freezing, heat above 40 C (104 F) avoided, protected from light
The OTC Narcan label lists 2-25 C (36-77 F), no freezing, avoidance of heat above 40 C (104 F), and light protection.
q9r2ehr: A diver has a dull ache in one shoulder after a dive. The full neurological exam is normal and the pain is gone within 10 minutes at 60 fsw on oxygen. Which table is used?
Pain-only (Type I) DCS with a normal full neurological exam that is relieved within 10 minutes at 60 fsw fits Treatment Table 5.
q1m7l481: Same shoulder pain, but it is not relieved after 10 minutes at 60 fsw. Which table is used?
Type I symptoms not relieved within 10 minutes at 60 fsw move the diver to Treatment Table 6.
q198j61x: A diver surfaces from a fast ascent and is confused with weakness on one side within 5 minutes. Which table is used?
Surface oxygen and observation for 24 hours
Neurological symptoms within 10 minutes of surfacing are treated as arterial gas embolism, which is treated on Treatment Table 6.
q1b0immr: How long is Treatment Table 6 without extensions?
Treatment Table 6 runs 4 hours 45 minutes (285 minutes), not counting descent. 2 h 15 min is Treatment Table 5.
q1c0semm: Treatment Table 5 runs 2 hours 15 minutes (135 minutes), not counting descent.
qiqtfwt: On Treatment Tables 5 and 6, when does oxygen time start?
Oxygen time starts on arrival at 60 fsw.
q1k4rkp7: What is the ascent rate between stops on Treatment Tables 5 and 6?
Ascent is no faster than 1 ft per minute on these tables, on oxygen. Descent is 20 ft per minute.
qsiz4dp: A diver has a seizure from oxygen toxicity at 60 fsw during Treatment Table 6. How does the schedule continue?
It resumes at the point of interruption 15 minutes after the reaction fully subsides
The table restarts from the beginning
The diver is brought straight to the surface
The rest of the table is done on air
After a CNS oxygen toxicity reaction, the schedule resumes at the point of interruption 15 minutes after the reaction has fully subsided.
q1ol6r12: A tender had a hyperbaric exposure 10 hours before running a Treatment Table 6. What changes for the tender?
60 more minutes of oxygen for the tender
The tender breathes air the whole time
A tender with a hyperbaric exposure in the past 18 hours breathes 60 more minutes of oxygen on Treatment Table 6 (20 more minutes on Table 5).
q1hdr4v8: Table 5 or Table 6 is unclear for a diver. Which is chosen?
Neither until a medical officer arrives
When in doubt, the longer table is used.
q1drddm0: After a treatment for pain-only symptoms, how long is the diver observed near the chamber?
The diver is observed for 2 hours after pain-only symptoms and 6 hours after serious symptoms.
q4hyfbb: After a treatment for serious (Type II) symptoms, how long is the diver observed?
The diver is observed for 6 hours after serious symptoms.
q55yjzt: A pulseless diver is pulled from the water. What comes first?
Treatment Table 6 with CPR at depth
ABCs come first. CPR and an AED take priority over recompression, and defibrillation is not done at depth.
qnvp6ht: A diver with suspected DCS is moved by air to a chamber. How is the flight planned?
At the lowest safe altitude or with the cabin pressurized to sea level
Lower pressure at altitude lets bubbles grow, so flight is at the lowest safe altitude or in a cabin held near sea level.
qbb9ohs: Three hours after a dive, a diver has a dull, deep ache in the elbow at rest. The full neurological exam is normal.
Dull, localized joint pain with a normal neurological exam is Type I (pain-only) DCS.
q1qpq9rf: After a dive, a diver has pain wrapping around the trunk like a belt.
Girdle pain points to spinal cord involvement and is treated as Type II. Chest, abdominal and hip pain also count as Type II.
q63agcq: A diver has marbled, bluish, patchy skin on the trunk after a dive.
Type I skin DCS, observation only
Cutis marmorata (marbling) can come before serious DCS and is treated as Type II.
q93y83l: After a dive, a diver has mild itching with no rash and no other symptoms.
Itching alone is usually transient and does not need recompression. Observation continues in case other symptoms appear.
qsj2mq7: After a dive, a diver has a cough, chest pain on breathing in and fast breathing.
These are the chokes, cardiopulmonary Type II DCS, which can progress to collapse.
qt1o0i6: A diver has vertigo, nausea and ringing in one ear after a deep dive with no problems clearing the ears on descent.
Inner ear DCS (the staggers), Type II
Vertigo, nausea and tinnitus after a deep dive can be inner ear DCS, which is Type II. Inner ear barotrauma is the main look-alike; trouble equalizing on descent points to barotrauma instead.
q1bfqj6y: A diver has ear pain and muffled hearing that started on descent while struggling to equalize.
Pain that starts on descent with trouble equalizing is middle ear barotrauma. DCS symptoms start after ascent, not on the way down.
qgwzvt6: A diver who held his breath on ascent has a crackling feeling under the skin of the neck and a hoarse voice, with a normal neurological exam.
Mediastinal and subcutaneous emphysema from lung overpressure
Breath-holding on ascent can rupture lung tissue and push air into the chest and neck (emphysema). The diver is watched closely for arterial gas embolism and pneumothorax.
qlb1inw: A diver who held his breath on a rapid ascent has sharp chest pain and shortness of breath, with breath sounds decreased on one side.
Lung overpressure can cause a pneumothorax. A pneumothorax is decompressed before or during recompression, because air in the chest expands on ascent from the table.
qv2zpzi: A diver collapses unconscious within 2 minutes of surfacing. What is assumed?
Any diver who breathed compressed gas and loses consciousness within 10 minutes of surfacing is assumed to have arterial gas embolism.
q18gcmal: A diver has numbness and tingling in both legs and trouble urinating 1 hour after a dive.
Numbness, weakness and bladder problems point to spinal cord DCS, a Type II emergency.
qazdo9c: A diver has unusual fatigue and mild headache only, 2 hours after a long dive, with a normal exam.
Possible DCS; a full neurological exam and observation continue
Vague fatigue and headache can be early DCS. A careful full neurological exam decides the type, and the diver stays under observation.
qnhuti3: When do most cases of decompression sickness start?
Within hours of surfacing, nearly all within 24 hours
Most DCS starts within hours of surfacing and nearly all within 24 hours. It can occur even within no-decompression limits.
qn82ocl: Why is pain medicine avoided as a way to make a DCS patient comfortable before treatment?
The pain shows where the problem is and whether treatment is working
Pain shows where the problem is and whether recompression is working, so masking it can hide progress or relapse.
q1x7nujx: A casualty with a pelvic injury still has a weak radial pulse after the first unit of whole blood. An arterial sample is run. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.24, PCO2 31 mmHg, HCO3 13 mmol/L, Base excess -15 mmol/L, Lactate 6.8 mmol/L, PO2 94 mmHg. What is the main problem these results point to?
Ongoing hemorrhagic shock with lactic acidosis and breathing compensation
Low blood oxygen from a chest injury

Low pH, low bicarbonate, a deep base deficit and high lactate together show tissue hypoperfusion from continued bleeding. Low pH, low bicarbonate, a negative base excess and high lactate form the signature of hemorrhagic shock. Hemorrhage control and blood are the core of care, and lactate and base deficit are trended
qum14cx: Fifteen minutes after a thigh gunshot wound, a tourniquet is in place. Heart rate is 128 and the casualty is pale. A sample is run before any fluid or blood. i-STAT (CG8+): Hematocrit 42%, Hemoglobin 14.3 g/dL, pH 7.31, PCO2 34 mmHg, HCO3 16.5 mmol/L, Base excess -10 mmol/L, Potassium 4.0 mmol/L, Glucose 142 mg/dL. How is the normal hemoglobin best interpreted here?
It reflects the lag of hemoglobin after acute bleeding; the base deficit is the earlier warning
It shows the blood loss was minor
It suggests the acidosis is a lab error
It means the tourniquet has fully stopped the shock process

Hemoglobin falls only after dilution. Base deficit and lactate rise sooner and track hemorrhage severity better. In the first hour after injury, hemoglobin and hematocrit can look normal even after large blood loss. Base deficit, lactate and the clinical exam are the earlier markers. Hematocrit is trended, and a fallin
qf027jj: A casualty with an abdominal wound had a lactate of 6.1 mmol/L and base excess of -12 an hour ago. After two units of whole blood and calcium, a repeat arterial sample is run. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.36, PCO2 37 mmHg, HCO3 20 mmol/L, Base excess -5 mmol/L, Lactate 2.8 mmol/L, PO2 98 mmHg, sO2 97%. What does the trend suggest?
Resuscitation is restoring perfusion and acid is clearing
The casualty is getting worse because lactate is still high
A new respiratory problem has appeared
The results are normal, so no more trending is needed

Lactate fell by more than half and the base deficit narrowed from -12 to -5, a strong sign that shock is reversing. Lactate clearance (the percent fall over time) and an improving base deficit are among the best signs that resuscitation is working. A single high lactate means less than the trend. Ongoing values guide w
q25jdon: A casualty has a fragment wound to the forearm with minimal bleeding, now dressed. Heart rate is 96 and the casualty is anxious. An arterial sample is run as part of a routine work-up. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.41, PCO2 39 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L, Base excess -1 mmol/L, Lactate 1.3 mmol/L, PO2 96 mmHg, sO2 98%. What do these results show?
No lab evidence of shock at this time
Compensated shock hidden by a normal pH

Every value is within range. The mild tachycardia fits anxiety and pain, and the exam and vital signs remain the main tools going forward. Most results in a minor injury are normal, and reading them as normal is a skill. A normal lactate and base excess make significant hidden hemorrhage unlikely at the time of the sam
qehk90g: A casualty has received four units of cold-stored whole blood and tranexamic acid (TXA) during a long hold. Calcium has not yet been given. i-STAT (CG8+): pH 7.29, Ionized calcium 0.91 mmol/L, Potassium 5.6 mmol/L, Sodium 141 mmol/L, Glucose 128 mg/dL, Hematocrit 33%, Hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL. Which finding is most directly caused by the transfusion and most urgent?
Low ionized calcium from citrate in the stored blood
Low calcium caused by the TXA
The hematocrit, which proves the transfusion failed

Citrate binds calcium. Low ionized calcium weakens clotting and heart contraction, which is why TCCC pairs calcium with the first unit of blood. Low ionized calcium is one of the most common and most treatable findings after transfusion. Citrate in each unit binds calcium, and hypocalcemia worsens bleeding and blood pr
q5ccqrp: During a massive transfusion of stored red cells and plasma, the cardiac monitor shows taller, peaked T waves. A sample is run. i-STAT (EG7+): Potassium 6.6 mmol/L, Ionized calcium 0.88 mmol/L, pH 7.22, PCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3 16 mmol/L, Sodium 140 mmol/L, Hematocrit 30%. Which combination raises the most concern for a dangerous heart rhythm?
High potassium together with low ionized calcium and acidosis

Each one adds to cardiac risk, and calcium stabilizes the heart muscle against potassium. The peaked T waves fit this combination. Massive transfusion can raise potassium (from stored red cells and acidosis) while lowering calcium (from citrate). The pair is especially dangerous for the heart. Calcium, correction of ac
qp3yfcc: Blood is being given rapidly through a fluid warmer. The casualty reports tingling around the mouth and fingers, and blood pressure has dropped despite the blood. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Ionized calcium 0.78 mmol/L, Potassium 4.6 mmol/L, Sodium 142 mmol/L, Chloride 104 mmol/L, Glucose 140 mg/dL, Hematocrit 35%, Hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL. What best explains the tingling and low blood pressure?
Citrate toxicity causing very low ionized calcium

Perioral and finger tingling with low blood pressure during rapid transfusion fits a very low ionized calcium. Calcium supports blood vessel tone and heart contraction. Rapid transfusion, liver injury and hypothermia slow citrate clearance, so ionized calcium can fall quickly. Numbness, tingling, muscle cramps, low blo
q19whk46: A casualty received two units of fresh whole blood collected from screened unit members. A blood gas and a clotting test are run together. i-STAT (CG8+ and PT/INR): Potassium 4.1 mmol/L, Ionized calcium 1.08 mmol/L, Hematocrit 37%, Hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, pH 7.34, INR 1.2, PT 13.0 sec. Which statement fits these results?
Fresh whole blood supplies working clotting factors with little potassium load, but calcium can still fall
Fresh whole blood has no effect on calcium
The INR shows a worsening coagulopathy
The potassium shows a transfusion reaction

Normal potassium and a near-normal INR fit fresh product; the mildly low ionized calcium reflects citrate. Fresh whole blood replaces red cells, plasma and platelets in one product with little stored-cell potassium. It is still anticoagulated with citrate, so ionized calcium is still trended. A stable INR and potassium
q1woy6y3: Midway through a unit of blood, a casualty develops fever, chills, low back pain and dark red urine. Hematocrit was 35% before this unit. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Potassium 5.9 mmol/L, Hematocrit 29%, Hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, BUN 24 mg/dL, Ionized calcium 1.15 mmol/L, Sodium 139 mmol/L, Glucose 118 mg/dL. What is the most likely explanation?

Fever, back pain and dark urine during a unit, with rising potassium, falling hematocrit and rising creatinine, point to destruction of incompatible red cells. An acute hemolytic reaction is usually from blood group incompatibility. Stopping the transfusion and supporting blood pressure and kidney function are the core
q1slh5qy: Three hours after a blast, a casualty has a GCS of 14, headache and repeated vomiting. The TBI cartridge and a chemistry panel are run. i-STAT (TBI and CHEM8+): GFAP Elevated, UCH-L1 Elevated, Sodium 140 mmol/L, Glucose 98 mg/dL, Hematocrit 43%, Hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL. What does an elevated TBI result mean here?
It indicates a higher chance of a CT-visible brain injury, supporting the need for CT imaging
It confirms a severe brain injury requiring surgery
It is explained by the vomiting and dehydration

The i-STAT TBI test is cleared to help decide on CT in mild head injury (GCS 13 to 15) within 24 hours of injury. The TBI cartridge reports GFAP and UCH-L1 against set cutoffs. An elevated result means CT imaging is more likely to show an injury, which affects evacuation priority. It does not replace the neurologic exa
q1y74wjm: Six hours after a nearby blast, a casualty has a GCS of 15, a mild headache and a normal neurologic exam. The TBI cartridge and a chemistry panel are run. i-STAT (TBI and CHEM8+): GFAP Not elevated, UCH-L1 Not elevated, Sodium 140 mmol/L, Potassium 4.1 mmol/L, Glucose 94 mg/dL, Hematocrit 44%. How is this result best interpreted?
A CT-visible brain injury is unlikely, but concussion is still possible and symptoms are followed
Concussion is ruled out and the casualty is cleared
The test is invalid because the chemistry is normal
A CT scan is urgent because of the headache

A negative TBI test has a high negative predictive value for CT findings. Concussion is a clinical diagnosis that the test does not exclude. A not-elevated TBI result can help show that a CT scan, and the evacuation needed to get one, may not be needed. It does not rule out concussion, so symptom tracking, rest and rep
q3ghri9: A head-injured casualty has received hypertonic saline twice for signs of rising brain pressure. Sodium was 141 mmol/L before the first dose. i-STAT (CHEM8+): Sodium 156 mmol/L, Chloride 121 mmol/L, TCO2 20 mmol/L, Anion gap 19 mmol/L, Potassium 3.9 mmol/L, Glucose 182 mg/dL, Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. How is the sodium of 156 mmol/L best read?
It reflects the intended effect of hypertonic saline, with limited room left before about 160 mmol/L
It shows dehydration and the need for more free water
It is a lab error because sodium cannot rise this fast

Head injury protocols accept a raised sodium to pull fluid out of the brain, and many treat values above about 160 mmol/L as a ceiling. Hypertonic saline raises sodium and chloride by design. q1wy7f3o: An intubated head-injured casualty is being bagged quickly during a bumpy ground transport. End-tidal CO2 reads low. An arterial sample is run. i-STAT (CG4+): pH 7.53, PCO2 26 mmHg, HCO3 21 mmol/L, Base excess -2 mmol/L, PO2 112 mmHg, Lactate 1.4 mmol/L. What is the main problem?

Lactated Ringer's boluses until blood pressure is normal
Hetastarch to expand volume and save the blood for later
No fluid until the radial pulse is lost completely

Whole blood is the preferred TCCC resuscitation fluid, and TXA in the first 3 hours reduces death from bleeding. TCCC lists cold-stored low titer O whole blood as the preferred fluid, then plasma with red cells, plasma alone, or red cells alone. The end point is a palpable radial pulse, improved mentation, or a systoli
q10qpk3t: A 26-year-old male stepped on a pressure-plate IED. He has a traumatic above-knee amputation on the right and a below-knee amputation on the left. H+0:40 (Casualty collection point): Two units of whole blood are in. He reports tingling around his mouth. An i-STAT CG8+ is run. How is the low ionized calcium handled?
Calcium replacement alongside ongoing blood products, with a repeat i-STAT
Sodium bicarbonate to fix the pH first, then a calcium recheck
Calcium deferred until four units are in
No treatment because he has no arrhythmia

Citrate in stored blood binds calcium, and hypocalcemia is part of the lethal diamond with acidosis, hypothermia and coagulopathy. The lethal diamond is hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy and hypocalcemia. TCCC calls for calcium with or right after the first unit of blood product, and i-STAT ionized calcium guides fur
q2k7kf2: A 26-year-old male stepped on a pressure-plate IED. He has a traumatic above-knee amputation on the right and a below-knee amputation on the left. H+1:30 (Patrol base): He is moved into an abandoned stone building. His uniform is soaked and he is shivering on the concrete floor. What is the best way to address his temperature?
Wet clothing removed, insulation under him, a hypothermia prevention kit with an active heater, and warmed blood products
Warm Lactated Ringer's boluses to heat him from the inside
A blanket over the torso, leaving the stumps exposed for monitoring
Shivering allowed to continue since it is the body's own warming

Insulation from the ground, dry layers, active heat and warmed fluids together limit heat loss from every route. Even mild hypothermia worsens clotting. In TCCC, hypothermia prevention starts at the point of injury and continues through every move: off the ground, out of the wind, dry, covered and actively warmed.
q16l0hb3: A 26-year-old male stepped on a pressure-plate IED. He has a traumatic above-knee amputation on the right and a below-knee amputation on the left. H+2:30 (Patrol base): The tourniquets have been on for about 2.5 hours. A teammate asks whether it is time to convert them to pressure dressings. Blood pressure is rising, and there is new oozing past the left tourniquet. What fits best for the tourniquets?
Tourniquets left in place, the left one tightened or a second added above it, and times recorded on the DD1380
Both tourniquets converted to pressure dressings now that the 2-hour mark has passed
Tourniquets loosened every 30 minutes to let the limbs perfuse
A pressure dressing added over the left stump while the tourniquet stays loose

Amputation tourniquets stay on. As resuscitation raises blood pressure, a tourniquet that was effective can start to leak and needs reassessment. TCCC: tourniquet conversion is not attempted on an amputation, on a casualty in shock, or when the casualty cannot be watched closely. Every tourniquet is reassessed after ea
qsvxa8z: A 26-year-old male stepped on a pressure-plate IED. He has a traumatic above-knee amputation on the right and a below-knee amputation on the left. H+3 (Patrol base): He is nauseated and has vomited once. Both stumps are open, contaminated wounds packed with dirt and fabric. No antibiotic has been given yet. Which antibiotic plan fits best?
IV ertapenem or ceftriaxone now, with the time recorded
Oral moxifloxacin from the combat wound medication pack
Antibiotics held until signs of infection appear
Topical antiseptic poured into the wounds instead of systemic antibiotics

TCCC calls for antibiotics as soon as possible for open combat wounds, by IV, IO or IM route when oral intake is not possible. TCCC antibiotics: moxifloxacin by mouth when the casualty can swallow; ertapenem or ceftriaxone IV, IO or IM when the casualty cannot. The time each dose is given goes on the DD1380 so redosing
qv9fmca: A 26-year-old male stepped on a pressure-plate IED. He has a traumatic above-knee amputation on the right and a below-knee amputation on the left. H+6 (Patrol base): He rates his pain 8 out of 10 and is grimacing. His blood pressure is better but he is still tachycardic. Which analgesic approach fits best?
Ketamine titrated to effect, with pain and sedation scores recorded and an antiemetic as needed
Repeated IV morphine until he is comfortable
Meloxicam, since it does not depress breathing
Analgesia withheld until his blood pressure is completely normal

Ketamine provides strong analgesia while preserving blood pressure and breathing, which makes it the TCCC choice for a casualty in or at risk of shock. TCCC analgesia: the combat wound medication pack for mild pain, fentanyl or ketamine for moderate to severe pain, and ketamine preferred when shock or respiratory distr
q1i63fi7: A 26-year-old male stepped on a pressure-plate IED. He has a traumatic above-knee amputation on the right and a below-knee amputation on the left. H+12 (Patrol base): A Foley catheter has been placed. All four stored units are used. Urine output over the last two hours is low and dark. What is the best next step?
Fresh whole blood from prescreened walking blood bank donors, calcium as needed, and a teleconsult
Large crystalloid boluses to bring up urine output
Current status accepted because his systolic pressure is above 90

Low urine output, falling hemoglobin and persistent lactate point to ongoing under-resuscitation that blood corrects. In prolonged care, urine output via a Foley, lactate and hemoglobin trends guide resuscitation better than one blood pressure. Teleconsultation through the ADVISOR line helps plan ongoing blood needs an
qujx3co: A 26-year-old male stepped on a pressure-plate IED. He has a traumatic above-knee amputation on the right and a below-knee amputation on the left. H+40 (Long hold, day 2): He has a new fever and a foul smell from the right stump dressing. The skin above the wound is red and warm. What is the best response?
Wound exposed, irrigated and debris removed, clean dressing applied, antibiotic redosing verified, sepsis screen and teleconsult
More dressing layers added on top to contain the smell
Acetaminophen for the fever and observation
Antibiotics stopped because they appear to have failed

Source control in the field means cleaning and opening the wound, confirming antibiotics are on time, and getting expert input. JTS Prolonged Casualty Care guidance includes daily wound checks, irrigation and dressing changes. New fever with a rising heart rate prompts a sepsis screen, lactate check, antibiotic review
q1e1rl9z: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+0:10 (Point of injury): His abdomen is firm and slowly distending. He is pale and anxious with a weak radial pulse. No external bleeding is visible. Which plan fits best?
Whole blood resuscitation to a radial pulse and clear mentation, TXA early, and an urgent surgical evacuation request
Hemostatic gauze packed deep into the abdominal wound
An abdominal aortic junctional tourniquet applied over the abdomen
Crystalloid to bring blood pressure back to normal

Non-compressible bleeding needs blood, TXA and a surgeon. Hypotensive resuscitation limits clot disruption until surgery. Non-compressible torso hemorrhage is the leading cause of preventable combat death. TCCC: resuscitate to a palpable radial pulse, normal mentation or a systolic pressure near 100, with whole blood a
qupxj1e: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+0:30 (Casualty collection point): He is thirsty and asks for water. A teammate offers the combat wound medication pack. Which antibiotic plan fits best?
IV or IO ertapenem now, nothing by mouth, mouth moistened with a damp gauze
Oral moxifloxacin with a sip of water
Oral cephalexin to cover the skin bacteria
Antibiotics deferred until the surgeon sees him

Ertapenem covers bowel flora including anaerobes and suits a casualty who cannot take oral medication. Penetrating abdominal wounds are presumed to involve bowel. Ertapenem is the TCCC parenteral choice. Keeping the casualty without food or drink protects the airway and a later surgery, and a damp gauze eases thirst.
qksrnzz: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+1 (Casualty collection point): Both stored units are in. His pressure has dipped again. i-STAT results are back. What is the best next step?
Walking blood bank activated with ABO confirmation on donors and recipient, and calcium replacement
Hetastarch to stretch the remaining resources
Vasopressin to support blood pressure until surgery
No more blood because systolic pressure is above 80

Fresh whole blood supplies red cells, plasma and working platelets. Calcium corrects the citrate effect seen on the i-STAT. The walking blood bank uses prescreened donors whose type is confirmed in the field with a rapid typing card. Ionized calcium falls with every citrated unit, and repeat i-STAT checks guide replace
q18h4oom: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+3 (Patrol base): After a unit of fresh whole blood, his radial pulse is stronger and he answers questions clearly. The team plans the night. Which monitoring plan fits best?
A Foley with hourly urine output, vitals every 15 to 30 minutes, serial abdominal exams and a PCC flowsheet
Vital signs every 4 hours to let him sleep
Blood pressure alone as the trigger for action
A nasogastric tube passed blind to check for blood in the stomach

Frequent, structured reassessment catches re-bleeding early and creates the trend record for teleconsult and handoff. The PCC flowsheet records vitals, intake, urine output, medications and products over time. Trends drive decisions during a long hold and give the receiving surgeon the story.
q1k6ddvh: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+6 (Patrol base): His pain is 9 out of 10 and he is guarding his abdomen. A teammate worries that pain medication will hide a worsening exam. Which analgesic approach fits best?
Titrated IV fentanyl or ketamine, with pain and sedation scores recorded
Ketorolac, since it avoids opioid side effects
Analgesia withheld to keep the abdominal exam reliable
IM morphine for its longer effect

Both work quickly with IV or IO access and are TCCC options for severe pain. Ketamine is favored if pressure drops again. Pain control is part of care, not a threat to diagnosis. TCCC and the JTS Analgesia and Sedation CPG favor titrated fentanyl or ketamine for severe pain and avoid NSAIDs other than meloxicam in casu
q1uogg8m: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+12 (Patrol base): He is stable through the night. Hemoglobin is holding. A teammate suggests raising his pressure further with fluid and starting clot prevention. What fits best now?
Measured maintenance fluid with ongoing reassessment, nothing by mouth, and a teleconsult update
Enoxaparin started to prevent DVT during the long hold
Large crystalloid boluses to push systolic pressure higher
A regular meal to support healing

With bleeding controlled for now, the goal is steady perfusion without over-resuscitation while surgery is awaited. After the shock phase, prolonged care shifts to careful maintenance and watching for re-bleeding. DVT prophylaxis waits until bleeding is surgically controlled, a decision made with a teleconsult.
q1cb4sxe: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+30 (Long hold, day 2): He is confused and breathing fast. His abdomen is rigid and tender everywhere. His skin is warm and flushed. What is happening, and what fits best?
Septic shock from peritonitis; fluid bolus with reassessment, antibiotic coverage reviewed by teleconsult, lactate repeated, evacuation priority raised
Fever only; acetaminophen and recheck in 4 hours
Fluids withheld to avoid abdominal swelling

Fever, confusion, fast breathing, low pressure and high lactate after bowel injury add up to septic shock that needs source control. The JTS Sepsis in PFC CPG uses early recognition, fluid boluses with reassessment, broad antibiotics and vasopressors when needed. Source control means surgery here, so the casualty's eva
q18u4xfa: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+32 (Long hold, day 2): After two fluid boluses his lungs are still clear, but his mean arterial pressure stays low and his urine output is falling. What is the best next step?
Norepinephrine titrated to a MAP of at least 65 through secure access
A MAP of 58 accepted since he is still mentating

Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor for septic shock once initial fluid has been given. Septic shock: MAP target of 65 or more, norepinephrine first, vasopressin as a second agent. Infusions in the field need a secure line, a pump or careful drip counting, and close blood pressure checks.
qzocp3f: A 31-year-old male was shot in the left upper abdomen. There is an entry wound and no exit wound. H+48 (Long hold, day 2): A helicopter is inbound. He is on norepinephrine with improving lactate. The team prepares for handoff. Which handoff fits best?
DD1380 and PCC flowsheet with trends, all products and donor IDs, antibiotic and infusion times, plus a MIST verbal report
A quick verbal summary to the flight medic
A blank DD1380 sent with a promise to email details later
Only the most recent set of vital signs

Complete documentation lets the surgical team act right away and avoid repeating or missing treatments. The DD1380 and PCC flowsheet travel with the casualty. They include tourniquet and product times, walking blood bank donor information, medications with times, and trends in vitals, urine output and labs.
q8z0e3m: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+0:10 (Point of injury): He has snoring respirations and does not open his eyes to pain. External bleeding is controlled. What fits best for his airway?
Rapid sequence intubation with a hemodynamically stable induction agent and a paralytic, with preoxygenation and waveform capnography
Hyperventilation by bag right away to reduce brain swelling

With a GCS of 7 and hypoxia, he needs a definitive airway. Ketamine or etomidate with rocuronium keeps blood pressure stable. In TBI, a single episode of hypoxia or hypotension raises mortality. TCCC and the JTS TBI in PFC CPG aim for SpO2 above 90% and avoid hypotension during airway management. Ketamine is acceptable
q1g2db7r: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+0:40 (Casualty collection point): He is intubated and on the ventilator. A teammate set a high rate to protect his brain. How is ventilation best adjusted?
Rate reduced to bring EtCO2 to 35 to 40 mmHg
EtCO2 kept at 28 to protect the brain
EtCO2 allowed to rise to 50 for lung protection
Only FiO2 adjusted, since EtCO2 is not relevant in TBI

Normal CO2 keeps cerebral blood flow steady. Hyperventilation is a short bridge only for active herniation. JTS TBI in PFC targets: SpO2 above 90%, normal EtCO2 near 35 to 40 mmHg, systolic pressure above 110 mmHg, head of bed raised about 30 degrees, and normal temperature and glucose.
qvbom4n: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+1:30 (Casualty collection point): His right pupil is now 6 mm and sluggish, the left is 3 mm. His blood pressure is rising and his heart rate is falling. What fits best now?
Hypertonic saline bolus, head of bed at 30 degrees with the neck straight, brief hyperventilation to EtCO2 near 30 to 35 as a bridge, and an urgent teleconsult
Metoprolol to bring blood pressure down
Observation until both pupils are fixed

A blown pupil with the Cushing triad signals herniation. Hypertonic saline draws water from the brain and supports pressure. Herniation signs: a dilated or sluggish pupil, posturing, falling GCS, or the Cushing triad of high blood pressure, slow heart rate and irregular breathing. JTS favors hypertonic saline. Mannitol
q3vr6m1: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+2 (Casualty collection point): He has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting more than 2 minutes. The ventilator alarms. What fits best?
A benzodiazepine to stop the seizure, then levetiracetam for ongoing prophylaxis
A paralytic to stop the movement
Levetiracetam alone, then waiting for it to work
Observation, since seizures stop on their own

Midazolam or lorazepam stops the seizure quickly, and levetiracetam covers the early post-injury period. The JTS TBI in PFC CPG recommends seizure prophylaxis with levetiracetam for severe TBI for about 7 days. Active seizures are stopped first with a benzodiazepine while watching blood pressure.
qkjpgg4: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+4 (Patrol base): He is settled after the seizure. Labs come back. A teammate wants to start a dextrose-containing maintenance fluid. Which fluid plan fits best?
Isotonic fluid such as Plasma-Lyte or normal saline, with sodium and glucose rechecked every 4 to 6 hours
Large volumes of Lactated Ringer's to keep the kidneys perfused
Fluids stopped to keep the brain dry

Isotonic fluid avoids pulling water into the brain, and repeat checks catch dangerous sodium or glucose shifts. In TBI, sodium is kept normal to mildly high with a target set by teleconsult, and swings are avoided. Glucose is kept roughly in the 80 to 180 mg/dL range because both low and high glucose harm the injured b
q153553w: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+8 (Patrol base): He coughs and bucks against the ventilator during suctioning. His heart rate and blood pressure spike. What fits best?
Analgesia and sedation deepened with ketamine and fentanyl, propofol only if blood pressure allows
Rocuronium alone to stop the bucking
Restraints only, since medications cloud the neuro exam

Coughing and agitation raise intracranial pressure. Analgesia first, then sedation, protects the brain while keeping pressure up. Analgesia-first sedation reduces intracranial pressure spikes. Ketamine does not raise intracranial pressure in ventilated patients when CO2 is controlled. Propofol lowers intracranial press
q15be9x2: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+14 (Patrol base): After propofol was increased, his blood pressure dropped. A teammate says a systolic of 92 is fine under TCCC. What fits best?
Propofol reduced, volume status checked, and a vasopressor such as norepinephrine or phenylephrine to keep systolic above 110
A systolic of 92 accepted as within TCCC targets
Head of bed lowered flat to raise blood pressure

Removing the cause and supporting pressure maintains brain perfusion. TBI blood pressure target: systolic above 110 mmHg in the JTS TBI in PFC CPG. When sedation lowers pressure, the sedative is adjusted first and a vasopressor is added as needed.
q1hsfsa7: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+24 (Long hold, day 2): Urine output has jumped to about 300 mL per hour of pale, watery urine. No hypertonic saline has been given in 10 hours. What is most likely, and what fits best?
Diabetes insipidus from pituitary injury; teleconsult, hypertonic saline held, and water replacement guided by frequent sodium checks
Response to earlier hypertonic saline; more hypertonic saline
Fluid restriction to slow urine output

Large volumes of dilute urine with rising sodium after severe TBI point to diabetes insipidus. Central diabetes insipidus can follow severe TBI. Clues are high urine output, dilute urine and rising sodium. Treatment needs teleconsult guidance, and sodium is lowered slowly.
q1sx2ud4: A 24-year-old male was thrown from a vehicle by a roadside blast. His helmet is cracked and he has a scalp laceration. H+30 (Long hold, day 2): His temperature is climbing. His eyes are not fully closed, and his skin over the sacrum is pink. Which care fits best?
Cooling and acetaminophen, a search for infection, eye lubrication and taping, and repositioning every 2 hours
Fever left alone as a normal response
Ice packs to the head only
Turning stopped to avoid raising intracranial pressure

Fever control, eye protection and pressure injury prevention are core nursing tasks in prolonged TBI care. Prolonged TBI nursing includes normal temperature, eye care, oral care, head of bed at 30 degrees, repositioning every 2 hours, and recording GCS and pupil checks on the flowsheet.
q1v1mnbt: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+0:10 (Point of injury): His nasal hair is singed, his voice is hoarse and he is coughing up black sputum. Mild stridor has started. What fits best for his airway?
Early rapid sequence intubation by the most experienced provider, with a cricothyroidotomy kit ready
Nebulized racemic epinephrine as the main airway treatment

Hoarseness, stridor and carbonaceous sputum predict airway swelling. Intubating early is easier and safer. Signs of inhalation injury: facial burns, singed hair, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness and stridor. The JTS Burn CPG supports early intubation when these are present and transport will be prolonged.
qf3mmew: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+0:30 (Casualty collection point): He is intubated. He was confused before intubation and the fire was in an enclosed space. The pulse oximeter reads high, but the i-STAT lactate is very high. What fits best?
100% oxygen and hydroxocobalamin for suspected cyanide poisoning
SpO2 of 99% taken as proof of good oxygenation
Sodium bicarbonate to correct the acidosis

An enclosed-space fire, altered mental status, hypotension and very high lactate suggest cyanide, and hydroxocobalamin is the preferred antidote. Smoke from burning plastics and furnishings contains carbon monoxide and cyanide. High-flow oxygen treats CO, and hydroxocobalamin treats cyanide. Hydroxocobalamin turns skin
q1irt0xn: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+1 (Casualty collection point): His burns are mapped and estimated at 40% TBSA, not counting superficial redness. A teammate wants a large fluid bolus based on the Parkland formula. Which fluid approach fits best?
Lactated Ringer's started at the Rule of Ten rate, then titrated hourly to urine output
The full first 8-hour Parkland volume given as a bolus
Hetastarch to reduce the total volume
Fluids withheld until 2 hours after the burn

The Rule of Ten gives a quick starting rate from TBSA and weight, and urine output guides changes from there. TCCC and the JTS Burn CPG use the Rule of Ten for adults 40 to 80 kg: TBSA rounded to the nearest 10, times 10, gives the starting hourly rate. Superficial (first-degree) burns are not counted in TBSA.
qmkpcar: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+3 (Patrol base): A Foley catheter is in. Urine output over the last hour is low and dark. Heart rate is climbing. What is the best adjustment?
Lactated Ringer's rate increased stepwise, with urine output rechecked each hour toward a target of about 30 to 50 mL per hour
A large bolus to catch up
Low urine output accepted as expected in burns

Hourly titration to urine output is the standard way to adjust burn fluid. In burns, urine output is the main resuscitation gauge: about 30 to 50 mL per hour for adults. The fluid rate is raised or lowered in steps, and every hour is recorded on the burn flowsheet.
q827bnd: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+6 (Patrol base): Ventilator peak pressures have risen and his chest barely moves. The circumferential chest burn is leathery and tight. After a quick DOPE check is normal, what fits best?

A tight chest eschar can restrict ventilation, and releasing it restores chest wall movement. Circumferential burns of the chest or limbs can restrict breathing or circulation. Escharotomy is a high-risk procedure in the field, usually done with teleconsult guidance when ventilation or limb perfusion is failing.
q1hxqye: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+10 (Patrol base): The burns are exposed while being checked. The room is cool and his temperature is dropping. Which wound and temperature plan fits best?
Clean, dry burn dressings, an active warming blanket, a warm room, and warmed fluids
Cool, wet dressings over all the burns for comfort
Burns left open to air to let them dry
Prophylactic systemic antibiotics for the burns

Burned skin cannot hold heat, so covering, warming the room and warming fluids prevent hypothermia. Burn casualties lose heat quickly through damaged skin. The JTS Burn CPG emphasizes dry dressings, active warming and a warm environment. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for burns alone.
qwrlx59: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+16 (Patrol base): He grimaces during dressing changes and his heart rate jumps. He is ventilated. Which analgesia and sedation approach fits best?
Ketamine and fentanyl titrated to pain and sedation scores, with extra analgesia before dressing changes
Dressing changes stopped to avoid pain

Burn pain is severe and spikes with dressing changes, so analgesia-first sedation with ketamine and fentanyl fits. Burns are among the most painful injuries. Analgesia-first sedation with ketamine and opioids is common. Burn patients often need more than expected, and pain and sedation scores are recorded on the flowsh
q1hpgoj2: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+30 (Long hold, day 2): His endotracheal tube cuff fails and he needs re-intubation. A teammate grabs succinylcholine. Which paralytic fits best?
Succinylcholine for its fast onset and short duration
Succinylcholine with calcium given ahead of time

Rocuronium avoids the burn-related hyperkalemia risk and still allows rapid sequence intubation. After about 24 hours, burns increase muscle acetylcholine receptors, and succinylcholine can cause a life-threatening rise in potassium. The same risk applies to crush injury, prolonged immobility and denervation injuries.
q1byvxpr: An 80 kg, 28-year-old male was trapped in a burning building for several minutes. He has partial and full thickness burns to the face, both arms circumferentially and the chest, about 40% TBSA. H+48 (Long hold, day 2): Urine output has been 80 to 100 mL per hour for several hours. His face, arms and abdomen are very swollen. What fits best?
Lactated Ringer's rate reduced stepwise, with abdominal pressure and airway pressures checked
The fluid rate kept the same
An extra bolus to protect the kidneys
Hetastarch to pull fluid back into the vessels

Over-resuscitation causes abdominal compartment syndrome, worsening lung function and limb compartment problems. Fluid creep is a major cause of burn complications. When urine output exceeds the target, the rate is lowered stepwise. A tense abdomen with rising airway pressures can signal abdominal compartment syndrome.
qckd156: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+0 (Point of injury): He is awake and talking. Engineers are ready to lift the slab in about 10 minutes. What fits best before release?
IV or IO access with isotonic fluid running before the slab is lifted, and the cardiac monitor attached
Immediate lift, with fluids started once he is out
Lift delayed several hours to plan the evacuation

Fluid before release dilutes the potassium, acid and myoglobin that flood in when blood returns to the crushed muscle. Crush syndrome develops after compression of large muscle groups, often more than an hour. Preparation before release includes access, fluid, a cardiac monitor and medications for hyperkalemia ready to
q131ts4p: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+0:40 (Casualty collection point): Minutes after release, the monitor shows peaked T waves and a widening QRS. His heart rate is slowing. What comes first?
Calcium to stabilize the cardiac membrane
Insulin with dextrose to lower potassium

Calcium protects the heart within minutes and buys time for the potassium-lowering treatments. Hyperkalemia with ECG changes: calcium first to stabilize the heart, then shift potassium into cells with insulin and dextrose, albuterol, and bicarbonate if acidotic. Only dialysis or the kidneys remove potassium from the bo
q1yd7loz: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+0:50 (Casualty collection point): After calcium, the QRS narrows. A teammate says the problem is fixed. What fits best next?
Regular insulin with dextrose, nebulized albuterol, and sodium bicarbonate for the acidosis
No further treatment since the ECG improved

These shift potassium into cells and lower the serum level while the kidneys recover. Calcium stabilizes but does not lower potassium. The JTS Hyperkalemia CPG lists insulin and dextrose, albuterol and bicarbonate as shift therapies, with potassium and glucose rechecked often.
q113ahdl: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+2 (Patrol base): He is sweaty and confused. The i-STAT is rechecked. What fits best?
Dextrose, with glucose checked every hour while insulin effects last
More insulin to keep potassium falling

Hypoglycemia is a common complication of insulin for hyperkalemia and is quickly reversed with dextrose. Insulin for hyperkalemia commonly causes hypoglycemia 1 to 3 hours later. Hourly glucose checks for several hours are part of the treatment.
q1jnvhut: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+4 (Patrol base): His urine is dark brown like tea. A Foley is in, and output is low. Which plan fits best?
Isotonic fluid titrated to a high urine output target of about 200 to 300 mL per hour, with lung and edema checks
Fluids restricted to protect the lungs

High urine flow flushes myoglobin through the kidneys and lowers the risk of kidney failure. Rhabdomyolysis from crush injury releases myoglobin that damages the kidneys. The goal is high urine output with isotonic fluid, while watching for lung crackles and edema.
qym4ku9: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+8 (Patrol base): His left calf is tense and shiny. He has severe pain when his toes are moved and numbness on top of his foot. Pulses are present. What fits best?
Leg kept at heart level, tight dressings loosened, hourly compartment checks, and a teleconsult about fasciotomy
Leg elevated high to reduce swelling

Pain with passive stretch and numbness suggest compartment syndrome. Present pulses do not rule it out. Compartment syndrome signs: severe pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, tense swelling and numbness. In crush injury, the fasciotomy decision is complex and is made with expert teleconsult input.
q1nxw719: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+14 (Patrol base): Potassium is rising again. Urine output has dropped despite fluids, and there are new crackles in both lungs. What fits best?
Repeat shift therapy, fluids reduced, oxygen, and an urgent teleconsult to raise evacuation priority for dialysis
More fluid boluses to restart urine flow
Potassium chloride in the IV fluid

Kidney failure with rising potassium needs dialysis, which only a hospital can provide. Oliguric kidney failure after crush injury needs dialysis. In the field, potassium is managed with repeated shift therapy and the evacuation priority rises.
q1wffrj5: A 34-year-old male has been pinned at the thighs by a concrete slab for about 4 hours. H+24 (Long hold, day 2): He is awake and in severe pain from his legs. Kidney function is poor. Which analgesic approach fits best?
Fentanyl or ketamine titrated to pain, with sedation and breathing watched
Ketorolac or meloxicam for non-opioid pain control
Pain medication withheld because of kidney failure

Neither relies on the kidneys for clearance as much as morphine, so they are better choices in kidney failure. In kidney failure, NSAIDs are avoided and morphine is used with caution. Fentanyl and ketamine are preferred. Pain and sedation scores are recorded with each dose.
q18ss8xj: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+0:05 (Point of injury): The wound bubbles with each breath. He is short of breath but talking in full sentences. Breath sounds are present on both sides. What fits best for the wound?
A vented chest seal applied, then close watch for progressive respiratory distress
Wound left open to air so tension cannot build
Needle decompression before the seal goes on
Hemostatic gauze packed into the chest wound

A vented seal stops air entry through the wound while letting pleural air escape, and tension can still develop later. TCCC: open or sucking chest wounds receive a vented or non-vented chest seal, then the casualty is monitored for tension pneumothorax. Placing the casualty in the sitting or recovery position, injured
q1ngz5t5: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+0:30 (Casualty collection point): He is gasping and anxious. Breath sounds are absent on the right. The chest seal was burped and briefly removed without improvement. What fits best?
Needle decompression at the 5th intercostal space anterior axillary line or the 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line
Observation until tracheal deviation confirms tension
A fluid bolus to treat the falling blood pressure
Intubation and positive pressure ventilation first

Suspected tension pneumothorax with shock and hypoxia is decompressed right away, and TCCC lists both sites. TCCC: suspected tension pneumothorax with progressive respiratory distress on the injured side is decompressed with a needle, and repeated if signs return. Simple thoracostomy is an option for providers trained
q1qgkzr1: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+1:30 (Casualty collection point): He improved, then tired and was intubated with ketamine and rocuronium. On the ventilator, his oxygen and pressure fall again and peak pressure climbs. What fits best?
Finger (simple) thoracostomy at the 4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line
More needle decompressions, one every few minutes
Tidal volume increased to improve oxygen

Positive pressure keeps refilling the pleural space, and an open finger thoracostomy decompresses it reliably in a ventilated casualty. In a ventilated casualty, recurrent tension after needle decompression is an indication for simple thoracostomy by a trained provider. A chest tube follows when the hold is long and a
q1e9imr: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+3 (Patrol base): A chest tube placed with teleconsult guidance drains about 900 mL of blood at once and then keeps dripping. His pressure is still low. What fits best?
Whole blood, TXA because he is within 3 hours of injury, calcium, warming, and hourly chest tube output tracking
Chest tube clamped to tamponade the bleeding
Crystalloid bolus to bring pressure up
Output ignored now that the lung has re-expanded

Hemorrhagic shock from a hemothorax needs blood, and hourly output tells whether surgery is urgent. Surgical bleeding is suggested by about 1,500 mL drained at once, or about 200 mL per hour for 2 to 4 hours. Chest tube output is recorded hourly on the PCC flowsheet alongside vitals and products.
qcb678v: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+6 (Patrol base): His SpO2 drops suddenly and the ventilator alarms high pressure. The EtCO2 waveform is still present but smaller. The chest tube has stopped draining. What fits best?
Disconnection from the ventilator, bag ventilation, and a DOPE check that includes chest tube patency
FiO2 and PEEP raised and the alarm silenced

DOPE finds the cause in a structured way; a kinked or clotted tube with a new pneumothorax fits these findings. DOPE: Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, Equipment. Bagging off the ventilator separates a patient problem from a machine problem, and a chest tube that suddenly stops draining is checked for kinks, clo
qneh3ke: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+10 (Patrol base): Chest tube output has been about 150 to 200 mL per hour for 3 hours. All stored units are used. What fits best?
Teleconsult reporting the trend, evacuation priority raised to urgent surgical, and fresh whole blood from the walking blood bank
A second chest tube to drain faster
Output accepted as normal after a chest wound
Chest tube clamped to slow the loss

This bleeding likely needs a thoracotomy, so the team raises priority and replaces blood until then. Ongoing hemothorax output is one of the clearest field signals that surgery is needed. The teleconsult report includes hourly output, products given, and vital sign and lab trends.
qpvd5dc: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+18 (Patrol base): Bleeding has slowed. An arterial i-STAT is run on FiO2 0.6. He has a large pulmonary contusion. Which ventilator adjustment fits best?
Lung-protective tidal volume kept, PEEP titrated for oxygenation, and rate increased for CO2
Sodium bicarbonate for the low pH
Tidal volume increased well above the lung-protective range to clear CO2
FiO2 at 1.0 for the rest of the hold

Rate clears CO2 and PEEP recruits lung without the overstretch of larger breaths. Lung-protective ventilation uses tidal volume based on ideal body weight, a plateau pressure under 30, and PEEP and FiO2 adjusted together. Mild permissive hypercapnia is acceptable when there is no brain injury.
q1i97qjx: A 29-year-old male has a gunshot wound to the right chest just below the nipple line. No exit wound is found. H+30 (Long hold, day 2): He has a new fever and thick yellow secretions on suctioning. The head of the litter has been flat most of the night. What fits best?
Pneumonia bundle with head of bed at 30 degrees, oral care, suctioning, and an antibiotic chosen with teleconsult
Chest tube removed as the likely source
Suctioning reduced to rest the airway

Fever with purulent secretions in a ventilated casualty suggests pneumonia, and the bundle limits further aspiration. Ventilator-associated pneumonia prevention includes head of bed at 30 degrees, oral care, suctioning and daily sedation checks. New fever in prolonged care prompts a source search and antibiotic choice
qfx9kud: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+0 (Point of injury): He is confused and combative. His skin is hot and still sweaty. A rectal thermometer is in the aid bag. What fits best?
Immediate whole-body cooling with cold water immersion or tarp-assisted cooling with ice water
Shade, loosened gear and oral water
Evacuation first, with cooling at the aid station

Time above about 40 C (104 F) drives organ injury, and rapid cooling within 30 minutes gives the best outcomes. Exertional heat stroke is a high core temperature with central nervous system dysfunction. Sweaty skin does not rule it out. Cold water immersion is the fastest method, with tarp-assisted cooling or ice sheet
q179emdm: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+0:20 (Point of injury): His rectal temperature is falling quickly. A teammate wants to keep cooling until it reaches 37 C (98.6 F). When is active cooling stopped?
At about 39 C (102.2 F), with continued rectal temperature checks
Only once mental status is fully normal

Stopping near 39 C (102.2 F) avoids overshoot, and ongoing checks catch rebound. Active cooling stops near 39 C (about 102 F) measured rectally. Oral, ear and forehead readings are unreliable in heat stroke, and rebound hyperthermia is common in the first hours.
q13ouhl8: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+0:30 (Point of injury): During cooling he has a generalized seizure and fights the tarp. What fits best?
A benzodiazepine to stop the seizure, with cooling continued and the airway protected
Cooling paused until the seizure ends
Restraints to keep him on the tarp

Midazolam or diazepam stops seizures and shivering, both of which generate heat. Benzodiazepines are the agents of choice for seizures, agitation and shivering during heat stroke cooling. Antipsychotics are avoided.
q12z853k: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+0:45 (Casualty collection point): Cooling is done but he is still slow to answer. An i-STAT CHEM8+ is run. What fits best?
Free water by mouth for the low sodium
Insulin with dextrose for the potassium
Observation, since confusion is expected after heat stroke

Hypoglycemia after prolonged exertion adds to his confusion and corrects quickly. Glucose is checked in every casualty with altered mental status. Exertional illness can also cause hyponatremia, so sodium guides fluid choice. Both are trended on the PCC flowsheet.
q1rdaklk: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+2 (Patrol base): A Foley drains a small amount of cola-colored urine. His legs ache. What fits best?
Isotonic fluid titrated to a high urine output target, with lung checks and potassium trends
A diuretic to increase urine flow
Cola-colored urine accepted as dehydration that will clear

Brisk urine flow protects the kidneys from myoglobin, and potassium is watched as muscle breaks down. Exertional heat stroke often causes rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury. Isotonic fluid is titrated to a high urine output, watching for crackles, edema and falling sodium.
q19s943q: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+8 (Patrol base): There is new oozing from IV sites and his gums, and petechiae on his chest. What fits best?
Teleconsult, whole blood or plasma if available, and a higher evacuation priority

Heat stroke can trigger DIC, which needs factor replacement and hospital care. DIC is a late, ominous complication of heat stroke, often with liver injury. Field care is supportive: blood products when available, avoidance of drugs that worsen bleeding, and urgent evacuation.
q19bov0s: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+16 (Patrol base): His temperature rebounds. His right upper abdomen is tender. A teammate reaches for fever medication. What fits best?
External cooling restarted with ice water and fanning, with rectal temperature monitored
Ketorolac to bring the temperature down
Acetaminophen to bring the temperature down
Observation, since the peak has passed

Rebound hyperthermia is treated the same way as the first episode: physical cooling. Rebound hyperthermia is common after heat stroke. External cooling is the treatment, and liver injury from heat stroke is another reason to avoid acetaminophen.
qqsxrn5: A 22-year-old male collapsed near the end of a long, heavy ruck march in high heat and humidity. H+24 (Long hold, day 2): He is awake and oriented and says he feels fine. Evacuation is inbound. What fits best?
DD1380 and PCC flowsheet with cooling times, temperatures, glucose, labs and urine output, plus a MIST report
Return to duty since he feels better
The last set of vital signs only

This record lets the hospital judge kidney, liver and clotting injury and plan follow-up. Feeling well does not mean organ recovery. Kidney, liver and clotting injury evolve over days, and the record of cooling start time, peak temperature and lab trends guides care and return-to-duty decisions.
q1nl7bcw: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+2 (Patrol base): He is bucking the ventilator, grimacing and reaching for the tube. What fits best?
Analgesia first with ketamine or fentanyl, then sedation titrated to a RASS goal of 0 to -2
Rocuronium to stop him fighting the ventilator

Pain is the most common driver of agitation in a fresh trauma casualty. The JTS Analgesia and Sedation CPG uses analgesia-first sedation. Pain is scored with a tool such as CPOT or a behavioral scale when the casualty cannot talk, and RASS is recorded with every check.
qvat3eu: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+6 (Patrol base): A teammate added propofol for better sedation, and his pressure dropped. What fits best?
Propofol reduced or stopped, with ketamine as the main agent and volume status checked
Propofol continued and a vasopressor added to cover it

Ketamine supports blood pressure and breathing, which fits a recently bled trauma casualty. Propofol is short acting but causes vasodilation and hypotension. In prolonged casualty care with limited monitoring, ketamine is often the backbone agent, with fentanyl for analgesia.
q1h4jjz8: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+10 (Patrol base): While turning him, the team hears gurgling at the mouth. The EtCO2 waveform disappears and his SpO2 falls. What fits best?
Tube displacement recognized, bag-mask ventilation, and re-intubation confirmed by waveform capnography

A lost waveform after moving a casualty is displacement until proven otherwise. Waveform capnography is the fastest monitor for displacement. DOPE starts with D, and tube depth at the teeth is recorded on the flowsheet and checked after every move.
qdofozw: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+18 (Patrol base): He does not open his eyes to voice or move to shoulder shaking. His sedation has not been lightened since H+6. What fits best?
Sedation lightened toward a RASS of 0 to -2, with pain reassessed as he wakes

Light sedation is the goal, and reassessing pain avoids swinging into agitation. Daily sedation lightening and a set RASS target reduce ventilator days and delirium. Reversal agents are for overdose emergencies, not routine sedation adjustment.
ql1yw23: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+24 (Long hold, day 2): Skin checks show a patch of non-blanching redness over the sacrum and red heels. He has been on a litter for a day. What fits best?
Repositioning every 2 hours, padding over bony areas, heels floated off the litter, and skin documented
Massage of the red area to restore blood flow
Turns every 6 hours to let him rest
A donut-shaped cushion under the sacrum

Non-blanching redness is a stage 1 pressure injury, and offloading prevents progression. Litters and ventilated immobility cause pressure injuries fast. JTS PCC guidance includes turns every 2 hours, padding, skin checks, and keeping skin dry, all recorded on the PCC flowsheet.
q14wtfa1: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+30 (Long hold, day 2): Hemoglobin has been stable on three checks, the leg wound is dry, and he has no brain or spinal cord injury. A teammate asks about clot prevention. What fits best?
Enoxaparin started now that bleeding is controlled, after a teleconsult
No prophylaxis until he reaches a hospital
Enoxaparin given at H+1, right after the wound was packed

With hemorrhage controlled and no brain injury, the benefit of prophylaxis outweighs the bleeding risk. Trauma casualties are hypercoagulable after the first day. Enoxaparin prophylaxis begins once bleeding is controlled, often around 24 to 36 hours, with teleconsult input. Intermittent compression devices can be used
q1yq1kt8: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+36 (Long hold, day 2): He has been ventilated with nothing by mouth for 36 hours. There is a small amount of coffee-ground fluid in the mouth during suctioning. What fits best?
Stress ulcer prophylaxis, an orogastric tube to decompress the stomach, and a teleconsult about starting enteral feeding
No action, since the amount is small
An oral diet once he is lighter

Acid suppression protects the stomach, and gastric access allows decompression and early nutrition. Ventilated trauma casualties are at high risk for stress ulcers. Pantoprazole or famotidine and early enteral nutrition through a gastric tube are standard in prolonged care, and nutrition is planned with teleconsult gui
q9khei6: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+48 (Long hold, day 3): Dexmedetomidine was added to ease agitation as sedation was lightened. His heart rate falls and he looks pale. What fits best?
Dexmedetomidine reduced or stopped, with atropine or glycopyrrolate ready if he becomes unstable
Dexmedetomidine increased because he is still restless
Observation only, since heart rate often drops with sedation

Bradycardia and hypotension are expected effects of dexmedetomidine and usually improve when it is reduced. Dexmedetomidine allows light, rousable sedation but causes bradycardia and hypotension. It is reduced or stopped first. Atropine or glycopyrrolate treats symptomatic bradycardia.
q1e85ph0: A 27-year-old male was intubated after blast injuries to the face and chest. A leg wound was packed, and bleeding has been controlled since H+1. H+72 (Long hold, day 3): The evacuation aircraft is inbound. He is on ketamine and fentanyl at a RASS of -1. Which handoff fits best?
PCC flowsheet with RASS and pain scores, ventilator settings, tube depth, line and drain times, medications with times, skin checks and intake and output
A verbal report to the flight crew
A blank DD1380 with a note to call later
The last set of vital signs only

A complete record supports safe continuity of care and avoids missed or repeated treatments. In a 72-hour hold, the PCC flowsheet is the medical record. It includes sedation and pain scores, ventilator settings, devices with placement times, medications with times, skin and wound checks, and intake and output.
q1e922fc: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+1 (Casualty collection point): Stored blood is gone and he is still in shock. Several soldiers volunteer to donate. Which donor approach fits best?
Prescreened donors from the roster, with ABO confirmed by rapid typing on both donor and recipient and each unit labeled
Any volunteer whose ID tag says type O
The first available volunteer, to save time

Pre-deployment screening plus field confirmation and labeling lower the risk of mismatch and clerical error. The JTS Whole Blood Transfusion CPG relies on prescreened donors, low titer O when the recipient type is unknown, field ABO confirmation, and careful labeling. Most severe reactions come from identification erro
q1yfg99r: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+1:40 (Casualty collection point): Fifteen minutes into the first fresh unit he develops a high fever, back and flank pain, oozing around the IV, and dark red urine in the Foley bag. What fits best?
Transfusion stopped at once, the line kept open with saline through new tubing, and donor and recipient identity and typing rechecked
Transfusion slowed and the casualty watched closely
Acetaminophen for the fever and the unit continued

Fever, flank pain, hypotension, oozing and dark urine early in a unit point to an acute hemolytic reaction. Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction: fever, chills, flank or back pain, hypotension, red or dark urine and oozing from DIC, usually early in the unit. The first step for any suspected reaction is stopping the tr
q19z8br6: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+1:50 (Casualty collection point): The transfusion is stopped. He remains hypotensive and urine output is low and dark. What fits best?
Blood pressure supported with fluid and norepinephrine, high urine output maintained, potassium and calcium treated, and a teleconsult
The same unit restarted once his pressure improves
Sodium bicarbonate as the main treatment

Hemolysis causes shock, kidney injury, high potassium and DIC, so support focuses on each. Hemolytic reactions release potassium and free hemoglobin. Support includes blood pressure, urine output to protect the kidneys, treatment of hyperkalemia, and watching for DIC.
quuurlg: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+2:30 (Casualty collection point): Retyping shows the recipient is type A. The donor recorded as O retypes as B. The tube labels were swapped during collection. Which donor fits best for the next unit?
Type A or low titer O donor, both confirmed by rapid typing, with one collection labeled at a time
Any type O donor without a known titer
No more blood after a reaction

These are compatible with a type A recipient, and one-at-a-time labeling prevents another swap. Fresh whole blood is type-specific or low titer O. Collecting and labeling one donor at a time, with two-person checks, prevents most clerical errors.
q178aocs: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+4 (Casualty collection point): During a type A unit his temperature rises and he shivers. Blood pressure is stable, urine is clear, and there is no pain or rash. What fits best?
Transfusion paused, hemolysis and contamination looked for, acetaminophen for fever, and a teleconsult decision on resuming or using a new unit
All transfusion stopped for the rest of the hold

Isolated fever and chills with stable vitals fit a febrile non-hemolytic reaction once worse causes are excluded. Febrile non-hemolytic reactions are common, especially with fresh whole blood. Hemolysis and bacterial contamination are excluded before deciding to resume or use another unit.
q1vrhe03: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+5 (Casualty collection point): During the next unit, hives appear on his chest and he itches. Breathing, voice and blood pressure are normal. What fits best?
Transfusion paused, diphenhydramine, and the unit resumed if hives resolve and nothing else develops
All transfusion stopped for the rest of the hold
Methylprednisolone and the unit continued without a pause

Isolated hives are a mild allergic reaction, which is the one reaction where the same unit is often resumed. Mild allergic reactions cause hives and itching only. Wheezing, throat tightness, swelling or hypotension change the picture to anaphylaxis, which is treated with epinephrine and the transfusion is not resumed.
qmyoc2m: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+6:30 (Casualty collection point): About 90 minutes after the last unit he becomes acutely short of breath with frothy secretions and crackles in both lungs. His neck veins are flat. What fits best?
Oxygen and ventilatory support with PEEP, any running blood stopped, and a teleconsult, treated as TRALI
Another unit of blood for the low pressure
Observation, since the transfusion is already finished

Hypoxia within 6 hours of transfusion with fever, hypotension and flat neck veins points to TRALI, which is treated with supportive care. TRALI: hypoxia within 6 hours, fever, hypotension and normal or flat neck veins. TACO: hypoxia with high blood pressure, distended neck veins and a positive fluid balance, and it res
q13hihr3: A 25-year-old male with a thigh gunshot wound and hemorrhagic shock has received two units of stored low titer O whole blood. The tourniquet controls the bleeding. H+12 (Patrol base): His oxygen requirement is falling and his pressure is stable. The team prepares records for the morning evacuation. Which documentation fits best?
Each unit's donor ID, ABO results, start and stop times, reactions with vitals, treatments, and the set-aside unit, recorded on the DD1380 and PCC flowsheet
Records of the mismatched unit discarded to avoid confusion
The last set of vital signs only

This record supports donor follow-up for infection testing, reaction investigation and safe care at the next level. Walking blood bank records link every unit to a donor for later infection testing and reaction review. The mismatched unit and samples are kept when possible.
qepkgfo: A 30-year-old male has an open midshaft right femur fracture from a gunshot wound. A tourniquet was placed at the point of injury. H+0:20 (Casualty collection point): The tourniquet has been on for 20 minutes. He is alert with a strong radial pulse. The team can watch him closely. What fits best for the tourniquet?
Conversion to a hemostatic or pressure dressing, with the loosened tourniquet left in place and the wound watched
Tourniquet left in place until evacuation
Tourniquet removed and the leg elevated without a dressing

He is not in shock, the wound is not an amputation, and he can be monitored, which fits TCCC conversion criteria. TCCC: tourniquets are reassessed and converted when possible within 2 hours if the casualty is not in shock, can be monitored, and does not have an amputation. A loosened tourniquet stays in place for quick
qninrxv: A 30-year-old male has an open midshaft right femur fracture from a gunshot wound. A tourniquet was placed at the point of injury. H+0:40 (Casualty collection point): The bleeding is controlled. The thigh is shortened and deformed, and bone is visible. What fits best?
Wound dressed, then a traction splint applied, with distal pulses and sensation checked before and after
No splint, to avoid disturbing the wound
Exposed bone pushed back into the wound before splinting
Tight elastic wrap around the whole thigh

Traction stabilizes the fracture, reduces bleeding and pain, and limits fat embolism risk. Traction splints are used for midshaft femur fractures without contraindications such as pelvic or knee injury. Distal pulse, motor and sensory checks are recorded before and after.
qak3yq2: A 30-year-old male has an open midshaft right femur fracture from a gunshot wound. A tourniquet was placed at the point of injury. H+1 (Casualty collection point): No antibiotics have been given. He is not vomiting and has IV access. Which antibiotic plan fits best?
IV cefazolin, or ertapenem or ceftriaxone if that is what the kit carries, now
The wound sutured closed to keep bacteria out

Early IV antibiotics reduce infection after open fractures, and the JTS favors cefazolin for open extremity fractures.
