qpa39279a2: A sample contaminated with lactated Ringer's may show which change?
Lactated Ringer's contains lactate, potassium and calcium, and also dilutes other analytes.
qp97899e39: An aPTT drawn from a line that was just flushed with heparin will most likely be:
Heparin contamination prolongs aPTT; line draws need a proper discard per protocol.
qp2a87ecf8: Both arms have IVs. What is the acceptable approach?
Draw below an IV site and document it
Draw above the IV for better flow
Draw through the IV catheter yourself
Below the IV is acceptable when no other site exists; the nurse decides whether the infusion can be interrupted, and the site is documented.
qp9805b175: Per CLSI order of draw, which tube comes right after blood cultures?
Order: cultures, light blue, red/gold serum, green heparin, lavender EDTA, then gray.
qp7f9d4069: Drawing a lavender EDTA tube before a chemistry tube can cause which result?
Falsely high potassium and low calcium
K2 or K3 EDTA carryover adds potassium and chelates calcium, causing misleading results.
qp08157daa: Why is the green heparin tube drawn after the light blue citrate tube?
Heparin carryover would prolong coag results
Green tubes need the most blood
Even small amounts of heparin carried into a coag tube can falsely prolong clotting times.
qp8a4b5aea: A patient takes high-dose biotin supplements. Which test is known to be falsely affected on some immunoassays?
The FDA has warned that biotin can cause falsely low troponin on biotin-streptavidin assays, risking a missed heart attack.
qpce9a54ee: How can biotin affect thyroid immunoassays?
Falsely low TSH and falsely high T4
Biotin interference can mimic hyperthyroidism; report supplement use per lab policy.
qp360f2a96: What is the phlebotomist's role when a lab requires biotin screening?
Ask about biotin use and record it per policy
Advise the patient to stop biotin
Draw the sample in a gray tube
The phlebotomist gathers and documents the information; the lab and provider decide how to handle interference.
qpfc359813: A patient on an IV insulin drip has a glucose drawn above the IV. What result might be misleading?
Glucose not matching the patient's true level
Infused fluid dilutes and alters the sample; glucose checks must come from the opposite arm or as directed.
qpb803f9d4: A vancomycin level is drawn from the same arm the vancomycin is infusing in. What is the likely result?
Drug from the infusion contaminates the sample; always draw drug levels from the arm without the infusion.
qpcf11afb8: Saline contamination of a sample typically shows which pattern?
High sodium and chloride with diluted other values
Normal saline adds sodium and chloride and dilutes everything else, such as protein and calcium.
qp339aa4e5: A patient started on metoprolol now has a heart rate in the 40s with a normal P before every QRS. What rhythm is this most likely?
Beta-blockers slow the SA node, producing sinus bradycardia with normal P-QRS relationships.
qp89abbd37: Diltiazem is given to a patient in rapid atrial fibrillation. What change on the monitor shows the intended effect?
Diltiazem slows AV node conduction, so fewer atrial impulses reach the ventricles and the ventricular rate falls.
qp3d3fd0cb: Which effect of verapamil explains why it can cause AV block?
It slows conduction through the AV node
It speeds up the SA node
It blocks potassium channels in the ventricles
Verapamil is a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that slows AV nodal conduction, lengthening the PR and possibly causing block.
qp2d2afe7c: A patient on atenolol shows a PR interval that is long but constant, with every P followed by a QRS. What is this?
A prolonged but constant PR with no dropped beats is first-degree AV block, a common beta-blocker effect.
qp0d38a3c9: A patient on both metoprolol and diltiazem has a new slow rhythm. Why is this combination watched closely?
Their AV node slowing effects add together
Beta-blockers and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers both slow the SA and AV nodes, so together they raise the risk of bradycardia and heart block.
qp5f6d9f70: What is atropine's main use in an emergency cardiac setting?
Atropine blocks vagal tone, increasing SA node firing and AV conduction in symptomatic bradycardia.
qpae070c3f: After atropine, what change would the monitor tech expect to see?
Atropine removes vagal slowing, so the sinus rate and AV conduction usually increase.
qp950c63f9: For which rhythm is atropine least likely to help?
Third-degree block with wide ventricular escape
Sinus bradycardia from high vagal tone
Atropine acts on the SA and AV nodes; blocks below the AV node with wide escape rhythms often do not respond, and pacing may be needed.
qpeedc0f83: Adenosine is given for a narrow-complex tachycardia. What should the tech expect on the strip right after it is given?
Adenosine briefly blocks the AV node; a short pause or asystole for a few seconds is expected before the rhythm resumes.
qp65d3b9c6: Adenosine is mainly used to treat which rhythm?
Adenosine interrupts reentry circuits that use the AV node, converting many SVTs to sinus rhythm.
qp23c9dbac: Why is a continuous rhythm strip recorded while adenosine is given?
To capture conversion or reveal an underlying rhythm
Recording during adenosine documents conversion and can unmask flutter waves or atrial fibrillation hidden by a fast rate.
qp5a0575a2: A patient with a fast regular rhythm gets adenosine. The rate slows briefly and sawtooth waves appear. What rhythm was hidden?
Adenosine slows AV conduction briefly, uncovering flutter waves; it does not convert atrial flutter itself.
qpb3b4f208: How long does adenosine's effect usually last?
Adenosine has a half-life of under ten seconds, so its pause is brief.
qp556ed715: Isoproterenol is a beta-agonist. What strip change is expected when it is running?
Isoproterenol stimulates beta receptors, increasing heart rate and AV conduction; it is used for some bradycardias and pause-dependent torsades.
qpde24f839: Esmolol is a very short-acting beta-blocker. Which strip change should be reported while it is infusing?
New heart block or marked bradycardia
A slightly lower ventricular rate in A-fib
Some slowing is the goal, but new AV block or marked bradycardia is an adverse effect to report.
qp42283182: Ivabradine lowers heart rate by acting on which part of the conduction system?
Ivabradine blocks the funny current in the SA node, slowing sinus rate without affecting AV conduction much.
qpc016cd09: What does the QT interval measure?
Start of the QRS to the end of the T wave
Start of the P wave to start of the QRS
End of the QRS to start of the T wave
Peak of one R wave to the next
The QT reflects ventricular depolarization and repolarization, from QRS onset to T-wave end.
qpfbfbc720: Why is the QTc used instead of the raw QT?
It corrects the QT for heart rate
It measures only the ST segment
QT shortens as heart rate rises, so the corrected QT allows comparison across different rates.
qpbfb4682e: At a normal heart rate, which quick visual check suggests a long QT?
The QT is longer than half the R-R interval
The PR is longer than one large box
The QRS is narrower than the P wave
The T wave is upright in lead II
If the T wave ends past the midpoint between two R waves at a normal rate, the QT is likely prolonged.
qpfb1ce871: Which rhythm is most associated with a prolonged QT?
A long QT increases the risk of torsades de pointes, a polymorphic VT.
qp021c4f01: On the strip, torsades de pointes looks like:
Polymorphic VT whose QRS height twists around the baseline
Regular narrow complexes with sawtooth waves
Wide complexes of identical shape and height
Irregular narrow complexes with no P waves
Torsades means 'twisting of the points': the QRS amplitude waxes and wanes around the baseline.
qpc0d32256: Which medicine is the usual first treatment for torsades with a pulse?
Magnesium stabilizes the cell membrane and is the common first-line treatment for torsades.
qpfd92c074: A patient on amiodarone has a QT that has lengthened. How is this best described?
An expected drug effect that still needs monitoring
A sign the drug has stopped working
A finding that rules out torsades
Amiodarone prolongs the QT by design, though torsades is less common than with some other drugs; trends should still be reported.
qp1755a22c: Why are patients usually placed on telemetry when sotalol is started?
To monitor the QTc for prolongation
To watch for peaked T waves
To check for U waves from high calcium
To confirm a faster heart rate
Sotalol is a beta-blocker with class III effects; it can prolong the QT and cause torsades, so starts are monitored.
qpdbdd9f6b: Besides QT prolongation, what other strip change would you expect from sotalol?
Sotalol also has beta-blocking activity, so it slows heart rate and can lengthen the PR.
qp91c7db12: Dofetilide is started in a monitored setting for several days mainly because of which risk?
Dofetilide labeling requires an inpatient start with continuous ECG monitoring and repeated QTc checks.
qp369c41ec: Which antiemetic commonly given in hospitals can prolong the QT?
Ondansetron has a dose-related QT effect, especially with other QT drugs or low electrolytes.
qp6a184a66: A patient receiving IV haloperidol for agitation should be watched for which strip change?
Haloperidol, especially given IV, can prolong the QT and has been linked to torsades.
qpc9ebb619: Which opioid is best known for prolonging the QT interval?
Methadone blocks cardiac potassium channels and can prolong the QT; ECG monitoring is often recommended.
qpee6d3782: A patient on amiodarone is started on azithromycin. Why might the provider want ECG follow-up?
Both drugs can prolong the QT
Both drugs cause peaked T waves
Azithromycin is a macrolide that can lengthen the QT; combining it with another QT drug adds risk.
qpa2840ce6: Which antidepressant has an FDA warning about QT prolongation?
Citalopram carries an FDA warning for dose-dependent QT prolongation.
qpa9ccb83d: Which antibiotic class, which includes levofloxacin, is linked to QT prolongation?
Fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin and moxifloxacin can prolong the QT.
qp5737244c: A patient on digoxin has sagging, scooped ST segments but no new arrhythmia. What is this most likely?
The scooped ST ('Salvador Dali mustache') is a common digoxin effect and does not by itself mean toxicity.
qp7a97b4bd: Which strip finding in a patient on digoxin suggests toxicity rather than normal effect?
New frequent PVCs in a bigeminy pattern
Ventricular ectopy such as bigeminy is one of the most common signs of digoxin toxicity.
qpbc4ce2ba: A patient on digoxin with A-fib suddenly has a slow, regular rhythm. Why is this concerning?
It may be a junctional rhythm from digoxin toxicity
It means the A-fib has safely resolved
It shows the potassium is high
It is a normal adenosine effect
Regularization of A-fib can mean complete heart block with a junctional escape, a digoxin toxicity sign.
qp8e12647c: Which rhythm is classically linked to digoxin toxicity?
Digoxin increases automaticity while slowing AV conduction, producing atrial tachycardia with AV block.
qp2df9b8de: Which electrolyte problem raises the risk of digoxin toxicity?
Hypokalemia makes heart cells more sensitive to digoxin, increasing the risk of toxic arrhythmias.
qp5f910ec7: A patient on digoxin reports nausea and yellow-green halos around lights. What should the tech do with this information?
Report it with a current rhythm strip
Document it only at shift end
Ask the patient to skip meals
Nausea and vision changes are signs of possible digoxin toxicity and should be reported promptly.
qp615e0d2c: What is usually the earliest ECG sign of hyperkalemia?
Peaked T waves usually appear first, before PR prolongation and QRS widening.
qp8903b204: As hyperkalemia worsens, which change is most dangerous?
Widening QRS heading toward a sine-wave pattern
A widening QRS and sine-wave pattern signal severe hyperkalemia and can quickly progress to VF or asystole.
qpe4063c44: In severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes, which medicine is commonly given to protect the heart?
IV calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane against high potassium; it does not lower potassium itself.
qp3f25dc24: A patient on spironolactone and lisinopril develops peaked T waves. Which electrolyte is most likely high?
Spironolactone and ACE inhibitors both raise potassium, which can cause peaked T waves.
qp40352b82: A patient on furosemide has small extra waves after the T wave. What are these and what do they suggest?
Loop diuretics waste potassium; prominent U waves are a classic sign of hypokalemia.
qp21bce5e5: Which ECG change is linked to hypocalcemia?
Prolonged QT from a long ST segment
Low calcium lengthens the ST segment, which prolongs the QT.
qp532240b2: Which ECG finding is linked to hypercalcemia?
High calcium shortens the ST segment and QT interval.
qp6f397e33: Low magnesium is most closely linked to which dangerous rhythm?
Hypomagnesemia prolongs the QT and raises the risk of torsades; it often occurs with low potassium.
qp3a8e4ca8: Which electrolyte finding should be reported to the nurse or provider immediately?
Peaked T waves with a widening QRS
Peaked T waves with QRS widening suggest severe hyperkalemia, which can cause cardiac arrest.
qp7bfb8ddf: A patient started lisinopril 6 weeks ago and now has a dry, tickling cough. Lungs are clear and weight is stable. What is the most likely cause?
Fluid backing up into the lungs
Beta-2 receptor blockade in the airways
ACE also breaks down bradykinin, so ACE inhibitors cause a dry cough in a notable minority of patients. Clear lungs and stable weight argue against HF fluid overload; ARBs rarely cause this cough.
qp834deb68: A patient who has taken enalapril for 4 years has sudden swelling of the lips and tongue. Which statement is correct?
ACE inhibitor angioedema can first appear even after years of use
Angioedema only occurs within the first few doses
This swelling is a sign of high potassium
This is fluid overload from worsening heart failure
ACE inhibitor angioedema is bradykinin-mediated, can occur at any time, and threatens the airway. It responds poorly to antihistamines alone.
qp57cc4186: A discharge list shows both lisinopril and sacubitril-valsartan as active. Why is this a concern to report?
Taking them together greatly raises angioedema risk
They cancel each other's blood pressure effect
Together they cause severe low potassium
Sacubitril-valsartan only works with a diuretic
Neprilysin inhibition plus ACE inhibition sharply raises bradykinin and angioedema risk. A washout of at least 36 hours is required when switching from an ACE inhibitor.
qpdd55b60c: Which counseling point appears in carvedilol labeling for patients with heart failure?
Taking it with food slows absorption and lowers orthostatic dizziness
It should be taken only at bedtime on an empty stomach
It must be separated from all meals by several hours
It is a rescue medicine used only when short of breath
Carvedilol is a nonselective beta-blocker with alpha-1 blockade. Taking it with food reduces the risk of orthostatic hypotension.
qpb7287a6e: A patient ran out of metoprolol succinate several days ago. Which problem is most associated with abruptly missing a beta-blocker?
Abrupt beta-blocker withdrawal can cause rebound sympathetic activity, angina and even MI. Running out of medicine should be reported and resolved promptly.
qp77f50cca: A heart failure patient on furosemide is taught to report weight gain. Which threshold is most commonly used?
A gain of 2-3 lb in one day or about 5 lb in a week
Any gain of a half pound over a month
Only gains greater than 15 lb in a week
Weight gain only if legs are also swollen
Rapid weight gain reflects fluid retention and often precedes dyspnea by days. Early reporting allows diuretic adjustment and can prevent admission.
qp478a9c16: Which method gives the most reliable daily weights for a heart failure patient?
Same scale each morning, after urinating, before eating
Any scale at any time, as long as it is daily
Each evening after dinner, fully dressed
Once a week at the clinic on its scale
Consistent timing, scale and clothing removes day-to-day noise so true fluid trends can be seen.
qp5a21daf5: A patient on lisinopril and spironolactone recently began using a salt substitute to cut sodium. What is the main concern?
Salt substitutes contain potassium chloride and can cause hyperkalemia
Salt substitutes cause severe low sodium
There is no concern; salt substitutes are recommended
Most salt substitutes are potassium chloride. Combined with an ACE inhibitor and a potassium-sparing diuretic, this can cause dangerous hyperkalemia.
qp89d991d6: A patient on furosemide reports leg cramps, weakness and palpitations. Which electrolyte problem is most likely?
Loop diuretics waste potassium and magnesium. Hypokalemia causes cramps, weakness and arrhythmias and should be reported for lab testing.
qp9b279e0b: An older patient on digoxin and furosemide has nausea, poor appetite and sees yellow-green halos around lights. What is the concern?
Digoxin toxicity, made more likely by low potassium
Expected side effects that will fade with time
Visual changes, GI symptoms and arrhythmias suggest digoxin toxicity. Hypokalemia from diuretics and declining kidney function increase toxicity risk.
qp933ef340: Which finding meets the usual definition of orthostatic hypotension?
Systolic drop of 20 or diastolic drop of 10 within 3 minutes of standing
Any heart rate rise of 5 beats on standing
Systolic drop of 5 within 10 minutes of standing
Diastolic rise of 10 after sitting up
Orthostatic hypotension is a sustained fall of at least 20 systolic or 10 diastolic mmHg within 3 minutes of standing. It is a major fall risk with antihypertensives and diuretics.
qp24a7cc89: A patient on clonidine has missed doses for 2 days and now has headache, agitation and very high blood pressure. What is the most likely explanation?
Rebound hypertension after abrupt clonidine interruption
Clonidine is a central alpha-2 agonist. Abrupt loss of effect causes sympathetic rebound with severe hypertension, which should be reported promptly.
qp959c696e: A patient on amlodipine has ankle swelling, but stable weight, clear lungs and no dyspnea. What is the most likely cause?
Deep vein thrombosis in both legs
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers dilate arterioles, causing dependent edema that responds poorly to diuretics. Treating it with a diuretic can start a prescribing cascade.
qp9907fa1f: A patient on lisinopril and furosemide has had vomiting and diarrhea for 2 days and is dizzy on standing. What is the main concern?
Volume depletion with hypotension and acute kidney injury
Diuretics plus ACE inhibitors or ARBs during dehydrating illness raise the risk of hypotension and AKI. Many patients have sick-day plans; poor intake should be reported.
qpe069afb2: Why can a beta-blocker be a concern for a patient with insulin-treated diabetes?
It can mask warning signs of hypoglycemia such as tremor and fast heart rate
It causes rapid weight gain that raises insulin needs
It makes insulin work much more slowly
Beta-blockers blunt adrenergic symptoms of low sugar like tachycardia and tremor. Sweating is usually preserved, so it remains a useful warning sign.
qp3aeccde7: A patient injected insulin lispro for lunch, then skipped the meal. When is hypoglycemia risk highest?
About 1 to 3 hours after the injection
About 8 to 12 hours after the injection
Rapid-acting insulin starts in about 15 minutes and peaks around 1-2 hours. Skipping the meal leaves that peak unopposed.
qpc5cd13a6: Which statement best describes insulin glargine?
Long-acting basal insulin with no pronounced peak
Rapid-acting insulin given right before meals
Intermediate insulin that peaks at 4 to 12 hours
Insulin that may be mixed with any other insulin
Glargine lasts about 24 hours with a relatively flat profile and should not be mixed with other insulins in the same syringe.
qpab721ce5: A patient taking NPH insulin at bedtime reports night sweats, nightmares and morning headaches. What is the most likely explanation?
NPH peaking overnight causing nocturnal hypoglycemia
Insulin resistance from too little insulin
NPH peaks around 4-12 hours, so a bedtime injection can peak in the early morning hours. Night sweats and nightmares are classic nocturnal hypoglycemia clues.
qp43d575b0: An alert patient with a low glucose takes fast-acting carbohydrate. When should glucose be rechecked under the Rule of 15?
The Rule of 15 pairs about 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate with a recheck in about 15 minutes, repeating if still low, then a snack or meal.
qp61c30b74: Which statement about nasal glucagon is correct?
It is absorbed through the nasal lining, so the patient does not need to inhale
It only works if the patient takes a deep breath
It must be mixed with sterile water before use
It is ineffective when the patient is unresponsive
Nasal glucagon is absorbed passively across the nasal mucosa and works in unresponsive patients, making it easy for family members to use.
qp1712223f: In which home patient is glucagon least likely to raise blood glucose effectively?
A malnourished patient who has been drinking heavily
A well-fed patient with type 1 diabetes
A patient who took extra rapid-acting insulin
A patient on a sulfonylurea who ate breakfast
Glucagon works by releasing liver glycogen. Starvation and alcohol deplete glycogen stores, so the response may be weak.
qp447865c0: Which situation most raises the risk of lactic acidosis in a patient taking metformin?
Severe dehydration or acute kidney injury
Metformin is cleared by the kidneys. Dehydration, AKI, iodinated contrast and hypoxia raise the risk of rare but serious lactic acidosis.
qpe9b5d170: A patient on metformin for many years reports new numbness and tingling in both feet. Which deficiency is associated with long-term metformin use?
Long-term metformin reduces B12 absorption, which can cause or worsen neuropathy. Periodic B12 checks are recommended.
qp7a1ef183: A patient on empagliflozin has vomiting, abdominal pain and rapid breathing. Fingerstick glucose is only mildly elevated. What should be suspected?
Gastroenteritis only, since glucose is near normal
SGLT2 inhibitors can cause DKA with near-normal glucose. Ketones and a blood gas or metabolic panel are needed; a normal-looking glucometer reading does not rule it out.
qp64c3898b: Why do sick-day plans for diabetes specifically address SGLT2 inhibitors?
Vomiting and poor intake raise the risk of ketoacidosis and kidney injury
They cause severe hypoglycemia during any illness
They stop working when the patient has a fever
Fasting and dehydration promote ketosis and volume depletion on SGLT2 inhibitors. Patients should have a written plan from their prescriber for acute illness and before surgery.
qpe14a3048: Which adverse effect is common with SGLT2 inhibitors such as canagliflozin?
Glucose in the urine promotes genital mycotic infections and UTIs. Rare Fournier gangrene (perineal pain, swelling, fever) needs emergency evaluation.
qp90aa43fb: A patient on semaglutide has severe, constant upper abdominal pain radiating to the back with vomiting. What should be suspected?
Nausea is common with GLP-1 agonists, but persistent severe pain radiating to the back suggests pancreatitis, which needs prompt evaluation.
qp37203f2e: Which history is a labeled contraindication for GLP-1 agonists such as dulaglutide?
Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma
History of type 2 diabetes for over 10 years
GLP-1 agonists carry a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors and are contraindicated with a personal or family history of MTC or MEN2.
qp77bbe2ec: A patient on tirzepatide and glipizide has lost weight and now logs several low readings. What is the best explanation?
Improved glucose control plus the sulfonylurea is raising hypoglycemia risk
Tirzepatide alone commonly causes severe lows
Weight loss always raises blood glucose
GLP-1 and GIP/GLP-1 agonists rarely cause lows alone, but combined with insulin or sulfonylureas they can. The pattern should be reported for medication review.
qpf553bc1e: Reviewing a glucose log, which pattern most needs prompt reporting to the provider?
One high reading after a holiday meal
Readings recorded in a different notebook
Recurrent hypoglycemia is dangerous, especially in older adults, and usually means a medication or meal-timing mismatch that needs adjustment.
qp3c475fbf: What is the usual INR target range for a patient taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation?
Most warfarin indications, including AF and VTE, target an INR of 2-3. Some mechanical valves need higher ranges.
qp445d64ec: A patient on warfarin asks about eating leafy green vegetables. What is the correct teaching point?
Keep vitamin K intake consistent from week to week
Eat as many greens as possible to prevent bleeding
Greens do not affect warfarin at all
Vitamin K counteracts warfarin. Sudden changes in intake shift the INR; a steady diet allows stable dosing.
qp307ba5e4: A patient on warfarin was just prescribed an antibiotic for a UTI. Which antibiotic is most likely to markedly raise the INR?
TMP-SMX inhibits warfarin metabolism (CYP2C9) and can sharply raise the INR. An early INR check after starting interacting antibiotics is common.
qp9ac6a60f: Which agent reverses the effect of warfarin?
Vitamin K restores clotting factor production; four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate is used for rapid reversal in serious bleeding.
qpe4f57d91: Why is adherence especially critical for direct oral anticoagulants like apixaban?
Short half-lives mean protection fades within about a day of missed doses
They build up for weeks before working
Missed doses cause sudden severe bleeding
DOACs act quickly and wear off quickly. Missed doses leave patients unprotected against stroke or clot, unlike warfarin's slower offset.
qp8768e503: Which administration point is important for the higher-strength rivaroxaban tablets?
They should be taken with food for adequate absorption
They must be crushed and mixed with juice
They must be taken on an empty stomach
They should be taken with an antacid
The higher-strength rivaroxaban tablets are absorbed much better with food, typically the evening meal for once-daily AF dosing.
qp40bd45c0: Which storage point applies to dabigatran capsules?
Keep them in the original bottle or blister to protect from moisture
Store them in a weekly pill organizer
Open the capsules to make swallowing easier
Dabigatran is moisture-sensitive and capsules should not be opened, which can greatly increase absorption and bleeding risk.
qpc215b539: An 84-year-old on apixaban tripped and hit her head an hour ago. She is alert with no complaints. What is the best action?
Arrange emergency evaluation for possible intracranial bleeding
Reassure her since she is alert
Apply ice and have family watch her for a month
Anticoagulated patients with head trauma are at risk of delayed intracranial hemorrhage and generally need imaging even when they appear well.
qp7fead8af: A patient on warfarin has been taking OTC ibuprofen for knee pain. What is the main concern?
Increased risk of GI and other bleeding
NSAIDs impair platelet function and injure the GI lining, adding to anticoagulant bleeding risk. Acetaminophen is usually preferred, within limits.
qpe58d7341: A COPD patient has been refilling an albuterol inhaler far more often than before. How should this be interpreted?
Worsening disease control that should be reported
A sign the inhaler is defective
Rising rescue inhaler use is an objective marker of worsening control and may precede an exacerbation.
qpe1cee6bf: Which statement about tiotropium is correct?
It is a once-daily maintenance bronchodilator, not a rescue inhaler
It is the preferred inhaler for sudden breathlessness
It is taken only during exacerbations
Tiotropium is a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) used daily to prevent symptoms. A short-acting bronchodilator is used for rescue.
qp1bd76502: When using a metered-dose inhaler, what should the patient do right after the puff is inhaled?
Keep the breath in for about 10 seconds if possible
Breath-holding lets the medicine settle in the airways. Technique: exhale, seal lips (or use a spacer), press at the start of a slow deep breath, then hold.
qp23e81b97: What is the correct inhalation technique for a dry-powder inhaler such as fluticasone-salmeterol (Diskus)?
A quick, forceful, deep breath in
A slow, gentle breath in over several seconds
Use with a spacer to slow the powder
Exhale into the device before inhaling
Dry-powder inhalers rely on a strong inspiratory effort to break up the powder. Exhaling into them can clump the dose; spacers are not used.
qp6daa063b: A patient using an inhaled corticosteroid has white patches in the mouth. Which teaching point helps prevent this?
Rinse the mouth with water and spit after each use
Use the inhaler only at night
Swallow the medicine instead of inhaling
Shake the inhaler for one minute
Oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush) is a common local effect of inhaled steroids. Rinsing and spitting, and using a spacer with MDIs, reduces it.
qpb7b240ee: A COPD patient with diabetes is on a prednisone burst for an exacerbation. Which change is most expected in the glucose log?
Higher readings, especially in the afternoon and evening
Glucocorticoids raise glucose by increasing insulin resistance. Morning prednisone typically peaks its effect later in the day.
qpde7f7c93: During home medication reconciliation, which approach gives the most complete picture?
Review every bottle in the home, including OTCs and supplements, against all lists
Rely on the most recent discharge summary
Ask the patient to list medicines from memory
Use only the primary care office list
A brown-bag review often reveals duplicates, discontinued drugs still in use, and OTC or herbal products missing from every official list.
qpd5f0c93a: An 80-year-old uses diphenhydramine nightly for sleep and has new confusion and urinary retention. Why is this drug on the Beers list?
Strong anticholinergic effects cause confusion, retention and falls
It causes severe low blood sugar
The AGS Beers Criteria list first-generation antihistamines as potentially inappropriate in older adults because of anticholinergic burden.
qp91d5711c: Why are benzodiazepines such as lorazepam listed in the Beers Criteria for older adults?
Higher risk of falls, fractures and cognitive impairment
Older adults are more sensitive to benzodiazepines and clear some of them slowly, raising the risk of sedation, delirium and falls.
qpd9499757: Why is glyburide considered potentially inappropriate in older adults?
It causes prolonged hypoglycemia, especially with reduced kidney function
Glyburide is long-acting with active metabolites. Beers Criteria advise avoiding it in favor of options with lower hypoglycemia risk.
qp3777f380: At a home visit, a patient has bottles labeled Zestril and lisinopril from two pharmacies and takes both. What is this?
Therapeutic duplication of the same drug
Zestril is brand-name lisinopril. Brand-generic duplication, often across pharmacies, is a common reconciliation finding to report.
qpd76c36b3: A patient takes Tylenol for arthritis and an OTC nighttime cold product. What is the main concern?
Hidden acetaminophen in the cold product raising liver injury risk
Acetaminophen causes bleeding with cold products
No concern; they have different uses
Many combination cold, sleep and prescription opioid products contain acetaminophen. Unrecognized stacking is a leading cause of liver toxicity.
qpd3765c0d: Which medicine should stay in its original container instead of a weekly pill organizer?
Sublingual nitroglycerin loses potency with exposure to air, light and moisture and should be kept in its original glass bottle.
qpeec1c0a9: A patient developed ankle edema on amlodipine and was then prescribed furosemide for it. What is this pattern called?
A prescribing cascade occurs when a drug side effect is mistaken for a new condition and treated with another drug, adding risk.
qp2324039d: Which medication groups cause the most ER visits for adverse drug events in older US adults?
Anticoagulants, insulin, and oral diabetes medicines
CDC surveillance shows anticoagulants, diabetes agents and antiplatelets account for a large share of emergency hospitalizations for adverse drug events in older adults.
qp490c5955: A patient with heart failure on lisinopril and furosemide has been taking daily ibuprofen. What is the main risk?
Fluid retention and acute kidney injury
NSAIDs cause sodium retention and reduce kidney perfusion. Combined with an ACE inhibitor or ARB and a diuretic, this is the 'triple whammy' for AKI.
qp2448a1be: Which technique best confirms that a patient understands a new medication schedule?
Ask the patient to explain in their own words how they take each medicine
Ask whether they have any questions
Have a family member sign the list
Teach-back reveals misunderstandings that yes-or-no questions miss and is a core adherence strategy.
qp8aa5f748: A patient admits skipping doses of an expensive inhaler to make it last. What is the best response?
Discuss cost openly and connect them with pharmacy or social work resources
Tell them the inhaler is optional
Advise buying a similar product online
Cost-related nonadherence is common. Pharmacists, assistance programs and prescribers can often find affordable alternatives.
qpfecbf48e: Which home medication combination most strongly warrants a conversation about having naloxone available?
An ACE inhibitor plus a diuretic
Opioids combined with benzodiazepines or other sedatives sharply raise respiratory depression risk; naloxone in the home is recommended.
qp229dbe10: An 82-year-old has new confusion that began about a week after a medication change. What is the best reconciliation approach?
Treat any recently started or changed medicine as a possible cause and report
Wait for the next annual visit
Adverse drug events often present atypically in older adults, with confusion, falls or functional decline. Recent changes are prime suspects.
qpcb27fe1a: Which finding gives the most objective evidence of nonadherence at a home visit?
Pill counts and refill dates that don't match the prescribed schedule
The patient says they never miss doses
The pill bottles are neatly organized
The patient knows the names of the medicines
Self-report overestimates adherence. Comparing remaining pills and pharmacy refill history to the expected use is more objective.
qp8eff994d: According to CoTCCC guidelines, tranexamic acid should be given within what time window after injury?
As soon as possible, within 3 hours of injury
TXA benefit is greatest when given early; CRASH-2 data showed possible harm when started more than 3 hours after injury.
qpb795768a: What is the mechanism of action of tranexamic acid?
Blocks plasminogen activation, preventing clot breakdown
Activates platelets at the wound site
TXA is an antifibrinolytic: it inhibits conversion of plasminogen to plasmin, stabilizing clots that have formed.
qpba77de11: Why do current TCCC guidelines call for calcium with the first unit of blood product?
Citrate preservative in blood binds the casualty's calcium
Calcium speeds up the onset of TXA
Citrate anticoagulant chelates ionized calcium; hypocalcemia impairs clotting and cardiac contractility, and is common in trauma even before transfusion.
qp422615be: Compared with calcium chloride, calcium gluconate has which characteristic?
Less elemental calcium per volume and less tissue irritation
Cannot be given through an IO line
Calcium chloride delivers about three times the elemental calcium but is more caustic if it extravasates; gluconate is gentler on tissue.
qp9a463525: Which resuscitation fluid is preferred for a casualty in hemorrhagic shock under current TCCC guidelines?
Whole blood replaces red cells, plasma and platelets in one product and is the preferred fluid; crystalloids dilute clotting factors.
qpa0a704f1: Which three conditions make up the trauma lethal triad?
Each element worsens the others; many now add hypocalcemia to make a lethal diamond.
qpbbd42776: A casualty is evacuated on a warm desert day after major blood loss. Why is hypothermia prevention still a priority?
Hemorrhagic shock impairs heat production and clotting enzymes slow when cool
Hypothermia only matters in cold climates
Heat loss improves tissue oxygen delivery
Warm weather makes blood products more effective
Every trauma casualty is at risk. Even mild hypothermia impairs clotting enzymes and platelet function.
qpe966e8e9: When blood products are not available, why is large-volume crystalloid resuscitation discouraged?
It dilutes clotting factors and worsens coagulopathy and acidosis
It cannot be given through an IO line
It raises the blood pressure too slowly to help
Crystalloids carry no clotting factors or oxygen; large volumes worsen dilutional coagulopathy and may raise pressure enough to dislodge clots.
qp16545571: In a hemorrhaging casualty without head injury, what is the usual field endpoint of resuscitation?
Improved mental status and a palpable radial pulse
Normal blood pressure and heart rate
Permissive hypotensive resuscitation aims for adequate perfusion without raising pressure enough to disrupt clots.
qp379b5bd0: How does resuscitation targeting change for a hemorrhaging casualty who also has a traumatic brain injury?
A higher blood pressure target is used to protect brain perfusion
A lower blood pressure target is used
Hypotension sharply worsens TBI outcomes, so a higher systolic target is maintained.
qp9cdee443: A casualty with a head injury shows a blown pupil and posturing. What is the purpose of hypertonic saline in this setting?
Draws water out of brain tissue to lower intracranial pressure
Raises blood sugar to fuel the brain
Hypertonic saline creates an osmotic gradient that pulls fluid from brain tissue in suspected herniation.
qp5b2acbe5: Why has hetastarch (Hextend) largely been replaced in TCCC resuscitation?
Blood products provide oxygen carrying and clotting ability it lacks
Hetastarch is a colloid volume expander with no clotting factors or oxygen carriage and can worsen coagulopathy and kidney injury.
qp40031db1: Which is a recognized risk to monitor for after tranexamic acid?
Antifibrinolysis can contribute to clots; seizures are also reported. TXA does not inhibit platelets.
qpd4f72ecd: Why does acidosis contribute to death in hemorrhagic shock?
It impairs clotting enzyme function and cardiac performance
It causes direct red cell destruction
It blocks all oxygen uptake in the lungs
Poor perfusion produces lactic acid; acidosis degrades coagulation factor activity and myocardial function.
qp2a7f337e: Why is Plasma-Lyte or lactated Ringer's generally preferred over normal saline when crystalloid must be used?
Balanced solutions cause less hyperchloremic acidosis
Large volumes of normal saline produce hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, worsening the lethal triad.
qpf54a1441: Why is meloxicam included in the combat wound medication pack instead of ibuprofen?
It has minimal effect on platelet function
It works faster than any other analgesic
Meloxicam is COX-2 preferential; older NSAIDs like ibuprofen impair platelets and are avoided in combat casualties.
qp4c8330dc: Which two pain relievers make up the analgesic portion of the combat wound medication pack?
The CWMP pairs acetaminophen and meloxicam for mild to moderate pain in a casualty who can still fight, along with an oral antibiotic.
qp4091161a: A casualty with severe pain is hypotensive. Which analgesic is preferred in TCCC guidelines?
Ketamine maintains blood pressure and airway reflexes, so it is preferred for casualties in shock or respiratory distress.
qpabd3161f: Which side effect is commonly seen with analgesic ketamine?
Emergence reactions such as hallucinations or agitation
Severe respiratory depression at analgesic levels
Dissociative and emergence reactions are common; midazolam may be considered. Nystagmus and increased secretions also occur.
qp849187ca: When oral transmucosal fentanyl is used, why is the lozenge taped to the casualty's finger?
If sedation develops, the hand falls and the lozenge leaves the mouth
It improves absorption through the skin
It tracks the time it was given
This safety measure limits absorption if the casualty becomes drowsy.
qpfc4d80b7: Which casualty is the best candidate for oral transmucosal fentanyl under TCCC?
Moderate to severe pain, no shock or respiratory distress
Mild pain while still able to fight
Opioids can worsen hypotension and breathing, so casualties in shock or respiratory distress receive ketamine instead.
qp0404fcf7: A casualty given fentanyl becomes unresponsive with slow, shallow breathing. Which medication reverses this?
Naloxone is an opioid antagonist. It also reverses analgesia, and its effect may wear off before the opioid's.
qp07c2987b: Why should a casualty be reassessed after naloxone reverses opioid sedation?
Naloxone can wear off before the opioid, so sedation may return
Naloxone causes delayed seizures in all patients
Naloxone raises blood pressure dangerously high
Naloxone blocks the effect of TXA
Many opioids outlast naloxone; continued monitoring for recurrent respiratory depression is required.
qp28f31b85: What is ondansetron used for in tactical field care?
Nausea and vomiting, including from opioids or ketamine
Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 antagonist antiemetic; it is available as an orally dissolving tablet and IV or IM.
qp7029ae88: Which adverse effect should be watched for with ondansetron?
Ondansetron can prolong the QT interval, especially with other QT-prolonging drugs such as fluoroquinolones.
qpeadd1806: Which antibiotic is the oral option for open combat wounds when the casualty can swallow?
Moxifloxacin is the broad-spectrum oral fluoroquinolone in the combat wound medication pack.
qp93ed6941: A casualty with an open wound is in shock and cannot take oral medication. Which antibiotic is an IV or IM option?
Ertapenem or ceftriaxone are the parenteral options when the casualty cannot take oral medication.
qp05de753c: Ceftriaxone, one parenteral TCCC wound antibiotic, belongs to which drug class?
Ceftriaxone is a once-daily third-generation cephalosporin; ertapenem is the carbapenem option.
qpfbd26174: In which phase of TCCC are point-of-injury antibiotics given?
Antibiotics fall under the PAWS portion of Tactical Field Care, given for all open combat wounds.
qp10536f2b: Which injury besides an open extremity wound is a TCCC indication for early oral antibiotics?
A penetrating eye injury gets a rigid shield and an oral antibiotic; the eye is not patched with pressure.
qpd6623832: What clinical endpoint guides repeated atropine in nerve agent poisoning?
Drying of airway secretions and easier breathing
Heart rate above a set number
Atropine treats muscarinic effects; it does not fix pupils quickly or nicotinic twitching. Secretions guide titration.
qpe75c9185: How does pralidoxime work in organophosphate or nerve agent poisoning?
Reactivates acetylcholinesterase before the bond ages
Stimulates GABA receptors to stop seizures
Oximes pull the agent off the enzyme; once aging occurs, the bond is permanent and oximes no longer help.
qpa90e44d6: Which nerve agent is notable for very rapid aging, limiting pralidoxime benefit to the first minutes?
Soman ages within minutes; VX ages slowly. This is why early auto-injector use matters.
qpc9d8dfdd: The DUMBELS mnemonic describes which type of toxic effect?
Diarrhea, urination, miosis, bronchorrhea/bradycardia, emesis, lacrimation, salivation reflect muscarinic stimulation.
qpb936fbd2: Which finding reflects nicotinic effects of nerve agent poisoning?
Nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction cause twitching, then weakness and paralysis; atropine does not reverse these.
qpbe4e0643: Which drug class is used for nerve agent-induced seizures?
Benzodiazepines such as midazolam or diazepam
Benzodiazepines treat seizures and may protect the brain; a midazolam auto-injector is FDA approved for nerve agent status epilepticus.
qpe9bc4c36: What does the combined atropine-pralidoxime auto-injector deliver?
A muscarinic blocker plus an enzyme reactivator in one injection
An opioid and its reversal agent
A cyanide antidote and a sulfur donor
The combined device (such as DuoDote or ATNAA) speeds self-aid and buddy-aid by delivering both antidotes intramuscularly.
qp27086186: How does hydroxocobalamin treat cyanide poisoning?
Binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, excreted in urine
Donates sulfur to convert cyanide to thiocyanate
Blocks cyanide absorption in the gut
Hydroxocobalamin directly combines with cyanide to form vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin).
qp7bcad6b5: Which effect is expected after hydroxocobalamin and should be reported to receiving staff?
Red skin and urine that can interfere with lab tests
The red color interferes with colorimetric labs and pulse oximetry; receiving staff should know it was given.
qpb3539940: Why is sodium nitrite risky in a smoke inhalation casualty with suspected cyanide poisoning?
It induces methemoglobin, further reducing oxygen carrying with carbon monoxide
Nitrite works by creating methemoglobin; combined with carboxyhemoglobin, oxygen delivery may fall critically. Hydroxocobalamin is preferred.
qp77876f6a: What is the role of sodium thiosulfate in cyanide poisoning?
Sulfur donor helping rhodanese convert cyanide to thiocyanate
Chelates heavy metals in the blood
Thiosulfate enhances the body's own detoxification to thiocyanate, which the kidneys excrete.
qp82bb889d: Which single decontamination step removes the majority of chemical contamination?
Clothing removal removes most contamination; cut away and roll outward away from the casualty.
qp7856af2c: In a chemical environment, what is the responder's first priority before treating casualties?
Don protective mask and gear to avoid becoming a casualty
Self-protection comes first; an incapacitated medic cannot help anyone.
qp9f77e687: Physostigmine is used to reverse which chemical agent's effects?
Anticholinergic incapacitating agents such as BZ
BZ causes anticholinergic delirium; physostigmine is a cholinesterase inhibitor and would worsen nerve agent toxicity.
qp5f0b88f5: Atropine reverses which of these nerve agent effects?
Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors in airways and glands; nicotinic effects need oxime and supportive care.
qp9bc4797d: Which oral antibiotics are first-line post-exposure prophylaxis for inhalational anthrax?
Ciprofloxacin or doxycycline are first-line; prophylaxis typically lasts about 60 days alongside vaccination.
qpb475bea6: Why is anthrax prophylaxis continued for an extended period after inhalational exposure?
Spores can germinate weeks after inhalation
The antibiotic works only after a month
Anthrax spreads person to person for weeks
The vaccine requires antibiotics to activate
Spores can persist in the lungs and germinate long after exposure, so prolonged prophylaxis is needed.
qp35803137: Which counseling point applies to doxycycline used for biothreat prophylaxis?
Photosensitivity and esophageal irritation; stay upright after a dose
Doxycycline can cause pill esophagitis and sun sensitivity; minerals like calcium and iron reduce absorption.
qp4f0fb4a0: Which adverse effect is associated with ciprofloxacin?
Fluoroquinolones carry boxed warnings for tendinopathy, neuropathy, CNS effects and myasthenia worsening.
qp0d2cf8d8: What does potassium iodide protect against after a nuclear incident?
Uptake of radioactive iodine by the thyroid gland
All forms of radiation to every organ
KI saturates the thyroid with stable iodine. It does not protect other organs or against other isotopes.
qpc5a1013e: When is potassium iodide most effective?
Shortly before or soon after exposure to radioactive iodine
Only when combined with Prussian blue
Protection drops sharply as hours pass after exposure because the thyroid has already taken up radioiodine.
qp689cb486: Prussian blue is used for internal contamination with which elements?
Prussian blue traps cesium and thallium in the gut, interrupting their recirculation and speeding fecal elimination.
qp5b5afb5b: Which expected effect of Prussian blue should be explained to the patient?
Prussian blue is not absorbed; it passes in stool, coloring it blue, and commonly causes constipation.
qp37178fd3: Ca-DTPA is used for internal contamination with which elements?
DTPA chelates transuranic elements, forming complexes excreted in urine.
qp5d814ec5: Why is Ca-DTPA preferred over Zn-DTPA in the first 24 hours after contamination?
It is more effective at chelation early after exposure
It is the only form that can be inhaled
It has no effect on zinc levels
It is the only form safe for pregnancy
Ca-DTPA is more effective initially; after the first day the two forms are similar and Zn-DTPA is used for continued therapy.
qp9615c685: Which patient group is Zn-DTPA preferred for over Ca-DTPA?
Ca-DTPA depletes zinc and other trace metals and has shown fetal harm in animals, so Zn-DTPA is preferred in pregnancy.
qp770af9d0: A trauma casualty is contaminated with radioactive debris. What is the priority?
Treat life threats first; radiation contamination rarely endangers providers
Complete decontamination before any hemorrhage control
Wait for radiation survey before touching
Give potassium iodide before anything else
Life-saving interventions are never delayed for radiological decontamination; standard precautions protect providers.
qp3108cc99: After radiation exposure, why is the time from exposure to first vomiting documented?
Shorter time to vomiting suggests a higher radiation dose
It predicts the need for potassium iodide
Early onset of vomiting correlates with higher absorbed dose and worse prognosis; antiemetics like ondansetron treat symptoms.
qpa626a6b2: In which TCCC phase are medications such as analgesics and antibiotics generally not given?
During Care Under Fire the priorities are returning fire, moving to cover and tourniquets for massive bleeding.
qp3ca8ddc9: During TACEVAC, what is an important medication-related task?
Reassess and continue resuscitation, analgesia and documentation
Repeat the entire Care Under Fire phase
TACEVAC continues TFC interventions with more resources, including blood products, and requires a handoff of medications given and times.
